title: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour  | Science | The Guardian
description: International delegates agree leap second no longer tenable, but first leap hour not likely to happen for thousands of years
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: International delegates agree leap second no longer tenable, but first leap hour not likely to happen for thousands of years
Content: A clock at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, through which the prime meridian passes.Photograph: coward_lion/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA clock at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, through which the prime meridian passes.Photograph: coward_lion/Getty ImagesScienceHow an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hourInternational delegates agree leap second no longer tenable, but first leap hour not likely to happen for thousands of yearsIan SampleScience editorThu 15 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter decades of discussion, quibbling and worrying about clocks in computer systems, the world’s official timekeepers have voted to replace what many viewed as a tiresome correction: the leap second. It’s time, they say, for the leap hour.Delegates from 69 countries cast their votes on Thursday at a conference inFranceof the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which ensures the world sticks to the same standards of time, weight, distance and more.The decision to adopt the leap hour from next year aims to reduce the risk of computers and other technical systems tripping over as their software grapples with minutes lasting 61 seconds – and, worse, 59 seconds – instead of a round 60.“After 30 years of debate, the leap second is making way for the leap hour,” said Dr Setnam Shemar, principal scientist in the time and frequency department at the UK’s National Physical Laboratory (NPL). “This will reduce the risks to the systems and national infrastructure that depend on accurate time while still preserving the fundamental link between our global time system and the rotation of the Earth.”The vote at Versailles means that coordinated universal time (UTC) can drift up to an hour from astronomical time before a leap hour is needed, but that is unlikely to happen for thousands of years.“We already have daylight saving where we change by an hour and no one gets bothered about that, apart from losing sleep or getting an extra hour’s sleep,” said Shemar, who sat on the international timekeeping expert committee that proposed the leap hour.The more familiar leap year was introduced more than 2,000 years ago to ensure that the calendar year did not fall out of step with the time that the Earth takes to circle the sun. Adding a day to the end of February every four or so years does the job, because Earth orbits the sun every 365 and a quarter days.Leap seconds are a much more modern invention. In 1955, Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the NPL built the world’s first practical, high-precision caesium atomic clock. The device revolutionised timekeeping, and in 1967 the astronomical definition of a second, based on the rotation of the Earth, was abandoned. Ever since, the formal definition of one second has been 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the caesium atom.Atomic clocks are exceptionally stable and precise. Their timekeeping has become critical for modern computer systems, communications, satellites, trading systems and electricity grids. But the Earth’s rotation is far less reliable. Its spin is affected by the planet’s molten core, the shift of the oceans, global jet streams and other natural forces.View image in fullscreenComputers linked with the atomic clock at the National Physical Laboratory in Teddington, England, and other international atomic clocks.Photograph: David Gee/AlamyBroadly, Earth’s rotation is slowing down: when an asteroid doomed the dinosaurs, a day lasted about 23 and a half hours. Because of this, officials have added 27 leap seconds since 1972 to ensure UTC is aligned with astronomical time.The strategy endured for more than 50 years until scientists spotted a fresh reason to fear technological mayhem. In the past decade, Earth’s rotation has sped up, meaning officials might have needed to add the first negative leap second, equivalent to lopping a second off UTC. The 30% probability of a negative leap second in the next decade brought the Versailles vote forward.“Leap seconds can be tricky enough to deal with,” said Shemar. Telecommunications, electricity grids and navigation systems used high-accuracy timing, he explained, but software updates could apply leap seconds at the wrong time, knocking networks out of sync.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“After the leap second applied in 2012, there were some computer systems whose operating systems couldn’t cope with 61 seconds in a minute. The servers froze, they seized up. Systems went offline. And those are the sorts of failures that can happen with positive leap seconds,” Shemar said.Among the crashed websites were Reddit and LinkedIn. Separately, Qantas flights were hit with delays. Negative leap seconds come with even greater risks. “There could be software out there that hasn’t been tested on negative leap seconds because we’ve never had to apply one before,” Shemar said.To test all the computer systems that talk to one another around the world would cost companies a fortune. It was this concern that swung the vote.Historically, the UK has grumbled about canning leap seconds because of the link with Greenwich mean time. Russia has also opposed the move, citing concerns of the impact on its Glonass satellite navigation system.The IERS Earth Orientation Centre, in Paris, tracks changes in the Earth’s rotation and other movements that feed into UTC. The centre also issues notices when leap seconds must be added.Dr Christian Bizouard, the director of the centre, approved of the vote, but said it passed the decision to people far in the future. “It’s kind of a philosophical discussion, because if a leap hour happens, it won’t be for a very, very long time,” he said. “What we are doing is pushing back the decision.”Explore more on these topicsScienceFrancefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Klara and the Sun review – Taika Waititi’s manic pixie dream robot sci-fi is a sentimental mess | Movies | The Guardian
description: The director of Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Jojo Rabbit turns Kazuo Ishiguro’s AI fable into a twee, tiresome tale of love and grief
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The director of Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Jojo Rabbit turns Kazuo Ishiguro’s AI fable into a twee, tiresome tale of love and grief
Content: Supremely lovable … Jenna Ortega in Klara and the Sun.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenSupremely lovable … Jenna Ortega in Klara and the Sun.Photograph: AlamyMoviesReviewKlara and the Sun review – Taika Waititi’s manic pixie dream robot sci-fi is a sentimental messThe director of Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Jojo Rabbit turns Kazuo Ishiguro’s AI fable into a twee, tiresome tale of love and griefPeter BradshawThu 15 Oct 2026 16.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 18.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaika Waititi detonates an explosion of postmodern quirkiness and ironic dorkiness in this unbearably mannered, unspeakably acted film. It’s a slice of sentimental whimsy-futurism and non-satire, adapted by Waititi from the Kazuo Ishiguro novel, which winds up saying nothing substantial or meaningful (or funny) about artificial intelligence, love or grief. Klara and the Sun is soft-centred sci-fi-lite, simultaneously demanding we laugh at its (unfunny) humour and wipe away a tear at its pass-agg poignancy. With earlier films like Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Thor: Ragnarok, Waititi showed he can do comedy. But this, sadly, is closer to his notoriousfey-Hitler fantasy Jojo Rabbit– misjudged and self-admiring.In the world to come in an uncanny valley of the almost-real, families can buy “artificial friend” or AF robots for their kids. In terms of tech plausibility overall, incidentally, their status isn’t entirely clear: AF salesperson (Natasha Lyonne) says that the recent third world war has wiped out the internet. (This post-WW3 world looks in pretty good shape apart from that.) And these AF humanoids incidentally have a kind of purple blood called PEC-9 running through them which one character incidentally tells us is “highly flammable”. (Uh-oh. Quite the design fault.)One such AF is teen girl Klara, played byJenna Ortegaas a ditsy, cutesy, supremely lovable innocent: a manic pixie dream robot – only nice – who is solar-powered and who therefore, in her adorable childlike robot way, worships the sun as a god. But Klara is an earlier, more rudimentary AF model, less sophisticated and robust apparently than the newer upgrades which run on Bluetooth as opposed to solar. (Is that really better?)At all events, her flaws are presented as analogous to the vulnerabilities of the human teen who wants Klara; this is Josie (Mia Tharia), a 14-year-old genius-prodigy due to be expensively “lifted” into a super-IQ class via a new surgical procedure, but who is also very lonely and suffering from an unspecified illness. Her uptight mom is played byAmy Adamsand the grumpy housekeeper Melania – whose appearance is the nearest the film comes to comedy – is played by Rachel House. Klara goes to live with her new family in their distant home in a weirdly dreamlike Midwest farming landscape from which the city can only be glimpsed distantly, like Oz. Klara becomes certain that the sun lives in the nearby barn above, from which she can see it rising every morning; what a sweetly naive belief. And so it goes on, to a twist ending that is as unsatisfying and contrived as everything that has gone before.The thought of robots or replicant youngsters having real intelligence or real feelings is a difficult subject; Hirokazu Kore-eda came unstuck with the idea of robot child replacements inhis recent film Sheep in the Box. Kogonada’s parableAfter Yang, about AI child robots, was a more interesting and persuasive movie. But this is a sentimental and laborious mess.Klara and the Sun screened at the London film festival; released on 22 October in Australia, and 23 October in the UK and US.Explore more on these topicsFilmScience fiction and fantasy filmsTaika WaititiJenna OrtegaLondon film festivalRobotsFilm adaptationsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Just as Saint Nige thought it was safe to reappear, along comes pesky ITV | John Crace | The Guardian
description: How dare the channel reveal more racism and bigotry within Reform just as he was planning a press conference?
Author: John Crace
Headline: How dare the channel reveal more racism and bigotry within Reform just as he was planning a press conference?
Content: ‘I mean, why does this stuff keep happening to me?’Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘I mean, why does this stuff keep happening to me?’Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersThe politics sketchNigel FarageJust as Saint Nige thought it was safe to reappear, along comes pesky ITVJohn CraceHow dare the channel reveal more racism and bigotry within Reform just as he was planning a press conference?Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.11 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.20 EDTShareSometimes the world can be very unfair. As though life is just one cruel joke. How else to make sense of everything? For when the history books come to be written,Nigel Faragewill go down as one of the century’s unluckiest politicians.Poor Nige. All he has ever wanted is a better Britain. A country united in a shared vision where everyone gets along with one another. Where people of all faiths and none look out for each other. Where men and women of all colours are treated as equals. Where Nige can teach the world to sing in perfect harmony.So why do so many bad things keep happening to such a good person? Where’s the justice in that? How come Nige has been given a lead role in the rewrite of Little Britain’s Book of Job. Nige as a latter day Old Testament prophet put on Earth to show us all the value of eternal suffering. Because Nige is a decent man. The very best of us. And yet time and again he is made to feel pain. No more so than in the last few months.First there was the money. Few would have batted an eyelid if he had been given £5m by the RNLI. For all he has done to support the work that unpaid volunteers do in rescuing all people in trouble on the sea. Let’s face it, a modern day ministry doesn’t pay for itself and no demigod-like politician can expect to get by on less than £1m a year. Those houses and bottles of champagne aren’t going to pay for themselves. Yet because the £5m came from a Thai crypto-billionaire, suddenly everyone wasasking difficult questions. Anyone would think Reform might have crypto-friendly policies.Then there wasthe Channel 4 sting. And yet again our Messiah was the innocent victim of an establishment plot. Compared to Nige, Jesus had it easy in Holy Week. How could he be expected to realise that two associates whom he had barely known for years might allegedly be trying to secure an illegal donation from overseas? And what were the chances that Nige might be caught on camera giving considered responses as part of a conversation he hadn’t even been listening to? Some days you just can’t buy a break.11:20Reform donations scandal: is this the final blow for Farage? - The LatestOn Thursday morning, Farage had been scheduled to host a press conference near Southend where we were promised he would spread goodwill to all men with yet another major policy announcement. Only for the event to be cancelled late on Wednesday evening. The official reason given was that Reform didn’t want to clash with the fifth anniversary of the murder of the former Southend MP David Amess. Yet more bad luck for Nige. Imagine only being given five years’ notice to plan your schedule.Or perhaps there was another reason for the cancellation. One related toanother sting, this time by ITV, that had sent undercover journalists into the Reform operations room and uncovered the only bad apples in the entire organisation. Again, what were the chances of finding racists and misogynists attracted to a party that loved women and people of all colours?How could this ever have happened? The chances were slimmer than winning the EuroMillions lottery. And surely had nothing to do with Nige’s would-be chancellor, Honest Bob Jenrick, saying he would consider allowing soldiers to be able to blow up migrants in small boats in the Channel. What’s wrong with killing a few thousand people for the sake of a greater good? The country is just too woke for its own good sometimes. Then there’s the wannabe home secretary Zia Yusuf, who is on a one-man mission to round up all immigrants – even women and children – and send them back to countries where they may be killed. So again we are left with the question. Why are so many racists attracted to Reform?Let’s take Dean Miller. A vetted Reform councillor from Bromleywho was filmed campaigningduring the Makerfield byelection. Quite how extensive the vetting process was is anyone’s guess. “Tell us, Dean. Are you in any way prejudiced against people of colour?”. “Absolutely not. I just don’t want them anywhere near me.” “That’s great. Thanks Dean. Welcome to Reform.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReform’s Zia Yusuf is sounding more and more like Trump every day | Zoe WilliamsRead moreAnyway, Dean was caught on camera saying that it was kill or be killed with illegal immigrants. “They’re all fucking black and they’re like animals,” he said. “I’m not a racist, but you know what I mean.” Yes, Dean. We know exactly what you mean. And he couldn’t have been clearer about his intentions towards the king. Charles was a Muslim and deserved to be beheaded. It’s a view.When Miller was asked for a comment before the film is aired this weekend, his defence was that he had been on heavy medication at the time. And suddenly that all made sense. Because I too am on regular medication both for my psyche and for my heart. So I chose to reread the common known side effects of one of my drugs. And there among the small print about causing faster breathing, fever, muscle stiffness and drowsiness, one thing stood out. “Never take in the presence of a black person or royalty. Can make you prone to racist outbursts and in extreme cases can provoke urges to kill the monarch.”I guess I must just have been extremely lucky so far.Miller was not the only one to have been caught out this way. Others – also apparently vetted – declared that all foreigners were parasites, that the UK should have a 1% limit on all immigrants and made disgusting comments about a female Reform councillor. Raymond Dunning said he was so far-far right it was unbelievable. Then there were those who thought it best to try to sound moderate until after they had been elected. Then the gloves would come off and they could give foreigners hell.And in the middle of all this we have the saintly Nige. Scratching his head and wondering why all this was happening to him again. He hadn’t come in to politics to stir grievance and division. He was the god of love, the man of peace. Others among the Reform elite knew exactly where the blame lay. And it wasn’t with the innocent men who had been caught saying the only racist and sexist words they had ever said. Dicky Tice and the former Tory MP Ben Bradley were pointing the finger at ITV for daring to do its job properly. It was outrageous they had recorded Reform councillors going about their everyday jobs. Every man and woman was entitled to be as racist as they like in the comfort of their workplace.For now, Nige was determined to rise above it. He would survive. He was doing God’s work. Just a shame that God didn’t seem to like him much.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageThe politics sketchReform UKFar rightImmigration and asylumIslamophobianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A powerful act of imagination and self-affirmation’: experts on how to start writing a book | Creative writing | The Guardian
description: Thinking about writing a book and doing it are two very different things – so how to get started and follow through?
Author: Madeleine Aggeler
Headline: Thinking about writing a book and doing it are two very different things – so how to get started and follow through?
Content: Writing a memoir, murder mystery or steamy romantasy is an accomplishment.Illustration: Carmen Casado/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWriting a memoir, murder mystery or steamy romantasy is an accomplishment.Illustration: Carmen Casado/The GuardianHow to startCreative writing‘A powerful act of imagination and self-affirmation’: experts on how to start writing a bookThinking about writing a book and doing it are two very different things – so how to get started and follow through?Madeleine AggelerThu 15 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt some point in their lives, many people are confronted with a big question: what if I wrote a book?Writing a memoir, murder mystery or steamy romance is an accomplishment. Like running a marathon or successfully filing your taxes, it speaks to grit, determination and hours of research and effort.But thinking about writing a book and actually doing it are two very different things. According to a 2021 survey byThriftBooks, more than half of respondents thought they had a good idea for a novel, but only 15% had started writing, and only 8% had finished.So how does one get started and follow through? We asked experts.Why do so many people want to write a book?“So many reasons”, says Jami Attenberg, bestselling author and founder of the annual writing project 1000 Words of Summer.For some, it’s a necessary form of artistic expression. “They’re born writers, and this is how they communicate with the world,” Attenberg says.For others, she says, there’s a story in them that’s dying to get out, and writing provides “that cathartic release”.Still others are motivated by the difficulty of the task.“Writing a book is a powerful act of imagination and self-affirmation,” says Marita Golden, novelist and co-founder of the Zora Neale Hurston/Richard Wright Foundation, which fosters and celebrates Black writers. “It is demanding, scary and the kind of personal challenge that many people find irresistible.”That there are so many different reasons for so many different people is encouraging, Attenberg says: “It means people still read, love and value books.”What stops people from writing books?And yet, lots of people who talk about writing books don’t actually do it – or they start, and never finish. (For example, without naming any names: me.)For a lot of people, “it’s difficult and they don’t know how to do it”, says novelist Christopher Moore. “Once you’ve written one, it’s difficult, but you know how to do it,” he adds.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’Often, Golden says, aspiring writers are stopped by their own negative self-talk. Perhaps others have questioned their abilities, or they feel writing a book is only for “certain types of people”, she says.Some fret that they won’t accomplish what they set out to do. “People fear that if they begin the process, they won’t complete it, and that will reinforce their insecurity or open them to criticism and judgment,” Golden says.And, Attenberg says: “Life can get in the way.”If you want to write a book, where do you start?Read.While everyone’s writing process is different, experts agree one practice is non-negotiable: reading. A lot. This allows you to figure out what you like and don’t like, identify the different tools authors use, and get inspired.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Figure out who your influences are, what kind of books you want to be writing, what genre, what length, what kind of vibe,” says Attenberg, adding that she starts every workday by reading someone else’s writing. “Literature, to me, is a big, beautiful, noisy conversation, and we can all learn from and be inspired by other people’s work.”Figure out why you want to write.“Having something to say is important,” says Moore. Even if you’re not writing a polemic, Moore says, in the process of writing a book, you should regularly be asking yourself: “What am I saying here?”“It doesn’t have to be profound,” he says. “It might be showing your unique perspective on a topic that’s been covered.”Research.“Some kind of research is where I start,” says Moore. This is more than looking up dates and places, he explains – it is finding out “what has been written before on the subject I’m interested in”, and then “creating characters to carry the story”.More from How to start:How to start meditatingHow to start weightliftingHow to start budgetingHow to start runningSet a start date.It’s easy to slip into a trap of endlessly preparing to write – telling yourself you’re just going to do a little more reading or add further detail to your outline before you start. To escape this, Moore suggests setting a start date. “On that date, I begin,” he says. Sometimes, all he writes that first day is a paragraph: “And that’s OK.”Take a writing class.In addition to learning the basics of the craft, taking a writing class can help you meet other writers who can support you on your journey, Golden says.If you started writing a book and stopped, how do you start (again)?Write yourself a letter.“Try to recall what your intentions were when you began this project,” Attenberg suggests. “Think about why it’s important to you to finish it. What would it mean for you to complete this project?”Then, she says, set a reasonable but firm timeline for yourself and get going.Write a scene.Even if it’s not in order, even if it’s a hundred pages from where you last stopped writing, “giving your characters a chance to talk to each other or make decisions will give you guidance for where to go next”, says Moore.Don’t rewrite.“People get stopped because their expectation for themselves is too high,” says Moore. Allow yourself to write until you have a full first draft, and only then go back and edit. “Once you have a thing that vaguely resembles a book, you can always go back and shape and polish it until it’s what you want,” he says. “No one will ever know that, for a while, your masterpiece was absolute shit.”Explore more on these topicsCreative writingHow to startWell actuallyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Repressive, secretive and highly militarised: Eritrea, the east African country facing UK visa ban threat | Eritrea | The Guardian
description: Country has not had an election in 33 years and has withdrawn cooperation with UK on migrant returns
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Country has not had an election in 33 years and has withdrawn cooperation with UK on migrant returns
Content: People on a busy street in Asmara, Eritrea’s capital, in June.Photograph: Monicah Mwangi/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople on a busy street in Asmara, Eritrea’s capital, in June.Photograph: Monicah Mwangi/ReutersEritreaExplainerRepressive, secretive and highly militarised: Eritrea, the east African country facing UK visa ban threatCountry has not had an election in 33 years and has withdrawn cooperation with UK on migrant returnsCarlos Mureithiin NairobiThu 15 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEritrea, the east African countryembroiled in a row with the UKover its refusal to accept the return of rejected asylum seekers and criminals, is considered one of world’s most secretive and repressive states, with reports of arbitrary detention and severe restrictions on freedom of expression, opinion and religion.Situated in the Horn ofAfricaand bordering Sudan, Ethiopia and Djibouti, it became a sovereign state after gaining independence from Ethiopia in 1993 following a 30-year war.The country is run by an authoritarian regime under Isaias Afwerki, who led separatist forces to defeat Ethiopian forces in 1991 and became president in 1993. He has served as president since independence and heads the People’s Front for Democracy and Justice, the country’s only legal political party.Eritrea has not held a national electionsince independence. A constitution that was ratified in 1997 by the constituent assembly has still not been implemented nearly three decades later.In 2001, the government shut down all independent newspapers after the publishing of an open letter by senior ruling party officials calling on the government to implement the constitution and hold elections.A highly militarised state, Eritrea runs a compulsory national service system that requires students to study at a military training centre in their final year of secondary school. They undergo military training and political education before working in either military units or civilian national service roles that can last decades.The repression and conscription has forced many Eritreans to risk harsh punishment for evading, deserting or escaping the military by fleeing the country. It is estimated thatup to one-thirdof the Eritrean-born population lives abroad.View image in fullscreenIsaias Afwerki has been president since the country gained independence in 1993.Photograph: Kirill Kukhmar/Tass/EPAEritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat to the UK in the year ending June 2026. Earlier this year, Eritrea abruptly withdrew cooperation with the UK on migrant returns, and on Thursday the UK home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said all Eritreanscould be stopped from coming to the UKunless the country agreed to accept more rejected asylum seekers and criminals.Eritrea’s political, economic and social framework has been defined by a doctrine of economic self-reliance, with the country notably rejecting foreign aid.It was an Italian colony and parts of the country feature early to mid-20th-century Italian modernist architecture. The capital, Asmara, was inscribed as a world heritage site in 2017, with Unesco describing it as “an exceptional example of early modernist urbanism at the beginning of the 20th century and its application in an African context”.A multi-ethnic country, Eritrea is mainly made up of the Tigrinya people. Its extensive Red Sea coastline (1,388 miles) gives it a strategic position along the Red Sea corridor.The country has been in the spotlight in recent weeks because of fears of war with Ethiopia. Both countries have accused each other of aggression. Ethiopia has claimed Eritrean troops crossed up to 60km (37 miles) into Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, while Eritrea has said the accusation is a fabrication to create a pretext for war.The escalation is linked torenewed fightingbetween Ethiopian government forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), an armed opposition group, in Tigray, which borders Eritrea.Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, a claim that Eritrea has denied. On Tuesday, Ethiopian forces advanced to Zalambessa, ​a town on the border with Eritrea that was under Tigrayan rebel control.Explore more on these topicsEritreaAfricaImmigration and asylumShabana MahmoodexplainersShareReuse this content

title: ‘Don’t do this!’ Why Paul McCartney cares about looking shorter than John Lennon in Sam Mendes’ Beatles films | The Beatles films | The Guardian
description: You’re Paul McCartney. So how come you’re still getting het up at a fictional version of you being marginally smaller than a fictional version of John Lennon?
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: You’re Paul McCartney. So how come you’re still getting het up at a fictional version of you being marginally smaller than a fictional version of John Lennon?
Content: The height of fame … Harris Dickinson (Lennon), Paul Mescal (McCartney), Barry Keoghan (Starr), and Joseph Quinn (Harrison).Photograph: John Russo/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe height of fame … Harris Dickinson (Lennon), Paul Mescal (McCartney), Barry Keoghan (Starr), and Joseph Quinn (Harrison).Photograph: John Russo/REX/ShutterstockThe Beatles films‘Don’t do this!’ Why Paul McCartney cares about looking shorter than John Lennon in Sam Mendes’ Beatles filmsYou’re Paul McCartney. So how come you’re still getting het up at a fictional version of you being marginally smaller than a fictional version of John Lennon?Stuart HeritageThu 15 Oct 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere has been a lot of discourse and conjecture surrounding Sam Mendes’s forthcoming Beatles biopics. Some of this is logical (will people really turn out to see four near-identical films on the same day?), some creative (what animal did they have to shave to make John Lennon’s Abbey Road beard?). At every turn the film has been examined and factchecked and cross-referenced against testimonies fromthe band’s actual hairdresser.But until now the remaining Beatles have managed to keep fairly quiet about the whole thing. Last year Ringo Starr mentioned that he’d sat down with Mendes to rework a scene he wasn’t happy with, andPaul McCartneyhas praised the guitar playing of Paul Mescal, but it appeared that no real red lines had been crossed. Until now.On the most recent episode of Amy Poehler’s podcast, McCartney hinted at one underlying tension that might just rip the whole project apart: under no circumstances should he be seen to be shorter thanJohn Lennon.View image in fullscreenA line has been crossed … Paul Mescal as Paul McCartney.Photograph: Chiabella James/©2026 CTMG, Inc., All Rights Reserved.Informing Poehler that he, Lennon andGeorge Harrisonwere all roughly equal height – with Starr slightly smaller – McCartney revealed that he was moved to text Mendes after shots of the actors recreating the Abbey Road album cover were published. In them, it looked an awful lot like Harris Dickinson (playing Lennon) loomed above Mescal’s McCartney. As per McCartney’s retelling, the text read “Sam! Smaller? Don’t do this! You said you wouldn’t do it!”While he was quick to point out that Mendes’s reply assured him that this was simply down to their respective strides in the shot, even going as far as sending another one that showed them both equally tall, you can understand his dismay here. By his own admission, McCartney is still sore about 2009’s Nowhere Boy, which depicted him as Lennon’s slighter and weedier sidekick.But this has always persisted. In the 1960s, the official and now genuinely bewilderingBeatles cartoon seriessimilarly depicted McCartney as a relative pixie compared with the strapping Lennon and, even though the Yellow Submarine film fastidiously kept Lennon and McCartney at the same height, there’s still a perception that McCartney was the smaller half of the partnership.In a sense, you can feel his pain. McCartney is a man who has spent the last couple of decades fastidiously building a counterargument to the once-prevalent claim that he was simply the sappy hanger-on to Lennon’s towering genius. Remember in 2002, when he released the live album Back in the US and changed the credits of 19 of its songs from “Lennon-McCartney” to “Paul McCartney and John Lennon” to better show the world that he had been in the driving seat?View image in fullscreenLooming … Harris Dickinson as John Lennon.Photograph: Chiabella James/©2026 CTMG, Inc., All Rights Reserved.This ended up with threats of legal action from Yoko Ono and subsequent editions were released with the credits reverted. But McCartney was more successful recently with both Peter Jackson’s Get Back (which recontextualised the Let It Be film from “Paul McCartney irritates everyone into leaving the Beatles” to “Paul McCartney singlehandedly keeps the Beatles afloat”) and the Now and Then single (which had been vetoed by Harrison on the basis that it was “fucking rubbish” and then released anyway after his death). Slowly but surely, McCartney has won the war. His undoubted talent is now recognised at every turn, to the point where you have to do some searching to find any recent interview that doesn’t end with the interviewer tearily thanking McCartney for his genius.So physical height is the final hurdle. Making sure that Harris Dickinson never looks taller thanPaul Mescalis the last T that McCartney has to cross to secure his legacy for ever. And, sure, it might seem a little petty – it is the biopic equivalent of the contracts in the Fast and Furious films that stipulate The Rock must never be seen to lose a fight, even if that means inventing a bizarre contrivance to render it a draw – but this is important.If these films do as well as they’re likely to, then these four actors, with their weird wigs and pubey faces, may well become a generation’s lasting depictions of the band. The slightest inaccuracy could rewrite all of history as we know it. Nobody, especially the man himself, wants Paul McCartney’s gravestone inscription to be “Composer and musician (slightly shorter than John Lennon)”.Explore more on these topicsThe Beatles filmsThe BeatlesPaul McCartneyJohn LennonRingo StarrGeorge HarrisonSam MendesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: John Healey poised to raise taxes on banks in budget | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Chancellor to target sector in his first budget, to help offset Iran war’s damage to public finances
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Exclusive: Chancellor to target sector in his first budget, to help offset Iran war’s damage to public finances
Content: John Healey talking to Germany’s Lars Klingbeil and Australia’s Jim Chalmers during the IMF/World Bank meeting in Bangkok on Thursday.Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/ReutersView image in fullscreenJohn Healey talking to Germany’s Lars Klingbeil and Australia’s Jim Chalmers during the IMF/World Bank meeting in Bangkok on Thursday.Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/ReutersBudget 2026John Healey poised to raise taxes on banks in budgetExclusive:Chancellor to target sector in his first budget, to help offset Iran war’s damage to public financesHeather Stewart,Jessica ElgotandKalyeena MakortoffThu 15 Oct 2026 12.17 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey is poised to tax Britain’s banks in his 28 October budget, to help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East, the Guardian understands.The chancellor is in Bangkok, where the International Monetary Fund has praised the UK’s progress towards balancing the books, urging him to “stay the course”.To keep the Treasury’s deficit reduction plans on track in the face of rising government borrowing costs, the Guardian understands Healey has decided to tap the financial sector for additional revenue.One option understood to be under discussion – reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt – would raise upwards of £2bn a year.Lenders have been logging strong earnings on the back of rising interest rates, with the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and LloydsBankingGroup – alone having generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years.Thinktanks and trade unions have repeatedly urged Healey to tax Britain’s banks more heavily, an option considered but rejected by his predecessor Rachel Reeves, who was wary of deterring future investment.Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), said: “Britain’s big four banks are making a billion pounds a week, while bonuses have hit a post-crash record. These are bumper profits, driven by high interest rates and households’ mortgage misery. It’s time to make sure banks pay their fair share.”Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, Healey praised the banks as crucial to supporting economic growth. “People too often see them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects,” he said.But he is nevertheless believed to be minded to increase the surcharge banks pay on their profits, over and above corporation tax. Industry figures believe that will probably mean raising the surcharge back to 8%, from 3% at present.The UK’s cost of borrowing has risen sharply in recent weeks,alongside that of other big economies, as bond markets have responded to the prospect of higher inflation as a result of the Middle East conflict.Analysts have suggested that could as much as halve the £24bn cushion Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules at the time of the spring forecast in March.View image in fullscreenBank bosses have been lobbying intensively against tax rises since narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersHealey is understood to be willing to accept a narrower “headroom”, but is also keen to convince bond markets he is wedded to deficit reduction.Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against tax rises since narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget. UK bosses of lenders including HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest, Barclays and Santander met Healey last week but were given no reassurance that bank tax hikes had been ruled out.Their lobby groups – including UK Finance and TheCityUK – wrote to Healey days later, saying that on top of “weakening investors confidence and damaging UK attractiveness”, higher taxes would force them to move staff and business out of the country.That echoed warnings by the chief executive of JP Morgan, Jamie Dimon, who said in May he couldscrap plans for a new £3bn London headquartersif the UK government became hostile towards banks. News of the tower – which will house more than half of the US investment bank’s 23,000 UK staff – was came days after Reeves spared the sector further tax rises in her 2025 autumn budget.One industry source said banks were resigned to a rise in the surcharge. They believe Healey is minded to reverse Hunt’s cut – taking it back to 8% – but not go further. Such a move would raise £2.25bn a year, according to analysis by the TUC.Another industry source said they were caught off guard by the change in messaging, having come just hours after Healey hailed banks as a“jewel” in the crown of the British economy. “We’re surprised to see this following earlier comments which appeared to be more supportive of the sector.”When asked about how much the banking industry might be able to absorb in terms of tax rises, the head of policy at TheCityUK, John Godfrey, said banks “do not want to get into debating the menu of taxation. The fact is that we don’t want to eat in that restaurant.”Healey has also been “listening to representations” from specialist banks, including Revolut and Shawbrook, that want the profit threshold at which the surcharge kicks in to be raised from £100m to £500m.One government source said Labour was mindful of the UK needing to offer a positive environment for startup banks, especially the lending they offered to small businesses.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe TUC has lobbied for a much more punitive increase, to 16%, saying that could raise £24bn in tax revenues over the next four years.View image in fullscreenHealey stressed government departments would have to stick to the budgets Reeves set out at her 2025 spending review.Photograph: House of Commons/ReutersHealey said he wanted his first budget as chancellor to give “breathing space” to both consumers and businesses in the face of rising energy prices.There will be little additional funding for other Whitehall departments, however, which he stressed would have to stick to the budgets Reeves set out at her spending review in June 2025.“It’s important that they do manage within what they’ve got, and it’s part of the job,” Healey said. “You have to reprioritise if you want to do fresh things, or more.”The Institute for Fiscal Studies has said Reeves’s plans could result in real-terms spending cuts for some departments in the later years of the spending review period.UK economy unexpectedly grows in August despite fall in consumer spendingRead moreThe Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, used a visit to a financial services firm in Edinburgh on Thursday to caution against further banking tax rises, saying the sector already faced a higher effective tax rate than in many other big global financial centres.Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Britain needs growth. But a raid on the financial services sector will stifle it. Labour should be backing businesses and wealth-creators, not making their lives even harder. Rather than hiking taxes yet again, Labour should cut spending.”As well as an energy support package for households and businesses, Healey’s first budget is expected to set out more details of plans to devolve income tax to mayoralties, and explain how the government will fully fund the four-year defence investment plan announced by Keir Starmer before he stepped down as prime minister.Healey is expected to duck the longer-term question of when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence, the issue over which he resigned as defence secretary in June, contributing to Starmer’s downfall.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026Tax and spendingBanks and building societiesEconomic policyJohn HealeyPublic financeGovernment borrowingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nineteen injured in collision between minibus and train on Eurotunnel loading platform | France | The Guardian
description: Two people critically hurt when vehicle carrying HGV drivers hit stationary train in Calais, say French authorities
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Two people critically hurt when vehicle carrying HGV drivers hit stationary train in Calais, say French authorities
Content: The Eurotunnel site on Thursday evening.Photograph: Maxppp/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Eurotunnel site on Thursday evening.Photograph: Maxppp/AlamyFranceNineteen injured in collision between minibus and train on Eurotunnel loading platformTwo people critically hurt when vehicle carrying HGV drivers hit stationary train in Calais, say French authoritiesNadeem Badshahand agenciesThu 15 Oct 2026 17.38 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 16.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNineteen people have been injured after a minibus collided with a stationary freight train at the loading platform of the Eurotunnel nearCalais, French authorities have said.Pas-de-Calais underprefect Agathe Cury said 18 passengers and the bus driver were injured in the incident.She told reporters that two people – including the driver – were critically injured and airlifted to the University hospital in Lille.The remaining 17 were taken to hospitals in Helfaut, Calais, Boulogne, Montreuil-sur-Mer and Dunkirk.Cury added: “There is no risk to anyone’s life.”The minibus was carrying lorry drivers bound for a shuttle train service through the tunnel on Thursday evening.About 200 emergency responders and other personnel rushed to the scene. The shuttle service through the tunnel was suspended for 90 minutes before gradually resuming by late evening, authorities said.Cury said an inquiry had been launched into the causes of the incident.She added “for reasons currently unknown” the minibus struck the shuttle “as it was departing”.Eurostar said the incident was not expected to affect its service. It said in a status update: “An incident occurred several kilometres away from the Channel tunnel. This incident does not involve or impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected.”The Pas-de-Calais prefecture said earlier in a statement: “An accident involving a minibus carrying heavy goods vehicle drivers, headed to board a LeShuttle train, occurred this evening at the loading platform of the Eurotunnel site.“Significant resources were immediately deployed by Eurotunnel, and subsequently placed under the authority of the Prefect of the Pas-de-Calais department.“Early reports suggest that 19 people were involved, including the driver. At this stage, there are no fatalities, and no one’s life is considered to be in danger.”A photograph published by local news outlet La Voix du Nord showed a badly damaged minibus on the platform, with police officers and staff in high-visibility jackets present at the scene.The tunnel, which opened in 1994, carried 3.4m vehicles last year along with millions of Eurostar passengers.Explore more on these topicsFranceCalaisEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump cancels plan to livestream execution after global condemnation | Capital punishment | The Guardian
description: Soldier who killed 13 people in 2009 will still be executed, but president said ‘people would rather not watch him die’
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Soldier who killed 13 people in 2009 will still be executed, but president said ‘people would rather not watch him die’
Content: A memorial for the victims of the shootings at Fort Hood army base in Killeen, Texas, on 8 November 2009.Photograph: Jessica Rinaldi/ReutersView image in fullscreenA memorial for the victims of the shootings at Fort Hood army base in Killeen, Texas, on 8 November 2009.Photograph: Jessica Rinaldi/ReutersCapital punishmentTrump cancels plan to livestream execution after global condemnationSoldier who killed 13 people in 2009 will still be executed, but president said ‘people would rather not watch him die’Anna Bettsin New YorkThu 15 Oct 2026 13.03 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has shelved awidely condemnedplan to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood inTexasin 2009.In asocial media poston Thursday, Trump argued that broadcasting such an execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan” but said that “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device”.“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” Trump added. “That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose.”Archbishop of US military condemns Pentagon plans to livestream executionRead moreHasan, who was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot by law enforcement officers during the shooting at Fort Hood, now uses a wheelchair.The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth,saidlast week that the execution of Hasan would be a public event. Hasan’s sentence will be the first military execution in more than 60 years, and would have been the first in US history to be publicly broadcast.In a statement to the Guardian on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Pentagon said Trump and Hegseth “spoke about the decision to not livestream Hasan’s execution” before Trump’s statement. Hegesth “supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned”, they added.In an interview with Real America’s Voice last Thursday, Hegseth said he supported the public execution “because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things”.But since then, the Trump administration has facedsweeping criticism, and comparisons to dictatorships inIranandAfghanistan. Many US lawmakers, from across the political spectrum, have come out and condemned the announcement, andurged Hegseth to reconsider.Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, wrotein a post on social media: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.”In another post, Lisa Murkowski, a Republican senator from Alaska,saidthat there was “no need to livestream any execution, including this one”, adding that she “would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America”.The representative Rob Bresnahan, a Republican from Pennsylvania,saidin a post on social media that “an execution shouldn’t be a live-streamed spectacle”, adding that “the focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment”.“Their pain deserves respect, not a public show,” he said.On Friday of last week, the United Nations’office of the high commissioner for human rightswarned that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”, and the president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops also condemned the Pentagon’s plan,saying in a statementthat “in no way can Hassan’s actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.“The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people,” the statement added.That same day, JD Vance appeared to cast doubt on whether the Pentagon would actually livestream the execution,tellingreporters that “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen” when asked about the plans. The vice-president also said that if it were livestreamed, “I’m not going to be watching it.”But over the weekend, Markwayne Mullin, who heads the Department of Homeland Security, stood behind the administration’s decision to livestream the execution.Speaking withCBS News,Mullin said that “no one has to watch it” and said: “I follow President Trump. He’s the commander in chief of the country, and he does a phenomenal job. He leads this country with a very, very, very direct, forward, straight hand, and he’s restoring American values.”Trump himself had made contrasting remarks in recent days on whether the live stream would happen. On Friday, he told reporters that he“absolutely”approved the plan to livestream the execution, but on Saturday he said that hehad not yetmade a final decision on whether to go through with it.“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it” hesaid. “’Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I’ll make a decision.”Explore more on these topicsCapital punishmentDonald TrumpPete HegsethTrump administrationInternational lawGun crimeUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Matt Gaetz accused in suit of sex trafficking two women in Florida | US news | The Guardian
description: Jane Does allege ex-congressman and two others coordinated ‘payments, drugs and travel’ for sexual acts
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Jane Does allege ex-congressman and two others coordinated ‘payments, drugs and travel’ for sexual acts
Content: Matt Gaetz attends the cocktail hour of New York Young Republican Club's annual gala in New York on 15 December 2024.Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APView image in fullscreenMatt Gaetz attends the cocktail hour of New York Young Republican Club's annual gala in New York on 15 December 2024.Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APUS newsMatt Gaetz accused in suit of sex trafficking two women in FloridaJane Does allege ex-congressman and two others coordinated ‘payments, drugs and travel’ for sexual actsRichard Luscombein Miami andAnna Bettsin New YorkThu 15 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Republican former congressmanMatt Gaetzhas been accused of participating in the sex trafficking of two young women in a civil lawsuit filed on Thursday in district court in Florida.The allegations, which Gaetz denied in a statement to the Guardian, are the latest developments in a long-running sexual abuse scandal involving the politician whoresigned from Congressin November 2024.In the 38-page lawsuit, filed in US district court for the middle district ofFlorida, the women identified as Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2 claim Gaetz and two others “coordinated the recruitment, payments, drugs, and travel to obtain commercial sexual acts” from them “during 2017 through January 2019”.“The defendants collectively used their public office, power, and wealth to prey on the economic vulnerability of Plaintiffs to commit the acts,” according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit contends that the alleged victims “were recent high school graduates” at the time of the alleged misconduct.One of the defendants, Joel Micah Greenberg, aclose associate of Gaetz, and the former tax collector of Seminole county,pleaded guilty in May 2021to six federal offenses: sex trafficking of a child, illegally producing a false identification document, aggravated identity theft, wire fraud, stalking, and conspiracy. Greenberg wassentencedto 11 years in federal prison.Gaetz rejected the new lawsuit’s allegations in a statement to the Guardian.“I look forward to taking the plaintiffs’ depositions because much of the conduct alleged against me is false,” he wrote. “The lawsuit relies almost exclusively on a Congressional Committee Report that didn’t allow me to confront my accusers. Now I will finally have that chance.”Gaetz attached a photograph of three women in swimsuits from a social media post in September 2018 that appeared to show them on a beach in the Bahamas, with the caption: “#beers and #babes are all you ever need”.Gaetz added: “I don’t know if this is Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2 or not. But if it is they seemed to portray their Bahamian trip differently on social media than in their lawsuit seeking money.”Thecongressional reportGaetz refers to was part of a bipartisan House ethics committee investigation into his alleged misconduct. That investigation was terminated when he resigned in November 2024 from his north Florida congressional seat shortly afterbeing nominatedby Donald Trump to become attorney general.Later that month, Gaetzwithdrew from considerationto serve as attorney general amid intense scrutiny around the allegations of sex trafficking and drug use. He has repeatedly denied these accusations.Weeks later, in December 2024, the House ethics committee said its investigation found that Gaetz madepayments totalingtens of thousands of dollarsto women for sex and drugs on at least 20 occasions.It also found that in 2017, Gaetz“engaged in sexual activity with a 17-year-old girl”. Gaetz denied any wrongdoing.The complaint filed on Thursday alleges that Greenberg recruited the women through the website SeekingArrangement.com and “introduced them to Gaetz”.The lawsuit contends that Jane Doe 1 was 20 years old when she was first introduced to Gaetz in the summer of 2017 and that Jane Doe 2 was 22 years old when Greenberg first contacted her.“Gaetz was a sitting member of Congress, holding himself out to be one of President Donald J. Trump’s closest confidants and most loyal supporters,” the lawsuit states.Jane Doe 1 alleges that she had sex with Gaetz at a July 2017 party at the home of one of the other named defendants. She said she was invited by Greenberg and that Gaetz “introduced himself” to her before giving her “a tour of the upstairs”. The complaint claims that the tour “ended with Gaetz having sex with Jane Doe 1 in a guest bedroom”.Later that night, Jane Doe 1 alleges she saw Gaetz “having sex with ‘Victim A’,” who was “only 17 years old” at the time, and that Gaetz “gave Victim A $400 in cash that night, which Victim A understood to be payment for sex”.The complaint also alleges that three days after the party, Gaetz sent Jane Doe 1 $500 by PayPal, and that it was “the first of thirteen payments he would make to her”.“Between July 2017 and January 2019, Gaetz and Greenberg paid Jane Doe 1 on at least nineteen documented occasions,” the complaint reads, noting that “the payments ranged from $150 to $1,000”.Jane Doe 1 said she had “no meaningful savings and no stable income” and alleges that “they led her to believe they could solve her financial problems as long as she kept performing sexual acts for them and their associates”.Jane Doe 2 alleges that she first met Greenberg in 2017 and that he later invited her to a party at a rented house.“Greenberg promised Jane Doe 2 that she would be ‘well compensated’ for attending but gave her little details about what would be required from her,” the complaint claims. Jane Doe 2 alleges she met Gaetz that night, that “pressed MDMA pills” were “handed out” at the party, and that she took one with Greenberg.“Greenberg then had sex with Jane Doe 2, and Gaetz had sex with her afterward,” the complaint alleges.The lawsuit alleges that the “defendants arranged and funded travel for Plaintiffs, other victims, and other prominent political figures to Venice Beach, Miami, Las Vegas, the Florida Keys, the Bahamas, and New York City between December 2017 and January 2019.“These trips took Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2 to places they had never been and into rooms with men they would never otherwise have met, and every part of that access, from the flights to the hotel rooms, was paid for by men, including the Defendants, who expected sex in return,” it reads.Explore more on these topicsUS newsUS politicsUS crimeLaw (US)Sex traffickingFloridaMatt GaetznewsShareReuse this content

title: Farage accused of ‘protecting’ Reform candidate over racist slurs against David Lammy | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: ITV investigation shows leader stood by mayoral candidate who said Labour MP should ‘go home to the Caribbean’
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Exclusive: ITV investigation shows leader stood by mayoral candidate who said Labour MP should ‘go home to the Caribbean’
Content: Nigel Farage on a walkabout in Chelmsford.Photograph: Will Colebourne/PAView image in fullscreenNigel Farage on a walkabout in Chelmsford.Photograph: Will Colebourne/PANigel FarageFarage accused of ‘protecting’ Reform candidate over racist slurs against David LammyExclusive: ITV investigation shows leader stood by mayoral candidate who said Labour MP should ‘go home to the Caribbean’Ben QuinnPolitical correspondentThu 15 Oct 2026 15.09 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 17.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage was told by a senior Reform official that he was “protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about David Lammy, an undercover investigation has revealed.The latest footage from an undercover investigation by ITV also shows Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”.1:18‘They are so chauvinistic’: Reform MP caught on camera in ITV investigation – videoOther footage shows Farage himself discussing thecase of Chris Parry, a retired rear admiral picked to contest the Hampshire and the Solent mayoral election for the party.The party stood by Parry for months after it emerged that he had said the former foreign secretary should “go home to the Caribbean” last year, and suggested that at least eight other politicians from minority ethnic backgrounds do not have a primary loyalty towards the UK.However, while Reform eventuallysuspended him in Marchafter the Guardian revealed other remarks by Parry, clips from an ITV documentary show Farage pushing back against senior advisers who said the candidate had to be sacked. They included Ed Sumner, Reform’s head of communications, who had told another press officer in an earlier disucussion that Parry was “clearly a racist”.“He needs to go, I’m getting rid of him,” Sumner was filmed saying when the controversy broke last December. However, Parry was still the candidate three weeks later, while Farage told a press conference that the candidate could stay if he apologised.In a conversation between Farage and Sumner, which was recorded by the undercover reporter, the Reform leader said that Parry “must apologise to Lammy” and was told that a text had been written for the candidate.“He must do it and move on … Tell him that from me,” Farage said, to which Sumner said: “You’re protecting him.”To laughter, Farage replied: “It’s showing a bit of … bit of sorrow. Look, ‘I’m sorry’ is probably a good thing to hear. Just take the fucking deal. Trouble is he’s a rear admiral. That’s the problem.”Parry was suspended on 26 March after the Guardian reported that he had described members of a Jewish neighbourhood watch group as“cosplayers”and likened them to “Islamists on horseback”.Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said these “latest shocking and deeply disturbing revelations go right to the top of Reform”, adding: “Nigel Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him. He also must urgently explain why he allegedly stood by a blatant racist instead of kicking him out of his party.”The revelations are the latest in a number of recent controversies for Reform. The full ITV documentary, Undercover: A Year in Reform, airs on Sunday.A number of councillors have already stood down after segments from the investigation aired on Wednesday showed them making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views.Reform UK councillors and candidates filmed making racist and misogynist commentsRead moreThe undercover reporter for ITV also met Pochin, Reform’s MP for Runcorn and Helsby, at a time when she was the party’s only female member of parliament.When Pochin was told that a new female press officer was starting work, she was recorded as saying: “Oh thank fuck for that. God! We so need women press officers … They are so fucking chauvinistic.“I go out on all the shows and go: ‘Oh no, it’s lovely, oh they’re all so welcoming.’ Shit … they just exclude you if you’re a woman. It’s really tough being a girl with all of this alpha male shit going on.”Pochin did not provide a statement when approached by ITV.Reform UKused a statement issued on Thursday to accuse ITV and the company behind the documentary, Hardcash Productions, of using “extreme methods of deception”.It said: “They have infiltrated our workplace including commissioning an undercover journalist to provide altered identification documents, a false address, and false credentials so that they could be given access to Reform’s headquarters, computer systems, and spy on its employees.“That same journalist did not limit themselves to recording candid conversations in the workplace. That journalist also sought to find out sensitive security information, travel arrangements, and financial information outside of the scope of this investigation.”Reform went on to claim that ITV had failed to address this in correspondence, despite this conduct being drawn to its attention. “This is at a time when Nigel Farage and other members of Reform are being targeted by individuals who wished them harm and caused a security issue which was documented during the course of the undercover investigation,” it added.“There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases.”When approached for comment, Parry referred the Guardian to a statement given to ITV. In it he said: “I would urge people to go back to the original contexts and tweets to see what was said and why. They related to reparations and failures by the police and government. They will see I always exercise my right to criticise anyone in power or the public eye whom I judge to be acting against the interests of the British people.”Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageReform UKDocumentary filmsFar rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wes Streeting urges US to back Ukraine on Washington visit after Starlink row | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: UK defence secretary says he has been ‘reassured directly’ counterpart Pete Hegseth that Starlink system has been restored as he seeks to cool tensions
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: UK defence secretary says he has been ‘reassured directly’ counterpart Pete Hegseth that Starlink system has been restored as he seeks to cool tensions
Content: Wes Streeting is welcomed to the Pentagon by Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary.Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/APView image in fullscreenWes Streeting is welcomed to the Pentagon by Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary.Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/APForeign policyWes Streeting urges US to back Ukraine on Washington visit after Starlink rowUK defence secretary says he has been ‘reassured directly’ counterpart Pete Hegseth that Starlink system has been restored as he seeks to cool tensionsDan SabbaghDefence and security editorThu 15 Oct 2026 19.49 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 14.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWes Streeting urged the US to stand by Ukraine on his visit to the American capital and sought to cool tensions between the two countries in the wake of the Starlink row that is threatening to set back Kyiv’s war effort.The British defence secretary, giving a speech before a meeting with his US counterpart,Pete Hegseth, argued that supporting Ukraine was in the long-term interests of Washington, and a business opportunity.Taking questions after his address, Streeting acknowledged “the challenges of recent days”, a reference to the row over the sudden decision of the US government on Monday to limit the use of Starlink by Ukraine’s military.He said it was “a reminder of two things – one is that American support in Ukraine has been significant and it has made, I think, a real impact in the Ukrainian war effort. And we and the Ukrainians would feel the absence of that.”The second was that there was “an enormous opportunity for the US in terms of the support for Ukraine”, a reference to the future “defence-industrial relationship” between the countries.Streeting was speaking at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US thinktank, before meeting Hegseth amid tensions over Ukraine, Iran and the Middle East.Speaking to the BBC after the meeting, Streeting said he had been “reassured directly” by his US counterpart that access to the vital Starlink communications system had been restored. The defence secretary said it was not yet clear to the UK why the disruption occurred, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.”The two men were also expected to discuss the safety of US military bases in the UK, after an Iranian threat prompted the US to withdraw B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, and whether the two countries would come together to help Saudi Arabia, which has come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis.View image in fullscreenStreeting and Hegseth during a meeting at the Pentagon.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersBut it is Ukraine that is the most urgent issue. A day ago, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said hefelt personally betrayedby Donald Trump after the US government appeared to have throttled aversion of the Starlinksatellite internet service used by Ukraine’s military.Ukrainian officials have reported that the US has also threatened to cut the sharing of intelligence used by Ukraine to detect incoming missiles if it does not abandon its attacks on refineries, aimed at hurting the Russian economy.The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, meeting Zelenskyy in London on Wednesday, said the UK would stand by Ukraine.Developing the theme, Streeting made a direct appeal to the US audience, saying: “There’s rarely been a more important time for Britain and America to come together.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The people of Ukraine are fighting for a principle that runs through the finest traditions of American political thought,” he said, which was “that a free people have a right to determine their own destiny”.Trump has vacillated over supporting Ukraine against Russia since returning to the White House, while support among US Republicans for Kyiv has been mixed. But Streeting argued that helping Ukraine was also a matter of national self-interest for the US as well as the UK.“Ukraine may be thousands of miles from American shores, but if aggression is rewarded, if borders can be redrawn by force, if the sovereignty of nations becomes negotiable, the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine or to my continent,” he said.The change to Starlink happened without warning at about 1am, when Ukrainian soldiers reported that terminals on drones were no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph, rendering communications inoperable.It led to a dramatic halt to mid-strike drone attacks on targets in Russian occupied territories on the frontline, andconcerns about Ukraine’s ability to interceptnew Russian jet-powered attack craft that are bombing its cities.Trump has been trying to put pressure on Ukraine to halt its bombing of Russian oil refineries in a desperate attempt to reduce world oil prices before the US midterm elections. He agreed to buy diesel from Russia earlier this month.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyDefence policyWes StreetingUkraineRussiaEuropePete HegsethnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s new press secretary says it’s ‘unknown’ how much she’ll deal with media | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Katie Zacharia tells Guardian her first, widely panned, press briefing followed whirlwind sprint to appoint her to key role
Author: Shrai Popat
Headline: Katie Zacharia tells Guardian her first, widely panned, press briefing followed whirlwind sprint to appoint her to key role
Content: Trump’s press secretary, Katie Zacharia, arrives in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Tuesday.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenTrump’s press secretary, Katie Zacharia, arrives in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Tuesday.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APTrump administrationTrump’s new press secretary says it’s ‘unknown’ how much she’ll deal with mediaKatie Zacharia tells Guardian her first, widely panned, press briefing followed whirlwind sprint to appoint her to key roleShrai Popatin WashingtonThu 15 Oct 2026 18.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 20.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s new White House press secretary says it is “unknown” how much she will engage with the press or hold briefings with reporters, as she faces mounting questions over her legal credentials.In a brief interview with the Guardian on Thursday, Katie Zacharia detailed the whirlwind sprint to replace her predecessor Karoline Leavitt as the US president’s chief spokesperson.Just six days after receiving a call from the White House, Zacharia stepped behind the podium for her first briefing as press secretary, in a debut that has beenwidely panned.Last Wednesday, 7 October, a White House official called Zacharia and asked her to travel from Los Angeles, where she lives with her family, to Washington for a meeting. (She declined to specify who made the call.)Zacharia made the trip the following day, before meeting officials on Pennsylvania Avenue on Friday. She was offered the job later that day – and accepted.“I flew home, packed two bags, said hi to my kids and husband and dogs,” Zacharia said, before returning to Washington on Sunday ahead of her first day on Monday.Enter the Zachbot: Trump’s new press secretary malfunctions on podium debutRead moreBut her first briefing, which Zacharia said she was “asked to do” on her second day in the job, was criticized as lackluster.And she has since faced intense scrutiny over her claimed legal qualifications. After her debut briefing on Tuesday, reporters asked Zacharia to name the state where she passed the bar exam. “When I moved to China”, she replied.She latertold the New York Timesshe had “misheard” the question over the sound of Marine One on the South Lawn and thought the reporter had asked: “Where were you after law school?” However, she did not confirm to the Times whether she had passed the bar exam. According to her LinkedIn profile, after graduating from Pepperdine University’s law school in 2011, Zacharia was an “associate” at the Beijing law firm Zhong Lun from 2011 to 2013.This week, the Wall Street Journalreported, citing a person familiar with the matter, that Zacharia failed the California bar exam after graduating from law school.The State Bar of California told the Guardian it had no record of Zacharia being licensed in the state under either her married name or her maiden name, Katie Black. While Trump has referred to Zacharia as an “attorney”, that title is reserved for those licensed to practice law.In a differentinterviewwith the conservative outlet Human Events on Thursday, Zacharia acknowledged to the rightwing influencer Jack Posobiec that she didn’t pass the California bar. At the time, she said she was “distracted and overwhelmed and excited” to join her new husband in China, where he was working, after being in a long-distance relationship for more than a year.A person familiar with the matter said Zacharia “stands by” referring to herself as a lawyer, and that she considered the designation a “valid title”, given her law degree and “international transactional law experience”. She did so after “consulting with other legal professionals and attorneys” about whether it was an appropriate designation, the source claimed, adding that Zacharia had “never given legal advice”; just “legal analysis”.However, many legal experts note that “lawyer” and “attorney” are often used interchangeably. On Wednesday,the Campaign for Accountability, a non-profit watchdog organization, asked the State Bar of California to investigate whether Zacharia misled the public, and potentially violated state law, by describing herself as a lawyer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter her time in China, there is a 10-year gap on Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile. Wiredreportedon Thursday that during that period she worked as an “affiliate marketer” for Beachbody, a multi-level marketing company she described to the outlet as “sort of a pyramid scheme”.She later claims to have served as “general counsel” for Fix California, a conservative group founded by Richard Grenell, a longtime Trump ally and the special presidential envoy for special missions. The Guardian has approached both Zhong Lun and Fix California seeking additional details about Zacharia’s legal roles at the organizations.Zacharia also said she “did not want to be seen lobbying” for the press secretary role, in her interview with the conservative outlet Human Events. Instead, she said she closely monitored Trump’s social media posts before appearing on conservative talkshows to “audition” for the job.When Trump announced that Zacharia had been tapped for the post, he described her as a “devoted fan of Maga” who has “an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning”.Asked by the Guardian what reasons the White House gave for offering her the position, Zacharia – who previously served as an adviser to Trump Media Group, which owns the president’s Truth Social platform, and had a brief stint as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security – declined to comment.Now the White House press secretary, she also would not clarify on Thursday how often she intended to brief the press. She said that was “unknown at this time” and that Trump “is his best spokesperson, and I will interact as needed”.“I follow the president’s lead,” Zacharia added.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS politicsDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand made alleged rape victim take photos of him half naked, trial told | UK news | The Guardian
description: Woman claims comedian ‘pranced around like an ostrich’ before forcing himself on her in hotel room attack
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Woman claims comedian ‘pranced around like an ostrich’ before forcing himself on her in hotel room attack
