Content: A photograph of Russell Brand that his alleged rape victim says he made her take in a Bournemouth hotel room.Photograph: Metropolitan police/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA photograph of Russell Brand that his alleged rape victim says he made her take in a Bournemouth hotel room.Photograph: Metropolitan police/AFP/Getty ImagesUK newsRussell Brand made alleged rape victim take photos of him half naked, trial toldWoman claims comedian ‘pranced around like an ostrich’ before forcing himself on her in hotel room attackEmine SinmazThu 15 Oct 2026 14.01 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Brand transformed into a “monster” when he allegedly made a woman take half-naked photographs of him before raping her in a hotel room at a Labour party conference, a court has heard.The 51-year-old comedian has denied attacking the woman, who broke down in tears in the witness box at Southwark crown court as she told how she could not fight him off.“He was really heavy,” she said. “I couldn’t struggle. I couldn’t breathe. I know he raped me, I know I said: ‘No, no, I don’t want this.’”Brand faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.8:24‘I couldn’t breathe’: Russell Brand trial hears from first alleged victim - The LatestBrand fixed his gaze on one of the TV screens in court on Thursday morning as a video of the woman’s interview from 27 September 2023 was played. She told police she met Brand at a fringe cabaret event that he was performing in during the Labour party conference in Bournemouth in 1999. She was not attracted to the then unknown performer, whom she assumed was gay and who showered her with compliments.But she found him polite and intelligent, and the pair spoke about their work before going back to her hotel room to continue their conversation.The woman said she “froze” in the run-down single room when she returned from the toilet to find that Brand was partly naked and “prancing around” like an ostrich. She said she asked him why he had undressed, and he told her: “Don’t worry, I’m mostly naked at home.”The woman told how she became “frightened” when Brand made her take half-naked photographs of him.“I took pictures of him on my camera – he made me take them,” she said. “I remember feeling: ‘What on earth have I got myself into?’”She told police he then raped her in an attack that lasted up to 10 minutes and left her feeling scared, in pain, and as if she couldn’t breathe.“He did rape, he did push me on the bed,” she told police. “He did pull my clothes off, he took my trousers off.“I remember him on me, very heavy. I know I said no. I kind of drifted out of my head. I couldn’t get out of the situation – ‘do I shout, do I scream?’ He was very heavy, I couldn’t breathe, it didn’t take long.”View image in fullscreenRussell Brand’s alleged victim said she felt ‘frightened’ when he asked her to take photographs of him half naked.Photograph: Metropolitan police/AFP/Getty ImagesShe described his body as snake-like and “disgusting” and said his tongue was “horrible” like a lizard. “I’m saying ‘no, no’ but I was really scared,” she told police. “I know he groped me. I know he was touching me, I know he grabbed my breasts. I know he tried to kiss me and I moved my neck. I didn’t want his mouth on mine.“He was just pulling my trousers down and pulling my underwear off, and he was inside me. It was not nice, it was painful and it hurt.”Giving evidence from behind a screen in the afternoon, the woman added: “I was like a zombie on the bed. All I could think was he’s inside me and the quicker the better.”In tense exchanges during cross-examination with the defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, the woman denied that Brand had persuaded her to have sex. “He was frightening, he seemed menacing at that point,” she replied. “He’s scary. I didn’t know what to do.”She rejected Winter’s suggestion that she had fallen under the spell of Brand, whom the barrister described as charismatic with a magnetic personality. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, had to interrupt the lawyer during one exchange to object to one of his questions, saying: “Shush please. I’m the judge, you have to let me talk.”The woman told the court Brand was a “completely different persona” in the hotel room. When pressed further by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones, the woman said: “He just changed suddenly from camp, friendly and effeminate to monster-like.“I felt very scared in that moment. He was big, I felt threatened and he’s half naked. And while I’m naive, I didn’t think at that moment his intentions were good.“He was just dark and arrogant and performing – he was scary, he was demanding. He was the centre of the show, it was like it was back on stage – he wasn’t the [same] person I was chatting to.”The woman told police she closed her eyes during the attack and that Brand made her feel sick and dirty. She recalled: “He was making noises, a lot of noises of enjoyment and saying how pretty I was. I remember him complimenting me, saying: ‘Are you enjoying it’? I remember him asking me. Obviously I didn’t answer.”She alleged that Brand spoke as the attack was unfolding. She told police: “He was just saying: ‘We’re having fun, it’s fine, it’s all good, don’t worry about it, it’s just fun, it’s normal.’”View image in fullscreenBrand (left) leaves Southwark crown court after Thursday’s proceedings.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersThe woman, who had been a victim of abuse in the past, said Brand made her compare earlier experiences, and it “stuck in her head … is this what abusers do?”She told police: “It was almost like to convince me it’s all OK and that I’d enjoy it, that I’d have to learn to enjoy it.”In the aftermath, she said Brand acted “like nothing was wrong”, wrote down his email address, and suggested that his mother might like to meet her.She told the court: “He is so arrogant in his mindset that he’s God’s gift that I must’ve enjoyed it and I must’ve wanted more.”The following morning, she banged her head against the wall because she felt numb. She told police she had had nightmares about being pregnant and said she kept quiet about the incident for years as she watched Brand becoming “more and more famous”.The woman said a 2023 Dispatches documentary about allegations of sexual misconduct by Brand “triggered” her to go to police.Brand denies the allegations. The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I am still a child, it cannot be good to be married’: how drought forces Afghan families to sell girls as brides | Global development | The Guardian
description: As climate breakdown pushes families to starvation, many feel forced to ‘sacrifice’ daughters to save siblings, with girls as young as eight and 10 engaged or married to repay debts or pay for food
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As climate breakdown pushes families to starvation, many feel forced to ‘sacrifice’ daughters to save siblings, with girls as young as eight and 10 engaged or married to repay debts or pay for food
Content: Khatirah, 11, who was sold into marriage to a 20-year-old man, at her family home in Qala-e-Naw, north-west Afghanistan. All photographs by Elise BlanchardAs climate breakdown pushes families to starvation, many feel forced to ‘sacrifice’ daughters to save siblings. Photographer Elise Blanchard travelled the country speaking to girls as young as eight, 10 and 14 who have been engaged or married to repay debts or pay for foodByElise BlanchardSupported byAbout this contentThu 15 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘I’m not happy about this,” says 11-year-old Khatira, who was sold into marriage to repay debts, sitting in her home in Qala-e-Naw, capital of Badghis province in north-westAfghanistan. “She was healthy before her engagement, now she is worried and cries a lot,” says her 40-year-old mother, Noor Bibi.When her 20-year-old husband-to-be comes to her home, Khatira runs away. Since her engagement, she has stopped going outside because she “is ashamed of having a husband in front of the other girls”, says her mother.Khatira’s father grew wheat and herded cattle before the family was displaced from its rural village by drought.In Badghis,95% of the populationrelies on rain-fed agriculture and livestock to live. But droughts, made more frequent and extreme by climate breakdown, have robbed people of their incomes.View image in fullscreenShepherds watch over their sheep in the hills of Bala-Murghab, Badghis province, north-west Afghanistan. By March, the pasture was already too dry for the seasonAs a result, selling young daughters into marriage to repay debts, feed the family or pay for medical treatment has become a common way to cope.“As a mother, I cried a lot, but I knew my husband had no choice,” says Gul Bobo, who does not know her own age, regarding her daughters, aged two and five, at her home in Tayz Nāwah, a village 12 hours’ drive from Qala-e-Naw. Both girls are engaged to be married.Like many there, Gul Bobo’s husband used to buy seeds each year and rent a tractor or donkey to cultivate a wealthier man’s plot of land.“I know they are too young to be engaged but we had no choice – otherwise we would have waited until after 18,” says Gul Bobo.“I expect them to be beaten, but there is nothing I can do about it. And at 14, they will be pregnant.”View image in fullscreenGul Bobo in the courtyard of her home with her daughters, Rubina, two, and Nazila, five, who have both been sold into marriageUnderage brides are often expected to have children when they reach puberty, leading to well-documented health problems – in a country wherematernal mortality is among the highest in the world.They are also expected to know how to run a household. When they are unable to do so like adults would, domestic violence from in-laws is not unusual.Five-year-old Nazila’s husband-to-be is 15. According to Gul Bobo, she could leave to live with her in-laws in two or three years.‘Iwould have preferred for her to be dead rather than be married off to such an old man,” says Bana, the mother of Gulalai, 11, who is engaged to a shopkeeper in his late 40s. Her parents owed him money.The story is always much the same. Gulalai’s father was a farmer and the family were displaced by crop failure from their remote village in Qadis, Badghis province.View image in fullscreenGulalai, who is now 11 and was engaged to become the second wife of a shopkeeper, playing with her sister, Farzana, in Balochha, Badghis, in September 2023“We have to sacrifice a family member to save the others,” says Gulalai’s father, Niaz Mohammad, who says he would have preferred to wait until his daughters turned 20 to marry them off – instead, four were married as children.The family only eat homemade bread, tea and wild mallow leaves they gather and boil, using rubbish to make a fire.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenLeft: Zartila, then eight, at home in Qala-e-Naw, where the family was displaced by droughts, in 2023. Every day, she collects rubbish to help them survive. Right: Nazia, 10, was sold into marriage for £2,300 to pay off the family’s debts after they were displaced by droughts. ‘When her future husband comes to visit us, she does not want to see him and starts to cry,’ her mother saysWhen asked about climate change, most people in Badghis do not know what it means. In villages, most live in mud homes, with no electricity besides the occasional solar-powered battery, and little transport aside from an occasional motorcycle. The population relies on so little to live that notions of overconsumption or greenhouse gas emissions are completely alien.In a desperate attempt to survive droughts over the past nine years, thousands have abandoned their ancestral villages to try to find work in Qala-e-Naw, often in vain.View image in fullscreenBoys in Badghis play football in April this year. The land is parched despite it being the rainy seasonTo feed his family, Mohammad Yawaz, 55, sells ice-cream on the roadside for 100 afghanis (£1.20) a day, after spending his mornings with his six-year-old daughter Zubaida, collecting cans and bottles. They make, at best, 500 to 1,000 afghanis a month reselling them.View image in fullscreenEvery morning, Zubaida, six, who was sold into marriage, collects rubbish with her father to resell in Qala-e-NawYawaz eventually felt he had no choice but to marry off his first daughter, now 15, who has already left for her husband’s home, and Zubaida, who was engaged last year to a 12-year-old boy.His neighbour, Surgul, is in the same situation. In the morning, he collects rubbish with his daughters Zartila, 10, and Bibi Aisha, seven, who are both engaged. The decision to sell Zartila into marriage was taken after the family had to endure “three days and three nights with nothing to eat”.Recently, Surgul sold the only battery he had for lighting in his mud home to buy medications for one of his daughters. A few years ago, he and his wife lost an infant to illness.But this was not always their life. Surgul once had cattle in his village. As droughts hit the area, he sold them.Cattle markets in Badghis are full of men selling their precious animals because they cannot afford to buy fodder to compensate for the lack of grass. In some areas, villages have become ghost towns.View image in fullscreenKhatera, nine, Jamila, 10, and Alaida, seven, help their father weed a field in Balocha. All have already been sold into marriageSome families go to Herat, the third-biggest city in Afghanistan, where the Shahrak-e-Sabz camp houses tens of thousands of displaced people. They come here in the hope of finding humanitarian aid – but it has dried up. Then they resort to selling their daughters into marriage to repay debts.Darellah, 15, lives with her 30-year-old husband, Mollah. Her family was displaced from their village in 2018.That year,Badghis suffered a historic drought, and since 2021, droughts have ruined harvests and starved livestock every year.View image in fullscreenDarellah, who is 15 and pregnant, with her sisters Rahimah, 11, and Bibi Zat, nine, both of whom have also been sold into marriage, in their father’s mud house in Herat’s Shahrak-e-Sabz camp in March 2026Now pregnant, Darellah is visiting her family. “I am still a child … it cannot be a good decision to be married at that age,” she says. Her sisters, Bibi Zat, nine, and Rahimah, 11, are both engaged but still live with their parents.View image in fullscreenZiauddin, 10, shows the scar left after his father sold his son’s kidney to feed the familyTheir neighbours were all displaced by the drought as well. Bahahuddin, 40, had to sell his land.When he found himself unable to feed his family by collecting rubbish and begging, he sold his 10-year-old son Ziauddin’s kidney for 100,000 afghanis. He wanted to sell his own but said he was not healthy enough for people to buy it.In the camp, stories like these do not raise an eyebrow. Residents say children have often died from not being able to access health services.Khomakha, 30, is another neighbour displaced by the droughts. Her husband made a deal to marry off their two-year-old daughter Fatemah only three months after the girl was born.The urgency came as they could not afford the small fee for shared transport to take their eight-year-old son, Ehsanullah, who has blood cancer, to the hospital for a transfusion each week.View image in fullscreenKhomakha, 30, sits with her daughter, Fatemah, two, who is already sold into marriage, and her son Ehsanullah, eight, in the Shahrak-e-Sabz camp, HeratKhomakha may not see Fatemah ever again after she marries and moves to a village 15 hours’ drive away. “I will not be able to afford transport to visit my daughter once she leaves,” Khomakha says.But life is not much easier for families who stay in their villages. In Khoshkian, Abdul Aziz’s wheat harvest failed seven times in eight years. Over the years of drought, he sold five of his daughters into marriage, for between 90,000 and 150,000 afghanis (£1,000-£1,750), to repay debts.Mazari, one of Abdul Aziz’s daughters, left home at about 12 or 13. Now 16 or 17, she lives with her husband in his 40s, their two-year-old son, and a baby born just one day ago.View image in fullscreenMazari holds her newborn baby, with her husband, Mirajan, and their son, Khan Ali, in Khoshkian, Ghormach district, in April this year“Getting married at 12 was really hard; when I came to his home, I wasn’t able to cook, but my husband and in-laws have been really kind,” she says.Her younger sisters, aged between three and 13, will live at home until their bride prices are paid. While they weed a field, they remember the years of war when soldiers from the previous government used to shoot from the mountains behind them.“There was no difference – the previous government’s army shot whether we were Taliban or civilians,” says Shamael, Mazari’s 13-year-old sister. “We feel better now because we are not woken up by fighting.”Sitting in the field, Shamael’s sisters nod as they continue weeding.“People cultivate their land for several years. People invested a lot to do so, and there is no harvest, so they are in debt,” Shamael says. “Then some people sell their lands, some sell their daughters – to survive.”View image in fullscreenFawzia, 10, Kabuli, 10, Alima, nine, and Khandia, seven, are sisters and neighbours all sold into marriage by families in Tangi Buzbay, Bala Murghab district, BadghisView image in fullscreenPregnant 14-year-old Bulbul with her father, Mansour, 35, in their house in Khushkian. After his wife fell sick, Mansour decided he needed a second wife, and, unable to pay the bride-price, he exchanged Bulbul for the daughter of a 45-year-old man, and married her to that manThere is no law regarding the age at which girls can leave home for marriage. Bride prices range from hundreds to a few thousand pounds and are paid in instalments. Once the dowry is paid in full, the in-laws are free to claim the bride. In many cases, it happens at the beginning of puberty.“Everything that is happening to us is because of poverty,” Shamael says.On her wedding day, in the village of Nookhil, Bibi Samia, 14, at first appears calm. She had cried a lot the night before, says her mother. She has remained stoical for hours but, just before she has to leave her home, bursts into tears. “I am not happy because I am very small,” she says.As foreign aid dries up, programmes that should provide support for these girls are disappearing.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenClockwise from top left: Bibi Samia, 14, cries before leaving home on her wedding day in March. As is traditional, men gather outside the house in Nookhil, Badghis, as a mullah dresses the groom, Fateh Mohammad, 16, while another man recitestaranas(Taliban chants) andnaats(religious odes). Bibi Samia goes to join her husband, veiled in a cloth as a sign of modesty and protection against the ‘evil eye’, and adorned with banknotes gifted by guests. Bibi and Fateh are welcomed at his home. She will live there now, while he will leave for Iran to find workMark Calder, advocacy director for Afghanistan at the aid organisation World Vision International, says: “Early marriage exposes girls to potentially deadly health risks, but the clinics treating them are disappearing as aid is cut.”The psychological toll for child brides is immense. Despite her crushing poverty, Sara brings her daughter, Aisha, 12, to primary school every morning, walking from the same slum Khatira lives in, bordering Qala-e-Naw, since they fled droughts in 2021.Still, Sara’s husband sold Aisha into marriage to a 20-year-old to repay debts; when it is paid, she will have to go.View image in fullscreenAisha, 12, at home with her mother, Sara, and two-month-old brother Ekmatullah in Qala-e-Naw in AprilThe bride price has done little to alleviate the family’s poverty: their rent of 1,000 afghanis has not been paid for two months and the landlord has told the family to leave. When her last baby was born, Sara had to walk to the hospital, unable to pay for a lift.Despite this, Sara says: “I try not to contact the in-laws to ask them for the rest of the bride price, so that Aisha will not have to leave.”Sara cannot speak about her daughter’s impending marriage in front of her, as it makes Aisha cry. She prefers to let her continue quietly doing her homework while she still can.Explore more on these topicsRights and freedomChild marriageWomen's rights and gender equalityChildren's rightsAfghanistanSouth and central AsiaDroughtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: They asked for 80 homes – she gave them 157! Council-housing miracle named Britain’s best new building | Architecture | The Guardian
description: Rising from bluebell woodlands and framed by rolling hills, this cluster of pink and brown brick towers in Croydon is a bittersweet winner of the prestigious RIBA Stirling prize
Author: Oliver Wainwright
Headline: Rising from bluebell woodlands and framed by rolling hills, this cluster of pink and brown brick towers in Croydon is a bittersweet winner of the prestigious RIBA Stirling prize
Content: ‘Oozing quality’ … Lion Green Road in Coulsdon, Croydon, designed by Mary Duggan Architects.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightView image in fullscreen‘Oozing quality’ … Lion Green Road in Coulsdon, Croydon, designed by Mary Duggan Architects.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightArchitectureThey asked for 80 homes – she gave them 157! Council-housing miracle named Britain’s best new buildingRising from bluebell woodlands and framed by rolling hills, this cluster of pink and brown brick towers in Croydon is a bittersweet winner of the prestigious RIBA Stirling prizeOliver WainwrightThu 15 Oct 2026 16.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf Andy Burnham is looking for inspiration for his great “council housebuilding comeback”, he would do well to visit Croydon. There, nestled into a steeply sloping site, sheltered by a canopy of mature trees, stands a cluster of crystalline pink and brown brick towers, where generous flats look on to a landscape of allotments, playgrounds and to the rolling hills of south London beyond. Designed by Mary Duggan Architects, with Ruff Architects, it is a model of council-led housebuilding – so much so that it has also been named this year’s best building in the UK, confounding the bookies’ outsider odds.Only once before has the RIBA Stirling prize ever been awarded to a council housing project, whenGoldsmith Street in Norwichscooped the gong in 2019, for its rows of low-energy brick terraces, designed by Mikhail Riches Architects and Cathy Hawley. This year’s winner,Lion Green Roadin Coulsdon, is an entirely different animal, and it puts a welcome spotlight back on housing design at a time when the government plans to pump £39bn into the sector. It is also a bittersweet vindication of Croydon council’s erstwhile housebuilding company, Brick by Brick, a bold and sadly brief experiment by the previous Labour administration, which was halted in 2020 when the council went bankrupt, seeing numerous projects cancelled.double quotation markIt puts a welcome spotlight back on housing design – at a time when the government plans to pump £39bn into the sector“At a time when we urgently need to deliver more homes,” says RIBA president, Chris Williamson, “Lion Green Road shows that density can be achieved without compromising the quality of the places we create. Through a consistent specification, with subtle variation in height and orientation, it offers housing at scale without uniformity.”Burnham’s first allocation of £10bn, announced in August, is planned to kickstart 70,000 affordable homes across the country. Yet few people in Britain welcome the prospect of new housing in their backyards, even if it’s prize-winning. The planning application for Lion Green Road, submitted in 2017, received 18 letters of support and 257 objections, mostly about the loss of parking. Now built, almost a decade later, the project demonstrates how more homes than you might imagine can be constructed on the most unpromising of sites in a sympathetic way, without sacrificing greenery, views and public access – and keeping plenty of parking, too.View image in fullscreenEach home is dual aspect, maximising natural light, cross-ventilation and views.Photograph: Oliver Wainwright“We really pushed against the suburban model of terraces dominated by cars, with little front and back gardens,” says Duggan. The original brief asked for 80 homes, arranged as she describes, but Duggan proved she could fit 157 flats, distributed between five pavilion-like towers, retaining the mature trees and bluebell woodland on the site. The result feels like it has grown out of its woodland setting, with a public route that winds its way through the site, up to a historic railway embankment at the rear, and not a perimeter fence in sight.“Brick by Brick was an amazing client,” says Duggan, who also hada small mews project in Crystal Palaceon the drawing board for the council’s housebuilder, before the plug was pulled. “It was a refreshing change from how private developers think about affordable housing. Here, they weren’t talking about the land as a commodity, but as a genuinely public asset.”View image in fullscreenDetailling … brick walls at Lion Green Road.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightThe council cared about the interior spaces, too. Thanks to the “pinwheel” plan of the blocks, with flats radiating outwards from a central lift core, each home is dual aspect, maximising natural light, cross-ventilation and views. The flats all enjoy an inset loggia balcony, with a bulge at the base of the balustrades to accommodate plant pots, while cuts in the form (to preserve historic views) create some with larger roof terraces. In the interests of efficiency, the five towers all have the same star-shaped plan, but each is subtly rotated to reduce direct overlooking between neighbouring homes, enabling the buildings to stand close together without sacrificing privacy. Half of the flats are private rental, in two towers, while half are affordable, in three blocks retained by the council, rented at local housing allowance rates. Unlike the Norwich project, this is not true social housing.The RIBA judges describe the project as a “new kind of garden neighbourhood”. The space between the blocks feels consciously planned, rather than a leftover afterthought, designed with landscape architecture practice Planit-IE to include a sensory garden, allotment plots and play areas. Walking around the development’s zig-zagging slopes and stepped pathways gives the feeling of exploring a bucolic hill town. Little bug hotels in the same faceted star-shaped form as the towers are a delightful touch; even the insects get a dignified dwelling.Duggan says the project “expands the idea of the threshold”, and the arrival feels more welcoming than most. The entrance of each block is framed by a paved terrace, with seating and planting, while all have generous lobbies, no matter the tenure. It’s a far cry from the “poor door” apartheid of so much developer-built housing, where private owners get the hotel concierge treatment, while affordable tenants enter around the back by the bins. It all oozes quality on a budget, down to the choice of three dusty colours of brick, some projecting to create a textured, tweedy finish. The quality belies the tight construction budget of £2,500/sq metre – making it the cheapest project on the shortlist by far. OtherStirling Prize contenders this yearincluded two exquisitely built projects for well-heeled Cambridge colleges, a large private house in Essex, an arts centre in Hertford, and an £825m office block in Paddington.‘Our hallway’s big enough to play football in!’ The council housing that feels like a holiday resortRead moreIf there is a cloud hanging over Croydon’s triumph, it is the fate of Brick by Brick. It was established in 2015, as a wholly council-owned company, because the conventional development model wasfailing to deliver enough affordable homes. The idea was that Croydon would use its own land, often small leftover sites, and borrow against its own resources, to build a mix of private and affordable housing, while turning a profit for the public purse. But the sites often proved to be trickier than expected, adding additional costs, while the financial forecasts were overly optimistic, with Brexit and Covid introducing huge delays. Housing expertsattribute its collapseto poor financial structuring, governance and risk management, rather than a failure in development expertise or quality of delivery.Nonetheless, Brick by Brick built 751 homes, over half of which are affordable, of a design quality higher than most standard developer fare. With renewed housing cash from central government, might there be a chance for some of the halted schemes to be resurrected, and more of the imagination and innovation of Lion Green Road spread across the borough and beyond?Explore more on these topicsArchitectureStirling prizeSocial housingThe RIBALondonCommunitiesHousingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK HRT shortages: which products are affected and what to do about it | Menopause | The Guardian
description: Experts say seeking alternatives that deliver the same dose of oestrogen by the same method is key
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Experts say seeking alternatives that deliver the same dose of oestrogen by the same method is key
Content: Estradot, one of the products affected, is the second longest running individual medicine shortage in the UK.Photograph: Nicola K photos/AlamyView image in fullscreenEstradot, one of the products affected, is the second longest running individual medicine shortage in the UK.Photograph: Nicola K photos/AlamyMenopauseExplainerUK HRT shortages: which products are affected and what to do about itExperts say seeking alternatives that deliver the same dose of oestrogen by the same method is keyNicola DavisScience correspondentThu 15 Oct 2026 13.58 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWomen in the UK are again facing shortages of some HRT products, with warnings they could persist for weeks. We take a look at the situation.What is HRT?Hormone replacement therapy is widely used to help women manage symptoms of menopause. It can take many forms, from gels and sprays to patches, pills, creams and intrauterine systems.As the NHS notes,HRT typically involves two hormones – oestrogen and progestogen – and replaces levels lost as women go through menopause. These can be given separately or in a single type of HRT. Women who have had a hysterectomy only require oestrogen-containing HRT.According to theNHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA), almost 2 million women in England aged 40 and above were prescribed HRT for menopause symptoms in 2025-26. Experts, however, say thataccess variesand shortages have been a problem.Which items are affected by the current shortages?According to amedicine supply notificationissued by the Department of Health and Social Care this week, FemSeven Contipatches are out of stock and are expected to remain so until late November. The patches contain estradiol – a type of oestrogen– and a synthetic progestogen called levonorgestrel.There are alsoshortages of various Estradot patches– a type of HRT that contains estradiol – and the situation is not expected to end until January.This isnot the first timethere have been HRT shortages, and the supply issues affecting Estradot have been long-lasting. The shortages of some products began in December 2024, according toNHSBSA.“When you have found an HRT treatment that helps you sleep, manage hot flushes and feel more like yourself, being told it is unavailable can be unsettling,” said Sobia Qasim, a pharmacist at the online pharmacyCurely.Sehar Shahid, a member of the National Pharmacy Association’s board, also raised concerns. “We are deeply frustrated and concerned by shortages to a number of HRT products, with shortages of Estradot being the second longest running individual medicine shortage in the UK,” she said.“Certain HRT products are specialised and cannot always be easily substituted for an alternative.”What alternatives are there?According to the FemSeven Conti notification, alternative patches include Evorel Conti, Estradot Conti 30/95 and Estradot Conti 40/130. These contain estradiol and a different type of synthetic progestogen called norethisterone, and are used twice rather than once a week.Paula Briggs, a consultant in sexual and reproductive health and a former chair of the British Menopause Society, said keeping the same dose of estradiol was the important aspect. “They have different progestogens, but I do not think that that would have any adverse impact on symptom control,” she said, noting progestogens are required to protect the lining of the womb rather than manage symptoms.Serious shortage protocols for the Estradot products also list alternatives, such as estradiol-containing patches by Estraderm MX and Evorel. “If we’re using the same dose of oestrogen delivered in a similar patch through the skin, really there is no need to worry,” said Briggs.What should women do if they are affected by the shortages?Shahid said people who had experienced disruption to their usual HRT regime should speak to their clinician, while Qasim cautioned against leaving a patch on for longer than prescribed, cutting patches up or borrowing HRT treatments from others.What needs to happen next?Briggs said shortages were likely to occur in the future “because year on year we’re seeing a more than 10% increase in use”, she said.Shahid urged the government to take action. “The new secretary of state should convene a taskforce to fully grasp this issue, bringing together all aspects of the supply chain,” she said.Explore more on these topicsMenopauseWomen's healthNHSHealthDrugsPharmaceuticals industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Cable and camera: selfies in 1970s Handsworth | Photography | The Guardian
description: Nearly 50 years ago in inner-city Birmingham, photographers Derek Bishton, Brian Homer and John Reardon set up an impromptu studio in the street and invited their neighbours along. With no camera phones in 1979, long cable releases gave participants the power to decide how they wished to be seen and represented. The project’s original aim was to counter negative media images of Handsworth and its people. Now, in collaboration with Dewi Lewis Publishing, a Kickstarter fund has been set up to bring them together in book form
