title: Just what damage can the emissions from a new fossil fuel facility cause? A new tool has estimates  | Coal | The Guardian
description: From crop failures to coral bleaching, a new tool developed by climate scientists aims to predict in detail the impacts of each megatonne of carbon emissions
Author: Nick Evershed
Headline: From crop failures to coral bleaching, a new tool developed by climate scientists aims to predict in detail the impacts of each megatonne of carbon emissions
Content: One big chartCoalJust what damage can the emissions from a new fossil fuel facility cause? A new tool has estimatesFrom crop failures to coral bleaching, a new tool developed by climate scientists aims to predict in detail the impacts of each megatonne of carbon emissionsWant to get more charts in your inbox every fortnight?Sign up for The Crunch hereNick EvershedThu 15 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 17.39 EDTShareThe emissions from a single coalmine expansion might not seem like a lot when compared with the scale of global emissions, which are measured in gigatonnes (that’s one thousand million tonnes).However, scientists have been saying for years thatevery tonne of carbon dioxide adds to global warming, and every fraction of a degree increase matters.Now, a group of climate scientists have released a new tool that shows the possible consequences of those emissions in detail. TheCarbon Impacts Traceruses peer-reviewed studies to estimate the impact of every megatonne of emissions on people and the environment.Here, you can see how theemissions from a coalmine expansion in Australia’s Hunter Valleycould affect food security and human exposure to heat stress globally.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenobc emissions AN fallbackIllustration: Guardian DesignasdasdasYou can read about the science underlying these projections on theCarbon Impacts Tracer website here.There are further predicted impacts from releasing 809m tonnes of emissions not listed in the graphic above, including an estimated 107 deaths in Europe, 41,800 additional people put into extreme poverty, 19.4km square of additional glacier area lost, and 38.8m additional heavy labour hours lost annually.

title: ‘A guy held a knife to my throat and said: play something normal!’ Richard Thompson on crazy crowds, his beloved beret and Sandy Denny’s driving skills | Richard Thompson | The Guardian
description: As he releases new album Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, the 77-year-old British folk legend answers your questions about Billy Connolly, Californian fish and chips and whether he nearly joined the Eagles
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: As he releases new album Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, the 77-year-old British folk legend answers your questions about Billy Connolly, Californian fish and chips and whether he nearly joined the Eagles
Content: ‘I wanted to do my Anglo-Celtic thing and sing in my own accent’ … Richard Thompson.Photograph: Paul ClampinView image in fullscreen‘I wanted to do my Anglo-Celtic thing and sing in my own accent’ … Richard Thompson.Photograph: Paul ClampinFilm & Music reader interviewRichard ThompsonInterview‘A guy held a knife to my throat and said: play something normal!’ Richard Thompson on crazy crowds, his beloved beret and Sandy Denny’s driving skillsAs told toDave SimpsonAs he releases new album Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, the 77-year-old British folk legend answers your questions about Billy Connolly, Californian fish and chips and whether he nearly joined the EaglesThu 15 Oct 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBilly Connolly recalled being in a room with you, Sandy Denny, Nick Drake and John Martyn. Did you feel you were collectively doing something special?poscopyThat might have been at the Royal Festival Hall [in 1969], where Fairport Convention had Nick and John as openers and Billy must have been backstage. He’d have been in the Humblebums with Gerry Rafferty, before he evolved from a banjo player who told jokes into a comedian who played a bit of banjo. He was always a fantastic bloke and we’ve been friends for a long time.There was a great camaraderie between the stable of acts Joe Boyd produced: Fairport, the Incredible String Band, John Martyn, Chris McGregor. We felt different, not special, and didn’t feel successful because we weren’t. None of these people really sold many records in their lifetimes, but people are still discovering them now. This album is my latest attempt to sell some units.Have you ever been on a1952 Vincent Black Lightningand did that inspire the song?llamapacaI’ve never ridden a Vincent Black Lightning. There’s only about 15 left, but when I was a kid one of the neighbours had a Vincent Black Shadow – a very similar motorcycle – and us kids thought it was one of the most beautiful things we’d ever seen. I was casting around for a British equivalent to American romantic imagery, so thought it would be a good object to build a drama around. Boy, girl, motorcycle, armed robbery …The narrator in your songCold Kissesis one of the most chilling characters I’ve ever met in a song. How much of that rogue is you?If it’s none, where did you summon him up from?LeroyDeSwoonHe wants to compare himself with her old boyfriends. Some of us have been there – not necessarily going through someone’s drawers, but looking at someone’s diary or emails, trying to find out more about a new partner. It’s a sneaky thing to do, obviously, but in the guise of entertainment songwriting can dig below the surface of what’s considered civilised and into an area that’s slightly uncomfortable. I love that.On the new album, the song Cocaine Walking, Booze Talking is based on people I met in the psychedelic era who were a bit edgy or violent. Then acid came along and they suddenly went all peace and love, but it wouldn’t last. So the last verse asks: “Who’ll win the battle before the nurse pulls the plug? The Kings Road hippy or the Sauchiehall thug?” Conflicted human beings. I thought John Lennon was a bit like that.Listen to Cocaine Walking, Booze Talking.Could you tell a nice – not sad – story that I haven’t heard about Sandy Denny or Nick Drake?katstuNick was so taciturn and hard to know that I couldn’t say a lot of uplifting stuff about him. Sandy was a terrible passenger, hypersensitive. In a car, she’d be going: “What was that noise?” “Why did you put the brakes on?” Eventually, our tour manager [in Fairport Convention] had to teach her about the internal combustion engine: “I’m now changing gear.” On an airplane, she was impossible. Flying to Los Angeles, she spilled a gin and tonic in my lap in the first hour, although on a boat she was totally at ease, in her element, hence so many of her songs about the sea. From what I’ve heard, when she finally got a licence, she was driving into ditches and all sorts. Bless her.Who is the inspiration behind Beeswing?EddieHaskellPeople say: “Oh, what a beautiful song about [the folk singer] Anne Briggs,” but it’s more complicated. When I lived in Suffolk in the 1970s, a tramp used to come looking for odd jobs. He’d do a bit of gardening, we’d wash his clothes and feed him and he’d tell extraordinary stories about his life. So his stories were part of the song, but also Sandy and Anne were great friends and it was really Sandy’s sense of Anne being this free spirit. But I need credit as a writer of fiction, too, because it’s not about anybody.Do you have a favourite cover of any of your songs? Mine isWall of Death by REM.MrsGRaffertyWall of Death was a memo to myself: take risks, go to the edge, don’t be complacent. But my favourite cover is The Great Valerio by Swan Arcade, a vocal trio around the folk scene in the 60s and 70s. They did a fantastic job of getting all the dissonant, unusual harmony that exists in the guitar arrangement and ended up with a wonderful piece of music. [Swan Arcade’s] Dave Brady had one arm. The story was that he’d been on his motorcycle and was hurtling towards a brick wall, so stuck his arm out to grab a lamp-post. But he managed to shape a chord with his left hand and strum with his little finger. A great character.Would you have liked to have worked more closely with John Martyn – at least before he became “difficult” and his music moved in a different direction?archiebargie“Difficult” is a bit cheeky. John was one of those guitar players, likeMartin Carthy, who cover all bases. I’m a bit like that myself, so if you put us together there’s a lot of treading on each other’s toes, but we were neighbours for a while in the late 60s and early 70s and used to jam together. Once, we were in Olympic Studios for one of John’s sessions and he played acoustic and I played electric. We jammed for about 20 minutes and it was just wonderful and joyous, but they didn’t have the machine running. We should have done more of that.View image in fullscreenFairport Convention in in 1970. From left: Dave Mattacks (front), Dave Pegg, Simon Nicol, Richard Thompson and Dave Swarbrick.Photograph: Jim McCrary/RedfernsHow did the offer to join Eagles come about?BobinDayOffers would come through lawyers or management. I don’t think it was ever someone from a band phoning up saying: “We’d love to have you.” When I was on tour with Sandy in ’71, I did get a firm approach to join Linda Ronstadt’s band because four of them had left to form Eagles. I thought: I can’t jump ship. Sandy would kill me … and do I wanna live and work with a bunch of Californians? I wanted to do my Anglo-Celtic thing and sing in my own accent. I was asked to join a later incarnation of the Animals when they wanted to dump [the guitarist]Hilton Valentine. Shocking stuff. I was asked to join the Band twice, but I thought they were gonna drink themselves to death.You were originally a fervent enthusiast for all things British and yet now you live in the US,which seems at odds with everything the UK stands for. Why?DozyDannyFor the last 40 years, I’ve had a place in London and a place in America. I lived in Santa Monica for a long time, but you’re surrounded by Brits in the music and film business. You can’t go 10 or 20 yards without a pub screening Premier League games or a fish and chip shop. Plus, when I open up my computer, the Guardian is my homepage. You can be connected anywhere in the world, but I’ve never felt connected with American culture. I’m not going to sing Jan and Dean songs about surfing. My inner landscape is London, Scotland or some dark moor in Brontë country.What was it like being on stage with Bob Dylan at theGuitar Legends festival in Seville in 1991? You looked on high alert, or anxious. Was there any rehearsal beforehand?MaskedTortillaI was on the road with [the American singer-songwriter]Bonnie Raittwhen I got a call from [the guitarist]Phil Manzanera. Word was Bob wanted to do some acoustic numbers together, which was great. We did rehearse in the dressing room, and rehearsed All Along the Watchtower with his band. When we went on stage, the acoustic guitars had gone out of tune, so I spent the first song trying to tune up – that was probably high alert – but once things settled down it was great fun; a great honour to work with Bob.Your first band wasEmil and the Detectives, withHugh Cornwell, later of the Stranglers. Did you cross paths again?Haigin88We had the band in school, but by 16 I was playing with Fairport Convention, so I didn’t see Hugh for 40 years. Then, in the 2000s, we were both playing a festival in Spain and picked up the conversation where we left it. Since then, we’ve done some musical things and gigs together anda splendid version of Tobacco Roadfor charity.View image in fullscreenThompson playing at the New Orleans jazz festival in 1980.Photograph: David Redfern/RedfernsWhat has been your most improbable backing role as a guitarist?thoughtwhackerIn the band with Hugh, we backedHelen Shapiro, but I’ve played unlikely places like care homes, funerals, weddings and schools. Singing at my own mum’s funeral was the toughest gig. I played a girls’ school in Connecticut because we knew the teacher. The kids knew a bit of Chaucer, so I could do something like Sumer Is Icumen In plus a Britney Spears song or something. The kids went nuts. Best audience ever.Bonospent a small fortune having his favourite hat flown in first class for a gig in Italy. How far would you go to ensure your trademark beret [a Balmoral] was in place come showtime?SalfordianBlueThat must have cost Bono £20,000. For the price of a stapler, I have someone staple it to my head before I go to the airport. I sometimes forget to pack any shoes, but people don’t notice ’cause I wear black socks.The last time I saw you, a fire alarm cleared the theatre. What’s your best, worst or most memorable moment playing live?RobFramptonIn the 70s, I did a solo tour of Sweden and played somewhere in the Arctic Circle where I was singing my precious little folk-rock numbers between the disco. A guy held a knife to my throat and said: “Why don’t you play something normal?” I wasn’t afraid; I was wondering: what’s normal? I might have done a Buddy Holly cover. At school, when I deputised for some local poppy covers band, there was a real fight in the audience, kids throwing chairs; hang on to your equipment and get off stage.The Mary Wallopers review – legs and pints go flying to the sound of rowdy folk ragersRead moreAt one point, you became an antiques dealer. Why was this and howdid you acquirethe expertise?rjoncasA friend of mine took over an antique shop in Marylebone. I knew a bit, but I was too nice to the old ladies, too honest: I’d tell them we’d offer £1,000, but they’d get double that at auction. I sold a couple of porcelain Ming dynasty lions for £60, thinking they were fakes. They were worth thousands. I soon went back to music, but I still annoy my family by watching Antiques Roadshow and correctly guessing what something’s worth, so they look at me like I’m some sort of genius.Hippies, Thugs and Heroes byRichard Thompsonis released on 16 October on New West Records. He tours North America until 18 February, then Europe and the UK from 15 April to 7 MayExplore more on these topicsRichard ThompsonFilm & Music reader interviewFolk musicPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Stranger than stranger-than-fiction’: how Lance Oppenheim made the year’s two buzziest films | Movies | The Guardian
description: Primetime and You Can See Everything are both clammy, audacious awards contenders that challenge our sense of reality. Ahead of the release of his drama starring Robert Pattinson as a TV vigilante, the 30-year-old director talks crime, punishment and South Park
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: Primetime and You Can See Everything are both clammy, audacious awards contenders that challenge our sense of reality. Ahead of the release of his drama starring Robert Pattinson as a TV vigilante, the 30-year-old director talks crime, punishment and South Park
Content: ‘Rob’s quite possibly the actor of our time’ … Lance Oppenheim on the star of Primetime, Robert Pattinson.Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/APView image in fullscreen‘Rob’s quite possibly the actor of our time’ … Lance Oppenheim on the star of Primetime, Robert Pattinson.Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/APMoviesInterview‘Stranger than stranger-than-fiction’: how Lance Oppenheim made the year’s two buzziest filmsRyan GilbeyPrimetime and You Can See Everything are both clammy, audacious awards contenders that challenge our sense of reality. Ahead of the release of his drama starring Robert Pattinson as a TV vigilante, the 30-year-old director talks crime, punishment and South ParkThu 15 Oct 2026 10.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo direct one movie that is on everyone’s lips in awards season is remarkable. To make two begins to look like sorcery. That is the position in which the 30-year-old Florida-born film-maker Lance Oppenheim now finds himself. Next month brings the release of You Can See Everything, the three-hour documentary which he co-directed with faux-naif deadpan prankster Nathan Fielder, in which they spend a month living with the disgraced health-tech mogulElizabeth Holmesbefore she begins her 11-year prison sentence for fraud and conspiracy. The film, described by Oppenheim as “head-spinning” and so shrouded in secrecy that Variety magazine’s list of Oscar predictions identifies one of its cast members only as “[Redacted]”, is expected to become the first documentary nominated for best picture.‘In our deepest hearts we are voyeurs’: the paedophile-hunting show that inspired Robert Pattinson’s new filmRead moreWhen I meet Oppenheim in a London hotel, it is to discuss his other hot ticket, Primetime, for whichRobert Pattinsonis the one attracting Oscar buzz. The Batman actor gives a high-wire performance as Chris Hansen, the sensationalist US television vigilante renowned for ambushing paedophiles on To Catch a Predator, which was a disreputable and highly addictive segment of the current affairs show Dateline NBC between 2004 and 2007. Hansen later parlayed the idea, and his crusading shtick, into a succession of spin-offs. Some, including Hansen Vs Predators, had the same sleazy catnip quality. Others, such as a sting to collar bicycle thieves, did not.The format of To Catch a Predator is simple. A volunteer from the website Perverted-Justice enters an online chatroom pretending to be underage. Once a paedophile takes the bait, chats with the supposed teen and then pitches up at the agreed location (which is in fact a “sting house” rigged with cameras), he is met by an actor posing as the adolescent. Suddenly, Hansen slinks out of the shadows and calmly invites the offender to “have a seat,” an offer which quickly became his catchphrase. He then reads aloud excerpts from the incriminating online chat as the guilty party squirms and panics. Reality television this may be, but it is also a theatrical performance with its own unvarying props from one sting to the next: cookies and pizza the pre-sex snacks, a table or kitchen island Hansen’s equivalent of a CEO’s desk or judge’s bench.“The show is so tonally strange,” marvels Oppenheim. “It feels like an alien object beamed in from Mars. You’re seeing this horrific situation where someone who’s sick in the head has shown up to do a terrible thing. Then they’re confronted by Chris Hansen, who has these catchphrases and one-liners. He’s a crime-stopper but he’s also there to make a TV show out of their miserable state. It oscillated between making me nauseated and making me laugh. The challenge for me was how to create something that’s even stranger than stranger-than-fiction.”View image in fullscreenRighteous avenger or meretricious huckster … Pattinson as Chris Hansen in Primetime.Photograph: A24In person, you would never take this boyish chatterbox for a zeitgeist-surfing A24 auteur whose fanclub includes Ari Aster, Darren Aronofsky and the Safdie brothers. In fact, you might think twice before serving him alcohol, at least without ID. His mini pompadour gives him an Eraserhead Jr look; his black, round-framed glasses might have been felt-tipped on to his face by a classmate. A black-and-white striped shirt worn under his suit jacket lends him the appearance of a well-dressed humbug.Though based in fact, Primetime is Oppenheim’s first non-documentary feature. His haunting 2020 debut,Some Kind of Heaven, was set in a Florida retirement community where happiness becomes oppressive and tyrannical. Its 2024 follow-up, Spermworld, delved into the private lives of men who donate sperm, including one who has fathered more than a hundred children.“I’ve always wanted my documentaries to feel like Hollywood dramas,” the director explains. “With Primetime, I was curious about what it would be like to make an actual Hollywood drama with actors.” The resulting character study is almost as kaleidoscopic and overripe asRen Faire, Oppenheim’s masterful 2024 HBO “docu-fantasia” featuring a mercurial, Viagra-popping elderly theme-park despot, his back-stabbing underlings and a giant talking lizard.View image in fullscreen‘It oscillated between making me nauseated and making me laugh’ … Oppenheim on the show that inspired Primetime.Photograph: Sinna NasseriThe film-maker’s own introduction to Chris Hansen came as a child when he saw him spoofed on an episode of South Park, in which Cartman is strong-armed by the presenter into appearing on a TV special about Tourette syndrome; a group of paedophiles inadvertently come to his rescue by shooting themselves en masse. From there, Oppenheim became hooked on To Catch a Predator and its derivatives. A few years ago, his girlfriend (now wife) even bought him a personalised Cameo video message from Hansen. He scoots forward now to play it to me on his phone. In the video, the silver-haired paedophile-hunter cheekily invites Oppenheim to “have a seat … not because I suspect you of anything predator-like,” before plugging his own upcoming shows.It is this confusion between righteous avenger and meretricious huckster that makes Hansen such an irresistible subject. “I think he started off with noble intentions, but he turned serious reporting into entertainment and willingly transformed himself into a meme. He’s on Cameo presenting what he does as a service you can pay for; then he puts his whole project into this moral register where he talks about good and evil. What happens to you psychologically when you believe you’re doing something good for the world? Does that turn you into a superhero?” He grins: “And now we’ve got the guy who plays Batman as Chris Hansen.”View image in fullscreen‘Head-spinning’ … Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24It was Pattinson, already a diehard Hansen fan, who brought the project to Oppenheim intending only to produce rather than star in it. “Rob’s quite possibly the actor of our time,” the director says. “Every movie he’s done this year has been a defining cultural moment.” Primetime follows The Drama, his prickly black comedy with Zendaya, and The Odyssey; Dune: Part Three arrives in December. “As I’ve gotten to know him, I feel like he also stitched some very human and vulnerable parts of himself into Primetime. Rob became an overnight celebrity when he went to Comic-Con with Twilight in 2008. He was instantly a public figure with expectations about how he should behave. That’s part of what Chris Hansen goes through in the movie.”The special alchemy of Primetime lies in the way it renders Hansen’s story in the clammy style of To Catch a Predator so that we are simultaneously inside the show, with its churning moral tumult, and outside, looking on in appalled and impotent horror. “It is very muchnota biopic,” agrees Oppenheim. “I wanted it to be experiential and phantasmagorical. I was wondering what would happen if you took Billy Wilder’s Ace in the Hole, Oliver Stone’s JFK and Brian De Palma’s Body Double, then threw them in a blender with the real-life events of To Catch a Predator. Would it taste weird or delicious? Maybe you sprinkle a little Sexy Beast in there, too, and it’s, like, ‘Boom!’”Boom, indeed. Hansen, who has griped bitterly about not being consulted or even informed about the film, has accused Primetime of “weaponised empathy”, “[making] audiences feel sorry for the predators” and portraying him and his staff “as ratings-obsessed, maniacal people”. On the other hand, he has insinuated himself enthusiastically into the Primetime experience, booking trailers for his own true-crime streaming platform, TruBlu, to run immediately before screenings of the movie in US cinemas.‘He stole the show’: do Oscars beckon for Robert Pattinson, star of four of the year’s biggest films – and Batman?Read moreOppenheim is full of admiration. “The way he has created a media circus around his reaction to the film is on a par with what we’ve seen of him on television. He contains multitudes. He is a journalist but also an entertainer, a circus ringleader and maybe a compulsive performer.” Are there parallels with the current US president? “Well, they were both on television around the same time and both on shows which were made or green-lit by Jeff Zucker, who plays himself in the film.” He stops short, though, of calling them kindred spirits.Perhaps Hansen’s persona is too closely intertwined with the development of Oppenheim’s own sensibility for him to make any such damning judgment. “I saw To Catch a Predator long before I saw Abbas Kiarostami’s Close-Up or Orson Welles’s F For Fake,” he says, citing two films in which documentary and drama form an unstable concoction. “But I feel the show has a lot in common with them because it’s such a reality bender. It has short adult actors pretending to be children in a house that looks like a set from Blue Velvet.” He shakes his head as if experiencing afresh the insanity of To Catch a Predator. “I don’t think I’d be making nonfiction films the way I do if I hadn’t seen that show as a kid.”Primetime is in UK cinemas from 30 October. You Can See Everything is in UK cinemas from 20 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsRobert PattinsonElizabeth HolmesinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Amol Rajan Connection review – another wrong move after lasting one night in The Celebrity Traitors? | Television | The Guardian
description: The broadcaster has bullet-proof confidence as he departs the BBC. But his first YouTube show with Gareth Southgate is nowhere near as radical as you’d expect – and he sounds like yet another tech guru
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The broadcaster has bullet-proof confidence as he departs the BBC. But his first YouTube show with Gareth Southgate is nowhere near as radical as you’d expect – and he sounds like yet another tech guru
Content: He certainly dreams big … The Amol Rajan Connection.Photograph: YouTubeView image in fullscreenHe certainly dreams big … The Amol Rajan Connection.Photograph: YouTubeTelevisionReviewThe Amol Rajan Connection review – another wrong move after lasting one night in The Celebrity Traitors?The broadcaster has bullet-proof confidence as he departs the BBC. But his first YouTube show with Gareth Southgate is nowhere near as radical as you’d expect – and he sounds like yet another tech guruPhil HarrisonThu 15 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhatever you think ofAmol Rajan, he can’t be accused of not dreaming big. In the clip trailing the launch of his YouTube project The Amol Rajan Connection, he acknowledges the seismic volatility of our times but locates himself firmly at the heart of them. “We are about to get 100 years of change in a single decade,” he says. “And that’s scary. But maybe I can help.” Big talk for someone who somehow managed the singular feat of being outlasted by Richard E Grant in The Celebrity Traitors. But joking aside, Rajan’s bulletproof self-confidence remains titanium-tough.The branding of The Amol Rajan Connection features a mock-up of the poster from The Harder They Come, a Jamaican film about a renegade insurgent whose reckless defiance of the establishment’s rules culminates in him dying in a hail of bullets. But however he might see himself, it’s impossible to regard Rajan as an outsider. From his editorship of a national newspaper, via University Challenge and Today, he has shown an uncanny facility for arriving, briskly, at the very heart of one national institution after another. The sponsors of this show are two world-bestriding tech corporations, one of Britain’s largest banks and an upmarket supermarket chain. He soft-launched with an appearance on former Tory chancellor George Osborne’s podcast. Rajan’s connections are clearly being worked very efficiently.View image in fullscreenMildly soporific … Rajan with Gareth Southgate on the first episode of The Amol Rajan Connection.Photograph: YouTubeIn the course of the conversation with Osborne, he explained himself thus: “The BBC, and BBC News, is going to get smaller at an accelerating rate. And I want to go to where the action is.” But what constitutes the action in this context? The long-form, one-on-one video podcast (which, essentially, this is) has become a crowded field. In fact, co-presenting Today on Radio 4 remains a much more influential position for a media operative to occupy.Since leaving Today, Rajan has hinted at certain low-key beefs with the limitations of the BBC, mainly revolving around the sense of being unable to say what he really thinks. Unpromisingly, these feelings were initially articulated in an article in the Spectator, and the piece contained, more unpromisingly still, an expression of agreement with some of the ideas of Dominic Cummings. Rajan is an undeniably fluent communicator but there’s a sense that his quickness can devolve into something slightly less palatable. There is a touch of the tech guru about him – his self-belief sometimes borders on the messianic. Can he listen to an expert? Or, in keeping with the current affairs interlocutor he has recently been, does he interrupt?Perhaps his first guest can be seen as reassuring.Gareth Southgateis arguably the anti-Amol. He is unflashy, measured and occasionally even a little ponderous. Rajan reads the room: like most right-thinking people, he’s clearly full of admiration and fondness for the former England manager, and so he allows himself to be incorporated into his steady, sometimes mildly soporific rhythm. The result is a very traditional piece of broadcasting.Gareth Southgate: Changing the Game for Young Men review – boys are crying out for help like thisRead moreInitially, it wanders at length down some well-trodden paths. Rejection by Southampton, a second chance at Crystal Palace, captaincy, England,thatpenalty miss, club management – and then back to England; this time in a waistcoat, searching for footballing redemption but finding himself, at a sensitive time, forced to take the lead in cultural areas, too. It’s gently enjoyable, like a lulling, familiar bedtime story.In the second of the conversation’s two hours, the pair navigate choppier waters, talking about Fifa governance, theManchester City situationand, eventually, Southgate’s pet subject: his heartfelt concerns about the problems afflicting young men.None of this is dull, exactly. In fact, much of it is engaging and worthwhile. It just doesn’t feel particularly dynamic or radical. If this interview is “where the action is”, it’s hard to see how it provides proof of concept for the venture as a whole.Obviously, tone and mood will vary with the guests – the version of Rajan we see here is certainly more thoughtful than usual, and that’s refreshing. But at first glance, The Amol Rajan Connection plays things safe. Maybe something more reflective of the times that spawned it will emerge. For the time being, though, this isn’t it.The Amol Rajan Connection is onYouTubenowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionYouTubeAmol RajanGareth SouthgatereviewsShareReuse this content

title: A perfect storm: how the super El Niño is devastating the fishing industry | El Niño southern oscillation | The Guardian
description: Peru’s anchoveta have made up about a 10th of the entire global commercial fishing catch since 1970, more than any other fish. A combination of warming seas and decades-long overfishing spells disaster
Author: Geoff Mann
Headline: Peru’s anchoveta have made up about a 10th of the entire global commercial fishing catch since 1970, more than any other fish. A combination of warming seas and decades-long overfishing spells disaster
Content: Anchoveta being sucked into the hold of a fishing boat off the coast of Lima, 19 November 2023. Photograph: Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty ImagesPeru’s anchoveta have made up about a 10th of the entire global commercial fishing catch since 1970, more than any other fish. A combination of warming seas and decades-long overfishing spells disasterByGeoff MannThu 15 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 09.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn 10 June 2026, the government of Peru made a decision that it knew would hurt one of the world’s major fishing industries. It stoppedallanchoveta fishing boatsfrom going out to sea, suspending the fishing season. At first the order was temporary, but in mid-August, the suspension turned into atotal closure. This was no easy call. For one thing, it was a brutal blow to the Peruvian economy.Peruvian anchovies – the scientific name isEngraulis ringens– are not the salty, punch-packing little fillets in a puttanesca sauce or caesar salad dressing. That is a different species –Engraulisencrasicolus– which is smaller, tastier and found mostly in the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Only a small part of Peru’s anchoveta catch is eaten in fish form. The rest – more than 90% – is immediately processed as fishmeal and fish oil, packed in sacks and barrels, and shipped to fish, shellfish and seaweed farms, factory farms and nutritional supplement producers around the world.The vast majority of the anchoveta industry is concentrated off the coast of north-central Peru, and it is hard to overstate how economically significant this fish is. By weight, Peruvian anchoveta have made up about a 10th of the entire global commercial fishing catch since 1970, more than any other fish. Some years, the anchoveta catch is worth close to $3bn and directly employs almost 50,000 people, close to a quarter of a million if you include indirect jobs. The Peruvian central bank is forecasting a30.7% contractionfor the fishing sector and about 78,000 job losses in 2026, and another 44,000 in 2027.The ripples will be felt far beyond Peru’s borders. The country is by a long way the world’s most important exporter of fishmeal – a crucial input to aquaculture and livestock agriculture virtually everywhere – and prices are skyrocketing as a result. This anchoveta closure will have a direct impact on jobs, food supplies and supermarket prices the world over. Peru’s then minister of production, César Quispe Luján, defended the decision as the only one possible: “The government has the responsibility to manage marine resources based on scientific criteria, timeliness and a long-term vision. When there is a need to strengthen conservation measures, it is necessary to act with prudence and responsibility to ensure the sustainability of the fishery.”When the June suspension was announced, the fishing boats had already been back in port for weeks. At the start of the season, in early April, Peru’s ministry of production had set a totalallowable catch of 1.9m tonnes. But in May, it closed the fishery for 15 days, with only 24% of the quota harvested. When the closure was extended to a full shutdown, there were even hints there would be no second fishing season this autumn. The main concern of the Instituto del Mar del Perú, which recommended the closure, was the risks already posed by this year’s El Niño, and a fear of what is to come.We are heading into what global climate models forecast as themost severe El Niñosince the 1880s, the earliest for which we have accurate records. The super El Niño that is developing “may end up the strongest by a truly mind-blowing margin,” said climatologistZeke Hausfather in July. Peru’s anchoveta population was already down before the suspension of fishing. We cannot know how the anchoveta would have fared in the absence of El Niño, but we know that its presence makes things considerably more volatile. The warmer waters produced by El Niño threaten the plankton on which anchoveta feed, which in turn threatens the anchoveta population.The oceans, which cover 71% of the Earth’s surface, are among the most gloriously alive parts of the Earth. While there are vast oceanic deserts, there are also marine versions of the Amazon basin and the Okavango Delta. These rich zones are the result of a host of wonderful contingencies: the shape of the continents, the force of gravity, the chemistry of the ocean and the crazy network of ocean currents.Most years, the Humboldt current, which flows north along the west coast of Chile and Peru, produces the most fertile fishing grounds on Earth. The current generates massive upwellings of deep colder waters that bring nutrients up from the depths, creating some of the most biologically productive zones in the ocean. This extraordinary biological abundance astounded the first Europeans who witnessed it. Islands piled tens of metres deep with the guano of innumerable birds feeding on sea life; the ocean boiling with million-tonne anchovy and sardine shoals; tuna, bonito and mackerel virtually leaping from the water. By comparison, today’s Humboldt current system is much impoverished – industrialised extraction has taken its toll – but even so, it remains exceptionally productive. Intensive commercial fishing continues, and the most intensive of all is for Peruvian anchoveta, 6in (15cm) flashes of big-eyed, blue-backed silver.In an average year, Peru produces 20% of the world’s fishmeal. But that word “average” obscures the extraordinary volatility of the anchoveta catch in the decades since the fishery was fully commercialised after the second world war. In 1970, Peru landed more than 12m tonnes of anchoveta. In 1973, the catch fell by 88%. The shock of this stock collapse was so existential for Peru that the military dictatorship introduced the first regulatory regime for the anchoveta fishery. In 1984, the catch plummeted again, to less than 100,000 tonnes, a fraction of what it had been 15 years earlier. The catch recovered in 2000 to about 9.6m tonnes, but has declined since then. Recent annual catches have been in the 2m-4m tonne range.Overfishing has played a crucial role in this ecological and economic rollercoaster ride. But the crazy seesaw of the anchoveta fishery is not merely a tale of rapacious industrial extraction, but of how overfishing combines with the bouts of accelerated oceanic warming driven by El Niño, which always hit Peruvian coastal waters especially hard.El Niño (“the little boy”) is the name that fishermen four centuries ago gave periods of unusually warm water off the coast of western South America. It is so named because the episodes usually reach their peak towards Christmas.Like most oceanic and atmospheric dynamics, both El Niño and the anchoveta fishery are partly born of the fact that the Earth is a spinning ball, turning upon an axis that runs through the middle of the planet from pole to pole. Since the ball is rotating at a fixed rate, different latitudes on its surface spin at different speeds: in the span of one Earth day, places near the equator have a lot more distance to cover to get all the way around than places near the poles, so they rotate faster. Vancouver, the city where I live, is moving around Earth’s axis at 1,100km an hour. If you are reading this in London, you are a little bit closer to the north pole, so spinning a little slower (1,042km/h), but if you are in Jakarta, near the equator, you are whirling about at 1,665km/h. Had someone granted Patsy Cline her wish to Stop the World and Let Me Off, she would have shot out of Nashville at 1,350km/h.View image in fullscreenAn anchovy fishing boat off the coast of Lima.Photograph: Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty ImagesIf everything on the Earth’s surface just stayed where it was relative to everything else, things might be fairly straightforward, but that is not how it works. While the terrestrial parts of the Earth spin at a constant rate and in the same direction, the parts of it that are fluid – its molten core, the atmosphere and the oceans – can move at different speeds and in different directions. Often, from our perspective on the surface, it seems as though the fluid parts are somehow moving against the direction of spin. The easterly trade winds of the tropics, for example, which have carried ships across the oceans for as long as we have sailed the seas, are the result of atmospheric patterns shaped by the planet’s eastward rotation, and the higher rotational speeds around the equator. From one perspective, you might even say these “winds” are something of an illusion: it’s not the air that’s blowing past us, but we who are racing through the slower moving air.Among the most fundamental fluid dynamics resulting from the Earth’s spin are the patterns of circulation of the oceans. These include the planet’s five massive oceanic gyres: two each (north and south of the equator) in the Atlantic and Pacific, and one in the Indian Ocean. These gyres are great circular systems of currents that span each ocean from coast to coast and from the poles almost all the way to the equator, and they too are partly created by the Earth’s roundness and rotation.The gyres in both hemispheres are like vast oceanic gears spinning in opposite directions: the northern gyres rotate clockwise, while the southern gyres turn anticlockwise. In the Atlantic and Pacific, they meet at the equator, driving wind and water westwards. Along the eastern side of all these gigantic rotating marine gears, cold waters are moving from the poles toward the equator: the Humboldt current is the South Pacific’s version of this process. As these currents push up against the oceans’ eastern coastlines they are driven towards the surface, bringing nutrient-rich cold water to the pelagic zone. In non-El Niño or “neutral” years, the Humboldt current runs all the way up to the seas off northern Peru, where the anchoveta and everything else feast.During El Niño events, the trade winds weaken and atmospheric pressure builds up over the coasts of Asia. As a result, the higher-temperature water spreads eastwards. With milder El Niño events, it reaches into the central Pacific, south of Hawaii, but in stronger phases it piles up off equatorial South America. Warmer water, much less hospitable to anchoveta, is driven south along the coast into the Humboldt current system, sometimes as far as Lima, Peru, 12 degrees south of the equator. There it sits at the surface, pushing the colder water into the depths and severely limiting the upwelling flows that bring nutrients to the upper layers of the ocean.For the anchoveta and everything above it in the food web, the result is a disaster. The warm surface waters have the devastating double effect of shrinking the area of the ocean in which the anchoveta find suitable habitat, and robbing them of their main food source, the plankton that depend on the nutrients carried by upwelling. Anchoveta populations shrink, sometimes dramatically; birds starve, predators higher up the food chain that rely on anchoveta scatter  or die; and there are a lot fewer fish for the fishing fleet to catch.Every massive crash in the anchoveta fishery is the consequence of a severe El Niño event hitting already intensely exploited stocks. The climate crisis increases ocean temperatures and acidification, all of which is bad for most marine life, anchoveta included, and further exacerbates the situation by intensifying El Niño.In its latest report on the state of the world’s marine fisheries in 2025, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization deemedmore than a third to be overfished, meaning harvests exceed the rate of reproduction. Though the report classifies most of the anchoveta stocks in Peru as “maximally sustainably fished”, it is worth remembering that calling a fishery sustainable does not take account of the fact that populations are at historically low levels – and, since the onset of industrial fishing, are more vulnerable than ever before.As with many other shrinking natural resources, what brought us to this point is a combination of increasingly efficient technology and too little regulation for too long. In the case of anchoveta, as regulation has increased, so too has fishing technology adapted itself to the behaviour of the fish. The anchoveta disperse at night to feed, but during the day, when predators like tuna can easily see them, they form large shoals or “schools”. Schooling, when vast numbers of fish mass together in a huge ball, evolved as a strategy to minimise predation. Schooling protects the bulk of the shoal by sacrificing those unlucky enough to end up on the outside edges.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian GraphicsThe problem, at least from an anchoveta’s perspective, is that this behaviour evolved before they ran into humans and our modern fishing gear. From the deck of a fishing boat, a school is an enormous swarm of fish conveniently clustered in a tight space near the sea’s surface. Huge fishing vessels can pull anchoveta from the water in enormous volumes. When a boat finds a shoal, it circles the fish while dropping a long float line from its stern. From the float line, which can be as much as 600 metres long, hangs a 50-metre net. Once the net is set in a ring around the shoal, a cable at the bottom edge is pulled tight, and the lower reaches of the net close like the mouth of a drawstring purse, capturing the shoal in what is now a massive mesh bag full of fish. The boats have enormous holds, some as large as 800 cubic metres (equivalent to about 12 40ft-long shipping containers), and can bring millions of anchoveta to port for processing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long ReadLose yourself in a great story: from politics to psychology, food to technology, culture to crimeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSchooling behaviour presents a challenge to scientists monitoring fish populations, because it means anchoveta are not evenly dispersed across their habitat, but massed together in great fish balls. We might catch a lot of them, but we can’t assume there are a lot more fish out there.A further cause for alarm, and not just for commercial fisheries, is that in the web of predatory relationships, anchoveta are a crucial link between plankton and larger animals: the anchoveta feed on plankton, their population flourishes, which provides food for scores of predator species higher up the food chain, including humans. When anchoveta numbers plummet, it is a potential catastrophe for the whole ecosystem and those who depend on it. When this happened to the Black Sea anchovy late in the 20th century, phytoplankton populations exploded, depleting oxygen levels in the water and threatening an already fragile marine ecosystem, and the other commercial fisheries that depended on it.The anchoveta matter in all these economic and ecological ways, but they also epitomise a widespread problem in our extractive age: in ecosystems around the world, we are pushing species into conditions of such fragility that we are no longer in control of the situation. Even if we slow or even stop destroying habitat or harvesting, things are now so precarious that “natural” environmental variability could tip them over the edge.Anchoveta have proven resilient in the face of remarkable levels of environmental variation, from extreme El Niño events to the frenzied overfishing of decades past, but the prognosis isn’t good: research suggests that ocean warming and its effects will lead to a decrease in the amount of anchoveta in the ocean of between 8% and 14% per decade across the 21st century. As sea surface temperatures rise, and salinity and oxygen levels change, the anchoveta’s territorial range shifts, as does the stock’s fertility, spawning seasons and the distribution of the population across different life stages (a crucial consideration in fisheries, because it is imperative to avoid catching fish that are too young to reproduce). All of this is unfolding against the background of ongoing climate heating at a planetary scale, to which El Niño introduces additional and increasing stresses.This year’s closure of the anchoveta fishery before the quota was reached came as a surprise to some in the industry, but it is not the first time it has happened. Just last year, Peru set the first season quota at 3m tonnes, but when scientists noted the juvenile population – the younger fish yet to reach reproductive age – was especially at risk, the government called the fleet off the water with just 2.5m tonnes landed. “The sustainable extraction of anchovy is a strategic priority for the country,” Jesús Barrientos, the vice minister of fisheries and aquaculture, said at the time.The anchoveta harvest limit is usually binding: the fleet generally catches its allowance, or very near to it, by the time the season closes. Getting so close to the limit may seem like a bad thing, but it is taken as an indicator of success. A lot of what we know about fish populations is based on industry data about where, when and how many fish are captured, and how old those fish are. However, illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing are estimated to be as large as a fifth of the legal commercial harvest worldwide. For that very reason, the Peruvian government polices all commercial fisheries very tightly: in 2024 alone it undertook 163,000 inspections, and confiscated 1,000 tonnes of illegally harvested anchoveta.View image in fullscreenCrates of anchoveta being unloaded from a fishing boat at the port of El Callao, Peru.Photograph: Rodrigo Abd/APIf all these efforts work out as planned, then when a fishery hits the quota in a fishing season, it means (at least in theory) that the industry is accurately reporting their operations, the stock assessment was more or less correct, and the regulators and inspectors are doing their jobs. The alternative – a quota that is never reached – might at first glance seem better, but would be very bad news if the whole fleet was out there and couldn’t find enough fish to meet the allowance. This has happened before, most famously during what fisheries expert Dean Bavington calls the “managed annihilation” of Atlantic cod. For centuries, cod had made Newfoundland’s Grand Banks one of the planet’s most productive fisheries. By the time thefishery collapsed completelyin the early 1990s, the absurdly high quota didn’t matter because the boats couldn’t find anywhere near enough fish to meet it. The oceans had been emptied; the cod were gone.In contrast to Newfoundland, Peru’s fisheries managers decided to protect the anchoveta population, despite pressure from an industry that has a lot of sway with the government and is increasingly concentrated in the hands of massive corporations, foreign and domestic. (In November 2024, the Canadian conglomerate Cooke Incorporated paid $1bn for Copeinca, the largest anchoveta firm in Peru. Cooke now controls a sixth of Peru’s anchoveta fishery, and a fifth of its meal and oil processing.) Corporate power like that doesn’t take massive revenue losses lying down. When the government delayed the start of the fishing season in 2023, the CEO of an anchoveta conglomerate moaned that regulators were “lost in a sea of ignorance”, creating an existential crisis for an industry that was “fighting to survive”. At that point, the ministry budged a little, and temporarily reopened the fishery. This year, it held firm: “Sustainability takes precedence over any short-term decision,” Juan Carlos Requejo, the minister of production, said in mid-August.The stakes are enormous. Peru’s fisheries sector contracted by almost 75% in June and July, and fishmeal production is plummeting just as prices have skyrocketed to almost $3,500 a tonne, more than twice what they were at the same time last year. The same is true of all the fisheries for high-value species that prey on anchoveta: the bonito, jack mackerel and the rest of the bigger torpedo-shaped beauties that bring in premium prices.The privatisation of the Peruvian anchoveta fishery began in 1992 and culminated in the introduction of a vessel quota system under the guidance of the World Bank in 2009. The creation of private property rights in the fishery has had complex repercussions, not least the increasing marginalisation and impoverishment of tens of thousands of smaller-scale fishers and their communities. Almost all the anchoveta catch is controlled by a collection of wealthy boat owners and big firms with close ties to the state.Monitoring is continuous, sophisticated and data-driven. The idea is to operate a sensitive, real-time regulatory regime based on the assumption that there is no longer any such thing as “normal” – and there isn’t. Every day of the anchoveta season, Peru’s ministry of production pays close attention to scientists’ advice and is ready to step in, not just to end the season altogether but to make tweaks on the fly, for example ordering temporary closures of local fishing zones.In August, the ministry declared a national fisheries and aquaculture emergency, which included launching a marine survey,Operation Eureka LXXVIII, to undertake an intensive stock assessment coordinated with the largest vessel owners. The outcome has not yet been officially announced, but in early October, Diario de Chimbote, the newspaper of Peru’s main fishing port (one of the largest in the world), reported that 2026’s second season will be cancelled entirely: the water is too warm, forcing the anchoveta in deeper and closer to shore, and the risks to juveniles are too great. Though this decision has not been confirmed, if it goes ahead, the closure is expected to cost Peru’s economy about $1.4bn. As Jessica Luna, president of Peru’s National Fisheries Society, an industry organisation, put it, the sector is “in the ICU”.Prior to these most recent calamities, many industry observers have noted that by some measures, Peru’s management of fish populations is a remarkable success story, all the more impressive in light of the way that multinational capital often gets what it wants in similar situations. In the past 20 years, the see-sawing catch numbers that plagued the industry for so long have declined considerably. But so too have average harvests, and the trend is decidedly downward. In the midst of what has been called a “Godzilla” El Niño, it is worth reconsidering what counts as success in a world in which crisis has become normal. Is the goal just a slightly slower road to the same destination?So far, despite everything, the anchoveta keep coming back, albeit in drastically diminished numbers compared with a few decades ago. It does sometimes seem as though they can survive whatever we throw at them, and their persistence can easily be mistaken for indestructibility. But there are limits to the robustness of any species or natural system. The fact that we don’t know where those limits are doesn’t mean they aren’t there, and as we push the anchoveta, and so much of the planet, we inevitably press upon fragilities we never knew were there, sometimes because until very recently they probably weren’t. Many of our leaders would have us believe that we can continue as before, but we have never been here before, and we need to proceed with modesty and care. Often, you only recognise a threshold once you have crossed it.Listen to our podcastshereand sign up to the long read weekly emailhere.Explore more on these topicsThe long readEl Niño southern oscillationFishingMarine lifePerufeaturesShareReuse this content

title: It’s not the old two-party politics – but Labour and the Tories now know they can shun their populist challengers | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: Though Burnham and Badenoch may still need the votes of Green and Reform supporters, both leaders have drawn clear lines in the sand, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: Though Burnham and Badenoch may still need the votes of Green and Reform supporters, both leaders have drawn clear lines in the sand, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianOpinionAndy BurnhamIt’s not the old two-party politics – but Labour and the Tories now know they can shun their populist challengersGaby HinsliffThough Burnham and Badenoch may still need the votes of Green and Reform supporters, both leaders have drawn clear lines in the sandThu 15 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTShareAsk a straight question, get a straight answer. It’s how politics is supposed to work but almost never does, which is why on the rare occasions it happens the result can be faintly chaotic. What did Andy Burnham mean when he said – in response to a question from the Tory MP Harriett Baldwin – thatLabour couldn’t partner with the Green partywhile it remains wedded to the “Zionism is racism” motion its members have just endorsed? Were Green MPs now barred from a future coalition government? If so, what about councils where they are currently sharing power with Labour?Though Burnham was only confirming what ministers have been arguing privately for days, at first nobody seemed to know: tellingly, it took almost 24 hours for theLabourparty chair, Bridget Phillipson, to confirm that unless local Green groups disowned that idea sharpish, “Labour will bring any such local arrangement to an end”. So much for cuddly cross-party Andy, who always seemed so relaxed about rainbow coalitions. Now elected Greens in places such as Sheffield or Lewes must choose between power and members’ wrath, a useful rehearsal for what a hung parliament might feel like.Westminster is increasingly realising that while nobody knows quite what’s in Burnham’s head except Burnham, unlike most prime ministers he is surprisingly liable just to tell you. He did it earlier this week on a podcast, pointing out thatRussia tried to interfere in the Brexit vote(which is true, albeit the sort of truth that for complicated reasons prime ministers don’t generally dwell on). Now the safety catch is off again.What did he mean with his comments about Labour and the Greens? Most likely just what he said: that the Greens crossed a line and it cannot be overlooked, especially by a party still recovering from its own battle with antisemitism. Green members did not just vote to adopt a policy that would condemn every Jew who believes in the right to a Jewish homeland, including those who simultaneously support the creation of a Palestinian state. The motion they backedadvocates turning all of historic Palestine into a Palestinian state, a one-state solutionwiping Israel off the map.Much as Kemi Badenoch did recently by insisting that herEnglish-born children have every right to be considered English,no matter what the ethno-nationalists of Reform and Restore say,Burnham was simply showing that he has limits: this far, and no further.Something has shaken loose over the party conference season. What we are seeing isn’t the return of two-party politics – things are still too volatile for that – but the return of leaders confident enough to set boundaries on what had become an almost abusive relationship with the public. They are no longer quite so terrified of naming extremism when they see it. More surprisingly, neither is behaving like a party needing to beg for coalition partners, whatever the electoral maths says.Andy Burnham says Russia interfered in Brexit referendum – videoAfter a period shadow boxing a prime minister who never seemed to know what he thought, Badenoch now faces one who does. That has brought drama back to the middle of politics and not just the radical edges, with genuine differences emerging between Labour and the Tories ahead of the budget over tax and spend, national security v social security, public v private ownership and the respective claims of younger and older people.Her new strategy is not a million miles from the one outlined this week by thethinktank Bright Blue,in a paper on how the traditional European right can combat far-right populism: adopt draconian immigration policies but make the economy the actual focus of your campaign, and hold the line that citizenship can be earned rather than being determined by ethnicity (the chilling line peddled by some of those in Reform and Restore who argue openly that you have to be white to be properly English).Though the polls still suggest the Tories can’t win without some kind of deal with Reform, the broad message of aconference speechin which Badenoch painted her rivals as aggressive weirdos who “threaten journalists, call veterans traitors and debate whether my mixed-race children are English” was that it would be a cold day in hell before that happened. That decision looks smarter with every passing journalistic exposé involving the kind of Reform councillor whothinks King Charles should be decapitatedfor supposedly being a secret Muslim.Burnham didn’t go quite so studs-up on the Greens, but then he doesn’t need to. The party is alreadyopenly agonisingabout that anti-Zionism motion, opposed byfour out of fiveof its elected MPs. The prospect of being politically ostracised for it may now strengthen the hand of Greens who think this freakishly hot summer might have been better spent campaigning on the climate crisis, not swervingquestions about Israel’s right to exist. Yet there are risks for Burnham here, all the same.Research by the pollster More in Common suggests that “progressive activists”, the group most commonly torn between voting Green or Labour, are significantly more likely than the average British voter to think worse of someone identifying as a Zionist. When Burnham called the Green motion antisemitic and wrong, he was confronting people whose support he may need in some Labour seats.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis civil war on the British right is a charade – its politics are more united than ever | Jonathan LiewRead moreSanctioning West Bank settlements, as this government has now done, isn’t enough for some of them: they want Burnham explicitly tocall the Gaza war a genocideand stop proscribingPalestine Actionas a terrorist organisation.(Polanski was notably quick toleap to the defence ofthe Irish novelist Sally Rooney, after it emergedher books arebeing withdrawn from salein Britainbecause of her promise to donate royalties to Palestine Action: knowing where the money could be going leaves her publishers open to potential prosecution under anti-terrorism law, just for handing over her earnings.)It’s technically possible that like some desiccated calculating machine, Burnham has crunched the numbers on all this and concluded that distancing himself from a row that has reportedly madeone in three British voters less likely to vote Green(according to Opinium) is mathematically preferable.But it’s more likely he was just doing the thing that got him here in the first place, and following his gut. If he can’t say what he thinks even now, in what passes for a honeymoon period, he never will. If basic norms are not enforced, they very quickly cease being norms. And if the Labour party can only win by sidling uncomfortably close to the kind of people it was until recently expelling for antisemitism – well, it’s not much of a Labour party. The chaos, in that sense, is probably just beginning.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
