title: Sally Rooney’s stand on Palestine is brave and humane  | Sally Rooney | The Guardian
description: The Normal People author’s determination to support Palestine Action, even if it means that her books are withdrawn from sale in the UK makes a mockery of Britain’s terrorism laws
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The Normal People author’s determination to support Palestine Action, even if it means that her books are withdrawn from sale in the UK makes a mockery of Britain’s terrorism laws
Content: Sally Rooney … chose the thorniest possible path for this cause.Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSally Rooney … chose the thorniest possible path for this cause.Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The GuardianSally RooneySally Rooney’s stand on Palestine is brave and humaneZoe WilliamsThe Normal People author’s determination to support Palestine Action, even if it means that her books are withdrawn from sale in the UK, makes a mockery of Britain’s terrorism lawsThu 15 Oct 2026 06.56 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.34 EDTShareIt’s hard to think of a published author in living memory who risked arrest in the UK for their political beliefs, hard to think of one whose books could be published anywhere but here. Sally Rooney went into this debacle with her eyes open: she said last July that royalties from her books, and their BBC adaptations, would be used to supportPalestine Action.Rooney’s courage is not so much in risking imprisonment, since there is a fix for that, which is what she’s doing – avoiding the UK. Rather, she has chosen the thorniest possible path for this cause. Authors can write essays and sign letters in support of the Palestinian people; actors can voice it in interviews, musicians can say it from the stage, and there is always a cost to it, whether it’s in plain sight and they’ve been kicked off a global tour, or it’s behind closed doors and they are simply excluded from opportunities. But such actions, even if they logically suggest support for a proscribed organisation, don’t entail actively breaking the terrorism laws. Rooney had taken a financial hit anyway, by pledging support for Palestine Action with her royalties; but that’s a price at least you can count. The lost sales and opportunities that ripple out from being effectively both barred from and banned in the UK are innumerable.double quotation markRooney has never been an apolitical writer and now she has taken on the idea that caring about Gaza is somehow a crank’s life choiceYet, speaking as not-her-accountant, but as someone living in the culture she also inhabits and has made such an impact describing, the value of her stand is similarly hard to put a price on. Her authorial voice and body of work makes this intervention distinctive in its reach. She’s never been an apolitical author.Normal Peoplewas razor sharp on class,Conversations With Friendswasn’t shy of a Marxist analysis. But the work is also intimate, often domestic, I mean, the clue’s in the name – these were always normal people. It was from a reputation of delicately challenging but everyday subtlety that Rooney assumed her outrider position, and in so doing, took on the idea that caring about Gaza is somehow a crank’s life choice; insisted that it is a human response, as natural and quotidian, as passionate and important, as friendship.It also, come on – surely at some point we’re allowed to say this – makes an absolute mockery of the terrorism legislation thus applied. Nobody anywhere thinks Sally Rooney poses a danger to the British state, or any state, just as nobody anywhere thinksa 94-year-old human rights barristerwho was a friend of Ed Miliband’s late mother does. Keir Starmer, paradoxically, given that the two things in his favour were his caution and his legal hinterland, painted himself into an absurd corner, whereterrorism arrests went up between 2024 and 2025 from 250 to nearly 3,000. On demos where anyone crunched the numbers,more of them were over 80 than under 20.Sally Rooney says she can no longer sell books in UK due to Palestine Action supportRead moreThe history and particularity ofIrish solidarity with the Palestinian cause have been discussed a lot since the painful Ed Sheeran tour, in which the singer thought a support act could be quietly ditched over a pro-Palestine song,without losing his backing band – Beoga, founder members of Irish Artists for Palestine. More broadly, Ireland has a vibrant tradition of young women with no reason to think they have the right to opine on geopolitics sticking their oar in anyway.The Dunnes Stores strike of 1984kicked off when 21-year-old Mary Manning refused to handle some South African grapefruit, leading to her receiving only £21 a week in strike pay for two years and nine months. It reached its political crescendo less than three years later, when Ireland banned South African goods altogether in protest at apartheid. In between, though, in 1985, Desmond Tutu met Manning and her fellow strikers on his way to get the Nobel peace prize, extending as he did an invitation to visit him in South Africa – which they took him up on, only to be turned away at the border. There’s an instant echo, here, of a state showing its might at customs only to draw attention to its weakness; and of an author who, as well as that, is an ordinary citizen, whose forgone royalties are almost the least of the sacrifice, but are still a powerful emblem.This article was amended on 15 October 2026. An earlier version said that the Dunnes Stores strike of 1984 “cost [Mary Manning] £21 a week”. In fact, this was her weekly strike pay for the two years and nine months of industrial action.Explore more on these topicsSally RooneyProtestPalestine ActionActivismUK security and counter-terrorismPalestineMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: The water torture goes on at Thames. Sector-wide reform isn’t moving much faster | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: If ‘public control’ bit is delaying overhaul, that needs to be nailed down sharpish or continued uncertainty could be costly
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: If ‘public control’ bit is delaying overhaul, that needs to be nailed down sharpish or continued uncertainty could be costly
Content: A person wears an Andy Burnham face mask during a protest against Thames Water outside the Labour party conference last month.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenA person wears an Andy Burnham face mask during a protest against Thames Water outside the Labour party conference last month.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PANils Pratley on financeThames WaterThe water torture goes on at Thames. Sector-wide reform isn’t moving much fasterNils PratleyIf ‘public control’ bit is delaying overhaul, that needs to be nailed down sharpish or continued uncertainty could be costlyThu 15 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 14.02 EDTShareIt is strange now to recall that Thames Water had a prominent slot on what was known as“Sue’s shit list”– the internal Labour dossier, compiled by Keir Starmer’s first chief of staff, Sue Gray, of potential crises that could erupt at short notice and force the incoming administration to make some big decisions quickly.That was July 2024. Here we are – more than two years later – and the Thames script has barely advanced. We’re still waiting to see if the financial crisis at the over-indebted, under-performing water company will be resolved by a creditor-led recapitalisation, special administration or something else.Now Thames isseeking another £2.4bn slug of funding from creditorsto stay afloat for another year and survive yet more back and forth between ministers, regulators and those same lenders. The new mystery element in the talks is what the prime minister, Andy Burnham, actually means by “greater public control”.Still, Thames was an outlier – albeit a biggie – one might say. At least the government in 2024 cracked on with the job of deciding how to overhaul the wider water sector in England and Wales. Indeed it did: Sir Jon Cunliffe, a former deputy governor of the Bank of England, was commissioned to review what was needed andhis detailed reportlanded in summer last year. The centrepiece was the abolition of Ofwat, the regulator.Steve Reed, the environment secretary at the time, embraced Cunliffe’s proposals anddeclared the “the biggest overhaul of water regulation in a generation”via a new water bill. Game on?Not exactly. The bill, which should have arrived this autumn, was delayed by the change of PM. Burnham has promised a “strengthened” version, which presumably will include the “public control” elements. In the meantime, Ofwat is still in place, and nobody knows which bits of the Environment Agency will be absorbed into the new super-regulator, or what the new body’s formal status will be. Will it, for example, be as formally independent as Ofwat, or will it be under a tighter ministerial leash?Credit rating agencies have noticed the uncertainty. In dry language, Moody’s on Thursday issued a report noting that regulatory changes “appears to have stalled”, that “political scrutiny is heightened and may cause further delay” and the “potential increase in business risk will require stronger financial ratios to maintain credit quality”.Moody’s, note, did not downgrade its assessment of the “stability and predictability” of UK water regulation, as it did in late-2024. But it did tiptoe up to the line: one of its slides at Thursday’s conference warned: “Our score could fall further.” Why does Moody’s opinion matter? Simply because rating agencies influence the price at which companies can borrow, which can itself affect the financing costs passed on to customers in bills.The government should take the hint and decide what it actually wants from water reform. Emma Hardy, the water minister, at least indicated to the same conference that a formal transition plan to the regulator is coming soon. But that’s not the same as an actual water bill, which would reveal if the rest of the Cunliffe changes have survived.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is, of course, entirely fair for an incoming PM to review what he wants from a bill. But the “public control” bit, if that’s delaying everything, needs to be nailed down sharpish. Is it simply the Cunliffe-compliant idea of greater powers of influence for mayors and local authorities? Or bigger changes to match the summer rhetoric? It’s impossible to tell – but it’s all taking far too long.And make a decision one way or another on Thames. Half a parliament to address a supposedly urgent 2024 problem is extreme water torture.Explore more on these topicsThames WaterNils Pratley on financeWater industryUtilitiesNationalisationcommentShareReuse this content

title: How Gaza changed Europe, exposing cracks that grow bigger by the week | Shada Islam | The Guardian
description: Solidarity with Palestine’s suffering is punished but MEPs allow a witch-hunt of European Muslims, says Brussels-based commentator Shada Islam
Author: Shada Islam
Headline: Solidarity with Palestine’s suffering is punished but MEPs allow a witch-hunt of European Muslims, says Brussels-based commentator Shada Islam
Content: Large crowds gathered in Amsterdam on 11 October 2026, calling for an end to violence against Palestinians.Photograph: Mouneb Taim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLarge crowds gathered in Amsterdam on 11 October 2026, calling for an end to violence against Palestinians.Photograph: Mouneb Taim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionGazaHow Gaza changed Europe, exposing cracks that grow bigger by the weekShada IslamSolidarity with Palestine’s suffering is punished but MEPs allow a witch-hunt of European MuslimsThu 15 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 00.01 EDTShareFor three painful years, Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, in retaliation for the Hamas terror attacks on 7 October 2023, haskilled more than 74,000 Palestinians, wounded thousands more and reduced most of the territory to rubble. It has changed views of Israelacross the world, increased support for Palestine andraised questionsabout US power.Europe’s failure to hold Israel’s government to account has cost itglobal credibilityand influence. But I fear something even more consequential than that: Gaza is changing Europe itself.European governments did nothing to try to stop the genocide; there have beenno collective sanctions, no trade restrictions or ending of arms sales to Israel. The EU sanctions Russia over its war in Ukraine but retains almost-business-as-usual ties with Israel, a blatant double standard.Gaza has exposed how Europe’s supposedly universal commitment to human rights is now conditional onwhose suffering is recognised, whose resistance is considered legitimate and whose demands for justice are considered worthy of attention. EU policymakers are selective even in thegroups of women they choose to celebrateas heroic in struggles against occupation and the children whose right to life they defend.After these three years I am convinced that the question of Palestine has become a stress test for European democracy itself. Democratic societies can only thrive when there is space for dissent, including dissent that is uncomfortable, disruptive and politically inconvenient. Yet today, across Europe, governments – which speak up against undemocratic conduct abroad – are now unapologetic in imposing restrictions on free expression and peaceful protest at home.Police violence at pro-Palestinian demonstrationshas become the norm, and those whose only crime is to speak up publicly for Palestinian rights areincreasingly criminalisedor made the target of suspicion.When this happens repeatedly it undermines public trust in the legitimacy of democratic governments and institutions. As Rabin Baldewsingh, the Netherlands’ national coordinator against discrimination and racism tells me: “Governments and public institutions have a responsibility not to reinforce polarisation when society is deeply divided.” Sadly, the opposite appears to be happening.Many societal fractures existed before Gaza, but they have received new oxygen and traction over the past three years. The EU’s Fundamental Rights Agency has long warned of bothanti-Muslim racismandantisemitism. What has become increasingly troubling over the past three years is the political framing under which antisemitism inconnection with Gaza is rightly treated as a threat to democracy, while Islamophobia is viewed through a security and anti-terrorism lens.This can’t all be blamed on the far right, either. True, some extremist groups hide their age-old prejudices behind accusations that it is Muslims and refugees who have “imported” antisemitism into Europe. But the European People’s party (EPP) – the EU’s largest political “family” for pro-European centre-right and conservative politicians, includingUrsula von der Leyenand Magnus Brunner, the EU’s most senior official for migration – is also giving old and debunked Islamophobic tropes a new and dangerous lease of life.The partybacked a resolutionin June condemning the “interference of political Islam” in European democratic processes. If “political Islam” was interfering in European democracy, the resolution may have some validity. But there is no evidence for the claim, and certainly none advanced in this document, which merely echoes French conspiracy theories about “Islamist entryism” and calls for a crackdown on alleged members ofMuslim Brotherhoodnetworks. It claims to make a distinction between “political Islam” and the Islamic faith itself but it reads more like the start of a witch-hunt of European Muslims.An even tougher EPP resolution, backed by amajority in the European parliamenton 8 October, goes a step further by casting suspicion on Muslim civil society groups’ loyalty, activity and participation in European democracy.Hiba Latreche, president ofFemyso, a pan-European network of young Muslim organisations that is explicitly mentioned in the EPP’s attack, points out the double bind of such unfounded allegations. “When we are not active we are accused of communitarianism, separatism and lack of integration. When we engage and exercise active citizenship we are accused of having a hidden agenda.”Such an environment demands even stronger anti-discrimination action. Yet Europe’s most powerful pro-equality body, theEuropean Network Against Racism(ENAR), has just lost European Commission funding. Worried that this could mean it has tocease operationsby the end of the year, ENAR has launched a legal challenge against the decision at the EU’s general court.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBeyond the visible, there are many unwritten post-Gaza codes being applied inside the EU’s corridors of power that are harder to measure and challenge. Islamophobia has become “quite blatant”, EU officials tell me, with micro‑aggressions and remarks about Muslims’ supposedly “irrational and emotional” behaviour. Likevon der Leyenin her recent “state of the union” speech,many now talk about Gaza as a humanitarian emergency, but not as a human-made genocide. There is agreement on the need for action againstsettler violenceand illegal settlement in the West Bank, which is framed as the work of “extremists”, but confronting the Israeli government remains difficult.For many, it has also been a time of uncomfortable conversations, ruptured personal relationships and disillusionment. But there are also moments of intense solidarity, as across Europe pro‑Palestinian movements have extended to include trade unions, faith groups – including Jewish activists – students, celebrities and senior politicians. Every Thursday, members of theEU Staff for Peacegather for a vigil outside the commission and the EU Council. Former EU commissioners, ambassadors and senior staff continue towrite to their bossesurging stronger action against Israel.So all hope is not lost. But Gaza has stripped away a great deal of self-soothing assumptions that many of us harboured aboutEurope. As the far right becomes more influential, too many have forgotten that democratic freedoms rarely disappear all at once. They begin to erode when some voices are silenced, some suffering is ignored and the rights of some citizens are treated as less deserving than others.Shada Islam is a Brussels-based commentator on EU affairs. She runs New Horizons project, a strategy, analysis and advisory companyDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Can Lena Dunham’s new Girls do for 40-year-olds what she did for 23-year-olds? I know it can | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: I was in my early 20s when the classic series debuted and I recognised so much in it. I can’t wait to see how the reboot takes on a new stage of life, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: I was in my early 20s when the classic series debuted and I recognised so much in it. I can’t wait to see how the reboot takes on a new stage of life, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Content: Shoshanna, Hannah, Marnie and Jessa in the original Girls.Photograph: Mark Schafer/HBOView image in fullscreenShoshanna, Hannah, Marnie and Jessa in the original Girls.Photograph: Mark Schafer/HBOOpinionGirlsCan Lena Dunham’s new Girls do for 40-year-olds what she did for 23-year-olds? I know it canRhiannon Lucy CosslettI was in my early 20s when the classic series debuted and I recognised so much. I can’t wait to see how the reboot takes on a new – equally messy – stage of lifeThu 15 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.10 EDTShareHBO’s Girls is coming back,Lena Dunhamand her fellow cast members announced this week, and the internet is already abuzz. Women of a certain age, myself included – approaching, turning or having turned 40 – are genuinely thrilled, if also slightly trepidatious. When you’ve loved, loathed and most importantly grown with characters in the way many of us did with Girls, you feel protective of a show’s legacy. But with Dunham, I’m confident it is in good hands.Girls means a lot to me, in part because it was the topic ofmy first ever column for this newspaper: in 2012, shortly after the show premiered, it was already generating a bananas amount of internet discourse and I was on work experience. I was in my early 20s and not long off the dole. I didn’t share the privilege of Dunham’s characters, which is perhaps why I so enjoyed how she skewered it. (I never understood the criticism that the show was about spoilt rich girls. So many people missed the satire.) Yet there were aspects of it that I related to, as I wrote at the time:“The experiences of Dunham’s characters, where they languish in unpaid jobs and have emotionless, awkward sex in grotty flats with pretentious males, resonate … with my experience and that of my friends.”It’s not the finest piece of journalism I’ve ever produced (and my God, I would never make reference to my sex life in print these days), but I feel as though history has vindicated me. The series has aged spectacularly well, and in the past few years has been discovered and appreciated anew by younger women. There are popular rewatch podcasts; it’s been big on TikTok. Without all the surrounding noise that constituted 2010s Twitterstorm hell, the quality of the writing, direction and acting has been allowed to speak for itself.What will Hannah, Jessa, Marnie and Shoshanna’s lives look like now they are more women than girls? When we left them, Hannah had just had a baby who would now be approaching tweenagehood. Will she have made it as “the voice of her generation”? Shoshanna had cut them all out of her life (in a prescient nod to the cult of going “no contact”) and was engaged to a man called Byron: will she be back in touch? Marnie was already divorced – Dunham has jokingly imagined she’d be on her third divorce by now – and Jessa was single in New York. How will we meet them again? And most importantly: will Elijah have become a Broadway star, and will he still have the bitchiest lines?I can’t wait to find out because, as Dunham wrote in apost announcing the new series, there are so many ways to be 40: “You can live with roommates and get drunk every night, or you can be a parent of four keeping a bustling household in check. You can proudly sleep around, or be in perimenopause and never want to be touched again. I have friends who are in marriage crises but think they’re too old to move on, and still others switching careers for the ninth time.”View image in fullscreenLena Dunham attending the Metropolitan Museum of Art Gala in New York, 4 May 2026.Photograph: Matt Crossick/PAIt’s true. Of the women I know and love, our lives all look quite different – from each other’s, and also from what we imagined in our 20s. Some marriages are imploding while others are just getting started. Some have tiny babies, some have teenagers and some are child-free. The sandwich years of caring for both offspring and elderly parents are beginning for some, while others don’t yet have those responsibilities. Some own huge houses and others are still renting. Many of us are grappling with our careers – whether that’s realising our ambitions and being given more power, or struggling with the juggle and paying the motherhood penalty (sometimes all of these at once). There are affairs. Perhaps most poignantly, there are the dreams that were never realised – and now may never be. There are the people we have loved and lost.Dunham won’t be the first screenwriter to pay homage to this complicated stage of life, but she will be one of the first to be exactly of our generation, just as she was the first time around. It’s always cathartic to see art that speaks so directly to your experience, especially when it’s so, so funny.Reading that first column, I cringe a little at my younger, wide-eyed self, but mostly I think about just how lost I was, how unsure of what my future would look like. That article helped convince my then editors that my perspective was worth sharing, that readers were interested in writing by young women. It still feels like an absurd stroke of luck and I’ll always be grateful to Dunham for saving me from the traditional nine to five. To quote Jessa: “You know what the weirdest part about having a job is? You have to be there every day. Even on the days you don’t feel like it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWill this new, short run of episodes generate similar levels of controversy? I expect not. We have all grown up, examined the bruises left by those years and moved on.Girlsis widely accepted to be one of the finest, funniest works about female experience that has ever been made for television. Will Dunham do for perimenopause, divorce, fertility issues, care work and postpartum what she did then for abortion, HPV, one-night stands and unpaid internships? I have a feeling she will, and I can’t wait.Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Martínez has drawn back the curtain on Manchester United’s ruinous ownership | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Defender may not be blameless in team’s struggles but his criticism goes to the heart of what has gone wrong at the club
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: Defender may not be blameless in team’s struggles but his criticism goes to the heart of what has gone wrong at the club
Content: Lisandro Martínez has spoken frankly about the club’s ownership – perhaps more so than any other serving Manchester United player.Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenLisandro Martínez has spoken frankly about the club’s ownership – perhaps more so than any other serving Manchester United player.Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy Live News.Manchester UnitedMartínez has drawn back the curtain on Manchester United’s ruinous ownershipJonathan LiewDefender may not be blameless in team’s struggles but his criticism goes to the heart of what has gone wrong at the clubThu 15 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTShareHeartbreaking: the worst defender you know just made a great point. And no, nobody would describe Lisandro Martínez as the ideal person toscrutinise Manchester United’s indifferent start to the season, given that his high-profile defensive errors against Fulham and Tottenham are partly responsible for it. “We’re all trying to find the guy who did this,” Martínez burbles on Amazon Primeafter United’s 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madridon Tuesday night, dressed in a hot dog costume and throwing his arms out in mock innocence.For those with no interest in engaging with what Martínez actually had to say, this alone will be sufficient grounds to ignore him. Already you can sense the squeamishness of former players for whom the violation of an omertà is the real cardinal sin here, a phantom limb that still tingles years after they last stepped into a dressing room. “Disrespectful,” reckoned Wayne Rooney. “I don’t feel like he’s got the right,” agreed Ashley Young. “These things don’t end well, man,” Rio Ferdinand observed on his podcast.Jason Wilcox: ‘best eyes’ at Manchester United or promoted too far and too fast?Read moreBut traducing the messenger will always be easier than hearing the message, even if Martínez’s views arewidely shared within the United dressing room. If the fallout from the Manchester City legal case has demonstrated anything, it is English football’s ingrained reluctance to scrutinise the owners and executives whohold more influence over the sport than anybody else. Men in boots, not men in suits. Hey, watch the ball. It’s going to move!All the same, it’s worth parsing exactly what Martínez was complaining about, because it’s a good deal more complex than it may appear on first viewing. Player calls out board – andspecifically “technical director” Jason Wilcox– for failing to invest sufficiently in the squad over the summer. This was a summer in which United brought in three midfielders (Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans, Carlos Baleba), a reserve goalkeeper (Karl Darlow), nobody up front and nobody in defence. So far, so simple.But let’s begin to unpick the threads. Why did United not buy a defender in the summer, despite pursuing deals for Lewis Hall and Myles Lewis-Skelly? Because they were unable to sell a defender. There was no interest in Diogo Dalot or Noussair Mazraoui, nor in Harry Maguire, nor in Luke Shaw or Martínez, whose contracts are up next summer in any case. This is the product of recruitment decisions made and deals signed years ago. But why do United, one of the world’s most lucrative clubs, need to sell to buy in the first place?Perhaps for the same reason they baulked at the asking price for Elliot Anderson and decided to sign the inconsistent Santos and the adequate but overpromoted Tielemans instead: this is a club in austerity measures, whose part-owner Jim Ratcliffe has been furiously cutting costs and raising ticket prices, determined to curb the years of excess that preceded him, where mediocre players were signed on ridiculous money, where failing coaches were paid to leave. But why would United, one of the most commercially successful clubs in footballing history, ever need to cut costs?Perhaps as a result of the more than £1bn drained out of the club by the Glazers in their 21 years of ownership, not just in dividends but share sales and interest payments on the debt they undertook to buy the club, while neglecting the maintenance of Old Trafford and the training ground at Carrington. Whether he knows it or not, when Martínez is criticising the lack of investment he is in effect holding the Glazers accountable for more than two decades of avarice and mismanagement.All of which lends a certain significance to Martínez’s intervention that goes beyond the churn of the weekly news cycle. Has any serving United player spoken out so frankly about the ruins of the Glazer ownership? Ole Gunnar Solskjær made a minor stand in early 2005, before they had arrived at the club. Cristiano Ronaldo threw some hand grenades over his shoulder a few days before he left for the second time in 2022. Countless others waited for the safety of retirement, when their disgruntlement could be monetised for personal gain, rather than used to stigmatise them, as Martínez will doubtless be stigmatised in the coming days.View image in fullscreenA Manchester United supporter shows off a jumper protesting against the club’s owners and executives.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesDoes any of this help United to win games in the short term? Almost certainly not. Martínez attempted to clarify his commentsin a social media poston Wednesday night. He may still be dispatched to the bomb squad anyway, for the crime of pointing out that the emperor secured his throne almost entirely through the use of payment-in-kind loans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInevitably Michael Carrick too will be gone before long, away to the great Overlap podcast in the sky. A few months ago I wrote hopefully thatCarrick might be the ideal manto cut through the noise and nonsense. I was wrong. The noise has beaten him; the nonsense always wins; any accumulated credit from last season has long since evaporated.Of course it’s not Carrick’s fault that United haven’t signed a new defender in almost two years, that Bruno Fernandes is so clearly playing through discomfort, that Joshua Zirkzee is still somehow hanging around the place, that the ownership decided to embark on a purge of season-ticket holders in the summer, generating a huge wave of ill-feeling and apathy that can be felt at Old Trafford on matchdays: an entire fanbase trying to work out whether they actually still care about this.But accountability is for the little people, and far easier to replace a coach on a modest 20-month contract than to oust Ineos or the Glazers, to replace Wilcox or Omar Berrada, even if we now know they partly built their reputations on the success of a club that has been found to have serially cheated. Bumper returns for the owners, price hikes for the fans, corners cut on the pitch; this is the story of the modernManchester United, which by no coincidence is also the story of modern football.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickcommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump should fear the BBC. Instead he’s picked a fight – and he seems to be losing  | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: The president is used to bullying his media targets. The quagmire that is his libel actions shows the broadcaster is working to a different script, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: The president is used to bullying his media targets. The quagmire that is his libel actions shows the broadcaster is working to a different script, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: An image of Donald Trump appears on video screens before his speech to supporters in Washington DC on 6 January 2021.Photograph: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn image of Donald Trump appears on video screens before his speech to supporters in Washington DC on 6 January 2021.Photograph: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesOpinionBBCTrump should fear the BBC. Instead he’s picked a fight – and he seems to be losingEmma BrockesThe president is used to bullying his media targets. The quagmire that is his libel actions shows the broadcaster is working to a different scriptThu 15 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 10.18 EDTShareFor the greatest account of the BBC’s finest hour, one must turn to Penelope Fitzgerald’s novel, Human Voices, written in 1980 and set 40 years earlier, at the corporation’s Portland Place wartime HQ. Flanked by sandbags and infused with a smell of cooking “from the deep hold that suggested more strongly than ever a cruise on the Queen Mary”, the organisation that Fitzgerald describes is at once noble and deeply eccentric. “Broadcasting House stood headed on a fixed course south,” she writes. “With the best engineers in the world, and a crew varying between the intensely respectable and barely sane, it looked ready to scorn any disaster.”In other words, a formidable foe, one that in the spring of 1940, in the face of anticipated Nazi invasion, decided “without prompting, that truth was more important than consolation, and, in the long run, would be more effective”. I bring this up in respect to the gathering storm of Donald Trump versus the BBC, a fight triggered by the US president’s$10bn defamation lawsuit– $10bn! It’s a wonder he didn’t go for $10 gazillion – brought against the corporation at the end of last year in response to a poorly edited episode of Panorama. The BBC was at fault, editing together comments made by the US president at a rally on 6 January 2021 to give, as the corporation’sapologyput it, “the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action”. But it is fighting the lawsuit.This will have come as a surprise to the president, who in his own country has had great success frightening media companies into craven submission. This week, as news broke that the BBC has beenclearedby a judge to serve legal papers on Trump’s children, while stillseeking judicial interventionto force him to show up to his own deposition, the president must be wondering what’s going on. In August last year, Trumpapplied to the courtto block the BBC from deposing Donald Trump Jr and Ivanka Trump, and yet … the corporation simply ignored him and ploughed on with its mission.Well. Welcome to the British Broadcasting Corporation, Mr President, let me give you a little insight into what you’re up against. There is no institutional power in the world to rival the BBC’s ability to drone on, a constant background hum for the nation. We all, at some level, consist of an interior mix-tape made up of Melvyn Bragg saying, “Hello. In the 13th century …” and Libby Purves opening an episode of Midweek with, “all my guests this week are time travellers, in a way”. The US president simply has no idea of the effect on this country’s nervous system of the opening bars of EastEnders, or a BBC newsreader interrupting normal programming with the line, “This is BBC television from London.”Nor will he have encountered that very particular BBC mindset, which, unlike the workforce at Google, doesn’t run on can-do energy and corporate good cheer, but rather on toxic gas released by an underpaid, overworked labour force, seething with resentment and, as Fitzgerald put it, “bitterly loyal” to its employers – which, as it happens, is a very high standard of loyalty indeed. You don’t get that at Fox News.Or indeed at ABC News, which in December 2024,agreed to pay Trump $15min an uncontested defamation suit. And while CNN, MS Now and Politico are allsuing the White Housefor banning them, CBS rolled over like a dog, announcing it would be axing Stephen Colbert’s highly critical show days after settling another defamation suit with the president. Meanwhile the Federal Communications Commission, the regulatory body run by arch-conservative Brendan Carr, threatened to review the licences of misbehaving broadcasters. A day after the president called for Trump-mocking Jimmy Kimmel’s dismissal from his late night ABC show,Carr orderedan early licence review of all eight of Disney’s ABC television stations.The BBC isn’t bound by these forces. There are financial pressures on it to settle, of course, but in public broadcasting money is never the be-all and end-all, and I would bet Trump has never come up against a force so stubborn, so irrational, so inexplicable to the American corporate or political mindset as his opponents at Langham Place. If the president prizes his own unpredictability as a key weapon in his arsenal, I’d like to introduce him to the people who brought us Noel’s House Party and Grandstand.Yes, the BBC loves nothing more than to don a hair shirt and report on its own failings. Yes, it could do with relying a bit less on Clare Balding. And yes, the corporation is a lunatic in so many ways. But it’s our lunatic and if you come for it, you come for us all. In the BBC’s long history of standing up to tyranny, it has seen off bigger enemies than Trump. I would bet the Shipping Forecast it will come out victorious.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmma Brockes is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBBCOpinionDonald TrumpMedia lawLaw (US)Trump administrationNoel EdmondscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on food security: we have just-in-time, we need just-in-case | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Experts are warning that the UK is unprepared for crises. A refrigerator cyber-attack scare in France is the latest reminder of the risks
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Experts are warning that the UK is unprepared for crises. A refrigerator cyber-attack scare in France is the latest reminder of the risks
Content: ‘The fifth of the population with the lowest incomes would need to spend 85% of their disposable income on food to meet governmental advice on healthy diets.’Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The fifth of the population with the lowest incomes would need to spend 85% of their disposable income on food to meet governmental advice on healthy diets.’Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianOpinionFood securityThe Guardian view on food security: we have just-in-time, we need just-in-caseEditorialExperts are warning that the UK is unprepared for crises. A refrigerator cyber-attack scare in France is the latest reminder of the risksThu 15 Oct 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.38 EDTShareWhat’s worrying French supermarket bosses should be prompting British ministers to action. On Sunday, hackersforced up the temperatures of refrigeratorsin hundreds of food stores across France to as high as 50C, resulting in waste and fires. Beyond the immediate destruction and inconvenience, it raised the prospect of other malicious actors finding new ways to play havoc with the food chain.Only weeks before, 150 expertstogether warnedthe British government that it does not have a plan to feed people in a crisis ­– and that the west is entering an era in which not only disruption but the weaponisation of food is a real possibility. “The public has been led to assume that food will simply be there,” they wrote. “It may not be.”The Covid pandemic was a salutary reminder of how vulnerable modern systems are – a shock for consumers used to strawberries in October.Brexit, climate stress and the wars in Ukraine and Iran have underlined the risks and raised prices. One issue is overall supply in the UK, which imports about 40% of its food. But affordability, logistics, distribution and nutrition are also essential components of food security.View image in fullscreenTim Lang.Photograph: Andy Hall/The ObserverWhile food inflation hasslowed, the cumulative impact has been severe. The Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit says that by September 2027, UK food prices are likely to be50% higherthan at the start of the cost of living crisis in mid-2021. That scale of increase previously took almost two decades. Food is a far smaller proportion of household budgets than it was 50 years ago. But the fifth of the population with the lowest incomes would need to spend85% of their disposable incomeon food to meet governmental advice on healthy diets.Fruit and vegetables often give wayto more filling but less nutritious options.The government has encouraged households to stockpile several days’ worth of tinned goods and bottled water in case of an emergency. But outsourcing food security to individuals is a woefully inadequate response. Buildingcivil food resiliencewill require more effort, including working with civil society.Real improvement requires a structural shift away from the “leave it to Tesco” approachdecried by Prof Tim Lang, a leading food-policy expert. As he points out, “framing markets is the job of politics”. Reliance on just-in-time last-minute deliveries and a few hubs makes economic sense for retailers, but is not conducive to national food security. Crises often winnow out smaller firms. But diversity is key to resilience. Geographical distribution – including relocalisation of food production – is also central. Almost 95% of retail food comes via131 food-distribution centres. Disruption to just one supermarket chain’s infrastructure could have a mammoth impact.Experts have rightly called for food supply shortages and disruption to be included as risks in their own right in the national security risk assessment. There is also a strong case for a dedicated national food council to focus on food security. The UK abandoned its strategic food stockpile in the 1990s. It should think again, as other countries around the worldare doing.Almost one in 10 householdsare already food-insecure. Others have become used to an age of abundance. None can count on food security without sustained action from the government, beginning with the recognition that this problem can’t be left to the market.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Stormont: voters in Northern Ireland deserve more than an endless cycle of dysfunction | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: After the executive’s failure to set a budget, and renewed culture war confrontations, faith in Stormont’s ability to act in the common good is evaporating
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: After the executive’s failure to set a budget, and renewed culture war confrontations, faith in Stormont’s ability to act in the common good is evaporating
Content: ‘Northern Ireland now risks being governed by a zombie administration until elections next May.’Photograph: Clodagh Kilcoyne/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Northern Ireland now risks being governed by a zombie administration until elections next May.’Photograph: Clodagh Kilcoyne/ReutersOpinionNorthern IrelandThe Guardian view on Stormont: voters in Northern Ireland deserve more than an endless cycle of dysfunctionEditorialAfter the executive’s failure to set a budget, and renewed culture-war confrontations, faith in the government’s ability to act in the common good is evaporatingThu 15 Oct 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.38 EDTShareLate last month, protestersdepositeda sizable amount of foul-smelling green water on the steps of Stormont to draw attention to the appalling state of Lough Neagh, the largest freshwater lake in the British Isles. Years of agricultural pollution havecreatedan environmental disaster in an area of huge ecological significance that once inspired the poetry of Seamus Heaney. Its plight should be a top priority for Northern Ireland’s devolved government. But the executive currently has other matters on its mind.The sentencing of the former leader of the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) Jeffrey Donaldson, after he was convicted of child sexual abuse, dominated Thursday’s headlines. Meanwhile, a cross-party political crisis continues to play out. Halfway through the financial year, Stormont has yet to set abudget. The current deadlock in negotiations with the Northern Ireland secretary, Sir Chris Bryant, could lead to one being imposed from Westminster. Cuts are already being made by default amid an atmosphere of stasis and policy drift.An unwelcome revival of sectarian tension on the streets is further undermining the fragile political institutions established by the Good Friday agreement. On Monday, Northern Ireland assembly membersdebateda motion of no confidence in the first minister, Michelle O’Neill. The move followed the Sinn Féin vice-president’s participation in protests against a proposed Orange Order march on the Garvaghy Road in Portadown, controversially sanctioned by the Parades Commission for the first time in 28 years.View image in fullscreenMichelle O’Neill.Photograph: Oscar Rihll/PAA prolongedstandoffbetween unionists and mainly Catholic residents ended peacefully, after Sir Chris banned the parade on police advice. The absence of violence was a silver lining, but the episode showcased the dangers of what one politiciandescribedas “negative nostalgia”. As those seeking to revive a route notoriously associated with loyalist violence surely anticipated, the bitter row has reopened old wounds and unleashed latent animosities.The motion of no confidence in Ms O’Neill was a performative exercise, with no chance of obtaining the necessary cross-community support. But the combination of no budget and a renewed culture-war confrontation means thatNorthern Irelandnow risks being governed by a zombie administration until elections next May.Given the dismal recenttrack recordof Stormont collapses and suspensions, that should prompt some hard thinking in London and Dublin as well as Belfast. The scandalous condition of Lough Neagh symbolises the deficiencies of a polity that now seems trapped in an endless cycle of dysfunction. The steady deterioration ofpublic servicessuch as healthcare, education and policing can partly be attributed to underfunding. But matters have been made much worse by the existence of a political vacuum and sectarian grandstanding where effective government should be.Power-sharing designed to reassure nationalist and unionist communities remains indispensable. But a loveless-marriage model that allows the largest party on either side of the divide to routinely bring assembly business to a halt is in urgent need ofreform. Otherwise, faith in Stormont’s ability to act in the name of the common good is in danger of evaporating. Huge strides have been made in civil society since the Good Friday agreement was struck nearly three decades ago. But Northern Ireland’s voters currently do not have the politics they deserve.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: An autism diagnosis, but where’s the treatment? | Mental health | The Guardian
description: Letters: Rebecca Hope Duncan says she has not received any help after being assessed as autistic, in response to Prof Peter Fonagy’s review of mental health, ADHD and autism services. Plus letters from Jeremy Seymour, John Bryant, Peter Deadman, Steve Bamford and another reader
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Rebecca Hope Duncan says she has not received any help after being assessed as autistic, in response to Prof Peter Fonagy’s review of mental health, ADHD and autism services. Plus letters from Jeremy Seymour, John Bryant, Peter Deadman, Steve Bamford and another reader
Content: ‘The diagnosis explained my life; it did not come with any help to live it.’Photograph: BongkarnThanyakij/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The diagnosis explained my life; it did not come with any help to live it.’Photograph: BongkarnThanyakij/Getty ImagesMental healthLettersAn autism diagnosis, but where’s the treatment?Rebecca Hope Duncansays she has not received any help after being assessed as autistic, in response to Prof Peter Fonagy’s review of mental health, ADHD and autism services. Plus letters fromJeremy Seymour,John Bryant, Peter Deadman, Steve Bamfordand another readerThu 15 Oct 2026 12.51 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTShareYour coverage of the Fonagy review concentrates on children and on the risk of diagnosing too readily (NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry finds, 9 October). I’d like to speak for those of us who were not diagnosed at all.I first asked for help at 17. For 34 years I was treated for anxiety, depression and trauma. All were real; none were the whole story. I was diagnosed as autistic at 51. The same report identified ADHD, which until 2013 could not officially be diagnosed alongside autism.I am still waiting for that ADHD assessment. ADHD is the one for which there is medication, but I cannot get to it. For autism there is nothing: you are given the diagnosis and sent home to deal with it.The review asks for support based on need, not labels. I’d welcome that. But I have the label and the need, and neither has brought support. The diagnosis explained my life; it did not come with any help to live it.Rebecca Hope DuncanSouthamptonYour editorial (11 October) correctly identifies the need for improved prevention and treatment of neurodevelopmental disorders, rather than rehearsing debates about diagnosis. Here are three additional suggestions.First, neurodevelopment largely occurs during sleep: neuroplasticity is what sleep is for. Many infants and children are sleep-deprived, so a national public health programme on improving child sleep hygiene will prevent and ameliorate the severity of future neurodevelopment disorders.Second, depression. Many young people with autism spectrum disorder and ADHD also fulfil criteria fordepression, which is treatable at GP surgeries with combinations of exercise and pluralistic psychological therapy.Third, work: to not work is bad for the mental health of young people with neurodivergence. If you can exercise, you can work, so the government could followDutch and Danishmodels and return to the supported employment and tax credits previously devised by Gordon Brown, undone by the political vandalism of Tory/Liberal Democrat austerity.Jeremy SeymourRetired consultant psychiatrist, SheffieldYour editorial mentions that “the rises in psychological distress, and the need for support with neurodevelopmental differences, are real and tied to social changes”.If the problems are tied to social changes, why is it primarily a healthcare issue? Wouldn’t we be better off calling out the “social changes” and addressing them?It’s possible to do that while acknowledging the reality of the suffering of those involved, dignifying it in fact. By focusing entirely on the symptoms, we risk ignoring the root, and in doing so will allow more children to suffer.John BryantGP, BristolGiven the alarming rise in childhood mental health problems, why do we allow our children to be fed on ultra-processed foods (UPFs)? Childhood anxiety is on the rise globally, but the UK is in theworst-performing groupof wealthy nations in virtually every measure of child and adolescent mental health. Coincidentally, British children also have the equal worst diets in the world – along with the US – in terms of consumption of UPFs, which make up aroundtwo-thirds of their diet. A 2026systematic reviewfound a clear association between child and adolescent consumption of UPFs and mental health problems such as anxiety, depression, irritability, sleep disturbances and suicidal ideation. And aCanadian studyof over 2,000 children found that as children ate more UPFs, they faced increasing risk of emotional and behavioural problems, and that replacing just 10% of UPF calories with minimally processed real food, lowered children’s behaviour problem scores. Until the government is ready to stand up to the powerful food industry and ignores the inevitable cries of “nanny state”, this won’t change.Peter DeadmanHove, East SussexThe differing explanations for the huge rise in diagnoses for autism and ADHD arise, I believe, from a general problem in the diagnosis of mental health conditions. In physical medicine, diagnosis includes not just the description and classification of symptoms, but identifying the underlying pathology that gives rise to the symptoms, and where possible the cause of this pathology.A symptom such as a headache, for example, can arise for a variety of reasons, and a diagnosis will determine what its origin is. The characteristics of the headache, such as severity, exact location and duration, will give clues as to the underlying cause, but this can only be determined accurately by medical tests. There are some conditions where a group of symptoms regularly occur together but where the underlying pathology is unknown; these are classed as syndromes, and the names for them are descriptive rather than true diagnoses.In the area of mental health, there are few if any diagnoses in the strict sense, and the terms used are descriptive rather than truly diagnostic. Even for the most severe conditions, such as schizophrenia, the underlying pathology is unknown, and this is even more true of conditions such as depression and anxiety, where the distinction between normal reactions and conditions severe enough to be regarded as illnesses is unclear.Nobody seriously questions that the phenomena of autism and ADHD exist; the question is whether the concept of diagnosis is appropriate. If not, the distinction between what is “normal” and what is a “disorder” is arbitrary, based on the severity of the problems experienced and how well someone is able to function. The criteria for autism have been broadened to include people on the “spectrum” with much milder difficulties than in the past, while ADHD is a condition that has only recently been recognised at all. It is therefore not surprising that many more have been diagnosed than in the past. However, it also raises the question of whether, in the milder cases, they should be regarded as “disorders” as opposed to differences in personality.Steve BamfordLittlehampton, West SussexIt’s not just young people who have been let down by the lack of diagnosis and care available to those with ADHD andAutism. My 70-year-old wife has suffered from one of these conditions throughout her life, along with many others of her generation. Had she been diagnosed at an early age, she would have had a much easier, more successful and fulfilling life. However, National Institute for Health and Care Excellence and NHS guidelines in the UK did not recognise ADHD as a valid condition in adults until 2008, when she was aged 52 and her condition began to become more evident postmenopause.Being born in the north of England in the 1950s meant there was little or no chance of her receiving a childhood diagnosis that would have made her life much more understandable. Today, living in Scotland where the NHS does not offer the “right to choose” for ADHD assessments, she would face a median wait time of 111 weeks, with some waits as long as 266 weeks and currently8,886 adults in the queue. Not surprisingly she continues to remain undiagnosed along with many others.Name and address suppliedHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Eritrean aggression must not be overlooked | Ethiopia | The Guardian
description: Letter: Biruk Mekonnen, the Ethiopian ambassador, responds to an editorial on the war in Tigray
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Biruk Mekonnen, the Ethiopian ambassador, responds to an editorial on the war in Tigray
Content: A person collects recyclable materials from the wreckage of an abandoned truck damaged by a drone strike during fighting between the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) in southern Tigray, 9 October 2026.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenA person collects recyclable materials from the wreckage of an abandoned truck damaged by a drone strike during fighting between the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) in southern Tigray, 9 October 2026.Photograph: ReutersEthiopiaLettersEritrean aggression must not be overlookedBiruk Mekonnen, the Ethiopian ambassador to the UK, responds to an editorial on the war in TigrayThu 15 Oct 2026 12.51 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTShareYour attention to Ethiopia is welcome, but your editorial (8 October) presents an incomplete account of the crisis, framing Ethiopia’s national interests as sources of regional instability while insufficiently examining the actions of other actors.The opening reference to the Nobel peace prize is particularly telling. By suggesting that the committee will hope its next choice “ages better than 2019’s”, the editorial invites readers to question Abiy Ahmed’s award because of the war that followed a year later. Yet the prime minister received the prize for his efforts to achieve peace withEritrea. The subsequent war in Tigray does not erase that achievement or, by itself, establish that the award was undeserved.Describing the rapprochement with Eritrea as having “facilitated a war with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front” implies causation without adequately explaining the evidence. Likewise, claiming Mr Abiy’s coalition is “held together by his patronage” reduces political support to personal favours without establishing that this is what sustains it.More seriously, the editorial overlooks the broader context of Eritrean aggression. The current crisis must also be understood in the context of an Eritrean foreign policy that, from Ethiopia’s perspective, has treated a weakEthiopiaas serving Eritrea’s interests.The call for a truce also fails to address responsibility for renewed hostilities. Dialogue is welcome, but it must not reward armed aggression with political leverage or pressure Ethiopia into concessions. Ethiopia’s pursuit of Red Sea access and its right to develop the Nile’s resources should not be portrayed as threats simply because they challenge neighbouring states’ preferences.Whether or not Eritrea’s strategic value to Washington explains its approach, that should not eclipse the consequences of its actions for Ethiopia’s sovereignty and security.Biruk MekonnenEthiopian ambassador to the UKHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Endless fun with a legendary book of placenames | Rural affairs | The Guardian
description: Letters: Ian A Anderson reminds readers of The Meaning of Liff. Plus letters from Peter Lewis, John Davies, Penelope Fletcher, Phil Ivens and Chris Skelcher
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Ian A Anderson reminds readers of The Meaning of Liff. Plus letters from Peter Lewis, John Davies, Penelope Fletcher, Phil Ivens and Chris Skelcher
Content: ‘Finding ourselves in Lincolnshire, we made a detour just to get a selfie with the village sign for Mavis Enderby.’Photograph: Lee Beel/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Finding ourselves in Lincolnshire, we made a detour just to get a selfie with the village sign for Mavis Enderby.’Photograph: Lee Beel/AlamyRural affairsLettersEndless fun with a legendary book of placenamesIan A Andersonreminds readers of The Meaning of Liff. Plus letters fromPeter Lewis, John Davies,Penelope Fletcher, Phil IvensandChris SkelcherThu 15 Oct 2026 12.51 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTShareNeither Adrian Chiles, in his column about placenames (7 October), nor the writers of the follow-up letters (9 October) mentioned Douglas Adams and John Lloyd’s legendary 1983 dictionary of placenames, The Meaning of Liff, still in print.Not so long ago, finding ourselves inLincolnshire, we made a detour just to get a selfie with the village sign for Mavis Enderby (“the almost-completely-forgotten girlfriend from your distant past for whom your wife has a completely irrational jealousy and hatred”). The book is full of delightful definitions of placenames like Nempnett Thrubwell (“the feeling experienced when driving off for the first time on a brand new motorbike”) and Mellon Udrigle (“the ghastly sound made by traditional folk-singers”). Hours of endless pleasure.Ian A AndersonCambridgeFriends and I in the Oxfordshire/Buckinghamshire area have long believed that the names of certain local villages could double as those of 1980s West Indies fast bowlers. Step forward the fearsome pace attack of Sutton Courtenay, Stanton Harcourt and Grendon Underwood.Peter LewisOxfordThere also are, or have been, real people whose names should be Dorset villages. Just a few from the world of stage and screen: Franklin Pangborn, Wensley Pithey, Lynton Brent, Weston Blakesley.John DaviesWanstead, LondonI always think that Wootton Rivers in Wiltshire is a country and western singer.Penelope FletcherKintbury, BerkshireAdrian Chiles assumes that Hope Bagot in Shropshire and Preston Bagot in Warwickshire – just across the valley from my home of Claverdon – are related. Indeed they are, as is Morton Bagot, also in Warwickshire. The Bagot family, who as lords of the manor lent their name to all these places, have their ancestral seat at Blithfield Hall in Staffordshire, which is one of the stops of the famous horn gance from the neighbouring village of Abbots Bromley.Phil IvensClaverdon, WarwickshirePink Green, Worcestershire: too garish for Adrian Chiles to mention?Chris SkelcherBirminghamHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The UK must have digital sovereignty  | Data protection | The Guardian
description: Letters: The government must stop allowing foreign companies to have access to our sensitive data, writes Ian White. Plus a letter from Bill Cawley
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: The government must stop allowing foreign companies to have access to our sensitive data, writes Ian White. Plus a letter from Bill Cawley
Content: A protest in London against Palantir’s role in the NHS, 1 October 2026.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenA protest in London against Palantir’s role in the NHS, 1 October 2026.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAData protectionLettersThe UK must have digital sovereigntyThe government must stop allowing foreign companies to have access to our sensitive data, writesIan White. Plus a letter fromBill CawleyThu 15 Oct 2026 12.51 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTShareThe UK cannot become dependent on foreign AI technology that can be switched off at short notice, says George Williamson, head of the Alan Turing Institute (Report, 10 October). The growing opposition to Palantir, an American company, having government contracts that give it access to sensitive data are all part of the same issue. The UK does not have digital sovereignty.This is not a theoretical problem. TheUS governmentimposed targetedsanctionson the international criminal court, stopping all digital services to certain individuals. This could happen to a country.Even if you use European email and cloud services, our computer operating systems require constant software updates. This is not just to add new features. There is a constant race between the good guys patching the software bugs and the bad guys trying to gain entry to your computer using those same software bugs.Recently, Holland and France took active steps to break thenear monopoly of big Amercian techby laying the foundations of a nationwide IT ecosystem that they would control. The UK needs to do the same.Ian WhiteCheltenham, GloucestershireThe concern about the NHS’s dependence on Palantir (Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contracts, 9 October) is justified, but the £330m contract is a symptom of a wider habit. Whenever the government wants joined-up data, it buys one large platform from one supplier – and such projects have a long record of overrunning, costing far more than planned and locking the buyer in.There is a working example of the alternative: the world wide web. It does not require everyone’s data to sit in one place or run on one company’s software. It simply defines how data is requested and transferred.TheNHSneeds the same: an open specification for exchanging records, plus a registry of where each patient’s data is held. Any authorised clinician could then assemble the full picture of my treatment, while each hospital or practice chose its own software supplier. Specialist firms could still compete to analyse the data for planning and research – but none would own the plumbing.The NHS already has the beginnings of this in itsinteroperability standards. Why do the money and political attention go to a single proprietary platform rather than to making open standards mandatory?Bill CawleyLudlow, ShropshireExplore more on these topicsData protectionPalantirNHSlettersShareReuse this content

title: Chris Woakes: ‘It’s unacceptable seeing the way some England players have acted’ | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Chris Woakes tells Donald McRae about his surreal last stand at the Oval, his ‘shabby’ treatment by Rob Key and the problem of cricket’s drinking culture
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: Chris Woakes tells Donald McRae about his surreal last stand at the Oval, his ‘shabby’ treatment by Rob Key and the problem of cricket’s drinking culture
Content: Warwickshire’s Chris Woakes poses for a portrait at  Edgbaston’s indoor cricket school – ‘I’ve played in teams where the majority enjoy a drink so it becomes the norm.’Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWarwickshire’s Chris Woakes poses for a portrait at  Edgbaston’s indoor cricket school – ‘I’ve played in teams where the majority enjoy a drink so it becomes the norm.’Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCricketInterviewChris Woakes: ‘It’s unacceptable seeing the way some England players have acted’Donald McRaeThe Test stalwart on his surreal last stand at the Oval, his ‘shabby’ treatment by Rob Key and the vexed problem of cricket’s drinking cultureThu 15 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a rainy October afternoon, after his 20th season as aprofessional cricketer, Chris Woakessits down at Edgbaston’s indoor nets and thinks of the advice that helped him when he was 17 and about to start a career in this consuming sport. “The words came from my parents, particularly my dad, and it was to always be myself,” he says in his thoughtful way.Woakes has just won his third CountyChampionship with Warwickshireand he played 62 Tests for England, taking 192 wickets and scoring 2,034 runs. He also won two World Cups and experienced a range of England coaches, from Andy Flower to Brendon McCullum, and played for captains as different as Sir Alastair Cook, Eoin Morgan, Joe Root and Ben Stokes.Woakes has been a positive and steadying presence in a tumultuous time for English cricket. “There were a couple of occasions where I stepped outside my character and tried to be something else and it backfired. I quickly learned that what I had, and the way I did it, was the way forward. I’m relatively reserved, but I had quite a bit of dog in me which I didn’t show verbally. You need that burning fire.”Woakes is routinely described as the nicest man in cricket, but it’s a reductive view that obscures the skill and tenacity that defines him. “Ask some batters over the years and I’m sure they said: ‘He isn’t that nice.’ Once you cross the line, you need to find a way to compete and win.”View image in fullscreenChris Woakes walks out to bat against India at the Oval, his left arm in a sling for his England swansong.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersThe Wizard, his fine new autobiography, has been written with the Guardian’s Ali Martin, who captures Woakes’s voice expertly while providing trenchant insights into the contrasting eras that span his long career. The book opens with his ending in Test cricket, on the bizarre morning last August when Woakes came in at No 11, with hisdamaged left arm in a sling,to try to help England score the 17 runs that would secure a 3-1 series victory over India.There was a fitting symmetry as Woakes walked down the stairs at the Oval, where he had made his Test debut 12 years earlier, while typically putting the interests of the team first. Woakes had dislocated his shoulder while fielding and could hold the bat only with one hand. The pain became excruciating when he tried to run and he knew India’s bowlers would show no mercy at the climax of a riveting series.“It was amazing to go out like that but, in another way, quite sad,” he says. “To walk out in front of a full house, and get a standing ovation, was maybe meant to be my farewell. But it was a horrible moment as well. I had the agony of the shoulder, but there’s no worse feeling, especially as a bowler, when you leave the team handicapped: 10 v 11. Not many teams win from that position. That hurts.”How did he feel as he stepped on to the field? “I don’t think I’ve ever been as nervous because I was going into the unknown. I was going to bat with one arm, which was never going to look pretty or be great. One of the things you have to get over is the thought that, when someone’s bowling at 90mph with a hard cricket ball, it can hurt even when you’re batting the right way round. It was a challenge to build up the courage to face that.”Was he scared? “Absolutely, because in international arena it’s dog eat dog. So there was certainly some fear in the cauldron. It would be stumps or head, so I was going to have to wear a few. Your brain naturally tells you: ‘I don’t want to do this.’ But you have to get over that. We got [the run chase] down to seven because Gus Atkinson did fantastically well. So close, yet so far.”Atkinson was bowled before Woakes could take his mark. “In a selfish way I didn’t want my wicket to be the deciding one, but part of me still wishes I could have faced a ball.”View image in fullscreenEngland’s Ben Stokes celebrates with teammate Chris Woakes during the 2019 Ashes series. Could the former captain return? ‘When it comes to Ben, anything is possible.’Photograph: Jon Super/APWoakes describes the harsh way he wassoon jettisoned by England. He could accept he had not been selected for the Ashes tour last year, and that his England contract was terminated, but he was hurt by Rob Key, the England team director, breaking the news in public. “Chris Woakes isn’t in our plans,” Key said, “at all.” “That final bit felt a bit cold,” Woakes writes. “A bit shabby, really.”He is too kind to put the boot in again. “I’ve always got on well with Rob and maybe those words slipped out, not necessarily how he meant it. But he could have easily had that conversation first with me, rather than the press.”Has he discussed the matter with Key? “We’ve barely spoken since. He’s a busy man and moved on to different things. I’m sure at some point we’ll discuss it. But in any walk of professional sport there isn’t much loyalty because the game moves on. Rob probably had bigger fish to fry at that time. There was an Ashes series and that was his priority, which I understand.”The Ashes were an unmitigated disaster with the familiar drubbing by Australia exacerbated bynocturnal mishaps featuring Harry BrookandBen Duckett. Those incidents added to the pressure on McCullum and Stokes. McCullum was relieved of his role, while retaining control of the white‑ball team. Stokes remained as captain, but after leading England to victory in the first Test of the summer against New Zealand he and Atkinson were caught up in a post‑match fracas with members of the Saracens rugby academy, breaking a curfew meant to curb such skirmishes.Stokes then looked exhausted as heannounced his unexpected retirementfrom international cricket a few weeks later. “Being Test captain does beat you up,” Woakes says. “We saw it with Joe [Root] last time round. Cookie was the same. We saw it with Ben.“He was desperate for that Ashes series to be a winning one, and he probably deserved it. But the game owes you nothing and he didn’t get it quite right on that tour. I think that was the nail in the coffin. Although he said he wanted to move forward, maybe deep down he knew he couldn’t re-energise himself.”What did he say to Stokes? “On the day itself I saw him briefly at Trent Bridge and it was: ‘What a career, mate. Hope you enjoy the moment.’ All that sort of stuff because it happened quite quickly. I was on Sky commentary that day. It was a very slow day and it got to three o’clock and all of a sudden we heard the news he was going to retire and it became a bit manic. It would be nice to be able to sit down with him and discuss it.”Woakes has always had a balanced relationship with alcohol. He enjoys a few beers after a big match but he is smart about his consumption and before the victorious 2019 World Cup he gave up drinking as part of his preparation for the sweetest moment of his career. But does English crickethave a drink problem?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I’d like to say no, but drinking culture is mentioned a lot. There are lads atWarwickshirethat enjoy a drink after a win or a hard four days of cricket. Other guys here are almost teetotal and this is the most professional county team I’ve ever seen. But I’ve played in teams where the majority enjoy a drink so it becomes the norm.View image in fullscreenChris Woakes with the trophy as Warwickshire are crowned county champions.Photograph: Jacob King/PA“People say within professional sport it should be zero alcohol. But cricket is very different to football and rugby. Test cricket is played over five days, on tours which last for months. It consumes you and people need to have a release. But that doesn’t mean they should get in trouble, like we’ve seen within the England team recently.”Yet curfews don’t solve anything. “No. You need to give players some freedom and treat them like adults. But it’s unacceptable seeing the way some England players have acted.”Woakes points out that, as cricketers, “we’re brought up on alcohol to a certain extent. In club cricket there’s a lot of alcohol and it becomes the norm from a young age. The professional game needs to be different, but the sport is so mentally draining it’s almost impossible to tell people they can’t have a drink. It’s a human release.”double quotation markAndy Flower was ridiculously hard. I was almost scared to train, but that was also what I needed at the timeHe is optimistic, however, that England havethe right Test coach in Stephen Fleming. Woakes also pays tribute to McCullum’s ability to free up players, while admitting that, as a senior player, he should have spoken out when he saw clearly that McCullum’s ultra-aggressive style, played without much thought of consequence, would fail against the best Test teams.“There were times where we had the opposition pretty much by the balls and could have played a little more conservatively in that moment to get us to a point where the other team didn’t have a sniff,” Woakes says. “But there were too many occasions where we let them back in. We could have been more vocal in those moments and say we need to shift gears within the game. We always went up the gears, but never really came back down.”His book offers some fascinating snapshots of how it felt being coached by men as opposite as Flower and McCullum. At the start of his Test career, Flower would shout at Woakes with withering ferocity. “He was ridiculously hard,” Woakes says. “I was almost scared to train, but that was also what I needed at the time. I just didn’t realise it. So it worked out perfectly. Flower was exactly what I needed at the start and McCullum was exactly what I needed at the back end of my career.”View image in fullscreenChris Woakes, the Warwickshire and former England cricketer, with Ali Martin, cricket correspondent of the Guardian, holding the autobiography they have just written together.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAfter such a successful county season he is open to playing one more year for Warwickshire for his love of red-ball cricket remains undimmed. But he has already shown a deft touch in his television work. It is easy to see Woakes becoming the face of cricket on Sky and he rocks in amusement when I say I would like to see him introduce the first day of the first Ashes Test at Trent Bridge next summer – as he confirms the sudden return of Stokes to Root’s team. “Wow,” Woakes laughs. “God, could you imagine that?”Could Stokes make one last comeback against Australia? “When it comes to Ben, I genuinely think anything is possible. A large part of me says it won’t happen. I think he’s done. But if there’s one person that could talk Ben Stokes round to playing again, it would be Joe Root. They’re very good friends and have known each other for a hell of a long time. If Joe was to say to Ben: ‘I want you back for one last series,’ it could happen. It would certainly be box office. It always is with Ben Stokes.”Look out for an exclusive extract from Chris Woakes’s book on the aftermath of England’s 2019 World Cup triumph. The Wizard by Chris Woakes (Penguin Books, £25). title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Henderson back on Merseyside, Farke threatens more misery for Carrick and Forest are a threat to Arsenal
Author: Guardian sport
