Headline: Henderson back on Merseyside, Farke threatens more misery for Carrick and Forest are a threat to Arsenal
Content: Coventry City’s Stephen Mfuni, Justin Kluivert of Bournemouth and Chelsea’s Jordan Henderson.Composite: Guardian Pictures; PA; Reuters; EPAView image in fullscreenCoventry City’s Stephen Mfuni, Justin Kluivert of Bournemouth and Chelsea’s Jordan Henderson.Composite: Guardian Pictures; PA; Reuters; EPATen things to look out for this weekendPremier LeaguePremier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendHenderson back on Merseyside, Farke threatens more misery for Carrick and Forest are a threat to ArsenalPremier League top scorers|Follow us on TikTokGuardian sportThu 15 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1Henderson’s return to MerseysideA lively reception awaits the former Liverpool midfielders Jordan Henderson and Xabi Alonso at Everton and, in the case of the former, any jeers can be considered an unintentional tribute. They will speak of what the 36-year-old is able to produce now as much as what, and where, he delivered in the past.With two goals and an assistagainst Bournemouth last Saturday, Henderson became the oldest player to contribute directly to three goals in a Premier League game, and demonstrated his role at Chelsea is not simply to elevate standards off the pitch. His midfield partnership with Moisés Caicedo gave Alonso’s team balance and enabled the front three of Morgan Rogers, João Pedro and Cole Palmer to flourish. Their confrontation against an Everton defence that had impressed this season, onlyto litter the draw at Hullwith costly mistakes, will provide a stern test of the hosts’ unbeaten start and may well be dictated by the veteran behind them.Andy HunterEverton vChelsea, Saturday 12.30pm (all times BST)Chart showing oldest players to make three goal contributions in a Premier League match for Chelsea2Bees a tougher test than LaskStill unbeaten in the top flight, Brentford’s commitment to pragmatism is serving them well. Keith Andrews’ side like to sit deep, close off the middle of the pitch and force opponents to play around them, while flooding the opposition box at set pieces and throw-ins allows them to create the chances from which most of their goals arrive. Inspanking six past Lask, the Austrian champions, Liverpool showed how good they can be on the front foot, but they will face far less obliging hosts at the Gtech Community Stadium. If Andoni Iraola’s side can dominate the ball and move it quickly enough to penetrate Brentford’s rearguard, they could win comfortably. However, the Bees’ efforts to turn the afternoon into a saloon brawl and capitalise on dead-ball situations may help to maintain their unbeaten run.Barry GlendenningBrentford vLiverpool, Saturday 3pm3García needs to find finishing touchGonzalo García has one league goal from 18 shots this season. The striker joined Fulham from Real Madrid in the summer and has looked promising in patches. García is 22 and capable of getting on the end of chances. He has an expected goals tally of 3.60 but is underperforming with his finishing. The challenge is to become more clinical. Fulham, bottom of the league, have six goals in six games and García is without a goal since scoring on his debut,against Chelsea. Álvaro Arbeloa has put a lot of faith in his fellow Spaniard. The head coach is under increasing pressure and winless Fulham need García to fire when they host Hull City.Jacob SteinbergFulham v Hull, Saturday 3pmView image in fullscreenFulham’s Gonzalo García (second left) attempts a shot on goal against Manchester United.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.4City still free-flowing after guilty verdictEven when losing for the first time this season in Wednesday’s 4-2 Champions Leaguedefeat by Paris Saint-Germain, Manchester City appeared the real deal as they rallied from 3-0 down after 32 minutes to give the European champions a scare. Enzo Maresca deserves credit for following Pep Guardiola serenely; his City, so far, are a free-flowing attacking machine and invigorating to watch. If not for the guilty verdict against the club for serious financial breaches of Premier League rules, the perma-twinkling Italian might be more widely lauded. Ipswich last beat City at home in the competition in November 2000: do not expect the statistic to change on Saturday.Jamie JacksonManchester City v Ipswich, Saturday 3pmPredicted outcomes of Premier League matches on 17 October 20265Jaissle should find his ‘inner Rafa’Newcastle’s latest attempt to play vertical football left Matthias Jaissle’s side horizontal at Coventry on Monday night. That4-1 defeatagainst Frank Lampard’s team has prompted quite an inquest on Tyneside where Jaissle could do without his players falling flat on their faces once more when Aston Villa visit St James’ Park. Jaissle maintains that his “vertical football” is the brand of high-octane, aggressive attacking that Newcastle’s hierarchy believes should become the club’s default, and is the way fans want to see the team play. That argument is not without validity but it is also worth remembering that, less than a decade ago, under Rafael Benítez’s charge, Newcastle often played a low block bolstered by three at the back, rarely took unnecessary risks and improved steadily. Admittedly resources were thinner then but the fans almost universally adored Benítez and were heartbroken when he eventually tired of Mike Ashley’s ownership and resigned. Quite apart from making his dislike for “chaotic football’ plain the Spaniard was a realist who knew a gung-ho approach would spell relegation. Granted tactical fashions have changed, but Jaissle could do worse than slow things down a bit and search for his “inner Rafa” against Villa.Louise TaylorNewcastle vAston Villa, Saturday 5.30pmChart showing which teams have conceded the most shots in fast break situations in the 2026-27 Premier League6Eyes on Kluivert and BrobbeyWith nine games each scheduled for the month between international breaks, Bournemouth v Sunderland will give an early indication of how both will cope during their first experience of such a relentless Thursday-Sunday autumnal grind. Sunderland are 17th, Bournemouth are 18th, and with seven points between them after sixPremier Leaguerounds, scaling similarly dizzy heights to last season already seems a lofty goal. For both clubs, European campaigns are far too much of an exciting novelty to be considered anything like a chore. In circumstances where squad depth is crucial, the returns of Justin Kluivert for the hosts and Brian Brobbey for the visitors will be welcomed by Marco Rose and Régis Le Bris. It would be no great surprise to see either Dutch international make a game-deciding contribution in what is already a six-pointer on the south coast.BGskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBournemouth v Sunderland, Sunday 2pm7Brighton must buck Palace trendBrighton’s momentum appears unstoppable at the moment, although supporters will be wary of Sunday’s showdown againstCrystal Palacegiven their recent history. They haven’t beaten Palace since a 4-1 thrashing at the Amex in February 2024 when Roberto De Zerbi was in charge, while Fabian Hürzeler managed only a point in four encounters with the Eagles under Oliver Glasner. Both are having to juggle European commitments this season and Brighton will start as heavy favourites against Pierre Sage’s side after their superb start to the campaign. Palace have big concerns in defence, but can the Frenchman defy the odds against the Premier League’s top scorers?Ed AaronsBrighton v Crystal Palace, Sunday 2pmView image in fullscreenJaouen Hadjam fires home Brighton’s final goal in their 2-0 victory at Sunderland.Photograph: Craig Cowan/Every Second Media/Shutterstock8Carrick confronts old nemesis FarkeMichael Carrick has lost five of his past six technical-area duels with Daniel Farke. Indeed the only time Manchester United’s manager has bested his Leeds counterpart was in a League Cup tie during his Middlesbrough tenure. If such statistics are not sufficient to put Manchester United’s currently beleaguered manager off a trip to West Yorkshire on Sunday, there is a sense that Leeds are overdue a first victory at Elland Road since 2002 against their arch-enemies from across the Pennines. One thing is certain; it will be a typically raucous latter-day War of the Roses. But, right now, while the White Rose blooms, its red counterpart is wilting alarmingly. Will Carrick survive this latest meeting with a manager who, at Championship level during his Middlesbrough days, proved something of a nemesis? He will not care to remember that, last January, a1-1 draw at Elland Roadproved to be Ruben Amorim’s final game in charge of Manchester United.LTLeeds vManchester United, Sunday 2pm9Forest a genuine threat to championsDespitelosing 3-1 to Crystal Palacelast weekend, Nottingham Forest played some excellent front-foot football only to be let down by extreme profligacy in front of goal and vulnerability to their hosts’ counterattacks. Oliver Glasner attributed his side’s defeat to karma upon his return to Palace, saying: “It was like I didn’t deserve to win at Selhurst Park because the players did everything.” When they welcome Arsenal to the City Ground on Sunday, they will give the champions plenty to ponder if they can play as well again. Mikel Arteta’s side were unconvincing for 65 minutesagainst Leedslast weekend and failed to impress until they brought their heavy artillery around the same timeagainst Lilleon Tuesday. If one or both of Morgan Gibbs-White and Liam Delap can convert the kind of chances they missed at Selhurst Park, Forest have every chance of getting something.BGNottingham Forest v Arsenal, Sunday 4.30pmChart showing points and expected points in the 2026-27 Premier League10On-song Coventry can pile angst on SpursThe last time Tottenham hosted Coventry in the Premier League, Steffen Iversen, Les Ferdinand and Serhiy Rebrov scored in a comfortable 3-0 win. And while Spurs fans will almost certainly have envisaged a similar scoreline when the fixtures were announced, they will now be viewing Monday night’s fixture with even more than the usual amount of apprehension and dread. Like Tottenham, Coventry’s main problem until recently was an inability to convert chances, but in their demolition of Newcastle on Monday they visibly grew in confidence and swagger as four different players took the plaudits. While it’s taken a while and they may still struggle, through back-to-back wins Frank Lampard’s side have now announced themselves as a Premier League force to be reckoned with, which is something Tottenham haven’t managed in more than two years.BGTottenham v Coventry, Monday 8pmPosTeamPGDPts1Man City611182Arsenal65153Brighton613134Brentford66105Everton63106Chelsea62107Leeds6398Hull6299Liverpool60910Ipswich6-3911Newcastle6-3812Crystal Palace6-3713Man Utd60614Coventry6-6615Nottm Forest6-3516Aston Villa6-5517Sunderland6-6418AFC Bournemouth6-6319Tottenham Hotspur6-6320Fulham6-42Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTen things to look out for this weekendEvertonChelseaBrentfordLiverpoolFulhamHull CityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Evanilson, Rayan and Rodríguez goals seal Bournemouth’s historic home win in Europe | Europa League | The Guardian
description: Evanilson scored Bournemouth’s first with a looping header before Rayan and Álvaro Rodríguez added to their 3-0 victory against Sturm Graz
Author: John Brewin
Headline: Evanilson scored Bournemouth’s first with a looping header before Rayan and Álvaro Rodríguez added to their 3-0 victory against Sturm Graz
Content: Bournemouth’s Evanilson after opening the scoring with a looping header.Photograph: Tony O Brien/ReutersView image in fullscreenBournemouth’s Evanilson after opening the scoring with a looping header.Photograph: Tony O Brien/ReutersEuropa LeagueEvanilson, Rayan and Rodríguez goals seal Bournemouth’s historic home win in EuropeJohn BrewinThu 15 Oct 2026 17.46 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn impossible dream realised: the Vitality Stadium staging European football, where the Europa League is becoming an oasis for Bournemouth. No wins yet in the Premier League, but beating Sturm Graz following upwinning away at Real Sociedadshould calm the domestic pressures mounting on Marco Rose. A pair of Brazilians secured club history, with Evanilson’s first-half header followed by Rayan’s later drive, a clincher coming just as the Austrian visitors were pushing hard for an equaliser. Álvaro Rodríguez’s stoppage-time penalty extended the celebrations.Flag day at the Vitality. Elvis Presley’s high baritone and Andy Williams’ tenor on the public address system marked a different type of occasion.Bournemouthhave come a significant distance. “Minus 17 to European dreams” read a banner in the Steve Fletcher stand, marking the journey from the foot of the Football League to becoming a model, continental club. Milan visit next week, an occasion to further broaden the smile of Bill Foley, Bournemouth’s financier present in the posh seats. “A long time coming,” said Bournemouth’s long-serving captain, Adam Smith. “The fans were up for it, the players were up for it.”Europa League: Lyon take down Crystal Palace, Cissè’s Milan hat-trick sinks SalzburgRead moreBournemouth’s new head coach has described the chaos of English football, midfield areas that can resemble a rolling maul, but he has pledged to learn and adapt. “I believe in this team and know they are always confident despite a difficult situation,” Rose said. “If we stick together and play like this and we have our fans then we are hard to play and it’s hard to beat us. That’s what we should take into the next game.”Missing Eli Junior Kroupi so far this season, and lately Alex Scott, are regrettable problems within a small squad. Selling Scott for £80m in January, as has been speculated, speaks to the financial balancing act clubs such as Bournemouth must perform to progress. Following the5-1 loss to Chelsea, Sunday’s Premier League meeting with Sunderland was prioritised in team selection though the second-half introduction of key men, including Rayan, proved decisive.“Everyone deserves to play and it’s good for us for the busy weeks to have a competitive squad,” said Rose, who revealed Smith had given a speech to his teammates after the loss at Stamford Bridge. “That’s my captain.”View image in fullscreenRayan doubles Bournemouth’s lead six minutes after coming off the bench.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersSmith supplied the first proper chance. Marcus Tavernier, cutting inside, shanked that wide before a Ben Gannon-Doak cross from the byline saw Rodríguez misjudge the flight. The summer signing, still raw at 22, finds decent positions only for his touch to betray him. His penalty, following an inadvertent handball from Jon Gorenc Stankovic, was his first goal and should help his confidence.Graz, fourth in this season’s Österreichische Bundesliga, hardly exuded ambition, a defensive trio often morphing into a shell-like five. Amid such squeezed space, after a corner, Bournemouth had the ball in the net, for what seemed an own goal though it had struck Bafode Diakité’s arm. Tavernier struck the outside of a post, before Graz at last began to advance. The away contingent celebrated a penalty, but Belmin Beganovic was shown a yellow card for simulation. Fabio Ingolitsch, the Graz coach and a Rose protege, spoke to his own team’s realities by saying: “Bournemouth is the team with the biggest market value in theEuropa League.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNoah Sadiki stunner earns Sunderland dramatic late win against TorreenseRead moreAnother Smith cross supplied Evanilson’s goal, a header full of neck muscle looping off the angle for a first European goal celebrated in Boscombe. “Many more to come from him,” said Smith of the perpetual motion No 9. Graz fans sang whatever the game state, that being the continental way, but there became more to encourage them beyond the break. Simon Seidl’s shot whistled wide, Jürgen Heil struck a post before Jacob-Peter Hödl forced a remarkable reflex save from Djorde Petrovic on the rebound. The spectre of Premier League travails, where positive play has been unrewarded, loomed as Graz interchanges became crisper.The 70th-minute triple introduction of Rayan, Justin Kluivert and Ryan Christie proved to be Rose’s successful method of locking down midfield and increasing his team’s attacking threat at the same time.Rayan, a decent finisher when coming inside, snatched the contest from Austrian reach. Daniil Khudyakov, Graz’s Russian goalkeeper, first flapped at a corner and then got only a weak hand to the Brazilian’s drive through the proverbial forest of legs. Bournemouth’s European homecoming had been coupled with the victory the occasion had demanded.Explore more on these topicsEuropa LeagueBournemouthSturm Grazmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Noah Sadiki stunner earns Sunderland dramatic late win against Torreense | Europa League | The Guardian
description: The midfielder scored his first goal for Sunderland as Régis Le Bris’s side came back from a goal down to beat Torreense 2-1 in the Europa League
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: The midfielder scored his first goal for Sunderland as Régis Le Bris’s side came back from a goal down to beat Torreense 2-1 in the Europa League
Content: Noah Sadiki races away after his stoppage-time goal puts Sunderland ahead.Photograph: Rodrigo Antunes/ReutersView image in fullscreenNoah Sadiki races away after his stoppage-time goal puts Sunderland ahead.Photograph: Rodrigo Antunes/ReutersEuropa LeagueNoah Sadiki stunner earns Sunderland dramatic late win against TorreenseLouise Taylorat Estádio Municipal de LeiriaThu 15 Oct 2026 15.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 18.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree minutes into stoppage time Noah Sadiki hurdled a set of advertising hoardings, sprinted across a running track and hurled himself towards the ecstaticSunderlandfans.Just as those supporters’ long-awaited party in Portugal had looked in peril of falling a little flat, the Democratic Republic of the Congo midfielder capitalised on excellent work from Enzo Le Fée and Granit Xhaka to half-volley an eye-catching first goal for Régis Le Bris’s side.Europa League: Lyon take down Crystal Palace, Cissè’s Milan hat-trick sinks SalzburgRead moreIt ensured a largely unconvincing Sunderland came from behind to secure a second straightEuropa Leaguewin and their relief was evident as every outfield player followed Sadiki in vaulting those hoardings to join the celebrations.“It was a difficult game,” said Le Bris, Sunderland’s manager, with considerable understatement. “Torreense are a good team.”With their home ground too small to accommodate European football, Leiria’s stadium stood in. It proved quite some substitute. An arena overlooked by a 12th-century castle constructed to defend this attractive medieval town against reconquest by the Moors created an imposing backdrop to Sunderland’s first competitive trip to the continent for 53 years.Back in 1973 they were second division FA Cup holders. Torreense know the feeling. Having provoked widespread shock by beating Sporting to win the Portuguese Cup last spring, Luís Tralhão’s second-tier side relish their underdog status.After winning at Lillestrøm last month, Torreense aimed to keep the surprises coming and duly left a heavily rotated Sunderland trailing at the break. Le Bris had left, among others, Xhaka, Le Fée and Nordi Mukiele on the bench ahead of Sunday’s vital Premier League trip to Bournemouth. This reshuffle permitted Luke O’Nien, a survivor from League One days, to captain Sunderland at a ground transformed into a sea of red and white. Although only 4,000 official tickets were allocated to the visitors more were readily available locally and estimates suggested the formal allocation had doubled.As the sun dropped and the temperature fell from a high of 28C those fans watched a disjointed first half on Sunderland’s part. It seemed telling that the normally fairly impassive Le Bris looked distinctly, and unusually, irritated and frustrated at times.View image in fullscreenSunderland supporters enjoy their club’s first competitive trip to the continent for 53 years.Photograph: Ana Brigida/APGranted his humour was hardly helped by the referee’s penchant for detecting phantom Sunderland fouls but ominously Malick Fofana, a £30m summer signing from Lyon, struggled wide on the left. Ditto Nilson Angulo on the right wing.Torreense, 15th in Portugal’s second tier might not have been threatening Robin Roefs’s goal but they succeeded in blocking and clearing pretty much everything that came their way. Indeed Tralhão’s defence looked almost as well fortified as that ancient castle towering over them.Admittedly, midway through the first half Timur Tutierov, Sunderland’s centre-forward, thought he had headed the opener but that effort was disallowed due to shirt pulling on Omar Alderete’s part.Then, with the interval fast approaching, Le Bris adopted hand-on-hips mode as Torreense reminded everyone precisely why they have built such a giantkilling reputation by scoring with their first shot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt came from centre-back Volnei Feltes. With Sunderland losing concentration and standing off, he was permitted to advance unopposed before cutting in on his right foot and sending a sublime 20-yard curler into the top corner.Although Angulo forced Lucas Paes into a fine save he, like Fofana, was soon replaced as Le Bris made a quadruple substitution involving the introduction of Le Fée, Xhaka, Mukiele and Reinildo.This infusion of quality left Torreense a little groggy and the midfielder Jules Ahoka –a highly impressive 20-year-old £8.5m summer buy from Royal Antwerp – was able to equalise by heading his first goal for Sunderland courtesy of Mukiele’s deft dink.View image in fullscreenJules Ahoka scores Sunderland’s first goal against Torreense.Photograph: Luis Loureiro/ShutterstockWhen the lively Tutierov went down in the box, the referee immediately pointed to the spot. However, a linesman’s flag indicated an offside so it seemed there would be no penalty. Or at least not until the video assistant referee intervened – lengthily; the eventual conclusion was no offside, no foul and no penalty.No matter; when Le Fée dinked a gorgeous ball into the box and Xhaka played it into Sadiki’s path, the scorer waited for it to drop across him before applying the expert finishing touch on the half-volley.Explore more on these topicsEuropa LeagueTorreenseSunderlandmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Martínez apologises to Manchester United’s director of football Wilcox after outburst | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: The Manchester United defender has apologised for his criticism of Jason Wilcox after the Champions League defeat by Atlético Madrid
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: The Manchester United defender has apologised for his criticism of Jason Wilcox after the Champions League defeat by Atlético Madrid
Content: Lisandro Martínez claimed Michael Carrick had not had sufficient backing.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenLisandro Martínez claimed Michael Carrick had not had sufficient backing.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAManchester UnitedMartínez apologises to Manchester United’s director of football Wilcox after outburstDefender says sorry after talks with Michael CarrickAny disciplinary action will not be made public by clubJamie JacksonThu 15 Oct 2026 15.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 18.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLisandro Martínez has apologised for claiming that Jason Wilcox, Manchester United’s director of football,failed to strengthen sufficiently in the summer windowafter discussions with the manager, Michael Carrick, and club hierarchy on Thursday.While any disciplinary action taken against him will not be made public by the club, it is thought that Martínez has been fined.Martínez has drawn back the curtain on Manchester United’s ruinous ownership | Jonathan LiewRead moreThe defender’s apology came on Thursday evening after the 28-year-old failed to offer one when issuing an initial statement on Wednesday regarding his outburst following Tuesday’s2-0 Champions League loss at Atlético Madrid.He posted on Instagram: “Today I met with the club’s leadership and the manager. It was a very positive conversation, where we were able to exchange views and speak openly about what happened after Tuesday’s game.“Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity. The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise.”The apology is a considerable climbdown. After the Atlético defeat, Martínez was scathing of Wilcox and his recruitment in the last window.He said: “I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Wilcox]. As players we have to do more but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night. Last season we did everything, we created the base to create an amazing team.”Martínez claimed that Carrick had not been backed sufficiently. “I don’t think so. He does his best. You can’t keep changing, changing, changing the manager. What about other areas?” he said.While it is understood Martínez’s apology was his decision alone, United spent £155m in the market – all on midfielders, Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans, and Carlos Baleba, despite Wilcox targeting a left-back.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe wider squadagrees with Martínez’s stanceregarding recruitment and has been left frustrated following a poor start to the season, with Carrick under considerable pressure.A return of six points from six league games is United’s poorest since 1986 and Carrick’s side have already been eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Brighton.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Alex Scott quits Disney+ role as Women’s Champions League presenter | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Disney+ has paid tribute to Alex Scott’s contribution after the presenter decided to walk away to focus on other projects
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Disney+ has paid tribute to Alex Scott’s contribution after the presenter decided to walk away to focus on other projects
Content: Alex Scott at last month’s launch event for Disney+ coverage of the Women's Champions League.Photograph: Mike Marsland/Getty Images for Disney+View image in fullscreenAlex Scott at last month’s launch event for Disney+ coverage of the Women's Champions League.Photograph: Mike Marsland/Getty Images for Disney+Women's Champions LeagueAlex Scott quits Disney+ role as Women’s Champions League presenterScott walking away to focus on other projectsDisney+ was criticised after opening round this seasonExclusive byTom GarryThu 15 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlex Scott, the former Football Focus host, has left her role as a presenter of the Women’s Champions League coverage on Disney+.It is understood it was Scott’s decision to walk away and focus on other projects, including her new show, One More Word WSL, with her fellow former England internationals Anita Asante and Fara Williams.Scott had fronted the streaming platform’s coverage of the elite women’s European club competition since it obtained the rights in 2025. However, Disney’s production levels werecriticised after the opening roundfollowing a series of technical problems. These included an unscheduled advert break that interrupted the second half ofArsenal’s 1-0 win over HB Køgefor more than three minutes.FC Copenhagen Women have a ‘startup-like’ brand. Now they need resultsRead moreA spokesperson for Disney+ told the Guardian: “We would like to extend our sincere thanks to Alex Scott for her contribution to our coverage of the Uefa Women’s Champions League on Disney+. Her passion for the women’s game and the competition shone through throughout her time with us, and we are grateful for all she contributed. We wish her every success.”Scott, a former England and Arsenal defender and former contestant on the BBC’s Strictly Come Dancing and ITV’s I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, has also presented major sports shows for the BBC, including coverage of the 2020 Olympics. Scott’s representatives said: “Alex is grateful for the opportunities she has had to work with the team at Disney+ and hopes that they continue to work together in the future.”Scott presented the BBC’s Football Focus show for five seasons beforeits closure this year. At the start of this season’s Women’s Super League campaign she launched One More Word through her own production company, First Cap Productions, and has previously explained that show was createdin response to the BBC cancelling its weekly WSL highlights show.Scott, who turned 42 on Wednesday, toldthe Observer, this month: “I feel like there’s always an excuse about women’s football shows not working because of the viewership or needing to save money. Whereas I think if they are done right, they can work, if things are given a fresh idea or a fresh format, they can work.”In the same interview, discussing some of the criticism aimed at Disney’s Women’s Champions League coverage this term, Scott said: “Ultimately, do I agree with all the decisions that were made? Absolutely not. Did I try and advise? Yes, but I can only do so much.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“But nobody sees the conversations, the fights I have behind the scenes. But I can hold my head up and know that I’ve always tried my best for the greater good of women’s sport.”Sources have told the Guardian the presenter’s relationship with Disney remains positive. Disney, whose coverage is produced by ESPN, secured an exclusive five-year deal to broadcast the Women’s Champions League across European broadcast territories in 2025. It is understood its presenting team will continue to include Shebahn Aherne, Nedum Onuoha and Lianne Sanderson. The lineup includes commentators such as Vicki Sparks and Jacqui Oatley. The competition resumes on 28 October.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nation-swappers show Rugby League World Cup is up for grabs in fiery opener | Rugby League World Cup 2026 | The Guardian
description: Kalyn Ponga stars for New Zealand but Australia edge Sydney clash as tournament promises fireworks on the pitch as well as off
Author: Angus Fontaine
Headline: Kalyn Ponga stars for New Zealand but Australia edge Sydney clash as tournament promises fireworks on the pitch as well as off
Content: Reece Walsh tackles Kalyn Ponga, who defected to New Zealand despite playing for Australia’s juniors team.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenReece Walsh tackles Kalyn Ponga, who defected to New Zealand despite playing for Australia’s juniors team.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesSportblogRugby League World Cup 2026Nation-swappers show Rugby League World Cup is up for grabs in fiery openerKalyn Ponga stars for New Zealand but Australia edge Sydney clash as tournament promises fireworks on the pitch as well as offAngus FontaineThu 15 Oct 2026 08.57 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 08.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnder new rules introduced for this World Cup, nation-swapping is not only possible, it is virtually encouraged. And like the cheeseburger spring rolls at Allianz Stadium on Thursday night, it’s a culture clash that delights as many people as it offends. But based on the intensity of last night’s Cup opener, it’s players and fans who are the winners.Australian success is not guaranteed but who can stop the Rugby League World Cup hosts?Read moreFireworks. Lasers. Shimmering projections. Allianz Stadium was lit up like a Las Vegas casino. This was intended to be a bold new era for rugby league. They had rejigged the tournament format to distil the talent pool, reducing the competing nations from 16 to 10 and boiling down the number of matches from 31 to 18.View image in fullscreenThe players walk onto the pitch at Allianz Stadium in Sydney.Photograph: Mark Evans/EPALast night’s Trans-Tasman clash was a sell-out and the 40,000+ arena was bristling with fans in black jerseys, keen to watch an all-star Kiwis side stomp the hosts and stamp themselves as the true favourites to take the trophy. And despite Australia winning nine of the last 10 Cups,their victory last night was truly a great escape.The Kangaroos met the James Fisher-Harris-led haka in a boomerang formation, hoping to capture the throat-slitting menace of the Maori war dance and send it back on their TransTasman foes. Instead they got mugged straight out of the gates, Casey McLean scoring one of the all-time great Cup tries with an aerial twist touchdown.New Zealand were boasting their strongest ever squad, bolstered by a Knights duo. Dane Gagai had defected after seven Tests for the Kangaroos in 2017-18 thanks to his Māori mother Tania, and Kalyn Ponga, a junior Kangaroo in 2019 was making his international debut in the black, by virtue of his Māori descent through father, Andre.Although he later finished with a broken arm that will rule him out of the tournament, Ponga rose to the storied occasion with anextraordinary individual performance. He created havoc every time he touched the ball, ghosting behind the lines, slipping and sliding out of tackles, picking up where he left off from his grand final heroics. Ponga scored two tries and should have had a third but for an incredible last-gasp tackle.The man who made that tackle was every bit Ponga’s equal. Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters had controversially given Reece Walsh first jump at the No 1 jersey over Clive Churchill medallist and premiership-winning captain, James Tedesco. Despite the diamond-eyed Broncos dynamo being sidelined two months, the gamble paid off in spades.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMen’s Rugby League World Cup 2026: group-by-group previewRead moreNot only did Walsh save Ponga’s near-try in the 36th minute to keep the Kangaroos in the contest, he then scored one of his own in the second half, hitting a Jack Bostock short ball at warp speed and then humiliating the converging defence to streak away and score in the corner. It was a mind-bending solo try in a spine-tingling return to the game’s centre stage.Although the Kangaroos prevailed 24-22 in the end, it was more arse than class. They stayed in the contest on the back of two runaway first-half tries, one to Jack Bostock – a Test debutant who scored three in the end – and another to Tom Trbojevic who streaked 90 metres to score in an otherwise rusty performance.Turbo’s vaunted centre partnership with Latrell Mitchell – a famous Origin success story – also fizzled with the erratic Rabbitohs star delivering little impact all night. Mitchell was bettered by Gagai for most of the Test and the pair’s lack of potency, albeit with poor ball from Harry Grant and Mitchell Moses, may force Walters to make several big calls for Australia’s next game against a fired-up Fiji on Sunday week.Friday night’s game is another clash of contrasting storylines. This World Cup was originally intended to be staged in France in 2025 but when Les Bleus couldn’t sniff a profit, Australia stepped in as hosts. The Trent Robinson-directed French take on Samoa, the 2022 runners-up, whose 2025 Test with Tonga drew 40,000 fans.England v Tonga on Saturday is another mouthwatering duel. The Kristian Woolf coached Tonga - whose two matches against Australia in the 2024 Pacific Championships drew crowds of 33,000 and 28,000 - have been especially rewarded in the international lolly scramble and are many pundit’s dark horse to shake up this 16th edition of the tournament.Until this year, players who had represented Tier 1 nations Australia, New Zealand or England, were unable to play for other nations. Rugby league’s diaspora are swearing new allegiances and reassembling under new colours. Players are honouring the ties that bind and the blood in their veins. Loyalties are up for grabs. And so is this World Cup.Explore more on these topicsRugby League World Cup 2026SportblogAustralia rugby leagueNew Zealand rugby leagueAustralia sportRugby leaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The one that got away: Tom Willis back to show what England are missing | Bordeaux Bègles | The Guardian
description: Bordeaux No8 takes on Gloucester in the Champions Cup on Friday after a spectacular start to the season for the title holders underlined the hole he will leave Borthwick for the World Cup
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Bordeaux No8 takes on Gloucester in the Champions Cup on Friday after a spectacular start to the season for the title holders underlined the hole he will leave Borthwick for the World Cup
Content: Tom Willis has been described as an ‘incredible competitor’.Photograph: Icon Sport/AlamyView image in fullscreenTom Willis has been described as an ‘incredible competitor’.Photograph: Icon Sport/AlamyBordeaux BèglesThe one that got away: Tom Willis back to show what England are missingBordeaux No 8 takes on Gloucester in Champions Cup to underline hole he will leave Borthwick for the World CupGerard MeagherThu 15 Oct 2026 12.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSwines are swirling above Twickenham, the cows have returned to their roots and hell is an icy sub-zero. Steve Borthwick has been given a free pass to pick one player based outside England. The consensus is that Jack Willis – Toulouse captain and two‑time Top 14 player of the season – would be the obvious choice. The smart money, however, would be on Borthwick picking brother Tom in a flash.For clarity, this is not going to happen. It is not World Cup season without acause celebrebut the reality is that you, dear reader, have more chance of selection. Still, the story of the younger Willis warrants re-examining. Firstly because hisdecision to head for Franceafter receiving an enhanced contract was unprecedented. Secondly because for Bordeaux he is pulling up trees, forests and anything else in his way this season. England’s No 8 depth is shallow and Willis is the type of player Borthwick would give his right arm for. AfterBordeaux have begun their Champions Cup defenceat Gloucester on Friday, chances are his left too.England boosted with Feyi-Waboso on track for Nations ChampionshipRead more“He’s an incredible competitor,” Bordeaux’s attack coach Noel McNamara says. “You can talk all you want about the technical and tactical but sometimes it’s just about desire. He won an aerial battle a couple weeks ago that I showed to the backs. Tom just wanted that ball, he’s an unbelievable competitor more than anything else. The Top 14 is incredibly competitive, because of relegation, because of the JIFF rule [which limits the number of foreign players]. That adds its own pressure and it’s not for everybody. We knew what we were getting, not just the player, he’s a fantastic human being.”Willis’s decision will not have been easy but by the time he informed Borthwick, shortly before the 2025 autumn internationals, his mind was made up despite having received the enhanced contract worth £150,000 a couple of months earlier. As someone who could offer ball-carrying heft, hard yards, Willis was a dead cert for the plane to Australia in 2027. Borthwick’s decision to leave him out immediately was equally difficult but he felt there was no choice with less than two yearsuntil the World Cup.What message would he have sent had he not?View image in fullscreenTom Willis’ brother Jack (above) seems the obvious choice for Steve Borthwick.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PA“I understand both sides, I understand the benefits for the [Prem], and I knew the rules before making my choice. I have no problem with it,” Willistold Midi Olympique last weekwhen asked about England’s selection policy. “There are strong arguments on both sides. Some say it’s bad, others that it’s necessary. I could have stayed in England to remain eligible, but I decided to leave.”It is clear Willis felt a strong draw to Bordeaux and there are obvious reasons why. After Wasps went bust he joined the club on a short‑term deal in November 2022 before moving to Saracens the following summer. He arrived in France just after the head coach, Christophe Urios, had left, did not speak French and had never lived alone before. The personal growth those circumstances precipitated meant that Willis had a deep-rooted connection with the club. It helps, too, they are one of Europe’s leading lights, the money is good and the lifestyle appeals. The opportunity to be close to Jack was an enormous factor too. The Willis family is exceptionally tight-knit.It is less clear precisely when in 2025 Bordeaux planted the seed. Saracens, for their part, were desperate to keep him. His first season in north London was disrupted by a knee injury but his second was mightily impressive. One performance against the Bulls in December 2024 stood out. Willis had been challenged to perform at “an elevated level” after being overlooked for the autumn Tests. Against the Bulls, he knocked a few Springboks around like they were nine-pins.By the 2025 Six Nations, Borthwick had been convinced. Willis had one cap in a World Cup warm-up match against Wales but returned to the fold initially as a replacement against Ireland. “I felt like I had not had a proper crack at playing for England and that is really what I wanted to do,” he said at the time. Starts followed in victories over France, Scotland and Italy but while Willis did little wrong, there was a feeling he wasn’t quite reaching his best at Test level. He was back on the bench against Wales and while a regular in the matchday 23, he had not managed to force his way into the British & Irish Lions conversation.View image in fullscreenTom Willis impresses for Bordeaux as he crashes through Lyon’s defence.Photograph: Philippe Lopez/AFP/Getty ImagesThen came the 2025 tour of Argentina and the USA. With Tom Curry, Ben Earl and Henry Pollock away, with less spotlight on England, Willis shone. His performances against the Pumas were emphatic and a few months later, Borthwick rewarded him with an enhanced deal. Willis had made strides when some of the bigger fish were away, when the pond was a little smaller.The suggestion is Willis does not possess self-belief by the bucketload as someone like Earl does, that he needs the odd reminder of his talents. Maybe the environment in Argentina was perfect for him then, particularly with the presence of Lee Blackett on the coaching staff. But speak to those who know him well and they reject any sense of timidity wholeheartedly. There may be a hint of shyness but “deep-thinking” and “diligent” are the words that come up. That he was spotted at Bordeaux’s base finishing a French lesson at 5pm recently bears that out.It also says much about Willis that in his third and final season with Saracens, despite his impending move, he was named Prem player of the year, producing more carries and beating more defenders than anyone in the league. Bordeaux evidently know how to harness those talents but McNamara cautions against pigeon-holing. “Jack is perceived as more of a defensive player and Tom as offensive but we can be very reductive,” says McNamara. “Against Clermont recently Tom had four turnovers. He’s a very smart player, he’s got leadership capabilities. He is doing that with his actions and he’s learning the language diligently so he can express himself.”The way Willis is performing does not suggest any regrets but if there is a tinge of sadness it is that we cannot be sure if he knew or understood quite how highly Borthwick regarded him at the very point Bordeaux turned his head. That is neither’s fault, it merely shows the importance of timing. The upshot is one of the most talented English players of his generation will not grace the World Cup stage next year. It is a testament to Willis’ character, however, that he left little open to interpretation when recently asked if he did not get a fair crack of the whip. “I did get the opportunities, and I was delighted to have them,” he said. “I have no issue with the coaching staff. I simply chose something different.”Explore more on these topicsBordeaux BèglesGloucesterRugby unionEngland rugby union teamChampions CupfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Apologetic Infantino ‘not fit’ to lead Fifa, claim European FA heads after meeting | Fifa | The Guardian
description: European football leaders are increasingly confident they will find a candidate to stand against Gianni Infantino in next year’s Fifa presidential election
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: European football leaders are increasingly confident they will find a candidate to stand against Gianni Infantino in next year’s Fifa presidential election
Content: Gianni Infantino faced critics at the Fifa council meeting in Zurich.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino faced critics at the Fifa council meeting in Zurich.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersFifaApologetic Infantino ‘not fit’ to lead Fifa, claim European FA heads after meetingInfantino failed to provide answers to questionsEuropean leaders expect someone will stand against himMatt Hughesin Zurich andNick AmesThu 15 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 15.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean football leaders are increasingly confident they will find a candidate to stand againstGianni Infantinoin next year’s Fifa presidential election, with the heads of the English and German football associations questioning his fitness to govern after a three-and-a-half-hour council meeting.Infantino began the long-awaited gathering of Fifa’s 37-strong executive board by apologising for failing to consult them over hisabandoned World Cup sell-off planbut failed to provide answers to dozens of questions posed by the European FAs on a range of subjects including the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal,Donald Trump’s Fifa peace prizeand theFolarin Balogun affair, when the USA striker’s World Cup suspension was overturned after lobbying from the US president.Infantino’s apology was followed by a 30-minute presentation on FFE from two American lawyers, who described the $20bn (£15.1bn) valuation and proposed sale of a 20% stake to Thrive Capital as a good deal forFifa. At the insistence of some attenders, the lawyers were asked to leave the meeting after they had presented. When questioned, one of them confirmed he had been commissioned and paid by Fifa to produce a review of FFE.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“The main objective for Gianni was to survive this meeting and nothing more,” one council member told the Guardian.Council members succeeded in deferring, until they receive more information on Balogun, a Fifa proposal to amend its disciplinary regulations by removing the scope for players shown a straight red card to have it rescinded. Infantino pledged to provide that information by their next meeting in Doha on 16 December, after nominations close on 18 November for March’s presidential election.The issue of whether the Fifa peace prize will be revived this year or Trump left as a standalone winner has been referred to Fifa’s social responsibility committee, and the Asian Football Confederation president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, has been appointed to chair a new committee examining governance reform. But otherwise the meeting broke up without tangible answers, to the frustration of the English FA’s chair, Debbie Hewitt.“We didn’t get answers to anything that we had specifically requested,” Hewitt said. “I think the man [Infantino] has to answer those questions, and if he doesn’t answer those questions, he’s not fit to be Fifa president. That was what was shared in the meeting.”The German FA’s president, Bernd Neuendorf, went further by calling for wholesale reforms of Fifa’s administration, which he hopes will fall within the purview of Sheikh Salman’s governance committee.“The whole administration has to be reformed and the whole governance has to be reformed,” Neuendorf said. “But I’m pretty clear here that this is not possible with Gianni as the responsible person at Fifa. So we need a complete restart, I think, a political restart of persons who represent Fifa.“Yes he apologised, but I didn’t have the feeling that this apology was because of the FFE project in total. My impression was it was just because it wasn’t brought forward to the council and no one was involved.”Neuendorf also said he was “very confident” that an alternative candidate would be found to stand against Infantino, a view shared by senior figures atUefa, who expect a late declaration to limit the amount of time for Fifa to scupper the nomination.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe respective presidents of the three continental confederations who have called for Infantino to go – Aleksander Ceferin of Uefa, Victor Montagliani of Concacaf and Sheikh Salman – have ruled themselves out and suggestions that high-profile figures such as Arsène Wenger or Michele Kang could put themselves forward have been dismissed.A proposal to distribute $3.5bn (£2.6bn) from Fifa’s financial reserves, which would involve each national association receiving $25m over the next four-year cycle, was approved by council.Montagliani is also understood to have been critical of Infantino, but Fifa’s president received strong support from council members from Asia and Africa.“I am certain that Gianni Infantino is the right president,” Ahmed Yahya, president of the Mauritania Football Federation said. “The majority want Gianni Infantino to stay. After finally withdrawing this proposal, president Gianni Infantino apologised to the members of the executive committee. This was followed by a responsible debate, during which this issue was more or less shelved.“In the interests of football, the executive committee is looking ahead and seeking solutions, by focusing on the good aspects that football has to offer and trying to move forward.”Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsUefaThe FAnewsShareReuse this content

title: Eritrea accuses Shabana Mahmood of ‘political gimmick’ over visa ban threat | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Home secretary says she will block all Eritreans from UK unless a returns deal is agreed for rejected asylum seekers and criminals
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Home secretary says she will block all Eritreans from UK unless a returns deal is agreed for rejected asylum seekers and criminals
Content: Shabana Mahmood: ‘My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK.’Photograph: Marcin Nowak/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood: ‘My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK.’Photograph: Marcin Nowak/Anadolu/Getty ImagesImmigration and asylumEritrea accuses Shabana Mahmood of ‘political gimmick’ over visa ban threatHome secretary says she will block all Eritreans from UK unless a returns deal is agreed for rejected asylum seekers and criminalsRajeev SyalandDiane TaylorThu 15 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShabana Mahmood has been accused of launching a “perfunctory political gimmick” by the Eritrean government in a row over the return of rejected asylum seekers and criminals.After the home secretary threatened to block all Eritreans from entering the UK unless a returns deal was agreed, the country’s embassy claimed the UK had failed to engage in “meaningful and appropriate” dialogue.The spat began on Thursday morning when theHome Officeclaimed the east African country had abruptly withdrawn cooperation on the return of unwanted citizens earlier this year.From Thursday, diplomats from the east African country also face restrictions on their movement outside London and VIPs will be stripped of access to fast-track visas as preferential processing is scrapped.It prompted a statement from Eritrea’s north London embassy “categorically” rejecting Mahmood’s claims.“Despite Eritrea’s repeated requests for constructive discussion with relevant UK authorities on the dignified return of its citizens, the UK has shown no interest to engage in meaningful and appropriate dialogue,” it said.Describing the home secretary’s decision as regrettable, the statement added: “The act is nothing more than a perfunctory political gimmick. The fact is, the UK has not issued a single visa to an Eritrean official since 2023.”UK government officials denied this. They insisted a confirmed exemption from immigration control for an Eritrean official took place as recently as August 2026.Sources said Eritrea previously cooperated with the UK on returns between 2024 and March 2026, while the UK has repeatedly sought to engage with Eritrean authorities, including repeatedly offering to send a Home Office delegation to Asmara to discuss returns.A Home Office spokesperson said: “The Eritrean government’s press notice misrepresents the UK’s position and contains numerous factual inaccuracies.”Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat in the year ending June 2026. Returns arrangements are vital for removing people who have been refused asylum and foreign criminals.Graph showing cumulative number of arrivals to the UK in small boats by nationality since January 2025, with those from Eritrea being the largest numberMahmood said on Thursday morning: “Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused.“My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK. I will not hesitate to impose further measures on other countries refusing to cooperate.”The move followed similar threats of visa sanctions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2025.Angola and Namibia subsequently agreed to cooperate with demands on migrant returns, while the DRC faced visa restrictions before reaching an agreement with the UK in February.In March, ministers also placed an emergency brake on visas for nationals from four countries after the home secretary accused them of exploiting Britain’s generosity to claim asylum.Study visas for nationals from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan were also halted, as were work visas for Afghans.Just over 100 refused asylum seekers from Eritrea have been deported – a figure comprising less than 4% of the 2,626 people whose claims were rejected in the past four years. Nearly 6,000 Eritreans have reached the UK across the Channel in the year to June, the highest number of any nationality.After the success of the previous sanction threats, Mahmood warned other countries that they faced similar visa restrictions if they continued to refuse to take back their criminals, illegal migrants and rejected asylum seekers.India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Somalia, Egypt and Gabon have been identified as resistant to taking back illegal migrants and could face sanctions.Madeleine Sumption, the director of theMigrationObservatory at Oxford University, said roughly 7,000 applications for asylum came from Eritreans, about 8% of the total.About 84% were successful on first application and more would be successful on appeal, she said.“There are different types of threats that can be made such as stopping student visas, or stopping visit visas. It will be interesting to see what kind of impact this has on the number of returns.”Reacting to Mahmood’s announcement, one Eritrean asylum seeker said any returnees would “be put in prison and may never be able to get out”.The advocacy group Justice for Eritreans condemned the announcement. “Many Eritreans have fled indefinite national service, arbitrary detention and severe human rights abuses,” it said. “These risks cannot be ignored for the sake of immigration targets. Refugee protection is a legal responsibility, not a political bargaining tool.”UN experts say the human rights situation in Eritrea continues to be dire. Mohamed Abdelsalam Babiker, the special rapporteur on human rights in Eritrea, said there were no signs of meaningful improvement in the country’s human rights situation.“There remain reasonable grounds to believe that crimes against humanity continue in Eritrea,” he said whenlaunching a reportthis year into the human rights situation.“Regrettably, the core human rights issues that prompted the creation of this mandate 14 years ago remain mostly unresolved.“The ongoing systematic, and widespread enforced disappearance and prolonged incommunicado detention without charge or trial, torture, and the persecution of political opponents, journalists, and members of religious communities remain central features of governance in Eritrea.”Steve Valdez-Symonds, Amnesty International’s policy lead on refugee and migrant rights, said: “As Amnesty and others have documented, Eritrea has an appalling human rights record.“It has not become any less unsafe following the election in this country of a Labour government in 2024 or Shabana Mahmood beginning her term at the Home Office in 2025.”Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said: “Severe political repression and widespread human rights abuses are the reason people are forced to flee Eritrea, and are, in the vast majority of cases, recognised by our government as in need of support.“It’s imperative that this policy only targets the Eritrean authorities, and does not undermine the UK’s moral and legal duty to provide protection to those who need it.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumEritreaShabana MahmoodMigrationRefugeesHome OfficenewsShareReuse this content

title: Lee Child backs launch of reading scheme to send prisons half a million books | Books | The Guardian
description: The Jack Reacher author, the UK’s first prison reading laureate, said drive to improve literacy skills was a practical way to address reoffending and support rehabilitation
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: The Jack Reacher author, the UK’s first prison reading laureate, said drive to improve literacy skills was a practical way to address reoffending and support rehabilitation
Content: ‘Proper books, proper storytellers’ … author Lee Child, third right, and Jake Richards MP talk to inmates in HMP Doncaster.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Proper books, proper storytellers’ … author Lee Child, third right, and Jake Richards MP talk to inmates in HMP Doncaster.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianBooksLee Child backs launch of reading scheme to send prisons half a million booksThe Jack Reacher author, the UK’s first prison reading laureate, said drive to improve literacy skills was a practical way to address reoffending and support rehabilitationEmma LoffhagenThu 15 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly half a million books will be distributed across prisons in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland this autumn, in a campaign backed by bestselling thriller writerLee Child.The initiative, delivered by the Reading Agency charity as part of its Quick Reads programme, will see copies of 11 short books distributed, with titles selected with input from prisoners as well as staff. A book will be distributed to every cell across the prison estate, as well as stock sent to prison libraries.Child, the UK’s first prison reading laureate, said the initiative was intended to address the “revolving door” – people leaving prison but struggling to cope outside and returning to custody.“If we can stop one in 10 of those people from coming back, that would be a major achievement,” he said. “It would be good for society as a whole, not just for that individual prisoner and their future employer.”Ministry of Justice statistics for 2024-25 show that 65% of initial-assessment results across public prisons in England, based on tests taken when people entered custody, were at entry levels 1-3,below the standardexpected of a typical GCSE student.Child said people who wanted to turn their lives around after prison could face compounded barriers if they had difficulty reading. “The obvious beneficiary will be somebody who is [in prison] due to some kind of mistake or unfortunate circumstance that they regret, and who wants to go straight afterwards and never come back,” he said. “But they face the problem of finding a job if they’ve got a conviction, and on top of that, if they’ve got poor literacy skills.”Everyday tasks could also become obstacles, he said. “You can’t read a lease if you want to rent a flat; you can’t deal with utilities or a TV licence if you can’t read the official notices.”The Quick Reads collection spans crime and thrillers, memoir, wellbeing, and a creative writing guide. Fiction titles include High Heat by Child himself; Cell One, a Lagos-set thriller by Leye Adenle; and Darkness Rising, from Bradford-based crime writer AA Dhand’s Harry Virdee series. Other books includeLemn Sissay’s memoir My Name Is Why, Andy McNab’s Today Everything Changes and Dr Alex George’s The Mind Manual. Authors featured also include Dreda Say Mitchell, Fiona Cummins, Cathy Rentzenbrink andAlex Wheatle.Child, who has made between 30 and 40 prison visits since beginning his work as laureate last year, said one of the most common explanations he heard from people who did not read was that the books they had been given at school were boring. Quick Reads, he said, offers an alternative. “They are proper books, proper storytellers, and there’s nothing simple or childish about them, they’re just short.”He added that improving access to books should be understood not as a soft approach to criminal justice but as a practical way to support rehabilitation and reduce reoffending. “The problem with public reaction to this kind of thing is a rather kneejerk reaction of ‘soft on crime’,” he said. “My point is that no, it’s actually hard on crime. It is focusing on where the budget and attention should really be.”Alongside distributing the books, the Reading Agency will organise author-led workshops, creative writing activities, content for National Prison Radio and resources for prison libraries, education teams and peer supporters. The initiative is funded by the Henry Smith Foundation, a poverty-focused non-profit.AA Dhand, whose Darkness Rising is among the selected books, said: “Books should be accessible to everyone, regardless of their circumstances or their previous relationship with reading.”View image in fullscreen‘Reading can build confidence, create empathy’ … AA Dhand.Dhand added: “In prison, reading can provide far more than temporary escape. It can build confidence, create empathy and give people the opportunity to see the world and themselves differently. If the right book reaches the right person at the right moment, it can open a door that may otherwise have remained closed.”Karen Napier, chief executive ofthe Reading Agency, said the programme was built with the intention of giving people in prison choice over what they read.“When we put a book directly into someone’s hands, we are offering more than words on a page,” she said. “Reading can offer escape, connection and space for reflection, while supporting wellbeing, confidence and learning. We want as many people as possible to have the opportunity to find a book that grabs them and discover where reading might take them.”Explore more on these topicsBooksLee ChildfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: France drops opposition to UK being included in ‘Made in Europe’ legislation | European Union | The Guardian
description: British government must however align with the European Union’s position over tariffs on Chinese EVs
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: British government must however align with the European Union’s position over tariffs on Chinese EVs
Content: The UK’s trade minister says Britain and the EU must ‘work together and act in lockstep’ to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.Photograph: Florence Lo/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe UK’s trade minister says Britain and the EU must ‘work together and act in lockstep’ to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.Photograph: Florence Lo/ReutersEuropean UnionFrance drops opposition to UK being included in ‘Made in Europe’ legislationBritish government must however align with the European Union’s position over tariffs on Chinese EVsLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentThu 15 Oct 2026 15.28 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 18.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrance has dropped its opposition to the UK being included in the EU’s “Made in Europe” legislation as long as the British government aligns with the bloc’s position over tariffs on Chinese EVs.In a breakthrough for Andy Burnham, France on Thursday came round to backing Germany, which has always supported the UK’s calls to be designated European for the purposes of the Industrial Accelerator Act. The legislation, which is in its draft stage, is designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition.According to a joint Franco-German paper seen by the Guardian, the two countries are now proposing that for the car industry specifically the UK could be included in Made in Europe.“For the automotive sector, ‘Made in Europe’ should comprise the EU27 and an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 01/01/2020, subject to an agreement on full reciprocity – i.e. adopting the European preference scheme relevant to the automotive sector,” it says in a clear reference to the UK, which was still in the single market as an EU member in January 2020.It would also include Norway, which is in the single market but not a member of the EU.The paper added that the opt-in would come with conditions, including alignment on trade defence measures, which have included tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the EU in 2024 and any future trade barriers, such as the quota deal being finalised withChinaon its exports of hybrid cars.The paper says that “as well as relevant anti-circumvention measures”, these “opt-in” countries would have to accept “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.Liam Byrne, the chair of the UK’s business, innovation, science and trade committee, said he believed aligning with the EU on trade defence measures was a small price to pay to save British manufacturing.“Sometimes politics is the least worst choice – aligning with Europe on trade defence against an over-subsidised China is the way we deliver for all of us,” he said.“Tariffs on these would be a small price to pay for the protection of a European manufacturing industry which safeguards jobs across supply chains in the UK and makes us less prone to coercion from China in the future.”On Wednesday the head of Mercedes implored EU leaders to let the UK join the package.Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial Made in Europe legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt”the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz said.The UK has been under pressure for weeks to align with the EU on tariffs on Chinese vehicles, but this week the business secretary Jonathan Reynolds said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.However the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK was locked out of supply chains in the EU.Earlier on Thursday trade minister Anas Sarwar hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs.He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.Bernd Lange, the chair of the European parliament’s influential international trade committee, told the Guardian the UK should “of course” be included in the Made in Europe legislation, calling France’s opposition “not rational”.A Downing Street spokesperson said it had yet to see the detail but saw the development as positive. “This is a Franco-German proposal and there is still a European process to run, but if confirmed, we welcome the objective to have UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act and this would be good news for the British automotive industry and the jobs and investment it supports across the UK.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionTrade policyAutomotive industryManufacturing sectorElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsBrexitChinaShareReuse this content

title: Top health official urged to recuse herself from private ADHD crackdown over ties to industry | Health policy | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Four MPs raise conflict of interest concerns over Samantha Jones’s past links to a big provider of ADHD assessments
Author: Anna Bawden
Headline: Exclusive: Four MPs raise conflict of interest concerns over Samantha Jones’s past links to a big provider of ADHD assessments
Content: Samantha Jones is responsible for overseeing the implementation of government decisions on health policy as the DHSC’s permanent secretary.Photograph: Andrew Parsons/No 10 Downing StreetView image in fullscreenSamantha Jones is responsible for overseeing the implementation of government decisions on health policy as the DHSC’s permanent secretary.Photograph: Andrew Parsons/No 10 Downing StreetHealth policyTop health official urged to recuse herself from private ADHD crackdown over ties to industryExclusive: Four MPs raise conflict of interest concerns over Samantha Jones’s past links to a big provider of ADHD assessmentsDenis CampbellandAnna BawdenThu 15 Oct 2026 11.35 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 10.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA senior civil servant should play no part in ministers’ crackdown on private attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism clinics because of her recent ties to the industry, MPs have said.Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs are demanding that Samantha Jones, the permanent secretary at the Department ofHealthand Social Care (DHSC), steps away from any role in plans to toughen regulation of the booming market in private neurodiversity assessments.They say Jones should not be involved because of her links to a company that is one of the biggest providers of NHS-funded neurodiversity assessments, which earned it £26m from the health service in England over the past six years.Ministers are drawing up plans for how to better regulate the “wild west” of private clinics offering assessment, diagnosis and treatment of ADHD and autism that has grown rapidly in recent years as people have struggled to access care via the NHS.The push comes after the government last week accepted thefindings of a reviewby Prof Peter Fonagy, which raised concerns about the “consistency and quality” of assessments by private providers of neurodiversity services that had inbuilt “financial incentives” to diagnose and treat people.NHS faces exodus of ADHD and autism services staff to private clinicsRead moreJones is responsible for overseeing the implementation of government decisions on health policy. She would therefore be expected to advise ministers on how best to strengthen the regulation of private providers of ADHD and autism services. Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, has vowed to introduce a much tougher regime.Four MPs have called for Jones to recuse herself from any role in those decisions because of her previous ties toADHD360, a provider of neurodiversity services. Her links to the private ADHD sector represent a serious conflict of interest, they claim.Jones was appointed as the permanent secretary on 22 April 2025. A month later, she was still thechairof and adirectorof andshareholderin the private care provider Keys Group when, on 16 May, it bought ADHD360, a clinic that has increased its NHS income considerably in recent years.At the time of the £22.5m purchase, Jones was also an operating partner inG Square Capital, the private equity company that owns Keys Group.Shesoldher shares in Keys Group andresignedher roles there and at G Square Capital before she started at the DHSC on 16 June. Jones has alreadyrecused herselffrom involvement in the department’s decision over whether to extendPalantir’s £330m, seven-year contractwith the NHS because of her past work for the lobbyists Carnall Farrar, which advised Palantir regarding the contract.MPs believe her tenure at Keys Group could represent a conflict of interest. Ben Coleman, a Labour MP on the health and social care committee, said: “People will want to feel reassured that future regulation of private ADHD and autism assessments is beyond reproach. Given her recent close involvement with ADHD360, I would encourage Ms Jones to recuse herself from that work, as she has done over Palantir, to avoid any perception of a conflict of interest.”In June, Jones apologised after she wasreprimanded by the Civil Service Commissionfor breaching lobbying rules by failing to ask the (now defunct) Advisory Committee on Business Appointments for prior approval before undertaking work for four healthcare companies.Helen Morgan, the Liberal Democrats’ health spokesperson, said: “Given Sam Jones oversaw the multimillion-pound acquisition of ADHD360 just weeks before entering the Department of Health, ministers must ensure she recuses herself immediately, just as she has over Palantir.”Jones, 55, was widely admired in the NHS when she ran West Hertfordshire NHS trust in 2013-15. After a role with NHS England, she began working in private healthcare. Boris Johnson as prime minister handed her a key role in Downing Street in 2021. She returned to private health in 2023 and by 2023-24 had paid roles or shareholdings in 13 health or consultancy organisations.Clive Lewis, the Labour MP for Norwich South, said Jones’s deep involvement in private healthcare meant she should not have been made DHSC permanent secretary in the first place, saying: “It just defies logic that anyone thought it was a good idea. Surely this must have come up during her recruitment process?”Jones did not answer questions put by the Guardian. The NHS has paid ADHD360 just over £26m for its services since 2020, according to figures supplied by the Tussell public expenditure database. “When it comes to the government’s response to the [Fonagy] review, there should be no suggestion that the top NHS official is being influenced by any past or current links to a major private provider of NHS ADHD services,” said Stella Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow. “This issue is too sensitive and complex to permit any conflicts of interest. As a result the permanent secretary should recuse herself from this area of policy.”David Rowland, the director of the Centre for Health and the Public Interest thinktank, said: “The permanent secretary at the department which has responsibility for regulating private ADHD providers appears to have a conflict of interest in this area and so may struggle to remain impartial when it comes to implementing the recommendations made by Prof Fonagy.”A DHSC spokesperson said: “There is no conflict of interest. The permanent secretary has appropriately declared all interests, in this post and when she was a non-executive director [of the DHSC]. She resigned from all her private sector posts before taking on the permanent secretary role at the department.”Explore more on these topicsHealth policyCivil serviceNeurodiversityAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderAutismHealthPrivate healthcarenewsShareReuse this content

title: Neanderthal remains may be earliest human ancestor find killed by a spear | Neanderthals | The Guardian
description: Adult excavated in an Iraqi Kurdistan cave died more than 70,000 years ago and bears ‘kill shot’ shoulder wound
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Adult excavated in an Iraqi Kurdistan cave died more than 70,000 years ago and bears ‘kill shot’ shoulder wound
Content: The left shoulder blade revealed three fractures spreading out from the 1.5cm-wide hole and fragments of bone that filled the wound.Photograph: University of CambridgeView image in fullscreenThe left shoulder blade revealed three fractures spreading out from the 1.5cm-wide hole and fragments of bone that filled the wound.Photograph: University of CambridgeNeanderthalsNeanderthal remains may be earliest human ancestor find killed by a spearAdult excavated in an Iraqi Kurdistan cave died more than 70,000 years ago  and bears ‘kill shot’ shoulder woundIan SampleScience editorThu 15 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA smooth round hole in the shoulder blade of a Neanderthal who died more than 70,000 years ago may be the oldest evidence so far of a human ancestor being killed by a wooden spear.Archaeologists spotted the distinctive injury after excavating skeletal remains of the adult and otherNeanderthalsfrom under nearly 8 metres of rock and sediment in the Shanidar cave in Iraqi Kurdistan.At least five Neanderthals were buried at the same spot over several years, in a depression no larger that a fridge that ran behind a huge boulder near the entrance to the cave.
