Some of the bodies appear to have been laid on top of others that were still decomposing.“They’re coming back to the same spot to place bodies over a number of years or several decades and that’s really quite unusual in in the Neanderthal archaeological record,” said Dr Emma Pomeroy, a biological anthropologist at theUniversity of Cambridge. “It suggests there’s some kind of meaningful behaviour in depositing the dead there.”View image in fullscreenArchaeologists spotted the distinctive injury after excavating skeletal remains of Neanderthals in Shanidar cave, Iraqi Kurdistan.Photograph: Prof Graeme BarkerResearchers found only partial remains of the injured Neanderthal, an adult aged about 45. The left shoulder blade that bears the wound was found with seven teeth, several ribs and fragments, and a near complete right hand that was leaning against the boulder.Close inspection of the shoulder blade revealed three fractures spreading out from the 1.5cm-wide hole and fragments of bone that filled the wound. The shards were probably punched out of the thin bone when the spear hit, the scientists said.The circular shape of the hole and the pattern of bone damage strongly suggest a wound inflicted by a wooden spear striking the body from the front.But whether it was a hunting accident or an intentional attack – a brutal jab from a foe, perhaps – is impossible to know.Pomeroy said the position of the wound and the force needed to push the spear through the chest, where it would have punctured the lung and probably severed arteries before punching out of the shoulder blade, pointed to a “kill shot” directed at the heart. “I don’t think that’s something you do accidentally,” she said.The spear wound was almost certainly lethal, but the individual was in bad shape before the fatal blow. Examination of the teeth revealed a lower incisor split vertically, leaving only half in place, its neighbours twisted inwards, according to details published inScientific Reports.View image in fullscreenExamination found the Neanderthal had a split-tooth caked in hardened plaque. ‘You’d need quite a severe hit in the face to split a tooth like that,’ said Dr Emma Pomeroy from Cambridge University.Photograph: Dr Emma Pomeroy“You’d need quite a severe hit in the face to split a tooth like that and to rotate the others,” said Pomeroy. “They might well have needed help because they would have been in terrible pain.” The split tooth was caked in hardened plaque that would have taken at least a year to build up.Chris Hunt, the emeritus professor at Liverpool John Moores University, who co-authored the paper, said Neanderthals at Shanidar were taking ibex as their main prey and could have used wooden spears shaped like modern javelins to kill the animals.Because plant material decomposes so easily, very few wooden objects survive from prehistory, but timber spears from about 200,000 years ago have been discovered in Germany, preserved in waterlogged ground. The pointed end of a rounded wooden spear discovered in Clacton-on-Sea in 1911 is the oldest known at over 400,000 years old.Last week, scientists in Spain described hundreds ofwooden imprints and artefactsthat show Neanderthals embraced woodwork, making trays, plates, tripods, spears and other items. But proof of fatal skirmishes is harder to find in fossils: we may never know how the wounded Neanderthal at Shanidar died. “Conceivably it was a hunting accident,” Hunt said. “We can’t, however, rule out that purposeful interpersonal violence was involved.”Explore more on these topicsNeanderthalsArchaeologyUniversity of CambridgeAnthropologyIraqnewsShareReuse this content

title: The hidden costs of fracking: boom in Argentina linked to trail of sickness | Global development | The Guardian
description: Families in Vaca Muerta, the centre of Patagonia’s shale operation, report cancers, miscarriages and pollution
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Families in Vaca Muerta, the centre of Patagonia’s shale operation, report cancers, miscarriages and pollution
Content: Analía Celeste Saldías suffered complications while pregnant with her son Joel, now five. He was born with a birth defect at home in Calle Ciega 10.Photograph: Erica Canepa/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAnalía Celeste Saldías suffered complications while pregnant with her son Joel, now five. He was born with a birth defect at home in Calle Ciega 10.Photograph: Erica Canepa/The GuardianSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanGlobal developmentThe hidden costs of fracking: boom in Argentina linked to trail of sicknessFamilies in Vaca Muerta, the centre of Patagonia’s shale operation, report cancers, miscarriages and pollutionSupported byAbout this contentElena Basso in Allen, Neuquén and Añelo, ArgentinaThu 15 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Allen, a small town in Argentine Patagonia, many people living on the same street ended up falling ill. For some, it was severe migraines, nausea or skin irritation. For others, cancers, congenital abnormalities, miscarriages or stillbirth seemed to affect foetuses or children. People say it all started 13 years ago – when a well was drilled near their homes to extract gas and oil.Calle Ciega 10[Dead-end Street 10] lies on the eastern edge of Vaca Muerta, a vital area forArgentina’s economy, home to theworld’s second-largest reserve of shale gasand fourth-largest reserve of shale oil. The region has more than2,600 active wells, including one on this small street where about 20 families live, most of them seasonal workers on fruit farms.View image in fullscreenRoxana Valverde, a resident of Calle Ciega 10, has lived in the area for nearly 30 years.Photograph: Erica Canepa/The Guardian“There have been cases of cancer, and several women had to move away because they could not carry their pregnancies to term. They kept losing their babies. Some were born with illnesses, or died shortly after birth,” says Roxana Valverde, who has lived in the area for nearly 30 years. “Before the well, we didn’t experience these illnesses, or if we did, they were much less common.”Valverde adds that, during medical appointments, doctors say the illnesses could be caused by pollution from fracking, while acknowledging that, without in-depth studies, it is hard to establish with 100% certainty.Vaca Muerta covers more than11,500 sq milesand spans four Argentine provinces. Since 2012, under the government led byCristina Kirchner,the area has been extracting gas and oil using fracking, a technique that injects water, sand and chemicals at high pressure to fracture rock and release trapped hydrocarbons.Now, under Javier Milei, the Argentine government isheavily reliant on Vaca Muerta’s gas and oilresources to help the country recover from years of economic crisis, and hasopened the doorto foreign companies to extract and export hydrocarbons.Bythe endof 2025, theall-time productionrecordhad been broken. For the first time in the country’s history,crude oilovertook soya bean meal asits leading export, partly driven by European companies that invested in theVaca Muerta regionto findanother optionas well as Russian gas.View image in fullscreenA resident of Calle Ciega 10 points toward the oil well located a short distance from their home in Allen, Rio Negro province.Photograph: Erica Canepa/The GuardianAccording to a report from the NGOOpSur, 33% of the unconventional gas and 39% of the unconventional oil extracted in Vaca Muerta are controlled by the state-owned energy company YPF, while the rest is handled by foreign companies, including the US company Chevron, France’s TotalEnergies and the UK’s Shell.Fracking is ahighly invasivetechnique that posesenvironmental risksand has been linked by numerousscientific studiestoecological harmandhealth issuesfor people living nearby, such as respiratory and skin conditions, cancer, congenital disabilities, miscarriages andpregnancy complications.Calle Ciega 10 is in the countryside, and the families living there come from low-income backgrounds. The houses are small and dilapidated. Children play and ride bikes just a few metres from the well, while workers and a crane operate nearby.View image in fullscreenDominik Joel Valverde, born with a congenital malformation, plays with a dog along a dirt road metres from an oil well in Calle Ciega 10.Photograph: Erica Canepa/The GuardianAccording to those who live in Calle Ciega 10, the well ceased operations in 2019, but work resumed in May this year. Theyhave repeatedly triedto file complaints, but the courts have never heard their pleas. They suspect that several incidents at the well could have contaminated a pond from which they draw water for their daily needs.The family of Analía Celeste Saldías has faced numerous health issues. In 2023, while pregnant with her youngest daughter, Bianca, Saldías faced complications, including what she described as the beginning of a stroke.View image in fullscreenLef Nawel of the Zonal Xawvn Ko Mapuche Cconfederation, an organisation that brings together 14 Indigenous communities living across different parts of Vaca Muerta.Photograph: Erica Canepa/The GuardianHer son Joel was born in 2020 with three lungs and had surgery as a baby to correct a severe congenital malformation. In 2019, her eldest daughter, Michelle, experienced serious skin problems, with painful patches on her back, arms and torso.Since fracking operations began, health concerns have spread beyond Calle Ciega 10. Lef and Jorge Nawel are members of theZonal Xawvn Ko Mapuche confederation, an organisation that brings together 14 Indigenous communities from different parts of Vaca Muerta.The Mapuche people, the largest Indigenous group in Argentina, are frequently amongthose most affectedin the region due to the widespread construction of wells on their ancestral lands.The Nawels say that the community has seen numerous cases of miscarriage and nervous and respiratory system disorders, particularly among children.View image in fullscreenA general view shows the town of Añelo, with trucks passing along the main road in Neuquén province, Argentina.Photograph: Erica Canepa/The GuardianIn Añelo, a small town considered theoperational coreof Vaca Muerta, Lorena Bravo Maripe, the ancestral leader of the Añelo Lof Campo MaripeMapuche communitywith 106 members, also reports numerous health issues in her group. That includes several cancer cases – such as her mother’s breast cancer and her own cervical cancer – as well as numerous respiratory and skin ailments.“This is a polluting industry and, instead of monitoring it, the state is completely absent,” she says, adding that the community raises livestock and has noticed that animals are often born disfigured or experience complications during birth.The rise in serious illnesses is raising concerns among doctors working in Vaca Muerta. Silvia Ávila, dean of the faculty of medicine at the National University of Comahue, says the government must monitor citizens’ health, ensure transparency and publish results.“The entire population, including healthcare workers, should be informed about the public policies and monitoring carried out by the state and companies regarding people’s health – but we are not,” she says.View image in fullscreenA lagoon sits beside an oil well next to Calle Ciega 10.Photograph: Erica Canepa/The Guardian“We lack medical andscientific research,” says Alan Rocha Varsanyi, a researcher at OpSur. “It is highly possible that we are already paying the health costs of this today, but we lack the tools to determine whether or to what extent this is the case.”When approached for interviews, health ministers in Neuquén and Río Negro provinces declined to comment. YPF, Chevron, TotalEnergies and Shell were approached for comment.Añelo is surrounded by hundreds of active wells, yet hydrocarbon extraction is not the only threat to the health of people living in Vaca Muerta. The region also hosts numerousopen-air toxic wastedumps, andhundreds of lorriespass through daily.People’s wellbeing is at the heart of Vaca Muerta’smost criticalenvironmental lawsuit: theComarsa case, initiated after complaints from local people, environmental groups and civic organisations.View image in fullscreenA road near the Comarsa landfill on the outskirts of Neuquén city. Road accidents in the area have surged due to a dramatic increase in heavy vehicle traffic linked to oil industry operations nearby.Photograph: Erica Canepa/The GuardianComarsa, a waste management company, is accused of storing rather than properly handling and disposing of more than300,000 cubic metres of toxic waste, now ina dump in Neuquén, a city with more than 300,000 inhabitants.If the courts have not yet considered the allegations, prosecutor Maximiliano Breide Obeid, the head of the environmental offences and special laws unit in Neuquén, leads the new case and has no doubt about the dangers posed by toxic waste such as that found at the Comarsa dump.“We have established that the nearest homes are just 200 metres from the toxic waste,” he says. “We believe there is an immediate danger to people’s health, and that there will be a future danger if the situation is not resolved.”‘Vaca Muerta was the future’: Argentina goes all in on frackingRead moreA crucial piece of evidence for the prosecution is a report by the forensic medical corps, where doctors state that contact with the toxic waste from the dump – polluting soil, water and air – can lead to severe health issues such as respiratory, skin, neurological, stomach and kidney problems, as well as cancer and miscarriages.According to the doctors, the waste contains barium, cadmium, lead, copper, mercury and arsenic – heavy metals that can be toxic to humans. Comarsa has been approached for comment.The prosecution says that the company stored toxic waste on the surface and underground without properly sealing the soil, violating safety regulations and risking contamination of water and soil. The air around the dump emits a very strong odour, making it unbearable to breathe, and within minutes, people’s eyes start to water.Yet new plots forresidential buildingare being developed around the dump, just a few dozen metres away.This article was developed with the support ofJournalismfund EuropeExplore more on these topicsGlobal developmentSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanPollutionFrackingEnergyGasFossil fuelsArgentinafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like selling wolves from Yellowstone’: how protected US sharks are being sold off to foreign aquariums | Oceans | The Guardian
description: While anglers cannot take endangered sand tiger sharks, a loophole lets private firms catch the fish to sell abroad, profiting from Delaware Bay’s conservation success
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: While anglers cannot take endangered sand tiger sharks, a loophole lets private firms catch the fish to sell abroad, profiting from Delaware Bay’s conservation success
Content: A marine researcher measures a male sand tiger shark in Delaware Bay, which has become a hotspot for the collection of sharks for the aquarium trade.Photograph: Maya Yang/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA marine researcher measures a male sand tiger shark in Delaware Bay, which has become a hotspot for the collection of sharks for the aquarium trade.Photograph: Maya Yang/The GuardianSeascape: the state of our oceansOceans‘Like selling wolves from Yellowstone’: how protected US sharks are being sold off to foreign aquariumsWhile anglers cannot take endangered sand tiger sharks, a loophole lets private firms catch the fish to sell abroad, profiting from Delaware Bay’s conservation successSupported byAbout this contentMaya Yangin Delaware BayThu 15 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShortly after 12.45pm, what remains of a 300-metre line goes taut. Somewhere beneath the murky green surface ofDelawareBay, on the eastern US coast, a sand tiger shark has taken the bait of a mackerel chunk. Marine researchers at the University of Delaware haul the line towards a small boat as the shark’s grey-brown outline emerges.It is a large animal: 225cm (7ft) long with a 90cm girth. Its mouth hangs open, revealing rows of jagged teeth. The researchers work quickly, measuring the shark, recording its sex, and taking blood and muscle samples. A tag is then fastened beneath its dorsal fin, through its thick sandpapery skin.The mature male seems to watch them as they work. Then it is lowered back into the bay. With a powerful flick of its tail, it disappears almost as quickly as it arrived.Several thousand miles away, sand tiger sharks collected from these same waters circle tanks in Abu Dhabi, moving among artificial reefs and through blue-lit tunnels in the desert city’s aquariums, where visitors pay up to $100 (£75) for day passes. They will never return to Delaware Bay.Tagging sand tigers – aspecies of concernthat isprohibited from being caughtin US waters – offers clues about the lives of these fish, which arecritically endangeredglobally.However, in recent years, the bay – aUS habitat of particular concernbetween the states of Delaware and New Jersey – has become a hotspot for private collection of specimens for the global aquarium trade.Arecent studyby marine researchers from the University of Delaware, Delaware State University and the University of Rhode Island shows that, since 2018, the number of sand tiger sharks collected from Delaware Bay for public display has risen sharply, from two that year to 40 in 2023. In total, 80 of the sharks were taken from Delaware waters for aquariums between 2018 and 2024.View image in fullscreenAaron Carlisle prepares mackerel bait in Delaware Bay with other colleagues from the University of Delaware’s School of Marine Science and Policy.Photograph: Maya Yang/The GuardianThe study, citing data from Delaware’s Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control (DNREC) shows that nearly all the sand tiger sharks collected from Delaware Bay were sent overseas: the highest numbers went to China and the United Arab Emirates, while others went to South Korea and Thailand. Some were sent to other countries – including Turkey, Scotland, Israel, Italy, France and Uzbekistan – with a few remaining in the US.“This [private collecting of sand tiger sharks] is like going into Yellowstone [national park] and catching wolves and then selling them to zoos in France or in the Middle East,” says Brad Wetherbee, a shark researcher atUniversity of Rhode Island who co-wrotethe study.“[These countries] used to have sand tigers. They could just go out in their own waters and catch them and collect them, but their populations are so low they can’t do that any more.”The US has spent decades restricting the killing of sand tiger sharks, yet in recent years, through a regulatory maze of federal and state permits, private collecting companies can legally remove these protected sharks from the wild for public display. A shark that an angler would be required to release after catching can instead be transported thousands of miles and placed in a foreign aquarium, with private companies profiting from the trade.“How can we say these people [private collectors] can remove them and functionally harvest them, whereas these ones [recreational anglers] can’t?” says Aaron Carlisle, an associate professor from the University of Delaware’s school of marine science and another of the study’s authors. “If our concern is sustainability, we need to know what is the impact of removal.”View image in fullscreenA sand tiger shark (centre) at SeaWorld Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates, March 2024.Photograph: CTK/AlamySand tigers, despite their fearsome appearance, are non-aggressive and docile. They have one of the lowest reproductive rates of any shark species, reaching sexual maturity at about six to 10 years old, depending on sex, and producing just one or two pups every two to three years.Once widespread across subtropical and temperate coastal waters, the species has declined across much of its range. Populations in parts of south-east Asia, west Africa and the Arabian Sea havefallen to critically low levels, largely because ofoverfishing, including bycatch, andhabitat degradation. In some regions, they are believed to have been wiped out entirely.The north-west Atlantic is one of the few regions where the species’ populations are not critically endangered, largely due to federal and state protections. Yet the population has never had a formal assessment, and how healthy it actually is remains difficult to determine.One private company has accounted for most of the recent collection in Delaware Bay. Dynasty Marine, a Florida-based supplier of live marine animals to aquariums and research institutions worldwide that drewbipartisan outragein Florida in 2025 after legally netting a manta ray for SeaWorld Abu Dhabi, began collecting sand tigers in Delaware in 2021.A spokesperson for Delaware state’s department of natural resources and environmental control (DNREC) says the company has “ramped up collection in the following years”.View image in fullscreenFishers off the coast of Panama City beach in Florida in 2025, catching a giant manta ray for SeaWorld Abu Dhabi.Photograph: Facebook/Planet Water USARecords reviewed by the Guardian show that Dynasty Marine collected 71 sharks between 2022 and 2024. The study also records 35 sand tiger harvest requests in 2025, with most destined for China.Recipients of the sharks caught between 2022 and 2024 included SeaWorld Abu Dhabi, Dubai Aquarium and Underwater Zoo, Sea Life Busan in South Korea, Aquaria Phuket in Thailand and Guangzhou Ocean World in China.Dynasty Marine was asked to comment on the number of sand tigers it collects a year but did not respond. In a statement to the Guardian, it said: “Every collection we conduct is done in full compliance with all applicable federal and state permits and regulations.“The animals we collect are cared for to the highest standards and go on to live in human care, where they play a vital role in educating millions of people each year about marine life and the importance of ocean conservation.”The company says it supports “numerous marine conservation, science and education initiatives”, including shark research, manatee rehabilitation and coral restoration efforts.Private companies seeking to collect sand tigers for public display must first obtain an exempted fishing permit from the US National Marine Fisheries Service (known as Noaa Fisheries). If the collection takes place in Delaware waters, the permit holder must then obtain a scientific collecting permit from DNREC.Noaa Fisheries says it reviews applications for capture of the sharks on a “case-by-case basis”.View image in fullscreenA blood sample is taken from the underside of a male sand tiger shark in Delaware Bay.Photograph: Maya Yang/The Guardian“We have an overall scientifically based annual quota for all shark research and public display,” says John Chu, a Noaa Fisheries spokesperson. “We consider that overall quota when issuing public display permits.”The state follows the federal lead in granting permits. The DNREC says Noaa Fisheries’ approval is “evidence enough for the state to believe that removal of the permitted number of individual sharks is sustainable”.However, scientists argue that, without knowing the population’s size or trend, it is difficult to determine what impact removing sharks for display in an aquarium may have.The concern is heightened by the size of many sand tigers collected in Delaware. Many are large juveniles or near-mature adults that could soon reproduce if left in the wild.The DNREC says the recent increase in collections is “an emerging concern”, but says it would be up to the federal government to act on that. It says an assessment on the number of sand tiger sharks in the area would “lend context” to a permit request from a private collection company.This uncertainty extends to what happens to the sharks after they leave Delaware Bay. Neither the DNREC or Noaa Fisheries record the sharks’ final status, including whether those animals become sick or die, though the DNREC says it intends to change this.Dewayne Fox, an assistant fisheries professor at Delaware State University who also worked on the study, says the issue is not just whether the collections are sustainable, but also who benefits from a population protected in US waters.“We have protected the habitat and yet we are going to allow some out-of-state company to come in, catch these animals and then ship them all the way around the world and make money,” he says. “Everybody else is benefiting from our conservation success.”Explore more on these topicsOceansSeascape: the state of our oceansSharksEndangered speciesFishingConservationAnimalsFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Indonesia fights fire with dry ice as toxic haze spreads across region | Indonesia | The Guardian
description: Having tried cloud seeding and water bombing, one pilot project will see dry ice dispersed by plane across the province of South Sumatra
Author: Kate Lamb
Headline: Having tried cloud seeding and water bombing, one pilot project will see dry ice dispersed by plane across the province of South Sumatra
Content: People walk through thick haze from wildfires in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, on Wednesday.Photograph: GENDES/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople walk through thick haze from wildfires in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, on Wednesday.Photograph: GENDES/EPAIndonesiaIndonesia fights fire with dry ice as toxic haze spreads across regionHaving tried cloud seeding and water bombing, one pilot project will see dry ice dispersed by plane across the province of South SumatraKate Lamband agenciesThu 15 Oct 2026 00.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs fires ravageIndonesia, emitting a toxic smoke that has drawn the ire of regional neighbours, the government is testing an unusual new approach to tackle the haze: dry ice.Having tried cloud seeding, water bombing and sending in army personnel to fight the fires, Indonesia’s coordinating security minister said dry ice would be dropped on the province of South Sumatra on Thursday.“This trial of dry ice dispersal is being conducted under the president’s direct instruction to help tackle the haze in South Sumatra,” minister Dudung Abdurachman was quoted as saying by state news agency Antara.“We will first observe the results, and if effective, there is a possibility that this method could be implemented in other regions.”Since January,almost 900,000 hectareshave been burned Indonesia-wide in the worst fire season in more than a decade, exacerbated by this year’s“godzilla” El-Ninoand as the practice of “slash and burn” to clear land for crops such as palm oil persists.View image in fullscreenMotorists ride through thick haze from wildfires in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia.Photograph: GENDES/EPAFor months, millions of Indonesians have been subject to thick smoke and an apocalyptic tangerine haze, with criticism mounting of the government’s response, including aclass action lawsuitfiled last week accusing it of “gross negligence”. Tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to the haze.Air quality has also plummeted in neighbouring countries, shuttering schools, grounding flights and driving a spike in respiratory illness.Marina Bay, Singapore, before and after smoke haze caused by fires in Indonesia.The haze has drifted into neighbouringSingapore, Malaysia and as far afield as the Philippines. Timor-Leste has said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday and urged families to keep children indoors or to use “respiratory protection” if going outside.Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment starting on Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes occurred. The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents.In the past week, the financial hub of Singapore was listed among the most polluted cities globally. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected, was at number two.View image in fullscreenKuala Lumpur’s skyline shrouded in haze from regional wildfires, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, on 9 October.Photograph: Hasnoor Hussain/ReutersOn Thursday, a Cessna aircraft will reportedly disperse 1.5 tons of dry ice over the South Sumatran city of Palembang, a move the government hopes will ease the smoke and improve air quality and visibility.The technique was first deployed in the 1940s to promote ice formation in clouds, Bloomberg reported.‘The physical toll is visceral’: How Indonesia’s fire haze affects millions - visual guideRead moreBut experts say the use of dry ice, or solid carbon dioxide, might only offer local, and limited relief.“It’s got some potential for local relief that might work for a while,” says Rick McRae, an adjunct professor from the University of New South Wales’ (UNSW) bushfire research group.View image in fullscreenA pedestrian wearing a mask walks along the boulevard at Marina Bay in Singapore this week.Photograph: Roslan Rahman/AFP/Getty Images“Weather systems are all moving from east to west. So if you’re in a town under that and you clear the smoke, there’s gonna be more blowing all the time,” he says, “So it’s a constant … It’s not going to be simple and it’s not going to be a permanent fix in any way.”In the Indonesian province of central Kalimantan ​on Wednesday, the ISPU air pollution index exceeded 1,200 – or four times the “hazardous” level of 300 – environment ministry data showed.Local news footage showed ​thick haze blanketing the provincial city of Palangka Raya, cutting visibility for motorists to a minimum.View image in fullscreenThick wildfire haze shrouds the Kahayan River in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia.Photograph: GENDES/EPAIndonesian presidentPrabowo Subiantohas ordered firefighting efforts to be stepped up, and called for a crackdown on those suspected of starting fires.But the government has struggled to combat the fires, the worst of which occur in peatland areas, can burn for weeks underground, and are difficult to extinguish.“As time goes by and climate change kicks in, I think it could become a global problem, not just the fix that one country needs to find,” said McRae, of the widening regional issue. “There’s a lot of interconnectedness on a global scale.”Explore more on these topicsIndonesiaAsia PacificPrabowo SubiantoWildfiresSingaporeMalaysianewsShareReuse this content

title: The day bad weather brought half a million birds to England | Birds | The Guardian
description: The ‘Great Fall’ of 1965 was caused by harsh conditions forcing migrating species to land on their way to Africa
Author: Stephen Moss
Headline: The ‘Great Fall’ of 1965 was caused by harsh conditions forcing migrating species to land on their way to Africa
Content: Vast numbers of redstarts were among the arrivals along the Suffolk coast in October 1965.Photograph: Kevin Elsby/AlamyView image in fullscreenVast numbers of redstarts were among the arrivals along the Suffolk coast in October 1965.Photograph: Kevin Elsby/AlamyWeatherwatchBirdsThe day bad weather brought half a million birds to EnglandThe ‘Great Fall’ of 1965 was caused by harsh conditions forcing migrating species to land on their way to AfricaStephen MossThu 15 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy birding mentor, the late Derek Moore, was also a keen cricketer. But one autumn day in 1965 he was unable to concentrate while fielding because many hundreds of songbirds were landing around him on the pitch at Lowestoft.The arrival of hundreds of thousands of birds along the Suffolk coast that day became known asthe “Great Fall”, and it was caused by a weather system bringing cloud, winds and heavy rain.The conditions caused migrating songbirds heading south across the North Sea from Scandinavia to become exhausted, with many falling into the waves and drowning. But an estimated half a million survived and made landfall along a 24-mile stretch of English coastline. Having rested and fed, they then continued their long journey south to sub-Saharan Africa.When I began birding in the 1970s, older birders waxed lyrical about the autumn falls from their youth. Yet today they are few and far between. Not because the weather patterns have changed, but simply because there are now far fewer songbirds breeding in northern Europe and migrating through Britain to Africa.One place they do still occur – though with smaller numbers of birds – is Spurn Head on the East Yorkshire coast. Last month, birders gathered there for the annualMigFest, which, since 2013, has celebrated the wonders of bird migration – with attenders ever hopeful of witnessing one of these extraordinary falls.Explore more on these topicsBirdsWeatherwatchUK weatherBirdwatchingWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Trans women no longer to be placed on female-only wards under new NHS England guidance | NHS | The Guardian
description: Rules mean single-sex wards, toilets and changing rooms will now be used by people based on their biological sex
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: Rules mean single-sex wards, toilets and changing rooms will now be used by people based on their biological sex
Content: The new guidance states that trans people should be ‘accommodated in line with their biological sex’.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenThe new guidance states that trans people should be ‘accommodated in line with their biological sex’.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PANHSTrans women no longer to be placed on female-only wards under new NHS England guidanceRules mean single-sex wards, toilets and changing rooms will now be used by people based on their biological sexJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentThu 15 Oct 2026 13.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrans women will no longer be placed on female-only wards under new NHSEnglandguidance on single-sex spaces.The new rules, published on Thursday, mean single-sex wards, toilets and changing rooms will be used by people based on their biological sex, not their gender identity.Theguidance statesthat trans people should be “accommodated in line with their biological sex” while ensuring their clinical needs are met and their “privacy, dignity and safety are maintained”, along with other patients sharing their accommodation.It adds that in cases where clinical needs and same-sex accommodation requirements cannot both be met, clinical needs are the priority.Updatedguidance for NHS England staff has also been published, stating that all organisations should carry out an audit of their provision to ensure it protects the “privacy, dignity and safety of all staff”.It states that inNHStrusts with mainly single-sex facilities, “suitable and accessible alternatives, such as single‑occupancy or mixed-sex facilities with individual lockable rooms, can be provided”.Previous NHS England guidance said patients and staff could be accommodated on wards or use facilities based on their gender identity.In a joint statement, TransActual and Trans+ Solidarity Alliance said the guidance would “not survive contact with reality in resource-strapped hospitals and will create unworkable operational challenges”.“This NHS guidance emphasises clinical judgment as the priority over blanket exclusion, but leaves individual healthcare professionals unclear on how to safely look after trans patients,” they said.“Forcing trans people into spaces for our sex assigned at birth will never be the most clinically appropriate decision, and would push trans people away from accessing care.”They added that “the government failing to get a grip of this legal mess was sadly putting politics over patient care”.The guidance has been updated after last year’s supreme court ruling that stated the terms “woman” and “sex” in the Equality Actreferred only to a biological woman and to biological sex, and did not include transgender women with gender recognition certificates.The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) code has already been revised to confirm a service must be used on the basis of biological sex for it to be classed as single sex under the Equality Act.Maya Forstater, the chief executive and co-founder of the charity Sex Matters, said the policies “represent a momentous shift back to reality”, but she was “concerned that NHS England has not said how rules based on biological sex will be implemented”.She also criticised the fact the guidance had been published 18 months after the supreme court judgment, saying it had initially been promised “within weeks”.She cited the case of the female nurses at Darlington memorial hospital whowon an employment tribunal case in Januaryafter being forced to share single-sex changing rooms with a trans colleague.The tribunal found that the nurses faced “a hostile, intimidating, humiliating and degrading environment” at work and were told to “broaden their mindsets” when raising their concerns.Bethany Hutchison, the lawyer who led the claim, said she welcomed the new “clear and necessary guidance from NHS England”.“The test now is whether NHS trusts will actually follow it. The Darlington nurses should never have had to take their own employer to court to secure privacy, dignity and lawful single-sex facilities,” she said.“Enforcement cannot continue to depend on the courage and personal sacrifice of individual nurses.”Explore more on these topicsNHSTransgenderWomenEnglandEquality Act 2010Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC)HealthShareReuse this content

title: Cost of balancing Great Britain’s power grid reaches nearly £50m a day | Energy industry | The Guardian
description: Grid operator paying large sums to switch off windfarms in areas of excess electricity generation while turning on gas plants elsewhere
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Grid operator paying large sums to switch off windfarms in areas of excess electricity generation while turning on gas plants elsewhere
Content: The Gwynt y Mor offshore windfarm. Great Britain’s £150bn power networks upgrade is not keeping pace with increasing renewable energy generation.Photograph: Robin Weaver/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Gwynt y Mor offshore windfarm. Great Britain’s £150bn power networks upgrade is not keeping pace with increasing renewable energy generation.Photograph: Robin Weaver/AlamyEnergy industryCost of balancing Great Britain’s power grid reaches nearly £50m a dayGrid operator paying large sums to switch off windfarms in areas of excess electricity generation while turning on gas plants elsewhereJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentThu 15 Oct 2026 11.55 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cost of balancing Great Britain’s power grid has soared to near-record highs of almost £50m a day after windfarms were turned off because of bottlenecks in transmitting power around the country.The grid operator paid £47.9m on Wednesday to turn windfarms off in areas with an oversupply of electricity and turn gas plants on in areas where supplies were tight.The costs, which are leviedon to household energy bills, included a £1.6m payment for one half-hour period, and were some of the highest recorded since the early months of the Ukraine crisis in 2022.Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to jump by £276 a year from JanuaryRead moreThey add to the increasing costs of balancing the grid, which reached a total of £505m in September alone, the highest monthly cost recorded, and are expected to reach £3.2bn over the next year.The costs underline the growing concerns over the pace ofGreat Britain’s £150bn power networks upgrade, which is failing to keep up with new renewable energy projects being connected to the grid.Overall, windfarms and hydropower plants with about 9 gigawatts of capacity were paid to not generate on Wednesday, according to the consultancy LCP Delta, enough to power more than 8m typical households.Instead, the grid operator was forced to pay for a string of gas and biomass plants to fire up and bought more electricity imports from Europe via high-voltage subsea power cables.The record costs have come to light days after the NationalEnergySystem Operator (Neso) was forced to call for “last resort” emergency assistance from its counterpart in France, which agreed to send last-minute power supplies to the UK on Monday and Friday last week.“The system overall wasn’t tight in terms of power supplies,” said Shivam Malhotra, the head of power trading at LCP Delta. “It’s the age-old story of a lack of infrastructure to transport power to where it’s needed, leading to lots of windfarms being turned off.”What is Burnham’s GB Grid plan and could it bring down energy bills?Read moreTypically, windfarms in Scotland are paid to turn off because there is not enough high-voltage cabling connecting the country to areas of growing electricity demand further south.“To resolve the energy needs in the south of the country Neso had to use one of their last resorts. It’s quite surprising for this time of year,” Malhotra said.During the summer Neso faced severe grid challenges when a high-pressure heat dome led to a drop in renewable energy output and surging electricity demand to power air conditioning and refrigerators.Neso was forced to bring in independent investigators to look into whistleblower claims that its staff were involved in a cover-up of a near-blackout during record high temperatures in late June.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe accusations, which wereraised in parliament last weekby the shadow energy secretary, Claire Coutinho, included claims that senior bosses at Neso were “risking blackouts to protect Neso’s reputation”.Fintan Slye, Neso’s chief executive, told an industry conference on Wednesday that there would be “lessons to be learned” coming out of a review into that period by the industry regulatorOfgem.Asked how he thought Neso handled the situation, Slye said: “Through that period, no customers were disconnected [and] frequencies stayed within statutory limits. But undoubtedly, it was a really challenging period for the system and right across Europe we saw power systems … under strain.“I think the control room and teams that were in it did an absolutely superb job managing what was a really difficult situation through the week.”A Neso spokesperson said Great Britain’s energy supplies were “secure” during both calls for emergency assistance, and that the “separate incidents” were “not signs of a wider problem with Britain’s electricity system”.“In both cases, our control room responded quickly to changing conditions and used established tools to keep the system running securely,” they said.“While Neso continues to deliver savings through operational reforms and innovation, the single biggest opportunity to reduce balancing costs is the timely delivery of new infrastructure by transmission owners, which could halve balancing costs by the end of the decade.”Explore more on these topicsEnergy industryRenewable energyWind powerInfrastructureOfgemEnergy billsConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pensioner pleads guilty to raping woman drugged by husband | UK news | The Guardian
description: Graham Brougham, 74, was one of a number of men invited to sexually assault victim while she was unconscious
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Graham Brougham, 74, was one of a number of men invited to sexually assault victim while she was unconscious
Content: Graham Brougham is set to be the oldest defendant on trial and has been bailed ahead of sentencing.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenGraham Brougham is set to be the oldest defendant on trial and has been bailed ahead of sentencing.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersUK newsPensioner pleads guilty to raping woman drugged by husbandGraham Brougham, 74, was one of a number of men invited to sexually assault victim while she was unconsciousHannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondentThu 15 Oct 2026 12.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man from Cheshire has pleaded guilty to the rape of a woman whose husband drugged her and invited other men to sexually assault her while she was unconscious.Graham Brougham, 74, pleaded guilty to rape at a hearing at Manchester Minshull Street crown court on Thursday afternoon.The husband, who cannot be named in order to protect the anonymity of his wife, has already admitted to more than 60 offences, and will be sentenced at a later date.The victim sat in the public gallery of the court as Brougham entered his guilty plea. She turned to watch him as he stood in the dock, while a relative sitting beside her held her hand throughout.Brougham, who was set to be the oldest defendant on trial, has been on bail throughout the proceedings, and Judge Greene again granted him bail before sentencing.However, addressing Brougham’s barrister, he said the defendant should not “be under any illusion”, as his “sentence will be custody, and a long time in custody”.Before his arrest Brougham, who lives in Northwich in Cheshire, had played in a 1970s tribute band and was a member of a walking football team.Two other men who were charged alongside the husband have also pleaded guilty at earlier hearings.Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee, a former technician at the city’s university, admitted a number of offences earlier this year, and last month Sean Peers, 38, pleaded guilty to one count of assault by penetration.Ten men are due to stand trial at the same court, denying a range of offences including rape andattempted rape, which are alleged to have taken place between 2018 and November 2025.They are Philip Wild, 59, from Stockport; Jordan Wallace, 31, from Manchester; Alan Keelan, 42, from Manchester; Jonathan Kirk, 43, from Stockport; Robert Stewart, 70, from Stockport; Mohammed Sabir, 28, of no fixed abode; Richard Townsend, 37, from Heywood in Greater Manchester; Karl Lindsay, 55, from Taunton in Somerset; Daniel Rayner, 42, from Whitstable in Kent; and David Graves, 60, from Ilkeston in Derbyshire.A jury has already been sworn in, and the trial was due to get under way on Monday, but it has been delayed for legal reasons.The prosecution is now scheduled to begin its case in early November, with the trial set to conclude by the end of January next year.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandCheshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Two 1960s London housing estates saved from demolition after decade-long battle | Social housing | The Guardian
description: Change of council leadership hands reprieve to residents of architecturally celebrated developments in Lambeth
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Change of council leadership hands reprieve to residents of architecturally celebrated developments in Lambeth
Content: Tenants of Cressingham Gardens in Lambeth faced years of limbo with their homes under threat of demolition.Photograph: David Rowe/AlamyView image in fullscreenTenants of Cressingham Gardens in Lambeth faced years of limbo with their homes under threat of demolition.Photograph: David Rowe/AlamySocial housingTwo 1960s London housing estates saved from demolition after decade-long battleChange of council leadership hands reprieve to residents of architecturally celebrated developments in LambethPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentThu 15 Oct 2026 11.57 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo architecturally celebrated council estates in southLondonthat have been under threat of demolition for more than a decade have been saved.Residents ofCressingham Gardensand theCentral Hill estatehave campaigned tirelessly for their homes to be saved, saying the low-density 1960s developments are significant in design and popular with those living there.Lambeth council argued that the estates were in poor repair and that razing them would create badly needed social and affordable homes.The plans were pursued when Lambeth was controlled by Labour but the Greens won the most seats at elections in May and now run the council as a minority administration.They oppose the demolition plans, which are expected to be reversed at a meeting of the cabinet next week.View image in fullscreenThe homes in Cressingham Gardens were built to encourage neighbourliness and play.Photograph: Sam Mellish/In Pictures/Getty ImagesThe fate of the estates attracted wider attention, in part because of their design but also because of the many years of limbo faced by tenants and leaseholders as the council pursued demolition.A2022 reviewof Homes Lambeth, the now defunct body which managed housing for the council, questioned the redevelopment plans, saying the net number of social rent homes to be created was very small.Sir Bob Kerslake, the former head of the civil service who led the review, said “feedback was uniformly negative”, with residents of estates earmarked for development citing inconsistent policy, delays and poor communication. He added: “As a consequence, levels of trust in the council are exceptionally low.”Both threatened estates were designed by a team of Lambeth architects led byTed Hollamby, who championed a move away from tower blocks toward lower-rise housing.Cressingham Gardens, which adjoins Brockwell Park, was built to encourage neighbourliness, with front doors facing each other and green spaces for play.View image in fullscreenThe Central Hill estate is built on a slope to maximise light and views.Photograph: Simon Elmer/Architects for Social HousingThe Central Hill project was led by Rosemary Stjernstedt when women were rare in social housing design. It was built on a sloping site near Crystal Palace, with homes maximising natural light.Martin Abrams, the Green leader of Lambeth, said: “This is a decisive moment for Central Hill and Cressingham Gardens. It recognises the relentless work of my colleagues in securing the future for these communities without demolition. We can now focus on investing in residents’ homes and bringing empty properties back into use.”Pete Elliott, the cabinet member for housing, said: “For over 12 years, we have fought for a better future for Central Hill and Cressingham Gardens. These proposals end years of uncertainty and put the focus where it belongs: repairing homes, supporting communities and filling empty properties.”Explore more on these topicsSocial housingLondonHousingArchitectureCommunitiesEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nicolás Maduro tells New York court new torture allegations are ‘false’ | Nicolás Maduro | The Guardian
description: Rewritten indictment accuses ex-Venezuela president and wife Cilia Flores of leading campaign of torture
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rewritten indictment accuses ex-Venezuela president and wife Cilia Flores of leading campaign of torture
Content: People protest against Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores outside a federal courthouse in New York on Thursday.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople protest against Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores outside a federal courthouse in New York on Thursday.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPANicolás MaduroNicolás Maduro tells New York court new torture allegations are ‘false’Rewritten indictment accuses ex-Venezuela president and wife Cilia Flores of leading campaign of tortureAssociated PressThu 15 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNicolás Maduro insisted on Thursday during an appearance in a New York court that torture allegations in a rewritten drug trafficking indictment against the deposed Venezuelan president and his wife were “false accusations”.Maduro, shackled at the ankles, was brought to court to face the new charges accusing the couple of leading a state-sponsored campaign of repression that tortured scores of victims, including three Americans.Judge Alvin K Hellerstein entered a not-guilty plea on behalf of Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores. They were seized from their Caracas home by the US military in a night-time raid in January.Hellerstein announced that he was entering the plea on behalf of Maduro after Maduro twice responded to the judge’s request to enter a plea by criticizing the indictment, saying it contained “false accusations and false testimony”. Maduro spoke through an interpreter.The vanishing of Nicolás Maduro: how the former dictator is being erased from VenezuelaRead moreAttorney Barry Pollack said when the charges were announced last week that Maduro, 63, denied them and “looks forward to his day in court”.According to the rewritten indictment, Maduro oversaw a violent torture system that beat, asphyxiated and delivered electric shocks to its victims. He is accused of personally recommending torture methods, receiving updates on specific victims’ treatment and threatening to kill one prisoner’s child as a form of psychological torture.Flores, 70, a former attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment alleges.When she was asked to enter a plea, she said through an interpreter: “I am completely innocent. I am not guilty.”Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the international criminal court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied wrongdoing.Prosecutors told the judge during the hearing that lawyers on both sides want the trial date moved from 1 June to 14 June.Torture is a crime under international law and can be prosecuted outside the country where the abuse occurred and regardless of the victims’ nationality. But the prosecution of foreign officials in the US is exceedingly rare, having been tried only a few times, including against the son of the former Liberian president Charles Taylor, Russians responsible for war crimes in Ukraine and a former prison warden in Bashar Assad’s Syria.Earlier this year, Maduro and his wife pleaded not guilty in the US drug case, which said they conspired to flood the US with cocaine. Their attorneys say the case should be dismissed on immunity grounds because they were the leader and first lady of a foreign country.The revised indictment covers allegations of torture stretching back to Maduro’s ascent to power in 2013, when he took over as president from his mentor Hugo Chávez, who died of cancer that year.Explore more on these topicsNicolás MaduroNew YorkVenezuelaTortureAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump business | Serbia | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Aleksandar Vučić personally intervened to push plans for controversial $500m Trump Tower in Belgrade, which sparked protests and a criminal case
Author: Tom Burgis
Headline: Exclusive: Aleksandar Vučić personally intervened to push plans for controversial $500m Trump Tower in Belgrade, which sparked protests and a criminal case
Content: The alleged scheme to override the protected status of a historic building in the Serbian capital looms over an election scheduled for 25 October.Composite: Guardian Design/PA/EPA/AP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe alleged scheme to override the protected status of a historic building in the Serbian capital looms over an election scheduled for 25 October.Composite: Guardian Design/PA/EPA/AP/Getty ImagesSerbiaRevealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump businessExclusive: Aleksandar Vučić personally intervened to push plans for controversial $500m Trump Tower in Belgrade, which sparked protests and a criminal caseTom Burgisin BelgradeThu 15 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 09.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSerbia’s authoritarian ruler personally intervened to advance an allegedly illegal scheme to hand over a protected site in Belgrade for a Trump tower, the Guardian can reveal.Aleksandar Vučić summoned officials to a meeting at his presidential offices about the project, which has culminated in a landmark indictment of senior figures from his regime on charges of abuse of public office.The criminal case is believed to be the first resulting from the Trumps’global moneymaking campaign, described by critics as a “pay to play” arrangement where everything from sanctions relief to cutting-edge chips is available to those who enrich the first family and their associates.The alleged scheme to override the protected status of a historic building in the Serbian capital looms over an election scheduled for 25 October, when Vučić will seek to extend his 12 years in power in the face of a mass protest movement spurred by government corruption.View image in fullscreenJared Kushner and the Serbian president, Aleksandar Vučić, in Belgrade.Photograph: Instagram/Aleksandar VucicA nationalist former propaganda chief under Slobodan Milošević, Vučić hosted the US president’s sonDonald Trump Jrand son-in-law Jared Kushner in Belgrade as they developed plans for a $500m hotel and residential tower to add to their global property portfolios.After the abuse of power charges were brought last December, Kushner’s company announced the project would not proceed “at this time”. Vučićthreatened reprisals, calling the prosecutors “corrupt gangs” who “fabricated cases”.View image in fullscreenScreenshot from Trumpbelgrade.com showing the renderings of the proposed Belgrade development.Photograph: Trumpbelgrade.com“We have lost an exceptional investment,” the Serbian president said. “I will personally ensure that everyone who participated in causing this damage is held accountable.”Vučić’s culture minister is among those charged with abuse of power. But a Guardian investigation, drawing on interviews and leaked documents, reveals that the Serbian president himself led the initial meeting where the alleged scheme was discussed. This crucial meeting is not mentioned in the indictment, raising questions about what information the prosecutors are holding back and why.Representatives of the Trumps and Kushner said they had no part in the removal of the building’s protected status and that it would be “false” to say the Belgrade project was part of a “pay to play” scheme.Vučić did not respond to requests for comment. His decision to call a snap election means that a hearing at which witnesses might reveal details of his involvement will not take place until after the vote.A free 99-year leaseOn 6 February 2024, Dubravka Đukanović, a Serbian conservation professor in her 60s, arrived for a meeting at the presidency, a domed former royal palace. For three years, she had been the director of the country’s institute for the protection of cultural monuments.The topic was the General Staff building, the former Yugoslav ministry of defence in central Belgrade. The building, an architectural gem seen as an emblem of resistance to the Nazis, was already cherished when Nato forces bombed it in 1999 during its campaign to force Milošević to withdraw from Kosovo, deepening its resonance.View image in fullscreenAleksandar Vučić and Donald Trump Jr in Belgrade.Photograph: Facebook/Aleksandar VucicVučić himself had reaffirmed the General Staff building’s legally protected status in 2016. Now, the president said he wanted Đukanović to rescind it, according to two people with knowledge of the meeting. Some unspecified “foreign investor” was keen on the site.Under Serbian law, stripping the General Staff building of its protected status was not in Đukanović’s gift. Her institute would have to commission an expert opinion, which would have to conclude that there were good reasons why protected status was no longer merited.But the president wanted it done. At 6ft 6in and intolerant of dissent, Vučić can be intimidating. His tone towards Đukanović and another heritage official present was unpleasant, the sources said. He told them they were lazy and incompetent. The message was clear: do what I want or resign.A plausible explanation for Vučić’s forceful intervention came the following month, when an agreement between the Serbian government and Kushner’s real estate companyleaked.Married to Trump’s daughter Ivanka, Kushner had been an influential White House aide during his father-in-law’s first term. Since Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 election, Kushner had been concentrating on his investment fund.By early 2024, Trump was storming to the Republican nomination and was favourite to win the coming election. If Trump took back the White House, Kushner would once more be one of the most influential people on the planet.The leaked agreement showed the Serbian authorities had granted Kushner’s company a 99-year lease over the General Staff site, free of charge.Kushner, whose spokesperson said he had been looking at the project since 2021, posted an image of the design on X, professing himself “excited”.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onplatform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThe news was not universally welcomed in Belgrade. “Serbia is not a buffet, and Vučić is not a waiter,”saidAleksandar Jovanović Ćuta, an environmental activist who revealed the agreement. “This is not his private property.”Yet Vučić’s regime proceeded to sign a contract, dated 13 May 2024 and seen by the Guardian, undertaking that the “cultural heritage designation” of the site would be removed “to the satisfaction” of Kushner’s company.Comply or resignThe week after the contract was signed, Đukanović was summoned to another meeting. The president was not there this time. Siniša Mali, his finance minister and right-hand man, took charge.Mali urged Đukanović and Olivera Vučković, Belgrade’s top heritage official, to cancel the General Staff site’s protected status, according to the indictment’s summary of testimony the two women would later give prosecutors. It makes no reference to the earlier meeting with the president but indicates that the subject had previously been broached.“Mali asked them if they had given it any thought,” the indictment says, “and if they would initiate the procedure to remove the building’s protected status.”The women refused, “believing that the legal conditions for it were not met”. In that case, Mali told them, repeating his boss’s ultimatum from February, they should resign. They did.In her resignation letter, which the Guardian has seen, Đukanović wrote that she could not agree “to inappropriate interventions that would permanently destroy all the values of the complex, which testifies to the highest achievements of contemporary Serbian architecture and is of incalculable importance for preserving enduring creative values, the education of future generations, and the strengthening of the cultural identity of the Serbian people”.Approached by the Guardian, Đukanović and Vučković confirmed the accuracy of this account. Đukanović added: “I prefer not to make any statement on this matter while the court proceedings are ongoing.”Little was heard of the General Staff plan for months. In November, Trump beat Kamala Harris to win re-election. Ten days later, Vučić’s government announced that the General Staff site had been stripped of its protected status.View image in fullscreenSerbian students and Belgrade residents hold a banner reading ‘We won’t give up the General Staff building’ in Belgrade in November 2025.Photograph: Andrej Isaković/AFP/Getty ImagesKeeping it in the familyOne of the first things Trump did upon regaining the presidency was to ditch the pledge he made in his first term that his family business would refrain from doing deals abroad while he was in office.“The scale of corruption will be orders of magnitude greater than what we saw in the first Trump administration,” Kathleen Clark, a government ethics lawyer at Washington University School of Law,warnedat the time. Trump had made it much easier, she said, to buy his favour.The family business remained officially under the control of his two oldest sons, Don Jr and Eric. In January 2025, four days after their father’s inauguration, Eric spoke about some new projects. The Trumps and the Kushners, New York real estate families united by marriage, had decided to embark on their first venture together: Kushner’s Belgrade hotel and tower would bear the Trump name.“It’s going to be fun to bring the family together,” Erictoldthe New York Times. “Serbia is one of the fastest-growing countries in Europe, and we’re incredibly honoured to be there.” Kushner, who had travelled to Belgrade for what Vučićcalledan “inspiring” meeting with the Serbian leader, added: “Our research showed that the Trump brand would be the best for this market.”That brand has enjoyed a surge in demand around the world during Trump’s second term, accompanied by allegations that it comes with a quid pro quo.View image in fullscreenJared Kushner joins Donald Trump and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, at the inaugural meeting of the Board of Peace at the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesIn Vietnam, Eric was showered with confetti at the groundbreaking ceremony for a £1.5bn golf resort, the permits for which were granted with unusual speed. Then Trump halved Vietnam’s tariffs. The Saudis poured money into Kushner’s fund, and plans emerged for a Trump plaza in Jeddah. Then Trump agreed to sell the kingdom new US fighter jets. A cryptocurrency baron’s company and senior Emiratis cut a lucrative transaction with World Liberty Financial, the digital currency venture Don Jr and Eric founded. Trump gave the crypto baron apardonand the Emiratis access to restrictedUS chips.Asked about such deals last year, Kushner, now a presidential envoy to Russia, Israel and elsewhere, said: “What people call conflicts of interests … I call experience and trusted relationships that we have throughout the world.”Those who strike up “trusted relationships” with the Trumps, even if there is not an obvious quid pro quo, gain something less tangible but maybe still more valuable: the aura of friendship with a president who is happy to wield his superpower to make or break smaller nations and their leaders.Vučić has plenty in common with Trump. Both are friendly with Vladimir Putin and contemptuous of the EU – in Vučić’s case, despite his country having applied to join. A shared disdain for Nato may help explain why the one part of the General Staff building’s heritage that the redevelopment pledged to retain was a memorial to the alliance’s “aggression” against Serbia.And there is a lot that Vučić could use US help with, not least the fate of Kosovo, which he says is still part of Serbia.Not long after his father returned to office, Don Jr landed in Belgrade. Vučić said that during their meeting he “emphasised the importance of the economic and political relations between Serbia and the USA and stressed the importance of strategic cooperation between the two countries and joint projects in the years to come”. When Don Jr returned the following month, Vučić fed him a choicesucking-pig.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueFor Vučić, the support of the first family was timely. Days before his regime stripped the General Staff site of its protection, thecollapse of a canopyat Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people, triggeredrolling protestsagainst graft. The student organisers’ slogan has become “Serbia or mafia”.Don Jr’s visit came on the eve of the biggest demonstration in Serbia’s history. He invited Vučić on to his podcast, Triggered, and declared that the Serb ruler’s opponents were “weaponising” the Novi Sad disaster, just as Trump’s had done with the Capitol riots after his 2020 election defeat.But the protesters maintained their momentum, and began to rally against the Trump tower. In May 2025, Vučić went to the US, hoping to visit Trump at Mar-a-Lago, his Florida members’ club. He got to see Rudy Giuliani, Trump’s disgraced lawyer, but not the president. State mediareportedthis was because Vučić fell ill.No sooner was Vučić home than police arrested Goran Vasić, the man who had been installed as head of the heritage institute to replace Dubravka Đukanović following her resignation. To achieve the cancellation of the General Staff building’s protected status, prosecutors said, Vasic hadforgeda supportive expert opinion.More arrests followed. In December 2025, Vučić’s culture minister was indicted for abuse of office for his alleged part in the General Staff scheme. Within days, Kushner’s company announced the project was off.Coup or cover-up?Vučić’s threat of reprisals was not idle.His allies attacked Đukanović, claiming that she had tried to profit personally from her time as a heritage official. Her deputy, who received a visit from the state security service after she went on television to denounce the cancellation of the General Staff building’s protection, has beenaccusedof unrelated misconduct. The Serbian conservators’ industry body said this had “the obvious aim of discrediting her”. Both are expected to give evidence in the criminal proceedings.For the specialist unit of organised-crime prosecutors who brought the charges, this is a watershed case. Never before has a serving Serbian minister been indicted.Vučić accuses the prosecutors of staging a coup. Others, though, fear they are pulling their punches. That concern increased when Nikola Selaković, the indicted culture minister, used a court appearance in April torevealthat, while police were raiding his ministry, he was in his office sipping plum brandy and smoking cigarettes with Mladen Nenadić, the head of the organised-crime prosecutors’ unit. The unit’s spokesperson said there was “no discussion regarding the course of the case”.“In everything that happened regarding potential investments, I saw a chance for our country and citizens,” said Selaković, who faces three years in prison if convicted.Vučić has not been charged. Neither has his lieutenant, Mali. Both deny wrongdoing.View image in fullscreenAleksandar Vučić addresses the 81st UN general assembly in September.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/ReutersThe indictment refers to evidence from witnesses who were present at the Vučić meeting in February 2024 but does not mention it, raising questions about the apparent decision to omit what would appear to be a key part of the narrative.The spokesperson for the organised crime prosecutors’ unit said that it had evidence regarding Vučić’s February 2024 meeting with the heritage officials. Beyond those already indicted, prosecutors were “conducting pretrial proceedings in this case to determine potential criminal liability of other persons as well”, the spokesperson added.Vučić has stepped down and cannot seek another term but is expected to retain his control over the regime if he is elected prime minister on 25 October. In one of his last acts as president, he issued 49 pardons. Some of the recipients have not been identified and it is not clear whether they include defendants in the General Staff case.Get in touchContact Tom Burgis about this storyIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact Tom using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’. To send a message to Tom Burgis please choose the ‘UK Investigations’ team.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreThe White House referred questions to the Trumps’ company. Its representative said: “The Trump Organization has no plans to develop any project in Belgrade, was never, at any point, involved in any discussions or negotiations to acquire any site in Belgrade and denies any involvement in or knowledge of the alleged claims.”Kushner’s spokesperson said: “The suggestion thatJared Kushnerpursued the Belgrade project as part of any political arrangement or ‘pay to play’ scheme is categorically false.” Rather, it was “an opportunity to transform a site associated with a painful chapter in Serbia’s history into a symbol of healing and reconciliation, while bringing substantial private investment, jobs and economic opportunity to Belgrade”.The spokesperson added: “Jared had no involvement in the Serbian government’s internal processes concerning the site’s protected status.”For all Vučić’s difficulties, the tale of the Trump Tower Belgrade does not appear to have put others off doing business with the first family. Trump retains stakes in dozens of his companies, even if his sons nominally run them. In July, he released his financial disclosure for his first year back at the White House. It showed he hadmade $2bn.Explore more on these topicsSerbiaTrump administrationDonald TrumpJared KushnerDonald Trump JrEric TrumpEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: UK economy unexpectedly grows in August despite fall in consumer spending | Economic growth (GDP) | The Guardian
description: Latest data showing surprise 0.1% growth is boost to John Healey a fortnight before his first budget
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Latest data showing surprise 0.1% growth is boost to John Healey a fortnight before his first budget
Content: The UK economy has shown more resilience than first feared at the start of the Iran war.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenThe UK economy has shown more resilience than first feared at the start of the Iran war.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAEconomic growth (GDP)UK economy unexpectedly grows in August despite fall in consumer spendingLatest data showing surprise 0.1% growth is boost to John Healey a fortnight before his first budgetBusiness news – live updatesRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentThu 15 Oct 2026 02.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK economy unexpectedly continued to grow in August despite a fall in consumer spending before John Healey’s first budget as chancellor.Figures from theOffice for National Statisticsshowed gross domestic product (GDP) rose by 0.1% last month, compared with 0.4% growth in July. That confounded a forecast by City economists of a 0.1% contraction.With less than a fortnight before Healey’s tax and spending announcement, the ONS reading represents a surprise boost given that the Middle East war is rattling the global economy and hitting British households and businesses with a surge in energy costs.After petrol and diesel prices rose and with higher energy bills hitting household spending, the ONS said the consumer-facing services sector fell by 0.3% on the month, after a decline of 0.1% in July.Despite the overall services sector showing no growth in August, the surprise headline improvement was driven by strength in manufacturing with 0.8% growth in the wider production sector, which includes manufacturing, mining and energy generation. Construction output fell by 0.2%..The largest negative contribution came from sports, amusement and recreation activities, alongside a slump in food and drink services. Analysts said the fall could be a sign of a reversal from an earlier boost from the World Cup and unusually hot weather, or could reflect households trimming their spending.The ONS said GDP over the wider three months to the end of August rose by 0.7%. On an annual basis, it said the economy had grown by 2.1%, the strongest growth rate since August 2022.It comes after the International Monetary Fund this weekupgraded its growth forecasts for the UKthis year but warned it expected a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll.Speaking from Bangkok, where he is attending the meetings of the IMF and World Bank, Healey welcomed the figures: “Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today’s figures offer more proof of Britain’s resilience in the face of these global shocks.“This week the IMF have upgraded UK growth for 2026 and said that our fiscal discipline stands out with the lowest deficit in the G7 forecast by 2029 … my budget will build on this approach to drive good growth in every postcode.”Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said: “Undoubtedly, there may be some hiccups to come in the runup to year-end, especially as energy prices continue to bite household incomes, and higher rates continue to drag on spending and investment.“The good news? The UK’s resilience story continues. It’s hard to overstate how strong the UK performance has been all year.”Against a volatile backdrop, the chancellor is under pressure to use his tax and spending address to the Commons on 28 October for a package of support to soften the blow for households, includinghelp with rising energy bills. However, he will face a delicate balancing act amid a sharpincrease in government borrowing costs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn recent months, Britain’s economy had shown more resilience than had been expected at the start of the Iran war after recording the strongest rate of growth in the G7 in the first half of 2026. Official figures suggested a strong expansion in AI-related business activity as one factor behind the surprise rise.Jake Finney, senior economist at PwC, said: “The UK’s growth performance has been a bright spot amid a less impressive run of economic news following events in the Middle East. Business investment has been an important driver, particularly spending on ICT hardware, likely linked to the build-out of AI infrastructure.”In a fillip for the chancellor, the IMF this weekupgraded its UK growth forecastsfor this year, but warned that it expected a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll.However, economists said momentum was likely to falter at the end of the year as households come under pressure from rising inflation.Financial markets now anticipate the Bank of England to raise interest rates next month from 3.75% to 4%, before four more quarter-point rate increases in 2027.Matt Swannell, the chief economic adviser to the Item Club, said: “We’re sceptical this strength can last … Some pullback looks inevitable.
