The impact of the conflict in the Middle East is also starting to be felt. Higher energy bills and petrol prices are pushing up inflation and hitting consumers’ spending power.”Explore more on these topicsEconomic growth (GDP)EconomicsBudget 2026US-Israel war on IranEnergy billsGlobal economyInflationnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I introduce myself to anyone who looks a bit jumpy’: a security guard’s take on anti-shoplifting fixes | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: A professional reveals the most effective tricks of the trade, from a little bit of empathy to hi-tech cameras
Author: George Bass
Headline: A professional reveals the most effective tricks of the trade, from a little bit of empathy to hi-tech cameras
Content: It is hard to identify who might be preparing to swipe something, especially given the rise of so-called ‘middle-class shoplifting’.Photograph: Vitalij Chalupnik/AlamyView image in fullscreenIt is hard to identify who might be preparing to swipe something, especially given the rise of so-called ‘middle-class shoplifting’.Photograph: Vitalij Chalupnik/AlamyRetail industry‘I introduce myself to anyone who looks a bit jumpy’: a security guard’s take on anti-shoplifting fixesA professional reveals the most effective tricks of the trade, from a little bit of empathy to hi-tech camerasGeorge BassThu 15 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 10.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve run into volatile thieves for years – from opportunistic phone snatchers to people ripping computers off desks and biofuel bandits trying to steal vats of used cooking oil – and every time I file an incident report, I try to make a recommendation for preventive measures.It’s safer to try to avoid a situation where things get physical with a suspected criminal. I don’t want to let my employers down, but I also don’t want anyone to have to go to hospital – myself included.Greggs seems to be following a similar train of thought: earlier this year the chainphased out self-service cabinetsin areas where shoplifting is rife and has installedsafe pod “robocops” with 120-decibel sirens in some stores.But snatch thefts seem to be on the rise everywhere, from “steaming” (large groups overwhelming a store) in city centres tomachinery being swiped from rural farm shops. The cost of this crime – in terms of lost merchandise and measures to tackle it – further erodes margins at a time when retailers are battlinghigher employment costsandincreases to business rates.Customers, ever squeezed byrising energy bills, are becoming doubly impatient: those who are not tempted by grabbable goods are rightly affronted by measures such assliding shieldsthat seem to imply that everyone is a criminal.But is it possible to make a store thief proof and welcoming to law-abiding clientele?Discreet high technology is a happy medium. PTZ cameras (pan/tilt/zoom, which can be adjusted to track and focus on a single suspect) are one of the most-effective choices. They’re more efficient than fixed-camera CCTV, less controversial than AI surveillance and a serious upgrade on the convex mirror mounted at the end of the aisle in your local corner shop.Sainsbury’s store pauses AI scanning after false shoplifting accusationRead morePTZ camera manoeuvrability means high-quality facial images, a must-have when trying to build evidence. Freeze-frames can also be used to generate stills that some premises owners choose to turn into warning posters, or share on a chat group with other local businesses.My advice here is to be wary of GDPR regulations and remember that an incorrect time signature can render recordings inadmissible.As useful as movable cameras are, they still require a human operator. Hiring guards can feel like a tax on businesses – but one that goes unpaid at considerable risk.Ask anyone who lives in a village whether they’d prefer a CCTV camera or a “bobby on the beat” and the answer would be probably unanimously the latter.The sight of a uniformed officer can be a strong deterrent. However, it comes with an upper limit. For example: if a 3,000 sq metre supermarket can accommodate 40,000 goods and 4,000 daily customers, one guard will not be able to cover it all.It is also hard to identify which customers might be preparing to swipe something, especially given the rise of“middle-class shoplifting”. As someone whose job pays just above minimum wage, this is an interesting phenomenon.I get that inflation presses down on all of us, but people further up the pyramid than me should know it won’t be shareholders or bonus-receiving bosses taking the hit for goods being pinched: it will be prices. Higher costs will further imperil the most vulnerable people who walk on site, the ones who already cannot afford breador baby formula.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy best approach in these cases is empathy. I try to introduce myself to anyone who hangs around but looks jumpy; explain that every tap of my bank card makes me sweat too.I also try to build local knowledge of repeat offenders: insight that made the bobbies on the beat so valuable. I know it won’t work against content creators who film me for “lols” while I’m administering first aid, and who half of all young Brits apparently want to emulate. I honestly fear them more than I do getting punched, stabbed or spat on.But doing your revision pays off, especially when encountering an unsettled local resident with a penchant for threatening people with kitchen utensils. As the resident in question strode towards the premises one morning, my shiftmate quickly asked me whether I knew his name and address (I did).“Morning, Mr Beddlington,” said my colleague as the resident got level with us and before he could grab his first frying pan. “Everything OK at Thorn Court today? Anything we can help with?”The resident did an about-face and left the site. Loss prevention done low-cost and painlessly.Names and addresses have been changedWhat the Bouncer Saw: Life on theFront Lineof the Security Businessby George Bass is published by Hachette. title: Poland’s ascent from communist state to top 20 economy reverses the brain drain | Poland | The Guardian
description: In the final part of our series on the country, Poles tell how wages have soared – along with the cost of living
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: In the final part of our series on the country, Poles tell how wages have soared – along with the cost of living
Content: A view of Warsaw from the observation deck of Varso Tower, the tallest building in the EU at 310 metres. In the background, the Palace of Culture and Science, built in the 1950s as a symbol of the postwar socialist era.Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA view of Warsaw from the observation deck of Varso Tower, the tallest building in the EU at 310 metres. In the background, the Palace of Culture and Science, built in the 1950s as a symbol of the postwar socialist era.Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The GuardianPolandPoland’s ascent from communist state to top 20 economy reverses the brain drainIn the final part of our series on the country, Poles tell how wages have soared – along with the cost of livingWill military spending help or hinder Poland’s growth story?Poland’s push for EU energy resilience amid Russian aggressionRichard Partingtonin WarsawThu 15 Oct 2026 01.56 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbove the rain-soaked streets of Warsaw, the observation deck of the Varso tower overlooks Joseph Stalin’s gift toPolandthat has divided opinion for decades.For some, the Soviet-eraPalace of Culture and Scienceis a drunk confectioner’s nightmare; standing as a relic of oppression that should have been demolished. For others, it is an icon on the skyline and a monumental warning from history.For the managers of the Varso – completed four years ago, as the tallest building in the EU – with its 310m-high spire rising symbolically above its Stalinist neighbour, it is a waypoint on Poland’s rapid path to economic prosperity.View image in fullscreenCezary Błaszczyk and Natalia Kasperska at the Varso Tower.Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The Guardian“We look down on it,” says Cezary Błaszczyk, the managing director of HB Reavis in Poland, which owns the tower, gesturing at the palace opposite. A few months ago aslackline walkertraversed the 500m gap between the buildings. “It was a symbolic walk from the past to the future,” says his colleague Natalia Kasperska.“Since we are higher and taller than the Palace of Culture, we treat it as: ‘We got over communism, and now we are a country with a strong economy,’” Błaszczyk says.Over the four decades since regaining its independence from Soviet-dominated rule, Poland has been transformed. Excluding oil-exporting states and financial hubs, incomes have converged with western levels at the fastest rate in the world; from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year.View image in fullscreenThe Estonian slackliner Jaan Roose walks on a 500-metre-long tightrope stretched between the Palace of Culture and Science and Varso Tower on 31 May.Photograph: Sergei Gapon/AFP/Getty ImagesNational income surpassed $1tn (£755bn) last year, ranking Poland among the world’s 20 largest economies. International Monetary Fund projections show income per capita will soon overtake Japan and Spain.“Four decades ago, we were in – excuse my English – deep, deep shit,” says Marcin Bosacki, the Polish deputy foreign minister.Stirring a cup of tea and lemon in his opulent Warsaw office, he recalls queueing after school in the 1980s for up to five hours to buy butter and meat as the communist government imposed martial law.However, the Gdańsk shipworkers’Solidarność movementand Pope John Paul II’s1979 pilgrimageto his home country paved the way for Poland’s transition to democracy in 1990 and an “economic miracle”. Integration with western institutions, includingNatoin 1999 andEUaccession in 2004, also helped.Poland GDP per capita graphicFor years, many Poles chose to emigrate to earn more abroad, in a brain drain accelerated by EU membership. Polish plumbersbecame shorthand in Britain for foreign labouramid the political battles over EU freedom of movement before the Brexit vote.Now Britons are increasingly likely to have their taps fixed by Romanians and Bulgarians, after a surge in the number of Polish nationals leaving. Ineach yearsince 2021, when Brexit was enacted after a year-long transition period, twice as many Poles left the UK than arrived.Meanwhile,Germany recordedmore non-Germans moving to Poland in 2024 than heading in the opposite direction for the first time on record.On the Varso’s 44th floor, in the Warsaw practice of Foster + Partners, Jedrzej Kolesinski and Krzysztof Gornicki are among those returnees. Both moved to London in their 20s to work in the British architecture firm’s head office – where they led the design team behind the tower they now occupy.Gornicki says Poland has changed dramatically in the years he was away. He always wanted to return to contribute to the country, and raising a family near his parents in a safe, green city that is more affordable than London also has its plus points. Now the pair are working to design Warsaw’s new airport – the biggest greenfield infrastructure project inEurope.“You can work globally from one location. In London we worked on projects from North America to Asia … right now, we’re doing the same thing, just from Warsaw.”On the streets below the Varso, the sights and sounds of progress are unmistakable. Modern electric trams glide past skyscrapers, there are cranes and construction work, giant advertising boards, and dockless e-scooters.The traditional working-classbar mleczny(milk bars) still do a roaring trade serving beetroot soup and Polish dumplings. But at the oldest, Prasowy, orders are taken on a digital touchscreen.Once an asphalt desert designed for columns of Soviet tanks, the old Parade Square surrounding the palace has had a green makeover. Further development is planned to bolster Warsaw’s bid for the 2040 summer Olympics.Living costs in Warsaw graphicThere are also growing pains. Just as the facades of Warsaw’s medieval old town –rebuilt from the rubble of the second world war– conceal 20th-century concrete, Poland’s stellar growth obscures tensions. The influx of global capital has driven up living costs, squeezing out poor Varsovians. Incomeinequality is among the highest in Europe, while growing political divisions set the stage for a fractious general election next year.Convergence with the west also presents a novel challenge for a country with a reputation as a low-cost hub within the EU.For years Poland’s cheap, skilled workforce attracted companies such as Volkswagen to build cars, Cadbury to make chocolate and banks such as JP Morgan to open global support centres. At €19.10 (£16.10) an hour, average labour costs (wages, taxes and other costs) are stillhalf the level of Germany and France, but the gap is closing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSince 2004, the average monthly wage has more than tripled in nominal terms to 8,904 złoty (£1,723) last year. The net monthly salary in Warsaw has risen by 120% since 2016, according to Deutsche Bank, lifting it above Rome and Lisbon. A meal for two in the capital now costs more than in Tokyo and the price of a cappuccino has doubled.Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire founder of InPost, the pan-European parcel locker company started in Kraków, says Poles deserve their reputation as hard workers. But now the country must focus on working smarter, in higher-value-added manufacturing and knowledge-intensive services.“The next phase will depend less on catching up, and more on productivity. We don’t have labour cost advantage at all. We need to focus on productivity, technology, cheaper energy and better regulation.”Capitals salaries graphicHe is, however, concerned about the tensions in Polish politics. Divisions between the nationalist president, Karol Nawrocki, and Donald Tusk’s liberal government havegrown increasingly acrimonious. Meanwhile, fringe far-right parties together hold afifth of public support. Poland is alsoinvesting heavily in defenceandenergy security– aiming to boost economic growth in the process – amid Europe’s response to Russian aggression and US disengagement.“People may put trust in someone else that has a magic remedy. [But] there is no magic remedy. We need to be super careful in terms of believing there is a secret sauce that will magically change things,” Brzoska says.“In my opinion – unfortunately for all of us – we still need to work hard.”As part of its growth plans, Poland is pushing to become a regional tech hub, bolstered by a$1bn investment fundbacked by public and private capital to support tech startups and AI companies. The number of high-growth firms is rising, includingElevenLabs, an $11bn AI audio generation and voice cloning company named after 11 November – Poland’s national independence day.There are strong foundations for its ambition. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s annual programme for international student assessment (Pisa) scoresranks Poland equal to the UKamong the top countries in Europe and globally for maths, while a greater share of adults have higher education qualifications than in Germany.On the eastern side of the Vistula River in the gritty and creative working-class district of Praga, the campus of the games company CD Projekt Red shows the progress being made.View image in fullscreenMarcin Łukaszewski, Social Media Manager at CD Projekt Red, gives a tour of the company’s headquarters in Warsaw.Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The GuardianAs the developer behind the smash hit games seriesThe WitcherandCyberpunk 2077, the company started life in the 1990s as an importer of CD games made by US publishers.Michał Nowakowski, its co-chief executive, says this was about the limit of Polish ambition in the early days. Now he competes globally to attract coders, games developers and graphic designers.“In the late 90s and early 2000s I feel there was a massive inferiority complex. Among everybody who was young, you wanted to catch up with the west.”Growing up in the 1980s, his family were expelled from Poland in the period of martial law. He recalls visiting London aged 15 and being “blown away” by the Virgin megastore and British culture. “I could never imagine Poland being like it.”Within a generation, though, he says this attitude would be alien to his own children. “For young people now they have no inferiority complex. They don’t stop and think: ‘Can we be as good as Brits, French, Spanish?’ It’s not holding them back.“We have really good universities and skills teaching people. I think that can take us to unprecedented heights as a country.“We’re a proper-sized country. Not too small, not too big; no inferiority complex any more. There’s nothing holding us back.”Explore more on these topicsPolandEconomicsTechnology sectorAI (artificial intelligence)EuropeEuropean UnionGentrificationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Frieze review – you’ll see more avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tent | Art | The Guardian
description:
Regents Park, London
This year’s art fair is a jumble sale of mediocre paintings for the super-rich, while its Masters sibling hawks dinosaur skulls and sleazy 19th-century nudes. Welcome to the art market as its most grotesque
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: Regents Park, LondonThis year’s art fair is a jumble sale of mediocre paintings for the super-rich, while its Masters sibling hawks dinosaur skulls and sleazy 19th-century nudes. Welcome to the art market as its most grotesque
Content: ‘Serves the tastes of a certain kind of consumer’ … the Carl Freedman stand at Frieze London, 2026.Photograph: Linda Nylind/Linda Nylind/FriezeView image in fullscreen‘Serves the tastes of a certain kind of consumer’ … the Carl Freedman stand at Frieze London, 2026.Photograph: Linda Nylind/Linda Nylind/FriezeArtReviewFrieze review – you’ll see more avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tentRegents Park, LondonThis year’s art fair is a jumble sale of mediocre paintings for the super-rich, while its Masters sibling hawks dinosaur skulls and sleazy 19th-century nudes. Welcome to the art market as its most grotesqueJonathan JonesThu 15 Oct 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNaked people climb out of the earth and run around waving their arms and screaming, while someone with a bird’s head and wings plays the bagpipes. It’s my favourite artwork at this year’s Frieze but don’t go looking for this wildly imaginative outrage among the heaps of contemporary art at Frieze London. It’s a painting by a 16th-century follower of Hieronymus Bosch and is on view at Frieze Masters, the posher tent on the other side of Regent’s Park.I’m sorry to say I was bored rigid in Frieze London. Many people attend, I imagine, hoping to be informed and excited by the newest, coolest art, but you’ll see more genuinely avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tent. There are endless paintings, none of which are much good, interspersed with photographs which tend to be a little better. The first thing here that held me at all was a two-metre-tall, inkjet print by Wolfgang Tillmans called Paul, nude, golf ball in which the naked Paul has his elbows on the floor and his close-cropped head bowed between them in apparent despair, while the white ball beside him eerily mirrors the pale flesh of his bony back. But it’s not new – it dates from 1994.And, oh Lord, those paintings. There seem to be millions of them. And an elegant white marquee full of gallery booths along endless white corridors is a ghastly way of showing them, a dreadful way of seeing. It’s not as rewarding as visiting galleries which can be interesting spaces. Here, everything is crammed in, like a huge shop – the Selfridges of art.View image in fullscreen‘The Selfridges of art’ … Spruth Magers stand at Frieze London, 2026.Photograph: Linda Nylind/Linda Nylind/FriezeFrieze, it is claimed, defines the new and finds the stars of tomorrow. But it’s obvious that it really serves the needs of sellers and the tastes of a certain kind of extremely wealthy consumer. This is most apparent on VIP day when I enter along with a host of tech bros, hedge-fund managers, retired hedge-fund managers, their children, and – is that George Osborne? – who were actually here to buy this stuff. At Frieze Masters, I was about to ask the price of an Anselm Kiefer work, matted vegetation clogging its surface, when an elderly couple beat me to it. They were genuinely interested in purchasing. The price was just shy of a million quid.Things you can put on your wall are still the most collectible art. At Frieze Masters, you will find works by established modern “masters”, many of whom are deceased: a series of stained, graffiti-laden visual poems by Cy Twombly, a grey, bleak nude by Leon Kossoff. But at the contemporary fair, some of it is jumble sale standard. At Los Angeles’ Night Gallery booth, Wanda Koop’s Radiance-Together depicts two candles burning side by side in a blue and purple setting. Aw, cute. Who on earth would take this seriously? Another of its artists, Andy Woll, shows a row of lazily brushed mountain views that are just as vacuous. Meanwhile, at the appropriately named Grimm Gallery, Rosalind Nashashibi – better known for her films – exhibits a silly painting of lovers between flowery borders.Now here’s something different – a row of white mineral-like growths, eerily lovely, enigmatically organic: they’re Helen Chadwick’s Piss Flowers, a chance to own examples of a modern classic by this tremendous artist who died in 1996. Why is she not over in Frieze Masters? And at the back of the Edel Assanti booth is Lonnie Holley’s assemblage of a water tap on a rusty pipe entwined with wire and two green bottles on a rough wooden plinth. It has the raw tang of real life. Holley, a musician and artist from Birmingham, Alabama who held me spellbound a couple of years ago when he showed how he can create beauty from a random piece of wire, is a true American great who stands out in this blandfest.View image in fullscreen‘A festival of capitalism run amok’ … Gagosian stand at Frieze London, 2026.Photograph: Linda Nylind/Linda Nylind/FriezeSo do Tracey Emin, Waqas Khan, Do Ho Suh, Catherine Opie and Zanele Muholi – but in all honesty the success rate at Frieze London is about one in 10. That’s far too low for an event claiming to define the artistic zeitgeist.Over at Frieze Masters, you’ve got the best certificate of quality there is: time. If something has value after 50, 500, or 68,000,000 years, it’s probably good. That 68m years is no exaggeration for here on sale is a triple-horned, fossilised Triceratops skull. Is this really going to end up as decoration in some rich dude’s house?Let’s get it in perspective. To call this head “museum quality” is an understatement. The Natural History Museum does not own a Triceratops fossil of this perfection. Palaeontologists,as the Guardian recently reported, are worried that the fashion for dinosaur specimens among the ultra-rich is inflating prices and locking out museums. There are several such marvels being sold here.View image in fullscreen‘Fruitier, stranger’ … a skull for sale at Frieze Masters.Photograph: Hugo Glendinning/ FriezeFrieze Masters is more visually exciting than Frieze London. It’s fruitier, stranger. You can buy armour, silverware, Arabian carpets, the stuff a decadent aesthete might have surrounded themselves with in 1896. It makes you realise how conformist the contemporary fair is. At Frieze Masters, you can indulge your most perverse tastes – there are loads of sleazy, 19th-century nudes.But if it is more interesting, it is also more disgusting. Stalls fetishise objects from the past, ripping them out of context to display them as brightly lit gewgaws: a manuscript page cut from its codex, a face mask off an ancient Egyptian coffin, a stone head of a priest from 2nd century AD Palmyra. These things belong in museums, but here they all are in the isolating spotlight of luxury and money.This is a festival of capitalism run amok. I could say jokingly you might buy this or that but you won’t, unless you are a squillionaire, nor will I. What was it Andy Burnham was saying about the tyranny of neoliberalism? Here it distorts art in a delirious orgy of commodification.The Colnaghi booth could have been designed as a Marxist exposé of the art market. African wooden carvings stand in front of a kitsch 1920 nude by Giacomo Grosso. The lavish view of the model’s bum as she lies on silks and the fact that she’s wearing high heels make it comically clear this is finely painted soft porn. The African art, made for religious purposes, is reduced to decor in front of this commodified body. John Berger, the radical critic who saw nude paintings and other forms of commodified art as playthings of western capitalism, might have said: told you so.Frieze London and Frieze Mastersare on until 18 OctoberExplore more on these topicsArtFrieze art fairCollectingExhibitionsPaintingSculptureHeritagereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Street Fighter review – nostalgia only goes so far in junky fighting game movie | Action and adventure films | The Guardian
description: There are brief, simple pleasures in the inevitable new big screen take on the classic game but like the recent Mortal Kombat movies, it’s a largely incoherent mess
Author: Radheyan Simonpillai
Headline: There are brief, simple pleasures in the inevitable new big screen take on the classic game but like the recent Mortal Kombat movies, it’s a largely incoherent mess
Content: Andrew Koji and Noah Centineo in Street Fighter.Photograph: Mark Rogers/Paramount Pictures, Capcom and LegendaryView image in fullscreenAndrew Koji and Noah Centineo in Street Fighter.Photograph: Mark Rogers/Paramount Pictures, Capcom and LegendaryAction and adventure filmsReviewStreet Fighter review – nostalgia only goes so far in junky fighting game movieThere are brief, simple pleasures in the inevitable new big screen take on the classic game but like the recent Mortal Kombat movies, it’s a largely incoherent messRadheyan SimonpillaiThu 15 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe just hadResident Evil, Zach Cregger’s giddy, nasty, devilishly fun spin on Capcom’s popular zombie franchise. It gave us renewed hope (after Sonic the Hedgehog, The Last of Us and Fallout) that video game adaptations could be good, actually.But now here comes Street Fighter, a garish and incoherent mess that amuses in fits and starts but barely improves on the Mortal Kombat movies before it, crushing those hopes in its atomic suplex.Whalefall review – slimy survival thriller traps us in a whale and struggles to make it digestibleRead moreFans certainly won’t mind. They’ve kept the box office’s life bar in the green for these one-on-one fighter adaptations going all the way back to the disastrous 1994 Street Fighter movie starring Jean-Claude Van Damme andhis $10,000-a-week coke problem. They’ll happily tolerate how the new Street Fighter, like those Mortal Kombat movies, can barely string together a cohesive plot, which has clearly been pencilled in as an afterthought between rounds of combat in yet another tournament-style narrative. None of that will matter because they’re just here for the dopamine hits by way of nostalgia.To that end, the movie exhaustively rolls out all the iconic characters and moves from the games – like Sumo warrior E Honda’s hundred-hand slap or military bro Guile’s flash kick – not to mention some at-times striking anime flashback sequences and a bevy of pop culture ephemera from its early-90s setting. Grainy, UHF quality MTV video segments show Ken (Noah Centineo) to be a self-destructive New Kids on the Block-era celebrity party boy with flashy blond curls, while the needle drops bring back bygone hits like MC Hammer’s 2 Legit 2 Quit and Montell Jordan’s This Is How We Do It.It’s all about keeping us pampered in those fond memories from our pubescent childhoods, including bits that bring back the way us preteen boys ogled the 16-bit version of hypersexualized Chun-Li. She’s played in the movie by the lively and commanding Callina Liang, who enters the frame thighs first and unfortunately plays the only character tasked with a gratuitous slow-motion shower scene.Liang doesn’t let that stuff drag down her performance, which is formidable, while her physicality during fight scenes is genuinely impressive. She’s one of the handful who bring some modest pleasures to the overcrowded mess. WWE wrestler Cody Rhodes, wearing a cartoonish trapezoid blond wig as Guile, is genuinely funny in the way he barks pleasantries and threats in equal measure. Indian movie star Vidyut Jammwal, who is trained in the ancient martial art Kalaripayattu, brings captivating authenticity and hypnotic movements to his all-too-brief scenes as yoga priest Dhalsim. Even controversial comic and manosphere podcaster Andrew Schulz gives a convincing performance worthy of an essay, playing Ken’s manager, who capitalizes on his bro’s brawn while coddling his wounded ego.But the likable performances get buried in a movie that often feels like it was made on a six-button control pad. Street Fighter is a barrage of character introductions and story arcs lifted from the games and animated spin-offs, colliding into one another in a way that makes a relatively linear plot (it’s a freakin’ fight tournament!) confusing. Did Vega edit this with his Wolverine-like claw hands?The movie’s most amusing fight arrives early, with Ken and Ryu (Andrew Koji) reunited in a hotel room after a years-long fallout, lured back together for a world championship tournament that the movie’s villain M Bison organized for nefarious purposes. Ken furiously takes wild swings at Ryu. Flying kicks miss the mark. Roundhouses hit nothing but air. Ryu quickly and calmly out-maneuvers, blocking with a pillow and then hilariously slipping the pillow below Ken’s head to catch his wipeout, or tiptoeing away from Ken while planted in a sofa seat. It’s a standout scene that really does feel like it belongs to another, smarter movie.Elsewhere, during a matchup between Ken and boxer Balrog (played by rapper 50 Cent), Sakurai learns the right lessons from Martin Scorsese’s Raging Bull, quick cutting between flashy hits and slow-motion impacts, the sloppy mix of blood and drool flying from Ken’s mouth hanging in the air long enough to appreciate its viscosity.And then there’s Liang’s Chun-Li, whose legwork delivers spectacular action, while her character tends to be the one dragging others down to earth with quick, frank, intermittently funny verbal jabs. She’s the grounded one, standing 10 toes down in purpose and principle. Whenever Ken or Ryu start emoting or waxing philosophical like Steven Seagal or Van Damme in those movies that inspire Street Fighter, Liang’s Chun-Li calls out in the most basic terms how stupid they sound.There’s several knowing winks at the fans like this, guarding against criticism by owning up to how silly this all is, which would land better if the movie ever rose above the stuff it’s making fun of. Instead, Street Fighter is satisfied punching down on itself, and everything that’s cringe about the 90s, while happily being stuck there, in the past, so it could pretend that this is as good as it gets for video game adaptations.We know better.Street Fighter is out in Australian cinemas now and in the UK and US on 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsAction and adventure filmsGamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Your full attention: Jesse Eisenberg’s 10 best film performances – ranked!  | Movies | The Guardian
description: As his new movie The Debut closes the London film festival, we count down the best of the actor’s shy, sly and sometimes hairy outings
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: As his new movie The Debut closes the London film festival, we count down the best of the actor’s shy, sly and sometimes hairy outings
Content: Two for the price of one … Jesse Eisenberg in The Double.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTwo for the price of one … Jesse Eisenberg in The Double.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianRankedMoviesYour full attention: Jesse Eisenberg’s 10 best film performances – ranked!As his new movie The Debut closes the London film festival, we count down the best of the actor’s shy, sly and sometimes hairy outingsPeter BradshawThu 15 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google10.The Double(2013)A doppelganger role can be a trap for an actor: either the two roles are not sufficiently distinct, or they are too hammily different, and either way the result can look like a film school graduation project. ButJesse Eisenberggives a stylish split-personality turn in Richard Ayoade’s adaptation of the Dostoevsky novella. He plays Simon, a nerdily shy and self-effacing computer programmer in a grim futureworld, ignored by his employers and by co-worker Hannah (Mia Wasikowska), with whom he is hopelessly in love. But then his carbon copy, James, arrives, also of course played by Eisenberg. James is a confident alpha-achiever who impresses his bosses and entrances Hannah – to Simon’s gibbering despair.9.The Squid and the Whale(2005)View image in fullscreen‘Poignant vulnerability’ … Eisenberg as Walt and Anna Paquin as Lili in The Squid and the Whale.Photograph: Samuel Goldwyn/AllstarNoah Baumbach’s brutally black-comic movie, based on his own parents’ unhappy relationship, features Eisenberg as the 16-year-old Walt, an unbearably precocious and self-important young man who has inherited all of his father’s pompous mannerisms. His dad is Jeff Daniels, a failed novelist and creative writing professor who enviously fell out with his wife, Walt’s mother (Laura Linney), when her own writing career took off. As Walt leaves the world of childhood behind, this becomes a rare unsympathetic performance for Eisenberg in many ways, and the nerdy mannerisms for which he became famous look spiky, high-handed and charmless – yet the poignant vulnerability is clear enough.8.Roger Dodger(2002)This was the teenage Eisenberg’s feature film acting debut, in which his persona of nerdiness, inexperience and bewilderment first arrived in the cinema, along with that patina of self-awareness with which all these things seemed nonetheless to be coated. He is the high school kid Nick, appalled by his own virginity and in dire need of advice on how to make it with girls. He approaches his Lothario uncle Roger – a glorious performance from Campbell Scott – who has just been dumped by his own girlfriend, and, in a frenzy of misogynist rage, Roger takes Nick on a tour of Manhattan’s pickup joints. Eisenberg’s innocence has a charm and openness that Nick’s womaniser lacks. In some ways, he is the opposite of his character in The Squid and the Whale.7.Adventureland(2009)View image in fullscreenComing of age … Kristen Stewart as Em and Eisenberg as James in Adventureland.Photograph: © 2007 Miramax Films. All Rights Reserved.Another of the “virgin” performances with which the younger Eisenberg made his name in the indie-adjacent cinema of the 00s, and he cleverly portrays the way in which the lack of sexual experience becomes the very centre of his character’s existence. It’s a coming-of-age story about a guy called James who has gone through a prestigious undergraduate career at college; the world, supposedly, is now his oyster. But he is still a virgin. And to earn cash for grad school he has to take a job in a scuzzy amusement park, ironically or perhaps not ironically called Adventureland, which is to provide education of a different sort and where he falls for his fellow employee, played byKristen Stewart.6.Sasquatch Sunset(2024)View image in fullscreenPrimitive … Eisenberg in Sasquatch Sunset.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyIt is a film and a role that would challenge any actor: Eisenberg, in full makeup and hairy costume, plays a grunting, nonverbal sasquatch loping through the empty northern California wilderness. He is one of four apelike bigfoot figures who are perhaps the only creatures left alive after some human-made apocalypse, or perhaps we have simply been allowed to share these creatures’ habitual seclusion, their secret existence away from humans. Eisenberg is, perhaps inevitably, the beta-male sasquatch who is less demonstrative than the alpha male grunter. It is a cult performance in a cult film.‘Every day is 24 hours of panic to just get out the door’: Jesse Eisenberg on self-indulgence, candid aunts and his Oscar-tipped Holocaust comedyRead more5.Café Society(2016)It was probably Eisenberg’s destiny to work with Woody Allen at some stage – he is in Café Society and, less prominently, in To Rome With Love, from 2012. Café Society is one of Allen’s innumerable light jeux d’ésprit comedies and perhaps not too memorable, but it has a very interesting performance from Eisenberg. He plays a nervy, gauche romantic who is, of course, ventriloquising Allen in the traditional way, but we also see him grow up from boy to man. Set in the US in the 30s, he’s the kid who gets a nepo job in LA as an assistant to his movie-agent uncle and then another in a New York club run by his brother, where he becomes a white-tuxedoed Bogartian figure, nursing a broken heart.4.Zombieland(2009)View image in fullscreen‘Potential hottie’ … Eisenberg as Columbus and Woody Harrelson as Tallahassee in Zombieland.Photograph: Columbia Pictures/AllstarThis came out the same year as Adventureland, creating the odd illusion that it was part of some kind of franchise – but no, the two films have nothing to do with each other, although Eisenberg’s appearance in both is not dissimilar; he is, as ever, the shy nerd who is also a potential hottie. (This film was followed up 10 years later by an underpar sequel entitled Zombieland: Double Tap, in which Eisenberg reprised his role.) He plays Columbus, a gauche, brainy guy in a post-apocalyptic landscape infested by zombies. Columbus teams up with Woody Harrelson’s redneck, who is overbearing and moreover keeps ruining his chances of making it with a young woman, played by Emma Stone, who goes on the road with them. His rage with Harrelson results in one of the most entertaining outbursts of Eisenberg’s movie career, as he screams: “You are like a giant, cock-blocking robot developed in some kind of secret government lab!”3.The Art of Self-Defense(2019)Film-maker and Brazilian ju-jitsu specialist Riley Stearns created a dark comedy that allowed Eisenberg to explore an interesting possibility to his habitual persona: what if that nerdy, maladroit shyness led not to romcom sexual success, but violence and a general outbreak of toxic masculinity? Eisenberg is Casey, a lonely office worker who is attacked by a gang of bikers and, traumatised, enrols in a karate class. It is led by a charismatic sensei (Alessandro Nivola) whose demands on him become increasingly disturbing.2.A Real Pain(2024)This understated, complex, contemporary film is Eisenberg’s directorial masterpiece. He also gives an outstanding performance, all the more interesting in that it is effectively a supporting turn, ceding the spotlight most of the time to Kieran Culkin. (The Polish-set film is also a very personal movie for Eisenberg, who has now taken up Polish citizenship.) Eisenberg plays David, Culkin is his cousin, Benji; the two are on a kind of buddy-movie road trip visit to Poland to visit the childhood home of their late grandmother, who was a Holocaust survivor. Eisenberg plays – inevitably – a strait-laced, uptight figure while Culkin is the more anarchic free spirit, but without the former’s sensibility and maturity, the latter’s performance wouldn’t make sense.1.The Social Network(2010)View image in fullscreen‘Mile-a-minute dialogue’ … Andrew Garfield, Joseph Mazzello, Eisenberg and Patrick Mapel in The Social Network.Photograph: Merrick Morton/Columbia Pictures/AllstarJesse Eisenberg: Privacy settings engagedRead moreCasting Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg, the young computer genius at Harvard who in 2004 invented Facebook in a frenzy of sexual and social rejection, was a stroke of genius. It allowed Eisenberg to weaponise and make sense of the nerdy onscreen persona that had come so readily to him; it also showed that he was a natural performer of screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s mile-a-minute dialogue. In Eisenberg’s other films, the underdog-nerd aspect was there as a kind of adorable (or perhaps disquieting) flaw, to be surmounted in the course of the narrative. Here it is the whole point. The nerdiness is the superpower; not getting it on with girls is the equivalent of lifting a car above his head. This was the sensational role which was to get Eisenberg the part of ubervillain Lex Luthor in DC films such as Batman V Superman: Dawn of Justice and Zack Snyder’s Justice League and the smart-alec illusionist J Daniel Atlas in the magician-heist caper Now You See Me. But none of those had anything like the quicksilver brilliance of his Zuckerberg, who is entitled and insufferable, driven and obsessive, always convinced of his intellectual superiority, never conceding any point to anyone in any argument, treating everyone to a nonstop fusillade of putdowns and zingers. Eisenberg convinced a whole generation that this was what Mark Zuckerberg was really like. It is a classic performance.Explore more on these topicsFilmRankedJesse EisenbergA Real PainThe Social NetworkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Whalefall review – slimy survival thriller traps us in a whale and struggles to make it digestible | Action and adventure films | The Guardian
description: Austin Abrams gets eaten by a sperm whale in an overlong and flashback-heavy adaptation of Daniel Kraus’s hit novel that only has us on edge in moments
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Austin Abrams gets eaten by a sperm whale in an overlong and flashback-heavy adaptation of Daniel Kraus’s hit novel that only has us on edge in moments
Content: Austin Abrams in Whalefall.Photograph: 20th Century Studios/PAView image in fullscreenAustin Abrams in Whalefall.Photograph: 20th Century Studios/PAAction and adventure filmsReviewWhalefall review – slimy survival thriller traps us in a whale and struggles to make it digestibleAustin Abrams gets eaten by a sperm whale in an overlong and flashback-heavy adaptation of Daniel Kraus’s hit novel that only has us on edge in momentsBenjamin LeeThu 15 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpare a thought for poor Austin Abrams, who, having just endured the world’s worst, and gloopiest, courier assignment inResident Evil, has now been trapped inside a sperm whale …You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreThe immensely likable Euphoria alum (has any show in recent memory provided quite as many genuine stars?) brings what he can to Brian Duffield’s rather soggy adaptation of Pulitzer prize-winner Daniel Kraus’s acclaimed novel Whalefall. But there’s not a great deal hecando, despite being in every scene of what’s his second studio lead in a month, other than scream and writhe and look understandably alarmed. It’s a setup that’s grabby enough to have us wonder just how the hell it’s going to play out (what if that one scene in Finding Nemo but a whole movie) but it just doesn’t work as a 106-minute adventure, too overstretched and too silly to have us rooting for his escape and caring how he might orchestrate it.There is something charmingly ambitious about a writer choosing to write himself into a corner, making an already hard job even harder, because while Kraus could clue readers into his protagonist’s inner thoughts and fears, Duffield decides against the easier choice of a voiceover. In order to keep the scenario as grounded as possible, Abrams’ unfortunate hero Jay is also unable to remove his breathing apparatus as the air inside the whale is toxic so whatever talking he might do is muffled through a mouthpiece. The authenticity is applaudable but it’s just one of many decisions that makes it harder to justify and enjoy the stage-to-screen adaptation, our connection to his plight hard to solidify.We learn more about Jay via a series of flashbacks, fleshing out his relationship to a gruff and difficult father (Josh Brolin), who recently chose killing himself in the ocean rather than dying slowly of mesothelioma, a rare cancer. Jay is determined to find his body, for reasons never quite fully explained, and after he’s trapped inside a whale, he looks back on their fractured dynamic, usefully accompanied by nuggets of diving wisdom from his father. Jay has something to prove (his mostly awful-seeming dad tells him he has “soft lungs”) and so his journey out of the beast is one that also aims to show what he can do by himself.Duffield’s scripts can often feel like pitches that are more sellable in an elevator than films that are watchable on the big screen, and while Whalefall might be his first adaptation, it suffers from the same disappointing follow-through. There was The Babysitter (what if your babysitter was a devil-worshipper),Spontaneous(what if spontaneous combustion at high school),No One Will Save You(what if home invasion but aliens) and the most relevant here,Underwater(what if monsters at the bottom of the ocean). As director, he does a better job than that film’s William Eubank did at capturing the majesty and terror of the water (he also only has one character to focus on and make distinguishable) but while treating the whale’s body as an alien landscape is an interesting idea, it’s also a limiting one.Given this year’sdeluge of shark movies, Whalefall makes an admirable initial case for finding drama elsewhere in the water. The otherworldly horror of the predicament is often wincingly effective (stomach acid burning hands, a swallowed-at-the-same-time giant squid causing added tentacled mayhem) and the film has a slick studio sheen that can be that much harder to find these days. But there are only so many set pieces that can take place in such a setting and only so much problem-solving that can be made legible without real dialogue. These scenes might get repetitive and viscerally unpleasant, yet they are at least more striking than the hopelessly rote and uninvolving father-son flashbacks that fail to add any real emotion or stakes to the story. What could have been a lean, mean 85-minute race to survive becomes weighed down by CW network-level soap, and Duffield never makes a decision we don’t already expect (his influences for the film, a list that bizarrely includes Brokeback Mountain, A Little Prayer, JFK and West Side Story, fail to add any personality to the finished product). A final hallucinatory chat is also laughably ineffective as dead father asks potentially dying son the questions he always wanted to know (spoiler: they include “did you ever want a dog?”). Abrams is an actor who has become incredibly easy to root for, but he struggles to make his scenes with Brolin feel like anything other than treading water (I would have liked to see more of the forever underused Elisabeth Shue as his mother).Flipping between a family drama of soul-searching and hackneyed advice-giving (“Survivors survive!”) and the more immediate 4DX-suited rush of thrashing, squelching, splashing and panicking makes Whalefall a disorienting and frustrating experience, like someone switching channels without your permission. You’ll want to grab the remote and watch something else entirely.Whalefall is out in Australian cinemas on 15 October and in the US and UK on 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsAction and adventure filmsJosh BrolinThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘To succeed meant to leave’: inside the jolting film about Brummie estate kids knocked flying by demolition | Movies | The Guardian
description: The novel had no hero, no dialogue and little action. So how was I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning turned into such a funny, rousing and acclaimed film? Director Clio Barnard reveals all
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: The novel had no hero, no dialogue and little action. So how was I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning turned into such a funny, rousing and acclaimed film? Director Clio Barnard reveals all
Content: ‘You end up as ghosts’ … Anthony Boyle, Joe Cole, Daryl McCormack, Jay Lycurgo and Lola Petticrew in I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning.Photograph: Chris HarrisView image in fullscreen‘You end up as ghosts’ … Anthony Boyle, Joe Cole, Daryl McCormack, Jay Lycurgo and Lola Petticrew in I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning.Photograph: Chris HarrisMoviesInterview‘To succeed meant to leave’: inside the jolting film about Brummie estate kids knocked flying by demolitionXan BrooksThe novel had no hero, no dialogue and little action. So how was I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning turned into such a funny, rousing and acclaimed film? Director Clio Barnard reveals allThu 15 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a kid in 90sBirmingham, Keiran Goddard would gather with his friends to watch the tower blocks coming down. That’s what passed for entertainment back then. Controlled explosions, collapsing buildings. The demolition of the city’s postwar council estates marked the end of one story and the start of another. It was a dust-blown display of regeneration and progress. The housing that replaced it would be an improvement. The people of east Birmingham would move on to better lives.Goddard, specifically, moved on to study English at Oxford University. He now lives in London and writes books for a living. Physically, he has left his home town far behind. Emotionally and spiritually, not so much. “So I feel quite splintered,” he says. “I’m not sure anyone ever really leaves the world they grew up in.”double quotation mark‘Work hard, rise out of your class – that was the story’Goddard’sBirmingham-set second novelhas just been made into a film. Enda Walsh wrote the script; Clio Barnard called the shots. Set in and around an anonymous housing estate, I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning is a jolting, stirring ensemble drama in which a tower block’s demolition serves as a kind of societal big bang, spinning five childhood friends into a fraught adulthood.When writing the book, Goddard identified with the character of Patrick, the idealistic graduate turned zero hours delivery driver who argues that decent housing is a basic human right, not a capital asset. But he’s also like Rian, the group’s breakout star, who made a killing on the stock market and bought a sterile London flat. Rian is the chief investor behind a new apartment complex that is to be built on the bones of the old estate. The film shows it rising in time-lapse leaps and bounds, just as historic strains set to work on Rian’s close-knit gang of mates.View image in fullscreen‘Joy in itself can be its own positive protest’ … Clio Barnard.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/the ObserverThe story scaffold may be simple, yet the drama that follows is anything but. It’s nuanced, thorny and possibly irresolvable, with no easy answers or obvious hero to root for. Goddard wrote the book as a series of interior monologues then delivered it to his agent and editor in a spirit of wild optimism. “I said, ‘You know, I think it’s got some cinematic potential.’ And both of them replied, saying, ‘There’s no dialogue and not much happens. It’s got the least cinematic potential of anything that we’ve seen.’”I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning by Keiran Goddard review – growing up and apartRead moreThe film was a challenge, Barnard admits. It’s about the pull of the past and the sharp edge of the present, stitching an intimate human story against the broader social canvas. “It feels to me that there is an equality in this group of friends,” the director says. “And that the antagonist is the system, which is a hard thing to represent.” She was fired up, however, by its brand of political rage and its fine-grained depiction of an embattled working-class community. “Also, it made me laugh,” she adds. Shared jokes are the glue of all successful friendship groups. Rian’s mates mock his lifestyle – his posh girlfriend and big fridge – but they are ruefully, lovingly pleased for him, too.Barnard has always been drawn to the margins of the UK. She likes outsiders, pariahs, survivors and scamps. She made an eye-catching debut with 2010’sThe Arbor, a brilliant lip-synced documentary about the Bradford-born playwright Andrea Dunbar, who died of a brain haemorrhage at the age of 29.The Selfish Giantwas arguably harsher still: a devastating coming-of-age drama, foraging for scrap metal on the tatty fringes of town. One hesitates to say that she has since lightened up. All the same, 2021’sAli & Ava– an interracial love story, as tender as a bruise – and I See Buildings at least come with an air of hard-won optimism.“I think that’s been a conscious choice,” she says. “With Ali & Ava, I wanted the audience to leave with the feeling that they were able to act. And what I got from the group of people in this film was a massive amount of compassion and hope. I see a lot of Keiran in [the character of] Patrick. And Patrick’s a hopeful person. He believes that political change is still possible.”The world has now slipped seriously out of whack, she admits. “Just look at the protests in France at the moment. There’s an economic imbalance everywhere. It’s hard to find a regular income and a roof over your head, especially for young people. But hope in itself can be an active resistance. Joy in itself can be its own positive protest.”View image in fullscreenTender as a bruise … Adeel Akhtar and Claire Rushbrook in Ali & Ava.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyAs for the film industry, that’s arguably out of whack, too. I See Buildings lands in the UK fresh from a triumphant unveiling at the Cannes film festival. The international critics adored it. The Guardian’s ownPeter Bradshaw gave it a five-star review. But Barnard’s film might also prove to be among the last of a dying breed. It’s a blast of impassioned old-school social realism, folded in amid a glut of studio sequels and mythic heroes’ journeys, crying out to an audience that may no longer exist.I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning review – sweet, sad portrait of gen Z discontent and disillusionRead moreGoddard begs to differ. Like Patrick, he has hope; he puts his faith in the people. “We’ve seen it in publishing where the types of issues – the economic precarity – that traditionally affected only working-class communities are creeping more into middle-class society,” he says. “That means there’s a greater middle-class appetite for these kinds of stories. ‘Oh, you know that thing you’ve been moaning about for years? Well, it’s happening to me now as well.’” On the most basic level, he adds, the maths doesn’t add up. “The fact that the lives that are most frequently lived are the ones that are least frequently depicted. Economically, that’s stupid. You can’t simultaneously hold the view that people want to relate to stories and that the stories about the most common lives just aren’t viable. Those two things cannot be true. They can’t coexist.”Probably every human life is one of explosions and upheaval, and it can take a while for the dust to settle. Nowadays, Goddard has a clearer view of who he is and where he came from. He is a product, he says, of Blair-era social mobility: the beneficiary of a fleeting, fitful period of wealth redistribution. He was told that if he worked hard and behaved he might one day, God willing, rise out of his class. “That was always the story,” he says. “To succeed meant to leave.”In I See Buildings, Rian (played by Peaky Blinders star Joe Cole) winds up as a square peg in his fancy London apartment, pining for the streets, pubs and friends that he has left behind. Goddard can relate. “I’ve been very lucky. I’m not the victim here. As far as there is a right side of the equation to be on, I’m on it. The structures that enabled me to be here no longer exist. If you ran my life again now, it wouldn’t be the same. But yes, I think it does cause problems. You’re never truly accepted, and you can never properly go home. So you end up as a ghost, haunting the edges of two lives.”A film of his book could have been a disaster, he knows. “There are a number of different flavours of wrong,” he says. It might have wound up as poverty porn, or an earnest slab of liberal doggerel. It might have involved flat caps and misery, or poured out eight pints of mindless, bleary-eyed hedonism. Instead, he thinks that Walsh and Barnard have improved on his work. They’ve made the tale funnier, more rousing and hopeful.Best of all, Barnard filmed it on the streets of Birmingham. Goddard’s brother Tom helped integrate the crew with the community. The Crown social club served as the chief base of operations, where an open casting call drew as many as 800 local people. In a traditional story arc, the wayfaring hero eventually returns home. Odysseus arrives at Ithaca. Dorothy wakes up in her cosy Kansas farmhouse. The social mobility kids, Goddard feels, have been denied their third act. It’s the price they must pay for all the advances they’ve made. “But there was something very moving about going through this whole journey and literally returning to the estate I grew up on,” he says. “That was beyond special. That doesn’t normally happen. It’s as though, out of nowhere, I’ve been gifted the rare opportunity to close the circle and go home.”I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning is in cinemas on 4 DecemberThis article was amended on 15 October 2026. An earlier version said that Odysseus arrived at “Icarus”; that should have said Ithaca.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsFilm adaptationsPovertyClio BarnardBirminghamEnda WalshfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Angèle: Instinct review – Belgium’s biggest star is determined to do pop differently | Music | The Guardian
description: Massive in her home nation but less so outside, Angèle is aided by Justice, Soulwax and Caroline Polachek in ​a bold bid for broader appeal – but her resultant album ​can be generic as well as daring
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Massive in her home nation but less so outside, Angèle is aided by Justice, Soulwax and Caroline Polachek in ​a bold bid for broader appeal – but her resultant album ​can be generic as well as daring
Content: Angèle.Photograph: Kenza Le BasView image in fullscreenAngèle.Photograph: Kenza Le BasAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewAngèle: Instinct review – Belgium’s biggest star is determined to do pop differently(RCA)Massive in her home nation but less so outside, Angèle is aided by Justice, Soulwax and Caroline Polachek in ​a bold bid for broader appeal – but her resultant album ​can be generic as well as daringAlexis PetridisThu 15 Oct 2026 07.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 09.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs has often been pointed out, we live in an era where the traditional Anglo-American stranglehold over pop has been broken. Partly because streaming has presented listeners with a far broader choice of music than would once have been imaginable, and partly as a result of social media accounts doing the promotional departments’ job for them, the charts are now as likely to include music made in Seoul or Lagos as London or LA. Spurs’ 62,000-capacity stadium has recently hosted not just Jay-Z, Gorillaz and System of a Down, but India’s Arijit Singh, South Korea’s BTS, BigBang and Stray Kids, and Puerto Rico’s Bad Bunny, who addressed the crowd almost exclusively in Spanish.View image in fullscreenCover art for Instinct.Photograph: Courtesy of Angéle and Grant James-ThomasClearly, British audiences’ disinclination to be welded to English-speaking artists is a cheering thing. Equally clearly, there seem to be limits: the same interest hasn’t been afforded Francophone pop. The biggest French-speaking stars in recent memory have either dealt in dance music or acquiesced to recording in English. Belgian rapper Stromae has attracted media interest and co-signs from Kanye West and Lorde without ever progressing beyond cult status in the UK.Likewise, Angèle Van Laeken, who kicked off her career in 2017, broke Stromae’s record for the most number of weeks at No 1 inBelgiumwith her 2018 single Tout Oublier – taken from a debut album that went seven times platinum in her homeland – and has been a household name to Francophone audiences ever since. The closest she has come to British success was her appearance on Dua Lipa’s 2020 single Fever, a minor hit.View image in fullscreenGlitterbeat stomp … Angèle.Photograph: Kenza Le BasYou could argue that some of her music is quite geographically specific. Her second album, Nonante-Cinq, opened with Bruxelles Je T’Aime, a song in praise of her her home town, terrible weather and all (one of its lyrics translates roughly, and rather splendidly, as: “Tonight the sky will certainly be covered by a storm / but after the storm people will party and get the beers in”). But it also fretted about the possibility that Belgium might end up divided between French and Flemish speakers, a topic that’s seldom hotly debated when the British get the beers in. Then again, Bad Bunny’s most recent album was at least partially consumed by the question of whether or not Hawaii was a suitable model for Puerto Rican statehood, and that didn’t stop it reaching the UK Top 10.You would struggle to call Angèle’s third album a concerted push for Anglo-American success, although there are more lyrics in English than on Nonante-Cinq and some of the names involved might cause ears to prick up. Justice collaborate on What You Want, a fruitful collision of maximalist rave synths and glitterbeat stomp. And Soulwax crop up on Trop, which is impressively noisy, with an edge to the electronics and its take on a house pulse; it’s driven by vocals that alternately lean towards rap and are scrambled into incomprehensibility. Love Triangle, meanwhile, involvesCaroline Polachekand French dance producer SebastiAn, a thrillingly discordant synthesiser arpeggio cutting through its killer chorus and sweaty-small-hours mood.Indeed, intermittently at least, Instinct makes a case that British audiences don’t know what they’re missing when it comes to Angèle, who has a penchant for suddenly grabbing the steering wheel and driving a song off road. On Verra starts out like a standard pop piano ballad – albeit with a hint of chanson about the melody – before it’s unexpectedly strafed with bursts of static and machine-gun-paced noise. You could initially imagine any number of pop stars essaying the sweet drift of Je Compte, but then it dramatically shifts gears, first into a four-to-the-floor rhythm topped with an assemblage of sampled gasps and warped vocals, then into a lo-fi piano ballad.This all carries the appealing sense of someone doing pop rather differently, although these moments are punctuated by more straightforward stuff. Some of it is great – the melody that floats above the chugging synths of Tout Décider is an unequivocal earworm – and some of it a little less so. The song F4ck 4ever is noticeably less diverting than its title; the cut-up samples and AutoTuned vocals that constitute Dis-le’s hook lie somewhere between unusual and tinnily annoying.Trash hits! Why a wave of hedonistic, feral female pop stars are rejecting respectabilityRead moreIt’s an album that is by turns really exciting and slightly frustrating, built for cherrypicking its highlights for a playlist rather than repeatedly listening to end-to-end. There’s enough here to grab the attention of anyone with an ear for left-field pop – one suspects any Caroline Polachek fans enticed by her appearance will be happy to stick around – but not quite enough to predict a broader shift in perceptions. One thing that unites all the disparate artists who have broken through pop’s language barrier is that they’re offering something that you really can’t get at home; so is Angèle, but only occasionally.This week Alexis listened toCameron Winter –$0 (Live at Carnegie Hall)A live version of the Heavy Metal highlight that alternately strips the song back – the string arrangement is gone – and somehow amplifies it: more simple, but more intense.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekPop and rockCaroline PolachekBelgiumJusticeDance musicalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Vermeer by Andrew Graham-Dixon audiobook review – a sharp and authoritative guide | Books | The Guardian
description: The author offers intriguing insights into the way this Dutch artist worked, including fresh perspectives on The Girl With the Pearl Earring
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The author offers intriguing insights into the way this Dutch artist worked, including fresh perspectives on The Girl With the Pearl Earring
Content: Vermeer's Girl With a Pearl Earring on display in Japan.Photograph: Jiji Press/EPAView image in fullscreenVermeer's Girl With a Pearl Earring on display in Japan.Photograph: Jiji Press/EPAAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewVermeer by Andrew Graham-Dixon audiobook review – a sharp and authoritative guideThe author offers intriguing insights into the way this Dutch artist worked, including fresh perspectives on The Girl With the Pearl EarringFiona SturgesThu 15 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the decades after the death of the Dutch artist Johannes Vermeer in 1675, few knew his name or work. He was so unknown that his paintings were sold with the forged signatures of more popular artists attached. All that changed in the mid-19th century, when his art was reassessed by French critics. Today Vermeer is one of the most admired painters in the world, although, says art historian Andrew Graham-Dixon, he has “proved stubbornly resistant to interpretation”.Vermeer: A Life Lost and Found, Graham-Dixon’s biography which was six years in the writing, endeavours to answer some unresolved questions, among them: what was Vermeer’s life like? Why did he paint the way he did? What was the intent behind his paintings, of which only 36 exist? Unlike the Dutch genre painters of his time, the Delft-born Vermeer painted solemn yet luminous works featuring women in domestic settings and engaged in activities such as reading, writing, playing music or pouring milk. His ability to render light, and its softening effect on rooms and people, was unparalleled.Graham-Dixon is the book’s narrator and his reading is sharp, authoritative and animated. As well as conjuring the world Vermeer inhabited and theorising about his relationship with his patrons, the author offers an intriguing new perspective – admittedly one that is impossible to prove – on the identity of the figure in The Girl With the Pearl Earring.Anyone doubting whether audio is the best medium to explore the life and work of a Dutch master will be pleased to find an attached file with the audiobook containing copious colour plates of Vermeer’s paintings.Available via Penguin, 15hr 1minFurther listeningKids, Wait Till You Hear This!Liza Minnelli, Hodder & Stoughton, 17hr 55minThe Cabaret star reads her uproarious and ferociously candid memoir, in which she reflects on her tumultuous love life, her relationship with her mother, Judy Garland, her struggles with alcohol and drug addiction and professional highs and lows.Good Good LovingYvvette Edwards,Little Brown, 7hr 47minSara Powell narrates this family saga about a British-Caribbean family spanning five decades. It opens with Ellen, the elderly matriarch, lying on a hospital bed waiting for the end while her family discuss her many shortcomings.Explore more on these topicsBooksAudiobook of the weekPaintingArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mendelssohn: Songs Without Words review – Chamayou makes each piece feel somehow familiar yet fresh  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The pianist brings a singing quality and seeming effortlessness to the complete set of Songs Without Words
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: The pianist brings a singing quality and seeming effortlessness to the complete set of Songs Without Words
Content: Effortless playing … Bertrand Chamayou.Photograph: Le Philtre / Parlophone Records Ltd 2026View image in fullscreenEffortless playing … Bertrand Chamayou.Photograph: Le Philtre / Parlophone Records Ltd 2026Classical musicReviewMendelssohn: Songs Without Words review – Chamayou makes each piece feel somehow familiar yet freshBertrand Chamayou(Warner Classics)The pianist brings a singing quality and seeming effortlessness to the complete set of Songs Without WordsErica JealThu 15 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 10.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMendelssohn wrote 48 Songs Without Words for solo piano: eight sets of six, mostly under three minutes long, emerging over a 16-year period that spanned most of his short adult life. The handful that still regularly make their way on to recital programmes are only the tip of the iceberg; the complete set hasn’t been recorded as much as you might think, which makes this new release fromBertrand Chamayoustill more welcome.View image in fullscreenBertrand Chamayou: Mendelssohn Songs Without WordsThese pieces belong to the world of Schubert Lieder, and Chamayou brings a singing quality to them from the off. The Duetto that rounds off the Op 38 set is beautifully done, the melodic lines alternating like a female and male voice, each lingering just slightly as the other voice takes over. Compared to other interpreters, Chamayou is often softer-edged, his playing a little smoother and more flowing, although there are exceptions: Op 62 No 6 – known as Spring Song, but originally titled Camberwell Green after the then-elegant London suburb where it was written – is given a perky, almost frothy touch in the accompaniment: spring bubbling under like frogspawn in a pond.Chamayou doesn’t present these miniatures as if he thinks they are profound, yet thanks to his seeming effortlessness they come across that way. For him, going through these pieces has been like “opening a trunk of family photos faded by time”. It’s also a good analogy for listening to him play them: each new piece feels somehow familiar and yet demands your fresh attention.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com.
