title: Finding the groove: what’s the best genre of music to dance to? | Dance music | The Guardian
description: What is it about music that makes even non-professionals want to hit the dancefloor, and is it disco, funk or even classical that does it best? Four leading choreographers discuss their theories, with the science to back them up
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: What is it about music that makes even non-professionals want to hit the dancefloor, and is it disco, funk or even classical that does it best? Four leading choreographers discuss their theories, with the science to back them up
Content: ‘I get lost and distracted because the beat is so funky’ … The Brown Suite.Photograph: Deborah JaffeView image in fullscreen‘I get lost and distracted because the beat is so funky’ … The Brown Suite.Photograph: Deborah JaffeDance musicFinding the groove: what’s the best genre of music to dance to?What is it about music that makes even non-professionals want to hit the dancefloor, and is it disco, funk or even classical that does it best? Four leading choreographers discuss their theories, with the science to back them upLyndsey WinshipThu 15 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Idon’t know what it is about house music that makes me move, but I just can’t help it,” says Faye Stoeser. “And I don’t care what I look like. I just go for it.” “If a Missy [Elliott] track comes on, that’s me, I’m in the zone,” says Dannielle “Rhimes” Lecointe. “With hip-hop it’s something deep within the gut that makes you want to move. It has so many rhythms to it – a heartbeat, a pulse, a ricochet – that you feel in so many different places of your body.”What is the best music to dance to? Is it house music, it is hip-hop, is it disco or funk? Stoeser and Lecointe should have some insight since, as performers and choreographers, dancing is what they do for a living. When it comes to popular floorfillers, theDJ Intelligenceplatform found the most-requested track from UK DJs last year was Whitney Houston’s I Wanna Dance With Somebody (with Abba’s Dancing Queen second, and Mr Brightside by the Killers third). In the US,Billboard’s top wedding songis Uptown Funk by Mark Ronson featuring Bruno Mars. A 2013Mixmag pollnamed Daft Punk’s One More Time as the ultimate dance track, whereas Radio 2 listeners in 2008 voted forMichael Jackson’s Billie Jean.But what about those for whom dancing is more than recreation? When it comes to dance on stage, there is plenty that isn’t driven by music at all. Back in the 1940s, the US choreographer Merce Cunningham began to disconnect dance and music in his collaborations with the composer John Cage, rehearsing the dancers in silence. Some choreographers use music to create dance in the studio that is totally different from what they’ll perform to on stage.Dancethat’s focused on musical connection definitely went out of fashion for a while, but there are a bunch of shows coming up where music is the absolute driving force.View image in fullscreenEbony Scrooge with Danielle Lecointe … ‘I’m vibrating at different levels’Photograph: Rebecca Warrand/Johan Persson“We won’t choreograph until we have the music,” says Nahum McLean, of dance company BlacBrik, “which sometimes can be scary because it will be a week before the show, and we’re, like: ‘Still not found that music yet!’”McLean and his BlacBrik co-founder Darius Drooh had no trouble with the music for their current showThe Brown Suite, which is soundtracked by godfather of funk James Brown – a legendary dancer himself – along with songs by Etta James and Sam Cooke. “It’s so infectious,” says McLean of Brown’s music. “Sometimes I’ll have the music on in my headphones, and I’m trying to block [some choreography] mentally or write something down, and then I get lost and distracted because I’m like: This beat is so funky!”Drooh agrees: “Sometimes we’re just too busy dancing in the studio when we should be trying to choreograph.”double quotation markI can see people tapping their feet. It’s an involuntary reactionWhat is it about funk that makes it so irresistible? “There’s something about the bassline and the way they used it during that era, and you can’t help it, your body starts to have this natural response,” says McLean. “The way it’s layered with the percussion and the horns. In performances, I can see people tapping their feet. It’s an involuntary reaction.”There’s actual science that bears this out. Oxford professor Morten Kringelbach is one neuroscientist who set out to pin down what’s so funky about funk. Heplayed his test subjects funk drum breakswith different amounts of syncopation – meaning the beats that land between the regular pulse – and found an inverted-U shape; simply put, too little syncopation equals not funky enough, too much and your body can’t hook into the rhythm. James Brown hits the sweet spot. Plenty of others have also investigated “groove” – that’s the official scientific term for the quality in music that makes people want to dance.In a 2012study, cognitive neuroscientist Petr Janata used various measures, including tracking people’s spontaneous movements, to find the grooviest piece of music. The result: Stevie Wonder’s stone-cold classic Superstition (1972). Neuroscientist and musician Daniel Levitin has pointed to Wonder’s drumming and clavinet-playing on the track and how he varies the tones so that even though there’s a strong pulse, it never sounds uniform; “ear candy”, he’s called it.People have been put in brainscanners while listening to groovy musicand areas in their basal ganglia, which control motor activity and reward, lit up. Other elements that have a positive correlation with groove include: a prominent pulse or rhythm; a high number of different notes in each bar; short or accented beats; harmonic complexity – it should be low to medium; and the presence of low-frequency sounds, ie, heavy bass. Tempo matters, too. Superstition hovers around the 100bpm mark, slightly slower than the perceived optimum – 107-126bpm, according to one2018 analysis; other studies landed on 120bpm.View image in fullscreenEkleido … ‘When someone scores a goal in football and people lose their sense of self. We’re trying to bring that into the theatre.Photograph: Jack ThomsonHannah Ekholm, who along with Stoeser leads dance company Ekleido, would agree with that. “One hundred and twenty to 126bpm, that’s when it’s really groovy,” says Ekholm.“We make work to 130-135bpm,” adds Stoeser, “but I agree that between the 120-128bpm range it feels like it has that steady pulse but you still have that groove within it; the space to play.” Ekleido are specialists in “new way vogue”(a progression from the type of voguing Madonna sang about), which is danced to house music. On stage, their soundtrack isn’t just a steady four-to-the-floor – Ekholm’s partner Sam Shepherd, AKAFloating Points, writes music for them, including for their latest showFemina– but they do like a thumping beat.double quotation markThe orchestra is like an engine for me. Until I hear the music live I can’t really access my full capacityIt is also more than just the technical aspects of the music. “When you’re in a club space, you almost transcend together collectively,” says Stoeser. “I learned this term the other day: ‘collective effervescence’, the feeling when someone scores a goal in football and people lose their sense of self for a minute. We’re trying to bring a piece of that into the theatre.”I ask Lecointe,who’s about to take the lead role in her hip-hop dance showEbony Scrooge, where exactly she feels the music. “In the solar plexus,” she says. “Hip-hop sometimes feels to me a bit like a speaker. I’m vibrating at different levels: the bass, the snare, the hi-hat, can be the isolation in the feet, the hips, the chest.”Music doesn’t need to have a banging bassline to make you want to dance, though. When Anna Rose O’Sullivan, principal dancer with the Royal Ballet, says “the music almost makes me want to take off”, she’s not talking about techno but Tchaikovsky – specifically the Act II pas de deux she dances inThe Nutcracker. “It’s the emotion that it evokes, the melody, the swell. It’s something deeply romantic, but it has this soar,” she says. “Tchaikovsky wrote some bangers.” He certainly did, and some of the most danceable tunes in ballet have kept The Nutcracker in business Christmas after Christmas.It helps that when O’Sullivan performs at the Royal Opera House, the music is played live. “The orchestra is like an engine for me,” she says. “I could be doing something in the rehearsal studio for months, but until I hear it live I can’t really access my full capacity. It’s like if someone’s listening to a piece of music and their hairs stand up,” she adds, “but for us it’s not just hairs, it’s everything, every muscle feels alive.” That’s borne out by the science, too: tactile sensation makes you want to dance, whether that’s vibration from a subwoofer or the orchestra in the pit.There is definitely no single answer to the question of groove. James Brown may have taken over BlacBrik’s playlist, but McLean and Drooh insist there’s no music they couldn’t dance to. “My father is from west Africa and I have an African dance background. We will always hear the rhythm,” Drooh says. “We will always hear the bass in anything. You can put on Beethoven and we can find a boom-taka, boom-taka!”The Brown Suiteis touringnationwide to May.Ekleido: Feminais atGulbenkian Arts, Canterbury,29 to 30 October;and The Place, London,5 to 7 November;Ebony Scroogeis at Sadler’s Wells East, London,24 November to 3 January;The Nutcrackeris at Royal Opera House, London,3 December to 13 January.Explore more on these topicsDance musicDanceHip-hopBalletStevie WonderJames BrownEtta JamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Floating World by Ben Eastham review – a compelling debut of art’s relation to money and power | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Following the death of his wife, a critic-teacher takes a job with an art-washing multinational, in a cinematic novel that is full of ideas
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Following the death of his wife, a critic-teacher takes a job with an art-washing multinational, in a cinematic novel that is full of ideas
Content: Slice of the art market … the National Museum of Qatar in Doha.Photograph: Patrick Baz/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSlice of the art market … the National Museum of Qatar in Doha.Photograph: Patrick Baz/AFP/Getty ImagesBook of the dayFictionReviewThe Floating World by Ben Eastham review – a compelling debut of art’s relation to money and powerFollowing the death of his wife, a critic-teacher takes a job with an art-washing multinational, in a cinematic novel that is full of ideasIan MaleneyThu 15 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 03.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the end of a night in a London pub, after last orders have been called, three friends are joking about what role they’d serve on a remote desert island, with no one but their fellow plane crash survivors for company. When one of them, an art critic turned reluctant schoolteacher, says that he would become an artist, he is, naturally, mocked. His friend Sybil, who actually is a painter, casts herself more sensibly as a demigod-queen of the island and employs her newly creative companion to “certify her glory”. “That’s what artists are for,” she says, “I pay you in fermented coconut water and you tell yourself you’re free and drink yourself to death.”This is about as clear a statement as one could wish for regarding the position of contemporary art as it relates to power: the boot of the latter is placed firmly on the former’s throat. This relationship is the central theme of The Floating World, Ben Eastham’s debut novel, which is narrated by the somewhat hapless and unnamed critic-teacher. And what has led to this existential pub conversation is an unexpected opportunity: following the death of the narrator’s wife in an unnamed war zone, he has been offered a job with the Morel Foundation, an art-washing spin-off of an arms-manufacturing multinational which extracts profit from all corners of a wartorn world while its cultural wing props up the ego of its eponymous overlord CEO.double quotation markIt's to its great credit that the novel's political awareness is more than stage‑dressing; it's the real heart of the bookThe narrator is unsure about taking up a position he knows to be morally indefensible, but which pays pretty well. Should he accept the nine-month contract – “helping with research, writing the press releases, editing the publications” – he would move from London to a tiny Greek island, where Morel is building “The Floating World”, a techno-utopian settlement inside a giant dome. A spectacular artistic event is planned to celebrate the official opening of what another of the narrator’s friends calls “literallya doomsday bunker for billionaires”. Is this really something he wants to be part of?Eastham knows this artistic milieu inside out. As a co-founder of the visual arts and literature magazine White Review and a busy and perceptive critic, Eastham has spent many years at the vanguard of contemporary art and literature. As a curator and writer, he has witnessed first-hand the tightening bonds between a globalised art market and international finance, from the widespread sponsorship of oil and opiate sellers to the geopolitical game-playing of projects like the Louvre Abu Dhabi, not to mention the use of artworks for money laundering, tax breaks and other kinds of financial engineering. Eastham threads examples of this interdependence throughout the book; sometimes as a nod to the knowing, but often more directly, as when a visit to a London museum is interrupted by a young woman throwing red paint at one of the paintings, screaming, “This is happening, open your eyes!”The narrator takes the job. He lands first in Athens, where he is welcomed by graffiti decrying the spread of short-term rentals for tourists, written deliberately in English – it is just about the only sign he can understand. Greece is the ideal setting for this book because there is arguably no place in Europe where it is easier to witness the contradictions of a world in which capital moves freely but people do not. In Athens, the most destitute struggle in statelessness and poverty, with the Acropolis as a backdrop. On the islands, victims of war, genocide, exploitation and climate catastrophe are airbrushed out of the escapist fantasies of the rich.It is to the novel’s immense credit that it manages to make this political awareness more than dutiful stage‑dressing; it is the real heart of the book. Eastham attempts an ambitious balancing act: on one side, the cynical gamesmanship of high-end contemporary art, and on the other, the emotional inner life of a man haunted by the memory of his deceased wife. The story becomes increasingly mysterious and action-packed, and it becomes inevitable that the two strands will be integrated through a conclusive narrative denouement. The form demands, and Eastham obliges with a blurry, dream-like conflagration of grief, panic and revenge. It’s all very cinematic, and neatly done – too neat, maybe, in the end. The Floating World is a book full of ideas and curiosity, but for all its well earned disillusion with the art world, it remains surprisingly sentimental.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Floating World by Ben Eastham is published by Fitzcarraldo (£14.99). title: Tim Jeal obituary | Biography books | The Guardian
description: Biographer who altered perceptions of Henry Morton Stanley, David Livingstone, Robert Baden-Powell and other figures active in Africa
Author: Justin Marozzi
Headline: Biographer who altered perceptions of Henry Morton Stanley, David Livingstone, Robert Baden-Powell and other figures active in Africa
Content: Henry Morton Stanley's expedition crossing the Makata swamp in central Africa in 1871, in search of David Livingstone.Photograph: Chronicle/AlamyView image in fullscreenHenry Morton Stanley's expedition crossing the Makata swamp in central Africa in 1871, in search of David Livingstone.Photograph: Chronicle/AlamyBiography booksObituaryTim Jeal obituaryBiographer who altered perceptions of Henry Morton Stanley, David Livingstone, Robert Baden-Powell and other figures active in AfricaJustin MarozziThu 15 Oct 2026 11.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThanks to the biographer and novelist Tim Jeal, who has died aged 81, we now know that one of the most famous sentences in journalism – “Dr Livingstone, I presume?” – was almost certainly never uttered.In November 1871, after a 700-mile expedition, the Welsh-American journalist and adventurerHenry Morton Stanleytracked down David Livingstone, the Scottish missionary and explorer. He had been lost to the outside world for six years and was now nearing death, in Ujiji, on the shores of Lake Tanganyika in present-day Tanzania.View image in fullscreenYet, as Jeal revealed in Stanley: The Impossible Life of Africa’s Greatest Explorer (2007), there was no mention of the greeting anywhere in Stanley’s original diary, from which the two following pages had been torn out and probably destroyed. Nor did Livingstone record it in his own journal. It all smacked of self-promoting sensationalism, eagerly trumpeted by the New York Herald.The reconstruction of the event, based on literary archaeology, exemplified Jeal’s strengths as biographer: a revisionist approach underpinned by tenacity in his research, empathy for his subjects and a vigorous narrative drive. In what was a controversial rehabilitation of a complicated man, the Stanley who emerged from these pages was a more nuanced figure, not so much a collaborator in brutal Belgian colonialism as a courageous, driven explorer and abolitionist with a powerful humanitarian streak and a tendency to exaggerate for effect. Widely acclaimed on both sides of the Atlantic, the book won the US National Book Critics Circle award.Jeal was drawn to figures who had been damaged in their childhood. His study of Stanley, a workhouse boy who managed to haul himself out of poverty to international fame and fortune, followed big biographies of two other sons of empire.Published when Jeal was still in his 20s, Livingstone (1973) offered a radical reappraisal of the definitive Victorian hero of African exploration. There were uncomfortable truths to confront.View image in fullscreenAs a missionary, Livingstone was a striking failure, gaining just one convert in three decades, a tribal leader named Sechele whose faith had to compete with an adherence to rainmaking and polygamy. Though revered by the Royal Geographical Society, Livingstone was equally unsuccessful as an explorer, failing to locate the elusive source of the Nile. Jeal’s biography, never out of print, remains the standard life.In Baden-Powell (1989), his biography of the founder of the Boy Scouts movement, Jeal brought his empathetic style and intensive research to bear on another troubled imperial servant. Here the revisionism was more positive, defending Robert Baden-Powell against the traditional accusations of moustachioed English racism and militarism and of having starved Africans as a colonel during theSiege of Mafekingin 1899-1900.One reviewer reckoned the book so far transcended earlier biographies as to make them “almost meaningless”. Contentiously Jeal also concluded that Baden-Powell, a married father of three, was a repressed homosexual.Explorers of the Nile (2011) drew some of his earlier themes together in another reappraising study which knocked the restless Richard Burton off his perch and championed John Hanning Speke as the man who discovered the source of Africa’s mightiest river.View image in fullscreenTim Jeal’s interest in Africa was sparked during his time there between school and universityBorn in London, Tim was the son of Norah Sabine (nee Sabine Pasley), from an aristocratic background, and her husband, Clifford Jeal, a pacifist vegetarian who belonged to the Order of the Cross, a fellowship of Christian mystics. The two first set eyes on each other at Heal’s, the London furniture store, where Clifford worked. An unlikely romance between the baronet’s daughter and the good-looking man on the shop floor followed.At the age of seven Tim was sent to Boarzell, a boarding school in East Sussex. The school’s nickname, “Boys’ Hell”, reflected a regime of cold showers, poor food and predatory teachers. As a young boy, his mother once sat him on a cushion with a pin underneath it and told him that if he kept silent for long enough it would turn into a golden egg. Despite these trials his childhood was tenderly described in Swimming With My Father, a moving memoir published in 2004.After Westminster school, Jeal disappeared to Africa on some far-ranging solo travels. The experience inspired his lifelong interest in some of the 19th-century explorers who made their name there. In 1963 he went to Christ Church, Oxford, to study history, before switching to English. In a party-filled undergraduate life he admitted to attending one lecture – and, later, to experimenting with fiction. His first novel, For Love and Money, was published to rave reviews when Jeal was 21. A later novel, Cushing’s Crusade, won the John Llewellyn Rhys Prize in 1975.As a graduate trainee producing arts and features for the BBC, Jeal met Joyce Timewell, a researcher. They married in 1969 and settled in north London, where they raised three daughters, walked Boz, the family dog, across Hampstead Heath, and entertained friends at spirited dinner parties. “He mesmerised everyone,” recalled his elder sister Thomasina. “He was in charge of the conversation. A great raconteur, he enjoyed amusing people.”View image in fullscreenAway from his books, Jeal was a convivial and mischief-loving man who took great delight in his family. He was said to be at his happiest in the Lizard in Cornwall, the scene of sailing holidays on the Helford River as a child and, later, as a father and grandfather of six. In recent years he was a devoted carer of Joyce, who had been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s.Asked by the Guardian in 2008what made him write, Jeal suggested it was perhaps “an inability to risk living without being intellectually occupied for hours on end. I’ve also got used to the idea of being a writer, and writers write, for goodness sake.”Jeal is survived by his wife, their three daughters, Jessica, Lucy and Emily, and his sister.John Julian Timothy Jeal, biographer and novelist, born 27 January 1945; died 5 August 2026Explore more on these topicsBiography booksAutobiography and memoirFictionAfricaobituariesShareReuse this content

title: From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics | Games | The Guardian
description: The studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action series
Author: Tom Regan
Headline: The studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action series
Content: Super smart shooter … Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Tactics.Illustration: UbisoftView image in fullscreenSuper smart shooter … Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Tactics.Illustration: UbisoftGamesFrom Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six TacticsThe studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action seriesTom ReganThu 15 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhere do you go after Mario? It’s a question the team at Ubisoft Paris found itself pondering three years ago after wrapping up work on the charming turn-based tactics adventure,Mario + Rabbids: Sparks of Hope, sequel to its unexpected crossover hit, Mario + Rabbids: Kingdom Battle. By melding a rather specialist genre with video gaming’s biggest household name, the developer introduced chin-stroking strategic play to a whole new audience.“Having the opportunity to work with the Mario franchise was a privilege, and it’s still something I’m very proud of,” says level designer director, Julien Vial. “I still remember seeing the first prototype and being blown away by all the possibilities.”Now, Ubisoft Paris has returned with a new project, but this time the studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action series Rainbow Six. Where Mario and Rabbids saw squishy creatures bounce harmlessly across levels as Mario encased foes in honey, Rainbow Six Tactics, a turn-based tactical spin-off fromRainbow Six Siege, sees balaclava-clad insurgents take shrapnel rounds to the chest. A seamless tonal shift, then.View image in fullscreenUnexpected hit …  Mario + Rabbids.Photograph: UbisoftOne of the most popular and testosterone-fuelled online shooters around, on paper Rainbow Six: Siege and turn-based strategy have little in common. Where Siege’s tight team play and ferocious first-person firefights sell out arenas at esports competitions in São Paulo and Atlanta, even the biggest brand in the tactical sim genre, X-Com, is unlikely to win energy-drink sponsorships or adorn a team jersey.Yet forUbisoftParis creative director Elie Benhamou, a veteran of the Ghost Recon series, the precision planning you need to be good at Siege is a natural fit for turn-based strategy. “What makes Rainbow Six unique is that it’s a smart shooter,” he says. “It’s not a shooter where it’s necessarily about who is the most brutal, but who is the most prepared ... Every decision matters because there are strong consequences. That is the exact recipe for a tactics game.”View image in fullscreenEvery decision matters … Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics.Photograph: UbisoftMy demo kicks off with a night-time operation in Nigeria. As I witness a team of four helmet-clad operators surveil their targets with drones and plant explosives during the prep phase – their synchronised teamwork soon breaches a heavily guarded warehouse. While smoke grenades blind their unsuspecting foes and sniper shots crackle through the air, the Rainbow Unit’s tight pincer formation makes short work of the remaining hostiles. It’s here that Benhamou’s words begin to ring true. Even with the bird’s eye view and pauses between gunfire, Tactics still oozes the tense thrills of its real-time brethren.Benhamou says he knew they were on to something after they invited sceptical first-person shooter stalwarts in to play test. Sitting alongside fans of real-time tactics, the hardcore FPS players swiftly used their Siege knowledge to execute a similar precision assault in Tactics, advising the tactics genre players next to them on how best to command Siege’s operators.The demo concludes with Rainbow Unit extracting a key hostage by racing towards a speedboat. Here, you can take a non-lethal approach with enemies, arresting combatants to gather intelligence points, which enhance your squad and improve gear for future missions.View image in fullscreen‘Freedom is key: there shouldn’t be only one single way to win.’ … Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics.Photograph: Ubisoft“The most important thing for me is when a game respects my intelligence – I don’t want to be over-guided,” says Benhamou. “It’s OK to fail and experiment … Freedom is key: there shouldn’t be only one single way to win. We have 15 unique operators, so the same problem can be solved or approached in many different ways.”Story wise, Rainbow Six Tactics promises to be your classic Tom Clancy fare, with shady government organisations and a globe-spanning conflict. You play as commander Paul “Big Boy” Bishop, the protagonist from Rainbow Six Vegas, as he attempts to re-establish Team Rainbow. “From a narrative standpoint, we try to bridge the gap with Siege and classic Rainbow, trying to have the best of all these worlds and eras of the series,” says narrative director, Barnabé Anglade. “Compared to Siege, it’s a much broader, zoomed-out point of view. Here, you’re at base and get to see the big picture … whereas Siege is much more moment-to-moment within the eyes of the operators. It’s still delivering that good old techno-thriller, but it’s closer to the books.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter working in a world of gravity-defying jumps and banana-shaped boomerangs, the biggest challenge after swapping Rabbids for Rainbow was creating compelling levels that strictly adhered to reality. “On Mario and Rabbids, most of the constraints were tied to the characters and their abilities, while the level design itself enjoyed a great deal of creative freedom,” says Vial. “We could come up with a gameplay concept first, then let the artists build a colourful and imaginative environment around it. On Rainbow Six Tactics, we have to take the reality of the location into account, which requires much closer collaboration between level designers and level artists.”Turn-based tactical sims have been an often overlooked mainstay of the games industry since the 1970s. Yet after the high-profile commercial failure of 2022’s Marvel’s Midnight Suns, things have looked bleak for fans of slowly moving units across maps. However, after last month’s one-two punch ofStar Wars Zero Companyand Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, the wonderfully nerdy genre is enjoying a revival.“The genre never disappeared – it was just niche or out of the spotlight,” says Benhamou. “Even in [such] a competitive business, when games are great, people will play them.”Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics is due for release in 2027 onPC, PS5 and XboxExplore more on these topicsGamesAction gamesUbisoftShooting gamesPCPlayStation 5Xbox series S/XfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From a VR gay sauna to the gothic pile that inspired Cluedo – Fierce festival storms back | Stage | The Guardian
description: As Britain’s longest-running live art festival returns, get ready for late-night artist dinners, a show in a swimming pool and Faye Driscoll’s incredible rotating disintegration
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: As Britain’s longest-running live art festival returns, get ready for late-night artist dinners, a show in a swimming pool and Faye Driscoll’s incredible rotating disintegration
Content: Epic work … Faye Driscoll’s Weathering at Philadelphia in 2025.Photograph: Kevin MonkoView image in fullscreenEpic work … Faye Driscoll’s Weathering at Philadelphia in 2025.Photograph: Kevin MonkoStageFrom a VR gay sauna to the gothic pile that inspired Cluedo – Fierce festival storms backVenues across BirminghamAs Britain’s longest-running live art festival returns, get ready for late-night artist dinners, a show in a swimming pool and Faye Driscoll’s incredible rotating disintegrationLyndsey WinshipThu 15 Oct 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe phrase “two things can be true” is a frequent refrain in popular psychology and it’s also a frequent response, I find, to witnessing the farther reaches of live art. Hmm, is this performance confusingly self-indulgent or utterly profound? Sometimes it can be both. In fact, it’s not just two things that can be true, it’s as many things as there are people in the audience, since this is all about the live subjective experience, in the moment; presence and connection.Launched in 1998, Fierce is Britain’s longest-running live art festival. For one week it takes over Birmingham’s conventional theatres alongside unconventional spaces, especially in ex-industrial Digbeth, which is fast becoming a creative hub. Also on the bill this year: late-night artist dinners, a show in a swimming pool, and a six-hour performance jam at a grand gothic hall that was apparently the inspiration for Cluedo.There’s a focus on the sensuous and sensory; it’s all about the physical body. But the first piece I experience is actually in virtual reality: Traversing the Mist, by Taiwanese artist Tung-Yen Chou. The setting is a gay sauna, and the VR tech is impressive. You walk through the grey concrete corridors, locker room, showers, cubicles, pushing aside curtains that you know aren’t really there. You can open doors, pick things up, press buttons in the lift. You’re an observer of the uncanny scene, which is peopled by identical blank-faced men; a sense of searching pervades, but there’s zero joy or pleasure to be found.View image in fullscreenLack of connection … Tung-Yen Chou, In the Mist at Fierce festival, 2026.Photograph: Kris KangThe experience is a combination of immersive and detached. It’s engaging, and yet eerily lonely – and also unnerving when the floor falls away, messing with your own proprioception. You feel, but what you feel is exactly the lack of connection. (Chou is also showing a short, sit-down VR piece called In the Mist, which was a precursor to the longer work, but is basically a sad porno.)What you’re missing in VR is the smells, the heat, the sweat. But don’t worry, there’s plenty of that elsewhere. Wojciech Grudziński’s sweaty, hairy, all-too-human fleshy body is front and centre in his solo Threesome, his bum in the air as he does upside down pliés in a shoulder stand and other yogic moves wearing bottomless frilly knickers. In voiceover he tells us of three Polish ballet dancers who were shamed for their homosexuality, and Threesome is his attempt to reclaim their true identities, and make peace with his own “ghastly” body. Is a series of bum-bearing contortions followed by a ravey, repetitive jig the best way to do that? Well, it’s Grudziński’s way. And it’s strangely compelling, building to a sort of catharsis, with lights and music and defiant mood.Artist Melissandre Varin is known as n:u, and calls themself an “atmosphere-maker”, which is interesting branding and perhaps modifies the expectations of the audience. Fierce is a thoroughly international festival, but n:u was previously based in Birmingham, although the work is rooted in Congolese, Guadeloupean, and Beninese heritage. I caught part of a rehearsal for the piece FREE(HOLD), an opaque ritual, in which performers drag ropes around their ankles and keen to the sky. Endurance, suffering, slavery and colonialism all rushed to mind.View image in fullscreenFront and centre … Wojciech Grudziński in Threesome at Fierce festival, 2026.Photograph: Manuel VasonThis is a festival full of intriguing, conversation-starting stuff, but American choreographer Faye Driscoll blows everyone else out of the water with her acclaimed, award-winning piece Weathering, which gets its UK premiere here. Driscoll’s work is a few levels up in terms of concept, commitment, execution and scale. It’s essentially 10 performers on a rotating platform, a tableau vivant, or maybe less a living tableau than one that’s slowly distorting and decaying and caving under the gravity of life’s pressures, or just the passage of time.It’s a piece full of wayward, messy bodies – it is indicated immediately that these are humans rather than “dancers” when the performers arrive in puffer jackets and cross-body bags and glasses, layers that will be gradually discarded, because this is live art after all. But these bodies also demonstrate a phenomenal amount of control, this multiperson sculpture moving at first so slowly it’s almost imperceptible. It’s intense and impressive, and importantly it sucks your attention and its imagery is ripe for extrapolation – especially the sense of precarity, of humans clinging to their unstable home as things start to spin out of control.Fierce festivalruns until 18 October, at various venues in BirminghamExplore more on these topicsStageDancePerformance artTheatreFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Balloon Girl review – tech tycoon swirls with tragic teen parachutist in a crackling, time-travelling climate romp | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Hannah McPake’s high-wire drama pokes fun at tech bro machismo, reality TV and Musk-style Martian escapes – think A Christmas Carol in space
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Hannah McPake’s high-wire drama pokes fun at tech bro machismo, reality TV and Musk-style Martian escapes – think A Christmas Carol in space
Content: Up, up and away … Mari Fflur, Oliver Wood and Elin Phillips in Balloon Girl at Sherman theatre, Cardiff.Photograph: Kirsten McTernanView image in fullscreenUp, up and away … Mari Fflur, Oliver Wood and Elin Phillips in Balloon Girl at Sherman theatre, Cardiff.Photograph: Kirsten McTernanTheatreReviewBalloon Girl review – tech tycoon swirls with tragic teen parachutist in a crackling, time-travelling climate rompSherman theatre, CardiffHannah McPake’s high-wire drama pokes fun at tech bro machismo, reality TV and Musk-style Martian escapes – think A Christmas Carol in spaceArifa AkbarThu 15 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis show takes local history as its starting point, that of a 19th-century balloonist’s assistant who performed a parachute stunt in the skies aboveCardiff. It throws in a current-day tech billionaire, the space race, a time-travelling hot-air balloon, and – for good measure? – a lifesize seagull that speaks.Surprisingly, given the complications of writer-director Hannah McPake’s high-wire drama, it lifts off, swirling through the clouds on its air-bound set, crackling with humour and effervescent imagination along with a keen sense of unwritten history, to become a complete blast.Louisa Maud Evans was the real-life 14-year-old girl from Bristol who was enlisted to perform a parachute jump from a hot-air balloon during the Fine Art, Industrial and Maritime Exhibition of 1896. She had little experience of parachuting and she perished in the Bristol Channel after an unfavourable wind cast her out to sea.View image in fullscreenRich imagination … Oliver Wood, François Pandolfo, Elin Phillips and Keiron Self.Photograph: Kirsten McTernanLouisa appears in different guises in McPake’s story,which begins with Carol Gaudron (Elin Phillips), a celebrity tech billionaire and descendant of Auguste Eugene Gaudron (Keiron Self), the balloonist who enlisted Louisa for the ill-fated stunt. The opening scene is a reality quizshow in which a guileless young woman from Bristol wins a televised rocket trip to Mars. “Let’s get humanity off this planet and into the stars,” declares Carol, who has all the integrity of a tech visionary turned rank capitalist. It’s a very nifty way to join up the 19th-century endeavour to conquer the skies and perform public displays of showmanship with modern-day tech bro ambitions in the space race.The story swivels from satire (on everything from reality TV to AI and journalism) to a picaresque journey of time travel for Carol, with a kooky young navigator, Louisa (Mari Fflur) and the talking seagull (Oliver Wood). There are shades of A Christmas Carol – in space – as this trio travels redemptively to the past and future before returning Carol,transformed, to her present.There is so much plot, such rich imagination and great zinging lines alongside a serious underlying message about climate and planetary resource. It occasionally comes too thick and fast, leaving you behind, but it is fun even in its confusions.Hayley Grindle’sset switches between gorgeous small-scale puppetry and grand hot-air balloon imagery. McPake has created several shows for this theatre but this surely has to be one of her best.An airborne triumph.AtSherman theatre, Cardiff, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreSherman theatreCardiffreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A tour around Amy Winehouse’s private junk: five free art exhibitions to see | Art | The Guardian
description: The Back to Black singer’s books, shoes and jigsaw puzzles have gone on display. Elsewhere, a leaky Barbican and some gloriously gloopy sculptures can be viewed in London galleries this week
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: The Back to Black singer’s books, shoes and jigsaw puzzles have gone on display. Elsewhere, a leaky Barbican and some gloriously gloopy sculptures can be viewed in London galleries this week
Content: Weirdly cold … Alex Margo Arden, Same Otherwise, 2026.Photograph: Eva Herzog/Courtesy the artist and the Nicoletta Fiorucci FoundationView image in fullscreenWeirdly cold … Alex Margo Arden, Same Otherwise, 2026.Photograph: Eva Herzog/Courtesy the artist and the Nicoletta Fiorucci FoundationEddy Frankel's gallery crawlArtA tour around Amy Winehouse’s private junk: five free art exhibitions to seeThe Back to Black singer’s books, shoes and jigsaw puzzles have gone on display. Elsewhere, a leaky Barbican and some gloriously gloopy sculptures can be viewed in London galleries this weekEddy FrankelThu 15 Oct 2026 06.28 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 06.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlex Margo Arden: Nothing Personal★★★★☆They tried to make her go to rehab and she said “no, no, no”. And she probably would’ve said no to letting the artist Alex Margo Arden mount an exhibition out of all her old junk, too, but sadlyAmy Winehouseisn’t around to protest, so Arden’s gone ahead regardless.In display cases and on shelves in a lush Chelsea flat, Arden has assembled a collection of objects and books based on what Winehouse once owned. Trawling through archive material and auction records, Arden has bought duplicates of Winehouse’s makeup, her copies of Vogue, her boardgames, her books.So you get to snoop through her private junk, imagining her reading all these biographies of jazzers and celebs, or the Claudia Roden book of Jewish food. The thought of her reading Roy Keane’s autobiography while slurping down matzah-ball soup is beautiful.Did Winehouse really do the 1,000-piece Cadbury jigsaw puzzle? Did she read the article on “the body we all want now” in that issue of Vogue? Arden is forcing you to ask these questions, imagine these scenarios, turning you into a celebrity stalker, someone who has become unable to separate idol from human.There’s a pair of ballet pumps signed by fans and left on her doorstep after Winehouse’s death, a birthday card from Mark Ronson and Adele that she never got to open. Now we’re too close, now it feels like we’re intruding.It’s a weirdly cold, unemotional display. But two things are opening at once here: there’s a portrait of an icon being created out of the objects and ephemera of their life, and there’s an uncomfortable exploration of the fetishisation of celebrity. There’s an act of love and devotion, and there’s an act of critical self-reflection. Joy and discomfort, rubbing awkwardly up against each other. It’s very smart, very critical conceptual art that makes you feel pretty grubby and intrusive.Nicoletta Fiorucci Foundation, until 23 January 2027Yuko Mohri: In Concert★★★★☆View image in fullscreenSurreal … Yuko Mohri: In Concert at the Barbican, London.Photograph: Thomas Adank/BarbicanThe Barbican has sprung a leak. Actually, it has sprung loads of them, which is why they’re investing so much in trying to repair this poor old brutalist beast.But in Yuko Mohri’s installation, those leaks aren’t maintenance problems, they’re creative collaborators. Water drips out of sinks and pipes in the Curve, gathering in buckets and tarpaulins, being funnelled and pumped through tubes. Each drip triggers a little cymbal, a triangle, a mallet on a drum. The Barbican’s collapsing infrastructure is playing you a tune.It’s surreal, cacophonous: repurposed Barbican lamps, flickering on and off, are being controlled by sensors measuring the moisture levels in rotting fruit, others by breezes blowing through the Barbican’s draughty walls – all at the will of mouldy fruit and crumbling concrete walls.It’s the best use of the Curve for years: Mohri has turned rot and disrepair into an instrument and made the building’s frailties into a symphony of survival. When life gives you lemons, you make lemonade. When it gives you a leaky roof, you make musique concrète.Barbican Curve, until 24 January 2027Yuyan Wang: Pilgrims★★★★☆View image in fullscreenDisconcerting … Yuyan Wang, Boring Billion, 2026, at Shoreditch church.Photograph: Yuyan WangLight is a positive thing in popular culture. We call smart people bright, we say good things are “lit”, etc. But there’s a darkness to how Chinese artist Yuyan Wang approaches it in this new film work.It takes as its starting pointa 2018 initiative from the Chinese governmentto launch artificial moons in order to provide continuous daylight.Moths and bugs flit across the screen downstairs, drawn to a lamp, their natural instincts duped by artificial light. Upstairs, found footage of drills and mines, LEDs, fireworks, lasers, rockets, torches and neon striplights flicker past, soundtracked by blasts of synthesiser choir chords. Wang is asking what it means to have no darkness, to be constantly productive, to have no rest or escape.I guess we are the moths now, being fooled by the artificial lights of a world that treats us like bugs.Over in the crypt of Shoreditch church next door, another video shows humanoid robots being constructed. You get the sense that Wang knows that our terrifying imminent future will just be more forgotten industrial detritus.This is what art cinema does well: non-narrative, alluring, disconcerting weirdness.Emalin, until 14 NovemberRebecca Warren: There Will Be Another You★★★★☆View image in fullscreenPerfectly imperfect … There Will Be Another You, 2026.Photograph: Mark Blower/Rebecca Warren/Maureen Paley, LondonTwenty years after her nomination for the Turner prize, Rebecca Warren has lost none of her angular, gritty, rough, weird power.The sculptor is back for her first London show in 16 years with more of her lumpy unfired clay and bronze figures, and they are still perfectly imperfect. The smaller sculptures look like a post-apocalyptic take on decorative rococo ceramics. Instead of glistening perfection and flowing, ornamental robes, we’ve got rough, gloopy, brittle nudes stretched out on rocks. They’re funny, ugly things. But you can’t help but feel like the avalanche of faux-amateurish, kindergarten-grade ceramics that are so popular these days might all be Warren’s fault.The big bronzes in the main space are the best. Lifesize nudes with hands and feet that have grown grotesque and lumpen, they’re somewhere between Henry Moore, Alberto Giacometti and Robert Crumb, like a bawdy grotesque take on modernism. It’s like all your favourite modernists have melted together, making one big, lumpy but pretty delicious visual soup.Maureen Paley, until 12 DecemberWilliam Kentridge: A Nicely Built City★★★☆☆View image in fullscreenWhimsical … William Kentridge, Composite for L’Orfeo (Unjustifiable), 2026.Photograph: Thys Dullaart/Goodman GalleryWilliam Kentridge is in a despairing mood. For decades, the South African artist – last seen round these parts with a major show at the Royal Academy in 2022 – has been making animated films about the fate of his home city, Johannesburg. The latest iteration is on show here, and it’s a pretty miserable thing. Whatever hope could be found in the earlier works is gone. Johannesburg has fallen further into ruin. A gas explosion has gutted a building, trees are blighted by fungus, women cradle their terrified children, protesters pack the streets, all rendered in filthy charcoal. The character of Soho Eckstein, a major industrialist in a modernist house, reappears – but now he seems to stand in for the artist, an isolated older man watching it all fall apart from the safety of his mansion.I’ve never been much of a Kentridge fan, and this all just feels a bit too whimsical for the subject matter. But it’s still classic Kentridge: experimental, theatrical art about deeply emotional issues. It’s a small, museum-quality show filled with drawings and sculptures that will make Kentridge fans very happy but probably won’t do much to get the rest of us on side.Goodman gallery, until 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsArtEddy Frankel's gallery crawlExhibitionsSound artCeramicsVideo artSculptureInstallationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pope.L review – savage satire from Y-fronts-wearing trickster famed for gruelling ‘crawl’ across New York | Art | The Guardian
description: The late American took on liberal presumptions and the commercialism of Black culture, even dressing in white bunny ears and underpants
Author: Ben Eastham
Headline: The late American took on liberal presumptions and the commercialism of Black culture, even dressing in white bunny ears and underpants
Content: What lies beneath … Real Kitsch #7.Photograph: Courtesy The Estate of Pope.L and Modern Art © The Estate of Pope.LView image in fullscreenWhat lies beneath … Real Kitsch #7.Photograph: Courtesy The Estate of Pope.L and Modern Art © The Estate of Pope.LArtReviewPope.L review – savage satire from Y-fronts-wearing trickster famed for gruelling ‘crawl’ across New YorkModern Art, LondonThe late American took on liberal presumptions and the commercialism of Black culture, even dressing in white bunny ears and underpantsBen EasthamThu 15 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 08.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeven squares are pinned to the wall, each one painted in the high style of American minimalism: pure, austere variations on a theme. At the centre of each is printed the phrase “negro idea” followed by an apparently random number (51, 37, 666). What is Pope.L, the late, great trickster of contemporary American art, getting at?Perhaps it is a critique of how minimalism, with its ethos of art-for-art’s sake, excluded politics from art? Or a comment on how racial categories are as constructed (and as subject to fashion) as the theories underpinning contemporary art? Or is it a riff on how the edifice of western modernism is built on stolen ideas? Then again, maybe the deployment of an outmoded racial category is simply designed to discomfort the liberal pieties of those people likely to visit this art gallery just off Piccadilly.All that is certain is that Pope.L cannot be pinned down. Best known for his gruelling “crawl” across New York, this influential artist and writer didn’t use art to make himself understood. Instead, he used its tools to dismantle the liberal presumption that other people and communitiescaneasily be understood, categorised and explained away. He was less interested in being “seen” than in making his audience look again at themselves and the world, and paved the way for a new generation of artists for whom identity – in the sense of conforming to external expectations – is not only a creative trap but a form of control.View image in fullscreenDada-esque … Identity What We Lose To Real For, 2022 (detail).Photograph: Courtesy The Estate of Pope.L, Gladstone and Modern Art © The Estate of Pope.LThis is most apparent in Pope.L’s deep suspicion of the commercialisation of Black culture, and the stereotypes that serve to commodify and defuse it. His satire is savage and furious, closer in spirit and ambition to the provocations of Dada than to any more straightforward satire of the art world. Take the photograph Foraging (Mr Mau Mau), in which he appears in white Y-fronts and white bunny ears, with a note pinned to his chest referencing the Kenyan anti-colonial uprising (and Britain’s notoriously brutal repression). More Y-fronts are framed on the walls, smeared in brown and white fluid and handwritten insignia (“I have something important to share with you – Cliff G”). The numbered series is entitled Real Kitsch.The way that words and images settle into fixed categories (cliche and kitsch, respectively) is a recurring theme. In Identity What We Lose to Real For, completed a year beforethe artist’s death in 2023, block wooden letters like those used to teach children the alphabet fall off their frame, further confusing a short text that reads like a dense concrete poem. The surface is spattered with paint, recalling painterly expressionism and a toddler’s paint-flinging (neighbouring series of scrawled Xs and Os likewise summon conceptual painting and a half-understood game of noughts and crosses). Art here is dismantling conventional ways of thinking and naming.View image in fullscreenCrawling critique … The Great White Way, 22 Miles, 5 Years, 1 Street (Segment #1, December 29, 2001), 2001.Photograph: Pope.L/Gladstone/Modern ArtShort films documenting a selection of Pope.L’s performances are screened in a back room. Dressed in a figure-hugging Superman costume and with a skateboard strapped to his back, the artist crawls on his belly from the Statue of Liberty to the Bronx. As he is barracked by strangers, you wonder why so many are offended by the performance yet unmoved by the numerous homeless people in New York.In a performance-lecture he situates his work on the “sidewalk of national consciousness”, and the world crowds into every work in this show: a white painting might look like a romantic abstraction but is in fact, as the text along its edge tells us, a picture of Martin Luther King’s Dick as Seen from Pluto. Fifteen years after Pope.L made this gag, incidentally, research was undertaken on Kazimir Malevich’s 1915 Black Square. It was discovered that the monochrome painting, long hailed as an icon of art’s transcendent possibilities, had a hidden title: Negroes Battling in a Cave.View image in fullscreenGold People Shit in Their Valet, 2014, mixed media on paper.Photograph: Pope.L/Modern ArtHere is more evidence for Pope.L’s argument that art can never entirely be insulated from the nature of the world that produces it, no matter how pure a painting might appear to the eye. This point is most clearly illustrated by his long-running and highly complex engagement with the work of Robert Ryman (a survey of whose monochrome white paintings is now on show at the Barbican in London).Pope.L memorably described himself as “the son” of Ryman and therefore duty-bound to “walk in his footsteps to the front door of the family mansion and burn it to the ground”. While it is a shame that this show does not include more of his direct responses to the painter, the two exhibitions can constructively be seen in counterpoint.Pope.L: Selected Works: 1978–2022is at Modern Art, London, from 13 October to 14 NovemberExplore more on these topicsArtExhibitionsPerformance artBlack US cultureLondonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Palestine book by Alana Hadid and Jenan Matari pulled from Random House before release | Penguin Random House | The Guardian
description: Authors withdraw book planned for young readers after disputes with editors over characterizations of 7 October
Author: Sam Levin
Headline: Authors withdraw book planned for young readers after disputes with editors over characterizations of 7 October
Content: Alana Hadid, a philanthropist, activist and older sister of models Bella and Gigi, and Jenan Matari, an author and communications strategist, signed a book deal with Random House Children’s Books, a division of Penguin Random House, in November 2024.Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreenAlana Hadid, a philanthropist, activist and older sister of models Bella and Gigi, and Jenan Matari, an author and communications strategist, signed a book deal with Random House Children’s Books, a division of Penguin Random House, in November 2024.Photograph: GettyPenguin Random HousePalestine book by Alana Hadid and Jenan Matari pulled from Random House before releaseAuthors withdraw book planned for young readers after disputes with editors over characterizations of 7 OctoberSam Levinin Los AngelesThu 15 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA book on Palestine for young readers was pulled atPenguin Random Housejust before its scheduled release, following editorial disputes between the publisher and the book’s Palestinian American authors over their account of Palestinian history.In November 2024, Random House Children’s Books, a division ofPenguinRandom House, signed the book deal with Alana Hadid, a philanthropist, activist and older sister of models Bella and Gigi, and Jenan Matari, an author and communications strategist. The book was promoted for release in September this year.The authors, both influential social media commentators, drafted a manuscript about the history ofPalestine, Israeli occupation, Palestinian resistance, and the diaspora, interwoven with references to their own families’ stories of displacement.But the writers withdrew their book after objecting to edits by Random House that they said sanitized and misrepresented their views, and which they said were introduced after they thought the book had been finalized. A Random House spokesperson said the process “followed our standard bookmaking procedures”, and that the publisher ultimately supported the authors’ decision to pull the book.Displacement and the Palestinian American Story would have been the eighth installment in Random House’s Race to the Truthseries, an ongoing collection of nonfiction books for youth ages 10 to 13. The books aimed to provide the “true story of American history”, written by members of marginalized groups telling the histories of their peoples. A co-creator of the project said she objected to the treatment of Displacement and would not be pursuing future installments in the series with the publisher.“It became clear that Penguin was never actually going to allow us just to write the book we wanted to write,” said Hadid. “It says a lot that they’re willing to tank an entire very powerful series that helps children learn history, just because of one book about Palestine.”View image in fullscreenAlana Hadid in 2025.Photograph: Edward Berthelot/Getty ImagesAccording to Hadid and Matari, who provided the Guardian with the draft manuscript and email excerpts of their communications with Random House, the authors and the publisher engaged in months of disagreements about language in the book, including a passage on the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks in southern Israel. The writers’ manuscript argued that people under “colonial domination” have the “right to resist”, but Random House urged them to incorporate arguments that the attacks that day violated international law. At an impasse, the authors withdrew their book in early September.The authors now plan torelease it through Interlink Books, a Palestinian-owned US publisher.Random House Children’s Books has other forthcoming books on Palestine, the spokesperson said, writing: “We remain committed to bringing the Palestinian perspective to young readers.” The spokesperson also said another Race to the Truth book remained on track for 2028 publication.The dispute over the book comes amid disproportionatescrutinyandcensorship of workby and on behalf ofPalestinians. The conflict also laid bare the wide gap between narratives around 7 October, one that could not be bridged in a book to be distributed by a mainstream publisher.“I believe it was a revolutionary book, which is why it was under so much scrutiny,” Matari said. “They continued to try to sanitize our history because they didn’t want to make certain communities uncomfortable. But decolonial history is supposed to make you uncomfortable.”‘No greater story to tell’The Race to the Truth series was conceived by Saira Rao and Regina Jackson, founders of Race2Dinner, a program launched in 2019 tofacilitate conversations with white womenabout racism. In 2020, Rao and Jackson sold a book called White Women to Penguin Random House, which became abestseller, then in 2021 sold the Race to the Truth children’s series to the publishing house. Random House has since publishedbooksin the series onslavery, the colonization of theWampanoagpeople, theexclusionof Chinese Americans,Mexican Americanhistory, and theforced assimilationof Indigenous youth.View image in fullscreenJenan Matari.Photograph: Courtesy of Jenan MatariAs the series progressed, Rao felt it was urgent to publish a Palestine installment: “There’s no greater story to tell right now. Palestine actually tells a story of all genocides, of all settler colonial violence.”After Random House greenlit the idea in summer of 2024, Rao brought on Matari and Hadid.The authors submitted their first draft of Displacement in July 2025. In the introduction, they wrote that the Palestinian story had long been missing from classrooms. “The deliberate erasure of our history has left generations of Palestinians struggling to explain not only where we come from but why nearly half of us are scattered around the world, including – as in our cases – in the United States,” the intro said.The book discussed the landscape and history of Palestine; the rise of Zionism; the Nakba, or catastrophe, of 1948 when more than 700,000 Palestinian people were expelled from their homes; their analysis of Israel as a “settler colony”; the relationship between the US and Israel; and life for Palestinians living under military occupation.They also documented their family histories. Hadid’s grandparents, they wrote, were expelled from Safed days after her father was born, becoming refugees in Syria. And relatives of Matari and her husband were displaced from Deir Yassin and Ein Karem after an April 1948 massacre claimed the lives of more than 100 Palestinians.“I just wanted children to see us as humans,” Hadid said.Disputes about 7 OctoberTensions arose on the project in June 2026 when, according to the authors, the book was distributed to reviewers and made available for preorder before Random House had shared a final version with the writers. When the authors received a copy, they said it included changes to a passage about 7 October made by Random House without their knowledge.In a chapter called The International Right to Armed Resistance, the authors cited a UN general assemblyresolutionthatsaidpeople under colonial domination are entitled to “the right to self-determination” and torestorethat right “by any means at their disposal”. The chapter also noted Hamas’s use of prisoner exchanges to free thousands of Palestinians imprisoned in Israel they called “effectively hostages of the state”. Referring to the 2011 exchange of captured Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit for more than 1,000 prisoners, they wrote: “This exchange was one of the most famous and showed Palestinians that resistance could bring real results.”On 7 October, the manuscript continued, Hamas fighters “crossed into Israel in a coordinated assault”. The authors said roughly 1,100 Israelis were killed, including 37 children, and said civilians and soldiers were taken captive “to be used in an exchange”.Their section on 7 October was brief, but argued that international law authorized Palestinian resistance “by any means necessary”, saying the attacks came after “decades of ignored suffering and repression”.“Palestinians, like other oppressed peoples before them, have demanded freedom in the face of overwhelming military power. What happened on October 7 was not the beginning of violence in this land – it was another moment in a long history of a people struggling to be free,” they wrote.The authors said they had, at Random House’s request, added details about the 7 October death toll, and they believed the language was finalized in May 2026. However, when they received an updated final copy of the book, they saw that a Random House editor had added a line about the 7 October attacks saying: “These actions were a violation of international law.”The authors objected to the insertion, emails show, saying it contradicted their analysis of international law. They claimed in an email it was also a violation of their contract to make changes without their approval. One Random House editor suggested in an email that without that line or something similar, “we will lose all credibility with our readers, including those who are open-minded about our perspective” and the book couldn’t be published.Back-and-forth negotiations surrounding the description of 7 October continued for weeks, emails show, with Random House’s head of publicity, legal department and children’s books president involved in discussions.In the meantime, Random House came back with other edits the authors found objectionable. In July, a senior Random House official suggested removing “Jewish” as a modifier in several places, including when the authors had referred to Zionist militias involved in the destruction of Palestinian villages during the Nakba as “Jewish gangs”. “Our concern is not accuracy, but whether the repetition adds necessary clarity,” the Random House official wrote.The authors responded that it was “shameful” for an editor to say accuracy was not the concern, prompting an editor to reply back: “Our editorial point was not about whether the word was accurate, but whether, given the context, repeating the [Jewish] modifier was necessary.”A Random House official again pressed the authors to expand on 7 October, writing in an email that the authors could add context along the lines of: “Some human rights organizations and commentators have described Hamas’s actions that day as violations of international law; others frame the legal and historical questions differently.”But the authors grew increasingly frustrated, writing in one email: “In a book about the history of slavery in the United States – neither of us can imagine a Black author being forced to condemn the slave rebellions or consider them a violation of international law.”In one email to their agent, Matari wrote, “It has become quite clear that Penguin is more focused and concerned with centering Jewish feelings over Palestinian life and lived experience.”Records show Random House repeatedly expressed their commitment to the book, with one official saying they were dedicated to publishing “a necessary and accessible book about the Palestinian American story for young readers, a perspective that remains far too rare in children’s nonfiction” and saying editors wanted to work in “good faith” to resolve issues.By August, Random House suggested keeping the author’s text as is, but adding a “publisher’s note” to the book with some of the suggested 7 October language and changing the age range to 14+. The publisher also said if the parties could not resolve their differences, the authors could take the book elsewhere and keep their advance.“Editorial discussion and revision are a standard part of the publishing process,” the Random House spokesperson said in an email. “We gave guidance to help ensure the intended readers for this book, ages 10 and up, had enough information to understand the subject matter and engage thoughtfully with the questions it raises, knowing that many readers would be coming to the subject matter for the first time.”The spokesperson said the company had made digital advance copies available to industry contacts, which were marked as “uncorrected” and not final, and that this process was halted after the authors expressed concerns. “We would not move forward with a book that the authors were not comfortable publishing,” the spokesperson said.‘No longer the book we wrote’In an interview, Matari said she felt it was unacceptable for Random House to publish a disclaimer that might contradict their writing. Termination, she said, seemed the only option: “It was no longer the book we wrote.”Matari was no stranger to backlash for her commentary on 7 October. Over the last year, severalscheduled book talksfor her debut children’s book, about a young Palestinian girl and her grandfather, were cancelled last-minute after people accused her of antisemitism, in part over social media posts describing the 7 October attacks as resistance against colonialism and declaring the US to be “under Zionist occupation”. She and a Jewish author recently sued the city of Los Angeles for free speech violations after the public library cancelled their planned joint book event. Matari has denied claims of antisemitism and defended her posts, saying she was “vehemently anti-Zionist”.View image in fullscreenSaira Rao.Photograph: Rebecca Stumpf/The GuardianHadid said they were not trying to minimize the harms of 7 October and had, at Random House’s request, been clear about the death toll. Their goal was to put the attacks into historical context. “I wasn’t going to publish this book with words I hadn’t written, where they were forcing us to tell the story from the perspective of the oppressors.”Rao, from the Race to the Truth series, said her relationship with Random House had been smooth before the conflicts over the Palestine book, with previous authors given significant leeway to write their stories without interference. Hadid and Matari’s experience was fundamentally different, Rao said: “You’ve got the entire company weighing in on this one little book.”The end of the series at Random House comes at a time when a wide range of industries and institutions are backtracking ondiversity, equity and inclusionefforts, raising fears about diminishing opportunities for people of color inacademia,publishing,entertainmentandmedia. The recent rise of book bans and open hostility to diverse works is further diminishing those opportunities, said Leyla Moushabeck, co-owner and longtime editor at Interlink, the publishing house taking on Hadid and Matari’s book.“As a second-generation Palestinian-American, it’s a book I wish I had had growing up,” Moushabeck said of the book, which Interlink plans to publish next year.Hadid added she was grateful their manuscript found a new home: “We hope that people read the book that Penguin didn’t want you to read.”Explore more on these topicsPenguin Random HousePalestinePenguinIsrael-Gaza warPublishingBella HadidGigi HadidnewsShareReuse this content

title: Her royal heilness: Berlin show revisits the artist who turned the Queen into a Nazi | Art | The Guardian
description: The late Christoph Schlingensief was one of German art’s great provocateurs. Can his B-Movie horror aesthetics still shock us into thinking anew about media power, colonialism, and the far right?
Author: Hanno Hauenstein
Headline: The late Christoph Schlingensief was one of German art’s great provocateurs. Can his B-Movie horror aesthetics still shock us into thinking anew about media power, colonialism, and the far right?
Content: Art and politics … Christoph Schlingensief, The African Twin Towers, 2005.Photograph: © Estate of Christoph SchlingensiefView image in fullscreenArt and politics … Christoph Schlingensief, The African Twin Towers, 2005.Photograph: © Estate of Christoph SchlingensiefArtHer royal heilness: Berlin show revisits the artist who turned the Queen into a NaziThe late Christoph Schlingensief was one of German art’s great provocateurs. Can his B-Movie horror aesthetics still shock us into thinking anew about media power, colonialism, and the far right?Hanno HauensteinThu 15 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChristoph Schlingensief certainly knew how to provoke. “Fury at German play that shows Queen as a Nazi,” read the Sunday Express’s headline after Kaprow City first premiered at Berlin’s Volksbühne theatre in 2006. Drawing on the happenings of US performance artist Allan Kaprow, the play turned its attention to Diana, Princess of Wales’s death. In one scene, the then queen performs a Hitler salute. Another re-enacts the paparazzi chase that led to Diana’s fatal crash. Diana appears in bed beside two men with Down’s syndrome; and Camilla is pelted with animal blood. Schlingensief insisted the work was not meant as provocation but as an investigation into how Diana turned into a modern icon. But his art thrived on outrage, exposing the absurdity of societies that glorify their idols while consuming their lives as entertainment.Kaprow City is at the heart of a new Berlin show – It’s Not My Problem Anymore, Deal With Your Own Shit – that revisits the artist’s legacy. In the Gropius Bau’s grand neo-Renaissance atrium, visitors encounter remnants of the carousel-like rotating stage he called the “animatograph”. Looking at this installation today feels like a glimpse into Schlingensief’s mind: a messy collage of childhood memories, violent fantasies and royal glamour.View image in fullscreenMaking headlines … It’s Not My Problem Anymore, Deal With Your Own Shit, Gropius Bau.Photograph: © Estate of Christoph SchlingensiefThe Gropius Bau installed roughly half of Schlingensief’s original set on the very same spot where Joseph Beuys, a major influence, once exhibited his Stag Monuments. In Kaprow City, flickering black-and-white footage of a crucifixion plays beneath a slate board listing the stage’s contents, from “Diana Girl Ballet” to “exorcism”. In the original production, audiences were distributed across 18 tiny, wedge-shaped rooms, echoing Allan Kaprow’s 18Happenings in 6 Parts. Spectators witnessed only fragments of the action. Now, most of the stage’s interior is draped in plastic. Excerpts of videos from the play loop throughout the installation on old-fashioned TV screens.Enlarged tabloid headlines and articles are plastered across the walls behind it. Beside the Sunday Expressheadline, a German newspaper asks: “Will Diana’s sons stop Schlingensief?” After rumours that the royals might pursue legal action, Schlingensief had invited William and Harry to Frieze, where he planned to present an iteration of the project.“The combination of Lady Di, the speculation surrounding the circumstances of her death, and the general myth that grew around her fascinated Christoph,” says stage designer Aino Laberenz, Schlingensief’s widow who now manages his estate. For the Volksbühne production, Schlingensief cast Jenny Elvers, a German TV personality whose private life, like Diana’s, was a fixture of tabloids, between fascination and intense scrutiny. Laberenz cautions against viewing Kaprow City only through the lens of Diana. It belonged to a wider artistic universe in which theatre, film and art collided and overlapped with questions of media power and spectacle, she says.View image in fullscreen‘We’re playing Germany’: Schlingensief outside the Schauspielhaus Zürich ahead of his Hamlet performance in 2001Photograph: David Baltzer/© Estate of Christoph SchlingensiefSchlingensief, who died of lung cancer just shy of his 50th birthday in 2010, grew up in the shadow of New German Cinema and was deeply influenced by film-makers such as Rainer Werner Fassbinder. Like Fassbinder, he blurred the lines between art and politics. In The African Twin Towers, he took actors including Patti Smith, Irm Hermann and Robert Stadlober to Namibia to re-enact Wagnerian myths, confronting the legacy of Germany’s colonial genocide. Namibian actors also took part.Seen today, Schlingensief’s artistic vocabulary – messy B-movie horror, drag, disabled performers, a taste for the extreme – sits awkwardly with Namibia as a stage. Watching his actors improvise on Shark Island, the site of a former German concentration camp where Herero and Nama prisoners endured forced labour and starvation, feels uncomfortable. Not because the provocation is empty (it isn’t), but because one wonders whether the team fully grasped what they were doing. Namibia feels less like the subject of a reckoning with Germany’s colonial past than a backdrop for a German artist’s grand vision. At Gropius Bau, The African Twin Towers appears as a patchwork of sequences across 18 screens.Schlingensief’s work on the far right, however, remains strikingly relevant – not only because of the AfD’s rise in Germany, but also because of his hands-on confrontational approach to anti-immigrant politics. In his version of Hamlet, he brought former far-right extremists on to the stage at Schauspielhaus Zürich and later Berlin’s Volksbühne, where they re-enacted Shakespeare’s central murder scene amid far-right rock music and Nazi aesthetics. “We’re not playing Hamlet, we’re playing Germany,” reads a Schlingensief quote taped to the exhibition wall. It captures the artist’s insistence that art must confront society, rather than offer an escape.View image in fullscreen‘How much he is missed’ … Christoph Schlingensief, Church of Fear, 2003, part of It’s Not My Problem Anymore, Deal With Your Own Shit.Photograph: © Estate of Christoph SchlingensiefThe same attitude runs through Ausländer Raus! Schlingensiefs Container, his 2000 project in which asylum seekers lived under surveillance in a Big Brother-style container beside Vienna’s State Opera, while audiences voted on who should be deported first, two people a day. Conceived in response to the far-right FPÖ’s entry into Austria’s government, the project turned deportation – or, in the AfD’s words, “remigration” – into an eerie spectacle. It exposed European racism while implicating viewers in its public reproduction.Looking at these works today, one cannot help thinking of how far-right actors have learned to adopt such aesthetic spectacle as a political tool. The AfD’s AI video Remigration Hit from 2024, for instance, revels in humiliating migrant men herded on to planes by Aryan-looking pilots. Schlingensief’s work reads as a warning of how easily such cruelty becomes entertainment. And how readily the media help normalise it, from the tabloid frenzy surrounding Diana to the far right’s supremacist language of “remigration”.“I keep noticing in the commentary how much he is missed,” says Laberenz toward the end of our interview. “But I also like to say that it’s up to us, whether we work in the arts or not, not to hand responsibility over to someone else so that we no longer have to act.”Christoph Schlingensief: It’s Not My Problem Anymore, Deal With Your Own Shit is atGropius Bau, Berlin, until 17 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArtGermanyEuropeExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content
