title: Wallace & Gromit maker Aardman falls short of return to profit | Aardman | The Guardian
description: Animation studio narrows annual loss to £1.1m amid ‘challenging market’ in children’s content
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Animation studio narrows annual loss to £1.1m amid ‘challenging market’ in children’s content
Content: The co-founders of Aardman Peter Lord (left) and David Sproxton alongside the Wallace & Gromit creator Nick Park (right) in August.Photograph: Ian West/PAView image in fullscreenThe co-founders of Aardman Peter Lord (left) and David Sproxton alongside the Wallace & Gromit creator Nick Park (right) in August.Photograph: Ian West/PAAardmanWallace & Gromit maker Aardman falls short of return to profitAnimation studio narrows annual loss to £1.1m amid ‘challenging market’ in children’s contentLauren AlmeidaThu 15 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 10.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDon’t break out the celebratory Wensleydale just yet.Aardman, the British animation studio behind the cheese-loving inventor Wallace and his beloved dog Gromit, has fallen short of a target to get back in the black, its accounts show.The employee-owned business was aiming to record a small profit in 2025 after two years of consecutive losses but was hit by production delays and a “challenging market” in children’s content.So although its revenues jumped 8% to £20.4m last year, it was in the red to the tune of £1.1m, albeit an improvement on the previous year’s £4.1m loss.Aardman, which also produces the popular Shaun the Sheep series, said the timing of some “significant” deals and weaker income in some parts of the business had hurt its bottom line.It will be hoping for a boost from new projects, such as arecently opened exhibition at Lightroom in Londonthat explores its 54-year history, as well as a third Shaun the Sheep film, which wasreleasedlast month.And the famously silent Gromit willsoon be getting a voice, with this month’s audiobook of his autobiography read by the actor Martin Freeman.In 2024 the studio launched a five-year business plan, which involved more investment in its intellectual property and cutting back costs.Since then it has enjoyed the success of Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl, which broke viewing records over Christmas in 2024 as the most watched animated film broadcast on British television since 2002.The film won two Baftas and received an Oscar nomination for best animated feature film.Aardman said in its annual accounts that it had undertaken a further strategic review in early 2026 as it looked for ways to manage inflationary cost pressures, which resulted in “several redundancies”.Its headcount for the 2025 financial year had already shrunk from 297 to 230 people, with permanent staff falling from 128 to 110.The studio also recognised artificial intelligence as a principal risk and uncertainty to its business. It wrote that AI and generative AI were “reshaping parts of the creative industries, creating opportunities to improve workflows and support innovation while also raising important legal, ethical and authorship issues”.It said it was vital this technology was developed and used responsibly and selectively, but only in ways that “support and celebrate human creativity and craft rather than replace it”.Peter Lord and David Sproxton co-founded the studio in the early 1970s in Bristol. They began animating as teenagers, selling their first short – starring a superhero called Aardman – to the BBC’s Vision On in 1972.They created Morph for the children’s programme Take Hart in 1977. The studio began appealing to adult audiences through Channel 4’s Conversation Pieces series, and its animators, including Nick Park, went on to make Wallace & Gromit.Aardman became employee-owned in 2018, with Lord and Sproxton transferring majority ownership to staff to safeguard the company’s independence. The pair wereknighted earlier this year.Explore more on these topicsAardmanAnnual resultsFilm industryTelevision industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: One week a year I escape my ‘real’ life as broke standup comic – and travel back to medieval times | Scout Boxall | The Guardian
description: Live action role play, or Larping, allows me to straddle two worlds with fellow weirdos – and enter a realm where death can be reversed and I’m a cashed-up bureaucrat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Live action role play, or Larping, allows me to straddle two worlds with fellow weirdos – and enter a realm where death can be reversed and I’m a cashed-up bureaucrat
Content: ‘My wardrobe is evenly split between the 21st, 16th and 14th centuries’, says Scout Boxall.Photograph: Trendy's PhotographyView image in fullscreen‘My wardrobe is evenly split between the 21st, 16th and 14th centuries’, says Scout Boxall.Photograph: Trendy's PhotographyOpinionRole playing gamesOne week a year I escape my ‘real’ life as broke standup comic – and travel back to medieval timesScout BoxallLive action role play, or Larping, allows me to straddle two worlds with fellow weirdos – and enter a realm where death can be reversed and I’m a cashed-up bureaucratThu 15 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 18.50 EDTShareEvery Friday night on a community sports field in Melbourne’s inner north, a few hundred nerds dress up in historical armour and attack each other with foam latex swords. It’s live action role play: turbocharged Dungeons & Dragons meets medieval re-enactment.I’ve been Larping for seven years. It’s the biggest thing in my life outside of comedy, and the two scenes have a lot in common. Everyone’s broke. Everyone was bullied in high school. No one gets into Larp or standup if things are going well.The biggest commonality is the gatekeeping. A crusted old comic in the corner of a greenroom gasps: “You’re a fan of standup, are you? Name three of Carl Barron’s best jokes.” His Larp counterpart, a polyamorous he/they in a top hat with a cog on it, twirls a cane: “So you like Warhammer Fantasy Battle? Name three spells an elven cleric can use in combat.” I’d like to see those two sit down and collectively name three women who feel safe around them.Larping’s reality bleed: ‘I’m basically falling in love with a person that does not exist’Read moreSwordcraft Quest is one of the biggest events on Australia’s Larp calendar. Hundreds of players pitch tents in a rocky cattle paddock in Pomborneit, Victoria, to roleplay living in a medieval fantasy village for a week called Sudenburg. It’s fully in character and immersive, save for a few modern conveniences. Even the most fearsome warrior needs a Portaloo and a soy flat white.You can be a noble paladin, a sage elven scholar or a tricksy halfling bard. But if you’re a real freak, like myself, you’ll spend the week as a fiscally conservative tax agent. This year I was appointed Master of Coin, responsible for overseeing the town’s finances. My parents are retired microeconomists and I was conceived on budget night of 1994, so perhaps it was inevitable.View image in fullscreenScout Boxall, second from right, with fellow Larpers.Photograph: Trendy’s PhotographyMoney works weirdly in Larp. Twelve copper to a silver, 20 silver to a gold. A copper is worth between $3 and $6 in “shadow currency” (Australian dollars or Aud, pronounced “Ow-dh”). Four coppers is an hour of unskilled labour; two gets you a coffee. You can’t cash them back in at the end of the game, so many of my Larp friends end up rich in coppers but live below the poverty line in the real world.As an itinerant touring performer and freelance writer, a steady nine-to-five data-entry job handling huge amounts of cash was the ultimate fantasy. And I revelled in the brutal bureaucracy of it all. Each day I opened up the tax office, made players present their in-character documentation and declare their assets and then place a few of their precious copper coins into a box marked TAX OFFICE COFFERS – LOOTABLE ITEM.Throughout the week, players produced elaborate disguises, fraudulent documents and even held me up at (fake foam) knife-point in fruitless attempts to steal the town’s hoard. Each of these heists was prenegotiated out of character. The final night of the event, someone simply broke into the tent and took the coins for real, which has since sparked a genuine out-of-character investigation.Tongue lodged firmly in cheek, Larpers love to replicate real-world dilemmas with a dirtbag medieval slant. Dwarven miners extract obsidian from a poisonous seam with indentured goblin child labour. (Fracking.) The Town Council funnels tax funds to their allies. (Cronyism.) Senate meetings grind to a standstill over whether to let in refugees who might bring an undead horde. (Xenophobia.)Beyond Dungeons and Dragons: can role play save the world?Read moreSometimes Larp and real life collide and form something that is technically “make-believe” but resonates beyond role play. Last year, a terminally ill player called Silas* knew it would be their last event, so they held their own funeral. Wearing elf ears and tucked into a mechanised wheelchair beneath heavy blankets, Silas laughed as friends took turns to deliver eulogies. Afterwards, they married their long-term partner in the tavern with a real celebrant presiding. The ceremony was soundtracked by live bards and emceed by a hulking man called The Mad Mage. It was a strange day that straddled two worlds: our collectively imagined realm of Sudenburg, where death can be reversed through magic, and the bleak reality of Silas’ diagnosis.Larp is a special interest that can verge into obsession. I’ve sunk thousands of dollars and hundreds of hours into it. My house is full to bursting with wool, linen and silk, plate armour, chain mail and a longbow. I have more Larp shoes than regular shoes, and my wardrobe is evenly split between the 21st, 16th and 14th centuries.I’m not the only one with a Renaissance streak. Fantasy is having a massive cultural resurgence. We’ve gone from twee cottagecore to wenchcore, maidencore and castlecore. Chappell Roan wears chain mail armour and wields a sword on the red carpet.View image in fullscreenChappell Roan performs in chain mail armour at the 2024 MTV Video Music Awards in New York.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Billboard/Getty ImagesEvery second queer in Brunswick Anytime Fitness has a gothic blackletter tattoo. An old high school Facebook friend who manages a Dunkin’ Donuts posts about craving a “little hobbity life”. Gen Z have even co-opted the term “Larper” to mean poser or fraud. In a time of relentless AI slop, fast fashion and impending climate apocalypse, we turn to the past. Well, a reimagining of a reimagining of the past: an ahistorical slurry of Arthurian romance, pre-Raphaelite idealism and dreamy Y2K aesthetics.The Ren Faire has become an ironically cool place for twentysomethings to gnaw a turkey leg and prance around in Shein princess costumes. Larp remains the domain of the weirdo, the loser and the pedant. That’s what makes it so special. It’s given me a chosen family, a community and – most importantly – the chance to go back in time for a week every year and pretend to be a cashed-up bureaucrat. Wouldn’t trade it for all the copper in Sudenburg.*Names have been changedScout Boxall is a standup comedian. Their latest solo show, God’s Favourite enjoyed a sold-out run at the Edinburgh fringe festival in 2026 and won the Pinder prize at Melbourne international comedy festival in 2025Explore more on these topicsRole playing gamesOpinionHobbiesAustralian lifestylecommentShareReuse this content

title: 20 of the best women’s shoes and boots for autumn, from ballet flats to knee-highs | Women's shoes | The Guardian
description: Whether it’s sleek slip-ons or stompers that mean business, we’ve got the standout pairs for the changing season
Author: Melanie Wilkinson
Headline: Whether it’s sleek slip-ons or stompers that mean business, we’ve got the standout pairs for the changing season
Content: Well-healed: a seasonal step in the right direction.Photograph: Photo by Edward Berthelot/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWell-healed: a seasonal step in the right direction.Photograph: Photo by Edward Berthelot/Getty ImagesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterWomen's shoes20 of the best women’s shoes and boots for autumn, from ballet flats to knee-highsWhether it’s sleek slip-ons or stompers that mean business, we’ve got the standout pairs for the changing season52 women’s autumn wardrobe updatesMelanie WilkinsonThu 15 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’ve dug out your knitwear, made a list of cosy TV shows to watch and posted a shot of your first pumpkin spice latte. Autumn is officially here!Now it’s time to start thinking seriously about your footwear. October is nice because it’s usually warm enough to still have a bit of flesh on show, so you can get away with Mary Janes or ballet flats. But it’s also not too hot for boots if you want something with a little more stomp.
