title: My autumn of comfort TV and comfort food | Food | The Guardian
description: From batch-cooked dal and chicken barley to sticky toffee pudding, these are the cosy dishes that make October evenings at home feel special
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: From batch-cooked dal and chicken barley to sticky toffee pudding, these are the cosy dishes that make October evenings at home feel special
Content: Perfect for the sofa and more than simple sugar hit … Felicity Cloake’s perfect sticky toffee pudding.Photograph: Stephen Conroy/the food passionates/CorbisView image in fullscreenPerfect for the sofa and more than simple sugar hit … Felicity Cloake’s perfect sticky toffee pudding.Photograph: Stephen Conroy/the food passionates/CorbisFeastFoodMy autumn of comfort TV and comfort foodFrom batch-cooked dal and chicken barley to sticky toffee pudding, these are the cosy dishes that make October evenings at home feel specialSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastGeorgina HaydenThu 15 Oct 2026 07.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 07.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a summer spent travelling here, there and everywhere, I am welcoming more time at home and bingeable telly with open arms. And, like a lot of the nation, I am obsessed with this season’sCelebrity Traitors. It is my achilles heel; so much so that, earlier this year, I politely declined an invite to a hot industry party because it clashed with the final, and there is no amount of free champagne or hobnobbing that would’ve got me off my sofa. The beauty of such shows is that they are on early enough to make an evening of it.Strictlyhas become our Saturday night family ritual, while my eldest will usually join us for Tuesday nights watchingBake Off. There are bowls of food, eaten by the spoonful, mugs of tea and endless biscuits. It’s a small, cosy ritual that makes the passing of summer feel a little less bleak.For ease, I try to live by the rule of one meal for everyone. On nights when we eat on the sofa, I like to make something in advance that the girls can eat after school and that we can return to later on. Nigella Lawson’schicken barley, for instance, is a firm favourite and, importantly, if a little less glamorously, it reheats well. The same goes for Laura Goodman’smac’n’cheese, a surefire hit and a fixture in our house.View image in fullscreenIt’s all about batch cooking … Nadiya Hussain’s carrot and cod curry.Photograph: Dan Matthews/The GuardianEssentially it’s all aboutbatch cooking, comfort and being prepared. I also love to make big pots ofcongeeanddal, which I freeze in portions for a rainy day. Both are perfect for feeding a range of appetites, too, with toppings and accompaniments added to suit. Ravinder Bhogal’s seasonalpumpkin and misovariation is firmly on my to-make list, as ispe hin, a Burmese dal recipe from Amy and Emily Chung.Sofa food isn’t all savoury, of course. If you’ve ever watched Bake Off, you’ll know that doing so without a sweet treat to hand is a form of torture. A mug of tea and a plate of biscuits will usually do that trick, particularly if those biscuits are homemade. Current favourites in our house are Ana Ortiz’salfajores de dulce de lecheand Rebecca Bishop’sbrown butter nutmeg shortbread. If something more substantial is required – because, let’s be honest, sometimes only a warming bowl of pudding will do – my first port of call is Felicity Cloake’ssticky toffee pudding(pictured top) with herproper custardon the side, naturally. And, being autumn, I’m also a sucker for Nigel Slater’sapple and blackberry crumble, ideally with more of that custard, too. Nothing says, “hello, autumn”, like a hedgerow-inspired crumble after all.My week in (sweet) foodView image in fullscreenPerfect to slice and share … Doreen’s rum cake.Photograph: doreensrumcakes.comA slice of Jamaica| I was recently lucky enough to be on the receiving end of one ofDoreen’s homemade Jamaican rum cakes, and I cannot stop thinking about it. I’m looking for any opportunity I can to send one as a gift. You can select a variety of shapes and sizes, but I do think the heart one is particularly endearing, as well as a gorgeous sentiment. Set up by Jackie Christian, the recipe was passed down to her from her Jamaican-born mum, Doreen. It’s a beautiful story and a stunning gift, and I’m already planning on buying myself another.Malt loaf magic| Friend and fellow food writerNicola Millerrecently introduced me toWooster’s Bakery, a 30-plus-year-old family business that takes bread and baking seriously. Based in Suffolk, it’s not somewhere I can frequent regularly, but luckily for those of us who aren’t local, you can order their incredible malt loaf online.Mail-a-maltis divine: a delicious, sticky, plump and rich loaf that comes in a glorious circular box.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSweet innovation| Hello, my name is Georgina Hayden and I am a full-blown chocoholic. And, fortunately for me, one of my favourite pastry chefs,Philip Khoury, has created an online shop where his chocolate creations can be enjoyed by everyone. They are all outstanding, but his latest ingenious creation may be my favourite to date: namely,fig chocolate. Made in the style of white chocolate, it’s packed with fresh figs, fig leaves and a little almond. Elegant yet playful, it feels like a more grown-up chocolate orange. Just don’t wait until Christmas.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastAutumn food and drinkVegetablesBiscuitsDessertFruitRicenewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for spaghetti with Marmite | Food | The Guardian
description: An umami-packed dish for when you need a flavour hit in a hurry
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: An umami-packed dish for when you need a flavour hit in a hurry
Content: ‘Exquisite’, maybe. Simple? You bet! – Rachel Roddy's Marmite spaghetti.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Exquisite’, maybe. Simple? You bet! – Rachel Roddy's Marmite spaghetti.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianA kitchen in RomeFoodRachel Roddy’s recipe for spaghetti with MarmiteAn umami-packed dish for when you need a flavour hit in a hurryRachel RoddyThu 15 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a simple, practical recipe that I trust will be useful to many who don’t have the time for lengthy kitchen preparations. Boil the spaghetti as usual, drain it, and toss it with a little butter and parmesan. Then, for four, take a spoonful of meat extract and dissolve it in a small saucepan with just a few drops of boiling water. Pour the meat extract over the pasta, stir and serve. You will be pleasantly surprised by the exquisite flavour the pasta acquires – achieved with such a negligible investment of time.This is a roughly word-for-word translation of an Italian recipe forspaghetti con l’estratto di carne(spaghetti with meat extract). It is another dish from Ada Boni’sIl Talismano della Felicità(The Talisman of Happiness), which waspublished in English for the first timelast month and, according to the food writer and editorAngela Frenda, is “still considered one of the most precise and accurate of all cookbooks”.I was alerted to spaghetti con l’estratto di carne by the food historian and author ofA Brief History of Pasta, Luca Cesari. I recently met Luca for dinner atSt John in Londonand, over bone marrow on toast, kidneys on toast, welsh rarebit and fried tripe, we talked about many things, including recipe outrage. Spaghetti withMarmitecame up as an example, and Luca pointed out that, in terms of approach, taste and spirit, it was more or less identical to Ada’s iconic and “exquisite” recipe.He also noted that using a spoonful of meat extract as a pasta sauce is in the spirit – and a short-cut version – ofpasta al sugo d’arrosto(pasta with sauce of the roast). That is, the pan juices, and those fat and tasty, crusty bits left at the bottom of the tin when you’ve roasted a joint of meat, are lengthened with a bit of water or wine, maybe more rosemary (or whatever you fancy) added, before being used as a pasta sauce. Pasta with gravy, if you like. (When I makebraised chicken with rosemary, garlic and wine, I particularly like the last of the congealed pan juices as a pasta sauce.)It was the great Anna del Conte, who was born in Milan in 1925 and moved to London in 1949, who first wrote about spaghetti with butter, cheese and Marmite, noting in her autobiographyRisotto and Nettlesthat this was a dish she herself made (and that was loved by her children). I wonder if Anna knew Ada’s version? She certainly mentionspasta al sugo d’arrostoin her writing. And Anna inspired Nigella Lawson to makeher own version of spaghetti with Marmite, which is the recipe I followed, although it is hardly a recipe.Marmite is, of course, a dark, sticky, salty-savoury spread made from concentrated yeast extract. What yeast extract and meat extract have in common is glutamic acid or free glutamates, an amino acid that provides a savoury, lip-smacking umami flavour. Tomatoes, mushrooms and cheese are high in free glutamates, too, so in the Ada-Anna-Nigella recipes all provide a double dose of umami by adding parmesan; butter is vital for adding fat, flavour and slippiness to the final dish. I hope you will be pleasantly surprised by the exquisite flavour this pasta acquires, and all achieved with such a negligible investment of time.Spaghetti with Marmite, Bovril or VegemiteServes4400-500g spaghettiSalt1-2 tspMarmite, or Bovril or Vegemite60gunsalted butter, cubed2-4 tspgrated parmesan, or grana padanoBoil the spaghetti in plenty of lightly salted water, because both the Marmite and the cheese are already salty.Meanwhile, in a very small saucepan on a low heat, warm two tablespoons of water with the Marmite until it has dissolved.Once the pasta is cooked but al dente, lift it into a warm bowl (reserve some of the pasta cooking water), then add the cubed butter and cheese, and toss well. Pour the dissolved Marmite over the spaghetti and stir again, adding a little of the reserved cooking water, if you think it needs it, until the sauce is soft and slippery. Serve immediately.Explore more on these topicsFoodA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkPastaStarterMain courserecipesShareReuse this content

title: Sedimentary rocks: why pét nat and cloudy wines are on the rise | Wine | The Guardian
description: There’s something refreshing about unfiltered or unfined wines. We filter through a selection …
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: There’s something refreshing about unfiltered or unfined wines. We filter through a selection …
Content: Cloudy with a chance of reigning: pét nats all in a row.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenCloudy with a chance of reigning: pét nats all in a row.Photograph: PRWineSedimentary rocks: why pét nat and cloudy wines are on the riseThere’s something refreshing about unfiltered or unfined wines. We filter through a selection …Mina HollandThu 15 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCenturies ago, Geoffrey Chaucer observed that “ther is no newe gyse that it nas old”. This truth – that there is nothing new under the sun – certainly applies to wine: every year, a well-documented or ancient viticultural practice is repackaged for a mainstream that greets it giddily as an innovation. Orange wine! Wine in kegs! Chilled reds! And, in 2026, cloudy wine, courtesy of Marks & Spencer’s peachy-opaque organic rosé, Trouble (a name that means “cloudy” in French.Trouble is the first cloudy still wine available in a British supermarket, a development that has seemed inevitable sincepét nat–pétillant naturel –hit the big time; it’s an ancestral method of making sparkling wine that involves bottling before fermentation has finished. Typically, pét nats are not disgorged (that is, the dead yeast cells left over from fermentation are not removed), which is what gives them a cloudy appearance. They are also often fresh and tangy, so they suit warm weather, but it’s hard to imagine a better pairing for a pizza takeaway on an autumn evening, and without prosecco’s divisive sherbety notes, to boot. (That said, look out for rustic, cloudycol fondo– bottle fermented, undisgorged prosecco – a hazy, lively and bracing take on the nation’s most popular fizz.) M&S, ever quick on the uptake, hasan own-label English rosé pét nat(currently out of stock), while Tesco sells a pét nat chardonnay from Argentina.The term “clarification” in viticulture refers to several processes that make conventional wines so crystalline – namely fining (where an agent is added to bind haze-forming particles or compounds such as proteins and tannins, causing them to clump and settle) and filtration, which physically removes suspended particles from the wine. There are ways of clarifying that involve neither fining nor filtering, such as racking or settling (as I suspect is the case with Trouble, which hasn’t a speck of sediment). So, cloudy wine can be filtered and an unfiltered wine can be clear. Waitrose has no “cloudy” wines on its shelves, but it does have several unfiltered ones, including surprisingly big players such asCatena malbec.So why choose a cloudy or unfiltered wine? “There’s texture, there’s fleshiness, there’s rounded fruit,” says Zainab Majerikova, head of wine for the Ottolenghi group, where the three house wines are unfiltered and cloudy natural numbers. “We think this makes them more moreish and a better fit for food with big, complex flavours,” says Majerikova.I always get the sense that longer contact with lees (those dead yeast cells) makes cloudy wine more food-like; it might be a drink, but there’s a crunchiness to it. For the full effect of its flavours and weight on the palate, Majerikova recommends shaking a bottle of cloudy wine before opening to mix the sediment with the liquid. Either way, she says, cloudiness “brings soul, vibrancy and complexity” to wines for old-fashioned fun.Four cloudy wines to lift the spiritsTrouble Cloudy Organic Rosé£12 Ocado, 12.5%. A slightly savoury, very drinkable take on a southern French rosé – bring on an Indian summer.Alma 4 Phos Pét Nat£12 Tesco, 12.5%. Food-versatile pét nat Argentinian chardonnay from the Uco Valley, lightly sparkling and textural.Alella “La Rumbera” 2022£32 Dynamic Wines, 11%. A serious unfined and unfiltered skin-contact wine from a legend of Catalonian winemaking.Ottolenghi Red Wine£26, 10%. This subtly cloudy pinot blend is Ottolenghi’s house red, and might well become mine: a wine you can almost crunch.Explore more on these topicsWineFoodBritish food and drinkFrench food and drinkSpanish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gen Z wrestle with shame from ordering delivery food: ‘This economy is not for the weak’ | Food | The Guardian
description: As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience
Author: Alaina Demopoulos
Headline: As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience
Content: ‘I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door … Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself,’ said Caroline Bauldree, 24.Photograph: Anastasiia Voloshko/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door … Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself,’ said Caroline Bauldree, 24.Photograph: Anastasiia Voloshko/Getty ImagesFoodGen Z wrestle with shame from ordering delivery food: ‘This economy is not for the weak’As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenienceTell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?Alaina DemopoulosThu 15 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 16.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen it comes to food, Caroline Bauldree does not like to “deprive” herself of anything. She does not like to cook either, so that means a lot of food deliveries. “If I want sushi, I’m getting sushi,” said the 24-year-old nanny, who lives in Raleigh, North Carolina. “I’m definitely lazy in that regard.”Bauldree got into the habit of near-daily DoorDashing back in college. “I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door – that’s the dream,” she said. “But then I just feel like crap about myself because I’m like, ‘wow, I’m a lazy piece of shit.’ Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself.”There is a term for that post-order clarity: delivery guilt. The pandemic turned food delivery apps such as DoorDash, Uber Eats and Grubhub, once only popular in major cities, into a full-fledged national lifestyle. One Purduestudyfound that two-thirds of consumers used a food-ordering app at least once in 2024; another recentsurveyfrom the marketing company FinanceBuzz in partnership with Bank of America found that 57% of Americans get takeout or delivery weekly or more. Gen Z is more likely to feed the habit, clocking in an average of five orders a month – roughly double the monthly orders made by Boomers.double quotation markIt doesn’t feel great to admit that we’re paying this extra money and contributing to these companies’ profitsJoy LuConsidering the price of food and those ever-pesky delivery fees, it’s an expensive habit; Bauldree estimates spending about $75 a week. And users might not feel comfortable broadcasting it to the world. According to the Finance Buzz survey, half of its gen Z respondents said they felt embarrassed about how much they spend on food delivery, sometimes so much that they lie about the amount to friends and family.Joy Lu is an assistant professor of marketing at Carnegie Mellon University who studies delivery app pricing. She calls food delivery an “affordable luxury”: a way for people to treat themselves without majorly splurging. But the fees on delivery apps can add up, resulting in sticker shock at checkout. Lu says people might be afraid to reveal their true delivery tab because they do not want to be perceived as wasting money.“People might be hesitant to talk about this because we have a sense that these food delivery apps are taking a cut and it’s not all going to the delivery person,” Lu said. “It doesn’t feel great to admit that we’re paying this extra money and contributing to these companies’ profits.”View image in fullscreenA DoorDash worker rides his bicycle along a path on the West Side Highway in New York.Photograph: John Minchillo/APThe Federal Trade Commission, which hassparredwith delivery apps in the past, is reportedly considering new rules that would address undisclosed fees resulting from dynamic and surge pricing,reportsthe industry publication Restaurant Business. Representatives for Grubhub and DoorDash told the Guardian that users are shown an itemized price, which includes all fees, before they place an order. “Customers can adjust their order at any time to stay within their budget,” the Grubhub rep said in an email. The DoorDash spokesperson wrote: “There are no hidden costs on our platform.”Last month, New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, announced a$131.5m fineagainst DoorDash for “systemic violations of New York City’s Delivery Worker Laws”, including lack of, late, or insufficient payment, and violations of the state’s mandatory minimum wage. It was the largest worker settlement in New York history, with $115m of the funds going to DoorDashers. In astatement, DoorDash said “our mistakes meant some DoorDashers were underpaid or paid late”, adding the errors were “unintentional”.As the cost of groceries continues to rise – this year, the USDApredictsthe cost of “food-at-home” (AKA groceries) will rise 2.4% – some shoppers say it’s becoming just as expensive to cook for themselves as it is to order out. That’s a tough claim to substantiate, as itdependson certain factors. For example, single people may be able to save money eating out compared with families, and people who live in grocery store deserts have to pay more for each trip once they factor in the price of gas.Lu believes people might not even realize how much they are spending on delivery, or consciously avoid looking into the cost. “You don’t really want to look into your app and see the total cost you spent,” she said. “It’s very easy to spend a bit at a time.”‘They’re playing dirty’: inside delivery apps’ pushback against tips after New York raises wageRead moreSome people are happy to reveal their reliance on food delivery. One New York-based influencer named Audrey Peters became TikTok’s villain of the week earlier this year when she revealed she DoorDashes almost every single meal.Petersdescribeda day where she spent $136.50 on a chicken salad, pizza, meatballs, hummus and ice-cream, among other indulgences. One order that particularly irked followers was her $19.44 Starbucks pumpkin spice latte, which she says was so expensive due to her tipping 20%. “I feel really guilty about what I spent today,” she said on the app. The content creator latertoldNew York magazine that she revealed this spending to “rage bait” an audience primed to judge her laziness.Ten years ago, millennials were told their weekly avocado toast or daily latte was the reason they would never be able to buy a house – never mind the fact that they came of age during a global financial crisis. Today, naysayers claim it’s food delivery that’s keeping gen Z from achieving their life goals. For example, a February Fox News segmentfoundanchor Sandra Smith telling viewers they could not complain about the cost of living while excessively DoorDashing too. Such finger-wagging could be the source of delivery shame.But, as economist Mike Konczalarguedon his Substack in February, it is also misguided: 2024 data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows that more of Americans’ food budgets are going to groceries than eating out and delivery. “Society as a whole is reallocating food spending toward cooking at home, not away from it,” Konczal wrote.Bauldree is trying to cut back on her delivery habit, mostly due to other rising costs such as rent and car insurance. “This economy is not for the weak,” she said. Lu, the college professor, does not put food-ordering apps on her phone – she doesn’t want the temptation. As she put it, “I know they’re dangerous.”Explore more on these topicsFoodGig economyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 18 again: I returned to my life in 1990. Who – and what – would I find there? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: I doused myself in Poison perfume and made the trip back to my childhood home, friends and college. What could I learn by re-immersing myself in a world that brimmed with hope and potential?
Author: Paula Cocozza
Headline: I doused myself in Poison perfume and made the trip back to my childhood home, friends and college. What could I learn by re-immersing myself in a world that brimmed with hope and potential?
Content: Paula Cocozza on the beach in Worthing, the town where she grew upPhotograph: Peter Flude/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPaula Cocozza on the beach in Worthing, the town where she grew upPhotograph: Peter Flude/The GuardianThe year I turned 18Life and style18 again: I returned to my life in 1990. Who – and what – would I find there?I doused myself in Poison perfume and made the trip back to my childhood home, friends and college. What could I learn by re-immersing myself in a world that brimmed with hope and potential?Paula CocozzaThu 15 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe house in which I turned 18 was full of clocks. Dark wooden things with aged faces. Every room ticked. If you stood in certain doorways, you could hear all the misaligned second hands racing. I could not understand why anyone would want to count away life like that or decorate their living quarters with so many symbols of mortality.There was no escaping time. Shortly before each hour, a mechanical whir heralded the first chime. We lived in a retirement town with an elderly and conservative population, which amplified the ticking. Worthing, on the south coast of England, was known as “God’s waiting room”. Death was there in our wide, slow roads and low bungalows, the grey sea mists and blue rinses.But I was young, and I scorned the clocks. Time was no master of mine. I answered only to love. And poetry. And fashion. And boys I liked.At least, I think I’ve got that right. But how well does any of us remember being 18? For 17 years, we set our sights on that beacon of independence, the coruscating wonder of adulthood and all the freedom we imagine it entails. But within a few years, the day slips from view.How did you celebrate? What did you wish for? Who did you hope to be? And if, like me, you’ve lost all memory of your 18th and need an HRT patch, creatine powder and phone alarms to recall anything, can you get it back? Over the past month, I have tried to return to April 1990 – when I became an adult – to turn back the clocks and rediscover what life was like then. And what I was like.Sadly, no one has invented the machine for this yet. But no worries. I have other tools: vintage Poison eau de cologne, a clutch of letters I wrote and never posted, photographs, books, college reports, my teenage poems, Facebook, a bottle of Southern Comfort and a bag of granny smith apples.With these, I hope to send myself back in time, to visit my old best friend, and the guy I loved, and to experience life, however fleetingly, as my 18-year-old self experienced it. I hope to see again how the world looked to my peers and me as we hatched into adulthood – right there at the dawn of the 90s, a decade coveted by natives of every decade since, but from which I longed to teleport to the 60s.The cap’s off the purple flask, wrists doused with Christian Dior’s Poison. I’m on my way. “Most sensory inputs go first to an area of the brain called the thalamus,” says Catherine Loveday, a podcast host and professor specialising in memory. “Smell goes directly to the memory centres.” I’ve been catapulted into my 18-year-old body. It’s a blitz. A spritz of pure joy and promise. I keep sniffing my own wrist: I can’t get enough of me. I smell dramatic. Strong. Sweet. Potent. Ready.Something is going to happen.Drenched in plum and spicy tuberose, I drive the 60 miles from my home in London to Worthing. At the general election in 2024, Worthing West got its first ever Labour MP, partly due to a spillover from edgier Brighton. Although the average age of the town’s population has risen by a few years since I turned 18 – 44 at the last census– it feels much younger.There are other changes. The phone box at the end of our road, where I made my private calls, has gone. I have a phone in my pocket, of course, which in the spirit of 1990 I’m trying to pretend doesn’t exist.I’m unable to access emails.For anything urgent, please write me a letter …View image in fullscreen‘Seeing the sameness and the differences simultaneously is like wearing bifocals’ …Paula outside her childhood home.Photograph: Peter Flude/The GuardianOur old house is painted yellow still, and the wooden gates my dad, a builder, made remain – though they’ve gone grey, and the house hasn’t been ours for 22 years. Seeing the sameness and the differences simultaneously is like wearing bifocals. I’m both here, and back there.As I set off to my former college, I’m amazed to find that my feet know exactly where to cross each road. I walked this route daily, no phone or headphones, and took in whatever the path put before me. The slope of a church roof; ivy lacing through the chain-link fence; litter snared in weeds. Each apparently insignificant sighting thrills me with a very specific sense, unfamiliar to my 54-year-old self, that I amin the right place.Thoughts fly up out of the paving cracks: the 1960s minidress pattern I found in a charity shop; phrases from the Italian library tapes I got on permanent renewal;“Moon Lady” and “Balloons”, the titles of the poems I was working on; the dream Saturday job I’d landed at Volume One bookshop in town; my next order from City Lights Bookstore in San Francisco, where I solemnly sent dollar notes, then waited six weeks for excitingly slim volumes of poetry to land on the mat, into whose pages I would tuck slips of paper bearing precious observations: “Vowel length.”I probably thought about my homework essays. “Why did race relations become an issue in British politics after 1945?”,and “Is the change in Mr Darcy credible, or do we believe it because we want to?”I certainly wanted to believe it. I thought about “the one” incessantly. In 1990, the median age for a first marriage in the UK was 24 for women. When we turned 18, we all heard the clocks ticking.And there was another, adjacent, race against time. The world divided into haves and have-nots, and I had not. If the internet had been built, it would have told me that most women in England lost their virginity at 18. It was a core belief of mine that this state of being must be addressed before my 19th birthday, and that failure to do so would mean there was something seriously wrong with me.There was no reprieve from self-consciousness about this. When my secondhand jeans tore at the ass, channelling my love of William Blake and the Beat poets, I patched them with a rose from some curtain fabric, and one day, as I was climbing the stairs at college, the boy behind me asked, “Is that your flower?” The shame.So many things have gone since then. The Lloyds bank tower I passed each day has been turned into apartments. Its huge digital clock was removed a decade ago, after it got stuck on 00:00. My college is a housing estate, the bakery a patisserie. The newsagent has stopped being anything at all. Only the butcher has retained its beguiling awning:National Award-Winning Sausages.I used to buy a Crunchie from that newsagent – the honeycomb was less fattening, and I sold enough copies of Rosemary Conley’s Hip and Thigh Diet on Saturdays to know the dangers – and a packet of salt and vinegar Discos. Thanks to the fetishisation of 1990s snacks, you can find them in Tesco; I’ve brought a pack with me.View image in fullscreen‘I walked this route daily’ … Paula retraces her old commute to sixth form.Photograph: Peter Flude/The GuardianThe salt is saltier and the vinegar more vinegary than any other crisp or chip I know. It could burn the bumps off your tongue. Good, because a postdoc research fellow at the University of North Dakota, Utkarsh Gupta, has shown that multi-sensory integration can help people who wish to undertake “mental time travel”. Last year he published research showing that “people who were embodying a younger version of themselves” – by seeing themselves virtually embodied with their childlike face – “had better childhood memory”. The Discos are doing the same for me.As I walk, I look around for friends. I keep an eye out for anyone interesting crossing the central reservation. Round the roundabout the cars come and go. Unlike them, I am heading somewhere.At high school, when I took on science subjects I wasn’t very good at, my grades sprawled from As to Ds. Our family had a tradition of work over further education, and at 16 my dad suggested I look for an accountancy apprenticeship. By then, I’d held 10 part-time jobs, in shops, a cafe, guest house, a supermarket and offices. Every week, the local paper had eight pages of situations vacant and I’d switch jobs for 10p more an hour. I rarely heard the word “university” – nobody had graduated in my family.But I loved books. In our house, shelves dense with clocks and ornaments, reading felt transgressive. Sometimes I’d bring a book to the dinner table, and be told to put it away. (“No phones at the table!” parent-me echoes.) As rebellions go, enrolling at college sounds pretty tame, but it was the first meaningful choice I made for myself, and it remains, to this day, my best. A door opened right then to a different life.Education made me feel special. In the staffroom, words like “delivery” and “impact” were creeping into the lexicon, but we students remained blissfully ignorant. “Impact – so much more violent thaneffect,” Mr Fraser, my old English teacher, muses now.Of course, we were all debilitatingly self-conscious – but not collectively so. We hadn’t yet been named generation X. Douglas Coupland’s book was still a year away. And I don’t recall hearing the word “anxiety”.We had a future.The world wasn’t ending anytime soon. Michael Jackson had his oxygen chamber and was going to live for ever. Maybe we would too. There was no climate crisis. As an advert in the local paper promised,1990 is going to be another scorching summer. At least for the lucky ones in a Mazda open top.I didn’t drive; I rode a bike, oiled myself with Hawaiian Tropic and bragged to a friend that it was “boiling” at 24C. Sure, there was a hole in the ozone layer, but it was small and far away. The girl I sat beside in government and political studies wore a CND badge, doodled mushroom clouds and taunted meat-eaters with mad cow disease, but we thought her a pessimist.View image in fullscreenRosemary Conley’s Hip & Thigh Workout VHS tape.Photograph: Brendan Bell/AlamyInitially, I took it easy at college. “Perhaps a more consistent effort across the board would enable her to raise her standard,” my report observed. But somewhere between 17 and 18, I grew serious. I spent lunch breaks in the library. The reports changed their tune. “Paula always gives of her best.” One morning, my form tutor told me: “Carry on like this and you’ll be applying to Oxbridge.”I knew about Oxford and Cambridge from the boat race, which was televised annually on BBC’s Grandstand. But I’d never heard of Oxbridge. I asked my tutor where it was. “Well, it’s a word for both of them,” he said irritably.Later, I studied matching towel bales, teasmades and filter coffee jugs in the Argos catalogue in preparation for my next life phase.The month I turned 18 was momentous in England. In the evenings leading to my birthday, I curled up in my corner spot on our brown Dralon sofa – it just about went with the orange carpet my dad brought home from an American Express refurb – to watch the BBC Nine O’Clock News. Inmates of Strangeways prison in Manchester paced their roofs. Riots spread to other prisons. There were riots against the poll tax and the egregiousness of a system that asked people living in council housing to pay the same as millionaires. Billionaires weren’t on anyone’s radar; there were fewer than 100 in the UK and US.View image in fullscreenPrisoners on the roof of Strangeways during the riots of April 1990.Photograph: John Giles/PAIn six months, Margaret Thatcher would be ousted. The week of my birthday, a poll reported her to be the least popular prime minister in half a century. And alongside the ads for lost cats, funeral directors, private vasectomies, Dial-a-Tan and cars with one careful lady owner, the “Coming of Age” section of the Worthing Herald announced, “COCOZZA – Congratulations, dear Paula. Good luck, health and happiness in the future. Much love Dad, Mum, Rob, Joe and Nan.”The Labour party was a joke in my house growing up – how we laughed when Neil Kinnock fell in the sea in nearby Brighton. My political awakening comprised a moderate shift to the left. My radicalism was confined to my reading – the Beats, Jean Genet, Arthur Rimbaud. There were drugs in those books but I went no further than an occasional smoke with friends on the forecourt of a beach hut.Members of my extended family had undergone shock treatment. Graylingwell psychiatric hospital loomed at the corner of my mind’s eye. Now, I wonder if the Beats appealed because they made mental illness seem heroic; swapped the stigma for a beatific glow. Maybe my folks weren’t crazy, but the best minds of their generation.I never made the connection. I was about to unwrap a rose-gold bracelet, a hardback copy of Federico García Lorca’s Poet in New York, and a Smith Corona electronic typewriter, on which I hoped to write better poems. (Exiling myself./I held the door;/Shut/On those sharp,/Intransigent, wood-chipped faces,/Quilted cuddles/Of oven glove and potpourri wraps.)The week after my birthday, I awoke in the middle of the night and fumbled for a pencil. Without switching on the light, I wrote a verse:“This World is Full of Words”Mmm hmmmand went back to sleep.View image in fullscreenPictures of Paula aged 18.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianThen, as now, I believed that the best answer to riots, the possibility of nuclear war, political upheaval, ticking clocks and pretty much anything else was love and books.I was so busy revising for my A-levels that when C, the boy I liked, phoned to invite me to play tennis, I told him I was busy.If I stepped back to consider the vastness of the continents, the world’s 5.3 billion population, and the needle-in-a-haystack odds of finding a soulmate, I felt incredibly lucky to have walked into the extracurricular English poetry class and seen him, floppy-fringed, bespectacled, watching Don’t Look Back,DA Pennebaker’s 1967 documentary aboutBob Dylanon the classroom television, which I too had recorded from TV on a VHS.He was a year older than me and already had a place at Cambridge. He gave me feedback on my practice essays. “It’s really not as important as you think,” he scribbled in red pen on a torn bit of A4. “It’s not as important as Chaplin, as Dylan, Kerouac, Ginsberg, Beatles, football, love, life, sex and death. It’s worthless in the face of these.”To me, he was sophisticated. His family wasn’t in the phone book. They had two sofas. His mother once told my mother, highly amused, that I’d asked her what broccoli was.C could quote from anything, including Casanova. Sometimes he brought his guitar to my house and sang, and I felt an immense release, and joy, listening, too shy to sing along. We sat for hours on opposite ends of my pink duvet, in my immaculate room that my mother tidied daily, with my pink carpet and matching velveteen wastebin Mum had made from a washed-out catering tin, and we talked and talked – though neither of us remembers what about – and we both smiled when the brooch holding my crossover sweater accidentally unpinned itself, but for now, nothing happened.“Men and women can’t be just friends because the sex part always gets in the way,” Harry told Sally; how I hoped he was right.“Yes, but do you love him? Or is it an obsession?” my best friend, D, in her infinite wisdom, asked. She liked psychology and could parse the meaning of things said and unsaid. I thought it was love. But I didn’t see the big difference.Obsession, as we all knew from Calvin Klein, was a very sexy, intense and stylish state of mind. It meant you couldn’t stop thinking about the other person, which sounded about right, and in some regards was more special than love.There are many loves, but only one obsession.View image in fullscreen‘I would have settled for Paolo Maldini’ … the footballer in a match between Italy and England in 1990.Photograph: SvenSimonSpo/United Archives/Getty ImagesI carried out endless feasibility debates with myself about my romantic path. I wanted what Lizzy Bennet and Mr Darcy had, Cindy Crawford and Richard Gere, or Fay Roadnight and Colin Benzie, the newlywed couple featured in the Worthing Herald the week of my 18th.Every Friday, when the paper came out, I’d sit at the pine kitchen table Dad had made, eating the salted peanuts my nan brought on her weekly visit, savouring the wedding announcements. Given away by her father, the bride wore a taffeta, Bo-peep-style dress and carried a bouquet of roses andgypsophila.I was by now an A-grade student, but I had no intellectual or ethical problem with spending hours immersed in the practicalities of my fantasies.Tom Cruise was officially The Sexiest Man Alive, but he wasn’t my type. Ideally, I wanted to go out with Bob Dylan as he was in 1967. I would have settled for LA Law’s Victor Sifuentes or Paolo Maldini, the young AC Milan defender. But mostly it seemed a travesty to my 18-year-old self that I was born 31 years after Dylan, an age gap that rendered him a romantic outlier. Maldini was more attainable, being four years my senior and on the same continent, and weren’t we soon all going to be in the Exchange Rate Mechanism? Mind you, he had his World Cup debut at Italia 90 to focus on.It is one of the puzzles of the age that all yearning seemed faintly plausible. Nothing was completely ruled out. I don’t know if this was naivety or arrogance or both. I bought Dylan’s Under the Red Sky when it came out in September, but the guy on the sleeve looked ancient. He was 49, an age I now know to be young.View image in fullscreen‘The guy on the sleeve looked ancient … he was 49.’Photograph: Shiiko Alexander/Alamy“Do you believe in women’s rights?” C asked one day.“I believe in human rights,” I told him. I wanted the same as the next person, but I wasn’t going to throw my love life under the bus for feminism; we still hadn’t kissed.“What did we talk about?” I ask him now. We’ve met up for lunch, as we do every few years. It’s a bit of a blur, he says. I shouldn’t take it personally. He has whole marriages he doesn’t remember. “We would have talked about books, played records …”He says memory has an evolutionary function. We remember what we need to survive. Of our time together at 18, there are only “pretty vague memories, because they’re essentially quite positive. They didn’t really serve,” he says.My laptop is open at a document of notes: scraps of dialogue, an exchange of looks, our first kiss, all as sharp and infinitely replayable as mental gifs. I wonder what this says about our relative threat to each other’s survival.Were we happy? Content? “You know, this notion of happiness,” C says. “You only know it in retrospect. The point when you’re happy, you don’t go: ‘I’m happy.’” Besides, he says, “I’ve never had a very good barometer on my actual feelings. There actually, genuinely, was the friendship level to us. Completely. We liked similar things, and not many people did. You were very observant. Somehow subtly you were always paying attention. You were always watching stuff. And you were very strong-willed underneath it all. You were introverted, a little shy, thoughtful, and you were always interesting to talk to. Even if I talked more than you. That’s my take.”On Monday morning, my alarm clock wakes me with a Saturday night feeling. I am going to see my friend D, and it doesn’t matter what the calendar says. D means Saturday nights. We used to get ready in her bedroom; kneeling on the carpet in front of her mirror, swigging from a 1.5l bottle of Liebfraumilch.Before I can recall any of the above, some ancient muscle memory has put me in matching underwear and knelt me on my bedroom floor, wondering why the mirror is so dusty and all my eyeshadows have crusted over. I haven’t seen D in 30 years. I no longer wear makeup. Or get ready. This might be because I’m always ready, or never ready.Who cares about makeup? You’ll only have to take it off tonight. Do you even own makeup remover? …I’m waiting for my middle-aged self to intercept, but she’s busy rummaging in the jewellery box, joy in her heart and a song on her lips. She snaps a gold bangle around her wrist – my 18th birthday gift – and bounds out the front door as if something very exciting is about to happen.And it is.I am going to hang out with the friend I hung out with at 18. The friend I went on Saturday-night pub crawls with. The friend who went to the bar because she looked 18 before she was 18, while I didn’t look 18 even when I was. For my milestone birthday, she laid the table in her family lounge with a red paper cloth, lit a candle and cooked me dinner. I loved her. But we haven’t met in 32 years.View image in fullscreenPaula at a birthday dinner for her 18th, cooked by her friend D.Photograph: Courtesy of Paula CocozzaD drank snakebite and black from pint glasses; I sipped Southern Comfort mixed with lemonade. Sometimes she was very sophisticated and asked for Perrier, a drink I was not confident of pronouncing. Over the course of an evening, we’d have five or six, but somehow only paid for one or two. I was the one who occasionally had to be pushed home along the promenade in a shopping trolley.Now here we are, sitting across the table at a lounge bar at midday, scanning QR codes for menus and wondering what it means that we both want the same salad and fizzy rhubarb drink.She remembers me as coy. We talked about our loves, our mothers, fathers, brothers, jobs, the Black Lace book series, Ann Summers parties. We vented, made each other laugh, barely thought about the future.“I do believe I LOVE people and have faith in human nature,” I wrote in a letter to her that year.And: “Sometimes it can do us good to put up with things we don’t like. It brings other elements in our personality out and makes us feel proud of our powers of endurance.”Sometimes I mailed letters to D even when we were both at home, a mile apart. “Would you like to go out early this wk? Will phone …”The day after D and I meet, my daughter turns 18. I ask her out for a drink. I want to taste Southern Comfort again, see if it will catapult me back, like the Poison, the sight of my teeth marks in the waxy green skin of a granny smith, or the detonating surprise of warm ketchup on a cold piece of iceberg lettuce, when I honour my 18-year-old self with a plate of Birds Eye chicken and chips.But our local pubs don’t stock Southern Comfort.“Is it a sipping whisky?” my daughter asks, and I laugh at her use of a phrase I have never needed, even at my age. We both get Cokes.So, did turning 18 feel like a big deal?“I didn’t give a fuck,” she says. “Everyone else seemed to, though.”When I was two months older than her, my A-levels done, I got a job in a secondhand bookshop. Few customers came in; most wanted to sell us John Braine’s Room at the Top. One day, a customer asked if we had any Kerouac. Did he know he was in Worthing? I lent him mine, he lent me his Neil Young tapes. He became a regular, rolling cigarettes into a little tin by the three-bar electric fire while we chatted.R had left school at 16, and was considering night school, something he clearly accomplished because he’s now a university professor. “There was a sense that it was a good time to be young,” he says. “Or that youth was something valuable. We were quite disillusioned – at 18 there’s always an existential stress – but it didn’t feel like a burden. If you think about our kids, and students now, the pressure … They can’t escape. They’re scrutinised all the time.”“You helped me realise that reading could be a momentous act, rather than just a way of filling time,” R says. “And that writing meant something.”A few months after we met, I found residential work at a hotel bar in the Italian alps, and R became another person I wrote letters to. In the mornings before my shift started, I’d sit on the balcony and write to friends au pairing in France, Germany, Panama, or in their first year at university. I listened to Neil Young on my Walkman and the drip-drip of melting snow. From noon till 8pm, I’d manage the bar, the fog of smoke lowering as the day wore on. I paid careful attention to the customers’ grammar.Non la trovi bellissima?one guy asked his friend about me.Don’t you find her beautiful?No, the friend replied. Oh, the things that stick in our heads.“I really believe there’s not much to leaving home,” I wrote to my brother. “When you want to get out, just DO it; cos it’s not true that you NEED things doing for you – cooking etc … There’s SO MUCH TO SEE.”I’m not sure how to explain my approach to personal safety back then to my own children, who are 15 and 18. “To get an offer of dinner, all you have to do is walk along the pavement,” I wrote. “Cars stop all the time. If they look OK, you jump in.”Ihave to order the Southern Comfort from Amazon. It’s a powerful time machine. At the first sip, I feel I’ve had too many. It tastes sweet and intense and full of things that might happen and haven’t happened. Sticky carpet. Worry I’ve laddered my stockings. The countdown of melting ice, leaving me with a watery drink that’s gone on too long and finished too soon …Above all, I suspect that life then was lived in a state of yearning, teetering between delight and disappointment.View image in fullscreen‘Meeting my 18-year-old self has felt exhilarating, debilitating, harrowing.’Photograph: Peter Flude/The GuardianThe year I turned 18, everything happened and nothing happened. It was the year I fell properly in love and, unrelated, lost my virginity. It was the year I first left home, travelled alone, made my own clothes, learned Italian, and admitted to myself that I wanted to be a writer, even if I forgot this till I read it in a letter 35 years later and realised I’d been living the dream all these years.I went to Cambridge. C met someone else.Meeting, and occasionally embodying, my 18-year-old self has felt exhilarating, debilitating, harrowing. Like being stuck between worlds. I’ve watched makeup tutorials, bought coloured eye sticks, ogled a silver leather miniskirt with my future 21-year-old self in mind, and found myself asking, “Are they the one?” of random souls who cross my path (sorry).When I’ve tried to make sense of the disorientation by writing – something that hasn’t changed – every key on the keyboard has felt like a mess I can’t put away. So how to evaluate my life since? I am not a published poet, as 18-year-old me would have loved me to be, but I have written two novels. I’ve found love a few times, and have a loving family.Three years ago, when I turned 50, I asked my parents for a carriage clock. It sits on the mantelpiece, and I only occasionally register its tick.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe year I turned 18Young peopleBob DylanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: You be the judge: should my husband stop looking up menus before we eat out? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: After losing a few stone, Abdeen now likes to plan his meals ahead, but Claire says he is taking the joy out of going to restaurants. Whose argument carries more weight? You decide
Author: Georgina Lawton
Headline: After losing a few stone, Abdeen now likes to plan his meals ahead, but Claire says he is taking the joy out of going to restaurants. Whose argument carries more weight? You decide
Content: Illustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianYou be the judgeLife and styleYou be the judge: should my husband stop looking up menus before we eat out?After losing a few stone, Abdeen now likes to plan his meals ahead, but Claire says he is taking the joy out of going to restaurants. Whose argument carries more weight? You decideFind out how to get a disagreement settled or become a jurorInterviews byGeorgina LawtonThu 15 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 09.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe prosecution: Clairedouble quotation markI want him to be more spur-of-the-moment because that will improve my dining experienceI love eating out. I’m lucky that I’m naturally slim and have never really had any issues with food. Abdeen, my husband of seven years, is different and has always struggled with his weight.When I met him, he was probably four stone (25kg) heavier than he is now. He’s lost a lot of weight using the jabs and is now very conscious of putting weight back on. I’m really proud that he’s taking his health seriously, and I don’t think the jabs are an “easy way out”, but eating out with Abdeen while he was losing weight was tricky, and it’s still a bit tedious at times.Before we go out to eat, Abdeen will look up the menus because he wants to watch his calories. His habit often ruins the surprise for me. He will download a menu and analyse his choices before we arrive, asking me: “What are you going to get?”double quotation markAbdeen will just sit down and say: ‘I know what I want,’ but I like to take my timeI don’t want to discuss a menu before we arrive at a restaurant. I like not knowing what I’m going to eat until I see another diner beside me order it, or speak to the waiting staff and think: “Ooh, that sounds nice.”Abdeen doesn’t even look at the menu when we arrive, and that makes me feel rushed. He will just sit down and say: “I know what I want,” but I like to take my time. It also cheapens the dining experience for me when we’re in a nice place. It makes me feel as if we’re in a canteen, waiting for a pre-ordered tray to be placed in front of us, and not people with sophisticated palates being given time to choose our food.Abdeen wants to feel he’s in control of his food. He wants to make sure he’s making healthy choices, but I think he can do that without consulting menus in advance. I want him to be a bit more spur‑of‑the‑moment, because that would improve my dining experience. I don’t think his way of doing things is any fun. If he really doesn’t want to change how he chooses his food, I’d happily compromise: he can look at the menu beforehand, but please don’t read it out to me or ask what I’m ordering. Let me have my surprise.You be the judge – send us your domestic disputesRead moreThe defence: Abdeendouble quotation markIt’s easy for someone who has never had to think much about their weight to choose food on the spotI understand that Claire likes the spontaneity of eating out, but for me, looking at the menu beforehand is partly how I’ve learned to manage my weight. I don’t think I should have to stop doing something that works for me just because she finds it less exciting.I lost a lot of weight using the jabs and I’m not ashamed of that, but I’ve been off them for about a year because I hit my goal and they were too expensive. Now, keeping the weight off is important to me, and that means being conscious of what I eat.Restaurants can be difficult because you don’t always know how calorific something is. There are lots of hidden fats. If I look at the menu beforehand, I can work out what my options are without feeling under pressure. I can decide that if I’m having a burger, for example, maybe I won’t have a starter, or I’ll make a healthier choice earlier in the day. It gives me a sense of control.double quotation markIf Claire really hates hearing about the menu in advance, I can stop reading it out to herI don’t like deciding in the moment because I can make bad choices. Claire can look at the menu for as long as she wants when we get there. If she wants to ask the waiter questions, look at what other people are eating and change her mind three times, that’s fine. I don’t think knowing what you’re going to eat turns dining out at a nice restaurant into a canteen experience. We’re still spending time together, having a drink, talking and enjoying the food.I do sometimes ask her what she’s going to order beforehand, but that’s because I’ve already looked at the menu at home before we go out. I’m not trying to make her choose in advance.If Claire really hates hearing about the menu, I can stop reading it out to her. But I don’t think it’s reasonable to ask me to wait until we arrive to make my own decision because being spontaneous around food is what caused me to gain weight. It’s easy for someone who has never had to think much about their weight to choose food on the spot. Claire can have her surprise; I just don’t want one myself.Names have been changedskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe jury of Guardian readersThere’s nothing wrong with wanting to look up a menu beforehand, especially given Abdeen’s reasons. However, he could still at least open the menu in the restaurant and discuss the options with Claire. I think that’s part of the dining experience, and it would give her time to decide without feeling rushed.Suvi, 27If Claire’s fine-dining fantasy hinges almost entirely on menu selection – a small part of the overall experience – she is neglecting the real fun of eating out: the company. Claire should be grateful for Abdeen’s laudable strategy, as many people managing their weight avoid restaurants entirely.Matthew, 54It’s a reluctant guilty from me, as I will often peruse the menu before going to a restaurant. However, there is nothing worse than a rushed experience. Perhaps not reading out the menu prior to going to the restaurant is the compromise.Shelly, 49Claire needs to accommodate Abdeen’s ways with the menu. While frustrating for her, the mental and physical impact on him seems significant. And maybe if Abdeen compromised a little (he could talk about it a bit less) it would help.Josephine, 33It’s good for Abdeen to look at a menu beforehand to decide on his choices due to his past issues. This enables him to be prepared rather than turning up to a restaurant and finding few things that would suit him. Claire has to see the bigger picture.Sakib, 53Now you be the judgeIn our online poll, tell us: should Abdeen stop making such a meal of eating out?The poll closes on Wednesday 21 October at 9am BSTLast week’s resultsWe asked whether Ruth should stillshare her tentwith her friend, Ava.16%of you said yes –Ruth is guilty84%of you said no –Ruth is not guiltyExplore more on these topicsLife and styleYou be the judgefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Welsh mountain inn that helped conquer Everest | Wales holidays | The Guardian
description: As a new film about Sherpa Tenzing Norgay is released, we visit Pen-Y-Gwryd, the Snowdonia hotel that served as British ‘base camp’ for the 1953 expedition and where the spirit of adventure lives on
Author: Gareth Roberts
Headline: As a new film about Sherpa Tenzing Norgay is released, we visit Pen-Y-Gwryd, the Snowdonia hotel that served as British ‘base camp’ for the 1953 expedition and where the spirit of adventure lives on
Content: Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel, at the foot of Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon), north Wales.Photograph: Pen-y-Gwryd HotelView image in fullscreenPen-Y-Gwryd hotel, at the foot of Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon), north Wales.Photograph: Pen-y-Gwryd HotelWales holidaysThe Welsh mountain inn that helped conquer EverestAs a new film about Sherpa Tenzing Norgay is released, we visit Pen-Y-Gwryd, the Snowdonia hotel that served as British ‘base camp’ for the 1953 expedition and where the spirit of adventure lives onGareth RobertsThu 15 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 16.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early hours of 2 June 1953, guests at thePen-Y-Gwryd hotelin the heart of Eryri (Snowdonia) were woken from their sleep by the sound of footsteps running down the corridor outside their rooms. The commotion was followed by gleeful shouting and the sound of champagne corks popping. A late-night telephone call to the hotel’s owner had moments earlier confirmed that Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay had successfully summited Mount Everest. It had taken two days for the news to travel from the Himalayas to London. Serendipitously, news of the historic achievement coincided with the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II later that day.In the days and weeks that followed, the two mountaineers were feted across the front pages of newspapers around the world. Posing awkwardly for the cameras, their beaming smiles shone out of frost-burnt faces. In the decades that followed, Tenzing Norgay’s role in the expedition was increasingly marginalised – he was a Sherpa, indigenous to the area, and the load-carrying guide, while Hillary firmly planted his ice axe in the history books.View image in fullscreenEdmund Hillary, left, with Tenzing Norgay, after their epic achievement.Photograph: Granger/Historical Picture Archive/Alamydouble quotation markTenzing had more experience on Everest than anyone else on that expedition. He wasn’t just helping another man achieve his dreamA new film, set for release this week on Apple TV, aims to set that record straight.Tenzing, starring Genden Phuntsok and Tom Hiddleston, tracks Tenzing Norgay’s life from a young boy growing up in the Khumbu Valley to his rise as one of the most accomplished climbers within the Sherpa community, and his eventual recruitment to the 1953 British expedition to Mount Everest (known locally as Chomolungma)led by Colonel John Hunt.Tenzing review – reconstruction of first summit of Everest puts Sherpa at the centre of the storyRead moreThe film opened the Zurich film festival last month, where its director, Australian film-maker Jennifer Peedom, told audiences: “It’s often reduced to a familiar shorthand: Hillary conquered Everest, assisted by a Sherpa. But Tenzing had more experience on Everest than anyone else on that 1953 expedition. He wasn’t just helping another man achieve his dream. He had his own dream.”View image in fullscreenTom Hiddleston as Edmund Hillary and Genden Phuntsok as Tenzing Norgay in the film Tenzing.Photograph: Apple TV+/PAIn the spring of 1952, a full year before the British expedition, Tenzing, alongside Swiss climber Raymond Lambert, came agonisingly close to reaching the summit – less than 250 metres stood between them and glory. After a storm-lashed night on the south-east ridge, and with little oxygen, they were forced to retreat, albeit having set a new altitude record.Meanwhile, back in the UK, Hunt, having been assigned by the Joint Himalayan Committee to assemble a team of climbers, set up base camp at the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel at the foot of the Llanberis Pass. It was here they would practise their technical climbing skills and test the state-of-the-art equipment that had been designed specifically for this adventure, in particular the closed-circuit oxygen tanks that would be critical in keeping them alive in the “death zone” above 8,000m. The teams spent weeks on Yr Wyddfa’s (Snowdon) notorious Crib Goch ridge and on Y Lliwedd mountain, testing the revolutionary new high-altitude boots that would replace the old leather and hobnail ones, which offered little to no protection from the freezing temperatures of Everest.double quotation markA beloved destination for those with a penchant for adventure and late-night conversations in front of roaring firesArtefacts from those pioneering days can be seen at the hotel today. A glass cabinet contains some of the summit team’s original equipment and mementoes: goggles, an ice axe, a ledger of Sherpas’ fingerprints as most could not read or write, a compass and a battered tin mug. Little has changed in the 73 years since Christopher Briggs woke his guests with those glasses of champagne. The Pen-Y-Gwryd is a time capsule; it remains in family hands, now run by Briggs’s grandsons, Nick and Rupert Pullee, who are determined to maintain the hotel’s legacy and the traditions that have made it a beloved destination for those with a penchant for adventure and late-night conversations in front of roaring fires.View image in fullscreenMementoes from the Everest expedition on display at Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel.“My grandfather was originally from Scarborough,” Nick says. “He was a chemist, but his shop was bombed during the war, so [in 1947] he persuaded a friend to lend him the money to buy a hotel in Wales. The building had been used to home children during the blitz and had fallen into terrible disrepair, but he somehow managed to turn it into a success.”Briggs also started the Snowdon Club, where guests under the age of 16 who have successfully climbed the mountain take part in a small ceremony in which they are quizzed on their mountain knowledge. Those who answer correctly get to drink (lemonade) from Hillary’s pewter tankard and are awarded a sterling silver ice-axe brooch, with their name added to a book of members – a ritual that still happens today.The Smoke Room serves as the residents’ bar, a tiny wood-panelled snug whose walls are adorned with photos of the Everest team, with Tenzing featuring prominently. In one, he’s perched in the bar drinking tea with George Band, the youngest climber on the 1953 expedition. Inanother, he’s on a rocky outcrop of Tryfan, another famous Snowdonia peak, with team leader Hunt.“I was only a toddler when Tenzing last visited the hotel,” says Nick. “I remember he was incredibly kind and was constantly smiling. He used to give Rupert and myself piggybacks up the stairs. He was great friends with my grandfather, who visited him in Nepal often.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLandlord Christopher Briggs with Tenzing Norgay and George Band in the Smoke Room.Photograph: Pen Y Gwryd ArchiveBuilt in 1810 on the bedrock that makes up the Glyderau range, the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel is also the original starting point of thePyg track, one of the most iconic routes to the summit of Yr Wyddfa, and today guests can walk directly from the hotel’s door to the path that snakes upwards towards Pen y Pass. The timeless interior of the hotel is devoid of TV screens or piped music, and the only concession to the 21st century appears to be the wifi.double quotation markThe ceiling of the Everest Room in the public bar has been signed by pretty much every big-name mountaineer of the past 100 yearsThis summer’s endless heatwaves saw sun-scorched hillwalkers cool their limbs in the natural outdoor pool in the grounds of the hotel. Fed by mountain streams, it offers unparalleled views of the hills and sweeping valley towards the mountain village of Capel Curig. The addition of an outdoor sauna and the popularity of cold-water swimming mean it’s now a year-round proposition.The 20 rooms are all named evocatively after local peaks: Pen yr Ole Wen, Elidir Fawr, Crib Goch, Y Garn. Each is as cosy as one would expect from a rain-lashed mountain hotel: softly lit and with comfy mattresses wrapped in vintage Welsh wool blankets. In the labyrinthine corridors upstairs, you’ll discover bathrooms with Victorian roll-top tubs and Heath Robinson-esque showers. The bathroom doors are adorned with illustrations in the style of Aubrey Beardsley, and photos and artworks capturing the surrounding landscape and its mountaineering history adorn virtually every wall.View image in fullscreenHikers on the challenging Crib Goch.Photograph: Bailey-Cooper Photography/AlamyDining at the Pen-Y-Gwryd is an event in itself: mealtimes are announced by the banging of a gong, the dining room is an unapologetic whirlwind of Axminster and silverware, and the menu features roast Welsh lamb and Welsh steak and ale pies, sticky toffee puddings or rhubarb crumble – everything you’ll need to replenish after a long mountain trek.The ceiling of the Everest Room in the public bar has been signed by pretty much every big-name mountaineer of the past 100 years, and each corner of the building appears to have a story and artefact attached. It’s this authenticity that Nick believes gives the hotel its charm.“I think our greatest attraction may be that things remain unchanged,” says Nick. “We have a lot of regular guests from all over the world, and for many people the opportunity to step back from the world in the wilds of Snowdonia is extremely enticing. It’s something we aim to protect and cherish.”Roomsat thePen-Y-Gwrydhotelrange from£114to £172B&B; three-course dinner£49.Tenzingis on Apple TVfrom16 OctoberThis article was amended on 15 October 2026. Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel is at the foot of Yr Wyddfa, not Llanberis Pass as an earlier version said. Also a mountain mentioned is Y Lliwedd, nor “Yr Lliwedd”.Explore more on these topicsWales holidaysClimbing holidaysUnited Kingdom holidaysMount Everest holidaysMount EverestfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Thursday news quiz: Nobel winners, ruined dinners and Claudia’s sinners | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Test yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare?
Author: Martin Belam
Headline: Test yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare?
Content: Claudia Winkleman.Photograph: Euan Cherry/Studio Lambert/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenClaudia Winkleman.Photograph: Euan Cherry/Studio Lambert/BBC/PAThursday quizLife and styleThursday news quiz: Nobel winners, ruined dinners and Claudia’s sinnersTest yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare?Martin BelamThu 15 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery now and again the Thursday quiz gets overexcited and goes off piste. Celebrity Traitors has been so omnipresent in the UK that the idea of doing questions based on awkward rhymes around it became overpowering. It is still the same old mix of topical news, general knowledge and pop culture questions, and there are no spoilers. You don’t even have to have watched the show. But if you’ve ever wanted to watch someone struggle to rhyme a question with Romesh Ranganathan, now is your chance.Allons-y!The Thursday news quiz, no 269 – Celebrity Traitors special1.Just how many? Count with King Kenny! The Tom Cruise vehicle Digger is set to lose how much at the box office, according to reports?$145m$245m$345m$445mReveal2.Big or small? With Jerry Hall! None of the tropical storms formed in the Atlantic so far this season had turned into hurricanes, until the one that made landfall across the Florida panhandle and southern Alabama at the weekend. It was called …HannaIsaiasJerryKylieReveal3.Fancy a bet? With Joe Lycett! Apparently more than $26m was bet on Polymarket before the announcement of the winner of the Nobel peace prize. Who won it?Yasmin SookaMame Mandiaye NiangArlinda XhaferiNavi PillayReveal4.Who did that art? With Miranda Hart! They are having a legal tizz at the Paris opera house over what should be displayed in the roof – the original decoration from the 1800s or the canvas that was put over it in the 1960s. Who are the two artists?Marc Chagall and Jules-Eugène LenepveuAndré Masson and Paul BaudryJoan Miró and William-Adolphe BouguereauRené Goscinny and Albert UderzoReveal5.Spot that queen, with Michael Sheen! Dolly Parton was an absolute queen, and her fans turned a place in Australia pink in her honour. Which place?Narromine, which was renamed Dollymine for the occasionGeelong, which was renamed Jolene-along for the occasionGlenwood, which was renamed Islands in the Streamwood for the occasionWildbarton, which was renamed Wildparton for the occasionReveal6.Name that plant, with Richard E Grant! A plant selfie in a Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily find. What is the scientific name of the new species discovered?Dodo colombianaLeela colombianaLethbridge colombianaVictoria colombianaReveal7.Who held it aloft? With Sebastian Croft! New Zealand beat Australia in the first tie of this year's Bledisloe Cup series. In which sport?NetballMen's rugby unionMen's T20 cricketWomen's beach volleyballReveal8.You've got some front, with beautiful James Blunt! In an astonishing turn of events, who has been elected mayor of a remote district in the Peruvian Andes?Hitler Mussolini Simeon FloresAdolf Stalin Simeon FloresLenin Goebbels Simeon FloresRon from SparksReveal9.Which was a cappella? With Game of Thrones' Bella! OK, the rhymes are getting harder to tie to current events now. So which of these hits by The Housemartins was a cappella?Me and the FarmerBuildThink for a MinuteCaravan of LoveReveal10.That's so very puny, with Sharon Rooney! Qantas had to ground a plane after finding it was infested with bed bugs. *Shudder*. Where?RomeParisBerlinMadridReveal11.Who's the master? With James Acaster! We all know Gromit is effectively the master of the Wallace and Gromit household in the wonderful Aardman animations. But who is going to finally give Gromit a voice for the first time in the audiobook of his autobiography?David TennantNigel HaversMartin FreemanJames AcasterReveal12.Lower or higher? With Love Island's Maya! Some supermarket refrigerators in France hit what temperature after they were hacked remotely?Up to 50C overnightUp to 60C overnightUp to 70C overnightUp to 80C overnightReveal13.Little Mix's Leigh-Anne asks: Sudan or Japan? Another extremely strained question. According to the archived version of the CIA World Factbook, which country has the largest total area – Sudan or JapanJapan is bigger than SudanSudan is bigger than JapanReveal14.It's time to wreck it, with lovely Rob Beckett! Who has just been ousted as US ambassador to Greece after being engulfed in reports of improper behaviour, which – the Guardian's lawyers are keen to stress – she deniesKatie ZachariaNatalie HarpKimberly GuilfoyleMorticia AddamsReveal15.A loss of concentration, with Romesh Ranganathan! Thanks to nobody looking at the CCTV, or something like that, thieves made off with a not inconsiderable 30,000 bottles of wine from the prestigious Marchesi Antinori winery in which part of Italy?PiedmontTuscanyEmilia-RomagnaLombardyReveal16.What was that burn? With Industry's Harper Stern! Last week a fan of the Thursday quiz emailed the quiz master to say 'Journalist? You are a piece of shit'. Thanks, mate. What activity did they then suggest the quiz master carry out?Go armchair-general a game of Duck, Duck, GooseGo micromanage a sandboxGo play Monday morning quarterback at the kinder gardenGo audit a lemonade standReveal17.Name that 'stan, with Ireland's Joanne! Ashgabat is the capital city of where?KyrgyzstanTajikistanUzbekistanTurkmenistanReveal18.Make it taste Cajan, with that ol' Amol Rajan! God, this is getting hard. Which of these spices is most associated with cajun food?TurmericPaprikaCardamomSumacReveal19.Where is the lie? With Prof Hannah Fry! One of these headlines appeared on the Guardian website this week. Which one?Boston moves to ban town criersPhiladelphia moves to end direct milk deliveryNew York City moves to ban horse-drawn carriagesDenver moves to ban 30-50 specific feral hogsReveal20.Truly unruly with Accrington's Julie! Nothing rhymes with Hesmondhalgh. Nothing. Anyway, across the Pennines from where Julie was born, there was a happy ending after a discarded 1950s wedding album was reunited with the son of the couple photographed in it. Where?HalifaxRotherhamWakefieldHarrogateReveal21.We really just can't, with EastEnders' Grant! Absolutely done for rhymes now. Instead tackle this: which Canadian-born musician announced this week they had become a US citizen?Joni MitchellNeil YoungAlanis MorissetteAvril LavigneRevealThis was a terrible idea. If you really do think there has been an egregious error in one of the questions or answers – and can show your working and are absolutely 100% positive you aren’t attempting to factcheck a joke – you can complain about it in the comments below. title: Country diary: Thrilled by Darwin, and the wonder of worms | Animals | The Guardian
description: Downe, Kent: It’s hard not to feel the earth move by a visit to the great man’s house. He truly valued these creatures of the dirt
Author: Lev Parikian
Headline: Downe, Kent: It’s hard not to feel the earth move by a visit to the great man’s house. He truly valued these creatures of the dirt
Content: An earthworm. ‘They were regarded by many as lowly creatures of the dirt, but Darwin understood their worth.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenAn earthworm. ‘They were regarded by many as lowly creatures of the dirt, but Darwin understood their worth.’Photograph: AlamyCountry diaryAnimalsCountry diary: Thrilled by Darwin, and the wonder of wormsDowne, Kent:It’s hard not to feel the earth move by a visit to the great man’s house. He truly valued these creatures of the dirtLev ParikianThu 15 Oct 2026 00.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe garden beds are moistened by steady rain, but the ground is still unyielding. A blackbird hops across bare soil. A dart, a jab, and up it comes – a wriggling tube of pink flesh. A simple catch. But when I rummage in the dirt, my only reward is loam under the fingernails. Perhaps I should have brought a bassoon.I’ve come toDown House. Here, Charles Darwin changed the world. And here he wrotehis last book, its title usually shortened for convenience: Earthworms.“I know not whether it will interest any readers, but it has interested me,” he said. Quite the understatement. When a subjectinterested Darwin, no aspect of it escaped scrutiny, and earthworms hadoccupied his mindfor decades. They were regarded by many as lowly creatures of the dirt, but he understood their worth.He tested their potential for intelligence, their sensitivity to atmospheric variations, their senses of taste, smell and hearing. The latter involved his son Frank attempting to stimulate them by tootling his bassoon. It’s no small wonder to stand in Darwin’s study, surrounded by his paraphernalia. All those years of painstaking labour and rigorous observation in the quest for truth… Crikey!View image in fullscreen‘When a subject interested Charles Darwin, no aspect of it escaped scrutiny, and earthworms had occupied his mind for decades.’Photograph: Cambridge University Library/PAOutside, a circular stone slab sits embedded in the grass. It’s the base for a “wormstone” – a wood-and-copper apparatus that measured the amount and rate of their soil displacement. A layer of about 2mm a year, it turned out. Darwin concluded that few animals “have played so important a part in the history of the world”. He wasn’t wrong – a modern estimate reckons that every 10 years, earthworms turn over the equivalent of all the soil on earth to a depth of one inch.I prod the ground. Still too hard. Away from the damp loam of the kitchen garden, they’ll be hard at work, aerating and mixing, grinding and digesting organic matter, their excretions converting unpromising clumps into fertile humus. Custodians of the soil.As I consider those worms, going about their business under my feet, I’m struck by a fanciful thought. Their ancestors were participants in the great man’s final project. Just for a moment, absurd though it is, the connection with something so special feels thrillingly tangible.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsAnimalsCountry diaryWildlifeCharles DarwinRural affairsfeaturesShareReuse this content
