title: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested | Global development | The Guardian
description: At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports
Author: Sarah Johnson
Headline: At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports
Content: HRW said arrests had been made based on information found on phones, third-party allegations or raids on private premises, while lawyers fear representing those detained.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenHRW said arrests had been made based on information found on phones, third-party allegations or raids on private premises, while lawyers fear representing those detained.Photograph: APGlobal developmentLGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrestedAt least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reportsSupported byAbout this contentSarah JohnsonThu 15 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to anew report.More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February,according to HIV Justice Network, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years.The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations.Larissa Kojoué, LGBTQ+ rights researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “LGBTQ+ people are being forced to curb their normal activities … for fear of arrest and increased stigma. Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.”Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Senegal in 1965, but hostility towards LGBTQ+ individuals has grown in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, who ended up winning the election, and the former prime minister Ousmane Sonkopromised to strengthen laws criminalising same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority.Arrests of men and women have happened all over the country. The police say they have arrested peoplebased on information extracted from seized phones, third-party allegations or raids on private premises.The changes to the penal code have had a chilling effect on lawyers, who said they were afraid to represent people for fear of being prosecuted themselves, according to the report. Doctors told Human Rights Watch that the changes were discouraging people from seeking HIV testing and treatment.While there was a49% fall in new HIV infectionsin western and central Africa from 2010 to 2022, sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected by the virus, with64% of all people living with HIVglobally.View image in fullscreenProtesters call for a crackdown on LGBTQ+ people in February in Senegal’s capital, Dakar. The issue was promoted as a national priority in elections.Photograph: Zohra Bensemra/ReutersSylvie Beaumont, a consultant with HIV Justice Network, said she had received anecdotal evidence that HIV clinics had seen a drop in attendance. “Obviously this is not good for the HIV response because people are going without treatment, they’re not going to get tested,” she said.“The consequences are really bad and it’s sad because Senegal was a country that was doing well with their HIV response. They are shooting themselves in the foot.”She said while the law criminalising deliberate HIV transmission was not part of the reforms to the penal code this year, there had been an “unprecedented” rate of arrests in recent months. She labelled the charges “nonsensical” because it was reported that most people had either only discovered their status upon arrest; were arrested with condoms; or were on treatment that renders transmission of the virus impossible.The report said police had breached confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBTQ+ people by leaking details to the media, which reported personal and confidential information, including HIV status – exposing individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats and violence.LGBTQ+ people interviewed by Human Rights Watch said the crackdown was instilling fear among their community, and causing them to feel anxious and depressed. Many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements or relocated; some have left the country.The report pointed out that the crackdown flew in the face of domestic and international laws that guaranteed the right to a fair trial, privacy and non-discrimination.The changes to Senegal’s penal code is part of a trend across sub-SaharanAfricatowards more punitive legislation directed against LGBTQ+ people.There have been dozens of arrests in Niger since it criminalised “sexual relations with a person of the same sex” in February. It was the first time in the country’s history that homosexuality had been criminalised, and followed the introduction of similar laws and penal codes in neighbouringMaliandBurkina Fasowithin the past two years. All three are ruled by military juntas.In May, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed legislationcriminalising LGBTQ+ “activities”. The bill, which has not been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of legislationfirst proposed in 2021. In 2023,Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Actmade homosexual acts punishable by death.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentSenegalLGBTQ+ rightsHuman rights (Global development)Human rights (Law)Anti-rights movementAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Nicolás Maduro tells New York court new torture allegations are ‘false’ | Nicolás Maduro | The Guardian
description: Rewritten indictment accuses ex-Venezuela president and wife Cilia Flores of leading campaign of torture
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rewritten indictment accuses ex-Venezuela president and wife Cilia Flores of leading campaign of torture
Content: People protest against Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores outside a federal courthouse in New York on Thursday.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople protest against Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores outside a federal courthouse in New York on Thursday.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPANicolás MaduroNicolás Maduro tells New York court new torture allegations are ‘false’Rewritten indictment accuses ex-Venezuela president and wife Cilia Flores of leading campaign of tortureAssociated PressThu 15 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNicolás Maduro insisted on Thursday during an appearance in a New York court that torture allegations in a rewritten drug trafficking indictment against the deposed Venezuelan president and his wife were “false accusations”.Maduro, shackled at the ankles, was brought to court to face the new charges accusing the couple of leading a state-sponsored campaign of repression that tortured scores of victims, including three Americans.Judge Alvin K Hellerstein entered a not-guilty plea on behalf of Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores. They were seized from their Caracas home by the US military in a night-time raid in January.Hellerstein announced that he was entering the plea on behalf of Maduro after Maduro twice responded to the judge’s request to enter a plea by criticizing the indictment, saying it contained “false accusations and false testimony”. Maduro spoke through an interpreter.The vanishing of Nicolás Maduro: how the former dictator is being erased from VenezuelaRead moreAttorney Barry Pollack said when the charges were announced last week that Maduro, 63, denied them and “looks forward to his day in court”.According to the rewritten indictment, Maduro oversaw a violent torture system that beat, asphyxiated and delivered electric shocks to its victims. He is accused of personally recommending torture methods, receiving updates on specific victims’ treatment and threatening to kill one prisoner’s child as a form of psychological torture.Flores, 70, a former attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment alleges.When she was asked to enter a plea, she said through an interpreter: “I am completely innocent. I am not guilty.”Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the international criminal court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied wrongdoing.Prosecutors told the judge during the hearing that lawyers on both sides want the trial date moved from 1 June to 14 June.Torture is a crime under international law and can be prosecuted outside the country where the abuse occurred and regardless of the victims’ nationality. But the prosecution of foreign officials in the US is exceedingly rare, having been tried only a few times, including against the son of the former Liberian president Charles Taylor, Russians responsible for war crimes in Ukraine and a former prison warden in Bashar Assad’s Syria.Earlier this year, Maduro and his wife pleaded not guilty in the US drug case, which said they conspired to flood the US with cocaine. Their attorneys say the case should be dismissed on immunity grounds because they were the leader and first lady of a foreign country.The revised indictment covers allegations of torture stretching back to Maduro’s ascent to power in 2013, when he took over as president from his mentor Hugo Chávez, who died of cancer that year.Explore more on these topicsNicolás MaduroNew YorkVenezuelaTortureAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Milei adviser claims UK being ‘colonised by Islam’ as Falklands row grows | Falkland Islands | The Guardian
description: Santiago Caputo cites election of Sagal Abdi-Wali as MP and calls UK a threat to the west in post shared by Argentina’s president
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Santiago Caputo cites election of Sagal Abdi-Wali as MP and calls UK a threat to the west in post shared by Argentina’s president
Content: A union flag outside a property in Stanley, the Falkland Islands capital.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA union flag outside a property in Stanley, the Falkland Islands capital.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianFalkland IslandsMilei adviser claims UK being ‘colonised by Islam’ as Falklands row growsSantiago Caputo cites election of Sagal Abdi-Wali as MP and calls UK a threat to the west in post shared by Argentina’s presidentDaniel Boffeyin Port Stanley, Falkland IslandsThu 15 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe chief adviser to Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has cited the election of Sagal Abdi-Wali to the UK parliament as evidence of the Islamisation of Britain and further reason for Argentina to take sovereignty over theFalkland Islands.In a post on social media, Santiago Caputo, who is reportedly taking a key role in Argentina’s strategy over the Falklands, suggested that the taking of the south Atlantic islands was necessary to prevent the “interference of an Islamic state” in the region.Milei shared Caputo’s post on the social media platform X.The intervention from Buenos Aires comes at a moment ofheightened tensionbetween Argentina and the UK over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory, which is 300 miles off the South American coastline.Labour’sAbdi-Wali was electedas the MP for Holborn and St Pancras in London this month, seeing off a challenge from the Green party leader, Zack Polanski. She took her seat in parliament on Monday.Milei has sought to criminalise executives involved in the Falkland Islands’ nascent oil industry and has threatened to target the fishing sector on which the islands’ economy depends.Argentina has long sought sovereignty over the islands. The intensity of Argentinian pressure relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by the then Argentinian dictator, Gen Leopoldo Galtieri.View image in fullscreenJavier Milei shared his adviser’s post on X.Photograph: Francisco Loureiro/ReutersThe 74-day conflict in 1982 ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of their military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.This week, Andy Burnham restated the UK’s position that it would respect the wish of the 3,600 islanders to remain British, and the government announced its intention to protect the interests of businesses working in the Falklands.The Guardian revealed that the Foreign Office hadwritten to Interpolseeking assurance that the law enforcement agency would not respond favourably to requests for the detention of individuals working in the Falklands.In his statement on X, Caputo – who has worked for Milei since 2021 – wrote that the “United Kingdom was, in many ways, the cradle of modern western civilisation” but that it now posed a threat to the west.He wrote: “Seeing the United Kingdom being colonised by Islam is not only an imminent risk to the cause of the west as a whole, but also a historical tragedy for those of us who defend the ideas of liberty.“This is yet another reason why Argentina must firmly project itself toward the south Atlantic and reclaim the Las Malvinas [Argentina’s name for the Falklands]. Given the strategic geopolitical importance the south Atlantic will assume in the coming decades, the west cannot afford the encroachment of an Islamic state within that sphere of influence. Reclaiming the Malvinas is not merely a national cause, it is a cause for the west.”Caputo accompanied his post with an image of Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee from Somalia, being sworn into parliament.Under the image, Javier Negre, a rightwing Spanish journalist, commented: “Here is a Somali Muslim woman taking her oath of office on the Qur’an in the English parliament. She has taken the seat formerly held by Prime Minister Keir Starmer. Islam is steadily gaining more power in the country.”In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of the Falkland Islands’ residents voted to remain a British territory, withonly three votes against.Explore more on these topicsFalkland IslandsArgentinaJavier MileiAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazil cuts work week to 40 hours in win for Lula ahead of runoff | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Congress approves constitutional amendment that bans six-day workweeks, which could affect up to 30 million
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Congress approves constitutional amendment that bans six-day workweeks, which could affect up to 30 million
Content: Senators celebrate the approval of a constitutional amendment bill that would end shorten the workweek in Brazil.Photograph: André Borges/EPAView image in fullscreenSenators celebrate the approval of a constitutional amendment bill that would end shorten the workweek in Brazil.Photograph: André Borges/EPABrazilBrazil cuts work week to 40 hours in win for Lula ahead of runoffCongress approves constitutional amendment that bans six-day workweeks, which could affect up to 30 millionTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroWed 14 Oct 2026 22.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrazil’s congress has approved a constitutional amendment to shorten the working week to a maximum of 40 hours, a move that could affect 30 million workers and that will hand a political victory to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead of thepresidential runoffin under two weeks.In an attempt to overturn thefirst-round leadsecured by his opponent, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula has strongly championed the amendment, which will give some workers an extra day off each week.Bolsonaro, by contrast, spent months opposing the change but reversed course on Tuesday, saying “the majority of Brazilian workers” supported it. On Wednesday, he joined 75 senators who approved the reform, which passed the lower house in May.Flávio Bolsonaro’s advance in Brazil’s election is grim jolt for climate campaignersRead moreOnly one senator voted against it: Hamilton Mourão, former vice-president to Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s father.The constitutional amendment bans six-day workweeks, currently worked by 16 million people, while cutting the maximum workweek from 44 to 40 hours for more than 30 million workers.The change is expected to affect mainly workers in retail, restaurants and hotels, most of them low-paid – one of the groups which Lulalost the most support fromsince the 2022 election, when he defeated Jair Bolsonaro.View image in fullscreenBrazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.Photograph: Evaristo Sa/AFP/Getty ImagesLula celebrated the amendment’s passing, writing on social media “ending the 6x1 schedule is about more than changing working hours. It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, look after yourself and enjoy life.”Victor Escobar, a researcher at the Laboratory of Parties, Elections and Comparative Politics, said the change “could indeed benefit Lula’s re-election campaign”.The proposal began as a TikTok movement called Life Beyond Work, founded by a pharmacy assistant who entered politics after its success and later was embraced by Lula.His party spent months pushing the senate to put the proposal to a vote and many believed that after the far right’ssweeping victorylast week secured a broad congressional majority in 2027, the Senate would no longer vote on it.But Senate president Davi Alcolumbre, whose relationship with Lula has at times been rocky, put it to a vote.Flávio Bolsonaro’s party had considered blocking it, but polls showed the change had more than 70% of the general population behind it, and more than half of the senator’s voters.In May, Bolsonaro said the proposal could cause “mass unemployment”, an argument employers’ associations opposed to the change have repeatedly made.The senator voted remotely while campaigning in the country’s south.Even after changing his position, Bolsonaro said on Tuesday that he “supports something even better,” referring to an alternative proposal he had long advocated in which pay would be based on the hours actually worked. The Folha newspaperreportedthat he told business leaders that, if elected, he would review parts of the new amendment, a point several allied senators also made during Wednesday’s vote.View image in fullscreenBrazil’s right-wing Senator and presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro delivers a speech on Wednesday.Photograph: Sílvio Ávila/AFP/Getty ImagesDespite its approval, none of the changes will take effect before the runoff on 25 October. After the Senate president promulgates it, a 60-day period will follow before six-day workweeks are abolished and the maximum working week is reduced from 44 to 42 hours, then to 40 hours after a further 14 months.However, Escobar believes its approval could already benefit Lula: “It will speak to how voters feel economically when they cast their ballot; they can feel more relieved with a change in their working schedule”.Marilane Oliveira Teixeira, a professor and researcher at a study centre at the University of Campinas whohas spent monthsexamining the possible impacts of the change, said there was no shortage of evidence showing how harmful having only one day off is to workers.“People who work a 6x1 schedule are practically prevented from having even a minimum level of social life,” she said, adding that the negative effects could include illness, workplace risks and exhaustion, “especially for women, who still carry the burden of unpaid domestic work”.Lilian Cristo dos Santos, 50, has only one day off from her job as a saleswoman at a home appliances shop in Salvador, Bahia. “There’s no time to go to the doctor, to the beach, to the salon, to look after myself; I wanted to have time to study and I can’t. On my only day off, I have to clean the house and look after my family,” she said.Santos said she voted for Lula, but has colleagues who chose Bolsonaro. “They say he represents change – well, yes, but certainly for the worse.”Escobar is among many political scientists who believe that,despite Bolsonaro’s lead, Lula has gained momentum not only from the change to the working schedule, but also from demonstrations by his supporters that have drawn thousands across the country and an effort to build a stronger presence on social media.Lula alsocontinued announcingbenefits just days before the vote, including debt relief for microentrepreneurs, and published a letter to evangelical Christians – who havehistorically favouredBolsonaro – stressing his commitment “to ensuring that everyone has two days off a week, because life is not just about work”.Escobar said: “Although most people have already decided their vote, there are some who are more responsive to political moves, and Lula has been trying very strongly to reach them. … The race still looks somewhat tangled, tied, with some degree of advantage for Bolsonaro, but it is still a very open election.”Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasFlávio BolsonaronewsShareReuse this content

title: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt | Stock markets | The Guardian
description: Chip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as potential interest rate hikes spook markets
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Chip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as potential interest rate hikes spook markets
Content: A Hana Bank screen shows the Kopsi index with a downward graph line. The tech-heavy South Korean index fell 8% overnight in Asia, triggering circuit breakers and halting stock trades.Photograph: Lee Jin-man/APView image in fullscreenA Hana Bank screen shows the Kopsi index with a downward graph line. The tech-heavy South Korean index fell 8% overnight in Asia, triggering circuit breakers and halting stock trades.Photograph: Lee Jin-man/APStock marketsTech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debtChip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as potential interest rate hikes spook marketsBusiness news – live updatesLarry Elliott: the global economy is muddling through. But a storm is comingKalyeena MakortoffThu 15 Oct 2026 10.33 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, asfears over rising inflationand future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix andSamsungElectronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5% respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.The global economy is muddling through against the odds. But a storm is coming | Larry ElliottRead moreMeanwhile, Japan’sNikkei225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in the memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI.The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where theNasdaqComposite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, its worst performance since July.US stocks fell further when trading resumed on Thursday. The Nasdaq dropped another 1.4% at the start of trading, with Dell, which makes datacentre servers, and Coherent, which manufactures components for AI datacentres, leading the early fallers.The sell-off came after US data on Wednesday showed stateside inflation jumped toa higher-than-expected 3.7% in September, marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May.Fresh data on Thursday showing US producers increased their prices by 6.3% year on year in September – the sharpest rise since December 2022 – added to inflationary jitters.The figures have rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month.“Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid said.Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe sell-offfollows warnings from the International Monetary Fund,which said this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets was putting world financial stability at risk.“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” the IMF said. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit.The latest jitters hit China, where the Shanghai Shenzhen CSI 300 slipped by as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits.European stocks also came under pressure, with Germany’s DAX down 0.36% in afternoon trading and the Italian FTSE MIB dropping by 1.3%.Explore more on these topicsStock marketsMarket turmoilTechnology sectorInflationInterest ratesUS marketsSamsungnewsShareReuse this content

title: Indonesia fights fire with dry ice as toxic haze spreads across region | Indonesia | The Guardian
description: Having tried cloud seeding and water bombing, one pilot project will see dry ice dispersed by plane across the province of South Sumatra
Author: Kate Lamb
Headline: Having tried cloud seeding and water bombing, one pilot project will see dry ice dispersed by plane across the province of South Sumatra
Content: People walk through thick haze from wildfires in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, on Wednesday.Photograph: GENDES/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople walk through thick haze from wildfires in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, on Wednesday.Photograph: GENDES/EPAIndonesiaIndonesia fights fire with dry ice as toxic haze spreads across regionHaving tried cloud seeding and water bombing, one pilot project will see dry ice dispersed by plane across the province of South SumatraKate Lamband agenciesThu 15 Oct 2026 00.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs fires ravageIndonesia, emitting a toxic smoke that has drawn the ire of regional neighbours, the government is testing an unusual new approach to tackle the haze: dry ice.Having tried cloud seeding, water bombing and sending in army personnel to fight the fires, Indonesia’s coordinating security minister said dry ice would be dropped on the province of South Sumatra on Thursday.“This trial of dry ice dispersal is being conducted under the president’s direct instruction to help tackle the haze in South Sumatra,” minister Dudung Abdurachman was quoted as saying by state news agency Antara.“We will first observe the results, and if effective, there is a possibility that this method could be implemented in other regions.”Since January,almost 900,000 hectareshave been burned Indonesia-wide in the worst fire season in more than a decade, exacerbated by this year’s“godzilla” El-Ninoand as the practice of “slash and burn” to clear land for crops such as palm oil persists.View image in fullscreenMotorists ride through thick haze from wildfires in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia.Photograph: GENDES/EPAFor months, millions of Indonesians have been subject to thick smoke and an apocalyptic tangerine haze, with criticism mounting of the government’s response, including aclass action lawsuitfiled last week accusing it of “gross negligence”. Tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to the haze.Air quality has also plummeted in neighbouring countries, shuttering schools, grounding flights and driving a spike in respiratory illness.Marina Bay, Singapore, before and after smoke haze caused by fires in Indonesia.The haze has drifted into neighbouringSingapore, Malaysia and as far afield as the Philippines. Timor-Leste has said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday and urged families to keep children indoors or to use “respiratory protection” if going outside.Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment starting on Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes occurred. The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents.In the past week, the financial hub of Singapore was listed among the most polluted cities globally. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected, was at number two.View image in fullscreenKuala Lumpur’s skyline shrouded in haze from regional wildfires, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, on 9 October.Photograph: Hasnoor Hussain/ReutersOn Thursday, a Cessna aircraft will reportedly disperse 1.5 tons of dry ice over the South Sumatran city of Palembang, a move the government hopes will ease the smoke and improve air quality and visibility.The technique was first deployed in the 1940s to promote ice formation in clouds, Bloomberg reported.‘The physical toll is visceral’: How Indonesia’s fire haze affects millions - visual guideRead moreBut experts say the use of dry ice, or solid carbon dioxide, might only offer local, and limited relief.“It’s got some potential for local relief that might work for a while,” says Rick McRae, an adjunct professor from the University of New South Wales’ (UNSW) bushfire research group.View image in fullscreenA pedestrian wearing a mask walks along the boulevard at Marina Bay in Singapore this week.Photograph: Roslan Rahman/AFP/Getty Images“Weather systems are all moving from east to west. So if you’re in a town under that and you clear the smoke, there’s gonna be more blowing all the time,” he says, “So it’s a constant … It’s not going to be simple and it’s not going to be a permanent fix in any way.”In the Indonesian province of central Kalimantan ​on Wednesday, the ISPU air pollution index exceeded 1,200 – or four times the “hazardous” level of 300 – environment ministry data showed.Local news footage showed ​thick haze blanketing the provincial city of Palangka Raya, cutting visibility for motorists to a minimum.View image in fullscreenThick wildfire haze shrouds the Kahayan River in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia.Photograph: GENDES/EPAIndonesian presidentPrabowo Subiantohas ordered firefighting efforts to be stepped up, and called for a crackdown on those suspected of starting fires.But the government has struggled to combat the fires, the worst of which occur in peatland areas, can burn for weeks underground, and are difficult to extinguish.“As time goes by and climate change kicks in, I think it could become a global problem, not just the fix that one country needs to find,” said McRae, of the widening regional issue. “There’s a lot of interconnectedness on a global scale.”Explore more on these topicsIndonesiaAsia PacificPrabowo SubiantoWildfiresSingaporeMalaysianewsShareReuse this content

title: Resources minister faces calls to correct her claim all Beetaloo emissions will be offset | Northern Territory | The Guardian
description: Madeleine King told press club emissions from NT fossil fuel basin ‘are accounted for and offset’ but research found 95% of emissions this decade would not have to be offset
Author: Adam Morton
Headline: Madeleine King told press club emissions from NT fossil fuel basin ‘are accounted for and offset’ but research found 95% of emissions this decade would not have to be offset
Content: At the National Press Club, Madeleine King defended her support for the development of the Beetaloo gas basin  in the Northern Territory.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenAt the National Press Club, Madeleine King defended her support for the development of the Beetaloo gas basin  in the Northern Territory.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPNorthern TerritoryResources minister faces calls to correct her claim all Beetaloo emissions will be offsetMadeleine King told press club emissions from NT fossil fuel basin ‘are accounted for and offset’ but research found 95% of emissions this decade would not have to be offsetSign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter hereAdam MortonandSarah Basford CanalesThu 15 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 15.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe resources minister, Madeleine King, is facing calls to correct her claim in a major speech that all greenhouse gas emissions from developing a massive fossil fuel basin in theNorthern Territorywill be offset to limit their impact on the climate.Speaking at the National Press Club in Canberra on Wednesday, King defended her support for the development of the Beetaloo gas basin south of Darwin after being asked if she was comfortable with the impact that the emissions from the gas would have on Australians.King was photographed laughing alongside the NT chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, as they celebrated the first gas being pumped from the basin last month. The minister told the press club the basin was a “very important resource” for the NT and to help supply gas to Australia’s east coast and export markets.Albanese’s resources minister celebrating the Beetaloo carbon bomb is a hell of a choice. Labor can’t say it wasn’t warned | Clear AirRead moreShe said it was being developed after a “landmark scientific study” in 2018 into whether fracking should be allowed in the territory. Known as the Pepper inquiry, that government-commissioned investigation made 135 recommendations, including that the NT and Australian governments should aim to ensure that any onshore shale gas developments did not increase the country’s total emissions.In practice, that would require any climate pollution from gas developments – from extraction, processing, transport and the fuel’s use – to be fully offset through the purchase of carbon credits.King told the press club that the NT government “took up and implemented” the inquiry’s recommendations. “My understanding from those recommendations is that the emissions are accounted for and offset, but I would have to check that,” she said.The NT government does not require emissions from Beetaloo basin to be offset. The Guardian revealed that the previous Labor territory government dropped the requirementafter the gas industry objected. The Country Liberal party government maintained that position when elected in 2024.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailSome emissions from gas developments in the NT will need to be offset under a federal climate policy, the safeguard mechanism, that is applied to operations that emit more than 100,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. But that applies only to pollution directly from the facility, not the full lifecycle emissions as recommended by the Pepper inquiry.King told the press club the safeguard mechanism would be applied to Beetaloo basin developments if emissions were above the threshold. “That is how we manage dealing with emissions in this country,” she said.Butresearch by Tim Baxter, of the consultancy Naru Research, found about 95% of emissions expected from four gas projects in the Beetaloo basin this decade would not have to be offset.Baxter said King either “isn’t across her brief or she’s being intentionally misleading”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When he publishesSign up toClear Air AustraliaAdam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The Pepper inquiry was clear. For the territory to begin to manage the risks of fracking and unconventional gas in the NT all emissions occurring in Australia must be fully offset,” he said.“The safeguard mechanism does not deliver this … If NT fracking is detonated, it could single-handedly undo all efforts to cut Australia’s climate emissions.”Kirsty Howey, a former head of Environment Centre NT, now leading the Wilderness Society, said governments had broken a promise to fully act on the recommendations of the Pepper inquiry. “It’s one of the greatest failures of climate policy in history,” she said.The acting chief head of Environment Centre NT, Bree Ahrens, called on the minister to “correct the public record”. She said an estimate by the energy company Santos suggested if the Beetaloo basin was fully developed and its gas burned it could lead to emissions 60 times what Australia releases into the atmosphere each year.“Frackers are being given a free pass on climate emissions, and it’s the territory that will pay the price,” she said.A spokesperson for King said successive NT governments had “accepted and implemented all 135 recommendations of the Pepper review”. They said the safeguard mechanism required all shale gas facilities, including Beetaloo basin gas extraction facilities, to have net zero emissions if they emitted more than 100,000 tonnes of CO2a year.Explore more on these topicsNorthern TerritoryCarbon offsettingGasGreenhouse gas emissionsFossil fuelsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Queensland’s LNP has trodden softly in government. It’s now baring its teeth over the power to break up workers’ strikes | Queensland politics | The Guardian
description: The controversial legislation may end up placing large sections of its suburban support – critical to the party’s lead in the polls – on the bonfire
Author: Ben Smee
Headline: The controversial legislation may end up placing large sections of its suburban support – critical to the party’s lead in the polls – on the bonfire
Content: The deputy premier of Queensland, Jarrod Bleijie, wants the power to break up strikes by public-sector workers.Photograph: AAPView image in fullscreenThe deputy premier of Queensland, Jarrod Bleijie, wants the power to break up strikes by public-sector workers.Photograph: AAPQueensland politicsAnalysisQueensland’s LNP has trodden softly in government. It’s now baring its teeth over the power to break up workers’ strikesBen SmeeThe controversial legislation may end up placing large sections of its suburban support – critical to the party’s lead in the polls – on the bonfireGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastThu 15 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 18.51 EDTShareFor almost two years, the Liberal National party’s strategy for government in Queensland has been to stay well clear of issues that risk burning through political capital.On Wednesday, one of the most tentative conservative governments in recent history announced plans for sweeping and controversial changes to workplace laws.In doing so, the LNP risks placing large sections of its suburban support – critical to the party’s lead in the polls – on the bonfire.The proposals would give the increasinglyinfluential deputy premier, Jarrod Bleijie, the power to break strikes by public-sector workers in certain circumstances, including if it is deemed “in the public interest”.The government will also make it more difficult for public servants, including emergency services workers, to claim compensation for psychological injuries. Under the proposed laws, workers with such claims will only be entitled to support if they can show their workplace was the primary cause.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailLaw firm Slater and Gordon said the changes would make it harder for Queenslanders to access support for psychological injuries. The United Workers Union, which represents paramedics and some healthcare workers, said the changes were “an underhanded attack onQueenslandambulance officers and other hospital staff”.Several business groups welcomed the changes.The opposition leader, Steven Miles, said on Thursday morning the proposals were a “Newman-era attack on workers”, and the only thing surprising about that statement was that it took so long (roughly 14 hours) for the spectre of Campbell Newman’s government to, once again, loom overQueensland politics.The collapse of the Newman government explains almost everything about the current one. The premier,David Crisafulli, and Bleijie had front-row seats for the “crash through” tactics that quickly turned voters off Newman, including proposals to sack public-sector workers, and led to mass protests.Rural Queenslanders have seen gas projects come and go – but a 725-hectare datacentre poses a whole new level of ‘stupidity’Read moreThe lessons since have been that most suburban voters are uncomfortable with the LNP putting ideology on show. And so it went to the 2024 election – and won comfortably – talking mainly about crime and keeping all those vote-losing positions on things like abortion and budget cuts off the table.Approaching the midway point of the term, the LNP has finally decided to show its teeth.There are readers who will, understandably, take issue with the idea that the Crisafulli government has been “tentative” or has been, up to this point, unthreatening.It has beenunapologetic in attacking Indigenous representation within government, trans healthcare, andsuppressing pro-Palestine protests.These moves have beenunderpinned by a simple calculation: that the issues are marginal for most suburban and regional voters, whose concerns are mostly the cost of living and crime.Those who care about evidence-based policy, human rights and civil liberties have every right to be furious. The polls suggest that fury hasn’t gone mainstream, and that suburban voters are OK with the government punching down, so long as it doesn’t affect them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWorkplace reforms affect them. If nothing else, those survivors of the Newman government who still sit in the cabinet room will have learned a lesson that in Queensland the public sector (which employs more than 320,000 people) is a powerful political bloc in its own right.The morning after announcing the changes, Bleijie seemed only too aware of the scale of the coming fight.“You’re going to see a mammoth campaign by the Labor party,” he told reporters at a press conference at Newstead.“It’s going to be a lot of mistruths and misinformation, and I think everything they will be able to say … we will be able to debunk with facts.”One Nation celebrated stunning success in Queensland in 1998 – then it all fell apart. What happened?Read moreThe Crisafulli government remains comfortably ahead in the relatively few public polls – arecent snapshot in Brisbane Timesseemed to show Labor in Queensland had taken the biggest hit from the rise in support for One Nation.But the bright orange cloud is still looming. And a simple look around the country reveals that in modern times, whether policy is decided by ideology or focus group, there’s no guarantee political capital will last.Better use that capital while you can. Even if it means, as it will for the Queensland LNP, picking a fight with many of the suburban middle-class voters who put the party into office.Ben Smee is Queensland state correspondentExplore more on these topicsQueensland politicsQueenslandDavid CrisafulliLiberal National partyIndustrial relationsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Woman charged after allegedly poisoning colleague’s curry lunch with snail pellets | Perth | The Guardian
description: Western Australian police say woman ‘experienced numbness to her tongue’ after tasting the curry at her workplace in Perth
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Western Australian police say woman ‘experienced numbness to her tongue’ after tasting the curry at her workplace in Perth
Content: A 43-year-old Perth woman allegedly contaminated a curry lunch with snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance.Photograph: Martin Lee/Rex FeaturesView image in fullscreenA 43-year-old Perth woman allegedly contaminated a curry lunch with snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance.Photograph: Martin Lee/Rex FeaturesPerthWoman charged after allegedly poisoning colleague’s curry lunch with snail pelletsWestern Australian police say woman ‘experienced numbness to her tongue’ after tasting the curry at her workplace in PerthGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressThu 15 Oct 2026 03.47 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 03.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman has been charged after allegedly poisoning a co-worker’s lunch curry with snail pellets.Western Australian police say a 58-year-old woman brought a container of curry to share with colleagues at her workplace in Perth’s southern suburbs in February.A 43-year-old woman allegedly contaminated it with snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance, a police spokesperson said on Thursday.“The curry had been experienced numbness to her tongue,” the police spokesperson said.It will be alleged the accused and the victim were in a personal relationship.Detectives arrested the 43-year-old woman last week.skip one count of unlawful act or omission with intent to harm (endangering the life, health or safety of any person).She is scheduled to appear before Armadale magistrates court on 5 November.Police title: ADF member ‘person of interest’ after video recorder found in HMAS Leeuwin women’s showers  | Australia news | The Guardian
description: Vice Adm Buckley calls incident an ‘act of sexual violence’ and a ‘despicable betrayal of trust’
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Vice Adm Buckley calls incident an ‘act of sexual violence’ and a ‘despicable betrayal of trust’
Content: The HMAS Leeuwin, pictured. A video recording device was found in a women’s bathroom onboard the ship.Photograph: Able Seaman Brenton Freind/Department of DefenceView image in fullscreenThe HMAS Leeuwin, pictured. A video recording device was found in a women’s bathroom onboard the ship.Photograph: Able Seaman Brenton Freind/Department of DefenceAustralia newsADF member ‘person of interest’ after video recorder found in HMAS Leeuwin women’s showersVice Adm Buckley calls incident an ‘act of sexual violence’ and a ‘despicable betrayal of trust’Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerThu 15 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 03.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe defence department says a member of the Australian Defence Force is a “person of interest” in investigations after a video recording device was found in a bathroom on HMAS Leeuwin, in what the chief of navy called a “despicable betrayal of trust”.A day after senator Jacqui Lambietold the Senate that a hidden camera had been found in a female shower facilityonboard the naval ship, docked in Cairns, navy chief Matt Buckley confirmed a “video recording device” had been located in one of the ship’s bathrooms.In a statement, Vice Adm Buckley called the incident an “act of sexual violence” and “the most despicable betrayal of trust”, and said the navy was conducting a review of all bathrooms across the service.Defence confirmed on Wednesday that a “video recording device” was found in the cabin of the vessel, which it had referred to the Joint Military Police Unit. It came hours after Lambie – an ADF veteran and advocate for defence personnel – told the Senate she’d been contacted by a former member of the navy with allegations about a camera being found aboard HMAS Leeuwin.Defence did not initially confirm where the device had been found, or any details about its investigation.On Thursday, the department gave a further update.“An Australian Defence Force member has been identified as a person of interest in the investigation into a video recording device being located on Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin,” the department said.“This person is now assisting the Joint Military Police Unit with its enquiries. Navy’s focus and priority is providing support to those who are impacted by this incident.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailIn a written statement, Buckley informed navy members of the update.“I consider this a most serious matter, and accordingly, the Ship’s program has been altered to enable a rapid and rigorous investigation by the Joint Military Policing Unit,” he wrote.“My highest priority, as always, is the wellbeing of our people.”Buckley said the navy was conducting a “100% audit of all of our bathrooms across the Fleet”.“This act is the most despicable betrayal of trust and is fundamentally misaligned with our values,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“You have my assurance and commitment that we will tackle this act of sexual violence with all of our energy. Any perpetrator will be held to account. Further, you should all know that eradicating sexual violence in our workplace is fundamental to the fighting efficiency of our Navy. I invite all of you to make this your priority.”The defence minister,Richard Marles, described the incident as “reprehensible, invasive and … the most despicable breach of trust”. He said he was receiving updates on the investigation as it continued.“There is no place for this behaviour in the Australian Defence Force. Our priority remains supporting the individuals who have been impacted,” he said in a statement on social media on Thursday.On Wednesday, Lambie asked whether images captured by the device had been published online.“How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask navy,” she said.Buckley said “all potentially impacted personnel are receiving our strongest support”, adding that the warrant officer of the navy was in Cairns to support the ship’s company.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsAustralian militaryRichard MarlesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Moscow sends swarms of drones to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine as Zelenskyy says Kyiv will restart strikes on Russian oil refineries
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Moscow sends swarms of drones to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine as Zelenskyy says Kyiv will restart strikes on Russian oil refineries
Content: A man stands at the site of his parents' house, destroyed by a Russian airstrikePhotograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenA man stands at the site of his parents' house, destroyed by a Russian airstrikePhotograph: ReutersUkraineRussia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapsesMoscow sends swarms of drones to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine as Zelenskyy says Kyiv will restart strikes on Russian oil refineriesAndrew Rothin KyivThu 15 Oct 2026 19.57 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 06.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia andUkrainehas collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries despite warnings from Donald Trump.Moscow accused Ukraine of launching a strike against a Russian oil refinery in the Ryazan region, its first since Trumpabruptly declared an “energy ceasefire”that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to.Trump has demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacking Russian oil refineries, claiming it is the cause of a global rise in the price of diesel fuel.An attack on two neutral ships in Romanian territorial waters at the mouth of the Danube River indicated that strikes against vulnerable commercial targets are set to expand.The Romanian president, Nicușor Dan, said two Russian drones violated Romanian airspace and struck two chemical tankers, setting the ships ablaze. Rescue crews were searching for at least seven missing sailors.“The situation in the Black Sea is serious,” he said. “Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk. Seafarers killed, injured and missing, very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria. This is unacceptable and it has to stop.”View image in fullscreenA San Marino-flagged ship caught fire in Romanian territorial waters.Photograph: Romanian interior ministry/ReutersZelenskyy said on Wednesday he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, after briefly halting them to demonstrate that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked a gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.Images from Ryazan showed flames at the refinery, which regional officials said had been targeted by 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. Moscow claimed debris from a drone struck by anti-aircraft fire had hit the refinery and sparked the fire.Ukraine also struck back at Russia’s military, hitting four Sukhoi Su-34 fighter/bomber jets and damaging two more, according to Zelenskyy. Ukraine’s military said it had used a Neptune cruise missile to strike an airfield in Russia’s southern Voronezh region.“These very warplanes were ready to launch new attacks on Ukraine and were loaded with aerial bombs,” Zelenskyy said, publishing a satellite photo of the damaged airfield.View image in fullscreenDestruction at Borisoglebsk airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region.Photograph: Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS/ReutersIn Ukraine, more than 360 Russian drones targeted Kirovohrad, a central region that has been hit less hard than others closer to Russia, in attacks that killed three people and injured six.“The enemy deliberately hit critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics ⁠facilities and residential homes,” the regional governor, Andriy Raikovych, said in a statement.Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 850 Shahed drones at a time when the speed of Ukraine’s defensive capabilities was being “artificially restricted”, a reference tosudden limitationson Ukraine’s use of the Starlink and Starshield mobile internet terminals.“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in a social media post on X, referring to a growing quarrel with theTrump administration.“Ukraine needs steady support, above all in defending our skies. We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security,” he said.Later, the British defence secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC that he had been “reassured directly” by his US counterpart Pete Hegseth that access to the vital Starlink communications system had been restored. The defence secretary said it was not yet clear to the UK why the disruption occurred, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.”View image in fullscreenWreckage of a Russian jet-powered drone lies inside a crater that appeared at the site of a residential area after a strike in Kyiv.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersTrump suddenly declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, writing on TruthSocial: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”Despite Trump’s claims, however, Russia continued to launch heavy strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, using hypersonic and ballistic missiles to target key Ukrainian power plants, leaving cities including Kyiv without power and water for hours. Ukraine said it would not strike Russian oil refineries in the interim in order to show that it was ready for negotiations.What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade Starlink system, and how will its restriction affect Ukraine?Read moreBut the White House piled pressure on Zelenskyy to capitulate to Russia by threatening to cut programmes to deliver arms to Ukraine and to stop sharing US battlefield intelligence with Ukraine.The US appeared to make good on some threats. Ukraine said it had not received advance warning from Washington of Russian missile strikes for several days this week. And on Wednesday, Ukrainian soldiers complained that their access to Starshield programmes controlled by the US military had been restricted, scuppering drone missions on the frontlines.On Thursday, a group of US senators from both major parties sent a letter to the Pentagon demanding it investigate whether the satellite and intelligence services had been deliberately restricted, and whether the Trump administration was responsible.“We are particularly alarmed by incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids, amid reported disruptions to intelligence-sharing and early-warning capabilities,” they wrote, according to the New York Times.The feud between Zelenskyy and Trump has spun out of control over the last week. Trump, who believes his support for Ukraine should come with a degree of control over the country’s leadership, has said Ukraine should “get a new president”.Zelenskyy, when asked on Thursday by Piers Morgan whether he felt betrayed, said yes. “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner,” he said.Musk, the head of SpaceX, which produces the Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military, has emerged as a leading critic of Zelenskyy in the US.On Thursday, Musk denied throttling the Starlink systems and said they were controlled by the US government. But in a social media post commenting on a Zelenskyy statement that Ukraine would continue to fight until Russia’s defeat, he wrote: “And so the slaughter continues … Time for Zelensky to go.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeUS foreign policyTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wes Streeting urges US to back Ukraine on Washington visit after Starlink row | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: UK defence secretary says he has been ‘reassured directly’ counterpart Pete Hegseth that Starlink system has been restored as he seeks to cool tensions
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: UK defence secretary says he has been ‘reassured directly’ counterpart Pete Hegseth that Starlink system has been restored as he seeks to cool tensions
Content: Wes Streeting is welcomed to the Pentagon by Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary.Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/APView image in fullscreenWes Streeting is welcomed to the Pentagon by Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary.Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/APForeign policyWes Streeting urges US to back Ukraine on Washington visit after Starlink rowUK defence secretary says he has been ‘reassured directly’ counterpart Pete Hegseth that Starlink system has been restored as he seeks to cool tensionsDan SabbaghDefence and security editorThu 15 Oct 2026 19.49 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 14.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWes Streeting urged the US to stand by Ukraine on his visit to the American capital and sought to cool tensions between the two countries in the wake of the Starlink row that is threatening to set back Kyiv’s war effort.The British defence secretary, giving a speech before a meeting with his US counterpart,Pete Hegseth, argued that supporting Ukraine was in the long-term interests of Washington, and a business opportunity.Taking questions after his address, Streeting acknowledged “the challenges of recent days”, a reference to the row over the sudden decision of the US government on Monday to limit the use of Starlink by Ukraine’s military.He said it was “a reminder of two things – one is that American support in Ukraine has been significant and it has made, I think, a real impact in the Ukrainian war effort. And we and the Ukrainians would feel the absence of that.”The second was that there was “an enormous opportunity for the US in terms of the support for Ukraine”, a reference to the future “defence-industrial relationship” between the countries.Streeting was speaking at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US thinktank, before meeting Hegseth amid tensions over Ukraine, Iran and the Middle East.Speaking to the BBC after the meeting, Streeting said he had been “reassured directly” by his US counterpart that access to the vital Starlink communications system had been restored. The defence secretary said it was not yet clear to the UK why the disruption occurred, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.”The two men were also expected to discuss the safety of US military bases in the UK, after an Iranian threat prompted the US to withdraw B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, and whether the two countries would come together to help Saudi Arabia, which has come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis.View image in fullscreenStreeting and Hegseth during a meeting at the Pentagon.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersBut it is Ukraine that is the most urgent issue. A day ago, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said hefelt personally betrayedby Donald Trump after the US government appeared to have throttled aversion of the Starlinksatellite internet service used by Ukraine’s military.Ukrainian officials have reported that the US has also threatened to cut the sharing of intelligence used by Ukraine to detect incoming missiles if it does not abandon its attacks on refineries, aimed at hurting the Russian economy.The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, meeting Zelenskyy in London on Wednesday, said the UK would stand by Ukraine.Developing the theme, Streeting made a direct appeal to the US audience, saying: “There’s rarely been a more important time for Britain and America to come together.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The people of Ukraine are fighting for a principle that runs through the finest traditions of American political thought,” he said, which was “that a free people have a right to determine their own destiny”.Trump has vacillated over supporting Ukraine against Russia since returning to the White House, while support among US Republicans for Kyiv has been mixed. But Streeting argued that helping Ukraine was also a matter of national self-interest for the US as well as the UK.“Ukraine may be thousands of miles from American shores, but if aggression is rewarded, if borders can be redrawn by force, if the sovereignty of nations becomes negotiable, the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine or to my continent,” he said.The change to Starlink happened without warning at about 1am, when Ukrainian soldiers reported that terminals on drones were no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph, rendering communications inoperable.It led to a dramatic halt to mid-strike drone attacks on targets in Russian occupied territories on the frontline, andconcerns about Ukraine’s ability to interceptnew Russian jet-powered attack craft that are bombing its cities.Trump has been trying to put pressure on Ukraine to halt its bombing of Russian oil refineries in a desperate attempt to reduce world oil prices before the US midterm elections. He agreed to buy diesel from Russia earlier this month.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyDefence policyWes StreetingUkraineRussiaEuropePete HegsethnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nineteen injured in collision between minibus and train on Eurotunnel loading platform | France | The Guardian
description: Two people critically hurt when vehicle carrying HGV drivers hit stationary train in Calais, say French authorities
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Two people critically hurt when vehicle carrying HGV drivers hit stationary train in Calais, say French authorities
Content: The Eurotunnel site on Thursday evening.Photograph: Maxppp/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Eurotunnel site on Thursday evening.Photograph: Maxppp/AlamyFranceNineteen injured in collision between minibus and train on Eurotunnel loading platformTwo people critically hurt when vehicle carrying HGV drivers hit stationary train in Calais, say French authoritiesNadeem Badshahand agenciesThu 15 Oct 2026 17.38 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 16.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNineteen people have been injured after a minibus collided with a stationary freight train at the loading platform of the Eurotunnel nearCalais, French authorities have said.Pas-de-Calais underprefect Agathe Cury said 18 passengers and the bus driver were injured in the incident.She told reporters that two people – including the driver – were critically injured and airlifted to the University hospital in Lille.The remaining 17 were taken to hospitals in Helfaut, Calais, Boulogne, Montreuil-sur-Mer and Dunkirk.Cury added: “There is no risk to anyone’s life.”The minibus was carrying lorry drivers bound for a shuttle train service through the tunnel on Thursday evening.About 200 emergency responders and other personnel rushed to the scene. The shuttle service through the tunnel was suspended for 90 minutes before gradually resuming by late evening, authorities said.Cury said an inquiry had been launched into the causes of the incident.She added “for reasons currently unknown” the minibus struck the shuttle “as it was departing”.Eurostar said the incident was not expected to affect its service. It said in a status update: “An incident occurred several kilometres away from the Channel tunnel. This incident does not involve or impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected.”The Pas-de-Calais prefecture said earlier in a statement: “An accident involving a minibus carrying heavy goods vehicle drivers, headed to board a LeShuttle train, occurred this evening at the loading platform of the Eurotunnel site.“Significant resources were immediately deployed by Eurotunnel, and subsequently placed under the authority of the Prefect of the Pas-de-Calais department.“Early reports suggest that 19 people were involved, including the driver. At this stage, there are no fatalities, and no one’s life is considered to be in danger.”A photograph published by local news outlet La Voix du Nord showed a badly damaged minibus on the platform, with police officers and staff in high-visibility jackets present at the scene.The tunnel, which opened in 1994, carried 3.4m vehicles last year along with millions of Eurostar passengers.Explore more on these topicsFranceCalaisEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Albania’s prime minister vows not to resign over student-led protests | Albania | The Guardian
description: Demonstrators demand resignation of Edi Rama after three days of clashes in capital Tirana
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Demonstrators demand resignation of Edi Rama after three days of clashes in capital Tirana
Content: An estimated 89 people, including 61 police officers, were injured during overnight clashes.Photograph: Hameraldi Agolli/APView image in fullscreenAn estimated 89 people, including 61 police officers, were injured during overnight clashes.Photograph: Hameraldi Agolli/APAlbaniaAlbania’s prime minister vows not to resign over student-led protestsDemonstrators demand resignation of Edi Rama after three days of clashes in capital TiranaHelena SmithThu 15 Oct 2026 13.52 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 06.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlbania’s prime minister has said he will not resign as a protest movement, initially prompted by a proposal to build a Trump family-backed resort in the Balkan state,turned violentwith clashes convulsing the capital for a third consecutive day.Speaking on Thursday after calls by students who this week assumed control of the anti-government demonstrationsthat have rattled Tirana since June, Edi Rama said: “Governments are changed through democratic elections. We had elections last year, not a revolution.”Rama’s comments to Reuters came hours before fresh clashes erupted outside the education ministry, where riot police responded to rock-throwing youths with teargas and water cannon. “My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keepAlbaniamoving forward,” he added.The alternative, he argued, would be tantamount “to a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership … I will not allow violence to derail Albania’s European future.”Rama,who won a historic fourth term last year, has vowed to get what was once the continent’s most isolated Stalinist state into the 27-member bloc by 2030.View image in fullscreenEdi Rama, pictured earlier this summer, has promised to secure EU membership for his country by 2030.Photograph: Malton Dibra/EPAThe unrest – in contrast to the largely peaceful protests of recent months – marks the veteran leader’s biggest challenge yet.On Thursday, after a night of running street battles between demonstrators and riot police, residents awoke to see the facades of shops smashed and traffic signals destroyed, with government buildings and banks burned and ransacked. An estimated 89 people, including 61 police officers, were injured.The renewed violence has created an atmosphere of unpredictability amid predictions that public patience may finally be running out for the socialist government after 13 years in power.“Young Albanians are tired of all the corruption, tired of all the arrogance. They want to live in a better country and they are not afraid to use violence,” said Afrim Krasniqi, the director of the Albanian Institute for Political Studies in Tirana. “There is no prognosis. Nobody can say what will come next.”But Rama, who emerged from the protest movement himself – becoming the face of state violence when he dared to criticise Albania’s first-post-communist government 30 years ago – also doubled down.“Students are the future. They are the ones who look ahead, who want to go further and faster,” he said as he visited the fire-damaged premises of Tirana’s College ofEuropeon Thursday. “Today, this is the ruin left by hands that are not, and can never be, the hands of students. These are the hands that try to push Albania down every time Albania tries to rise.”While he was willing to talk with the younger generation about the rising costs of education – a central complaint that has also spurred the unrest – vandalism would not be tolerated, he said.View image in fullscreenA hooded protester throws a petrol bomb at the College of Europe in Tirana on Wednesday night.Photograph: Hameraldi Agolli/APFor nearly five months, demonstrators have gathered daily outside Rama’s office, prompted by plans for a controversial tourism complex championed by the US president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. The venture foresees construction along pristine coastline deemed a conservation zone of unique natural beauty, includingthe uninhabited island of Sazan.Labelled the “flamingo revolution” because of the risk posed by the development to wildlife and delicate ecosystems, the rallies have attracted crowds big and small. They, too, have demanded the prime minister resign.Despite the opposition, Rama has steadfastly refused to back down, defending the project as a “gift” that will boost the economy and provide badly needed jobs by transforming Albania into a high-end tourist destination.View image in fullscreenPolice fired water cannon and teargas at protesters in the capital on Thursday.Photograph: Malton Dibra/EPABut Krasniqi said he believed the protest movement was at an inflection point – even if the demonstrations had also been inspired by similar student unrest sweeping Europe, particularly France.“I think this week we reached a turning point,” he said. “The government had more than four months to talk to people, who every day have been out on the street. It chose to belittle and dismiss them instead. And now students have joined in, and they appear to have the upper hand.”For the first time, Krasniqi said, he had heard young people saying they were prepared to be hurt or go to jail if that was the price “for ensuring democracy”.“Their demands are very different to the [flamingo] protesters. They want better education, better university buildings, a society that offers them hope. They also don’t believe Albania should be for sale.”At €4bn (€3.37bn), the Trump family-backed resort would be the biggest investment the nation has seen.Last week, addressing the controversy triggered by the project, Kushner admitted he and his investment firm, Affinity Partners, were “betting on a country that has never had a project of this scale”.View image in fullscreenA masked protester prepares to hurl an object.Photograph: Florion Goga/Reuters“There are no guarantees,” he said. “We are taking that risk because we believe in Albania and we believe in Albanians. If successful, the project would represent approximately €4bn of investment and create significant jobs, economic activity and international visibility for Albania.”This week environmentalists, who first led the charge against the development, begged to differ. Months after the protests began, people still felt as exercised about a venture many believed would only benefit the elite, said Aleksandër Trajçe, who heads the country’s leading conservation group, the Protection and Preservation of Natural Environment in Albania.“Anger over the [Kushner] project has prepared the ground for the violence we are seeing, because day after day protesters have been faced with the arrogance of a government that has refused to listen to them, or give an inch.”Explore more on these topicsAlbaniaEuropeProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Seven sailors missing after drones strike tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast | Russia | The Guardian
description: Nato source says drones came from Russia, while Romania’s president says attacking commercial ships ‘is unacceptable and has to stop’
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Nato source says drones came from Russia, while Romania’s president says attacking commercial ships ‘is unacceptable and has to stop’
Content: The Wine Trader after it was struck by drones in Romania waters.Photograph: Arsvom/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenThe Wine Trader after it was struck by drones in Romania waters.Photograph: Arsvom/AFP/GettyRussiaSeven sailors missing after drones strike tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coastNato source says drones came from Russia, while Romania’s president says attacking commercial ships ‘is unacceptable and has to stop’Jennifer Rankinin BrusselsThu 15 Oct 2026 13.31 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeven sailors are missing after drones struck two tankers near Romania’s Black Sea ⁠coast, setting them ablaze and raising ⁠fresh security concerns on a ​vital shipping route used by Ukraine.A Nato military source told Reuters the drones that had hit the Wine Trader and the Yara J came fromRussia. “The drones that caused ⁠the fires on board two tankers inside Romanian territorial waters were of Russian origin,” the source said.Romania’s president, Nicușor Dan, described the situation in the Black Sea as serious. “Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk,” he wrote on X. “Seafarers killed, injured and missing very close to the shores of Romania andBulgaria. This is unacceptable and it has to stop.”His statement followed a meeting with Bulgaria’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, and Nato’s secretary-general, Mark Rutte, on Thursday, where they agreed “to strengthen our defences in the Black Sea”, Dan said.Rutte said: “Nato will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed.”A Nato official said the issue would be discussed at a meeting of the North Atlantic Council next week.The missing crew were from the Wine Trader, a San Marino-flagged tanker travelling from Tunisia to Romania. All crew on the Yara J, which was struck just inside Romanian waters late on Wednesday, were safe.Similar incidents in recent weeks have raised fears that the zone is becoming another front in Russia’s war onUkraine.Dan said the two ships had been struck by drones, but declined to say whether Russia was responsible.Romania shares a 614km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube. The country has experienced frequent drone incursions since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, includinga daytime encroachment last November that led Nato to scramble fighter jets.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRussia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapsesRead moreEU leaders were already concerned about drone strikes on merchant ships off the coast of Bulgaria. On Tuesday, drone strikes on two ships off the coast of Bulgaria prompted emergency rescue operations, with 11 crew member from the HS Dignity, a cargo ship sailing under a Guinea-Bissau flag, still missing.On another ship, the Ukrainian-operated Chelsea 3 sailing under a Maltese flag, rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members, with five receiving treatment for minor injuries. The crew reported that the ship’s deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones.“The results of this attack favour Russia.
