However, we don’t have any solid evidence that the drones are Russians,” Radev said after arriving in Brussels for an EU summit on Thursday.At least 23 sailors have been reported missing or killed after attacks on commercial shipping near the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania in the past 10 days, according to Reuters.Russia has stepped up its bombing campaign on Ukraine’s Black Sea infrastructure, forcing Kyiv to turn to Danube river ports and Black Sea routes off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria to export its grain, sunflower oil and other products.According to a draft summit declaration, EU leaders will say that attacks against civilian shipping, including “member state-flagged vessels, such as the recent attacks in Bulgaria’s and Romania’s exclusive economic zones in the Black Sea, are unacceptable and constitute a serious violation of international and maritime law”.Explore more on these topicsRussiaUkraineShipping industryEuropeRomaniaBulgariaNatonewsShareReuse this content

title: Pakistan school roof collapse kills at least 34 children and teacher | Pakistan | The Guardian
description: Another three pupils from al-Khair school in Peshawar in critical condition after search for survivors
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Another three pupils from al-Khair school in Peshawar in critical condition after search for survivors
Content: A total of 110 students were attending lessons in three classrooms when the roof caved in.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenA total of 110 students were attending lessons in three classrooms when the roof caved in.Photograph: ReutersPakistanPakistan school roof collapse kills at least 34 children and teacherAnother three pupils from al-Khair school in Peshawar in critical condition after search for survivorsReuters in IslamabadThu 15 Oct 2026 04.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 34 schoolchildren and a female teacher have died after the roof of a school collapsed during morning classes in the northern Pakistani city ⁠of Peshawar.As panicked parents ​and relatives thronged the site of the privately run al-Khair school to search for their loved ones, rescue workers spent hours pulling children from the rubble.Most of the victims were under 13 years old ⁠and from low-income households. At least 45 children suffered injuries, ranging from minor wounds to severe trauma, said Arif Khattak, the regional director of emergency services.Map showing location of school and Lady Reading hospital in PeshawarTelevision footage showed rescuers clawing through debris with their bare hands and carrying bloodied children to ⁠waiting ambulances as people crowded the alley where the school stood.The roof of a higher floor collapsed on to classrooms below, crumpling two ​storeys of the building, a rescue official said. “The fatalities include ‌12 girl students and a female teacher,” said the Lady ‌Reading hospital spokesperson, Mohammad Asim. Three children remained in critical condition with head injuries, while most of the injured taken to the hospital ‌had been treated and discharged, he added.The incident took place at 8.48am local time (0348 GMT) and the rescue operation lasted for four to five hours, Khattak said. “It was a weak building structure,” said the Peshawar police chief, Mian Saeed. “Its roof was overloaded with construction on a weak structure, which caused the collapse.”Saeed said the school’s owner had been arrested and an investigation launched. A total of 110 students were attending lessons in three classrooms when the roof caved in.View image in fullscreenMourners attend funeral prayers for children who died in the roof collapse.Photograph: Maaz Awan/APDistraught relatives accused the school of ignoring concerns about ‌the building’s condition and demanded accountability. “Make an example of them, a lesson for all, so that no one dares open a school just to make money without providing facilities,” said Mohammad Zaman, who lost two nephews in the collapse.The ​school was located in a poor, crowded neighbourhood of Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, where Pakistan’s president imposed a state of emergency on Sunday, saying the provincial government had failed to tackle Islamist militancy from neighbouring Afghanistan, an allegation it denied.Pakistan spends less than 1% of its approximately $450bn (£340bn) GDP on education, leaving many families dependent on low-cost private schools.Many of those schools operate from poorly maintained rented buildings with limited oversight, contributing to recurring safety concerns. In June,at least ⁠14 children diedwhen the roof of a tutoring centre housed in a dilapidated building collapsed in the ​eastern city of Lahore.There was no immediate comment ​from school officials.The country’s prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, expressed ​sorrow over the tragedy and offered condolences to the victims’ families, his office said.Jawad Ahmad, whose son and daughter survived the incident, said the ‌news had left him devastated. “It felt ​as if someone had shot ​me in the chest when I learned that the school building had collapsed,” he said.The province, governed for years by the party of the jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, has frequently been at odds with the federal administration. Pakistan’s president, Asif Ali Zardari, imposed a new governor on the province when he declared the state of emergency on Sunday, sharpening the tensions.Explore more on these topicsPakistanSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Farage accused of ‘protecting’ Reform candidate over racist slurs against David Lammy | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: ITV investigation shows leader stood by mayoral candidate who said Labour MP should ‘go home to the Caribbean’
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Exclusive: ITV investigation shows leader stood by mayoral candidate who said Labour MP should ‘go home to the Caribbean’
Content: Nigel Farage on a walkabout in Chelmsford.Photograph: Will Colebourne/PAView image in fullscreenNigel Farage on a walkabout in Chelmsford.Photograph: Will Colebourne/PANigel FarageFarage accused of ‘protecting’ Reform candidate over racist slurs against David LammyExclusive: ITV investigation shows leader stood by mayoral candidate who said Labour MP should ‘go home to the Caribbean’Ben QuinnPolitical correspondentThu 15 Oct 2026 15.09 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 17.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage was told by a senior Reform official that he was “protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about David Lammy, an undercover investigation has revealed.The latest footage from an undercover investigation by ITV also shows Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”.1:18‘They are so chauvinistic’: Reform MP caught on camera in ITV investigation – videoOther footage shows Farage himself discussing thecase of Chris Parry, a retired rear admiral picked to contest the Hampshire and the Solent mayoral election for the party.The party stood by Parry for months after it emerged that he had said the former foreign secretary should “go home to the Caribbean” last year, and suggested that at least eight other politicians from minority ethnic backgrounds do not have a primary loyalty towards the UK.However, while Reform eventuallysuspended him in Marchafter the Guardian revealed other remarks by Parry, clips from an ITV documentary show Farage pushing back against senior advisers who said the candidate had to be sacked. They included Ed Sumner, Reform’s head of communications, who had told another press officer in an earlier disucussion that Parry was “clearly a racist”.“He needs to go, I’m getting rid of him,” Sumner was filmed saying when the controversy broke last December. However, Parry was still the candidate three weeks later, while Farage told a press conference that the candidate could stay if he apologised.In a conversation between Farage and Sumner, which was recorded by the undercover reporter, the Reform leader said that Parry “must apologise to Lammy” and was told that a text had been written for the candidate.“He must do it and move on … Tell him that from me,” Farage said, to which Sumner said: “You’re protecting him.”To laughter, Farage replied: “It’s showing a bit of … bit of sorrow. Look, ‘I’m sorry’ is probably a good thing to hear. Just take the fucking deal. Trouble is he’s a rear admiral. That’s the problem.”Parry was suspended on 26 March after the Guardian reported that he had described members of a Jewish neighbourhood watch group as“cosplayers”and likened them to “Islamists on horseback”.Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said these “latest shocking and deeply disturbing revelations go right to the top of Reform”, adding: “Nigel Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him. He also must urgently explain why he allegedly stood by a blatant racist instead of kicking him out of his party.”The revelations are the latest in a number of recent controversies for Reform. The full ITV documentary, Undercover: A Year in Reform, airs on Sunday.A number of councillors have already stood down after segments from the investigation aired on Wednesday showed them making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views.Reform UK councillors and candidates filmed making racist and misogynist commentsRead moreThe undercover reporter for ITV also met Pochin, Reform’s MP for Runcorn and Helsby, at a time when she was the party’s only female member of parliament.When Pochin was told that a new female press officer was starting work, she was recorded as saying: “Oh thank fuck for that. God! We so need women press officers … They are so fucking chauvinistic.“I go out on all the shows and go: ‘Oh no, it’s lovely, oh they’re all so welcoming.’ Shit … they just exclude you if you’re a woman. It’s really tough being a girl with all of this alpha male shit going on.”Pochin did not provide a statement when approached by ITV.Reform UKused a statement issued on Thursday to accuse ITV and the company behind the documentary, Hardcash Productions, of using “extreme methods of deception”.It said: “They have infiltrated our workplace including commissioning an undercover journalist to provide altered identification documents, a false address, and false credentials so that they could be given access to Reform’s headquarters, computer systems, and spy on its employees.“That same journalist did not limit themselves to recording candid conversations in the workplace. That journalist also sought to find out sensitive security information, travel arrangements, and financial information outside of the scope of this investigation.”Reform went on to claim that ITV had failed to address this in correspondence, despite this conduct being drawn to its attention. “This is at a time when Nigel Farage and other members of Reform are being targeted by individuals who wished them harm and caused a security issue which was documented during the course of the undercover investigation,” it added.“There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases.”When approached for comment, Parry referred the Guardian to a statement given to ITV. In it he said: “I would urge people to go back to the original contexts and tweets to see what was said and why. They related to reparations and failures by the police and government. They will see I always exercise my right to criticise anyone in power or the public eye whom I judge to be acting against the interests of the British people.”Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageReform UKDocumentary filmsFar rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand made alleged rape victim take photos of him half naked, trial told | UK news | The Guardian
description: Woman claims comedian ‘pranced around like an ostrich’ before forcing himself on her in hotel room attack
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Woman claims comedian ‘pranced around like an ostrich’ before forcing himself on her in hotel room attack
Content: A photograph of Russell Brand that his alleged rape victim says he made her take in a Bournemouth hotel room.Photograph: Metropolitan police/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA photograph of Russell Brand that his alleged rape victim says he made her take in a Bournemouth hotel room.Photograph: Metropolitan police/AFP/Getty ImagesUK newsRussell Brand made alleged rape victim take photos of him half naked, trial toldWoman claims comedian ‘pranced around like an ostrich’ before forcing himself on her in hotel room attackEmine SinmazThu 15 Oct 2026 14.01 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Brand transformed into a “monster” when he allegedly made a woman take half-naked photographs of him before raping her in a hotel room at a Labour party conference, a court has heard.The 51-year-old comedian has denied attacking the woman, who broke down in tears in the witness box at Southwark crown court as she told how she could not fight him off.“He was really heavy,” she said. “I couldn’t struggle. I couldn’t breathe. I know he raped me, I know I said: ‘No, no, I don’t want this.’”Brand faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.8:24‘I couldn’t breathe’: Russell Brand trial hears from first alleged victim - The LatestBrand fixed his gaze on one of the TV screens in court on Thursday morning as a video of the woman’s interview from 27 September 2023 was played. She told police she met Brand at a fringe cabaret event that he was performing in during the Labour party conference in Bournemouth in 1999. She was not attracted to the then unknown performer, whom she assumed was gay and who showered her with compliments.But she found him polite and intelligent, and the pair spoke about their work before going back to her hotel room to continue their conversation.The woman said she “froze” in the run-down single room when she returned from the toilet to find that Brand was partly naked and “prancing around” like an ostrich. She said she asked him why he had undressed, and he told her: “Don’t worry, I’m mostly naked at home.”The woman told how she became “frightened” when Brand made her take half-naked photographs of him.“I took pictures of him on my camera – he made me take them,” she said. “I remember feeling: ‘What on earth have I got myself into?’”She told police he then raped her in an attack that lasted up to 10 minutes and left her feeling scared, in pain, and as if she couldn’t breathe.“He did rape, he did push me on the bed,” she told police. “He did pull my clothes off, he took my trousers off.“I remember him on me, very heavy. I know I said no. I kind of drifted out of my head. I couldn’t get out of the situation – ‘do I shout, do I scream?’ He was very heavy, I couldn’t breathe, it didn’t take long.”View image in fullscreenRussell Brand’s alleged victim said she felt ‘frightened’ when he asked her to take photographs of him half naked.Photograph: Metropolitan police/AFP/Getty ImagesShe described his body as snake-like and “disgusting” and said his tongue was “horrible” like a lizard. “I’m saying ‘no, no’ but I was really scared,” she told police. “I know he groped me. I know he was touching me, I know he grabbed my breasts. I know he tried to kiss me and I moved my neck. I didn’t want his mouth on mine.“He was just pulling my trousers down and pulling my underwear off, and he was inside me. It was not nice, it was painful and it hurt.”Giving evidence from behind a screen in the afternoon, the woman added: “I was like a zombie on the bed. All I could think was he’s inside me and the quicker the better.”In tense exchanges during cross-examination with the defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, the woman denied that Brand had persuaded her to have sex. “He was frightening, he seemed menacing at that point,” she replied. “He’s scary. I didn’t know what to do.”She rejected Winter’s suggestion that she had fallen under the spell of Brand, whom the barrister described as charismatic with a magnetic personality. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, had to interrupt the lawyer during one exchange to object to one of his questions, saying: “Shush please. I’m the judge, you have to let me talk.”The woman told the court Brand was a “completely different persona” in the hotel room. When pressed further by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones, the woman said: “He just changed suddenly from camp, friendly and effeminate to monster-like.“I felt very scared in that moment. He was big, I felt threatened and he’s half naked. And while I’m naive, I didn’t think at that moment his intentions were good.“He was just dark and arrogant and performing – he was scary, he was demanding. He was the centre of the show, it was like it was back on stage – he wasn’t the [same] person I was chatting to.”The woman told police she closed her eyes during the attack and that Brand made her feel sick and dirty. She recalled: “He was making noises, a lot of noises of enjoyment and saying how pretty I was. I remember him complimenting me, saying: ‘Are you enjoying it’? I remember him asking me. Obviously I didn’t answer.”She alleged that Brand spoke as the attack was unfolding. She told police: “He was just saying: ‘We’re having fun, it’s fine, it’s all good, don’t worry about it, it’s just fun, it’s normal.’”View image in fullscreenBrand (left) leaves Southwark crown court after Thursday’s proceedings.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersThe woman, who had been a victim of abuse in the past, said Brand made her compare earlier experiences, and it “stuck in her head … is this what abusers do?”She told police: “It was almost like to convince me it’s all OK and that I’d enjoy it, that I’d have to learn to enjoy it.”In the aftermath, she said Brand acted “like nothing was wrong”, wrote down his email address, and suggested that his mother might like to meet her.She told the court: “He is so arrogant in his mindset that he’s God’s gift that I must’ve enjoyed it and I must’ve wanted more.”The following morning, she banged her head against the wall because she felt numb. She told police she had had nightmares about being pregnant and said she kept quiet about the incident for years as she watched Brand becoming “more and more famous”.The woman said a 2023 Dispatches documentary about allegations of sexual misconduct by Brand “triggered” her to go to police.Brand denies the allegations. The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK HRT shortages: which products are affected and what to do about it | Menopause | The Guardian
description: Experts say seeking alternatives that deliver the same dose of oestrogen by the same method is key
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Experts say seeking alternatives that deliver the same dose of oestrogen by the same method is key
Content: Estradot, one of the products affected, is the second longest running individual medicine shortage in the UK.Photograph: Nicola K photos/AlamyView image in fullscreenEstradot, one of the products affected, is the second longest running individual medicine shortage in the UK.Photograph: Nicola K photos/AlamyMenopauseExplainerUK HRT shortages: which products are affected and what to do about itExperts say seeking alternatives that deliver the same dose of oestrogen by the same method is keyNicola DavisScience correspondentThu 15 Oct 2026 13.58 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWomen in the UK are again facing shortages of some HRT products, with warnings they could persist for weeks. We take a look at the situation.What is HRT?Hormone replacement therapy is widely used to help women manage symptoms of menopause. It can take many forms, from gels and sprays to patches, pills, creams and intrauterine systems.As the NHS notes,HRT typically involves two hormones – oestrogen and progestogen – and replaces levels lost as women go through menopause. These can be given separately or in a single type of HRT. Women who have had a hysterectomy only require oestrogen-containing HRT.According to theNHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA), almost 2 million women in England aged 40 and above were prescribed HRT for menopause symptoms in 2025-26. Experts, however, say thataccess variesand shortages have been a problem.Which items are affected by the current shortages?According to amedicine supply notificationissued by the Department of Health and Social Care this week, FemSeven Contipatches are out of stock and are expected to remain so until late November. The patches contain estradiol – a type of oestrogen– and a synthetic progestogen called levonorgestrel.There are alsoshortages of various Estradot patches– a type of HRT that contains estradiol – and the situation is not expected to end until January.This isnot the first timethere have been HRT shortages, and the supply issues affecting Estradot have been long-lasting. The shortages of some products began in December 2024, according toNHSBSA.“When you have found an HRT treatment that helps you sleep, manage hot flushes and feel more like yourself, being told it is unavailable can be unsettling,” said Sobia Qasim, a pharmacist at the online pharmacyCurely.Sehar Shahid, a member of the National Pharmacy Association’s board, also raised concerns. “We are deeply frustrated and concerned by shortages to a number of HRT products, with shortages of Estradot being the second longest running individual medicine shortage in the UK,” she said.“Certain HRT products are specialised and cannot always be easily substituted for an alternative.”What alternatives are there?According to the FemSeven Conti notification, alternative patches include Evorel Conti, Estradot Conti 30/95 and Estradot Conti 40/130. These contain estradiol and a different type of synthetic progestogen called norethisterone, and are used twice rather than once a week.Paula Briggs, a consultant in sexual and reproductive health and a former chair of the British Menopause Society, said keeping the same dose of estradiol was the important aspect. “They have different progestogens, but I do not think that that would have any adverse impact on symptom control,” she said, noting progestogens are required to protect the lining of the womb rather than manage symptoms.Serious shortage protocols for the Estradot products also list alternatives, such as estradiol-containing patches by Estraderm MX and Evorel. “If we’re using the same dose of oestrogen delivered in a similar patch through the skin, really there is no need to worry,” said Briggs.What should women do if they are affected by the shortages?Shahid said people who had experienced disruption to their usual HRT regime should speak to their clinician, while Qasim cautioned against leaving a patch on for longer than prescribed, cutting patches up or borrowing HRT treatments from others.What needs to happen next?Briggs said shortages were likely to occur in the future “because year on year we’re seeing a more than 10% increase in use”, she said.Shahid urged the government to take action. “The new secretary of state should convene a taskforce to fully grasp this issue, bringing together all aspects of the supply chain,” she said.Explore more on these topicsMenopauseWomen's healthNHSHealthDrugsPharmaceuticals industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Thames Water asks for £2.4bn more to avoid going bust this year or early 2027 | Thames Water | The Guardian
description: Water company tells creditors it will not survive long enough to agree refinancing deal without more money
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Water company tells creditors it will not survive long enough to agree refinancing deal without more money
Content: Thames Water has drawn down most of a £3bn lifeline creditors gave it in February 2025 without reaching a long-term deal on cutting its debts and getting fresh investment.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenThames Water has drawn down most of a £3bn lifeline creditors gave it in February 2025 without reaching a long-term deal on cutting its debts and getting fresh investment.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAThames WaterThames Water asks for £2.4bn more to avoid going bust this year or early 2027Water company tells creditors it will not survive long enough to agree refinancing deal without more moneyJasper JollyThu 15 Oct 2026 13.14 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThames Water has asked its creditors for another £2.4bn as the embattled water company comes close to running out of cash.The UK’s largest water company said on Thursday it needed another short-term cash injection because it would be unable to reach a longer-term deal to sort out its giant debt pile before running out of cash by “the end of 2026 or the start of 2027”.Thames Water said in a statement to the stock market that it “does not expect to complete its recapitalisation process ahead of this date”, meaning it would run out of cash without creditors stumping up more.The utility company serves 16 million customers in London and the Thames valley. However, it has been on the brink of collapse for several years after it becameoverwhelmed by a debt pilethat is now about £20bn. Its shareholders walked away, leaving the company under the effective control of its creditors while they work out a deal to avoid bankruptcy.The creditors gave Thames a £3bn lifelinein February last yearto try to see it through negotiations on a deal to cut its debts and inject more money. Thecreditors, collectively called the London & Valley Water company, are led by a group of American hedge funds such as Elliott Management and Silver Point Capital, and institutional investors including BlackRock and M&G.However, those talks have dragged on, and the water company has now drawn down £2.65bn of the £3bn, leaving it perilously close to running out of cash even as it carries out a series of expensive repairs and upgrades.The Guardian view on Thames Water: Andy Burnham should nationalise this failed monopoly | EditorialRead moreThames said the extra cash would “extend […] liquidity into autumn 2027 and allow [it] to continue to deliver its capital programme and deliver improvements for customers and the environment”.Thames Water’s creditors have drawn up detailed proposals for a rescue plan that would involve them writing off £9.6bn in loans. However, that plan hinges on Ofwat agreeing to let the company pay set penalties for several years upfront, and effectively creating a special regime for the company. That prospect has proven politically unpalatable for the Labour government.Some Labour politicians and environmental campaigners called on Keir Starmer and then Andy Burnham to put Thames Water into special administration, a form of temporary government control while a new buyer is sought.Burnham has pledged more public control of the UK’s water industry, and has said that public ownership for Thames Water“is what should be done”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn addition, the change of prime minister has led to regulatory uncertainty for the broader water industry. Starmer’s government had committed to implementing recommendations on changes to the water system from the former Bank of England deputy governor Sir John Cunliffe, but Burnham’s government has not yet made clear what it plans to do.Thames Water said it “continues to work closely with stakeholders to secure a market-led solution”.Thames Water’s creditors are expected to vote on the proposals later in the month.Explore more on these topicsThames WaterWater industryUtilitiesLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Eritrea accuses Shabana Mahmood of ‘political gimmick’ over visa ban threat | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Home secretary says she will block all Eritreans from UK unless a returns deal is agreed for rejected asylum seekers and criminals
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Home secretary says she will block all Eritreans from UK unless a returns deal is agreed for rejected asylum seekers and criminals
Content: Shabana Mahmood: ‘My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK.’Photograph: Marcin Nowak/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood: ‘My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK.’Photograph: Marcin Nowak/Anadolu/Getty ImagesImmigration and asylumEritrea accuses Shabana Mahmood of ‘political gimmick’ over visa ban threatHome secretary says she will block all Eritreans from UK unless a returns deal is agreed for rejected asylum seekers and criminalsRajeev SyalandDiane TaylorThu 15 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShabana Mahmood has been accused of launching a “perfunctory political gimmick” by the Eritrean government in a row over the return of rejected asylum seekers and criminals.After the home secretary threatened to block all Eritreans from entering the UK unless a returns deal was agreed, the country’s embassy claimed the UK had failed to engage in “meaningful and appropriate” dialogue.The spat began on Thursday morning when theHome Officeclaimed the east African country had abruptly withdrawn cooperation on the return of unwanted citizens earlier this year.From Thursday, diplomats from the east African country also face restrictions on their movement outside London and VIPs will be stripped of access to fast-track visas as preferential processing is scrapped.It prompted a statement from Eritrea’s north London embassy “categorically” rejecting Mahmood’s claims.“Despite Eritrea’s repeated requests for constructive discussion with relevant UK authorities on the dignified return of its citizens, the UK has shown no interest to engage in meaningful and appropriate dialogue,” it said.Describing the home secretary’s decision as regrettable, the statement added: “The act is nothing more than a perfunctory political gimmick. The fact is, the UK has not issued a single visa to an Eritrean official since 2023.”UK government officials denied this. They insisted a confirmed exemption from immigration control for an Eritrean official took place as recently as August 2026.Sources said Eritrea previously cooperated with the UK on returns between 2024 and March 2026, while the UK has repeatedly sought to engage with Eritrean authorities, including repeatedly offering to send a Home Office delegation to Asmara to discuss returns.A Home Office spokesperson said: “The Eritrean government’s press notice misrepresents the UK’s position and contains numerous factual inaccuracies.”Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat in the year ending June 2026. Returns arrangements are vital for removing people who have been refused asylum and foreign criminals.Graph showing cumulative number of arrivals to the UK in small boats by nationality since January 2025, with those from Eritrea being the largest numberMahmood said on Thursday morning: “Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused.“My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK. I will not hesitate to impose further measures on other countries refusing to cooperate.”The move followed similar threats of visa sanctions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2025.Angola and Namibia subsequently agreed to cooperate with demands on migrant returns, while the DRC faced visa restrictions before reaching an agreement with the UK in February.In March, ministers also placed an emergency brake on visas for nationals from four countries after the home secretary accused them of exploiting Britain’s generosity to claim asylum.Study visas for nationals from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan were also halted, as were work visas for Afghans.Just over 100 refused asylum seekers from Eritrea have been deported – a figure comprising less than 4% of the 2,626 people whose claims were rejected in the past four years. Nearly 6,000 Eritreans have reached the UK across the Channel in the year to June, the highest number of any nationality.After the success of the previous sanction threats, Mahmood warned other countries that they faced similar visa restrictions if they continued to refuse to take back their criminals, illegal migrants and rejected asylum seekers.India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Somalia, Egypt and Gabon have been identified as resistant to taking back illegal migrants and could face sanctions.Madeleine Sumption, the director of theMigrationObservatory at Oxford University, said roughly 7,000 applications for asylum came from Eritreans, about 8% of the total.About 84% were successful on first application and more would be successful on appeal, she said.“There are different types of threats that can be made such as stopping student visas, or stopping visit visas. It will be interesting to see what kind of impact this has on the number of returns.”Reacting to Mahmood’s announcement, one Eritrean asylum seeker said any returnees would “be put in prison and may never be able to get out”.The advocacy group Justice for Eritreans condemned the announcement. “Many Eritreans have fled indefinite national service, arbitrary detention and severe human rights abuses,” it said. “These risks cannot be ignored for the sake of immigration targets. Refugee protection is a legal responsibility, not a political bargaining tool.”UN experts say the human rights situation in Eritrea continues to be dire. Mohamed Abdelsalam Babiker, the special rapporteur on human rights in Eritrea, said there were no signs of meaningful improvement in the country’s human rights situation.“There remain reasonable grounds to believe that crimes against humanity continue in Eritrea,” he said whenlaunching a reportthis year into the human rights situation.“Regrettably, the core human rights issues that prompted the creation of this mandate 14 years ago remain mostly unresolved.“The ongoing systematic, and widespread enforced disappearance and prolonged incommunicado detention without charge or trial, torture, and the persecution of political opponents, journalists, and members of religious communities remain central features of governance in Eritrea.”Steve Valdez-Symonds, Amnesty International’s policy lead on refugee and migrant rights, said: “As Amnesty and others have documented, Eritrea has an appalling human rights record.“It has not become any less unsafe following the election in this country of a Labour government in 2024 or Shabana Mahmood beginning her term at the Home Office in 2025.”Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said: “Severe political repression and widespread human rights abuses are the reason people are forced to flee Eritrea, and are, in the vast majority of cases, recognised by our government as in need of support.“It’s imperative that this policy only targets the Eritrean authorities, and does not undermine the UK’s moral and legal duty to provide protection to those who need it.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumEritreaShabana MahmoodMigrationRefugeesHome OfficenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s new press secretary says it’s ‘unknown’ how much she’ll deal with media | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Katie Zacharia tells Guardian her first, widely panned, press briefing followed whirlwind sprint to appoint her to key role
Author: Shrai Popat
Headline: Katie Zacharia tells Guardian her first, widely panned, press briefing followed whirlwind sprint to appoint her to key role
Content: Trump’s press secretary, Katie Zacharia, arrives in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Tuesday.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenTrump’s press secretary, Katie Zacharia, arrives in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Tuesday.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APTrump administrationTrump’s new press secretary says it’s ‘unknown’ how much she’ll deal with mediaKatie Zacharia tells Guardian her first, widely panned, press briefing followed whirlwind sprint to appoint her to key roleShrai Popatin WashingtonThu 15 Oct 2026 18.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 20.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s new White House press secretary says it is “unknown” how much she will engage with the press or hold briefings with reporters, as she faces mounting questions over her legal credentials.In a brief interview with the Guardian on Thursday, Katie Zacharia detailed the whirlwind sprint to replace her predecessor Karoline Leavitt as the US president’s chief spokesperson.Just six days after receiving a call from the White House, Zacharia stepped behind the podium for her first briefing as press secretary, in a debut that has beenwidely panned.Last Wednesday, 7 October, a White House official called Zacharia and asked her to travel from Los Angeles, where she lives with her family, to Washington for a meeting. (She declined to specify who made the call.)Zacharia made the trip the following day, before meeting officials on Pennsylvania Avenue on Friday. She was offered the job later that day – and accepted.“I flew home, packed two bags, said hi to my kids and husband and dogs,” Zacharia said, before returning to Washington on Sunday ahead of her first day on Monday.Enter the Zachbot: Trump’s new press secretary malfunctions on podium debutRead moreBut her first briefing, which Zacharia said she was “asked to do” on her second day in the job, was criticized as lackluster.And she has since faced intense scrutiny over her claimed legal qualifications. After her debut briefing on Tuesday, reporters asked Zacharia to name the state where she passed the bar exam. “When I moved to China”, she replied.She latertold the New York Timesshe had “misheard” the question over the sound of Marine One on the South Lawn and thought the reporter had asked: “Where were you after law school?” However, she did not confirm to the Times whether she had passed the bar exam. According to her LinkedIn profile, after graduating from Pepperdine University’s law school in 2011, Zacharia was an “associate” at the Beijing law firm Zhong Lun from 2011 to 2013.This week, the Wall Street Journalreported, citing a person familiar with the matter, that Zacharia failed the California bar exam after graduating from law school.The State Bar of California told the Guardian it had no record of Zacharia being licensed in the state under either her married name or her maiden name, Katie Black. While Trump has referred to Zacharia as an “attorney”, that title is reserved for those licensed to practice law.In a differentinterviewwith the conservative outlet Human Events on Thursday, Zacharia acknowledged to the rightwing influencer Jack Posobiec that she didn’t pass the California bar. At the time, she said she was “distracted and overwhelmed and excited” to join her new husband in China, where he was working, after being in a long-distance relationship for more than a year.A person familiar with the matter said Zacharia “stands by” referring to herself as a lawyer, and that she considered the designation a “valid title”, given her law degree and “international transactional law experience”. She did so after “consulting with other legal professionals and attorneys” about whether it was an appropriate designation, the source claimed, adding that Zacharia had “never given legal advice”; just “legal analysis”.However, many legal experts note that “lawyer” and “attorney” are often used interchangeably. On Wednesday,the Campaign for Accountability, a non-profit watchdog organization, asked the State Bar of California to investigate whether Zacharia misled the public, and potentially violated state law, by describing herself as a lawyer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter her time in China, there is a 10-year gap on Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile. Wiredreportedon Thursday that during that period she worked as an “affiliate marketer” for Beachbody, a multi-level marketing company she described to the outlet as “sort of a pyramid scheme”.She later claims to have served as “general counsel” for Fix California, a conservative group founded by Richard Grenell, a longtime Trump ally and the special presidential envoy for special missions. The Guardian has approached both Zhong Lun and Fix California seeking additional details about Zacharia’s legal roles at the organizations.Zacharia also said she “did not want to be seen lobbying” for the press secretary role, in her interview with the conservative outlet Human Events. Instead, she said she closely monitored Trump’s social media posts before appearing on conservative talkshows to “audition” for the job.When Trump announced that Zacharia had been tapped for the post, he described her as a “devoted fan of Maga” who has “an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning”.Asked by the Guardian what reasons the White House gave for offering her the position, Zacharia – who previously served as an adviser to Trump Media Group, which owns the president’s Truth Social platform, and had a brief stint as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security – declined to comment.Now the White House press secretary, she also would not clarify on Thursday how often she intended to brief the press. She said that was “unknown at this time” and that Trump “is his best spokesperson, and I will interact as needed”.“I follow the president’s lead,” Zacharia added.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS politicsDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: California faces more extreme weather as hot, windy days raise wildfire risk | California | The Guardian
description: Warnings come as Californians have already in autumn felt brutal heatwave and storm surge that battered coast
Author: Gabrielle Canon
Headline: Warnings come as Californians have already in autumn felt brutal heatwave and storm surge that battered coast
Content: A firefighter sprays a hotspot while fighting the Bike fire in the outskirts of Santa Clarita, California, earlier this week.Photograph: David Swanson/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA firefighter sprays a hotspot while fighting the Bike fire in the outskirts of Santa Clarita, California, earlier this week.Photograph: David Swanson/AFP/Getty ImagesCaliforniaCalifornia faces more extreme weather as hot, windy days raise wildfire riskWarnings come as Californians have already in autumn felt brutal heatwave and storm surge that battered coastGabrielle Canonin OaklandThu 15 Oct 2026 16.56 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCommunities acrossCaliforniaare bracing for more dangerous weather this week, with strong winds and high temperatures that could set the stage for rapid wildfire growth over the next several days.“A moderate to strong Santa Ana wind will bring widespread strong winds and critical fire weather conditions to much of south-west California through Saturday,” the National Weather Service said in a forecast issued on Thursday.Strong, dry winds could reach 20-40mph (32 to 64 km/h), with gusts from 50-70mph in the San Gabriel mountains in Los Angeles county and the Santa Susana mountains, which are mostly in Ventura county, officials said. Critical fire weather conditions are also forecast for portions of the Santa Lucia mountains in San Luis Obispo county.The elevated risks come amid a tumultuous start to autumn that has already brought severeheatwaves,high surfandflooding– and this may just be the beginning, according to experts.Destructive conditions fueled by apotentially historic El Niño brewing in the Pacificwill continue to mount through the end of this year and into next. The impacts, which have already raised sea levels, increased temperatures and supercharged storms in the Pacific, layer on top of natural hazards and those fueled by the human-caused climate crisis.The so-called Santa Ana winds in this week’s forecast are expected during this time of year, along with higher fire dangers that typically linger in the state through November. But on the heels of the recent storm surge that battered the California coast, the weather whiplash has left residents reeling.With the threat of fire, heat and sea level rise colliding, as the state readies for more incoming effects from El Niño, Kevin McGowan, the director of LA’s office of emergency management, urged residents to be ready. “People should continue to prepare not just for one hazard,” he said during a recent briefing, “but all hazards”.In Los Angeles, where strong Santa Ana winds fueled the devastating 2025 firestorm that killed more than 30 people, the warnings were sharply felt. Neighborhoods are still being rebuilt after multiple blazes consumed more than 16,000 structures, and the huge burn scars left behind have increased the dangers for debris flows and landslides, should the elevated chances of severe storms materialize over this winter.Officials are preparing to meet the fire risks head on to protect communities now and in months that follow. New fires will mean more risks in the season ahead.“If there is any significant fire activity this week, it would be somewhat poorly timed in the context of El Niño,” said climate scientist Daniel Swain in an online briefing on Wednesday. “We know the likelihood of a wet winter in southern California is now very high. [Fire] would further raise the stakes.”Thousands of people in California were without electricity on Thursday as utilities tried to reduce the risk of hot, windy weather that could blow over power lines and spark wildfires.In northern California, nearly 62,000 customers in 26 counties had no electricity, according to Pacific Gas and Electric Company. The company began proactively turning off power on Wednesday night. Weather conditions that increase the fire risk were expected to last through Saturday.Los Angeles Fire chief, Jaime Moore, said staffing has been augmented and equipment pre-deployed so crews will be ready.“We are asking residents to do their part too,” he added. “Clear the streets, have a plan and stay informed.”‘Like an earthquake’: El Niño is coming for California – is the state ready?Read moreWith the risks rising across California, the state’s office of emergency services has also increased its coordination and readied resources to support local officials should disaster strike, according to spokesperson Chris Dargan.The National Weather Service issued fire weather warnings for parts of central and northern California, starting on Thursday and lasting through Friday morning, saying any fires would spread rapidly.“It’s a pretty widespread event of elevated fire weather, so the whole SoCal region should really be on alert,” said Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.The Associated Press contributed in reportingExplore more on these topicsCaliforniaWildfiresUS weatherWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Key US voters say economy is getting worse ahead of midterms, exclusive poll finds | US economy | The Guardian
description: Nearly 61% believe country is in recession and 65% of independents say economy is worse, according to new Harris poll
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: Nearly 61% believe country is in recession and 65% of independents say economy is worse, according to new Harris poll
Content: Shoppers checking out at a Costco Wholesale store in Colchester, Vermont.Photograph: Robert Nickelsberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShoppers checking out at a Costco Wholesale store in Colchester, Vermont.Photograph: Robert Nickelsberg/Getty ImagesUS economyKey US voters say economy is getting worse ahead of midterms, exclusive poll findsNearly 61% believe country is in recession and 65% of independents say economy is worse, according to new Harris pollTell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?Lauren Arataniin New YorkThu 15 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 16.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith the midterm elections less than three weeks away, key voting groups including independents, rural voters and even some Republicans are increasingly disenchanted with Donald Trump’s economy, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian.The majority of those surveyed were pessimistic about the economy, with three-quarters of Americans saying they are concerned about a recession while 61% wrongly believe that the US is already experiencing one. By its typical definition, the US is not currently experiencing a recession.The poll shows growing weariness across the political spectrum over high prices.33:55Why are prices so high? Robert Reich answers your questions – Stateside with Kai and CarterRepublicans, fighting to keep control of Congress, are losing support with independent voters, who are expected to be the deciding factor in key swing races. Nearly two-thirds (65%) of independents said the economy was worse, up from 48% who said the same in September 2024 in the heat of the 2024 presidential election.Even within the Republican ranks, optimism has waned. In February 2025, just a few weeks after Trump was inaugurated, 39% of Republicans said the economy was getting better. By February 2026, just before the US launched attacks against Iran, that optimism was up to 49%. In the latest poll, just 28% of Republicans said the economy was getting better.A graphic showing percentage change in number of people who believe US is experiencing a recessionVoters say the high prices they are seeing at gas stations and grocery stores will be a key factor when they cast their votes in November. Two-thirds of those polled said that gas prices and grocery prices are their most important issues heading into the election, followed by living expenses, healthcare costs and foreign affairs.Graph showing food and gas prices are top midterm issuesRecentinflation datashowed that annualized prices increased 3.7% in September, the highest reading before a midterm election, excluding the pandemic, since 1990.Energy prices have been especially high since the Iran war, with average gas prices at the pump crossing $1.20 more per gallon compared with a year ago. California drivers, who are experiencing the highest gas prices, are paying on average $6.20 per gallon, according toAAA.Democrats in swing races have spent much of the last few months framing their midterm battles as a fight, in part, against a growing affordability crisis. James Talarico, the Democratic candidate in a closely watched US Senate race in Texas, has a campaign ad of him holding a paper bag of groceries. “Too many Texans feel like they’re drowning, the cost of groceries, gas, healthcare,” he says in thevideo.“They say I can’t win because of my name,” Abdul El-Sayed, another Democratic candidate for a US Senate race in Michigan,saidat a recent campaign event. “My name is not the reason your gas prices are through the roof. My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”In the new poll, a vast majority of Americans agreed that there was an affordability crisis, including 96% of Republicans. But Americans still remain divided over who has a solution.Democrats (71%) were more likely than Republicans (59%) to say that their own party had a solution.Republicans were more likely (26%) to say neither party had a solution compared with Democrats (17%)Half of independents said neither party had a solution, while 14% sided with Democrats and 10% with Republicans.A graph showing percentage of polled people who responded they are in ‘survival mode’ when asked about their financial situation today, by urbanicity.Rural Americans, considered a core base for Trump, were more likely to believe that neither party has a solution (41%) compared with their suburban (35%) and urban (27%) counterparts. Four out of 10 of rural Americans said they were living in “survival mode”, where one surprise bill could sink them, compared with 35% of urban and 27% of suburban Americans.When asked what is most affecting today’s gas prices, 46% of rural Americans said the US government compared with 28% of Republicans who said the same. Republicans were the least likely of any group to blame the US government, instead spreading the blame across oil companies, the Iranian government and natural economic fluctuations.This survey was conducted online within the US by The Harris Poll from 24 September to 3 October 2026 among a nationally representative sample of 3,998 USadults.Explore more on these topicsUS economyUS midterm elections 2026Donald TrumpInflationEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US lawmakers unveil bill to hold Wall Street’s ‘Epstein-connected’ bosses to account | Banking | The Guardian
description: Move comes as Senator Elizabeth Warren condemns Barclays response to questions over ex-boss’s ties to sex offender
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Move comes as Senator Elizabeth Warren condemns Barclays response to questions over ex-boss’s ties to sex offender
Content: The proposed bill follows a months-long investigation into Jeffrey Epstein who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.Photograph: Uma Sanghvi/APView image in fullscreenThe proposed bill follows a months-long investigation into Jeffrey Epstein who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.Photograph: Uma Sanghvi/APBankingUS lawmakers unveil bill to hold Wall Street’s ‘Epstein-connected’ bosses to accountMove comes as Senator Elizabeth Warren condemns Barclays response to questions over ex-boss’s ties to sex offenderKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentThu 15 Oct 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and histies tothe once well-connected billionaire.A bipartisan group of politicians, led by Warren and House representative Robert Garcia, are introducing a bill on Thursday known as the Epstein Wall Street Records Act. The bill follows a months-long investigation into the financier, whodied in prisonin 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.If passed, the bill would force regulators including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate “Epstein connected” financial firms and executives for potential breaches of banking, investment or illicit funding laws; and fine or even ban wrongdoers from the US financial sector.The bill – which is also being backed by House Republican Thomas Massie – will also force regulators to publicly disclose any records relating to Epstein and his associates; and refer any potential criminal violations to the US justice department.Warren said: “Since the big banks won’t hold themselves accountable – and the Trump administration won’t either – Congress must act to force real transparency and accountability for them and their executives who enabled Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”News of the bill came as Warren condemned the bosses at Barclays, one of the UK’s biggest banks, over their failure to adequately answer questions about its former chief executivesJes Staleyand his links to Epstein.Staley’s ties with the well-connected billionaire spelled the end of his career. The American bankerresigned from Barclays in November 2021, after UK regulators started investigating the true nature of his relationship with Epstein, whom he met in 2000 during his three-decade stint at JP Morgan.View image in fullscreenA FCA investigation concluded that Jes Staley and Jeffrey Epstein had a relationship that ‘went beyond one that was professional in nature’.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersThe Financial Conduct Authority’s original investigation, triggered by a cache of more than 1,200 emails between Staley and Epstein, concluded that the pair were“indeed close”and had a relationship that “went beyond one that was professional in nature”.Staley was eventuallybanned from the UK’s financial sectorin 2023 for playing down those ties, andfailed to overturnthat decision in a court battle that revealed intimate details of the pair’s friendship last year.That included Staleyadmitting to having sex with a member of Epstein’s staffin New York – an encounter he said was “consensual”. The case also revived a 2010 exchangereferring to Disney princesses,in which Staley said: “That was fun. Say hi to Snow White.” Staley denied knowledge of the exchange during a UK court hearing.After the loss of his legal challenge against the FCA, Staley said he was disappointed by the outcome but was “never dishonest”.In July, Warren and a team of House Democrats wrote to theBarclayschair, Nigel Higgins, asking how it had vetted its former chief executive, and whether the bank had investigated potential “deficiencies” in its executive hiring process, given it had “allowed the board to hire a CEO who held extensive professional and personal ties to a convicted sex offender”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenIn July, Elizabeth Warren and a team of House Democrats wrote to the Barclays chair asking how it had vetted its former chief executive.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersBarclays has since responded with a letter from its head of US government relations, Lance Williams, that Warren said was not sufficient.The letter focused on the findings of the UK regulators’ investigation. Williams stressed that Staley had “concealed information about his actions and the nature of his relationship with Mr Epstein” and only after Staley’s resignation had “previously unknown information come to light through various public disclosures”.“This information paints a fundamentally different picture of Mr Staley than what he presented to Barclays,” Williams said, noting that Barclays had relied on external executive search firms to recruit Staley in 2015, when he was “known for his accomplishments in the banking industry”.Warren said Barclays’ lacklustre response illustrated why it was time for regulators to launch formal investigations into Wall Street’s ties to Epstein: “Barclays continues to dodge responsibility over its apparent failure to vet its former CEO Jes Staley’s close professional and personal ties to Epstein.”Barclays declined to comment. Staley’s legal representatives were contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsBankingJeffrey EpsteinBarclaysJes StaleyElizabeth WarrenCorporate governanceFinancial sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt | Stock markets | The Guardian
description: Chip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as potential interest rate hikes spook markets
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Chip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as potential interest rate hikes spook markets
Content: A Hana Bank screen shows the Kopsi index with a downward graph line. The tech-heavy South Korean index fell 8% overnight in Asia, triggering circuit breakers and halting stock trades.Photograph: Lee Jin-man/APView image in fullscreenA Hana Bank screen shows the Kopsi index with a downward graph line. The tech-heavy South Korean index fell 8% overnight in Asia, triggering circuit breakers and halting stock trades.Photograph: Lee Jin-man/APStock marketsTech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debtChip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as potential interest rate hikes spook marketsBusiness news – live updatesLarry Elliott: the global economy is muddling through. But a storm is comingKalyeena MakortoffThu 15 Oct 2026 10.33 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, asfears over rising inflationand future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix andSamsungElectronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5% respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.The global economy is muddling through against the odds. But a storm is coming | Larry ElliottRead moreMeanwhile, Japan’sNikkei225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in the memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI.The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where theNasdaqComposite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, its worst performance since July.US stocks fell further when trading resumed on Thursday. The Nasdaq dropped another 1.4% at the start of trading, with Dell, which makes datacentre servers, and Coherent, which manufactures components for AI datacentres, leading the early fallers.The sell-off came after US data on Wednesday showed stateside inflation jumped toa higher-than-expected 3.7% in September, marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May.Fresh data on Thursday showing US producers increased their prices by 6.3% year on year in September – the sharpest rise since December 2022 – added to inflationary jitters.The figures have rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month.“Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid said.Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe sell-offfollows warnings from the International Monetary Fund,which said this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets was putting world financial stability at risk.“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” the IMF said. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit.The latest jitters hit China, where the Shanghai Shenzhen CSI 300 slipped by as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits.European stocks also came under pressure, with Germany’s DAX down 0.36% in afternoon trading and the Italian FTSE MIB dropping by 1.3%.Explore more on these topicsStock marketsMarket turmoilTechnology sectorInflationInterest ratesUS marketsSamsungnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gen Z wrestle with shame from ordering delivery food: ‘This economy is not for the weak’ | Food | The Guardian
description: As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience
Author: Alaina Demopoulos
Headline: As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience
Content: ‘I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door … Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself,’ said Caroline Bauldree, 24.Photograph: Anastasiia Voloshko/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door … Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself,’ said Caroline Bauldree, 24.Photograph: Anastasiia Voloshko/Getty ImagesFoodGen Z wrestle with shame from ordering delivery food: ‘This economy is not for the weak’As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenienceTell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?Alaina DemopoulosThu 15 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 16.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen it comes to food, Caroline Bauldree does not like to “deprive” herself of anything. She does not like to cook either, so that means a lot of food deliveries. “If I want sushi, I’m getting sushi,” said the 24-year-old nanny, who lives in Raleigh, North Carolina. “I’m definitely lazy in that regard.”Bauldree got into the habit of near-daily DoorDashing back in college. “I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door – that’s the dream,” she said. “But then I just feel like crap about myself because I’m like, ‘wow, I’m a lazy piece of shit.’ Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself.”There is a term for that post-order clarity: delivery guilt. The pandemic turned food delivery apps such as DoorDash, Uber Eats and Grubhub, once only popular in major cities, into a full-fledged national lifestyle. One Purduestudyfound that two-thirds of consumers used a food-ordering app at least once in 2024; another recentsurveyfrom the marketing company FinanceBuzz in partnership with Bank of America found that 57% of Americans get takeout or delivery weekly or more. Gen Z is more likely to feed the habit, clocking in an average of five orders a month – roughly double the monthly orders made by Boomers.double quotation markIt doesn’t feel great to admit that we’re paying this extra money and contributing to these companies’ profitsJoy LuConsidering the price of food and those ever-pesky delivery fees, it’s an expensive habit; Bauldree estimates spending about $75 a week. And users might not feel comfortable broadcasting it to the world. According to the Finance Buzz survey, half of its gen Z respondents said they felt embarrassed about how much they spend on food delivery, sometimes so much that they lie about the amount to friends and family.Joy Lu is an assistant professor of marketing at Carnegie Mellon University who studies delivery app pricing. She calls food delivery an “affordable luxury”: a way for people to treat themselves without majorly splurging. But the fees on delivery apps can add up, resulting in sticker shock at checkout. Lu says people might be afraid to reveal their true delivery tab because they do not want to be perceived as wasting money.“People might be hesitant to talk about this because we have a sense that these food delivery apps are taking a cut and it’s not all going to the delivery person,” Lu said. “It doesn’t feel great to admit that we’re paying this extra money and contributing to these companies’ profits.”View image in fullscreenA DoorDash worker rides his bicycle along a path on the West Side Highway in New York.Photograph: John Minchillo/APThe Federal Trade Commission, which hassparredwith delivery apps in the past, is reportedly considering new rules that would address undisclosed fees resulting from dynamic and surge pricing,reportsthe industry publication Restaurant Business. Representatives for Grubhub and DoorDash told the Guardian that users are shown an itemized price, which includes all fees, before they place an order. “Customers can adjust their order at any time to stay within their budget,” the Grubhub rep said in an email. The DoorDash spokesperson wrote: “There are no hidden costs on our platform.”Last month, New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, announced a$131.5m fineagainst DoorDash for “systemic violations of New York City’s Delivery Worker Laws”, including lack of, late, or insufficient payment, and violations of the state’s mandatory minimum wage. It was the largest worker settlement in New York history, with $115m of the funds going to DoorDashers. In astatement, DoorDash said “our mistakes meant some DoorDashers were underpaid or paid late”, adding the errors were “unintentional”.As the cost of groceries continues to rise – this year, the USDApredictsthe cost of “food-at-home” (AKA groceries) will rise 2.4% – some shoppers say it’s becoming just as expensive to cook for themselves as it is to order out. That’s a tough claim to substantiate, as itdependson certain factors. For example, single people may be able to save money eating out compared with families, and people who live in grocery store deserts have to pay more for each trip once they factor in the price of gas.Lu believes people might not even realize how much they are spending on delivery, or consciously avoid looking into the cost. “You don’t really want to look into your app and see the total cost you spent,” she said. “It’s very easy to spend a bit at a time.”‘They’re playing dirty’: inside delivery apps’ pushback against tips after New York raises wageRead moreSome people are happy to reveal their reliance on food delivery. One New York-based influencer named Audrey Peters became TikTok’s villain of the week earlier this year when she revealed she DoorDashes almost every single meal.Petersdescribeda day where she spent $136.50 on a chicken salad, pizza, meatballs, hummus and ice-cream, among other indulgences. One order that particularly irked followers was her $19.44 Starbucks pumpkin spice latte, which she says was so expensive due to her tipping 20%. “I feel really guilty about what I spent today,” she said on the app. The content creator latertoldNew York magazine that she revealed this spending to “rage bait” an audience primed to judge her laziness.Ten years ago, millennials were told their weekly avocado toast or daily latte was the reason they would never be able to buy a house – never mind the fact that they came of age during a global financial crisis. Today, naysayers claim it’s food delivery that’s keeping gen Z from achieving their life goals. For example, a February Fox News segmentfoundanchor Sandra Smith telling viewers they could not complain about the cost of living while excessively DoorDashing too. Such finger-wagging could be the source of delivery shame.But, as economist Mike Konczalarguedon his Substack in February, it is also misguided: 2024 data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows that more of Americans’ food budgets are going to groceries than eating out and delivery. “Society as a whole is reallocating food spending toward cooking at home, not away from it,” Konczal wrote.Bauldree is trying to cut back on her delivery habit, mostly due to other rising costs such as rent and car insurance. “This economy is not for the weak,” she said. Lu, the college professor, does not put food-ordering apps on her phone – she doesn’t want the temptation. As she put it, “I know they’re dangerous.”Explore more on these topicsFoodGig economyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Petey Halpin’s two-run homer lifts Guardians past Rays for 2-1 ALCS lead | MLB | The Guardian
description: Petey Halpin’s fifth-inning blast and a dominant bullpen performance lifted Cleveland to a 3-2 win over Tampa Bay and a 2-1 ALCS series lead
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Petey Halpin’s fifth-inning blast and a dominant bullpen performance lifted Cleveland to a 3-2 win over Tampa Bay and a 2-1 ALCS series lead
Content: The Guardians’ Petey Halpin celebrates after hitting a go-ahead, two-run homer in the fifth inning of Thursday’s ALCS Game 3 win over the Rays at Progressive Field.Photograph: Gregory Shamus/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Guardians’ Petey Halpin celebrates after hitting a go-ahead, two-run homer in the fifth inning of Thursday’s ALCS Game 3 win over the Rays at Progressive Field.Photograph: Gregory Shamus/Getty ImagesMLBPetey Halpin’s two-run homer lifts Guardians past Rays for 2-1 ALCS leadHalpin’s first playoff homer puts Cleveland aheadWilliams strikes out nine as Guardians win 3-2Cleveland bullpen retires 11 of final 12 Rays battersAgenciesThu 15 Oct 2026 16.51 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 16.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePetey Halpin hit a go-ahead two-run homer, Gavin Williams struck out nine over five innings and theCleveland Guardiansbeat the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 in Game 3 of the American League Championship Series on Thursday to take a 2-1 lead.Game 4 of the best-of-seven series is scheduled for Friday, though rain is forecast.José Ramírez had two hits and Nathaniel Lowe added an RBI for the Guardians, who have won five of their last six playoff games since falling 2-0 behind the Chicago White Sox in their AL Division Series.Williams allowed two runs over five innings while walking one. He is 2-0 with a 2.16 ERA and 33 strikeouts over 16 and two-thirds innings innings in four postseason appearances this year, including three starts.Cleveland retired 16 of the Rays’ final 17 batters. Daniel Espino, Erik Sabrowski, Hunter Gaddis and Cade Smith combined to allow just one baserunner over the final four innings.Smith stranded a runner at third in the eighth when he struck out Yandy Díaz after a 10-pitch at-bat, then retired the side in order in the ninth.Tampa Bay went down in order in seven innings, with Junior Caminero striking out four times. Rays batters struck out 13 times in Game 3 after combining for 14 in the first two games of the series.Lowe opened the scoring with an RBI double in the second that bounced off the right-field fence and past Victor Mesa Jr.Chandler Simpson put the Rays ahead with a two-run triple in the fourth.Patrick Bailey led off the fifth with a chopper that pitcher Griffin Jax was unable to field cleanly. Halpin then connected on an elevated 95.9mph sinker on a 2-2 count, driving it 385ft into the right-center-field stands to give Cleveland a 3-2 lead.It was Halpin’s first postseason home run and only the fifth of his two-year major league career. Jax had not allowed a homer since 9 September, a span of five appearances.Williams did not allow a baserunner and struck out five the first time through the order.Jax allowed three runs on five hits and two walks in four-plus innings.Explore more on these topicsMLBCleveland GuardiansTampa Bay RaysBaseballUS sportsShareReuse this content
