Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Longtime Monday Night Football announcer Troy Aikman said he is looking for his ‘next landing spot’ with ⁠his ESPN contract set to expire
Content: Joe Buck and Troy Aikman have been a broadcasting duo for 25 years.Photograph: Matthew Emmons/USA Today SportsView image in fullscreenJoe Buck and Troy Aikman have been a broadcasting duo for 25 years.Photograph: Matthew Emmons/USA Today SportsUS sports mediaTroy Aikman addresses reported rift with Joe Buck and says he is leaving ESPNFormer QB says he is looking ‘for next landing spot’Aikman and Buck said to have argued over contractsReutersThu 15 Oct 2026 14.36 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLongtime Monday Night Football announcer Troy Aikman said he is looking for his “next landing spot” with ⁠hisESPNcontract set to expire after February’s Super Bowl.“I’ll broadcast through this season, and I’ll be ⁠a free agent ⁠at ​the end of the year and kind of see what happens,” Aikman said in a radio interview ⁠with KTCK of Dallas on Thursday morning.The rise and fall of Tony Romo: what comes next for CBS’s $180m NFL analyst?Read moreAikman, a Hall of Fame quarterback who won three Super Bowls with ⁠the Dallas Cowboys, is in the final year of a five-year deal ​with ESPN that pays him $18m ‌annually.Joe Buck, Aikman’s ‌broadcast partner for the past 25 years, recently finalized a six-year extension ‌with ESPN that is worth more than $100m, according to the Athletic. Buck’s deal runs through the network’s next Super Bowl broadcast in 2031.In Thursday’s radio interview, Aikman appeared to confirmearlier reports from Front Office Sportsthat there was tension between ‌him and Buck over their contract situations. The pair reportedly had an argument before Monday’s game between the ​Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams.“There’s probably a time and a place for all that to be discussed,” Aikman said. “I don’t know if now ⁠is the time. I don’t know that it’s hard ​to figure out kind ​of what’s happened.“If Aikman does leave ESPN, he could explore his options ​at other ‌networks or streaming services ​or perhaps ​pursue a front-office role with anNFLteam.“I’m looking forward to whatever the rest of this season does hold, with the Super Bowl and all that, and where my next landing spot might be,” Aikman said.Explore more on these topicsUS sports mediaNFLESPNUS television industryUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Henderson back on Merseyside, Farke threatens more misery for Carrick and Forest are a threat to Arsenal
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Henderson back on Merseyside, Farke threatens more misery for Carrick and Forest are a threat to Arsenal
Content: Coventry City’s Stephen Mfuni, Justin Kluivert of Bournemouth and Chelsea’s Jordan Henderson.Composite: Guardian Pictures; PA; Reuters; EPAView image in fullscreenCoventry City’s Stephen Mfuni, Justin Kluivert of Bournemouth and Chelsea’s Jordan Henderson.Composite: Guardian Pictures; PA; Reuters; EPATen things to look out for this weekendPremier LeaguePremier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendHenderson back on Merseyside, Farke threatens more misery for Carrick and Forest are a threat to ArsenalPremier League top scorers|Follow us on TikTokGuardian sportThu 15 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1Henderson’s return to MerseysideA lively reception awaits the former Liverpool midfielders Jordan Henderson and Xabi Alonso at Everton and, in the case of the former, any jeers can be considered an unintentional tribute. They will speak of what the 36-year-old is able to produce now as much as what, and where, he delivered in the past.With two goals and an assistagainst Bournemouth last Saturday, Henderson became the oldest player to contribute directly to three goals in a Premier League game, and demonstrated his role at Chelsea is not simply to elevate standards off the pitch. His midfield partnership with Moisés Caicedo gave Alonso’s team balance and enabled the front three of Morgan Rogers, João Pedro and Cole Palmer to flourish. Their confrontation against an Everton defence that had impressed this season, onlyto litter the draw at Hullwith costly mistakes, will provide a stern test of the hosts’ unbeaten start and may well be dictated by the veteran behind them.Andy HunterEverton vChelsea, Saturday 12.30pm (all times BST)Chart showing oldest players to make three goal contributions in a Premier League match for Chelsea2Bees a tougher test than LaskStill unbeaten in the top flight, Brentford’s commitment to pragmatism is serving them well. Keith Andrews’ side like to sit deep, close off the middle of the pitch and force opponents to play around them, while flooding the opposition box at set pieces and throw-ins allows them to create the chances from which most of their goals arrive. Inspanking six past Lask, the Austrian champions, Liverpool showed how good they can be on the front foot, but they will face far less obliging hosts at the Gtech Community Stadium. If Andoni Iraola’s side can dominate the ball and move it quickly enough to penetrate Brentford’s rearguard, they could win comfortably. However, the Bees’ efforts to turn the afternoon into a saloon brawl and capitalise on dead-ball situations may help to maintain their unbeaten run.Barry GlendenningBrentford vLiverpool, Saturday 3pm3García needs to find finishing touchGonzalo García has one league goal from 18 shots this season. The striker joined Fulham from Real Madrid in the summer and has looked promising in patches. García is 22 and capable of getting on the end of chances. He has an expected goals tally of 3.60 but is underperforming with his finishing. The challenge is to become more clinical. Fulham, bottom of the league, have six goals in six games and García is without a goal since scoring on his debut,against Chelsea. Álvaro Arbeloa has put a lot of faith in his fellow Spaniard. The head coach is under increasing pressure and winless Fulham need García to fire when they host Hull City.Jacob SteinbergFulham v Hull, Saturday 3pmView image in fullscreenFulham’s Gonzalo García (second left) attempts a shot on goal against Manchester United.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.4City still free-flowing after guilty verdictEven when losing for the first time this season in Wednesday’s 4-2 Champions Leaguedefeat by Paris Saint-Germain, Manchester City appeared the real deal as they rallied from 3-0 down after 32 minutes to give the European champions a scare. Enzo Maresca deserves credit for following Pep Guardiola serenely; his City, so far, are a free-flowing attacking machine and invigorating to watch. If not for the guilty verdict against the club for serious financial breaches of Premier League rules, the perma-twinkling Italian might be more widely lauded. Ipswich last beat City at home in the competition in November 2000: do not expect the statistic to change on Saturday.Jamie JacksonManchester City v Ipswich, Saturday 3pmPredicted outcomes of Premier League matches on 17 October 20265Jaissle should find his ‘inner Rafa’Newcastle’s latest attempt to play vertical football left Matthias Jaissle’s side horizontal at Coventry on Monday night. That4-1 defeatagainst Frank Lampard’s team has prompted quite an inquest on Tyneside where Jaissle could do without his players falling flat on their faces once more when Aston Villa visit St James’ Park. Jaissle maintains that his “vertical football” is the brand of high-octane, aggressive attacking that Newcastle’s hierarchy believes should become the club’s default, and is the way fans want to see the team play. That argument is not without validity but it is also worth remembering that, less than a decade ago, under Rafael Benítez’s charge, Newcastle often played a low block bolstered by three at the back, rarely took unnecessary risks and improved steadily. Admittedly resources were thinner then but the fans almost universally adored Benítez and were heartbroken when he eventually tired of Mike Ashley’s ownership and resigned. Quite apart from making his dislike for “chaotic football’ plain the Spaniard was a realist who knew a gung-ho approach would spell relegation. Granted tactical fashions have changed, but Jaissle could do worse than slow things down a bit and search for his “inner Rafa” against Villa.Louise TaylorNewcastle vAston Villa, Saturday 5.30pmChart showing which teams have conceded the most shots in fast break situations in the 2026-27 Premier League6Eyes on Kluivert and BrobbeyWith nine games each scheduled for the month between international breaks, Bournemouth v Sunderland will give an early indication of how both will cope during their first experience of such a relentless Thursday-Sunday autumnal grind. Sunderland are 17th, Bournemouth are 18th, and with seven points between them after sixPremier Leaguerounds, scaling similarly dizzy heights to last season already seems a lofty goal. For both clubs, European campaigns are far too much of an exciting novelty to be considered anything like a chore. In circumstances where squad depth is crucial, the returns of Justin Kluivert for the hosts and Brian Brobbey for the visitors will be welcomed by Marco Rose and Régis Le Bris. It would be no great surprise to see either Dutch international make a game-deciding contribution in what is already a six-pointer on the south coast.BGskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBournemouth v Sunderland, Sunday 2pm7Brighton must buck Palace trendBrighton’s momentum appears unstoppable at the moment, although supporters will be wary of Sunday’s showdown againstCrystal Palacegiven their recent history. They haven’t beaten Palace since a 4-1 thrashing at the Amex in February 2024 when Roberto De Zerbi was in charge, while Fabian Hürzeler managed only a point in four encounters with the Eagles under Oliver Glasner. Both are having to juggle European commitments this season and Brighton will start as heavy favourites against Pierre Sage’s side after their superb start to the campaign. Palace have big concerns in defence, but can the Frenchman defy the odds against the Premier League’s top scorers?Ed AaronsBrighton v Crystal Palace, Sunday 2pmView image in fullscreenJaouen Hadjam fires home Brighton’s final goal in their 2-0 victory at Sunderland.Photograph: Craig Cowan/Every Second Media/Shutterstock8Carrick confronts old nemesis FarkeMichael Carrick has lost five of his past six technical-area duels with Daniel Farke. Indeed the only time Manchester United’s manager has bested his Leeds counterpart was in a League Cup tie during his Middlesbrough tenure. If such statistics are not sufficient to put Manchester United’s currently beleaguered manager off a trip to West Yorkshire on Sunday, there is a sense that Leeds are overdue a first victory at Elland Road since 2002 against their arch-enemies from across the Pennines. One thing is certain; it will be a typically raucous latter-day War of the Roses. But, right now, while the White Rose blooms, its red counterpart is wilting alarmingly. Will Carrick survive this latest meeting with a manager who, at Championship level during his Middlesbrough days, proved something of a nemesis? He will not care to remember that, last January, a1-1 draw at Elland Roadproved to be Ruben Amorim’s final game in charge of Manchester United.LTLeeds vManchester United, Sunday 2pm9Forest a genuine threat to championsDespitelosing 3-1 to Crystal Palacelast weekend, Nottingham Forest played some excellent front-foot football only to be let down by extreme profligacy in front of goal and vulnerability to their hosts’ counterattacks. Oliver Glasner attributed his side’s defeat to karma upon his return to Palace, saying: “It was like I didn’t deserve to win at Selhurst Park because the players did everything.” When they welcome Arsenal to the City Ground on Sunday, they will give the champions plenty to ponder if they can play as well again. Mikel Arteta’s side were unconvincing for 65 minutesagainst Leedslast weekend and failed to impress until they brought their heavy artillery around the same timeagainst Lilleon Tuesday. If one or both of Morgan Gibbs-White and Liam Delap can convert the kind of chances they missed at Selhurst Park, Forest have every chance of getting something.BGNottingham Forest v Arsenal, Sunday 4.30pmChart showing points and expected points in the 2026-27 Premier League10On-song Coventry can pile angst on SpursThe last time Tottenham hosted Coventry in the Premier League, Steffen Iversen, Les Ferdinand and Serhiy Rebrov scored in a comfortable 3-0 win. And while Spurs fans will almost certainly have envisaged a similar scoreline when the fixtures were announced, they will now be viewing Monday night’s fixture with even more than the usual amount of apprehension and dread. Like Tottenham, Coventry’s main problem until recently was an inability to convert chances, but in their demolition of Newcastle on Monday they visibly grew in confidence and swagger as four different players took the plaudits. While it’s taken a while and they may still struggle, through back-to-back wins Frank Lampard’s side have now announced themselves as a Premier League force to be reckoned with, which is something Tottenham haven’t managed in more than two years.BGTottenham v Coventry, Monday 8pmPosTeamPGDPts1Man City611182Arsenal65153Brighton613134Brentford66105Everton63106Chelsea62107Leeds6398Hull6299Liverpool60910Ipswich6-3911Newcastle6-3812Crystal Palace6-3713Man Utd60614Coventry6-6615Nottm Forest6-3516Aston Villa6-5517Sunderland6-6418AFC Bournemouth6-6319Tottenham Hotspur6-6320Fulham6-42Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTen things to look out for this weekendEvertonChelseaBrentfordLiverpoolFulhamHull CityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bueckers broadsides to Lady Magic’s spice: the greatest trash talkers in WNBA history | WNBA | The Guardian
description: With the season approaching its climax, we look at the players who have perfected the art of smack talking through the years
Author: Jacob Uitti
Headline: With the season approaching its climax, we look at the players who have perfected the art of smack talking through the years
Content: Paige Bueckers is known for clapping back at opponents.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APView image in fullscreenPaige Bueckers is known for clapping back at opponents.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APWNBABueckers broadsides to Lady Magic’s spice: the greatest trash talkers in WNBA historyWith the season approaching its climax, we look at the players who have perfected the art of smack talking through the yearsJacob UittiThu 15 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleToday, even the most casual ofWNBAfans have watched some of the league’s biggest stars talking trash on the court. But while the snarling convos look heated, most of the time, they are good-natured, competitive fun.Still, we wondered, who are the best trash talkers in the game? Which players over the years have turned talking smack into an art form? Let’s explore.Cheryl MillerOK, Miller never played in the league – she retired before the W’s launch in 1997 – but if there was a trash-talking trophy in the WNBA, it wouldhaveto be named after her. Miller is considered by many to be the best women’s basketball player of all time (sheonce scored 105 pointsin a high school game), and those who saw her at USC or heard her in the booth on TNT know that she can reallytalk. Of course, her talent for it began in the back yard playing against her younger brother, fellow Hall of Famer Reggie Miller. From there, a legend was made.Diana TaurasiAnother candidate for greatest player of all time and, like Miller, Taurasi had a knack for talking smack. She did it both on and off the court. For example, in 2016, when the men’s and women’s US basketball teams were together on a cruise ship, Taurasi yelled over to an already-blustery Draymond Green, “Hey, Draymond, how does it feel to be the only person in this room who’s never been double-teamed?” Taurasi doesn’t mind – she’ll even go after the league’s biggest names, chirping incessantly in the ears of playerslike Caitlin Clark.From Mahorn to Jordan: a brief guide to the NBA’s finest trashtalkersRead moreAngel Reese/Caitlin ClarkLike Larry Bird and Magic Johnson, these two players will for ever be linked. It all began in college in the NCAA Tournament when Reesetalked some legendary trash to Clark, pointing at her finger as if to say, “Where’s your championship ring?”Those images made global headlines. Since then, the two have been rivals. (Even the famed formerShowtime point guard has noticed.) “They jaw at each other,”offered Las Vegas Aces coach Becky Hammon. But their trash talking isn’t only reserved for each other.Clark is willing to talk smackto anyone after a big shot and Reese is on the brink of a title – something shepredicted loudly last year. But despite all their verbal battles, Reese and Clark, like Bird and Magic, seem to bemore than amicable off the floorthese days.Alyssa ThomasIn a poll by the Athletic last year, Thomas was voted by her peers as the biggest and best trash talker in the league. That’s saying something, but Thomas wears the crown proudly. Explained one opponent: “She smiles and talks shit, that’s the crazy part, it’s psycho stuff, she’s crazy, man.” Said another: “Everyone knows AT talks shit. I don’t even guard her, and she talks shit to me.” Certainly, Thomas is not one to back down from anything.She was even fined and suspendedearlier this year for throwing an elbow at Clark. While that isn’t exactly verbal communication, Thomas did send a message.Paige BueckersDrafted just last year, Bueckers has quickly become one of the WNBA’s best. She’s an assassin on the floor, capable of hitting game-winner after game-winner. And she’ll let you know about it, too. She’ll strike even if you’reon the bench, before nailing a three. Whethershe’s speaking up for fellow playersortalking smack to her opponentafter a hard foul, Bueckers is not someone to mess with. “I don’t reallystartit,”she told Jennifer Hudson, with a smile, “but if somebody gets me going …” Yes, that would be a bad idea.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNancy LiebermanLieberman is one of the legends of the women’s game. Known in her heyday as “Lady Magic” for her skill at point guard, she was also one of the most biting trash talkers, according to her former GM with the Women’s Professional Basketball League’s Dallas Diamonds, Nancy Nichols. “From my experience, Nancy Lieberman was pretty spicy!” Nichols tells the Guardian. “Especially when she played street ball with the Washington Generals on the Harlem Globetrotters’ tour.” That’s right: Lieberman was so good that she was a standout in the men’s and women’s game. More recently, though, when former NBA All-Star Jeff Teague criticized Lieberman’s friend and mentee Clark,Lieberman came to the Fever star’s defense, telling Teague, “Jeff, I love you, but, you weren’t a great player.”Cynthia CooperWhen the Guardian reached out to two-time WNBA champion coach Michael Cooper for his thoughts on the greatest trash talkers in league history, he was quick to mention Cynthia Cooper (unrelated). A two-time MVP and four-time champ with the 1990s Houston Comets, Cynthia was a marvel on the floor. But she didn’t go about her business silently, often making her feelings known to Michael’s LA Sparks in the playoffs. “We were playing them for their second title and I was an assistant coach,” Michael says. “She walked by me during a timeout and said, ‘Coop, we beating y’all like the Celtics did in 8’84.’ I couldn’t help but laugh. She was a shit talker!”Teresa WeatherspoonSpeaking of those 1990s Comets, one of their former players, Fran Harris, was quick to note Weatherspoon’s trash talking ability. Of course, Weatherspoon hit perhaps the biggest shot in WNBA history (against the 1999 Comets). But even before that, the two-time Defensive Player of the Year filled arenas with her biting smack talk, not unlike another former DPOY, Gary Payton.Skylar DigginsThere was another marquee player on the Athletic’s poll who received several votes – a veteran who has long been considered a premiere trash talker. If there was ever any doubt about Diggins’s smack talking prowess, it was silenced last year when she erupted during a gameat the Minnesota Lynxbench.Explore more on these topicsWNBABasketballUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Martínez has drawn back the curtain on Manchester United’s ruinous ownership | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Defender may not be blameless in team’s struggles but his criticism goes to the heart of what has gone wrong at the club
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: Defender may not be blameless in team’s struggles but his criticism goes to the heart of what has gone wrong at the club
Content: Lisandro Martínez has spoken frankly about the club’s ownership – perhaps more so than any other serving Manchester United player.Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenLisandro Martínez has spoken frankly about the club’s ownership – perhaps more so than any other serving Manchester United player.Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy Live News.Manchester UnitedMartínez has drawn back the curtain on Manchester United’s ruinous ownershipJonathan LiewDefender may not be blameless in team’s struggles but his criticism goes to the heart of what has gone wrong at the clubThu 15 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTShareHeartbreaking: the worst defender you know just made a great point. And no, nobody would describe Lisandro Martínez as the ideal person toscrutinise Manchester United’s indifferent start to the season, given that his high-profile defensive errors against Fulham and Tottenham are partly responsible for it. “We’re all trying to find the guy who did this,” Martínez burbles on Amazon Primeafter United’s 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madridon Tuesday night, dressed in a hot dog costume and throwing his arms out in mock innocence.For those with no interest in engaging with what Martínez actually had to say, this alone will be sufficient grounds to ignore him. Already you can sense the squeamishness of former players for whom the violation of an omertà is the real cardinal sin here, a phantom limb that still tingles years after they last stepped into a dressing room. “Disrespectful,” reckoned Wayne Rooney. “I don’t feel like he’s got the right,” agreed Ashley Young. “These things don’t end well, man,” Rio Ferdinand observed on his podcast.Jason Wilcox: ‘best eyes’ at Manchester United or promoted too far and too fast?Read moreBut traducing the messenger will always be easier than hearing the message, even if Martínez’s views arewidely shared within the United dressing room. If the fallout from the Manchester City legal case has demonstrated anything, it is English football’s ingrained reluctance to scrutinise the owners and executives whohold more influence over the sport than anybody else. Men in boots, not men in suits. Hey, watch the ball. It’s going to move!All the same, it’s worth parsing exactly what Martínez was complaining about, because it’s a good deal more complex than it may appear on first viewing. Player calls out board – andspecifically “technical director” Jason Wilcox– for failing to invest sufficiently in the squad over the summer. This was a summer in which United brought in three midfielders (Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans, Carlos Baleba), a reserve goalkeeper (Karl Darlow), nobody up front and nobody in defence. So far, so simple.But let’s begin to unpick the threads. Why did United not buy a defender in the summer, despite pursuing deals for Lewis Hall and Myles Lewis-Skelly? Because they were unable to sell a defender. There was no interest in Diogo Dalot or Noussair Mazraoui, nor in Harry Maguire, nor in Luke Shaw or Martínez, whose contracts are up next summer in any case. This is the product of recruitment decisions made and deals signed years ago. But why do United, one of the world’s most lucrative clubs, need to sell to buy in the first place?Perhaps for the same reason they baulked at the asking price for Elliot Anderson and decided to sign the inconsistent Santos and the adequate but overpromoted Tielemans instead: this is a club in austerity measures, whose part-owner Jim Ratcliffe has been furiously cutting costs and raising ticket prices, determined to curb the years of excess that preceded him, where mediocre players were signed on ridiculous money, where failing coaches were paid to leave. But why would United, one of the most commercially successful clubs in footballing history, ever need to cut costs?Perhaps as a result of the more than £1bn drained out of the club by the Glazers in their 21 years of ownership, not just in dividends but share sales and interest payments on the debt they undertook to buy the club, while neglecting the maintenance of Old Trafford and the training ground at Carrington. Whether he knows it or not, when Martínez is criticising the lack of investment he is in effect holding the Glazers accountable for more than two decades of avarice and mismanagement.All of which lends a certain significance to Martínez’s intervention that goes beyond the churn of the weekly news cycle. Has any serving United player spoken out so frankly about the ruins of the Glazer ownership? Ole Gunnar Solskjær made a minor stand in early 2005, before they had arrived at the club. Cristiano Ronaldo threw some hand grenades over his shoulder a few days before he left for the second time in 2022. Countless others waited for the safety of retirement, when their disgruntlement could be monetised for personal gain, rather than used to stigmatise them, as Martínez will doubtless be stigmatised in the coming days.View image in fullscreenA Manchester United supporter shows off a jumper protesting against the club’s owners and executives.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesDoes any of this help United to win games in the short term? Almost certainly not. Martínez attempted to clarify his commentsin a social media poston Wednesday night. He may still be dispatched to the bomb squad anyway, for the crime of pointing out that the emperor secured his throne almost entirely through the use of payment-in-kind loans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInevitably Michael Carrick too will be gone before long, away to the great Overlap podcast in the sky. A few months ago I wrote hopefully thatCarrick might be the ideal manto cut through the noise and nonsense. I was wrong. The noise has beaten him; the nonsense always wins; any accumulated credit from last season has long since evaporated.Of course it’s not Carrick’s fault that United haven’t signed a new defender in almost two years, that Bruno Fernandes is so clearly playing through discomfort, that Joshua Zirkzee is still somehow hanging around the place, that the ownership decided to embark on a purge of season-ticket holders in the summer, generating a huge wave of ill-feeling and apathy that can be felt at Old Trafford on matchdays: an entire fanbase trying to work out whether they actually still care about this.But accountability is for the little people, and far easier to replace a coach on a modest 20-month contract than to oust Ineos or the Glazers, to replace Wilcox or Omar Berrada, even if we now know they partly built their reputations on the success of a club that has been found to have serially cheated. Bumper returns for the owners, price hikes for the fans, corners cut on the pitch; this is the story of the modernManchester United, which by no coincidence is also the story of modern football.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickcommentShareReuse this content

title: Champions League review: PSG’s benchmark, Viking uprising and an Italian-German dilemma | Champions League | The Guardian
description: The competition returned after the international break as the reigning champions put on a devastating display and Italy looked for its next saviour
Author: John Brewin
Headline: The competition returned after the international break as the reigning champions put on a devastating display and Italy looked for its next saviour
Content: Ousmane Dembélé, Achraf Hakimi, Bradley Barcola and NicolòTresoldi were all on form this week.Composite: Getty, EPA, AlamyView image in fullscreenOusmane Dembélé, Achraf Hakimi, Bradley Barcola and NicolòTresoldi were all on form this week.Composite: Getty, EPA, AlamyChampions LeagueChampions League review: PSG’s benchmark, Viking uprising and an Italian-German dilemmaThe competition returned after the international break as the reigning champions put on a devastating display and Italy looked for its next saviourJohn BrewinThu 15 Oct 2026 09.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA big week forFamous faces in the crowd for English teams’ home matches on Wednesday. While Prince William delighted in his belovedAston Villa’s 6-0 romp over Fenerbahce, Pep Guardiola’sManchester City homecomingwas spoiled byParis Saint-Germain showingthey still represent the benchmark in European club football this season.The center-circle inquest led by Erling Haaland after Vitinha put PSG 3-0 up was a jarring contrast to the triumphalism shown when City were winning atLiverpoollast weekend. The Parisians put on a devastating display in the first half and, although the defiance City exhibited at Anfield on Sunday was on display again in the second half, PSG held on for a 4-2 win. “We could’ve lost this match if they scored the chances they created,” said a magnanimous Luis Enrique.City may soon be absent from the competition,after they were found guiltyof more than 100 charges of breaking the Premier League’s financial regulations. If City wish to sign off with a valedictory trophy lift they now know the standard they must meet – and beat. PSG have had their own issues with financial regulations in the era of petrodollar state ownership but, with the club president Nasser Al-Khelaifi a major powerbroker in European football, they have become an establishment club. While City are now pariahs, PSG have become near untouchables, not least on the field of play.“He who brings glory to Rome, Rome honors for ever,” read a banner in the Stadio Olimpico. “Your hands are blessed and the people will give you eternal glory!” José Mourinho won hearts during his time in charge of Roma. But his popularity ratings are nowhere near as high in Madrid, though the manner ofReal Madrid’s 4-3 comeback winover Roma will calm the gathering storm he has faced since returning to work for Florentino Pérez. The comeback came via Madrid’s next generation: Carlos Espí, 21, pulled the scoreline back to 3-2; the unlikely aerial threat of the 5ft 8in Endrick, 20, made it 3-3; and Antonio Rüdiger scored the winner, via a second assist for Arda Güler, 21. Mourinho embracing youth is a fresh development. This week saw Mourinho block a loan move to Milan for Endrick, and he admitted in Rome: “The first half was the coach’s fault; the second half was the players’ fault.”A record 78 goals flew in this game week; the previous record was 71. On the wrong end were the Serie A clubs. In addition to Roma’s defeat, Como lost 3-2 at Feyenoord, the decisive moment coming via an own-goal for Robert Sánchez, the keeper loaned from Chelsea. Inter also lost, 4-3 to Club Brugge, whose performances in the competition in recent years meant the result was not much of a surprise. Napoli lost 3-1 to Villarreal, the Yellow Submarines’ firstChampions Leaguewin in eight matches. Neapolitan focus was on a running battle between Massimiliano Allegri, the Napoli coach, and Kevin De Bruyne. Scott McTominay’s return to the team has pushed De Bruyne deeper. The Belgian made clear his feelings on playing there with some highly demonstrative body language.Player of the weekThere were two hat-tricks this week. Bradley Barcola ignited his Liverpool career with a treble at Lask, whose defending duringtheir 6-3 defeatwas suboptimal to say the least. That 4-3 Brugge win was mostly thanks to Nicolò Tresoldi. The striker was born in Italy, but moved to Hanover when he was 13, and he plays for Germany’s under-21s. Italian soul-searching after missing out on the last three World Cups has cast Tresoldi as a new savior. “I always speak Italian at home; I was born in Italy too,” he said post-match. “We’ll see.”Paolo Di Canio, on Sky Italia, was pessimistic: “He has already chosen.”View image in fullscreenIt was a memorable night for Viking.Photograph: Lise Åserud/NTB/APClub in focus: Viking StavangerAfter Bodø/Glimt’s exploits over the last couple of seasons and the national team’s admirable World Cup showing, the true football hipsters have a new destination in Norway. Viking play a thousand miles south-west of Bodø, in Norway’s oil capital, Stavanger.The club has co-managersin Bjarte Lunde Aarsheim and Morten Jensen: the pair were interviewed for the top job before deciding it was best they share duties. Viking are in the Champions League for the first time since the 1992-93 season, and at one point on Tuesday the Eliteserien champions led Bayern Munich 2-0. But a seismic shock was averted via two Harry Kane goals and another from Luis Díaz that put Bayern 3-2 up. Once Herman Haugen headed home at the back post, Viking had rescued a point with a 3-3 draw. “I could have played another 90 minutes,” said the captain, Zlatko Tripić, “I’m so incredibly proud.”They said it“I expect more. I’m not going to close my mouth; we need more ambition, we need to talk more about winning Champions Leagues and Premier Leagues in terms of other things.” Lisandro Martínez was undeterred by Peter Schmeichel’s soft-shoe questioning on Tuesday’s CBS broadcast after Manchester United’s defeat to Atlético Madrid.“If we don’t say the truth, nothing will change,” added Martínez, whose Manchester United contract expires in June. Martínez’s interventions exposed the cracks at United – and highlighted the dubious merits of having a football celebrity do a journalist’s job.Looking aheadA quick turnaround sees the third round staged next week, with Manchester United heading to Como for another examination of Michael Carrick’s regime. That follows a difficult Sunday trip to Leeds for United.A couple of heavyweight ties catch the eye. Barcelona’s 4-1 win at Galatasaray continued their perfect start to the season, and Tuesday sees them visit PSG, a meeting of the two favorites to claim the title. On Wednesday, Arsenal v Bayern may trigger unhappy memories among Gunners fans. Arsenal lost 5-1 to Bayern three times in succession over the 2015-16 and 2016-17 seasons, and lost in the 2023-24 quarter-finals to the Germans too. Arsenal did, though, beat Bayern in last season’s Champions League.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueParis Saint-GermainManchester CityLiverpoolManchester UnitedReal MadridViking FKfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: After struggles v Spain, the USWNT’s midfield puzzle won’t be easily solved | USA women's football team | The Guardian
description: The lack of cohesion in the center of the park is evident for the US, with Emma Hayes continuing to try different combinations
Author: Jeff Rueter
Headline: The lack of cohesion in the center of the park is evident for the US, with Emma Hayes continuing to try different combinations
Content: Lindsey Heaps started both of the United States’ recent friendlies against Spain.Photograph: Scott Taetsch/USSF/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLindsey Heaps started both of the United States’ recent friendlies against Spain.Photograph: Scott Taetsch/USSF/Getty ImagesUSA women's football teamAnalysisAfter struggles v Spain, the USWNT’s midfield puzzle won’t be easily solvedJeff RueterThe lack of cohesion in the center of the park is evident for the US, with Emma Hayes continuing to try different combinationsThu 15 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 05.27 EDTShareThe discourse around the US women’s national team may have been a harsh one if not for a fourth-half surge against Spain.In the latest of their back-to-back bookings, where Emma Hayes’ team plays the same opponent twice, Spain looked far more confident and effective than the four-time champions. Both teams were missing a handful of crucial players; Naomi Girma and Sam Coffey headlining the US’s absentees, while Aitana Bonmatí, Mariona Caldentey and Clàudia Pina were among Spain’s.Nonetheless, Spain controlled the game and forced the US to settle for scraps in the final third. The first game saw Spain rush to a 2-0 lead inside 15 minutes and maintain that margin for the rest of the match. On Tuesday, the US once again entered half-time facing an identical deficit.USWNT returnees earn 2-2 draw against Spain, an early World Cup wake-up callRead moreIt wasn’t until Hayes made five changes in unison that they regained a foothold in the latter match and clawed back two goals from direct, incisive attacks. That’s hardly a title-winning blueprint, and not just because a World Cup limits teams to five substitutions instead of the eight the teams agreed to for these games.This month, Spain’s alternates slotted into the lineup and executed the game model because of holistic familiarity. Each player understood what their role was after meticulous refinement, and the team around them continued to operate as expected as a result. This kind of synergy can be enough to beat a more talented team, and long gone are the days where the United States can expect to beat another top women’s national team on talent alone.Hayes has not, at any point, implied otherwise. And so, her staff has been immensely thorough in working towards building the best 26-player roster they can.This year, like 2025, was a year of deep talent evaluation. The October window saw four players included without previous caps, as well as returns to the pitch for longtime absentees Mallory Swanson and Ashley Sanchez, whose goals earned the US their draw on Tuesday. Kate Del Fava and Pietra Tordin became the 33rd and 34th players to debut since Hayes assumed her post in mid-2024. The efforts have made the pool deeper, but the duration and density of this search may be coming at the cost of that crucial synergy.A well-organized midfield is borderline mandatory to win a World Cup. Spain dominated in 2023 with awe-inspiring play in the heart of the park. So, too, did the United States during their successful repeat bid in 2019. Megan Rapinoe and Alex Morgan’s exploits were made possible by one of the most balanced midfield trios in recent memory: Sam Mewis as an ideal all-around central midfielder, Julie Ertz as a hard-nosed defensive midfielder and Rose Lavelle’s facilitation to link with the attack.View image in fullscreenSam Coffey missed this past US camp after suffering an injury on duty with Manchester City.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesAfter injuries forced Mewis into an early retirement and Ertz called time on her career after 2023, Hayes has had the tall task of crafting a worthy sequel. Her best Chelsea sides were built with midfielders whose technical acumen were bolstered by their tireless commitment to tracking back and pressing. Consistently doing so requires second-nature understanding of your teammates and how they operate, on the ball and especially without it. That synergy can’t be rushed, and Hayes tried giving herself a deadline of sorts to begin doing that work.“I want to get to the end of June where I have a really strong sense of a core group of players that will form part of the build towards the World Cup,” Hayestold CBS, “but also know that we need to get some consistency in relationships, connections on the pitch, and we have to forego that for now while we’re still evaluating players at an individual level.”That stated aim came before the April friendly window in 2025, hoping to pave a two-year runway to refine partnerships before the big games in Brazil. Injuries can partly be to blame for the delay, and more recent first-time call-ups (like this window’s) have been made with an eye toward the2028 Olympics. But the US still sufferers from a specific lack of clarity in the middle of the park.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOlivia Moultrie’s injury leaves the USWNT with a thinning midfield pool ahead of the World CupRead moreTuesday’s friendly was the United States’ 27th match since the start of 2025, and seven midfielders have made at least three starting lineups in this span. Coffey and Claire Hutton have been the preferred defensive midfielders; Lindsey Heaps, Lily Yohannes, and the injured Olivia Moultrie as central midfielders; and Rose Lavelle and Jaedyn Shaw in attacking midfield. Heaps has regularly floated between all three roles, the only player to start in each spot. While six of her 12 starts have come as the more all-around No 8, her other six have been evenly split between defensive midfield and attacking midfield.Despite this consistency of personnel, Hayes has used 17 different combinations of three midfielders in that span. Tuesday was just the second time that Hutton, Heaps, and Lavelle opened a match together. The consensus “first-choice” trio of Coffey, Heaps and Lavelle has also started together just twice in 20 months. The most common combination has been Lavelle playing in front of a Coffey-Hutton double pivot on four occasions.Unfortunately, testing either of those trios against Spain was impossible once Coffey withdrew from camp with an injured left ankle. The perceived drawbacks of that setup is that both Coffey and Hutton thrive in more withdrawn deployment, which can increase gaps between the defensive block and the attack. It’s possible that the full-backs (Emily Fox on the right and, increasingly often, Gisele Thompson on the left) can provide enough progression to mitigate for that, but it’s why that No 8 role is still one Hayes wants to incorporate.It’s also a factor that makes Moultrie’s torn ACL in August even more impactful. While Heaps remains Hayes’s captain and Yohannes has earned regular starts with her improving skill set, Moultrie wasarguably the most natural complement to Coffey, alongside whom she partnered in Portland for four seasons. And yet, she made just three starts since January 2025, and none alongside Coffey.Injuries are impartial and no individual can be assumed to arrive to World Cup camp at peak health. But continuous recalibration in midfield – for reasons of circumstance and experimentation alike – and a corresponding lack of system clarity in all phases threatens to keep a viable contender from maximizing its potential against fellow heavyweights like Spain.Explore more on these topicsUSA women's football teamEmma HayesUS sportsLA Olympic Games 2028Women's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Apologetic Infantino ‘not fit’ to lead Fifa, claim European FA heads after meeting | Fifa | The Guardian
description: European football leaders are increasingly confident they will find a candidate to stand against Gianni Infantino in next year’s Fifa presidential election
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: European football leaders are increasingly confident they will find a candidate to stand against Gianni Infantino in next year’s Fifa presidential election
Content: Gianni Infantino faced critics at the Fifa council meeting in Zurich.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino faced critics at the Fifa council meeting in Zurich.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersFifaApologetic Infantino ‘not fit’ to lead Fifa, claim European FA heads after meetingInfantino failed to provide answers to questionsEuropean leaders expect someone will stand against himMatt Hughesin Zurich andNick AmesThu 15 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 15.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean football leaders are increasingly confident they will find a candidate to stand againstGianni Infantinoin next year’s Fifa presidential election, with the heads of the English and German football associations questioning his fitness to govern after a three-and-a-half-hour council meeting.Infantino began the long-awaited gathering of Fifa’s 37-strong executive board by apologising for failing to consult them over hisabandoned World Cup sell-off planbut failed to provide answers to dozens of questions posed by the European FAs on a range of subjects including the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal,Donald Trump’s Fifa peace prizeand theFolarin Balogun affair, when the USA striker’s World Cup suspension was overturned after lobbying from the US president.Infantino’s apology was followed by a 30-minute presentation on FFE from two American lawyers, who described the $20bn (£15.1bn) valuation and proposed sale of a 20% stake to Thrive Capital as a good deal forFifa. At the insistence of some attenders, the lawyers were asked to leave the meeting after they had presented. When questioned, one of them confirmed he had been commissioned and paid by Fifa to produce a review of FFE.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“The main objective for Gianni was to survive this meeting and nothing more,” one council member told the Guardian.Council members succeeded in deferring, until they receive more information on Balogun, a Fifa proposal to amend its disciplinary regulations by removing the scope for players shown a straight red card to have it rescinded. Infantino pledged to provide that information by their next meeting in Doha on 16 December, after nominations close on 18 November for March’s presidential election.The issue of whether the Fifa peace prize will be revived this year or Trump left as a standalone winner has been referred to Fifa’s social responsibility committee, and the Asian Football Confederation president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, has been appointed to chair a new committee examining governance reform. But otherwise the meeting broke up without tangible answers, to the frustration of the English FA’s chair, Debbie Hewitt.“We didn’t get answers to anything that we had specifically requested,” Hewitt said. “I think the man [Infantino] has to answer those questions, and if he doesn’t answer those questions, he’s not fit to be Fifa president. That was what was shared in the meeting.”The German FA’s president, Bernd Neuendorf, went further by calling for wholesale reforms of Fifa’s administration, which he hopes will fall within the purview of Sheikh Salman’s governance committee.“The whole administration has to be reformed and the whole governance has to be reformed,” Neuendorf said. “But I’m pretty clear here that this is not possible with Gianni as the responsible person at Fifa. So we need a complete restart, I think, a political restart of persons who represent Fifa.“Yes he apologised, but I didn’t have the feeling that this apology was because of the FFE project in total. My impression was it was just because it wasn’t brought forward to the council and no one was involved.”Neuendorf also said he was “very confident” that an alternative candidate would be found to stand against Infantino, a view shared by senior figures atUefa, who expect a late declaration to limit the amount of time for Fifa to scupper the nomination.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe respective presidents of the three continental confederations who have called for Infantino to go – Aleksander Ceferin of Uefa, Victor Montagliani of Concacaf and Sheikh Salman – have ruled themselves out and suggestions that high-profile figures such as Arsène Wenger or Michele Kang could put themselves forward have been dismissed.A proposal to distribute $3.5bn (£2.6bn) from Fifa’s financial reserves, which would involve each national association receiving $25m over the next four-year cycle, was approved by council.Montagliani is also understood to have been critical of Infantino, but Fifa’s president received strong support from council members from Asia and Africa.“I am certain that Gianni Infantino is the right president,” Ahmed Yahya, president of the Mauritania Football Federation said. “The majority want Gianni Infantino to stay. After finally withdrawing this proposal, president Gianni Infantino apologised to the members of the executive committee. This was followed by a responsible debate, during which this issue was more or less shelved.“In the interests of football, the executive committee is looking ahead and seeking solutions, by focusing on the good aspects that football has to offer and trying to move forward.”Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsUefaThe FAnewsShareReuse this content

title: Martínez apologises to Manchester United’s director of football Wilcox after outburst | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: The Manchester United defender has apologised for his criticism of Jason Wilcox after the Champions League defeat by Atlético Madrid
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: The Manchester United defender has apologised for his criticism of Jason Wilcox after the Champions League defeat by Atlético Madrid
Content: Lisandro Martínez claimed Michael Carrick had not had sufficient backing.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenLisandro Martínez claimed Michael Carrick had not had sufficient backing.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAManchester UnitedMartínez apologises to Manchester United’s director of football Wilcox after outburstDefender says sorry after talks with Michael CarrickAny disciplinary action will not be made public by clubJamie JacksonThu 15 Oct 2026 15.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 18.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLisandro Martínez has apologised for claiming that Jason Wilcox, Manchester United’s director of football,failed to strengthen sufficiently in the summer windowafter discussions with the manager, Michael Carrick, and club hierarchy on Thursday.While any disciplinary action taken against him will not be made public by the club, it is thought that Martínez has been fined.Martínez has drawn back the curtain on Manchester United’s ruinous ownership | Jonathan LiewRead moreThe defender’s apology came on Thursday evening after the 28-year-old failed to offer one when issuing an initial statement on Wednesday regarding his outburst following Tuesday’s2-0 Champions League loss at Atlético Madrid.He posted on Instagram: “Today I met with the club’s leadership and the manager. It was a very positive conversation, where we were able to exchange views and speak openly about what happened after Tuesday’s game.“Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity. The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise.”The apology is a considerable climbdown. After the Atlético defeat, Martínez was scathing of Wilcox and his recruitment in the last window.He said: “I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Wilcox]. As players we have to do more but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night. Last season we did everything, we created the base to create an amazing team.”Martínez claimed that Carrick had not been backed sufficiently. “I don’t think so. He does his best. You can’t keep changing, changing, changing the manager. What about other areas?” he said.While it is understood Martínez’s apology was his decision alone, United spent £155m in the market – all on midfielders, Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans, and Carlos Baleba, despite Wilcox targeting a left-back.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe wider squadagrees with Martínez’s stanceregarding recruitment and has been left frustrated following a poor start to the season, with Carrick under considerable pressure.A return of six points from six league games is United’s poorest since 1986 and Carrick’s side have already been eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Brighton.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Evanilson, Rayan and Rodríguez goals seal Bournemouth’s historic home win in Europe | Europa League | The Guardian
description: Evanilson scored Bournemouth’s first with a looping header before Rayan and Álvaro Rodríguez added to their 3-0 victory against Sturm Graz
Author: John Brewin
Headline: Evanilson scored Bournemouth’s first with a looping header before Rayan and Álvaro Rodríguez added to their 3-0 victory against Sturm Graz
Content: Bournemouth’s Evanilson after opening the scoring with a looping header.Photograph: Tony O Brien/ReutersView image in fullscreenBournemouth’s Evanilson after opening the scoring with a looping header.Photograph: Tony O Brien/ReutersEuropa LeagueEvanilson, Rayan and Rodríguez goals seal Bournemouth’s historic home win in EuropeJohn BrewinThu 15 Oct 2026 17.46 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn impossible dream realised: the Vitality Stadium staging European football, where the Europa League is becoming an oasis for Bournemouth. No wins yet in the Premier League, but beating Sturm Graz following upwinning away at Real Sociedadshould calm the domestic pressures mounting on Marco Rose. A pair of Brazilians secured club history, with Evanilson’s first-half header followed by Rayan’s later drive, a clincher coming just as the Austrian visitors were pushing hard for an equaliser. Álvaro Rodríguez’s stoppage-time penalty extended the celebrations.Flag day at the Vitality. Elvis Presley’s high baritone and Andy Williams’ tenor on the public address system marked a different type of occasion.Bournemouthhave come a significant distance. “Minus 17 to European dreams” read a banner in the Steve Fletcher stand, marking the journey from the foot of the Football League to becoming a model, continental club. Milan visit next week, an occasion to further broaden the smile of Bill Foley, Bournemouth’s financier present in the posh seats. “A long time coming,” said Bournemouth’s long-serving captain, Adam Smith. “The fans were up for it, the players were up for it.”Europa League: Lyon take down Crystal Palace, Cissè’s Milan hat-trick sinks SalzburgRead moreBournemouth’s new head coach has described the chaos of English football, midfield areas that can resemble a rolling maul, but he has pledged to learn and adapt. “I believe in this team and know they are always confident despite a difficult situation,” Rose said. “If we stick together and play like this and we have our fans then we are hard to play and it’s hard to beat us. That’s what we should take into the next game.”Missing Eli Junior Kroupi so far this season, and lately Alex Scott, are regrettable problems within a small squad. Selling Scott for £80m in January, as has been speculated, speaks to the financial balancing act clubs such as Bournemouth must perform to progress. Following the5-1 loss to Chelsea, Sunday’s Premier League meeting with Sunderland was prioritised in team selection though the second-half introduction of key men, including Rayan, proved decisive.“Everyone deserves to play and it’s good for us for the busy weeks to have a competitive squad,” said Rose, who revealed Smith had given a speech to his teammates after the loss at Stamford Bridge. “That’s my captain.”View image in fullscreenRayan doubles Bournemouth’s lead six minutes after coming off the bench.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersSmith supplied the first proper chance. Marcus Tavernier, cutting inside, shanked that wide before a Ben Gannon-Doak cross from the byline saw Rodríguez misjudge the flight. The summer signing, still raw at 22, finds decent positions only for his touch to betray him. His penalty, following an inadvertent handball from Jon Gorenc Stankovic, was his first goal and should help his confidence.Graz, fourth in this season’s Österreichische Bundesliga, hardly exuded ambition, a defensive trio often morphing into a shell-like five. Amid such squeezed space, after a corner, Bournemouth had the ball in the net, for what seemed an own goal though it had struck Bafode Diakité’s arm. Tavernier struck the outside of a post, before Graz at last began to advance. The away contingent celebrated a penalty, but Belmin Beganovic was shown a yellow card for simulation. Fabio Ingolitsch, the Graz coach and a Rose protege, spoke to his own team’s realities by saying: “Bournemouth is the team with the biggest market value in theEuropa League.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNoah Sadiki stunner earns Sunderland dramatic late win against TorreenseRead moreAnother Smith cross supplied Evanilson’s goal, a header full of neck muscle looping off the angle for a first European goal celebrated in Boscombe. “Many more to come from him,” said Smith of the perpetual motion No 9. Graz fans sang whatever the game state, that being the continental way, but there became more to encourage them beyond the break. Simon Seidl’s shot whistled wide, Jürgen Heil struck a post before Jacob-Peter Hödl forced a remarkable reflex save from Djorde Petrovic on the rebound. The spectre of Premier League travails, where positive play has been unrewarded, loomed as Graz interchanges became crisper.The 70th-minute triple introduction of Rayan, Justin Kluivert and Ryan Christie proved to be Rose’s successful method of locking down midfield and increasing his team’s attacking threat at the same time.Rayan, a decent finisher when coming inside, snatched the contest from Austrian reach. Daniil Khudyakov, Graz’s Russian goalkeeper, first flapped at a corner and then got only a weak hand to the Brazilian’s drive through the proverbial forest of legs. Bournemouth’s European homecoming had been coupled with the victory the occasion had demanded.Explore more on these topicsEuropa LeagueBournemouthSturm Grazmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Noah Sadiki stunner earns Sunderland dramatic late win against Torreense | Europa League | The Guardian
description: The midfielder scored his first goal for Sunderland as Régis Le Bris’s side came back from a goal down to beat Torreense 2-1 in the Europa League
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: The midfielder scored his first goal for Sunderland as Régis Le Bris’s side came back from a goal down to beat Torreense 2-1 in the Europa League
Content: Noah Sadiki races away after his stoppage-time goal puts Sunderland ahead.Photograph: Rodrigo Antunes/ReutersView image in fullscreenNoah Sadiki races away after his stoppage-time goal puts Sunderland ahead.Photograph: Rodrigo Antunes/ReutersEuropa LeagueNoah Sadiki stunner earns Sunderland dramatic late win against TorreenseLouise Taylorat Estádio Municipal de LeiriaThu 15 Oct 2026 15.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 18.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree minutes into stoppage time Noah Sadiki hurdled a set of advertising hoardings, sprinted across a running track and hurled himself towards the ecstaticSunderlandfans.Just as those supporters’ long-awaited party in Portugal had looked in peril of falling a little flat, the Democratic Republic of the Congo midfielder capitalised on excellent work from Enzo Le Fée and Granit Xhaka to half-volley an eye-catching first goal for Régis Le Bris’s side.Europa League: Lyon take down Crystal Palace, Cissè’s Milan hat-trick sinks SalzburgRead moreIt ensured a largely unconvincing Sunderland came from behind to secure a second straightEuropa Leaguewin and their relief was evident as every outfield player followed Sadiki in vaulting those hoardings to join the celebrations.“It was a difficult game,” said Le Bris, Sunderland’s manager, with considerable understatement. “Torreense are a good team.”With their home ground too small to accommodate European football, Leiria’s stadium stood in. It proved quite some substitute. An arena overlooked by a 12th-century castle constructed to defend this attractive medieval town against reconquest by the Moors created an imposing backdrop to Sunderland’s first competitive trip to the continent for 53 years.Back in 1973 they were second division FA Cup holders. Torreense know the feeling. Having provoked widespread shock by beating Sporting to win the Portuguese Cup last spring, Luís Tralhão’s second-tier side relish their underdog status.After winning at Lillestrøm last month, Torreense aimed to keep the surprises coming and duly left a heavily rotated Sunderland trailing at the break. Le Bris had left, among others, Xhaka, Le Fée and Nordi Mukiele on the bench ahead of Sunday’s vital Premier League trip to Bournemouth. This reshuffle permitted Luke O’Nien, a survivor from League One days, to captain Sunderland at a ground transformed into a sea of red and white. Although only 4,000 official tickets were allocated to the visitors more were readily available locally and estimates suggested the formal allocation had doubled.As the sun dropped and the temperature fell from a high of 28C those fans watched a disjointed first half on Sunderland’s part. It seemed telling that the normally fairly impassive Le Bris looked distinctly, and unusually, irritated and frustrated at times.View image in fullscreenSunderland supporters enjoy their club’s first competitive trip to the continent for 53 years.Photograph: Ana Brigida/APGranted his humour was hardly helped by the referee’s penchant for detecting phantom Sunderland fouls but ominously Malick Fofana, a £30m summer signing from Lyon, struggled wide on the left. Ditto Nilson Angulo on the right wing.Torreense, 15th in Portugal’s second tier might not have been threatening Robin Roefs’s goal but they succeeded in blocking and clearing pretty much everything that came their way. Indeed Tralhão’s defence looked almost as well fortified as that ancient castle towering over them.Admittedly, midway through the first half Timur Tutierov, Sunderland’s centre-forward, thought he had headed the opener but that effort was disallowed due to shirt pulling on Omar Alderete’s part.Then, with the interval fast approaching, Le Bris adopted hand-on-hips mode as Torreense reminded everyone precisely why they have built such a giantkilling reputation by scoring with their first shot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt came from centre-back Volnei Feltes. With Sunderland losing concentration and standing off, he was permitted to advance unopposed before cutting in on his right foot and sending a sublime 20-yard curler into the top corner.Although Angulo forced Lucas Paes into a fine save he, like Fofana, was soon replaced as Le Bris made a quadruple substitution involving the introduction of Le Fée, Xhaka, Mukiele and Reinildo.This infusion of quality left Torreense a little groggy and the midfielder Jules Ahoka –a highly impressive 20-year-old £8.5m summer buy from Royal Antwerp – was able to equalise by heading his first goal for Sunderland courtesy of Mukiele’s deft dink.View image in fullscreenJules Ahoka scores Sunderland’s first goal against Torreense.Photograph: Luis Loureiro/ShutterstockWhen the lively Tutierov went down in the box, the referee immediately pointed to the spot. However, a linesman’s flag indicated an offside so it seemed there would be no penalty. Or at least not until the video assistant referee intervened – lengthily; the eventual conclusion was no offside, no foul and no penalty.No matter; when Le Fée dinked a gorgeous ball into the box and Xhaka played it into Sadiki’s path, the scorer waited for it to drop across him before applying the expert finishing touch on the half-volley.Explore more on these topicsEuropa LeagueTorreenseSunderlandmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Europa League: Lyon take down Crystal Palace as Benfica overwhelm Celtic | Europa League | The Guardian
description: Pierre Sage suffered a Europa League defeat as his Crystal Palace side lost 3-2 to his former employers Lyon while Celtic found clinical Benfica too much to handle
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pierre Sage suffered a Europa League defeat as his Crystal Palace side lost 3-2 to his former employers Lyon while Celtic found clinical Benfica too much to handle
Content: Corentin Tolisso takes the acclaim of his Lyon teammates after scoring an early opener against Crystal Palace.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersView image in fullscreenCorentin Tolisso takes the acclaim of his Lyon teammates after scoring an early opener against Crystal Palace.Photograph: Manon Cruz/ReutersEuropa LeagueEuropa League: Lyon take down Crystal Palace as Benfica overwhelm CelticSage loses 3-2 to former side; Benfica 4-1 CelticJuventus go top with 2-1 win over Celta VigoAgenciesThu 15 Oct 2026 15.18 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 18.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePierre Sage endured a frustrating return toLyonin the Europa League as hisCrystal Palaceside lost 3-2 to his former employers at the Groupama Stadium.Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half without a shot on target for the visitors. Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break before Pavel Sulc restored the Ligue 1 side’s two-goal advantage. The Palace substitute Daichi Kamada pulled one back with nine minutes remaining in a better second half for Palace, who could not find an equaliser.Noah Sadiki stunner earns Sunderland dramatic late win against TorreenseRead moreDays afterbeating his predecessor, the Nottingham Forest manager, Oliver Glasner, at Selhurst Park in the Premier League on Sunday, Sage found himself returning to the home of the club he managed for 14 months.Ismaïla Sarr, who claimed the Conference League golden boot last season, was in the Crystal Palace starting lineup for the first time this season.Celticfound a clinicalBenficaside too much to handle during a 4-1 defeat in Lisbon. The Colombia striker Jhon Durán scored for the hosts with a penalty after just five minutes having been fouled by Dane Murray and completed his double in the 35th minute, after the defender Alexander Bah had doubled Benfica’s lead earlier in the half.Martin O’Neill’s side were cut apart at times but could have scored themselves on a couple of occasions before the break. The visitors eventually reduced the deficit in the 63rd minute through a brave header from Camilo Durán – who had joined up with the squad late after remaining in Glasgow for the birth of his second child – but they could not close the gap any further before the substitute Vangelis Pavlidis fired in a fourth for the home side with two minutes remaining.Quick GuideConference League roundupShowGeorginio Rutter gotBrighton’s campaign off to a flying start and sent a message to his manager, Fabian Hürzeler. Rutter has lost his place to Charalampos Kostoulas and was making his first start since the opening day of the season against the Lithuanian championsKauno Zalgiris.The French forward responded by scoring twice and creating another as Brighton cruised to a 4-0 victory at the Amex Stadium, with Jack Hinshelwood and Matt O’Riley also on target.Heartssuffered a frustrating start to their campaign asNordsjællandscored a late equaliser to secure a 1-1 draw in an entertaining encounter at Tynecastle.The home side went ahead through Oisin McEntee’s close-range finish in the 33rd minute and had several chances to add to their lead.But they lost their way in the closing quarter of the match and Nordsjælland, fourth in the Danish Superliga, claimed a point through a deflected strike from Nicklas Røjkjær.Press AssociationWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Randal Kolo Muani scored a stoppage-time header to giveJuventusa 2-1 win atCelta Vigowhich leaves them top of the standings. Hugo Álvarez had put the home side in front early on before Nick Woltemade equalised on the hour and Kolo Muani then nodded in from close range during the second minute of added time.Milancruised to a 4-0 victory atRBSalzburg, courtesy of a hat-trick by the Italian teenager Alphadjo Cissè. Milan’s record signing Gonçalo Ramos made it four on 72 minutes before a red card for Filippo Terracciano took some of the shine off the win for Ruben Amorim’s side.View image in fullscreenMilan’s Alphadjo Cissè points to the crowd after scoring the opener in a 4-0 win at RB Salzburg.Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPABayer Leverkusenput themselves top of the standings after the early kick-offs as they followed up their opening 2-0 win with a 4-0 success at Polish sideLech Poznan. The Czech striker Patrik Schick was on target twice from the penalty spot in the first half, either side of a Malik Tillman goal, to ensure the points were wrapped up for Carles Martínez’s side before the interval. Ibrahim Maza added a late fourth.Real Sociedadfollowed up their opening defeat at home to Bournemouth with a 1-1 draw atUnion Saint-Gilloise.Explore more on these topicsEuropa LeagueLyonCrystal PalaceBenficaCelticMilanRed Bull SalzburgnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alex Scott quits Disney+ role as Women’s Champions League presenter | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Disney+ has paid tribute to Alex Scott’s contribution after the presenter decided to walk away to focus on other projects
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Disney+ has paid tribute to Alex Scott’s contribution after the presenter decided to walk away to focus on other projects
Content: Alex Scott at last month’s launch event for Disney+ coverage of the Women's Champions League.Photograph: Mike Marsland/Getty Images for Disney+View image in fullscreenAlex Scott at last month’s launch event for Disney+ coverage of the Women's Champions League.Photograph: Mike Marsland/Getty Images for Disney+Women's Champions LeagueAlex Scott quits Disney+ role as Women’s Champions League presenterScott walking away to focus on other projectsDisney+ was criticised after opening round this seasonExclusive byTom GarryThu 15 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlex Scott, the former Football Focus host, has left her role as a presenter of the Women’s Champions League coverage on Disney+.It is understood it was Scott’s decision to walk away and focus on other projects, including her new show, One More Word WSL, with her fellow former England internationals Anita Asante and Fara Williams.Scott had fronted the streaming platform’s coverage of the elite women’s European club competition since it obtained the rights in 2025. However, Disney’s production levels werecriticised after the opening roundfollowing a series of technical problems. These included an unscheduled advert break that interrupted the second half ofArsenal’s 1-0 win over HB Køgefor more than three minutes.FC Copenhagen Women have a ‘startup-like’ brand. Now they need resultsRead moreA spokesperson for Disney+ told the Guardian: “We would like to extend our sincere thanks to Alex Scott for her contribution to our coverage of the Uefa Women’s Champions League on Disney+. Her passion for the women’s game and the competition shone through throughout her time with us, and we are grateful for all she contributed. We wish her every success.”Scott, a former England and Arsenal defender and former contestant on the BBC’s Strictly Come Dancing and ITV’s I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, has also presented major sports shows for the BBC, including coverage of the 2020 Olympics. Scott’s representatives said: “Alex is grateful for the opportunities she has had to work with the team at Disney+ and hopes that they continue to work together in the future.”Scott presented the BBC’s Football Focus show for five seasons beforeits closure this year. At the start of this season’s Women’s Super League campaign she launched One More Word through her own production company, First Cap Productions, and has previously explained that show was createdin response to the BBC cancelling its weekly WSL highlights show.Scott, who turned 42 on Wednesday, toldthe Observer, this month: “I feel like there’s always an excuse about women’s football shows not working because of the viewership or needing to save money. Whereas I think if they are done right, they can work, if things are given a fresh idea or a fresh format, they can work.”In the same interview, discussing some of the criticism aimed at Disney’s Women’s Champions League coverage this term, Scott said: “Ultimately, do I agree with all the decisions that were made? Absolutely not. Did I try and advise? Yes, but I can only do so much.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“But nobody sees the conversations, the fights I have behind the scenes. But I can hold my head up and know that I’ve always tried my best for the greater good of women’s sport.”Sources have told the Guardian the presenter’s relationship with Disney remains positive. Disney, whose coverage is produced by ESPN, secured an exclusive five-year deal to broadcast the Women’s Champions League across European broadcast territories in 2025. It is understood its presenting team will continue to include Shebahn Aherne, Nedum Onuoha and Lianne Sanderson. The lineup includes commentators such as Vicki Sparks and Jacqui Oatley. The competition resumes on 28 October.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Southgate ‘hardly watches’ football and does not envisage Premier League return | Gareth Southgate | The Guardian
description: Gareth Southgate has revealed he ‘didn’t even enjoy the wins’ for more than a couple of minutes towards the end of his time in charge of England
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Gareth Southgate has revealed he ‘didn’t even enjoy the wins’ for more than a couple of minutes towards the end of his time in charge of England
Content: Gareth Southgate pictured after his last game as England’s manager, the Euro 2024 final defeat by Spain.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGareth Southgate pictured after his last game as England’s manager, the Euro 2024 final defeat by Spain.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianGareth SouthgateSouthgate ‘hardly watches’ football and does not envisage Premier League returnFormer England manager last went to game in May 2025He says he got only brief enjoyment from wins by the endJacob SteinbergThu 15 Oct 2026 06.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGareth Southgate has all but ruled out a return to Premier League management and revealed he “didn’t even enjoy the wins” for more than a couple of minutes towards the end of his time in charge of England.Southgate, who has moved away from football sincestepping down as the managerof the England men’s team after defeat by Spain in the Euro 2024 final, said he had not attended a game since watching his boyhood clubCrystal Palace beat Manchester City in the FA Cup finallast year.The 56-year-old’s only taste of club management came when he spent almost three-and-a-half years at Middlesbrough after replacing Steve McClaren in 2006. Southgate was unable to keep Middlesbrough in the Premier League in 2009 and he indicated during an appearance on theAmol Rajan Connectionpodcast that he had no interest in seeking a return to top-flight management.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“I don’t see a scenario where I do that,” he said. “Towards the end of my time with England, I stopped enjoying … at the very least for a period, the wins keep you going. By the end, I didn’t even enjoy the wins for any longer than a couple of minutes. So, I’ve hardly watched football.“I went to the FA Cup final to see my team, Crystal Palace, win their first trophy. I’ve not been to a football ground since. So my sort of desire to be involved in football has changed.”Southgate managed England for almost eight years and came close to ending their hunt for a first men’s trophy since the 1966 World Cup. But he has sought different opportunities since leaving the role. He has launched a podcast and fronted a BBC documentary this year in which he travelled across the UK to understand the challenges facing young men and boys.“I’ve loved the last 18 months of my life,” Southgate said. “I’ve had 37 years where my sense of self depended on did I win or lose on Saturday. And actually I’ve loved having different experiences.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I’ve met politicians, I’ve met people in the media industry, I have learned about leadership in all sorts of areas, I’ve travelled around the world learning things. I’ve just enjoyed playing a different film in my life.”Explore more on these topicsGareth SouthgatenewsShareReuse this content
