title: Giovanni Leoni’s return from injury delayed in fresh blow to Liverpool | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Liverpool defender Giovanni Leoni’s return from a lengthy spell out with a knee injury has been delayed, but Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitiké are approaching a return
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Liverpool defender Giovanni Leoni’s return from a lengthy spell out with a knee injury has been delayed, but Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitiké are approaching a return
Content: Giovanni Leoni sustained a serious knee injury on his Liverpool debut in 2025.Photograph: Jan Kruger/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGiovanni Leoni sustained a serious knee injury on his Liverpool debut in 2025.Photograph: Jan Kruger/Getty ImagesLiverpoolGiovanni Leoni’s return from injury delayed in fresh blow to LiverpoolDefender sustained ACL injury on debut for clubBradley and Ekitiké are on track with recoveryAndy HunterThu 15 Oct 2026 11.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGiovanni Leoni’s Liverpool return has been delayed because of the severity of the knee injury sustained on his debut,Andoni Iraolahas revealed.The central defender had been expected to resume team training during the recent international break but that schedule has been put back by about a month.Bradley Barcola’s clinical hat-trick inspires Liverpool to 6-3 rout of LaskRead moreLeoni, a £26m signing from Parma in 2025, sustained an anterior cruciate ligament injuryagainst Southampton13 months ago. Iraola has disclosed the damage extended beyond the ACL and Liverpool must tread carefully with the 19-year-old’s rehabilitation as a consequence.“It is taking more time than we wanted,” the head coach said. “With Gio, the plan was to train with the team in this past international break. It is probably now going to be the next international break [which starts on 9 November], so we have lost one month in the process.“With Giovanni’s injury, I wasn’t here but talking to the medical department it wasn’t just an ACL. It was a bad injury, a lot of things around the knee were involved apart from the ACL. I think he has to be very confident in the rehab and the process has to be very careful with him.“We want to make sure once he comes to the team he stays there in a good place. It’s true we’ve had a little bit of not a setback but a delay, if you want. The plan now is he starts in the next break. It’s not that far off, but a little bit later than we expected.”Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo remain doubts for Saturday’s Premier League trip to Brentford having missed Liverpool’s last two fixtures with injuries picked up on international duty.Iraola had more encouraging news concerning Liverpool’s other long-term injury casualties, Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitiké, with the former close to starting training with the squad. Bradley has been sidelined since sustaining a serious knee injury at Arsenal in January, and Ekitiké’s impressive debut season at Liverpool was cut short by an achilles injury against Paris Saint-Germain in April.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“They are both doing very well and they are in a good place,” he said. “Conor is not so far from training with the group – not full training but doing some things with the group. Hugo is a little bit behind that but that was always the plan. He is still doing very well according to the plan. When they have been injured for so long it’s difficult to say [when they will be back] but I think Conor is not very far from starting doing things with us.”Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolAndoni IraolanewsShareReuse this content

title: Vinícius claims he is targeted by referees and says flair players need protection | Real Madrid | The Guardian
description: Vinícius Júnior is not happy with how he is being treated by referees and wants more protection for talented players such as himself, Lamine Yamal and Julián Álvarez
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Vinícius Júnior is not happy with how he is being treated by referees and wants more protection for talented players such as himself, Lamine Yamal and Julián Álvarez
Content: Vinícius Júnior runs with the ball during Real Madrid’s Champions League win over Roma.Photograph: Ettore Ferrari/EPAView image in fullscreenVinícius Júnior runs with the ball during Real Madrid’s Champions League win over Roma.Photograph: Ettore Ferrari/EPAReal MadridVinícius claims he is targeted by referees and says flair players need protectionMadrid forward banned for four games after recent red‘In the end, the yellow cards always seem to go to Vini’Associated PressThu 15 Oct 2026 09.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 10.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVinícius Júnior is not happy with how he is being treated by referees and wants more protection for talented players such as himself, Lamine Yamal and Julián Álvarez.Vinícius spoke out afterReal Madrid’s 4-3 come-from-behind win at Romain the Champions League on Wednesday. The Brazil forward also acknowledged he was going through a slump, but said he had “no doubt” he would regain his best form soon.The match against Roma came hours after he was handed a four-game suspension in the Spanish league after beingsent off for pulling the hair of an opponentand for protesting against the referee. “I don’t recall any other player receiving a four-match suspension,” he said. “I tried to move the player in front of me out of the way, and I ended up getting caught in his hair.“That was it – a red card – which is why I was so surprised. I didn’t say a single offensive word to the referee that would warrant a four-match ban. But when it comes to Vini, it’s all too easy. The opposing team will always say it’s justified, and the press will say the same. I understand that. I’m here to keep evolving and improving, because I know where I’ve come from and what I’m capable of achieving.View image in fullscreenVinícius Júnior leaves the pitch after his red card against Villarreal.Photograph: Alejandro Martinez Velez/Reuters“It’s understandable for the opposing fans to jeer me, because my job is to score goals against their team, but I don’t get the referees. I’ve seen the stats: I’ve been on the receiving end of 500 fouls, yet that has only resulted in five red cards. In the end, the yellow cards always seem to go to Vini, to the attacking players. We need to protect the players who bring something different to the game, like Lamine at Barcelona or Julián at Atleti. Defenders are allowed to foul me the entire match but in the end it’s me who gets the card.”José Mourinho complained about the timing of the announcement of the suspension. “Do you think it’s normal for a player from a Spanish team, preparing for an important match that’s also crucial for Spanish football, to find out about his four-match suspension just two hours before kickoff?” Madrid’s manager said. “We were on the bus about to arrive at the stadium when we found out … they’ve started doing things without any shame.”Vinícius, who hasn’t scored for Madrid since August, was replaced in the 59th minute of Madrid’s victory before the team rallied from 3-1 down. “I’m working to get back to my best as soon as possible,” Vinícius said. “I know I’m not at my peak right now, but I’ve been through worse, and even when people have doubted me, I’ve always stood up for this club. That’s why I signed a six-year contract extension. The good run of form will return, and the goals will come back, too. I’m certain of that. I have no doubt. I’m here to help the team.”The 26-year-old downplayed his frustration after Mourinho substituted him. “It’s natural for me to get upset when I’m substituted because I always want to play every single match,” he said. “I’m well aware of my current form and how I’m playing. I’m here to help the team, and sometimes you have to come off so that other players can get on and change the dynamic.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Mourinho and I have a great relationship. He’s always straight with me. Of course I got a little annoyed when I came off today, but that’s normal. In the end he was right, the team improved, and that’s what matters most.” Vinícius was replaced by Endrick, who scored an 85th-minute equaliser before Antonio Rüdiger gave Madrid the win in the 90th.Among the games Vinícius will miss because of his suspension is theclásicoat Barcelona on 25 October.Explore more on these topicsReal MadridEuropean club footballLa LigaRefereesnewsShareReuse this content

title: FA spending on Wembley hospitality and free tickets for FA Council rises by 25% | The FA | The Guardian
description: The Football Association spent 25% more on Wembley hospitality and freebies for FA Council members last season, the Guardian can reveal
Author: Sam Cunningham
Headline: The Football Association spent 25% more on Wembley hospitality and freebies for FA Council members last season, the Guardian can reveal
Content: The FA has upgraded the hospitality on offer at Wembley to VIPs.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenThe FA has upgraded the hospitality on offer at Wembley to VIPs.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAThe FAFA spending on Wembley hospitality and free tickets for FA Council rises by 25%Expenditure rises to £564,000 in 2025-26 seasonCost of hosting FA Council meetings also almost doublesSam CunninghamThu 15 Oct 2026 07.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 15.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Football Association spent 25% more on Wembley hospitality and freebies for FA Council members last season, the Guardian can reveal. The latest accounts show expenditure on tickets and hospitality rose from £452,300 in the 2024-25 season to £564,400 in 2025-26.While fans across the country have staged protests and walkouts in recent years over ticket price rises, and the cost-of-living crisis has made football increasingly unaffordable, the FA has upgraded the hospitality it offers to VIPs. Liverpoolscrapped plans to increase ticket pricesover three successive seasons following widespread unrest from supporters at the end of last season.There are more than 120 FA Council members, including some of the most influential figures in the game, such as the English Football League chair, Rick Parry, Professional Footballers’ Association chief executive, Maheta Molango, and senior Premier League executives.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.FA Council members can attend England and FA Cup matches – including the FA Cup semi-finals and final – held at Wembley and bring one guest free of charge. They receive complimentary meals and drinks, and sit in premium seats.“FA Council members are invited as our guests to the England matches and FA competitions that we host,” an FA spokesperson said. “They are just one of the groups invited to these fixtures, alongside others such as the competing clubs and any visiting national associations. The hospitality offering at these matches was updated over the past year to better reflect the hospitality offered by clubs and other football stakeholders, which has resulted in an increase in expenditure in this area.”The accounts indicate ticket and hospitality costs are likely to increase further due to the Fellowship of Council, an honorary membership scheme introduced in 2017. It allows members who have served on the FA Council for at least nine years to continue receiving free tickets, food and drinks even after stepping down.“As the number of members of the Fellowship increases annually, the costs associated with match tickets and hospitality are likely to increase,” the FA company secretary, Richard McDermott, writes in the accounts. “We propose to introduce changes to the benefits that go with membership of the Fellowship so that from 2027 these costs will start to reduce.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe cost of hosting FA Council meetings also almost doubled, rising from £18,600 to £33,200, with much of the increase attributed to higher hospitality expenditure.Explore more on these topicsThe FAWembley StadiumnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brewers go one win from World Series as back-to-back homers sink Dodgers | MLB | The Guardian
description: Milwaukee overturned a sixth-inning deficit with two seventh-inning blasts off Blake Snell to beat Los Angeles 6-2 and move within one win of the World Series
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Milwaukee overturned a sixth-inning deficit with two seventh-inning blasts off Blake Snell to beat Los Angeles 6-2 and move within one win of the World Series
Content: Brewers pitcher Trevor Megill celebrates after his team’s 6-2 victory over the Dodgers in Game 3 of the NLCS on Wednesday in Los Angeles.Photograph: Luke Hales/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBrewers pitcher Trevor Megill celebrates after his team’s 6-2 victory over the Dodgers in Game 3 of the NLCS on Wednesday in Los Angeles.Photograph: Luke Hales/Getty ImagesMLBBrewers go one win from World Series as back-to-back homers sink DodgersMilwaukee rally past Los Angeles for 3-0 NLCS leadBauers and Mitchell homer back-to-back off Blake SnellDefending champions face elimination on ThursdayAgenciesWed 14 Oct 2026 23.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 07.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJake Bauers and Garrett Mitchell hit back-to-back home runs off Blake Snell to reclaim the lead in the seventh inning as the Milwaukee Brewers beat theLos Angeles Dodgers6-2 on Wednesday night to take a commanding 3-0 lead in the National League Championship Series.The Dodgers had just taken a 2-1 lead in the bottom of the sixth before being stunned. The loss pushed the two-time defending World Series champions to the brink of elimination. They had trailed 3-0 in a best-of-seven postseason series only once previously in franchise history, when they were swept by the Baltimore Orioles in the 1966 World Series.Game 4 is Thursday at Dodger Stadium.Snell had retired 14 consecutive batters entering the seventh. The two-time Cy Young Award winner’s first pitch of the game was driven out of the park by Jackson Chourio, and his last was Mitchell’s solo shot.Andrew Vaughn drew a seven-pitch walk to open the seventh and was replaced by pinch-runner Christian Yelich. Bauers followed with a 412ft drive to right field on the 11th pitch of the at-bat, giving Milwaukee a 3-2 lead as much of the Brewers’ dugout spilled on to the field in celebration. Mitchell came up next and launched a 428ft shot to right-center, chasing Snell.Snell allowed four runs on four hits over six-plus innings, striking out nine and walking two.The Brewers are on the verge of sweeping the Dodgers in a reversal of last year’s NLCS, when Los Angeles eliminated Milwaukee in four games. The Brewers have never beaten the Dodgers in three previous postseason series.Milwaukee extended their lead to 5-2 in the eighth on a wild pitch by Justin Wrobleski that scored Brice Turang, who had reached on an infield single to third and advanced on William Contreras’ single. They added another run on Joey Ortiz’s two-strike RBI single in the ninth.The offensively starved Dodgers had taken their first lead of the night, 2-1, on Will Smith’s two-run double off reliever Abner Uribe in the sixth.Uribe, who replaced rookie starter Robert Gasser, loaded the bases with walks to Teoscar Hernández, Kyle Tucker andShohei Ohtani. Smith, who entered the game batting .043, doubled to left-center for his first hit of the NLCS.View image in fullscreenMilwaukee’s Jackson Chourio celebrates with teammates after hitting a first-inning home run against Los Angeles in Game 3 of the NLCS on Wednesday at Dodger Stadium.Photograph: Luke Hales/Getty ImagesDL Hall replaced Uribe, allowing one hit and striking out two before handing the ball to Trevor Megill in the eighth.The Dodgers had fallen behind almost immediately when Chourio homered off Snell’s first pitch, with fans still making their way to their seats.Mitchell then walked and Cooper Pratt singled in the second before Snell retired 14 consecutive batters, six by strikeout, only to unravel in the seventh.Los Angeles put runners on base in all but three innings but struggled to bring them home. They have yet to hit a home run in the NLCS.Ohtani went 1 for 2 with a walk while batting sixth, his lowest spot in the lineup since joining the Dodgers three years ago.Explore more on these topicsMLBMilwaukee BrewersLos Angeles DodgersBaseballShohei OhtaniUS sportsWest CoastShareReuse this content

title: Online ads weaponised to deliver ‘zero-click’ spyware, researchers say | Hacking | The Guardian
description: Discover-Tech’s Controlium software lets clients mass-profile internet users then covertly hack targets, say researchers at University of Toronto
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Discover-Tech’s Controlium software lets clients mass-profile internet users then covertly hack targets, say researchers at University of Toronto
Content: Millions of users worldwide have been served ads by Discover-Tech since 2024, say researchers.Photograph: Sergio Azenha/AlamyView image in fullscreenMillions of users worldwide have been served ads by Discover-Tech since 2024, say researchers.Photograph: Sergio Azenha/AlamyHackingOnline ads weaponised to deliver ‘zero-click’ spyware, researchers sayDiscover-Tech’s Controlium software lets clients mass-profile internet users then covertly hack targets, say researchers at University of TorontoAisha DownThu 15 Oct 2026 08.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 14.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Israeli advertising agency has been serving millions of online adverts that allow “zero-click” spyware to be used against targets,researchers at a Canadian university have said.Citizen Lab, a digital investigations research unit at the University of Toronto, said it believed dozens of devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera had been compromised by spyware delivered through ads run by Discover-Tech, which describes itself as a specialised digital advertising agency.According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech operates a software platform called Controlium that allows its clients to “mass-profile and deanonymise” internet users then covertly hack targets with third-party spyware. Unlike infections that rely on people interacting with links or files, the spyware requires no interaction from the victim to be installed, making it a new delivery technique, Citizen Lab says.The infections happen without a user’s knowledge, and in a matter of seconds, according to Citizen Lab.“[The online advertising] ecosystem is being weaponised at a massive scale to profile millions of users, then silently infect targets with zero-click mercenary spyware,” the report says.According to the report, Controlium is able to harvest a user’s identity and IP address when the user is shown a seemingly benign custom-created ad – for example, for a digital game or a telecoms service. If the user has been selected as a target for hacking, a mercenary spyware firm can then send a malicious code containing spyware to their device, the researchers say.They say that millions of users worldwide have been served ads by Discover-Tech since 2024, including in Yemen, Brazil, Mexico and Czechia.Related work by the research group Confiant also suggests that Discover-Tech’s ads have been shown to users of the networks of government entities in Europe and the US, as well as the UN, Nato, the international criminal court and the International Atomic Energy Agency.“It’s disastrous that major ad vendors and organisations apparently were neither able to detect nor prevent the company’s malicious advertising operations for years,” said Wolfie Christl, a researcher at Citizen Lab. “The way the online advertising ecosystem works today is a security threat for states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike.”According to Citizen Lab, Controlium acts as a “facilitator” for third-party spyware firms that have targeted “government officials, journalists, businesspeople, activists, academics and embassy workers”. Citizen Lab claims it can deliver spyware that can access everything on the device of a target, extracting messages, photos and emails, recording calls and secretly activating microphones.The full extent of the targeting allegedly enabled by Discover-Tech is unknown. Citizen Lab’s findings join mounting evidence that the opaque arrangements underpinning the world of online advertising can be leveraged for surveillance.“There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a researcher at Citizen Lab.Discover-Tech has been approached for comment.When a user navigates to a website that shows advertisements, their details become part of a split-second programmatic auction involving dozens or hundreds of companies. These companies bid automatically to place an ad in front of that user.These bids are based on the user’s profile, which can include information about their device and data compiled on them by tracking their activity across the web. For example, companies given the profile of a 35-year-old interested in sports betting and crypto might bid to show that individual an advertisement for an energy drink.There is little regulation on this automated online market, and there is growing evidence that it is being exploited by malevolent actors.Reuters hasreportedthat billions of dollars’ worth of Meta’s ad revenue comes from ads for scams, illegal gambling, pornography and other banned content. In the US, ICE and other government agencies haveboughtsoftware that uses ad tech data to track people’s movements.“Cybersecurity agencies, regulators and lawmakers in the US, Europe and other regions must urgently step in. They must investigate the involved companies and fix the systemic risks that enable malicious ad targeting,” said Christl.Explore more on these topicsHackingInternet safetySurveillanceResearchHigher educationIsraelAdvertisingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Is your boss watching you? The rise of AI surveillance at work – podcast | Science | The Guardian
description: Workers have always been monitored by their bosses, first through output targets, and then via computer software labelled ‘bossware’. But AI is transforming the capabilities of these systems, processing huge volumes of data to provide minute-by-minute accounts of activity, and productivity. To find out more, Ian Sample hears from UK technology editor Robert Booth. He explains which sectors are adopting this approach, why they are doing it, and how it could end up being counterproductive.

title: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt | Stock markets | The Guardian
description: Chip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as potential interest rate hikes spook markets
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Chip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as potential interest rate hikes spook markets
Content: A Hana Bank screen shows the Kopsi index with a downward graph line. The tech-heavy South Korean index fell 8% overnight in Asia, triggering circuit breakers and halting stock trades.Photograph: Lee Jin-man/APView image in fullscreenA Hana Bank screen shows the Kopsi index with a downward graph line. The tech-heavy South Korean index fell 8% overnight in Asia, triggering circuit breakers and halting stock trades.Photograph: Lee Jin-man/APStock marketsTech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debtChip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as potential interest rate hikes spook marketsBusiness news – live updatesLarry Elliott: the global economy is muddling through. But a storm is comingKalyeena MakortoffThu 15 Oct 2026 10.33 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, asfears over rising inflationand future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix andSamsungElectronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5% respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.The global economy is muddling through against the odds. But a storm is coming | Larry ElliottRead moreMeanwhile, Japan’sNikkei225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in the memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI.The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where theNasdaqComposite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, its worst performance since July.US stocks fell further when trading resumed on Thursday. The Nasdaq dropped another 1.4% at the start of trading, with Dell, which makes datacentre servers, and Coherent, which manufactures components for AI datacentres, leading the early fallers.The sell-off came after US data on Wednesday showed stateside inflation jumped toa higher-than-expected 3.7% in September, marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May.Fresh data on Thursday showing US producers increased their prices by 6.3% year on year in September – the sharpest rise since December 2022 – added to inflationary jitters.The figures have rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month.“Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid said.Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe sell-offfollows warnings from the International Monetary Fund,which said this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets was putting world financial stability at risk.“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” the IMF said. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit.The latest jitters hit China, where the Shanghai Shenzhen CSI 300 slipped by as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits.European stocks also came under pressure, with Germany’s DAX down 0.36% in afternoon trading and the Italian FTSE MIB dropping by 1.3%.Explore more on these topicsStock marketsMarket turmoilTechnology sectorInflationInterest ratesUS marketsSamsungnewsShareReuse this content

title: Poland’s ascent from communist state to top 20 economy reverses the brain drain | Poland | The Guardian
description: In the final part of our series on the country, Poles tell how wages have soared – along with the cost of living
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: In the final part of our series on the country, Poles tell how wages have soared – along with the cost of living
Content: A view of Warsaw from the observation deck of Varso Tower, the tallest building in the EU at 310 metres. In the background, the Palace of Culture and Science, built in the 1950s as a symbol of the postwar socialist era.Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA view of Warsaw from the observation deck of Varso Tower, the tallest building in the EU at 310 metres. In the background, the Palace of Culture and Science, built in the 1950s as a symbol of the postwar socialist era.Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The GuardianPolandPoland’s ascent from communist state to top 20 economy reverses the brain drainIn the final part of our series on the country, Poles tell how wages have soared – along with the cost of livingWill military spending help or hinder Poland’s growth story?Poland’s push for EU energy resilience amid Russian aggressionRichard Partingtonin WarsawThu 15 Oct 2026 01.56 EDTFirst published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbove the rain-soaked streets of Warsaw, the observation deck of the Varso tower overlooks Joseph Stalin’s gift toPolandthat has divided opinion for decades.For some, the Soviet-eraPalace of Culture and Scienceis a drunk confectioner’s nightmare; standing as a relic of oppression that should have been demolished. For others, it is an icon on the skyline and a monumental warning from history.For the managers of the Varso – completed four years ago, as the tallest building in the EU – with its 310m-high spire rising symbolically above its Stalinist neighbour, it is a waypoint on Poland’s rapid path to economic prosperity.View image in fullscreenCezary Błaszczyk and Natalia Kasperska at the Varso Tower.Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The Guardian“We look down on it,” says Cezary Błaszczyk, the managing director of HB Reavis in Poland, which owns the tower, gesturing at the palace opposite. A few months ago aslackline walkertraversed the 500m gap between the buildings. “It was a symbolic walk from the past to the future,” says his colleague Natalia Kasperska.“Since we are higher and taller than the Palace of Culture, we treat it as: ‘We got over communism, and now we are a country with a strong economy,’” Błaszczyk says.Over the four decades since regaining its independence from Soviet-dominated rule, Poland has been transformed. Excluding oil-exporting states and financial hubs, incomes have converged with western levels at the fastest rate in the world; from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year.View image in fullscreenThe Estonian slackliner Jaan Roose walks on a 500-metre-long tightrope stretched between the Palace of Culture and Science and Varso Tower on 31 May.Photograph: Sergei Gapon/AFP/Getty ImagesNational income surpassed $1tn (£755bn) last year, ranking Poland among the world’s 20 largest economies. International Monetary Fund projections show income per capita will soon overtake Japan and Spain.“Four decades ago, we were in – excuse my English – deep, deep shit,” says Marcin Bosacki, the Polish deputy foreign minister.Stirring a cup of tea and lemon in his opulent Warsaw office, he recalls queueing after school in the 1980s for up to five hours to buy butter and meat as the communist government imposed martial law.However, the Gdańsk shipworkers’Solidarność movementand Pope John Paul II’s1979 pilgrimageto his home country paved the way for Poland’s transition to democracy in 1990 and an “economic miracle”. Integration with western institutions, includingNatoin 1999 andEUaccession in 2004, also helped.Poland GDP per capita graphicFor years, many Poles chose to emigrate to earn more abroad, in a brain drain accelerated by EU membership. Polish plumbersbecame shorthand in Britain for foreign labouramid the political battles over EU freedom of movement before the Brexit vote.Now Britons are increasingly likely to have their taps fixed by Romanians and Bulgarians, after a surge in the number of Polish nationals leaving. Ineach yearsince 2021, when Brexit was enacted after a year-long transition period, twice as many Poles left the UK than arrived.Meanwhile,Germany recordedmore non-Germans moving to Poland in 2024 than heading in the opposite direction for the first time on record.On the Varso’s 44th floor, in the Warsaw practice of Foster + Partners, Jedrzej Kolesinski and Krzysztof Gornicki are among those returnees. Both moved to London in their 20s to work in the British architecture firm’s head office – where they led the design team behind the tower they now occupy.Gornicki says Poland has changed dramatically in the years he was away. He always wanted to return to contribute to the country, and raising a family near his parents in a safe, green city that is more affordable than London also has its plus points. Now the pair are working to design Warsaw’s new airport – the biggest greenfield infrastructure project inEurope.“You can work globally from one location. In London we worked on projects from North America to Asia … right now, we’re doing the same thing, just from Warsaw.”On the streets below the Varso, the sights and sounds of progress are unmistakable. Modern electric trams glide past skyscrapers, there are cranes and construction work, giant advertising boards, and dockless e-scooters.The traditional working-classbar mleczny(milk bars) still do a roaring trade serving beetroot soup and Polish dumplings. But at the oldest, Prasowy, orders are taken on a digital touchscreen.Once an asphalt desert designed for columns of Soviet tanks, the old Parade Square surrounding the palace has had a green makeover. Further development is planned to bolster Warsaw’s bid for the 2040 summer Olympics.Living costs in Warsaw graphicThere are also growing pains. Just as the facades of Warsaw’s medieval old town –rebuilt from the rubble of the second world war– conceal 20th-century concrete, Poland’s stellar growth obscures tensions. The influx of global capital has driven up living costs, squeezing out poor Varsovians. Incomeinequality is among the highest in Europe, while growing political divisions set the stage for a fractious general election next year.Convergence with the west also presents a novel challenge for a country with a reputation as a low-cost hub within the EU.For years Poland’s cheap, skilled workforce attracted companies such as Volkswagen to build cars, Cadbury to make chocolate and banks such as JP Morgan to open global support centres. At €19.10 (£16.10) an hour, average labour costs (wages, taxes and other costs) are stillhalf the level of Germany and France, but the gap is closing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSince 2004, the average monthly wage has more than tripled in nominal terms to 8,904 złoty (£1,723) last year. The net monthly salary in Warsaw has risen by 120% since 2016, according to Deutsche Bank, lifting it above Rome and Lisbon. A meal for two in the capital now costs more than in Tokyo and the price of a cappuccino has doubled.Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire founder of InPost, the pan-European parcel locker company started in Kraków, says Poles deserve their reputation as hard workers. But now the country must focus on working smarter, in higher-value-added manufacturing and knowledge-intensive services.“The next phase will depend less on catching up, and more on productivity. We don’t have labour cost advantage at all. We need to focus on productivity, technology, cheaper energy and better regulation.”Capitals salaries graphicHe is, however, concerned about the tensions in Polish politics. Divisions between the nationalist president, Karol Nawrocki, and Donald Tusk’s liberal government havegrown increasingly acrimonious. Meanwhile, fringe far-right parties together hold afifth of public support. Poland is alsoinvesting heavily in defenceandenergy security– aiming to boost economic growth in the process – amid Europe’s response to Russian aggression and US disengagement.“People may put trust in someone else that has a magic remedy. [But] there is no magic remedy. We need to be super careful in terms of believing there is a secret sauce that will magically change things,” Brzoska says.“In my opinion – unfortunately for all of us – we still need to work hard.”As part of its growth plans, Poland is pushing to become a regional tech hub, bolstered by a$1bn investment fundbacked by public and private capital to support tech startups and AI companies. The number of high-growth firms is rising, includingElevenLabs, an $11bn AI audio generation and voice cloning company named after 11 November – Poland’s national independence day.There are strong foundations for its ambition. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s annual programme for international student assessment (Pisa) scoresranks Poland equal to the UKamong the top countries in Europe and globally for maths, while a greater share of adults have higher education qualifications than in Germany.On the eastern side of the Vistula River in the gritty and creative working-class district of Praga, the campus of the games company CD Projekt Red shows the progress being made.View image in fullscreenMarcin Łukaszewski, Social Media Manager at CD Projekt Red, gives a tour of the company’s headquarters in Warsaw.Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The GuardianAs the developer behind the smash hit games seriesThe WitcherandCyberpunk 2077, the company started life in the 1990s as an importer of CD games made by US publishers.Michał Nowakowski, its co-chief executive, says this was about the limit of Polish ambition in the early days. Now he competes globally to attract coders, games developers and graphic designers.“In the late 90s and early 2000s I feel there was a massive inferiority complex. Among everybody who was young, you wanted to catch up with the west.”Growing up in the 1980s, his family were expelled from Poland in the period of martial law. He recalls visiting London aged 15 and being “blown away” by the Virgin megastore and British culture. “I could never imagine Poland being like it.”Within a generation, though, he says this attitude would be alien to his own children. “For young people now they have no inferiority complex. They don’t stop and think: ‘Can we be as good as Brits, French, Spanish?’ It’s not holding them back.“We have really good universities and skills teaching people. I think that can take us to unprecedented heights as a country.“We’re a proper-sized country. Not too small, not too big; no inferiority complex any more. There’s nothing holding us back.”Explore more on these topicsPolandEconomicsTechnology sectorAI (artificial intelligence)EuropeEuropean UnionGentrificationnewsShareReuse this content

title: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour  | Science | The Guardian
description: International delegates agree leap second no longer tenable, but first leap hour not likely to happen for thousands of years
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: International delegates agree leap second no longer tenable, but first leap hour not likely to happen for thousands of years
Content: A clock at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, through which the prime meridian passes.Photograph: coward_lion/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA clock at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, through which the prime meridian passes.Photograph: coward_lion/Getty ImagesScienceHow an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hourInternational delegates agree leap second no longer tenable, but first leap hour not likely to happen for thousands of yearsIan SampleScience editorThu 15 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter decades of discussion, quibbling and worrying about clocks in computer systems, the world’s official timekeepers have voted to replace what many viewed as a tiresome correction: the leap second. It’s time, they say, for the leap hour.Delegates from 69 countries cast their votes on Thursday at a conference inFranceof the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which ensures the world sticks to the same standards of time, weight, distance and more.The decision to adopt the leap hour from next year aims to reduce the risk of computers and other technical systems tripping over as their software grapples with minutes lasting 61 seconds – and, worse, 59 seconds – instead of a round 60.“After 30 years of debate, the leap second is making way for the leap hour,” said Dr Setnam Shemar, principal scientist in the time and frequency department at the UK’s National Physical Laboratory (NPL). “This will reduce the risks to the systems and national infrastructure that depend on accurate time while still preserving the fundamental link between our global time system and the rotation of the Earth.”The vote at Versailles means that coordinated universal time (UTC) can drift up to an hour from astronomical time before a leap hour is needed, but that is unlikely to happen for thousands of years.“We already have daylight saving where we change by an hour and no one gets bothered about that, apart from losing sleep or getting an extra hour’s sleep,” said Shemar, who sat on the international timekeeping expert committee that proposed the leap hour.The more familiar leap year was introduced more than 2,000 years ago to ensure that the calendar year did not fall out of step with the time that the Earth takes to circle the sun. Adding a day to the end of February every four or so years does the job, because Earth orbits the sun every 365 and a quarter days.Leap seconds are a much more modern invention. In 1955, Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the NPL built the world’s first practical, high-precision caesium atomic clock. The device revolutionised timekeeping, and in 1967 the astronomical definition of a second, based on the rotation of the Earth, was abandoned. Ever since, the formal definition of one second has been 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the caesium atom.Atomic clocks are exceptionally stable and precise. Their timekeeping has become critical for modern computer systems, communications, satellites, trading systems and electricity grids. But the Earth’s rotation is far less reliable. Its spin is affected by the planet’s molten core, the shift of the oceans, global jet streams and other natural forces.View image in fullscreenComputers linked with the atomic clock at the National Physical Laboratory in Teddington, England, and other international atomic clocks.Photograph: David Gee/AlamyBroadly, Earth’s rotation is slowing down: when an asteroid doomed the dinosaurs, a day lasted about 23 and a half hours. Because of this, officials have added 27 leap seconds since 1972 to ensure UTC is aligned with astronomical time.The strategy endured for more than 50 years until scientists spotted a fresh reason to fear technological mayhem. In the past decade, Earth’s rotation has sped up, meaning officials might have needed to add the first negative leap second, equivalent to lopping a second off UTC. The 30% probability of a negative leap second in the next decade brought the Versailles vote forward.“Leap seconds can be tricky enough to deal with,” said Shemar. Telecommunications, electricity grids and navigation systems used high-accuracy timing, he explained, but software updates could apply leap seconds at the wrong time, knocking networks out of sync.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“After the leap second applied in 2012, there were some computer systems whose operating systems couldn’t cope with 61 seconds in a minute. The servers froze, they seized up. Systems went offline. And those are the sorts of failures that can happen with positive leap seconds,” Shemar said.Among the crashed websites were Reddit and LinkedIn. Separately, Qantas flights were hit with delays. Negative leap seconds come with even greater risks. “There could be software out there that hasn’t been tested on negative leap seconds because we’ve never had to apply one before,” Shemar said.To test all the computer systems that talk to one another around the world would cost companies a fortune. It was this concern that swung the vote.Historically, the UK has grumbled about canning leap seconds because of the link with Greenwich mean time. Russia has also opposed the move, citing concerns of the impact on its Glonass satellite navigation system.The IERS Earth Orientation Centre, in Paris, tracks changes in the Earth’s rotation and other movements that feed into UTC. The centre also issues notices when leap seconds must be added.Dr Christian Bizouard, the director of the centre, approved of the vote, but said it passed the decision to people far in the future. “It’s kind of a philosophical discussion, because if a leap hour happens, it won’t be for a very, very long time,” he said. “What we are doing is pushing back the decision.”Explore more on these topicsScienceFrancefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics | Games | The Guardian
description: The studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action series
Author: Tom Regan
Headline: The studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action series
Content: Super smart shooter … Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Tactics.Illustration: UbisoftView image in fullscreenSuper smart shooter … Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Tactics.Illustration: UbisoftGamesFrom Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six TacticsThe studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action seriesTom ReganThu 15 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhere do you go after Mario? It’s a question the team at Ubisoft Paris found itself pondering three years ago after wrapping up work on the charming turn-based tactics adventure,Mario + Rabbids: Sparks of Hope, sequel to its unexpected crossover hit, Mario + Rabbids: Kingdom Battle. By melding a rather specialist genre with video gaming’s biggest household name, the developer introduced chin-stroking strategic play to a whole new audience.“Having the opportunity to work with the Mario franchise was a privilege, and it’s still something I’m very proud of,” says level designer director, Julien Vial. “I still remember seeing the first prototype and being blown away by all the possibilities.”Now, Ubisoft Paris has returned with a new project, but this time the studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action series Rainbow Six. Where Mario and Rabbids saw squishy creatures bounce harmlessly across levels as Mario encased foes in honey, Rainbow Six Tactics, a turn-based tactical spin-off fromRainbow Six Siege, sees balaclava-clad insurgents take shrapnel rounds to the chest. A seamless tonal shift, then.View image in fullscreenUnexpected hit …  Mario + Rabbids.Photograph: UbisoftOne of the most popular and testosterone-fuelled online shooters around, on paper Rainbow Six: Siege and turn-based strategy have little in common. Where Siege’s tight team play and ferocious first-person firefights sell out arenas at esports competitions in São Paulo and Atlanta, even the biggest brand in the tactical sim genre, X-Com, is unlikely to win energy-drink sponsorships or adorn a team jersey.Yet forUbisoftParis creative director Elie Benhamou, a veteran of the Ghost Recon series, the precision planning you need to be good at Siege is a natural fit for turn-based strategy. “What makes Rainbow Six unique is that it’s a smart shooter,” he says. “It’s not a shooter where it’s necessarily about who is the most brutal, but who is the most prepared ... Every decision matters because there are strong consequences. That is the exact recipe for a tactics game.”View image in fullscreenEvery decision matters … Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics.Photograph: UbisoftMy demo kicks off with a night-time operation in Nigeria. As I witness a team of four helmet-clad operators surveil their targets with drones and plant explosives during the prep phase – their synchronised teamwork soon breaches a heavily guarded warehouse. While smoke grenades blind their unsuspecting foes and sniper shots crackle through the air, the Rainbow Unit’s tight pincer formation makes short work of the remaining hostiles. It’s here that Benhamou’s words begin to ring true. Even with the bird’s eye view and pauses between gunfire, Tactics still oozes the tense thrills of its real-time brethren.Benhamou says he knew they were on to something after they invited sceptical first-person shooter stalwarts in to play test. Sitting alongside fans of real-time tactics, the hardcore FPS players swiftly used their Siege knowledge to execute a similar precision assault in Tactics, advising the tactics genre players next to them on how best to command Siege’s operators.The demo concludes with Rainbow Unit extracting a key hostage by racing towards a speedboat. Here, you can take a non-lethal approach with enemies, arresting combatants to gather intelligence points, which enhance your squad and improve gear for future missions.View image in fullscreen‘Freedom is key: there shouldn’t be only one single way to win.’ … Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics.Photograph: Ubisoft“The most important thing for me is when a game respects my intelligence – I don’t want to be over-guided,” says Benhamou. “It’s OK to fail and experiment … Freedom is key: there shouldn’t be only one single way to win. We have 15 unique operators, so the same problem can be solved or approached in many different ways.”Story wise, Rainbow Six Tactics promises to be your classic Tom Clancy fare, with shady government organisations and a globe-spanning conflict. You play as commander Paul “Big Boy” Bishop, the protagonist from Rainbow Six Vegas, as he attempts to re-establish Team Rainbow. “From a narrative standpoint, we try to bridge the gap with Siege and classic Rainbow, trying to have the best of all these worlds and eras of the series,” says narrative director, Barnabé Anglade. “Compared to Siege, it’s a much broader, zoomed-out point of view. Here, you’re at base and get to see the big picture … whereas Siege is much more moment-to-moment within the eyes of the operators. It’s still delivering that good old techno-thriller, but it’s closer to the books.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter working in a world of gravity-defying jumps and banana-shaped boomerangs, the biggest challenge after swapping Rabbids for Rainbow was creating compelling levels that strictly adhered to reality. “On Mario and Rabbids, most of the constraints were tied to the characters and their abilities, while the level design itself enjoyed a great deal of creative freedom,” says Vial. “We could come up with a gameplay concept first, then let the artists build a colourful and imaginative environment around it. On Rainbow Six Tactics, we have to take the reality of the location into account, which requires much closer collaboration between level designers and level artists.”Turn-based tactical sims have been an often overlooked mainstay of the games industry since the 1970s. Yet after the high-profile commercial failure of 2022’s Marvel’s Midnight Suns, things have looked bleak for fans of slowly moving units across maps. However, after last month’s one-two punch ofStar Wars Zero Companyand Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, the wonderfully nerdy genre is enjoying a revival.“The genre never disappeared – it was just niche or out of the spotlight,” says Benhamou. “Even in [such] a competitive business, when games are great, people will play them.”Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics is due for release in 2027 onPC, PS5 and XboxExplore more on these topicsGamesAction gamesUbisoftShooting gamesPCPlayStation 5Xbox series S/XfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Trump should fear the BBC. Instead he’s picked a fight – and he seems to be losing  | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: The president is used to bullying his media targets. The quagmire that is his libel actions shows the broadcaster is working to a different script, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: The president is used to bullying his media targets. The quagmire that is his libel actions shows the broadcaster is working to a different script, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: An image of Donald Trump appears on video screens before his speech to supporters in Washington DC on 6 January 2021.Photograph: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn image of Donald Trump appears on video screens before his speech to supporters in Washington DC on 6 January 2021.Photograph: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesOpinionBBCTrump should fear the BBC. Instead he’s picked a fight – and he seems to be losingEmma BrockesThe president is used to bullying his media targets. The quagmire that is his libel actions shows the broadcaster is working to a different scriptThu 15 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 10.18 EDTShareFor the greatest account of the BBC’s finest hour, one must turn to Penelope Fitzgerald’s novel, Human Voices, written in 1980 and set 40 years earlier, at the corporation’s Portland Place wartime HQ. Flanked by sandbags and infused with a smell of cooking “from the deep hold that suggested more strongly than ever a cruise on the Queen Mary”, the organisation that Fitzgerald describes is at once noble and deeply eccentric. “Broadcasting House stood headed on a fixed course south,” she writes. “With the best engineers in the world, and a crew varying between the intensely respectable and barely sane, it looked ready to scorn any disaster.”In other words, a formidable foe, one that in the spring of 1940, in the face of anticipated Nazi invasion, decided “without prompting, that truth was more important than consolation, and, in the long run, would be more effective”. I bring this up in respect to the gathering storm of Donald Trump versus the BBC, a fight triggered by the US president’s$10bn defamation lawsuit– $10bn! It’s a wonder he didn’t go for $10 gazillion – brought against the corporation at the end of last year in response to a poorly edited episode of Panorama. The BBC was at fault, editing together comments made by the US president at a rally on 6 January 2021 to give, as the corporation’sapologyput it, “the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action”. But it is fighting the lawsuit.This will have come as a surprise to the president, who in his own country has had great success frightening media companies into craven submission. This week, as news broke that the BBC has beenclearedby a judge to serve legal papers on Trump’s children, while stillseeking judicial interventionto force him to show up to his own deposition, the president must be wondering what’s going on. In August last year, Trumpapplied to the courtto block the BBC from deposing Donald Trump Jr and Ivanka Trump, and yet … the corporation simply ignored him and ploughed on with its mission.Well. Welcome to the British Broadcasting Corporation, Mr President, let me give you a little insight into what you’re up against. There is no institutional power in the world to rival the BBC’s ability to drone on, a constant background hum for the nation. We all, at some level, consist of an interior mix-tape made up of Melvyn Bragg saying, “Hello. In the 13th century …” and Libby Purves opening an episode of Midweek with, “all my guests this week are time travellers, in a way”. The US president simply has no idea of the effect on this country’s nervous system of the opening bars of EastEnders, or a BBC newsreader interrupting normal programming with the line, “This is BBC television from London.”Nor will he have encountered that very particular BBC mindset, which, unlike the workforce at Google, doesn’t run on can-do energy and corporate good cheer, but rather on toxic gas released by an underpaid, overworked labour force, seething with resentment and, as Fitzgerald put it, “bitterly loyal” to its employers – which, as it happens, is a very high standard of loyalty indeed. You don’t get that at Fox News.Or indeed at ABC News, which in December 2024,agreed to pay Trump $15min an uncontested defamation suit. And while CNN, MS Now and Politico are allsuing the White Housefor banning them, CBS rolled over like a dog, announcing it would be axing Stephen Colbert’s highly critical show days after settling another defamation suit with the president. Meanwhile the Federal Communications Commission, the regulatory body run by arch-conservative Brendan Carr, threatened to review the licences of misbehaving broadcasters. A day after the president called for Trump-mocking Jimmy Kimmel’s dismissal from his late night ABC show,Carr orderedan early licence review of all eight of Disney’s ABC television stations.The BBC isn’t bound by these forces. There are financial pressures on it to settle, of course, but in public broadcasting money is never the be-all and end-all, and I would bet Trump has never come up against a force so stubborn, so irrational, so inexplicable to the American corporate or political mindset as his opponents at Langham Place. If the president prizes his own unpredictability as a key weapon in his arsenal, I’d like to introduce him to the people who brought us Noel’s House Party and Grandstand.Yes, the BBC loves nothing more than to don a hair shirt and report on its own failings. Yes, it could do with relying a bit less on Clare Balding. And yes, the corporation is a lunatic in so many ways. But it’s our lunatic and if you come for it, you come for us all. In the BBC’s long history of standing up to tyranny, it has seen off bigger enemies than Trump. I would bet the Shipping Forecast it will come out victorious.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmma Brockes is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBBCOpinionDonald TrumpMedia lawLaw (US)Trump administrationNoel EdmondscommentShareReuse this content

title: The global economy is muddling through against the odds. But a storm is coming | Larry Elliott | The Guardian
description: Finance ministers gathering for the IMF annual meeting know the need for multilateral cooperation to deal with many crises. There is little chance of that, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Author: Larry Elliott
Headline: Finance ministers gathering for the IMF annual meeting know the need for multilateral cooperation to deal with many crises. There is little chance of that, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Content: Illustration: Sébastien Thibault/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Sébastien Thibault/The GuardianOpinionInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)The global economy is muddling through against the odds. But a storm is comingLarry ElliottFinance ministers gathering for the IMF annual meeting know the need for multilateral cooperation to deal with many crises. There is little chance of thatThu 15 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.08 EDTShareNot much has gone right for the global economy this year, and plenty has gone wrong. Two big regional wars are destabilising prices and supply chains everywhere.Businesses and consumers are feeling the effects of a serious energy shock. Rising inflation has made it a lot more expensive for governments to finance their debts.Chinaand the US are at loggerheads over trade.Yet, so far, the impact has been modest. It is something of a miracle that the finance ministers and central bank governors gathered for this year’s annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok are not having to deal with a full-blown crisis. This is not like the autumn of 2008, when the meetings took place during the worst of the global banking meltdown.The IMF is right when it says countrieshave shown resiliencewhen having to cope with so many headwinds. It could have been worse. A lot worse. There was even some good news for the UK, with theIMF upgradingits growth forecast for this year and praising the government for its deficit-reduction plan.The better-than-expected performance of the global economy breaks with historical precedent. In the past, oil shocks of the magnitude witnessed since the start of Iran war have had a marked and immediate impact, but there are three key reasons why growth has remained robust and inflationary pressure has been muted this time.The first is the massive amount of investment in the development of artificial intelligence. This has been particularly important in the US, which is comfortably the fastest growing member of the G7 group of major developed economies year on year. The second is that countries have drawn on inventories of oil, and that has helped to alleviate the loss of crude from the Middle East. Had stockpiles not been run down, oil prices would have risen even more sharply. The third is that China’s economic strategy relies on exporting cheap goods to the rest of the world, and this is bearing down on the prices of imports elsewhere.All that said, the potential flashpoints for trouble are everywhere. The situation in the Middle East is deteriorating, with theconflict spreadingto Saudi Arabia. Oil stocks are running low and Donald Trump has got the US into just the sort of forever war that he used to rail against. The downside to cheap Chinese goods is that they are threatening manufacturing jobs in the west, with Germany especially vulnerable.Meanwhile, massive US investment in AI has pushed up the cost of borrowing and resulted in shortages of capital for non-AI sectors. Governments are coming under pressure to rein in spending or raise taxes in the hope that bond markets will be impressed by their efforts to cut budget deficits.Warnings from (among others) thehead of the IMF, Kristalina Georgieva, and thegovernor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, of the need to run a tighter fiscal ship come at a time when voters want politicians to do more, not less. There is little appetite for a new era of austerity, and finance ministers know it. If they follow through on the tough talk and actually deliver painful measures, the backlash is likely to be brutal.Just as big a problem for governments is the need – at a time when global supply chains are stretched and fragile – to boost national self-sufficiency. The student protests in India and France highlight the pressures on states to intervene. Yet the capacity of states to act effectively is much weaker than they care to admit.At a time when globalisation is in retreat, there is a need for a strong system of multilateral cooperation to cope with the strains. That is not currently the case. The World Trade Organization is moribund in this new age of protectionism, and the IMF and the World Bank are reluctant to call Trump out for his erratic behaviour.Yet the idea that a new era of partnership will flower when there is a new US president is for the birds. The problems of multilateralism run far deeper than that. The liberal world order that the IMF and World Bank have presided over since the end of the second world war was dysfunctional long before Trump arrived in office.As the former UN official Richard Kozul-Wright points out in a paper published next month, the IMF and World Bank – created at the 1944 Bretton Woods conference – may still be operational but they have lost their connection to the New Deal principles laid out 82 years ago: state intervention in the running of economies, active industrial policy, the pursuit of full employment and help for poor countries to develop. “Instead, they have in recent decades pursued an agenda which encourages footloose capital, bolsters (and protects) private profit, and reduces the policy space available to governments. As a result, they have acted as hand maidens to an age of rising inequality, debt distress and heightened anxiety.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe IMF’s own programmes for countries that come looking for financial assistance illustrate Kozul-Wright’s point aboutthe lack of policy space. Help comes with strings attached: an insistence on tax increases and spending cuts that are frontloaded so that half the measures are implemented in the first year and two-thirds within two years.The IMF argues that this “tough love” has a higher chance of success, although its view of what constitutes success is limited, and primarily means that a borrowing country doesn’t need another IMF programme in the next three years. It doesn’t mean living standards are improving or that fewer people are in poverty.Clearly it would help to return to New Deal principles. It would mean governments had more policy space to develop strategies tailored to their own needs. It would mean a boost to public investment. It would mean a newMarshall planto help poorer countries cope with the climate crisis. It would mean a serious attempt to tackle debt distress. But, in all honesty, none of that has a chance of happening any time soon. As a result, the world will become hotter, more fractured, more prone to conflict, less equal and a lot angrier.The IMF is worried that the limits of this resiliencemay soon be tested, and it is right to be worried. Peace in the Middle East would bring oil prices tumbling down, but unless that happens quickly a long winter lies ahead. This looks more like a crisis postponed than a crisis permanently avoided. A lull before the storm, in all probability.Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)OpinionGlobal economyEconomicsAusterityGlobalisationDonald TrumpAI (artificial intelligence)commentShareReuse this content

title: It’s not the old two-party politics – but Labour and the Tories now know they can shun their populist challengers | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: Though Burnham and Badenoch may still need the votes of Green and Reform supporters, both leaders have drawn clear lines in the sand, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: Though Burnham and Badenoch may still need the votes of Green and Reform supporters, both leaders have drawn clear lines in the sand, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianOpinionAndy BurnhamIt’s not the old two-party politics – but Labour and the Tories now know they can shun their populist challengersGaby HinsliffThough Burnham and Badenoch may still need the votes of Green and Reform supporters, both leaders have drawn clear lines in the sandThu 15 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTShareAsk a straight question, get a straight answer. It’s how politics is supposed to work but almost never does, which is why on the rare occasions it happens the result can be faintly chaotic. What did Andy Burnham mean when he said – in response to a question from the Tory MP Harriett Baldwin – thatLabour couldn’t partner with the Green partywhile it remains wedded to the “Zionism is racism” motion its members have just endorsed? Were Green MPs now barred from a future coalition government? If so, what about councils where they are currently sharing power with Labour?Though Burnham was only confirming what ministers have been arguing privately for days, at first nobody seemed to know: tellingly, it took almost 24 hours for theLabourparty chair, Bridget Phillipson, to confirm that unless local Green groups disowned that idea sharpish, “Labour will bring any such local arrangement to an end”. So much for cuddly cross-party Andy, who always seemed so relaxed about rainbow coalitions. Now elected Greens in places such as Sheffield or Lewes must choose between power and members’ wrath, a useful rehearsal for what a hung parliament might feel like.Westminster is increasingly realising that while nobody knows quite what’s in Burnham’s head except Burnham, unlike most prime ministers he is surprisingly liable just to tell you. He did it earlier this week on a podcast, pointing out thatRussia tried to interfere in the Brexit vote(which is true, albeit the sort of truth that for complicated reasons prime ministers don’t generally dwell on). Now the safety catch is off again.What did he mean with his comments about Labour and the Greens? Most likely just what he said: that the Greens crossed a line and it cannot be overlooked, especially by a party still recovering from its own battle with antisemitism. Green members did not just vote to adopt a policy that would condemn every Jew who believes in the right to a Jewish homeland, including those who simultaneously support the creation of a Palestinian state. The motion they backedadvocates turning all of historic Palestine into a Palestinian state, a one-state solutionwiping Israel off the map.Much as Kemi Badenoch did recently by insisting that herEnglish-born children have every right to be considered English,no matter what the ethno-nationalists of Reform and Restore say,Burnham was simply showing that he has limits: this far, and no further.Something has shaken loose over the party conference season. What we are seeing isn’t the return of two-party politics – things are still too volatile for that – but the return of leaders confident enough to set boundaries on what had become an almost abusive relationship with the public. They are no longer quite so terrified of naming extremism when they see it. More surprisingly, neither is behaving like a party needing to beg for coalition partners, whatever the electoral maths says.Andy Burnham says Russia interfered in Brexit referendum – videoAfter a period shadow boxing a prime minister who never seemed to know what he thought, Badenoch now faces one who does. That has brought drama back to the middle of politics and not just the radical edges, with genuine differences emerging between Labour and the Tories ahead of the budget over tax and spend, national security v social security, public v private ownership and the respective claims of younger and older people.Her new strategy is not a million miles from the one outlined this week by thethinktank Bright Blue,in a paper on how the traditional European right can combat far-right populism: adopt draconian immigration policies but make the economy the actual focus of your campaign, and hold the line that citizenship can be earned rather than being determined by ethnicity (the chilling line peddled by some of those in Reform and Restore who argue openly that you have to be white to be properly English).Though the polls still suggest the Tories can’t win without some kind of deal with Reform, the broad message of aconference speechin which Badenoch painted her rivals as aggressive weirdos who “threaten journalists, call veterans traitors and debate whether my mixed-race children are English” was that it would be a cold day in hell before that happened. That decision looks smarter with every passing journalistic exposé involving the kind of Reform councillor whothinks King Charles should be decapitatedfor supposedly being a secret Muslim.Burnham didn’t go quite so studs-up on the Greens, but then he doesn’t need to. The party is alreadyopenly agonisingabout that anti-Zionism motion, opposed byfour out of fiveof its elected MPs. The prospect of being politically ostracised for it may now strengthen the hand of Greens who think this freakishly hot summer might have been better spent campaigning on the climate crisis, not swervingquestions about Israel’s right to exist. Yet there are risks for Burnham here, all the same.Research by the pollster More in Common suggests that “progressive activists”, the group most commonly torn between voting Green or Labour, are significantly more likely than the average British voter to think worse of someone identifying as a Zionist. When Burnham called the Green motion antisemitic and wrong, he was confronting people whose support he may need in some Labour seats.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis civil war on the British right is a charade – its politics are more united than ever | Jonathan LiewRead moreSanctioning West Bank settlements, as this government has now done, isn’t enough for some of them: they want Burnham explicitly tocall the Gaza war a genocideand stop proscribingPalestine Actionas a terrorist organisation.(Polanski was notably quick toleap to the defence ofthe Irish novelist Sally Rooney, after it emergedher books arebeing withdrawn from salein Britainbecause of her promise to donate royalties to Palestine Action: knowing where the money could be going leaves her publishers open to potential prosecution under anti-terrorism law, just for handing over her earnings.)It’s technically possible that like some desiccated calculating machine, Burnham has crunched the numbers on all this and concluded that distancing himself from a row that has reportedly madeone in three British voters less likely to vote Green(according to Opinium) is mathematically preferable.But it’s more likely he was just doing the thing that got him here in the first place, and following his gut. If he can’t say what he thinks even now, in what passes for a honeymoon period, he never will. If basic norms are not enforced, they very quickly cease being norms. And if the Labour party can only win by sidling uncomfortably close to the kind of people it was until recently expelling for antisemitism – well, it’s not much of a Labour party. The chaos, in that sense, is probably just beginning.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionKemi BadenochLabourGreen partyZack PolanskiConservativesAntisemitismcommentShareReuse this content

title: One week a year I escape my ‘real’ life as broke standup comic – and travel back to medieval times | Scout Boxall | The Guardian
description: Live action role play, or Larping, allows me to straddle two worlds with fellow weirdos – and enter a realm where death can be reversed and I’m a cashed-up bureaucrat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Live action role play, or Larping, allows me to straddle two worlds with fellow weirdos – and enter a realm where death can be reversed and I’m a cashed-up bureaucrat
Content: ‘My wardrobe is evenly split between the 21st, 16th and 14th centuries’, says Scout Boxall.Photograph: Trendy's PhotographyView image in fullscreen‘My wardrobe is evenly split between the 21st, 16th and 14th centuries’, says Scout Boxall.Photograph: Trendy's PhotographyOpinionRole playing gamesOne week a year I escape my ‘real’ life as broke standup comic – and travel back to medieval timesScout BoxallLive action role play, or Larping, allows me to straddle two worlds with fellow weirdos – and enter a realm where death can be reversed and I’m a cashed-up bureaucratThu 15 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 18.50 EDTShareEvery Friday night on a community sports field in Melbourne’s inner north, a few hundred nerds dress up in historical armour and attack each other with foam latex swords. It’s live action role play: turbocharged Dungeons & Dragons meets medieval re-enactment.I’ve been Larping for seven years. It’s the biggest thing in my life outside of comedy, and the two scenes have a lot in common. Everyone’s broke. Everyone was bullied in high school. No one gets into Larp or standup if things are going well.The biggest commonality is the gatekeeping. A crusted old comic in the corner of a greenroom gasps: “You’re a fan of standup, are you? Name three of Carl Barron’s best jokes.” His Larp counterpart, a polyamorous he/they in a top hat with a cog on it, twirls a cane: “So you like Warhammer Fantasy Battle? Name three spells an elven cleric can use in combat.” I’d like to see those two sit down and collectively name three women who feel safe around them.Larping’s reality bleed: ‘I’m basically falling in love with a person that does not exist’Read moreSwordcraft Quest is one of the biggest events on Australia’s Larp calendar. Hundreds of players pitch tents in a rocky cattle paddock in Pomborneit, Victoria, to roleplay living in a medieval fantasy village for a week called Sudenburg. It’s fully in character and immersive, save for a few modern conveniences. Even the most fearsome warrior needs a Portaloo and a soy flat white.You can be a noble paladin, a sage elven scholar or a tricksy halfling bard. But if you’re a real freak, like myself, you’ll spend the week as a fiscally conservative tax agent. This year I was appointed Master of Coin, responsible for overseeing the town’s finances. My parents are retired microeconomists and I was conceived on budget night of 1994, so perhaps it was inevitable.View image in fullscreenScout Boxall, second from right, with fellow Larpers.Photograph: Trendy’s PhotographyMoney works weirdly in Larp. Twelve copper to a silver, 20 silver to a gold. A copper is worth between $3 and $6 in “shadow currency” (Australian dollars or Aud, pronounced “Ow-dh”). Four coppers is an hour of unskilled labour; two gets you a coffee. You can’t cash them back in at the end of the game, so many of my Larp friends end up rich in coppers but live below the poverty line in the real world.As an itinerant touring performer and freelance writer, a steady nine-to-five data-entry job handling huge amounts of cash was the ultimate fantasy. And I revelled in the brutal bureaucracy of it all.
