Each day I opened up the tax office, made players present their in-character documentation and declare their assets and then place a few of their precious copper coins into a box marked TAX OFFICE COFFERS – LOOTABLE ITEM.Throughout the week, players produced elaborate disguises, fraudulent documents and even held me up at (fake foam) knife-point in fruitless attempts to steal the town’s hoard. Each of these heists was prenegotiated out of character. The final night of the event, someone simply broke into the tent and took the coins for real, which has since sparked a genuine out-of-character investigation.Tongue lodged firmly in cheek, Larpers love to replicate real-world dilemmas with a dirtbag medieval slant. Dwarven miners extract obsidian from a poisonous seam with indentured goblin child labour. (Fracking.) The Town Council funnels tax funds to their allies. (Cronyism.) Senate meetings grind to a standstill over whether to let in refugees who might bring an undead horde. (Xenophobia.)Beyond Dungeons and Dragons: can role play save the world?Read moreSometimes Larp and real life collide and form something that is technically “make-believe” but resonates beyond role play. Last year, a terminally ill player called Silas* knew it would be their last event, so they held their own funeral. Wearing elf ears and tucked into a mechanised wheelchair beneath heavy blankets, Silas laughed as friends took turns to deliver eulogies. Afterwards, they married their long-term partner in the tavern with a real celebrant presiding. The ceremony was soundtracked by live bards and emceed by a hulking man called The Mad Mage. It was a strange day that straddled two worlds: our collectively imagined realm of Sudenburg, where death can be reversed through magic, and the bleak reality of Silas’ diagnosis.Larp is a special interest that can verge into obsession. I’ve sunk thousands of dollars and hundreds of hours into it. My house is full to bursting with wool, linen and silk, plate armour, chain mail and a longbow. I have more Larp shoes than regular shoes, and my wardrobe is evenly split between the 21st, 16th and 14th centuries.I’m not the only one with a Renaissance streak. Fantasy is having a massive cultural resurgence. We’ve gone from twee cottagecore to wenchcore, maidencore and castlecore. Chappell Roan wears chain mail armour and wields a sword on the red carpet.View image in fullscreenChappell Roan performs in chain mail armour at the 2024 MTV Video Music Awards in New York.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Billboard/Getty ImagesEvery second queer in Brunswick Anytime Fitness has a gothic blackletter tattoo. An old high school Facebook friend who manages a Dunkin’ Donuts posts about craving a “little hobbity life”. Gen Z have even co-opted the term “Larper” to mean poser or fraud. In a time of relentless AI slop, fast fashion and impending climate apocalypse, we turn to the past. Well, a reimagining of a reimagining of the past: an ahistorical slurry of Arthurian romance, pre-Raphaelite idealism and dreamy Y2K aesthetics.The Ren Faire has become an ironically cool place for twentysomethings to gnaw a turkey leg and prance around in Shein princess costumes. Larp remains the domain of the weirdo, the loser and the pedant. That’s what makes it so special. It’s given me a chosen family, a community and – most importantly – the chance to go back in time for a week every year and pretend to be a cashed-up bureaucrat. Wouldn’t trade it for all the copper in Sudenburg.*Names have been changedScout Boxall is a standup comedian. Their latest solo show, God’s Favourite enjoyed a sold-out run at the Edinburgh fringe festival in 2026 and won the Pinder prize at Melbourne international comedy festival in 2025Explore more on these topicsRole playing gamesOpinionHobbiesAustralian lifestylecommentShareReuse this content

title: How Gaza changed Europe, exposing cracks that grow bigger by the week | Shada Islam | The Guardian
description: Solidarity with Palestine’s suffering is punished but MEPs allow a witch-hunt of European Muslims, says Brussels-based commentator Shada Islam
Author: Shada Islam
Headline: Solidarity with Palestine’s suffering is punished but MEPs allow a witch-hunt of European Muslims, says Brussels-based commentator Shada Islam
Content: Large crowds gathered in Amsterdam on 11 October 2026, calling for an end to violence against Palestinians.Photograph: Mouneb Taim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLarge crowds gathered in Amsterdam on 11 October 2026, calling for an end to violence against Palestinians.Photograph: Mouneb Taim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionGazaHow Gaza changed Europe, exposing cracks that grow bigger by the weekShada IslamSolidarity with Palestine’s suffering is punished but MEPs allow a witch-hunt of European MuslimsThu 15 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 00.01 EDTShareFor three painful years, Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, in retaliation for the Hamas terror attacks on 7 October 2023, haskilled more than 74,000 Palestinians, wounded thousands more and reduced most of the territory to rubble. It has changed views of Israelacross the world, increased support for Palestine andraised questionsabout US power.Europe’s failure to hold Israel’s government to account has cost itglobal credibilityand influence. But I fear something even more consequential than that: Gaza is changing Europe itself.European governments did nothing to try to stop the genocide; there have beenno collective sanctions, no trade restrictions or ending of arms sales to Israel. The EU sanctions Russia over its war in Ukraine but retains almost-business-as-usual ties with Israel, a blatant double standard.Gaza has exposed how Europe’s supposedly universal commitment to human rights is now conditional onwhose suffering is recognised, whose resistance is considered legitimate and whose demands for justice are considered worthy of attention. EU policymakers are selective even in thegroups of women they choose to celebrateas heroic in struggles against occupation and the children whose right to life they defend.After these three years I am convinced that the question of Palestine has become a stress test for European democracy itself. Democratic societies can only thrive when there is space for dissent, including dissent that is uncomfortable, disruptive and politically inconvenient. Yet today, across Europe, governments – which speak up against undemocratic conduct abroad – are now unapologetic in imposing restrictions on free expression and peaceful protest at home.Police violence at pro-Palestinian demonstrationshas become the norm, and those whose only crime is to speak up publicly for Palestinian rights areincreasingly criminalisedor made the target of suspicion.When this happens repeatedly it undermines public trust in the legitimacy of democratic governments and institutions. As Rabin Baldewsingh, the Netherlands’ national coordinator against discrimination and racism tells me: “Governments and public institutions have a responsibility not to reinforce polarisation when society is deeply divided.” Sadly, the opposite appears to be happening.Many societal fractures existed before Gaza, but they have received new oxygen and traction over the past three years. The EU’s Fundamental Rights Agency has long warned of bothanti-Muslim racismandantisemitism. What has become increasingly troubling over the past three years is the political framing under which antisemitism inconnection with Gaza is rightly treated as a threat to democracy, while Islamophobia is viewed through a security and anti-terrorism lens.This can’t all be blamed on the far right, either. True, some extremist groups hide their age-old prejudices behind accusations that it is Muslims and refugees who have “imported” antisemitism into Europe. But the European People’s party (EPP) – the EU’s largest political “family” for pro-European centre-right and conservative politicians, includingUrsula von der Leyenand Magnus Brunner, the EU’s most senior official for migration – is also giving old and debunked Islamophobic tropes a new and dangerous lease of life.The partybacked a resolutionin June condemning the “interference of political Islam” in European democratic processes. If “political Islam” was interfering in European democracy, the resolution may have some validity. But there is no evidence for the claim, and certainly none advanced in this document, which merely echoes French conspiracy theories about “Islamist entryism” and calls for a crackdown on alleged members ofMuslim Brotherhoodnetworks. It claims to make a distinction between “political Islam” and the Islamic faith itself but it reads more like the start of a witch-hunt of European Muslims.An even tougher EPP resolution, backed by amajority in the European parliamenton 8 October, goes a step further by casting suspicion on Muslim civil society groups’ loyalty, activity and participation in European democracy.Hiba Latreche, president ofFemyso, a pan-European network of young Muslim organisations that is explicitly mentioned in the EPP’s attack, points out the double bind of such unfounded allegations. “When we are not active we are accused of communitarianism, separatism and lack of integration. When we engage and exercise active citizenship we are accused of having a hidden agenda.”Such an environment demands even stronger anti-discrimination action. Yet Europe’s most powerful pro-equality body, theEuropean Network Against Racism(ENAR), has just lost European Commission funding. Worried that this could mean it has tocease operationsby the end of the year, ENAR has launched a legal challenge against the decision at the EU’s general court.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBeyond the visible, there are many unwritten post-Gaza codes being applied inside the EU’s corridors of power that are harder to measure and challenge. Islamophobia has become “quite blatant”, EU officials tell me, with micro‑aggressions and remarks about Muslims’ supposedly “irrational and emotional” behaviour. Likevon der Leyenin her recent “state of the union” speech,many now talk about Gaza as a humanitarian emergency, but not as a human-made genocide. There is agreement on the need for action againstsettler violenceand illegal settlement in the West Bank, which is framed as the work of “extremists”, but confronting the Israeli government remains difficult.For many, it has also been a time of uncomfortable conversations, ruptured personal relationships and disillusionment. But there are also moments of intense solidarity, as across Europe pro‑Palestinian movements have extended to include trade unions, faith groups – including Jewish activists – students, celebrities and senior politicians. Every Thursday, members of theEU Staff for Peacegather for a vigil outside the commission and the EU Council. Former EU commissioners, ambassadors and senior staff continue towrite to their bossesurging stronger action against Israel.So all hope is not lost. But Gaza has stripped away a great deal of self-soothing assumptions that many of us harboured aboutEurope. As the far right becomes more influential, too many have forgotten that democratic freedoms rarely disappear all at once. They begin to erode when some voices are silenced, some suffering is ignored and the rights of some citizens are treated as less deserving than others.Shada Islam is a Brussels-based commentator on EU affairs. She runs New Horizons project, a strategy, analysis and advisory companyDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsGazaOpinionEuropean UnionPalestineUrsula von der LeyenIslamophobiaAntisemitismEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: The Victorian election put gas laws on the ballot. The Coalition and One Nation have chosen to fight for the indefensible | Saul Griffith | The Guardian
description: The ‘right to choose’ crowd would damage Victorians’ health and move costs on to those least able to pay
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The ‘right to choose’ crowd would damage Victorians’ health and move costs on to those least able to pay
Content: The gas industry is ‘largely foreign-owned, pays little back to the Australian people and pushes up the cost of healthcare’, Saul Griffith writes.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPView image in fullscreenThe gas industry is ‘largely foreign-owned, pays little back to the Australian people and pushes up the cost of healthcare’, Saul Griffith writes.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPOpinionEnergyThe Victorian election put gas laws on the ballot. The Coalition and One Nation have chosen to fight for the indefensibleSaul GriffithThe ‘right to choose’ crowd would damage Victorians’ health and move costs on to those least able to payFollow ourAustralian politics live blogfor latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastWed 14 Oct 2026 21.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 01.39 EDTShareAs an engineer I see the climate problem simply. We have a collection of machines – some burn fossil fuels, others don’t. We need to stop buying the ones that burn poisons and instead buy electric ones and run them on clean electricity. Live well, breathe easy, pay less.From January, new homes and most new commercial buildings inVictoriawill be built all-electric, locking in lower bills and lower emissions. From March, when a gas hot water system dies it must be replaced with an efficient electric one, so existing homes get the savings too. And when a renter’s gas heater fails, the landlord must install efficient electric heating. The tenant’s bills get slashed, not just the owner-occupier’s.Those laws are now on the ballot because the gas industry has the money and power to unduly influence our politics. Before November’s election, the Liberals, the Nationals and One Nation are all promising to scrap them before they start. They say they are defending your “right to choose”.As One Nation rises, Victorian Labor has promised to make abortions free. Is the timing pure politics?Read moreWhat they are defending is the right of a few very large, mostly foreign-owned gas companies to keep making enormous profits by making choices for you, choices we know damage your children’s health today and their future tomorrow.We did the modelling for the Liberals and Nationals under senator Andrew Bragg’s electrification inquiry. One Nation has been harder to reach, though I’ve tried. They could make their own spreadsheets and see the economics is better for electrification.Three parties are wrapping themselves in the flag and false liberties while opposing the most obviously national-interest energy policy on offer: running as much of Australia as possible on the thing Australia has more of than anyone else. Sunshine.Here is the moment that matters. Every gas appliance in Victoria will die, on average, once every 15 years or so. The day you replace it is the day the savings are won or lost. Choose electric heating, hot water and cooking, and a typical Victorian family of four saves about $2,000 a year. Add solar and a battery and that rises to about $3,800, every year. Add electric vehicles and it’s north of $5,000. Electric machines are simply better at their jobs: an electric car uses a third to a quarter of the energy to drive the same kilometre; a heat pump or reverse-cycle air conditioner uses a third to a quarter of the energy to heat the same water or air. Since 2023, Australian households that have electrified have saved a combined $185m on bills,according to IEEFA, and that figure only goes up.Plumbers and electricians tell me customers ask one question – “What’s cheapest to run?” – and the answer is electric every single time.Now to the part the “right to choose” crowd leaves out. Gas pipes are paid off over decades by whoever is still connected. As households leave, the cost lands on fewer and fewer people, and the people left holding it are the ones who can’t leave: renters, pensioners who can’t afford to upgrade, apartment dwellers with no say over the building. Sensible Australians will choose no gas. The “right to choose” crowd will keep the rest in thrall to the gas industry while the costs rise for those least able to pay. TheAustralian Gas Infrastructure Grouphas gone to the media with modelling of the terrible costs those stranded customers will face.When a tobacco shop opened next door, a Melbourne couple’s dream cafe went up in smoke: ‘It felt like a warzone’Read moreI agree. They will, unless they switch to electric, which will save them. The argument is circular: keep people on the expensive fuel, or the price of the expensive fuel will go up. This from an industry that is largely foreign-owned, pays little back to the Australian people and pushes up the cost of healthcare by poisoning us, as burning gas in a kitchen puts nitrogen dioxide into our lungs and carbon into everyone’s atmosphere. Their remedy is to keep everyone locked in to a thing they can’t afford. That is treating customers like mugs.Sensible people will see the costs they describe as an argument for an orderly, financed transition off gas, not against one. Exactly what Victoria already legislated. Victoria’s rules stop the hole getting deeper: stop connecting new homes and you stop laying pipe that someone will still be paying off in 2060.Upfront cost is the real barrier. A heat pump, solar and a battery pay for themselves, but plenty of households don’t have thousands of dollars in the bank to get started. New South Wales has worked this out: zero-interest loans for households earning under $210,000 a year, repaid out of the savings on the bill. Victoria should match it, then go further, extending rebates and discounts to renters and strata households. Otherwise the people who most need cheaper bills will be the last to get them.The politicians who want to tear up these laws say they are standing up for ordinary Victorians. What they are offering is a lifetime subscription to a foreign-owned technology that poisons them, heats the planet and costs more every year, sold by companies that profit from every year you stay subscribed.Politicians might call that a “right to choose”. I’d call it a waste of time, energy and money. Australia is going electric because it’s better for our wallets, communities and planet. So, let’s get on with it.Saul Griffith is co-founder and chief scientist of Rewiring Australia. He is an engineer and entrepreneur specialising in clean and renewable energy technologies. Saul has founded a dozen technology companies across 20 years in Silicon Valley and is the author of Electrify, The Big Switch, The Wires That Bind and Plug In!Explore more on these topicsEnergyOpinionRenewable energyVictoriaGasFossil fuelsLiberal partycommentShareReuse this content

title: They asked for 80 homes – she gave them 157! Council-housing miracle named Britain’s best new building | Architecture | The Guardian
description: Rising from bluebell woodlands and framed by rolling hills, this cluster of pink and brown brick towers in Croydon is a bittersweet winner of the prestigious RIBA Stirling prize
Author: Oliver Wainwright
Headline: Rising from bluebell woodlands and framed by rolling hills, this cluster of pink and brown brick towers in Croydon is a bittersweet winner of the prestigious RIBA Stirling prize
Content: ‘Oozing quality’ … Lion Green Road in Coulsdon, Croydon, designed by Mary Duggan Architects.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightView image in fullscreen‘Oozing quality’ … Lion Green Road in Coulsdon, Croydon, designed by Mary Duggan Architects.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightArchitectureThey asked for 80 homes – she gave them 157! Council-housing miracle named Britain’s best new buildingRising from bluebell woodlands and framed by rolling hills, this cluster of pink and brown brick towers in Croydon is a bittersweet winner of the prestigious RIBA Stirling prizeOliver WainwrightThu 15 Oct 2026 16.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf Andy Burnham is looking for inspiration for his great “council housebuilding comeback”, he would do well to visit Croydon. There, nestled into a steeply sloping site, sheltered by a canopy of mature trees, stands a cluster of crystalline pink and brown brick towers, where generous flats look on to a landscape of allotments, playgrounds and to the rolling hills of south London beyond. Designed by Mary Duggan Architects, with Ruff Architects, it is a model of council-led housebuilding – so much so that it has also been named this year’s best building in the UK, confounding the bookies’ outsider odds.Only once before has the RIBA Stirling prize ever been awarded to a council housing project, whenGoldsmith Street in Norwichscooped the gong in 2019, for its rows of low-energy brick terraces, designed by Mikhail Riches Architects and Cathy Hawley. This year’s winner,Lion Green Roadin Coulsdon, is an entirely different animal, and it puts a welcome spotlight back on housing design at a time when the government plans to pump £39bn into the sector. It is also a bittersweet vindication of Croydon council’s erstwhile housebuilding company, Brick by Brick, a bold and sadly brief experiment by the previous Labour administration, which was halted in 2020 when the council went bankrupt, seeing numerous projects cancelled.double quotation markIt puts a welcome spotlight back on housing design – at a time when the government plans to pump £39bn into the sector“At a time when we urgently need to deliver more homes,” says RIBA president, Chris Williamson, “Lion Green Road shows that density can be achieved without compromising the quality of the places we create. Through a consistent specification, with subtle variation in height and orientation, it offers housing at scale without uniformity.”Burnham’s first allocation of £10bn, announced in August, is planned to kickstart 70,000 affordable homes across the country. Yet few people in Britain welcome the prospect of new housing in their backyards, even if it’s prize-winning. The planning application for Lion Green Road, submitted in 2017, received 18 letters of support and 257 objections, mostly about the loss of parking. Now built, almost a decade later, the project demonstrates how more homes than you might imagine can be constructed on the most unpromising of sites in a sympathetic way, without sacrificing greenery, views and public access – and keeping plenty of parking, too.View image in fullscreenEach home is dual aspect, maximising natural light, cross-ventilation and views.Photograph: Oliver Wainwright“We really pushed against the suburban model of terraces dominated by cars, with little front and back gardens,” says Duggan. The original brief asked for 80 homes, arranged as she describes, but Duggan proved she could fit 157 flats, distributed between five pavilion-like towers, retaining the mature trees and bluebell woodland on the site. The result feels like it has grown out of its woodland setting, with a public route that winds its way through the site, up to a historic railway embankment at the rear, and not a perimeter fence in sight.“Brick by Brick was an amazing client,” says Duggan, who also hada small mews project in Crystal Palaceon the drawing board for the council’s housebuilder, before the plug was pulled. “It was a refreshing change from how private developers think about affordable housing. Here, they weren’t talking about the land as a commodity, but as a genuinely public asset.”View image in fullscreenDetailling … brick walls at Lion Green Road.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightThe council cared about the interior spaces, too. Thanks to the “pinwheel” plan of the blocks, with flats radiating outwards from a central lift core, each home is dual aspect, maximising natural light, cross-ventilation and views. The flats all enjoy an inset loggia balcony, with a bulge at the base of the balustrades to accommodate plant pots, while cuts in the form (to preserve historic views) create some with larger roof terraces. In the interests of efficiency, the five towers all have the same star-shaped plan, but each is subtly rotated to reduce direct overlooking between neighbouring homes, enabling the buildings to stand close together without sacrificing privacy. Half of the flats are private rental, in two towers, while half are affordable, in three blocks retained by the council, rented at local housing allowance rates. Unlike the Norwich project, this is not true social housing.The RIBA judges describe the project as a “new kind of garden neighbourhood”. The space between the blocks feels consciously planned, rather than a leftover afterthought, designed with landscape architecture practice Planit-IE to include a sensory garden, allotment plots and play areas. Walking around the development’s zig-zagging slopes and stepped pathways gives the feeling of exploring a bucolic hill town. Little bug hotels in the same faceted star-shaped form as the towers are a delightful touch; even the insects get a dignified dwelling.Duggan says the project “expands the idea of the threshold”, and the arrival feels more welcoming than most. The entrance of each block is framed by a paved terrace, with seating and planting, while all have generous lobbies, no matter the tenure. It’s a far cry from the “poor door” apartheid of so much developer-built housing, where private owners get the hotel concierge treatment, while affordable tenants enter around the back by the bins. It all oozes quality on a budget, down to the choice of three dusty colours of brick, some projecting to create a textured, tweedy finish. The quality belies the tight construction budget of £2,500/sq metre – making it the cheapest project on the shortlist by far. OtherStirling Prize contenders this yearincluded two exquisitely built projects for well-heeled Cambridge colleges, a large private house in Essex, an arts centre in Hertford, and an £825m office block in Paddington.‘Our hallway’s big enough to play football in!’ The council housing that feels like a holiday resortRead moreIf there is a cloud hanging over Croydon’s triumph, it is the fate of Brick by Brick. It was established in 2015, as a wholly council-owned company, because the conventional development model wasfailing to deliver enough affordable homes. The idea was that Croydon would use its own land, often small leftover sites, and borrow against its own resources, to build a mix of private and affordable housing, while turning a profit for the public purse. But the sites often proved to be trickier than expected, adding additional costs, while the financial forecasts were overly optimistic, with Brexit and Covid introducing huge delays. Housing expertsattribute its collapseto poor financial structuring, governance and risk management, rather than a failure in development expertise or quality of delivery.Nonetheless, Brick by Brick built 751 homes, over half of which are affordable, of a design quality higher than most standard developer fare. With renewed housing cash from central government, might there be a chance for some of the halted schemes to be resurrected, and more of the imagination and innovation of Lion Green Road spread across the borough and beyond?Explore more on these topicsArchitectureStirling prizeSocial housingThe RIBALondonCommunitiesHousingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Balloon Girl review – tech tycoon swirls with tragic teen parachutist in a crackling, time-travelling climate romp | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Hannah McPake’s high-wire drama pokes fun at tech bro machismo, reality TV and Musk-style Martian escapes – think A Christmas Carol in space
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Hannah McPake’s high-wire drama pokes fun at tech bro machismo, reality TV and Musk-style Martian escapes – think A Christmas Carol in space
Content: Up, up and away … Mari Fflur, Oliver Wood and Elin Phillips in Balloon Girl at Sherman theatre, Cardiff.Photograph: Kirsten McTernanView image in fullscreenUp, up and away … Mari Fflur, Oliver Wood and Elin Phillips in Balloon Girl at Sherman theatre, Cardiff.Photograph: Kirsten McTernanTheatreReviewBalloon Girl review – tech tycoon swirls with tragic teen parachutist in a crackling, time-travelling climate rompSherman theatre, CardiffHannah McPake’s high-wire drama pokes fun at tech bro machismo, reality TV and Musk-style Martian escapes – think A Christmas Carol in spaceArifa AkbarThu 15 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis show takes local history as its starting point, that of a 19th-century balloonist’s assistant who performed a parachute stunt in the skies aboveCardiff. It throws in a current-day tech billionaire, the space race, a time-travelling hot-air balloon, and – for good measure? – a lifesize seagull that speaks.Surprisingly, given the complications of writer-director Hannah McPake’s high-wire drama, it lifts off, swirling through the clouds on its air-bound set, crackling with humour and effervescent imagination along with a keen sense of unwritten history, to become a complete blast.Louisa Maud Evans was the real-life 14-year-old girl from Bristol who was enlisted to perform a parachute jump from a hot-air balloon during the Fine Art, Industrial and Maritime Exhibition of 1896. She had little experience of parachuting and she perished in the Bristol Channel after an unfavourable wind cast her out to sea.View image in fullscreenRich imagination … Oliver Wood, François Pandolfo, Elin Phillips and Keiron Self.Photograph: Kirsten McTernanLouisa appears in different guises in McPake’s story,which begins with Carol Gaudron (Elin Phillips), a celebrity tech billionaire and descendant of Auguste Eugene Gaudron (Keiron Self), the balloonist who enlisted Louisa for the ill-fated stunt. The opening scene is a reality quizshow in which a guileless young woman from Bristol wins a televised rocket trip to Mars. “Let’s get humanity off this planet and into the stars,” declares Carol, who has all the integrity of a tech visionary turned rank capitalist. It’s a very nifty way to join up the 19th-century endeavour to conquer the skies and perform public displays of showmanship with modern-day tech bro ambitions in the space race.The story swivels from satire (on everything from reality TV to AI and journalism) to a picaresque journey of time travel for Carol, with a kooky young navigator, Louisa (Mari Fflur) and the talking seagull (Oliver Wood). There are shades of A Christmas Carol – in space – as this trio travels redemptively to the past and future before returning Carol,transformed, to her present.There is so much plot, such rich imagination and great zinging lines alongside a serious underlying message about climate and planetary resource. It occasionally comes too thick and fast, leaving you behind, but it is fun even in its confusions.Hayley Grindle’sset switches between gorgeous small-scale puppetry and grand hot-air balloon imagery. McPake has created several shows for this theatre but this surely has to be one of her best.An airborne triumph.AtSherman theatre, Cardiff, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreSherman theatreCardiffreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Klara and the Sun review – Taika Waititi’s manic pixie dream robot sci-fi is a sentimental mess | Movies | The Guardian
description: The director of Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Jojo Rabbit turns Kazuo Ishiguro’s AI fable into a twee, tiresome tale of love and grief
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The director of Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Jojo Rabbit turns Kazuo Ishiguro’s AI fable into a twee, tiresome tale of love and grief
Content: Supremely lovable … Jenna Ortega in Klara and the Sun.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenSupremely lovable … Jenna Ortega in Klara and the Sun.Photograph: AlamyMoviesReviewKlara and the Sun review – Taika Waititi’s manic pixie dream robot sci-fi is a sentimental messThe director of Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Jojo Rabbit turns Kazuo Ishiguro’s AI fable into a twee, tiresome tale of love and griefPeter BradshawThu 15 Oct 2026 16.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 18.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaika Waititi detonates an explosion of postmodern quirkiness and ironic dorkiness in this unbearably mannered, unspeakably acted film. It’s a slice of sentimental whimsy-futurism and non-satire, adapted by Waititi from the Kazuo Ishiguro novel, which winds up saying nothing substantial or meaningful (or funny) about artificial intelligence, love or grief. Klara and the Sun is soft-centred sci-fi-lite, simultaneously demanding we laugh at its (unfunny) humour and wipe away a tear at its pass-agg poignancy. With earlier films like Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Thor: Ragnarok, Waititi showed he can do comedy. But this, sadly, is closer to his notoriousfey-Hitler fantasy Jojo Rabbit– misjudged and self-admiring.In the world to come in an uncanny valley of the almost-real, families can buy “artificial friend” or AF robots for their kids. In terms of tech plausibility overall, incidentally, their status isn’t entirely clear: AF salesperson (Natasha Lyonne) says that the recent third world war has wiped out the internet. (This post-WW3 world looks in pretty good shape apart from that.) And these AF humanoids incidentally have a kind of purple blood called PEC-9 running through them which one character incidentally tells us is “highly flammable”. (Uh-oh. Quite the design fault.)One such AF is teen girl Klara, played byJenna Ortegaas a ditsy, cutesy, supremely lovable innocent: a manic pixie dream robot – only nice – who is solar-powered and who therefore, in her adorable childlike robot way, worships the sun as a god. But Klara is an earlier, more rudimentary AF model, less sophisticated and robust apparently than the newer upgrades which run on Bluetooth as opposed to solar. (Is that really better?)At all events, her flaws are presented as analogous to the vulnerabilities of the human teen who wants Klara; this is Josie (Mia Tharia), a 14-year-old genius-prodigy due to be expensively “lifted” into a super-IQ class via a new surgical procedure, but who is also very lonely and suffering from an unspecified illness. Her uptight mom is played byAmy Adamsand the grumpy housekeeper Melania – whose appearance is the nearest the film comes to comedy – is played by Rachel House. Klara goes to live with her new family in their distant home in a weirdly dreamlike Midwest farming landscape from which the city can only be glimpsed distantly, like Oz. Klara becomes certain that the sun lives in the nearby barn above, from which she can see it rising every morning; what a sweetly naive belief. And so it goes on, to a twist ending that is as unsatisfying and contrived as everything that has gone before.The thought of robots or replicant youngsters having real intelligence or real feelings is a difficult subject; Hirokazu Kore-eda came unstuck with the idea of robot child replacements inhis recent film Sheep in the Box. Kogonada’s parableAfter Yang, about AI child robots, was a more interesting and persuasive movie. But this is a sentimental and laborious mess.Klara and the Sun screened at the London film festival; released on 22 October in Australia, and 23 October in the UK and US.Explore more on these topicsFilmScience fiction and fantasy filmsTaika WaititiJenna OrtegaLondon film festivalRobotsFilm adaptationsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Amol Rajan Connection review – another wrong move after lasting one night in The Celebrity Traitors? | Television | The Guardian
description: The broadcaster has bullet-proof confidence as he departs the BBC. But his first YouTube show with Gareth Southgate is nowhere near as radical as you’d expect – and he sounds like yet another tech guru
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The broadcaster has bullet-proof confidence as he departs the BBC. But his first YouTube show with Gareth Southgate is nowhere near as radical as you’d expect – and he sounds like yet another tech guru
Content: He certainly dreams big … The Amol Rajan Connection.Photograph: YouTubeView image in fullscreenHe certainly dreams big … The Amol Rajan Connection.Photograph: YouTubeTelevisionReviewThe Amol Rajan Connection review – another wrong move after lasting one night in The Celebrity Traitors?The broadcaster has bullet-proof confidence as he departs the BBC. But his first YouTube show with Gareth Southgate is nowhere near as radical as you’d expect – and he sounds like yet another tech guruPhil HarrisonThu 15 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhatever you think ofAmol Rajan, he can’t be accused of not dreaming big. In the clip trailing the launch of his YouTube project The Amol Rajan Connection, he acknowledges the seismic volatility of our times but locates himself firmly at the heart of them. “We are about to get 100 years of change in a single decade,” he says. “And that’s scary. But maybe I can help.” Big talk for someone who somehow managed the singular feat of being outlasted by Richard E Grant in The Celebrity Traitors. But joking aside, Rajan’s bulletproof self-confidence remains titanium-tough.The branding of The Amol Rajan Connection features a mock-up of the poster from The Harder They Come, a Jamaican film about a renegade insurgent whose reckless defiance of the establishment’s rules culminates in him dying in a hail of bullets. But however he might see himself, it’s impossible to regard Rajan as an outsider. From his editorship of a national newspaper, via University Challenge and Today, he has shown an uncanny facility for arriving, briskly, at the very heart of one national institution after another. The sponsors of this show are two world-bestriding tech corporations, one of Britain’s largest banks and an upmarket supermarket chain. He soft-launched with an appearance on former Tory chancellor George Osborne’s podcast. Rajan’s connections are clearly being worked very efficiently.View image in fullscreenMildly soporific … Rajan with Gareth Southgate on the first episode of The Amol Rajan Connection.Photograph: YouTubeIn the course of the conversation with Osborne, he explained himself thus: “The BBC, and BBC News, is going to get smaller at an accelerating rate. And I want to go to where the action is.” But what constitutes the action in this context? The long-form, one-on-one video podcast (which, essentially, this is) has become a crowded field. In fact, co-presenting Today on Radio 4 remains a much more influential position for a media operative to occupy.Since leaving Today, Rajan has hinted at certain low-key beefs with the limitations of the BBC, mainly revolving around the sense of being unable to say what he really thinks. Unpromisingly, these feelings were initially articulated in an article in the Spectator, and the piece contained, more unpromisingly still, an expression of agreement with some of the ideas of Dominic Cummings. Rajan is an undeniably fluent communicator but there’s a sense that his quickness can devolve into something slightly less palatable. There is a touch of the tech guru about him – his self-belief sometimes borders on the messianic. Can he listen to an expert? Or, in keeping with the current affairs interlocutor he has recently been, does he interrupt?Perhaps his first guest can be seen as reassuring.Gareth Southgateis arguably the anti-Amol. He is unflashy, measured and occasionally even a little ponderous. Rajan reads the room: like most right-thinking people, he’s clearly full of admiration and fondness for the former England manager, and so he allows himself to be incorporated into his steady, sometimes mildly soporific rhythm. The result is a very traditional piece of broadcasting.Gareth Southgate: Changing the Game for Young Men review – boys are crying out for help like thisRead moreInitially, it wanders at length down some well-trodden paths. Rejection by Southampton, a second chance at Crystal Palace, captaincy, England,thatpenalty miss, club management – and then back to England; this time in a waistcoat, searching for footballing redemption but finding himself, at a sensitive time, forced to take the lead in cultural areas, too. It’s gently enjoyable, like a lulling, familiar bedtime story.In the second of the conversation’s two hours, the pair navigate choppier waters, talking about Fifa governance, theManchester City situationand, eventually, Southgate’s pet subject: his heartfelt concerns about the problems afflicting young men.None of this is dull, exactly. In fact, much of it is engaging and worthwhile. It just doesn’t feel particularly dynamic or radical. If this interview is “where the action is”, it’s hard to see how it provides proof of concept for the venture as a whole.Obviously, tone and mood will vary with the guests – the version of Rajan we see here is certainly more thoughtful than usual, and that’s refreshing. But at first glance, The Amol Rajan Connection plays things safe. Maybe something more reflective of the times that spawned it will emerge. For the time being, though, this isn’t it.The Amol Rajan Connection is onYouTubenowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionYouTubeAmol RajanGareth SouthgatereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Frieze review – you’ll see more avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tent | Art | The Guardian
description:
Regents Park, London
This year’s art fair is a jumble sale of mediocre paintings for the super-rich, while its Masters sibling hawks dinosaur skulls and sleazy 19th-century nudes. Welcome to the art market as its most grotesque
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: Regents Park, LondonThis year’s art fair is a jumble sale of mediocre paintings for the super-rich, while its Masters sibling hawks dinosaur skulls and sleazy 19th-century nudes. Welcome to the art market as its most grotesque
Content: ‘Serves the tastes of a certain kind of consumer’ … the Carl Freedman stand at Frieze London, 2026.Photograph: Linda Nylind/Linda Nylind/FriezeView image in fullscreen‘Serves the tastes of a certain kind of consumer’ … the Carl Freedman stand at Frieze London, 2026.Photograph: Linda Nylind/Linda Nylind/FriezeArtReviewFrieze review – you’ll see more avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tentRegents Park, LondonThis year’s art fair is a jumble sale of mediocre paintings for the super-rich, while its Masters sibling hawks dinosaur skulls and sleazy 19th-century nudes. Welcome to the art market as its most grotesqueJonathan JonesThu 15 Oct 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNaked people climb out of the earth and run around waving their arms and screaming, while someone with a bird’s head and wings plays the bagpipes. It’s my favourite artwork at this year’s Frieze but don’t go looking for this wildly imaginative outrage among the heaps of contemporary art at Frieze London. It’s a painting by a 16th-century follower of Hieronymus Bosch and is on view at Frieze Masters, the posher tent on the other side of Regent’s Park.I’m sorry to say I was bored rigid in Frieze London. Many people attend, I imagine, hoping to be informed and excited by the newest, coolest art, but you’ll see more genuinely avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tent. There are endless paintings, none of which are much good, interspersed with photographs which tend to be a little better. The first thing here that held me at all was a two-metre-tall, inkjet print by Wolfgang Tillmans called Paul, nude, golf ball in which the naked Paul has his elbows on the floor and his close-cropped head bowed between them in apparent despair, while the white ball beside him eerily mirrors the pale flesh of his bony back. But it’s not new – it dates from 1994.And, oh Lord, those paintings. There seem to be millions of them. And an elegant white marquee full of gallery booths along endless white corridors is a ghastly way of showing them, a dreadful way of seeing. It’s not as rewarding as visiting galleries which can be interesting spaces. Here, everything is crammed in, like a huge shop – the Selfridges of art.View image in fullscreen‘The Selfridges of art’ … Spruth Magers stand at Frieze London, 2026.Photograph: Linda Nylind/Linda Nylind/FriezeFrieze, it is claimed, defines the new and finds the stars of tomorrow. But it’s obvious that it really serves the needs of sellers and the tastes of a certain kind of extremely wealthy consumer. This is most apparent on VIP day when I enter along with a host of tech bros, hedge-fund managers, retired hedge-fund managers, their children, and – is that George Osborne? – who were actually here to buy this stuff. At Frieze Masters, I was about to ask the price of an Anselm Kiefer work, matted vegetation clogging its surface, when an elderly couple beat me to it. They were genuinely interested in purchasing. The price was just shy of a million quid.Things you can put on your wall are still the most collectible art. At Frieze Masters, you will find works by established modern “masters”, many of whom are deceased: a series of stained, graffiti-laden visual poems by Cy Twombly, a grey, bleak nude by Leon Kossoff. But at the contemporary fair, some of it is jumble sale standard. At Los Angeles’ Night Gallery booth, Wanda Koop’s Radiance-Together depicts two candles burning side by side in a blue and purple setting. Aw, cute. Who on earth would take this seriously? Another of its artists, Andy Woll, shows a row of lazily brushed mountain views that are just as vacuous. Meanwhile, at the appropriately named Grimm Gallery, Rosalind Nashashibi – better known for her films – exhibits a silly painting of lovers between flowery borders.Now here’s something different – a row of white mineral-like growths, eerily lovely, enigmatically organic: they’re Helen Chadwick’s Piss Flowers, a chance to own examples of a modern classic by this tremendous artist who died in 1996. Why is she not over in Frieze Masters? And at the back of the Edel Assanti booth is Lonnie Holley’s assemblage of a water tap on a rusty pipe entwined with wire and two green bottles on a rough wooden plinth. It has the raw tang of real life. Holley, a musician and artist from Birmingham, Alabama who held me spellbound a couple of years ago when he showed how he can create beauty from a random piece of wire, is a true American great who stands out in this blandfest.View image in fullscreen‘A festival of capitalism run amok’ … Gagosian stand at Frieze London, 2026.Photograph: Linda Nylind/Linda Nylind/FriezeSo do Tracey Emin, Waqas Khan, Do Ho Suh, Catherine Opie and Zanele Muholi – but in all honesty the success rate at Frieze London is about one in 10. That’s far too low for an event claiming to define the artistic zeitgeist.Over at Frieze Masters, you’ve got the best certificate of quality there is: time. If something has value after 50, 500, or 68,000,000 years, it’s probably good. That 68m years is no exaggeration for here on sale is a triple-horned, fossilised Triceratops skull. Is this really going to end up as decoration in some rich dude’s house?Let’s get it in perspective. To call this head “museum quality” is an understatement. The Natural History Museum does not own a Triceratops fossil of this perfection. Palaeontologists,as the Guardian recently reported, are worried that the fashion for dinosaur specimens among the ultra-rich is inflating prices and locking out museums. There are several such marvels being sold here.View image in fullscreen‘Fruitier, stranger’ … a skull for sale at Frieze Masters.Photograph: Hugo Glendinning/ FriezeFrieze Masters is more visually exciting than Frieze London. It’s fruitier, stranger. You can buy armour, silverware, Arabian carpets, the stuff a decadent aesthete might have surrounded themselves with in 1896. It makes you realise how conformist the contemporary fair is. At Frieze Masters, you can indulge your most perverse tastes – there are loads of sleazy, 19th-century nudes.But if it is more interesting, it is also more disgusting. Stalls fetishise objects from the past, ripping them out of context to display them as brightly lit gewgaws: a manuscript page cut from its codex, a face mask off an ancient Egyptian coffin, a stone head of a priest from 2nd century AD Palmyra. These things belong in museums, but here they all are in the isolating spotlight of luxury and money.This is a festival of capitalism run amok. I could say jokingly you might buy this or that but you won’t, unless you are a squillionaire, nor will I. What was it Andy Burnham was saying about the tyranny of neoliberalism? Here it distorts art in a delirious orgy of commodification.The Colnaghi booth could have been designed as a Marxist exposé of the art market. African wooden carvings stand in front of a kitsch 1920 nude by Giacomo Grosso. The lavish view of the model’s bum as she lies on silks and the fact that she’s wearing high heels make it comically clear this is finely painted soft porn. The African art, made for religious purposes, is reduced to decor in front of this commodified body. John Berger, the radical critic who saw nude paintings and other forms of commodified art as playthings of western capitalism, might have said: told you so.Frieze London and Frieze Mastersare on until 18 OctoberExplore more on these topicsArtFrieze art fairCollectingExhibitionsPaintingSculptureHeritagereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Stranger than stranger-than-fiction’: how Lance Oppenheim made the year’s two buzziest films | Movies | The Guardian
description: Primetime and You Can See Everything are both clammy, audacious awards contenders that challenge our sense of reality. Ahead of the release of his drama starring Robert Pattinson as a TV vigilante, the 30-year-old director talks crime, punishment and South Park
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: Primetime and You Can See Everything are both clammy, audacious awards contenders that challenge our sense of reality. Ahead of the release of his drama starring Robert Pattinson as a TV vigilante, the 30-year-old director talks crime, punishment and South Park
Content: ‘Rob’s quite possibly the actor of our time’ … Lance Oppenheim on the star of Primetime, Robert Pattinson.Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/APView image in fullscreen‘Rob’s quite possibly the actor of our time’ … Lance Oppenheim on the star of Primetime, Robert Pattinson.Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/APMoviesInterview‘Stranger than stranger-than-fiction’: how Lance Oppenheim made the year’s two buzziest filmsRyan GilbeyPrimetime and You Can See Everything are both clammy, audacious awards contenders that challenge our sense of reality. Ahead of the release of his drama starring Robert Pattinson as a TV vigilante, the 30-year-old director talks crime, punishment and South ParkThu 15 Oct 2026 10.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo direct one movie that is on everyone’s lips in awards season is remarkable. To make two begins to look like sorcery. That is the position in which the 30-year-old Florida-born film-maker Lance Oppenheim now finds himself. Next month brings the release of You Can See Everything, the three-hour documentary which he co-directed with faux-naif deadpan prankster Nathan Fielder, in which they spend a month living with the disgraced health-tech mogulElizabeth Holmesbefore she begins her 11-year prison sentence for fraud and conspiracy. The film, described by Oppenheim as “head-spinning” and so shrouded in secrecy that Variety magazine’s list of Oscar predictions identifies one of its cast members only as “[Redacted]”, is expected to become the first documentary nominated for best picture.‘In our deepest hearts we are voyeurs’: the paedophile-hunting show that inspired Robert Pattinson’s new filmRead moreWhen I meet Oppenheim in a London hotel, it is to discuss his other hot ticket, Primetime, for whichRobert Pattinsonis the one attracting Oscar buzz. The Batman actor gives a high-wire performance as Chris Hansen, the sensationalist US television vigilante renowned for ambushing paedophiles on To Catch a Predator, which was a disreputable and highly addictive segment of the current affairs show Dateline NBC between 2004 and 2007. Hansen later parlayed the idea, and his crusading shtick, into a succession of spin-offs. Some, including Hansen Vs Predators, had the same sleazy catnip quality. Others, such as a sting to collar bicycle thieves, did not.The format of To Catch a Predator is simple. A volunteer from the website Perverted-Justice enters an online chatroom pretending to be underage. Once a paedophile takes the bait, chats with the supposed teen and then pitches up at the agreed location (which is in fact a “sting house” rigged with cameras), he is met by an actor posing as the adolescent. Suddenly, Hansen slinks out of the shadows and calmly invites the offender to “have a seat,” an offer which quickly became his catchphrase. He then reads aloud excerpts from the incriminating online chat as the guilty party squirms and panics. Reality television this may be, but it is also a theatrical performance with its own unvarying props from one sting to the next: cookies and pizza the pre-sex snacks, a table or kitchen island Hansen’s equivalent of a CEO’s desk or judge’s bench.“The show is so tonally strange,” marvels Oppenheim. “It feels like an alien object beamed in from Mars. You’re seeing this horrific situation where someone who’s sick in the head has shown up to do a terrible thing. Then they’re confronted by Chris Hansen, who has these catchphrases and one-liners. He’s a crime-stopper but he’s also there to make a TV show out of their miserable state. It oscillated between making me nauseated and making me laugh. The challenge for me was how to create something that’s even stranger than stranger-than-fiction.”View image in fullscreenRighteous avenger or meretricious huckster … Pattinson as Chris Hansen in Primetime.Photograph: A24In person, you would never take this boyish chatterbox for a zeitgeist-surfing A24 auteur whose fanclub includes Ari Aster, Darren Aronofsky and the Safdie brothers. In fact, you might think twice before serving him alcohol, at least without ID. His mini pompadour gives him an Eraserhead Jr look; his black, round-framed glasses might have been felt-tipped on to his face by a classmate. A black-and-white striped shirt worn under his suit jacket lends him the appearance of a well-dressed humbug.Though based in fact, Primetime is Oppenheim’s first non-documentary feature. His haunting 2020 debut,Some Kind of Heaven, was set in a Florida retirement community where happiness becomes oppressive and tyrannical. Its 2024 follow-up, Spermworld, delved into the private lives of men who donate sperm, including one who has fathered more than a hundred children.“I’ve always wanted my documentaries to feel like Hollywood dramas,” the director explains. “With Primetime, I was curious about what it would be like to make an actual Hollywood drama with actors.” The resulting character study is almost as kaleidoscopic and overripe asRen Faire, Oppenheim’s masterful 2024 HBO “docu-fantasia” featuring a mercurial, Viagra-popping elderly theme-park despot, his back-stabbing underlings and a giant talking lizard.View image in fullscreen‘It oscillated between making me nauseated and making me laugh’ … Oppenheim on the show that inspired Primetime.Photograph: Sinna NasseriThe film-maker’s own introduction to Chris Hansen came as a child when he saw him spoofed on an episode of South Park, in which Cartman is strong-armed by the presenter into appearing on a TV special about Tourette syndrome; a group of paedophiles inadvertently come to his rescue by shooting themselves en masse. From there, Oppenheim became hooked on To Catch a Predator and its derivatives. A few years ago, his girlfriend (now wife) even bought him a personalised Cameo video message from Hansen. He scoots forward now to play it to me on his phone. In the video, the silver-haired paedophile-hunter cheekily invites Oppenheim to “have a seat … not because I suspect you of anything predator-like,” before plugging his own upcoming shows.It is this confusion between righteous avenger and meretricious huckster that makes Hansen such an irresistible subject. “I think he started off with noble intentions, but he turned serious reporting into entertainment and willingly transformed himself into a meme. He’s on Cameo presenting what he does as a service you can pay for; then he puts his whole project into this moral register where he talks about good and evil. What happens to you psychologically when you believe you’re doing something good for the world? Does that turn you into a superhero?” He grins: “And now we’ve got the guy who plays Batman as Chris Hansen.”View image in fullscreen‘Head-spinning’ … Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24It was Pattinson, already a diehard Hansen fan, who brought the project to Oppenheim intending only to produce rather than star in it. “Rob’s quite possibly the actor of our time,” the director says. “Every movie he’s done this year has been a defining cultural moment.” Primetime follows The Drama, his prickly black comedy with Zendaya, and The Odyssey; Dune: Part Three arrives in December. “As I’ve gotten to know him, I feel like he also stitched some very human and vulnerable parts of himself into Primetime. Rob became an overnight celebrity when he went to Comic-Con with Twilight in 2008. He was instantly a public figure with expectations about how he should behave. That’s part of what Chris Hansen goes through in the movie.”The special alchemy of Primetime lies in the way it renders Hansen’s story in the clammy style of To Catch a Predator so that we are simultaneously inside the show, with its churning moral tumult, and outside, looking on in appalled and impotent horror. “It is very muchnota biopic,” agrees Oppenheim. “I wanted it to be experiential and phantasmagorical. I was wondering what would happen if you took Billy Wilder’s Ace in the Hole, Oliver Stone’s JFK and Brian De Palma’s Body Double, then threw them in a blender with the real-life events of To Catch a Predator. Would it taste weird or delicious? Maybe you sprinkle a little Sexy Beast in there, too, and it’s, like, ‘Boom!’”Boom, indeed. Hansen, who has griped bitterly about not being consulted or even informed about the film, has accused Primetime of “weaponised empathy”, “[making] audiences feel sorry for the predators” and portraying him and his staff “as ratings-obsessed, maniacal people”. On the other hand, he has insinuated himself enthusiastically into the Primetime experience, booking trailers for his own true-crime streaming platform, TruBlu, to run immediately before screenings of the movie in US cinemas.‘He stole the show’: do Oscars beckon for Robert Pattinson, star of four of the year’s biggest films – and Batman?Read moreOppenheim is full of admiration. “The way he has created a media circus around his reaction to the film is on a par with what we’ve seen of him on television. He contains multitudes. He is a journalist but also an entertainer, a circus ringleader and maybe a compulsive performer.” Are there parallels with the current US president? “Well, they were both on television around the same time and both on shows which were made or green-lit by Jeff Zucker, who plays himself in the film.” He stops short, though, of calling them kindred spirits.Perhaps Hansen’s persona is too closely intertwined with the development of Oppenheim’s own sensibility for him to make any such damning judgment. “I saw To Catch a Predator long before I saw Abbas Kiarostami’s Close-Up or Orson Welles’s F For Fake,” he says, citing two films in which documentary and drama form an unstable concoction. “But I feel the show has a lot in common with them because it’s such a reality bender. It has short adult actors pretending to be children in a house that looks like a set from Blue Velvet.” He shakes his head as if experiencing afresh the insanity of To Catch a Predator. “I don’t think I’d be making nonfiction films the way I do if I hadn’t seen that show as a kid.”Primetime is in UK cinemas from 30 October. You Can See Everything is in UK cinemas from 20 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsRobert PattinsonElizabeth HolmesinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A guy held a knife to my throat and said: play something normal!’ Richard Thompson on crazy crowds, his beloved beret and Sandy Denny’s driving skills | Richard Thompson | The Guardian
description: As he releases new album Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, the 77-year-old British folk legend answers your questions about Billy Connolly, Californian fish and chips and whether he nearly joined the Eagles
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: As he releases new album Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, the 77-year-old British folk legend answers your questions about Billy Connolly, Californian fish and chips and whether he nearly joined the Eagles
Content: ‘I wanted to do my Anglo-Celtic thing and sing in my own accent’ … Richard Thompson.Photograph: Paul ClampinView image in fullscreen‘I wanted to do my Anglo-Celtic thing and sing in my own accent’ … Richard Thompson.Photograph: Paul ClampinFilm & Music reader interviewRichard ThompsonInterview‘A guy held a knife to my throat and said: play something normal!’ Richard Thompson on crazy crowds, his beloved beret and Sandy Denny’s driving skillsAs told toDave SimpsonAs he releases new album Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, the 77-year-old British folk legend answers your questions about Billy Connolly, Californian fish and chips and whether he nearly joined the EaglesThu 15 Oct 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBilly Connolly recalled being in a room with you, Sandy Denny, Nick Drake and John Martyn. Did you feel you were collectively doing something special?poscopyThat might have been at the Royal Festival Hall [in 1969], where Fairport Convention had Nick and John as openers and Billy must have been backstage. He’d have been in the Humblebums with Gerry Rafferty, before he evolved from a banjo player who told jokes into a comedian who played a bit of banjo. He was always a fantastic bloke and we’ve been friends for a long time.There was a great camaraderie between the stable of acts Joe Boyd produced: Fairport, the Incredible String Band, John Martyn, Chris McGregor. We felt different, not special, and didn’t feel successful because we weren’t. None of these people really sold many records in their lifetimes, but people are still discovering them now. This album is my latest attempt to sell some units.Have you ever been on a1952 Vincent Black Lightningand did that inspire the song?llamapacaI’ve never ridden a Vincent Black Lightning. There’s only about 15 left, but when I was a kid one of the neighbours had a Vincent Black Shadow – a very similar motorcycle – and us kids thought it was one of the most beautiful things we’d ever seen. I was casting around for a British equivalent to American romantic imagery, so thought it would be a good object to build a drama around. Boy, girl, motorcycle, armed robbery …The narrator in your songCold Kissesis one of the most chilling characters I’ve ever met in a song. How much of that rogue is you?If it’s none, where did you summon him up from?LeroyDeSwoonHe wants to compare himself with her old boyfriends. Some of us have been there – not necessarily going through someone’s drawers, but looking at someone’s diary or emails, trying to find out more about a new partner. It’s a sneaky thing to do, obviously, but in the guise of entertainment songwriting can dig below the surface of what’s considered civilised and into an area that’s slightly uncomfortable. I love that.On the new album, the song Cocaine Walking, Booze Talking is based on people I met in the psychedelic era who were a bit edgy or violent. Then acid came along and they suddenly went all peace and love, but it wouldn’t last. So the last verse asks: “Who’ll win the battle before the nurse pulls the plug? The Kings Road hippy or the Sauchiehall thug?” Conflicted human beings. I thought John Lennon was a bit like that.Listen to Cocaine Walking, Booze Talking.Could you tell a nice – not sad – story that I haven’t heard about Sandy Denny or Nick Drake?katstuNick was so taciturn and hard to know that I couldn’t say a lot of uplifting stuff about him. Sandy was a terrible passenger, hypersensitive. In a car, she’d be going: “What was that noise?” “Why did you put the brakes on?” Eventually, our tour manager [in Fairport Convention] had to teach her about the internal combustion engine: “I’m now changing gear.” On an airplane, she was impossible. Flying to Los Angeles, she spilled a gin and tonic in my lap in the first hour, although on a boat she was totally at ease, in her element, hence so many of her songs about the sea. From what I’ve heard, when she finally got a licence, she was driving into ditches and all sorts. Bless her.Who is the inspiration behind Beeswing?EddieHaskellPeople say: “Oh, what a beautiful song about [the folk singer] Anne Briggs,” but it’s more complicated. When I lived in Suffolk in the 1970s, a tramp used to come looking for odd jobs. He’d do a bit of gardening, we’d wash his clothes and feed him and he’d tell extraordinary stories about his life. So his stories were part of the song, but also Sandy and Anne were great friends and it was really Sandy’s sense of Anne being this free spirit. But I need credit as a writer of fiction, too, because it’s not about anybody.Do you have a favourite cover of any of your songs? Mine isWall of Death by REM.MrsGRaffertyWall of Death was a memo to myself: take risks, go to the edge, don’t be complacent. But my favourite cover is The Great Valerio by Swan Arcade, a vocal trio around the folk scene in the 60s and 70s. They did a fantastic job of getting all the dissonant, unusual harmony that exists in the guitar arrangement and ended up with a wonderful piece of music. [Swan Arcade’s] Dave Brady had one arm. The story was that he’d been on his motorcycle and was hurtling towards a brick wall, so stuck his arm out to grab a lamp-post. But he managed to shape a chord with his left hand and strum with his little finger. A great character.Would you have liked to have worked more closely with John Martyn – at least before he became “difficult” and his music moved in a different direction?archiebargie“Difficult” is a bit cheeky. John was one of those guitar players, likeMartin Carthy, who cover all bases. I’m a bit like that myself, so if you put us together there’s a lot of treading on each other’s toes, but we were neighbours for a while in the late 60s and early 70s and used to jam together. Once, we were in Olympic Studios for one of John’s sessions and he played acoustic and I played electric. We jammed for about 20 minutes and it was just wonderful and joyous, but they didn’t have the machine running. We should have done more of that.View image in fullscreenFairport Convention in in 1970. From left: Dave Mattacks (front), Dave Pegg, Simon Nicol, Richard Thompson and Dave Swarbrick.Photograph: Jim McCrary/RedfernsHow did the offer to join Eagles come about?BobinDayOffers would come through lawyers or management. I don’t think it was ever someone from a band phoning up saying: “We’d love to have you.” When I was on tour with Sandy in ’71, I did get a firm approach to join Linda Ronstadt’s band because four of them had left to form Eagles. I thought: I can’t jump ship. Sandy would kill me … and do I wanna live and work with a bunch of Californians? I wanted to do my Anglo-Celtic thing and sing in my own accent. I was asked to join a later incarnation of the Animals when they wanted to dump [the guitarist]Hilton Valentine. Shocking stuff. I was asked to join the Band twice, but I thought they were gonna drink themselves to death.You were originally a fervent enthusiast for all things British and yet now you live in the US,which seems at odds with everything the UK stands for. Why?DozyDannyFor the last 40 years, I’ve had a place in London and a place in America. I lived in Santa Monica for a long time, but you’re surrounded by Brits in the music and film business. You can’t go 10 or 20 yards without a pub screening Premier League games or a fish and chip shop. Plus, when I open up my computer, the Guardian is my homepage. You can be connected anywhere in the world, but I’ve never felt connected with American culture. I’m not going to sing Jan and Dean songs about surfing. My inner landscape is London, Scotland or some dark moor in Brontë country.What was it like being on stage with Bob Dylan at theGuitar Legends festival in Seville in 1991? You looked on high alert, or anxious. Was there any rehearsal beforehand?MaskedTortillaI was on the road with [the American singer-songwriter]Bonnie Raittwhen I got a call from [the guitarist]Phil Manzanera. Word was Bob wanted to do some acoustic numbers together, which was great. We did rehearse in the dressing room, and rehearsed All Along the Watchtower with his band. When we went on stage, the acoustic guitars had gone out of tune, so I spent the first song trying to tune up – that was probably high alert – but once things settled down it was great fun; a great honour to work with Bob.Your first band wasEmil and the Detectives, withHugh Cornwell, later of the Stranglers. Did you cross paths again?Haigin88We had the band in school, but by 16 I was playing with Fairport Convention, so I didn’t see Hugh for 40 years. Then, in the 2000s, we were both playing a festival in Spain and picked up the conversation where we left it. Since then, we’ve done some musical things and gigs together anda splendid version of Tobacco Roadfor charity.View image in fullscreenThompson playing at the New Orleans jazz festival in 1980.Photograph: David Redfern/RedfernsWhat has been your most improbable backing role as a guitarist?thoughtwhackerIn the band with Hugh, we backedHelen Shapiro, but I’ve played unlikely places like care homes, funerals, weddings and schools. Singing at my own mum’s funeral was the toughest gig. I played a girls’ school in Connecticut because we knew the teacher. The kids knew a bit of Chaucer, so I could do something like Sumer Is Icumen In plus a Britney Spears song or something. The kids went nuts. Best audience ever.Bonospent a small fortune having his favourite hat flown in first class for a gig in Italy. How far would you go to ensure your trademark beret [a Balmoral] was in place come showtime?SalfordianBlueThat must have cost Bono £20,000. For the price of a stapler, I have someone staple it to my head before I go to the airport. I sometimes forget to pack any shoes, but people don’t notice ’cause I wear black socks.The last time I saw you, a fire alarm cleared the theatre. What’s your best, worst or most memorable moment playing live?RobFramptonIn the 70s, I did a solo tour of Sweden and played somewhere in the Arctic Circle where I was singing my precious little folk-rock numbers between the disco. A guy held a knife to my throat and said: “Why don’t you play something normal?” I wasn’t afraid; I was wondering: what’s normal? I might have done a Buddy Holly cover. At school, when I deputised for some local poppy covers band, there was a real fight in the audience, kids throwing chairs; hang on to your equipment and get off stage.The Mary Wallopers review – legs and pints go flying to the sound of rowdy folk ragersRead moreAt one point, you became an antiques dealer. Why was this and howdid you acquirethe expertise?rjoncasA friend of mine took over an antique shop in Marylebone. I knew a bit, but I was too nice to the old ladies, too honest: I’d tell them we’d offer £1,000, but they’d get double that at auction. I sold a couple of porcelain Ming dynasty lions for £60, thinking they were fakes. They were worth thousands. I soon went back to music, but I still annoy my family by watching Antiques Roadshow and correctly guessing what something’s worth, so they look at me like I’m some sort of genius.Hippies, Thugs and Heroes byRichard Thompsonis released on 16 October on New West Records. He tours North America until 18 February, then Europe and the UK from 15 April to 7 MayExplore more on these topicsRichard ThompsonFilm & Music reader interviewFolk musicPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From a VR gay sauna to the gothic pile that inspired Cluedo – Fierce festival storms back | Stage | The Guardian
description: As Britain’s longest-running live art festival returns, get ready for late-night artist dinners, a show in a swimming pool and Faye Driscoll’s incredible rotating disintegration
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: As Britain’s longest-running live art festival returns, get ready for late-night artist dinners, a show in a swimming pool and Faye Driscoll’s incredible rotating disintegration
Content: Epic work … Faye Driscoll’s Weathering at Philadelphia in 2025.Photograph: Kevin MonkoView image in fullscreenEpic work … Faye Driscoll’s Weathering at Philadelphia in 2025.Photograph: Kevin MonkoStageFrom a VR gay sauna to the gothic pile that inspired Cluedo – Fierce festival storms backVenues across BirminghamAs Britain’s longest-running live art festival returns, get ready for late-night artist dinners, a show in a swimming pool and Faye Driscoll’s incredible rotating disintegrationLyndsey WinshipThu 15 Oct 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe phrase “two things can be true” is a frequent refrain in popular psychology and it’s also a frequent response, I find, to witnessing the farther reaches of live art. Hmm, is this performance confusingly self-indulgent or utterly profound? Sometimes it can be both. In fact, it’s not just two things that can be true, it’s as many things as there are people in the audience, since this is all about the live subjective experience, in the moment; presence and connection.Launched in 1998, Fierce is Britain’s longest-running live art festival. For one week it takes over Birmingham’s conventional theatres alongside unconventional spaces, especially in ex-industrial Digbeth, which is fast becoming a creative hub. Also on the bill this year: late-night artist dinners, a show in a swimming pool, and a six-hour performance jam at a grand gothic hall that was apparently the inspiration for Cluedo.There’s a focus on the sensuous and sensory; it’s all about the physical body. But the first piece I experience is actually in virtual reality: Traversing the Mist, by Taiwanese artist Tung-Yen Chou. The setting is a gay sauna, and the VR tech is impressive. You walk through the grey concrete corridors, locker room, showers, cubicles, pushing aside curtains that you know aren’t really there. You can open doors, pick things up, press buttons in the lift. You’re an observer of the uncanny scene, which is peopled by identical blank-faced men; a sense of searching pervades, but there’s zero joy or pleasure to be found.View image in fullscreenLack of connection … Tung-Yen Chou, In the Mist at Fierce festival, 2026.Photograph: Kris KangThe experience is a combination of immersive and detached. It’s engaging, and yet eerily lonely – and also unnerving when the floor falls away, messing with your own proprioception. You feel, but what you feel is exactly the lack of connection. (Chou is also showing a short, sit-down VR piece called In the Mist, which was a precursor to the longer work, but is basically a sad porno.)What you’re missing in VR is the smells, the heat, the sweat. But don’t worry, there’s plenty of that elsewhere. Wojciech Grudziński’s sweaty, hairy, all-too-human fleshy body is front and centre in his solo Threesome, his bum in the air as he does upside down pliés in a shoulder stand and other yogic moves wearing bottomless frilly knickers. In voiceover he tells us of three Polish ballet dancers who were shamed for their homosexuality, and Threesome is his attempt to reclaim their true identities, and make peace with his own “ghastly” body. Is a series of bum-bearing contortions followed by a ravey, repetitive jig the best way to do that? Well, it’s Grudziński’s way. And it’s strangely compelling, building to a sort of catharsis, with lights and music and defiant mood.Artist Melissandre Varin is known as n:u, and calls themself an “atmosphere-maker”, which is interesting branding and perhaps modifies the expectations of the audience. Fierce is a thoroughly international festival, but n:u was previously based in Birmingham, although the work is rooted in Congolese, Guadeloupean, and Beninese heritage. I caught part of a rehearsal for the piece FREE(HOLD), an opaque ritual, in which performers drag ropes around their ankles and keen to the sky. Endurance, suffering, slavery and colonialism all rushed to mind.View image in fullscreenFront and centre … Wojciech Grudziński in Threesome at Fierce festival, 2026.Photograph: Manuel VasonThis is a festival full of intriguing, conversation-starting stuff, but American choreographer Faye Driscoll blows everyone else out of the water with her acclaimed, award-winning piece Weathering, which gets its UK premiere here. Driscoll’s work is a few levels up in terms of concept, commitment, execution and scale. It’s essentially 10 performers on a rotating platform, a tableau vivant, or maybe less a living tableau than one that’s slowly distorting and decaying and caving under the gravity of life’s pressures, or just the passage of time.It’s a piece full of wayward, messy bodies – it is indicated immediately that these are humans rather than “dancers” when the performers arrive in puffer jackets and cross-body bags and glasses, layers that will be gradually discarded, because this is live art after all. But these bodies also demonstrate a phenomenal amount of control, this multiperson sculpture moving at first so slowly it’s almost imperceptible. It’s intense and impressive, and importantly it sucks your attention and its imagery is ripe for extrapolation – especially the sense of precarity, of humans clinging to their unstable home as things start to spin out of control.Fierce festivalruns until 18 October, at various venues in BirminghamExplore more on these topicsStageDancePerformance artTheatreFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lee Child backs launch of reading scheme to send prisons half a million books | Books | The Guardian
description: The Jack Reacher author, the UK’s first prison reading laureate, said drive to improve literacy skills was a practical way to address reoffending and support rehabilitation
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: The Jack Reacher author, the UK’s first prison reading laureate, said drive to improve literacy skills was a practical way to address reoffending and support rehabilitation
