Content: ‘Proper books, proper storytellers’ … author Lee Child, third right, and Jake Richards MP talk to inmates in HMP Doncaster.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Proper books, proper storytellers’ … author Lee Child, third right, and Jake Richards MP talk to inmates in HMP Doncaster.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianBooksLee Child backs launch of reading scheme to send prisons half a million booksThe Jack Reacher author, the UK’s first prison reading laureate, said drive to improve literacy skills was a practical way to address reoffending and support rehabilitationEmma LoffhagenThu 15 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly half a million books will be distributed across prisons in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland this autumn, in a campaign backed by bestselling thriller writerLee Child.The initiative, delivered by the Reading Agency charity as part of its Quick Reads programme, will see copies of 11 short books distributed, with titles selected with input from prisoners as well as staff. A book will be distributed to every cell across the prison estate, as well as stock sent to prison libraries.Child, the UK’s first prison reading laureate, said the initiative was intended to address the “revolving door” – people leaving prison but struggling to cope outside and returning to custody.“If we can stop one in 10 of those people from coming back, that would be a major achievement,” he said. “It would be good for society as a whole, not just for that individual prisoner and their future employer.”Ministry of Justice statistics for 2024-25 show that 65% of initial-assessment results across public prisons in England, based on tests taken when people entered custody, were at entry levels 1-3,below the standardexpected of a typical GCSE student.Child said people who wanted to turn their lives around after prison could face compounded barriers if they had difficulty reading. “The obvious beneficiary will be somebody who is [in prison] due to some kind of mistake or unfortunate circumstance that they regret, and who wants to go straight afterwards and never come back,” he said. “But they face the problem of finding a job if they’ve got a conviction, and on top of that, if they’ve got poor literacy skills.”Everyday tasks could also become obstacles, he said. “You can’t read a lease if you want to rent a flat; you can’t deal with utilities or a TV licence if you can’t read the official notices.”The Quick Reads collection spans crime and thrillers, memoir, wellbeing, and a creative writing guide. Fiction titles include High Heat by Child himself; Cell One, a Lagos-set thriller by Leye Adenle; and Darkness Rising, from Bradford-based crime writer AA Dhand’s Harry Virdee series. Other books includeLemn Sissay’s memoir My Name Is Why, Andy McNab’s Today Everything Changes and Dr Alex George’s The Mind Manual. Authors featured also include Dreda Say Mitchell, Fiona Cummins, Cathy Rentzenbrink andAlex Wheatle.Child, who has made between 30 and 40 prison visits since beginning his work as laureate last year, said one of the most common explanations he heard from people who did not read was that the books they had been given at school were boring. Quick Reads, he said, offers an alternative. “They are proper books, proper storytellers, and there’s nothing simple or childish about them, they’re just short.”He added that improving access to books should be understood not as a soft approach to criminal justice but as a practical way to support rehabilitation and reduce reoffending. “The problem with public reaction to this kind of thing is a rather kneejerk reaction of ‘soft on crime’,” he said. “My point is that no, it’s actually hard on crime. It is focusing on where the budget and attention should really be.”Alongside distributing the books, the Reading Agency will organise author-led workshops, creative writing activities, content for National Prison Radio and resources for prison libraries, education teams and peer supporters. The initiative is funded by the Henry Smith Foundation, a poverty-focused non-profit.AA Dhand, whose Darkness Rising is among the selected books, said: “Books should be accessible to everyone, regardless of their circumstances or their previous relationship with reading.”View image in fullscreen‘Reading can build confidence, create empathy’ … AA Dhand.Dhand added: “In prison, reading can provide far more than temporary escape. It can build confidence, create empathy and give people the opportunity to see the world and themselves differently. If the right book reaches the right person at the right moment, it can open a door that may otherwise have remained closed.”Karen Napier, chief executive ofthe Reading Agency, said the programme was built with the intention of giving people in prison choice over what they read.“When we put a book directly into someone’s hands, we are offering more than words on a page,” she said. “Reading can offer escape, connection and space for reflection, while supporting wellbeing, confidence and learning. We want as many people as possible to have the opportunity to find a book that grabs them and discover where reading might take them.”Explore more on these topicsBooksLee ChildfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cult venue Prince Charles cinema ‘saved’ after lease renewal signed | Movies | The Guardian
description: The much-loved central London institution, which has been threatened with closure since January 2025, secures 25-year lease without break clause with current landlords
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The much-loved central London institution, which has been threatened with closure since January 2025, secures 25-year lease without break clause with current landlords
Content: The Prince Charles off London’s Leicester Square has been operating as a cinema since 1969.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The ObserverView image in fullscreenThe Prince Charles off London’s Leicester Square has been operating as a cinema since 1969.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The ObserverMoviesCult venue Prince Charles cinema ‘saved’ after lease renewal signedThe much-loved central London institution, which has been threatened with closure since January 2025, secures 25-year lease without break clause with current landlordsAndrew PulverThu 15 Oct 2026 11.20 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe celebrated Prince Charles repertory cinema in London’s Leicester Square has announced that the threat of closure has been staved off by signing a new 25-year lease with its landlords.In a post on social mediatitled “You Saved the PCC”, the cinema said that “after 21 months of uncertainty, we’re delighted to have secured the future of the cinema” and that they had “signed a new 25-year lease with no break clause, ensuring our projectors will keep rolling for years to come”.The cinema also expressed its gratitude for the “support, commitment and belief of many, many people”.In January 2025, the Prince Charleslaunched a petition, claiming that its landlord, Zedwell LSQ Ltd (owned by developer Criterion Capital) was trying to “bully us out of the building” by demanding a break clause in its lease, due for renewal in September 2025. The break clause would have enabled Zedwell to give the cinema six months’ notice if it had other plans for the site. At the time, Criterion Capital denied that it was attempting to intimidate or disadvantage the cinema.The news, however, triggered a groundswell of support, fromfilm fansand industry figures including theactor Paul Mescal and directors Danny Boyle, Robert Eggers, Christopher NolanandEdgar Wright.The building was opened as a live theatre in 1962, but converted to a cinema in 1969 after being bought by the Star Cinema chain, and subsequently showed adult movies. In 1991 it was taken over as a repertory cinema with cut-price seats. In May 2025,the Prince Charles was designated an asset of community valueby Westminster City Council.Ben Freedman, the owner of the Prince Charles, said in a statement: “Our cinema means an enormous amount to our team, our audiences and the wider arts community. Having this security gives us the confidence to invest in the cinema’s future and continue providing a home for film lovers. We are pleased to have reached an agreement that works for both parties and, most importantly, allows us to look forward with real confidence and excitement to the next chapter of the Prince Charles Cinema.”Vaqas Farooq, CEO of Criterion Capital, said: “We are delighted to have agreed terms which secure [the Prince Charles’] future … I’m particularly pleased that together we were able to work through a set of complex issues and find an equitable solution for both parties. A 25-year commitment provides real security for the cinema and its fans, and we are delighted to be continuing our partnership for many years to come.” Farooq added that the landlords plan to develop a hotel on the building’s upper floors.Lease issues are also behindthe threat to another key independent cinema, the Ultimate Picture Palace in Oxford, whose landlord, the University of Oxford’s Oriel College, is refusing to renew its current lease past 2037.Explore more on these topicsFilmLondonFilm industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Palestine book by Alana Hadid and Jenan Matari pulled from Random House before release | Penguin Random House | The Guardian
description: Authors withdraw book planned for young readers after disputes with editors over characterizations of 7 October
Author: Sam Levin
Headline: Authors withdraw book planned for young readers after disputes with editors over characterizations of 7 October
Content: Alana Hadid, a philanthropist, activist and older sister of models Bella and Gigi, and Jenan Matari, an author and communications strategist, signed a book deal with Random House Children’s Books, a division of Penguin Random House, in November 2024.Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreenAlana Hadid, a philanthropist, activist and older sister of models Bella and Gigi, and Jenan Matari, an author and communications strategist, signed a book deal with Random House Children’s Books, a division of Penguin Random House, in November 2024.Photograph: GettyPenguin Random HousePalestine book by Alana Hadid and Jenan Matari pulled from Random House before releaseAuthors withdraw book planned for young readers after disputes with editors over characterizations of 7 OctoberSam Levinin Los AngelesThu 15 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA book on Palestine for young readers was pulled atPenguin Random Housejust before its scheduled release, following editorial disputes between the publisher and the book’s Palestinian American authors over their account of Palestinian history.In November 2024, Random House Children’s Books, a division ofPenguinRandom House, signed the book deal with Alana Hadid, a philanthropist, activist and older sister of models Bella and Gigi, and Jenan Matari, an author and communications strategist. The book was promoted for release in September this year.The authors, both influential social media commentators, drafted a manuscript about the history ofPalestine, Israeli occupation, Palestinian resistance, and the diaspora, interwoven with references to their own families’ stories of displacement.But the writers withdrew their book after objecting to edits by Random House that they said sanitized and misrepresented their views, and which they said were introduced after they thought the book had been finalized. A Random House spokesperson said the process “followed our standard bookmaking procedures”, and that the publisher ultimately supported the authors’ decision to pull the book.Displacement and the Palestinian American Story would have been the eighth installment in Random House’s Race to the Truthseries, an ongoing collection of nonfiction books for youth ages 10 to 13. The books aimed to provide the “true story of American history”, written by members of marginalized groups telling the histories of their peoples. A co-creator of the project said she objected to the treatment of Displacement and would not be pursuing future installments in the series with the publisher.“It became clear that Penguin was never actually going to allow us just to write the book we wanted to write,” said Hadid. “It says a lot that they’re willing to tank an entire very powerful series that helps children learn history, just because of one book about Palestine.”View image in fullscreenAlana Hadid in 2025.Photograph: Edward Berthelot/Getty ImagesAccording to Hadid and Matari, who provided the Guardian with the draft manuscript and email excerpts of their communications with Random House, the authors and the publisher engaged in months of disagreements about language in the book, including a passage on the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks in southern Israel. The writers’ manuscript argued that people under “colonial domination” have the “right to resist”, but Random House urged them to incorporate arguments that the attacks that day violated international law. At an impasse, the authors withdrew their book in early September.The authors now plan torelease it through Interlink Books, a Palestinian-owned US publisher.Random House Children’s Books has other forthcoming books on Palestine, the spokesperson said, writing: “We remain committed to bringing the Palestinian perspective to young readers.” The spokesperson also said another Race to the Truth book remained on track for 2028 publication.The dispute over the book comes amid disproportionatescrutinyandcensorship of workby and on behalf ofPalestinians. The conflict also laid bare the wide gap between narratives around 7 October, one that could not be bridged in a book to be distributed by a mainstream publisher.“I believe it was a revolutionary book, which is why it was under so much scrutiny,” Matari said. “They continued to try to sanitize our history because they didn’t want to make certain communities uncomfortable. But decolonial history is supposed to make you uncomfortable.”‘No greater story to tell’The Race to the Truth series was conceived by Saira Rao and Regina Jackson, founders of Race2Dinner, a program launched in 2019 tofacilitate conversations with white womenabout racism. In 2020, Rao and Jackson sold a book called White Women to Penguin Random House, which became abestseller, then in 2021 sold the Race to the Truth children’s series to the publishing house. Random House has since publishedbooksin the series onslavery, the colonization of theWampanoagpeople, theexclusionof Chinese Americans,Mexican Americanhistory, and theforced assimilationof Indigenous youth.View image in fullscreenJenan Matari.Photograph: Courtesy of Jenan MatariAs the series progressed, Rao felt it was urgent to publish a Palestine installment: “There’s no greater story to tell right now. Palestine actually tells a story of all genocides, of all settler colonial violence.”After Random House greenlit the idea in summer of 2024, Rao brought on Matari and Hadid.The authors submitted their first draft of Displacement in July 2025. In the introduction, they wrote that the Palestinian story had long been missing from classrooms. “The deliberate erasure of our history has left generations of Palestinians struggling to explain not only where we come from but why nearly half of us are scattered around the world, including – as in our cases – in the United States,” the intro said.The book discussed the landscape and history of Palestine; the rise of Zionism; the Nakba, or catastrophe, of 1948 when more than 700,000 Palestinian people were expelled from their homes; their analysis of Israel as a “settler colony”; the relationship between the US and Israel; and life for Palestinians living under military occupation.They also documented their family histories. Hadid’s grandparents, they wrote, were expelled from Safed days after her father was born, becoming refugees in Syria. And relatives of Matari and her husband were displaced from Deir Yassin and Ein Karem after an April 1948 massacre claimed the lives of more than 100 Palestinians.“I just wanted children to see us as humans,” Hadid said.Disputes about 7 OctoberTensions arose on the project in June 2026 when, according to the authors, the book was distributed to reviewers and made available for preorder before Random House had shared a final version with the writers. When the authors received a copy, they said it included changes to a passage about 7 October made by Random House without their knowledge.In a chapter called The International Right to Armed Resistance, the authors cited a UN general assemblyresolutionthatsaidpeople under colonial domination are entitled to “the right to self-determination” and torestorethat right “by any means at their disposal”. The chapter also noted Hamas’s use of prisoner exchanges to free thousands of Palestinians imprisoned in Israel they called “effectively hostages of the state”. Referring to the 2011 exchange of captured Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit for more than 1,000 prisoners, they wrote: “This exchange was one of the most famous and showed Palestinians that resistance could bring real results.”On 7 October, the manuscript continued, Hamas fighters “crossed into Israel in a coordinated assault”. The authors said roughly 1,100 Israelis were killed, including 37 children, and said civilians and soldiers were taken captive “to be used in an exchange”.Their section on 7 October was brief, but argued that international law authorized Palestinian resistance “by any means necessary”, saying the attacks came after “decades of ignored suffering and repression”.“Palestinians, like other oppressed peoples before them, have demanded freedom in the face of overwhelming military power. What happened on October 7 was not the beginning of violence in this land – it was another moment in a long history of a people struggling to be free,” they wrote.The authors said they had, at Random House’s request, added details about the 7 October death toll, and they believed the language was finalized in May 2026. However, when they received an updated final copy of the book, they saw that a Random House editor had added a line about the 7 October attacks saying: “These actions were a violation of international law.”The authors objected to the insertion, emails show, saying it contradicted their analysis of international law. They claimed in an email it was also a violation of their contract to make changes without their approval. One Random House editor suggested in an email that without that line or something similar, “we will lose all credibility with our readers, including those who are open-minded about our perspective” and the book couldn’t be published.Back-and-forth negotiations surrounding the description of 7 October continued for weeks, emails show, with Random House’s head of publicity, legal department and children’s books president involved in discussions.In the meantime, Random House came back with other edits the authors found objectionable. In July, a senior Random House official suggested removing “Jewish” as a modifier in several places, including when the authors had referred to Zionist militias involved in the destruction of Palestinian villages during the Nakba as “Jewish gangs”. “Our concern is not accuracy, but whether the repetition adds necessary clarity,” the Random House official wrote.The authors responded that it was “shameful” for an editor to say accuracy was not the concern, prompting an editor to reply back: “Our editorial point was not about whether the word was accurate, but whether, given the context, repeating the [Jewish] modifier was necessary.”A Random House official again pressed the authors to expand on 7 October, writing in an email that the authors could add context along the lines of: “Some human rights organizations and commentators have described Hamas’s actions that day as violations of international law; others frame the legal and historical questions differently.”But the authors grew increasingly frustrated, writing in one email: “In a book about the history of slavery in the United States – neither of us can imagine a Black author being forced to condemn the slave rebellions or consider them a violation of international law.”In one email to their agent, Matari wrote, “It has become quite clear that Penguin is more focused and concerned with centering Jewish feelings over Palestinian life and lived experience.”Records show Random House repeatedly expressed their commitment to the book, with one official saying they were dedicated to publishing “a necessary and accessible book about the Palestinian American story for young readers, a perspective that remains far too rare in children’s nonfiction” and saying editors wanted to work in “good faith” to resolve issues.By August, Random House suggested keeping the author’s text as is, but adding a “publisher’s note” to the book with some of the suggested 7 October language and changing the age range to 14+. The publisher also said if the parties could not resolve their differences, the authors could take the book elsewhere and keep their advance.“Editorial discussion and revision are a standard part of the publishing process,” the Random House spokesperson said in an email. “We gave guidance to help ensure the intended readers for this book, ages 10 and up, had enough information to understand the subject matter and engage thoughtfully with the questions it raises, knowing that many readers would be coming to the subject matter for the first time.”The spokesperson said the company had made digital advance copies available to industry contacts, which were marked as “uncorrected” and not final, and that this process was halted after the authors expressed concerns. “We would not move forward with a book that the authors were not comfortable publishing,” the spokesperson said.‘No longer the book we wrote’In an interview, Matari said she felt it was unacceptable for Random House to publish a disclaimer that might contradict their writing. Termination, she said, seemed the only option: “It was no longer the book we wrote.”Matari was no stranger to backlash for her commentary on 7 October. Over the last year, severalscheduled book talksfor her debut children’s book, about a young Palestinian girl and her grandfather, were cancelled last-minute after people accused her of antisemitism, in part over social media posts describing the 7 October attacks as resistance against colonialism and declaring the US to be “under Zionist occupation”. She and a Jewish author recently sued the city of Los Angeles for free speech violations after the public library cancelled their planned joint book event. Matari has denied claims of antisemitism and defended her posts, saying she was “vehemently anti-Zionist”.View image in fullscreenSaira Rao.Photograph: Rebecca Stumpf/The GuardianHadid said they were not trying to minimize the harms of 7 October and had, at Random House’s request, been clear about the death toll. Their goal was to put the attacks into historical context. “I wasn’t going to publish this book with words I hadn’t written, where they were forcing us to tell the story from the perspective of the oppressors.”Rao, from the Race to the Truth series, said her relationship with Random House had been smooth before the conflicts over the Palestine book, with previous authors given significant leeway to write their stories without interference. Hadid and Matari’s experience was fundamentally different, Rao said: “You’ve got the entire company weighing in on this one little book.”The end of the series at Random House comes at a time when a wide range of industries and institutions are backtracking ondiversity, equity and inclusionefforts, raising fears about diminishing opportunities for people of color inacademia,publishing,entertainmentandmedia. The recent rise of book bans and open hostility to diverse works is further diminishing those opportunities, said Leyla Moushabeck, co-owner and longtime editor at Interlink, the publishing house taking on Hadid and Matari’s book.“As a second-generation Palestinian-American, it’s a book I wish I had had growing up,” Moushabeck said of the book, which Interlink plans to publish next year.Hadid added she was grateful their manuscript found a new home: “We hope that people read the book that Penguin didn’t want you to read.”Explore more on these topicsPenguin Random HousePalestinePenguinIsrael-Gaza warPublishingBella HadidGigi HadidnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wallace & Gromit maker Aardman falls short of return to profit | Aardman | The Guardian
description: Animation studio narrows annual loss to £1.1m amid ‘challenging market’ in children’s content
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Animation studio narrows annual loss to £1.1m amid ‘challenging market’ in children’s content
Content: The co-founders of Aardman Peter Lord (left) and David Sproxton alongside the Wallace & Gromit creator Nick Park (right) in August.Photograph: Ian West/PAView image in fullscreenThe co-founders of Aardman Peter Lord (left) and David Sproxton alongside the Wallace & Gromit creator Nick Park (right) in August.Photograph: Ian West/PAAardmanWallace & Gromit maker Aardman falls short of return to profitAnimation studio narrows annual loss to £1.1m amid ‘challenging market’ in children’s contentLauren AlmeidaThu 15 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 10.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDon’t break out the celebratory Wensleydale just yet.Aardman, the British animation studio behind the cheese-loving inventor Wallace and his beloved dog Gromit, has fallen short of a target to get back in the black, its accounts show.The employee-owned business was aiming to record a small profit in 2025 after two years of consecutive losses but was hit by production delays and a “challenging market” in children’s content.So although its revenues jumped 8% to £20.4m last year, it was in the red to the tune of £1.1m, albeit an improvement on the previous year’s £4.1m loss.Aardman, which also produces the popular Shaun the Sheep series, said the timing of some “significant” deals and weaker income in some parts of the business had hurt its bottom line.It will be hoping for a boost from new projects, such as arecently opened exhibition at Lightroom in Londonthat explores its 54-year history, as well as a third Shaun the Sheep film, which wasreleasedlast month.And the famously silent Gromit willsoon be getting a voice, with this month’s audiobook of his autobiography read by the actor Martin Freeman.In 2024 the studio launched a five-year business plan, which involved more investment in its intellectual property and cutting back costs.Since then it has enjoyed the success of Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl, which broke viewing records over Christmas in 2024 as the most watched animated film broadcast on British television since 2002.The film won two Baftas and received an Oscar nomination for best animated feature film.Aardman said in its annual accounts that it had undertaken a further strategic review in early 2026 as it looked for ways to manage inflationary cost pressures, which resulted in “several redundancies”.Its headcount for the 2025 financial year had already shrunk from 297 to 230 people, with permanent staff falling from 128 to 110.The studio also recognised artificial intelligence as a principal risk and uncertainty to its business. It wrote that AI and generative AI were “reshaping parts of the creative industries, creating opportunities to improve workflows and support innovation while also raising important legal, ethical and authorship issues”.It said it was vital this technology was developed and used responsibly and selectively, but only in ways that “support and celebrate human creativity and craft rather than replace it”.Peter Lord and David Sproxton co-founded the studio in the early 1970s in Bristol. They began animating as teenagers, selling their first short – starring a superhero called Aardman – to the BBC’s Vision On in 1972.They created Morph for the children’s programme Take Hart in 1977. The studio began appealing to adult audiences through Channel 4’s Conversation Pieces series, and its animators, including Nick Park, went on to make Wallace & Gromit.Aardman became employee-owned in 2018, with Lord and Sproxton transferring majority ownership to staff to safeguard the company’s independence. The pair wereknighted earlier this year.Explore more on these topicsAardmanAnnual resultsFilm industryTelevision industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Her royal heilness: Berlin show revisits the artist who turned the Queen into a Nazi | Art | The Guardian
description: The late Christoph Schlingensief was one of German art’s great provocateurs. Can his B-Movie horror aesthetics still shock us into thinking anew about media power, colonialism, and the far right?
Author: Hanno Hauenstein
Headline: The late Christoph Schlingensief was one of German art’s great provocateurs. Can his B-Movie horror aesthetics still shock us into thinking anew about media power, colonialism, and the far right?
Content: Art and politics … Christoph Schlingensief, The African Twin Towers, 2005.Photograph: © Estate of Christoph SchlingensiefView image in fullscreenArt and politics … Christoph Schlingensief, The African Twin Towers, 2005.Photograph: © Estate of Christoph SchlingensiefArtHer royal heilness: Berlin show revisits the artist who turned the Queen into a NaziThe late Christoph Schlingensief was one of German art’s great provocateurs. Can his B-Movie horror aesthetics still shock us into thinking anew about media power, colonialism, and the far right?Hanno HauensteinThu 15 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChristoph Schlingensief certainly knew how to provoke. “Fury at German play that shows Queen as a Nazi,” read the Sunday Express’s headline after Kaprow City first premiered at Berlin’s Volksbühne theatre in 2006. Drawing on the happenings of US performance artist Allan Kaprow, the play turned its attention to Diana, Princess of Wales’s death. In one scene, the then queen performs a Hitler salute. Another re-enacts the paparazzi chase that led to Diana’s fatal crash. Diana appears in bed beside two men with Down’s syndrome; and Camilla is pelted with animal blood. Schlingensief insisted the work was not meant as provocation but as an investigation into how Diana turned into a modern icon. But his art thrived on outrage, exposing the absurdity of societies that glorify their idols while consuming their lives as entertainment.Kaprow City is at the heart of a new Berlin show – It’s Not My Problem Anymore, Deal With Your Own Shit – that revisits the artist’s legacy. In the Gropius Bau’s grand neo-Renaissance atrium, visitors encounter remnants of the carousel-like rotating stage he called the “animatograph”. Looking at this installation today feels like a glimpse into Schlingensief’s mind: a messy collage of childhood memories, violent fantasies and royal glamour.View image in fullscreenMaking headlines … It’s Not My Problem Anymore, Deal With Your Own Shit, Gropius Bau.Photograph: © Estate of Christoph SchlingensiefThe Gropius Bau installed roughly half of Schlingensief’s original set on the very same spot where Joseph Beuys, a major influence, once exhibited his Stag Monuments. In Kaprow City, flickering black-and-white footage of a crucifixion plays beneath a slate board listing the stage’s contents, from “Diana Girl Ballet” to “exorcism”. In the original production, audiences were distributed across 18 tiny, wedge-shaped rooms, echoing Allan Kaprow’s 18Happenings in 6 Parts. Spectators witnessed only fragments of the action. Now, most of the stage’s interior is draped in plastic. Excerpts of videos from the play loop throughout the installation on old-fashioned TV screens.Enlarged tabloid headlines and articles are plastered across the walls behind it. Beside the Sunday Expressheadline, a German newspaper asks: “Will Diana’s sons stop Schlingensief?” After rumours that the royals might pursue legal action, Schlingensief had invited William and Harry to Frieze, where he planned to present an iteration of the project.“The combination of Lady Di, the speculation surrounding the circumstances of her death, and the general myth that grew around her fascinated Christoph,” says stage designer Aino Laberenz, Schlingensief’s widow who now manages his estate. For the Volksbühne production, Schlingensief cast Jenny Elvers, a German TV personality whose private life, like Diana’s, was a fixture of tabloids, between fascination and intense scrutiny. Laberenz cautions against viewing Kaprow City only through the lens of Diana. It belonged to a wider artistic universe in which theatre, film and art collided and overlapped with questions of media power and spectacle, she says.View image in fullscreen‘We’re playing Germany’: Schlingensief outside the Schauspielhaus Zürich ahead of his Hamlet performance in 2001Photograph: David Baltzer/© Estate of Christoph SchlingensiefSchlingensief, who died of lung cancer just shy of his 50th birthday in 2010, grew up in the shadow of New German Cinema and was deeply influenced by film-makers such as Rainer Werner Fassbinder. Like Fassbinder, he blurred the lines between art and politics. In The African Twin Towers, he took actors including Patti Smith, Irm Hermann and Robert Stadlober to Namibia to re-enact Wagnerian myths, confronting the legacy of Germany’s colonial genocide. Namibian actors also took part.Seen today, Schlingensief’s artistic vocabulary – messy B-movie horror, drag, disabled performers, a taste for the extreme – sits awkwardly with Namibia as a stage. Watching his actors improvise on Shark Island, the site of a former German concentration camp where Herero and Nama prisoners endured forced labour and starvation, feels uncomfortable. Not because the provocation is empty (it isn’t), but because one wonders whether the team fully grasped what they were doing. Namibia feels less like the subject of a reckoning with Germany’s colonial past than a backdrop for a German artist’s grand vision. At Gropius Bau, The African Twin Towers appears as a patchwork of sequences across 18 screens.Schlingensief’s work on the far right, however, remains strikingly relevant – not only because of the AfD’s rise in Germany, but also because of his hands-on confrontational approach to anti-immigrant politics. In his version of Hamlet, he brought former far-right extremists on to the stage at Schauspielhaus Zürich and later Berlin’s Volksbühne, where they re-enacted Shakespeare’s central murder scene amid far-right rock music and Nazi aesthetics. “We’re not playing Hamlet, we’re playing Germany,” reads a Schlingensief quote taped to the exhibition wall. It captures the artist’s insistence that art must confront society, rather than offer an escape.View image in fullscreen‘How much he is missed’ … Christoph Schlingensief, Church of Fear, 2003, part of It’s Not My Problem Anymore, Deal With Your Own Shit.Photograph: © Estate of Christoph SchlingensiefThe same attitude runs through Ausländer Raus! Schlingensiefs Container, his 2000 project in which asylum seekers lived under surveillance in a Big Brother-style container beside Vienna’s State Opera, while audiences voted on who should be deported first, two people a day. Conceived in response to the far-right FPÖ’s entry into Austria’s government, the project turned deportation – or, in the AfD’s words, “remigration” – into an eerie spectacle. It exposed European racism while implicating viewers in its public reproduction.Looking at these works today, one cannot help thinking of how far-right actors have learned to adopt such aesthetic spectacle as a political tool. The AfD’s AI video Remigration Hit from 2024, for instance, revels in humiliating migrant men herded on to planes by Aryan-looking pilots. Schlingensief’s work reads as a warning of how easily such cruelty becomes entertainment. And how readily the media help normalise it, from the tabloid frenzy surrounding Diana to the far right’s supremacist language of “remigration”.“I keep noticing in the commentary how much he is missed,” says Laberenz toward the end of our interview. “But I also like to say that it’s up to us, whether we work in the arts or not, not to hand responsibility over to someone else so that we no longer have to act.”Christoph Schlingensief: It’s Not My Problem Anymore, Deal With Your Own Shit is atGropius Bau, Berlin, until 17 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArtGermanyEuropeExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The world is falling apart’: Dominic Cooke plans boldly political first season at Almeida | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: London theatre’s new artistic director working with David Tennant and Caryl Churchill as he wrestles with Britain’s decline – and with smart glasses
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Exclusive: London theatre’s new artistic director working with David Tennant and Caryl Churchill as he wrestles with Britain’s decline – and with smart glasses
Content: Cooke said he also wanted to work more with young talent, as school drama cuts have dried up the pool of new directors.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenCooke said he also wanted to work more with young talent, as school drama cuts have dried up the pool of new directors.Photograph: AlamyTheatre‘The world is falling apart’: Dominic Cooke plans boldly political first season at AlmeidaExclusive: London theatre’s new artistic director working with David Tennant and Caryl Churchill as he wrestles with Britain’s decline – and with smart glassesHelena HortonThu 15 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 09.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA spate of highly political plays will feature in one of north London’s most storied theatres next season, as its new artistic director says the world “is falling apart”.An exploration of Britain’s decline featuring David Tennant and a searing series of new plays by Caryl Churchill are planned for Dominic Cooke’s first season at theAlmeida theatre.“It’s hard not to be political nowadays,” Cooke said of the programme. “I don’t believe in art telling people what to think but I do think that we should be putting situations on to stage, into culture, that aren’t being looked at. The world is falling apart and to not talk about that would be an abdication of responsibility.”The Almeida theatre has a coup in Dominic Cooke: this gifted director is also a proven talent spotter | Michael BillingtonRead moreCooke, who ran the Royal Court for several years, is a long-term friend of Tennant and will be directing him in a revival of John Osborne’s The Entertainer.“I am really excited about it,” he said. “I have known David since he was a drama student; I once stayed at his flat when I was doing a show in Edinburgh. I was so taken with his rigour and his intelligence.”He proposed the idea of putting on this play with Tennant: “I have been thinking about him doing this for a very long time. We are doing quite a radical repositioning of the play. It could really speak to our times; it deserves to be rescued. It has a lot about English identity and the empire. It’s all about that moment in the 50s when England viewed itself a second-rate power for the first time in its history.”Cooke said this was relevant to politics in the UK today: “We have this internalised memory of ourselves as this great nation. We are just one relatively big nation in world terms. There is this atmosphere of us trying to grapple with this change. Look at Brexit: that was about us ruling the waves, and obviously we aren’t any more.”Opening the season will be Three and a Bit, a collection of short plays by Churchill, who at 88 is “still as sharp as ever”, according to Cooke. “It’s thrilling; she is more than ever on the cutting edge, just as provocative, just as fascinating. She talks in Three and a Bit about being indifferent to suffering when it’s not on your doorstep. It arrests you and creeps up on you in a very unlikely way.”The play that changed my life: ‘Caryl Churchill’s Cloud 9 had us dancing in the aisles’Read moreThe Almeida will be joining other theatres, as well as cinemas and pubs, inbanning Meta’s new smart glasses. “They are ghastly, aren’t they? Because of the invasive nature of them, especially for women,” Cooke said. “For years people have been stopped from filming during a performance. Definitely we would crack down on them. The problem with the bloody things is they are hard to notice and crack down on.”Stars including Cate Blanchett, Rosamund Pike and Gillian Anderson have hit the news recently for telling audience members off for filming and being distracting during performances. “It is fair for theatres to want to control the use of phones, as people have the right to decide whether they want to be filmed or not,” Cooke said. “The concentration required to give a leading performance on stage is immense, and it is easy to feel distracted if a phone goes off and there is a camera in your face.”Another highlight of the season will be a production by the Almeida Young Company (ages 14-18), who will perform Angel to Olympus, an amalgamation myth by Flora Wilson Brown, directed by Takiyah Kamaria.Cooke wants to work more with young talent, after cuts to school drama programmes have dried up the pool of new directors. “It is a fascinating department in the theatre – they work with every single child in the borough. These things become more and more important when the arts are being reduced in education, they are being struck from the syllabus. It is so shortsighted,” he said.“One of the reasons I wanted the job is that I was concerned about the talent pipeline. We are trying to find ways through for emerging directors – we have a project coming down the line on that, which we will be talking more about soon. You only learn by doing, and you have to have the space to do that.”Explore more on these topicsTheatreDominic CookeDavid TennantAlmeida theatreShareReuse this content

title: South Park takes on looksmaxxing, aura-farming and influencer nonsense with grotesque glee | South Park | The Guardian
description: In the third episode of the latest season, the boys head into Sephora and eventually the Backrooms in a story that makes fun of app-mutated self-care
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: In the third episode of the latest season, the boys head into Sephora and eventually the Backrooms in a story that makes fun of app-mutated self-care
Content: It doesn’t feel like a betrayal to see South Park grappling with contemporary concepts like looksmaxxing and aura farming, writes Jesse Hassenger.Photograph: ParamountView image in fullscreenIt doesn’t feel like a betrayal to see South Park grappling with contemporary concepts like looksmaxxing and aura farming, writes Jesse Hassenger.Photograph: ParamountSouth ParkSouth Park takes on looksmaxxing, aura-farming and influencer nonsense with grotesque gleeIn the third episode of the latest season, the boys head into Sephora and eventually the Backrooms in a story that makes fun of app-mutated self-careJesse HassengerThu 15 Oct 2026 01.36 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 08.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrey Parker and Matt Stone have always been pretty upfront about howSouth Park, like all animated sitcoms from the past 35 years, lives in the shadow of The Simpsons. There are plenty of ways that The Simpsons, even in its more uneven recent seasons, still outshines South Park: greater depth of ensemble, stronger emotional moments, even in the sheer number of episodes.Something that South Park often does better, though, is react to contemporary social trends. Kyle, Stan, Cartman, Kenny and the rest are more or less the same age as Bart (and have been for decades); but The Simpsons has never been as adept at riffing on trends, tech and social issues as South Park, which has always been more immediate and responsive. Perhaps this is why it doesn’t feel like a betrayal to see the boys dealing with, say,looksmaxxingandaura farming, which is exactly what the third episode of South Park’s 29th season addresses.South Park has ​​AI datacentres​, sentient penises ​and a billionaire problem – in more ways than oneRead moreYou Like That On Your Face begins with Cartman breathlessly interrupting Kyle and Stan discussing Wendy’s mysterious desire for anti-ageing face cream with the news that Kyle’s toddler brother Ike is in danger of being “mogged” by another student. But Ike prevails in a livestreamed aura battle because he is now into looksmaxxing, the influencer-driven nonsense practice of using all means necessary to gain greater facial symmetry.As Stan later explains to his father, Randy, there are apps that will analyse and rate your appearance using AI and suggest products to improve your inevitably terrible score. Though Randy advises closing the app and simply eating well and exercising to take care of your body, he, too, is driven to assess his face on the app. Meanwhile, Ike faces a challenge from Chase Chadwick – the only person to ever get a perfect score from the Chadmaxx app.So where do all the tweens wind up at different points in the episode, in order to look their best? Sephora, of course, Parker and Stone riffing on the very real popularity of skin creams and beauty productsamong troublingly young children. Stan takes Wendy there for her birthday and encounters an old man who warns him that his granddaughter went in there six years ago, never to return. As Stan loses track of Wendy and wanders through the store, the familiar shelves and excited crowds drop away, the walls are increasingly yellow, the sights increasingly uncanny … and, whoops, Stan has enteredthe Backrooms.It’s an inspired juxtaposition – the capitalist graveyard depicted by the Backrooms with the trendy bustle of Sephora’s decidedly non-liminal space – suggesting (without anyone in the show ever saying so) that there may be less distance between the two than we realise and the dead-end nature of trend-chasing.Stan is able to escape the Sephora-Backrooms, freaked out but unscathed. Randy, however, comes back diminished to tween size, suddenly to scale with his son and the rest of the kids – the product of anti-ageing procedures working too well, apparently. He’s not the last character to visit Sephora; Kyle has given up attempting to intervene with Ike, so Cartman, never one to shrug off a meaningless totem of popularity, agrees to take the toddler there.When Stan and Kyle find out Cartman and Ike are in the Sephora-Backrooms (from Randy, who has now enrolled as a student atSouth Americaelementary), they rush to the rescue. Various Sephora workers offer various creams with the porny, suggestive phrase that gives the episode its title: “You like that on your face?” they insistently ask. The monstrous Sephora manager in the Backrooms takes it further, squirting lotion from a crotch-positioned bottle as she calls out the gross tagline.It’s part and parcel with South Park wanting to take things too far, and also kind of a shame; the blatant innuendo takes this episode from being kind of perfect for actual tweens in the midst of skincare routine trend-chasing back to, well, the TV-MA territory the show is known for – even though a younger audience may be the most likely to laugh in recognition of the episode’s absurdity. Then again, what are tweens more likely to seek out than something they’re not really supposed to watch? Maybe this is the best way to make fun of app-mutated self-care without seeming like cringe adults who don’t know what they’re talking about.The symbolism of a clueless adult barging into the weird realm of young-person trends emerges fully at the end of the episode, when a semi-drunk and still-childish Randy enters the aura battle between Ike and the supposedly “hot” Chase Chadwick (hilariously grotesque) and ends up “mogging” Chase by beating the ever-loving hell out of him. Problem … solved? Adults may not have the answers, but at least they can ruin everyone’s fun with a bloody mess.South Park is streaming on Paramount+ in the US, UK and Australia.Explore more on these topicsSouth ParkTelevisionAnimation on TVBeautyUS televisionTV comedyComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Crystal Lake review – Friday the 13th gets unnecessary expansion in gory and goofy series | US television | The Guardian
description: Linda Cardellini tries her best but this baffling attempt to add backstory to one of horror’s thinnest franchises is IP stretching at its most pointless
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Linda Cardellini tries her best but this baffling attempt to add backstory to one of horror’s thinnest franchises is IP stretching at its most pointless
Content: Linda Cardellini in Crystal Lake.Photograph: PEACOCK/Matt InfanteView image in fullscreenLinda Cardellini in Crystal Lake.Photograph: PEACOCK/Matt InfanteTV reviewUS televisionReviewCrystal Lake review – Friday the 13th gets unnecessary expansion in gory and goofy seriesLinda Cardellini tries her best but this baffling attempt to add backstory to one of horror’s thinnest franchises is IP stretching at its most pointlessBenjamin LeeThu 15 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 03.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe unending exhaustion of IP has forced us to ask questions we never really wanted or needed to ask. How did thePink Ladies in Greasecome tobethe Pink Ladies? What would happen if one of The Craft witcheshad a kid who wasalso a witch? Why is the yellow brick road thecolour of yellow? What is Linda Blairup to these days?VisionQuest review – Marvel’s latest TV show feels like it could have been made by a computerRead moreNo one or no thing ever really dies any more, something that has long been true in the world of slashers, where no amount of stabbing, shooting and exploding has stopped masked killers from killing again and again and again. Recent years have seen thetimeline of the Halloween franchise retooledso that Michael Myers could regain his head and restart his reign of terror, whileGhostface has resurfacedto stalk the younger relatives of his old frenemies. As Leatherface preparesan A24 comebackcourtesy of Obsession’s Curry Barker and dual Nightmare on Elm Street rebootssquare off, it’s time to return to Camp Crystal Lake to see what desperate rights-holders can do with Friday the 13th’s Jason Voorhees, the hockey mask-wearing giant who enjoys slicing and dicing horny youngsters.Given the success of the low-budget franchise (12 films since 1980 grossing almost $500m worldwide) and the killer’s still strong brand recognition, it’s surprising that we haven’t seen him since the middling 2009 remake (especially as quality has never been a preventive issue in the franchise). It’s partly down to a headache-inducing scramble over rights but also the difficulty of placing a killer as mechanically one-note as Jason in a horror genre that now places more importance on trauma over terror. Friday the 13th films were tiny-brained and thinly plotted excuses to make couples squeeze each other tighter in the dark, light on thought and heavy on blood. Some were better than others (1984’s The Final Chapter, which of course wasn’t the final chapter, being a notable high point), but the bar was low and the more a film-maker might add to the plate, the less it might feel like a Friday the 13th movie.Which brings us to Crystal Lake, an almost comically of-the-moment pitch for a 2026 return to the franchise. A schlocky sleepover slasher has now become an overstuffed eight-part streaming series exploring the backstory of Jason but mainly focused on the psychology of his murderous mother, Pamela, who was revealed to be the killer in the first film. What turned Pamela into a psychopath? Why was Jason able to survive his drowning? What exactlyarewe doing here?Pamela is a character who was in less than 15 minutes of a 46-year-old movie, best known since as a Halloween costume ora Scream gotcha question, more plot twist than person. But she’s now been turned into an ex-nightclub singer turned experimented-on Stepford Wife turned grieving mother turned avenging angel. It’s expansion for expansion’s sake in a show that isn’t as heinous as it could be, but more a passable answer to an LA conference room question that should never have been asked in the first place.In the lead, Linda Cardellini, fresh off an Emmy win, tries to bring some prestige to the pulp and almost succeeds. The violent hardening of her camp cook single mother, whose disfigured son accidentally dies in the cold open (far too soon for us to be emotionally invested), is only ever close to being tantalising because of how far she’s willing to go. But the tone of the show is far less surer than her at times ferociously compelling performance. Creator Brad Caleb Kane wills us to take the silliness seriously in moments as some vague commentary is made about the medical and societal treatment of women in the 70s before he leans into full-on, Syfy channel goofiness. To justify an entire series, he gives us flashbacks, a conspiracy, some romance, a spot of police corruption, a plucky journalist, a seance, a nefarious life coach and a shadowy corporation, an overbooked camp fit to burst. It’s Bates Motel but for a film without even a shred of the texture of Psycho and while meddling with a franchise as tinny as Friday the 13th is not exactly sacrilege, it’s just entirely pointless.It’s not that a TV series directly copying the stalk-and-slash formula of the films would have worked either (even an 80s attempt used Friday the 13th as a symbol of bad luck rather than a way to bring Jason to the small screen), but it’s just that a TV series maybe wasn’t the best idea in the first place. Horror stans might appreciate the fan service (and the staggeringly nasty gore) but for anyone else, the overcomplicated and underpowered Crystal Lake just doesn’t warrant the stay. Jason will inevitably be back (a new film is reportedly in the works) but, despite Cardellini’s best efforts, maybe it’s best to leave Pamela behind.Crystal Lake is available now on Peacock in the US, on Stan in Australia on 16 October and on Now in the UK on 19 OctoberExplore more on these topicsUS televisionTV reviewHorror (TV)TelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: can a breakup in a flatshare ever end well?  | Television | The Guardian

Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: It’s the final double bill of housing crisis romcom Break Clause. Plus, will the Traitors win their game of hide and seek? Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Road to nowhere? … Ben (Samuel Bottomley) and Lil (Lara Ricote) in Break Clause.Photograph: Kerry Spicer/Channel 4 / Vishal SharmaView image in fullscreenRoad to nowhere? … Ben (Samuel Bottomley) and Lil (Lara Ricote) in Break Clause.Photograph: Kerry Spicer/Channel 4 / Vishal SharmaTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: can a breakup in a flatshare ever end well?It’s the final double bill of housing crisis romcom Break Clause. Plus, will the Traitors win their game of hide and seek? Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson, Alexi Duggins andAli CatterallThu 15 Oct 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBreak Clause10.05pm, Channel 4Can a breakup in a flatshare end well? In the closing double bill, Ben (Samuel Bottomley) and Lil (Lara Ricote) are single and mingling – but they also find themselves back in each other’s arms, gallivanting around London … before reality hits again. With their six-month break clause in the lease coming up, they need to decide whether to get back together or move on for good.Hollie RichardsonThe Celebrity Traitors8pm, BBC OneMyha’la and Julie are banished, while Hannah is still – somehow – in the game. Does this mean that, after a rocky start with Richard E Grant, the traitors are starting to get good? Tonight we find out how the game of hide and seek turns out, and whether Leigh-Anne Pinnock’s shield means that no one gets murdered.HROur Tiny Islands8pm, Channel 4This series, looking at more than 400 small isles round the UK coast, visits a sheep farmer on Iona in the Hebrides with a unique wool product, and the Lundy Company, which allows residents of the Bristol Channel island to keep living there. Plus, a look at the gardening upkeep of a 3.8 hectare (9.5 acre) croft in North Uist – so brace for a bucolic watch that might inspire a digital detox.Alexi DugginsThe Yorkshire Vet8pm, Channel 5View image in fullscreenOld blue eyes … Frank Sinatra the cat is ready for his makeover.Photograph: Daisybeck StudiosPeter faces a desperate case when a newborn lamb arrives with a rare birth defect: “It hasn’t got a bottom.” Meanwhile, Shona treats Grace, a shire horse with a uterine infection; Rohin rescues an injured pheasant; and Julian and Lucy give Frank Sinatra, a ragdoll cat, a much-needed makeover: “What do you think about a mohawk?”Ali CatterallClassic Movies: The Story of a Matter of Life and Death8pm, Sky ArtsWith its tragically romantic opening scene – a second world war pilot chatting up a radio operator as his broken plane plummets – Powell and Pressburger’s strange, celestial wartime drama is a beloved classic. Here, critics gleefully dig into exactly why that is.HRAll Creatures Great and Small9.05pm, Channel 5Another testosterone-filled, action-packed episode of the veterinary period drama: Tristan has a bargain haircut from Josh for his final date with Charlotte before she heads off to New York. title: Sally Rooney’s stand on Palestine is brave and humane  | Sally Rooney | The Guardian
description: The Normal People author’s determination to support Palestine Action, even if it means that her books are withdrawn from sale in the UK makes a mockery of Britain’s terrorism laws
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The Normal People author’s determination to support Palestine Action, even if it means that her books are withdrawn from sale in the UK makes a mockery of Britain’s terrorism laws
Content: Sally Rooney … chose the thorniest possible path for this cause.Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSally Rooney … chose the thorniest possible path for this cause.Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The GuardianSally RooneySally Rooney’s stand on Palestine is brave and humaneZoe WilliamsThe Normal People author’s determination to support Palestine Action, even if it means that her books are withdrawn from sale in the UK, makes a mockery of Britain’s terrorism lawsThu 15 Oct 2026 06.56 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.34 EDTShareIt’s hard to think of a published author in living memory who risked arrest in the UK for their political beliefs, hard to think of one whose books could be published anywhere but here. Sally Rooney went into this debacle with her eyes open: she said last July that royalties from her books, and their BBC adaptations, would be used to supportPalestine Action.Rooney’s courage is not so much in risking imprisonment, since there is a fix for that, which is what she’s doing – avoiding the UK. Rather, she has chosen the thorniest possible path for this cause. Authors can write essays and sign letters in support of the Palestinian people; actors can voice it in interviews, musicians can say it from the stage, and there is always a cost to it, whether it’s in plain sight and they’ve been kicked off a global tour, or it’s behind closed doors and they are simply excluded from opportunities. But such actions, even if they logically suggest support for a proscribed organisation, don’t entail actively breaking the terrorism laws. Rooney had taken a financial hit anyway, by pledging support for Palestine Action with her royalties; but that’s a price at least you can count. The lost sales and opportunities that ripple out from being effectively both barred from and banned in the UK are innumerable.double quotation markRooney has never been an apolitical writer and now she has taken on the idea that caring about Gaza is somehow a crank’s life choiceYet, speaking as not-her-accountant, but as someone living in the culture she also inhabits and has made such an impact describing, the value of her stand is similarly hard to put a price on. Her authorial voice and body of work makes this intervention distinctive in its reach. She’s never been an apolitical author.Normal Peoplewas razor sharp on class,Conversations With Friendswasn’t shy of a Marxist analysis. But the work is also intimate, often domestic, I mean, the clue’s in the name – these were always normal people. It was from a reputation of delicately challenging but everyday subtlety that Rooney assumed her outrider position, and in so doing, took on the idea that caring about Gaza is somehow a crank’s life choice; insisted that it is a human response, as natural and quotidian, as passionate and important, as friendship.It also, come on – surely at some point we’re allowed to say this – makes an absolute mockery of the terrorism legislation thus applied. Nobody anywhere thinks Sally Rooney poses a danger to the British state, or any state, just as nobody anywhere thinksa 94-year-old human rights barristerwho was a friend of Ed Miliband’s late mother does. Keir Starmer, paradoxically, given that the two things in his favour were his caution and his legal hinterland, painted himself into an absurd corner, whereterrorism arrests went up between 2024 and 2025 from 250 to nearly 3,000. On demos where anyone crunched the numbers,more of them were over 80 than under 20.Sally Rooney says she can no longer sell books in UK due to Palestine Action supportRead moreThe history and particularity ofIrish solidarity with the Palestinian cause have been discussed a lot since the painful Ed Sheeran tour, in which the singer thought a support act could be quietly ditched over a pro-Palestine song,without losing his backing band – Beoga, founder members of Irish Artists for Palestine. More broadly, Ireland has a vibrant tradition of young women with no reason to think they have the right to opine on geopolitics sticking their oar in anyway.The Dunnes Stores strike of 1984kicked off when 21-year-old Mary Manning refused to handle some South African grapefruit, leading to her receiving only £21 a week in strike pay for two years and nine months. It reached its political crescendo less than three years later, when Ireland banned South African goods altogether in protest at apartheid. In between, though, in 1985, Desmond Tutu met Manning and her fellow strikers on his way to get the Nobel peace prize, extending as he did an invitation to visit him in South Africa – which they took him up on, only to be turned away at the border. There’s an instant echo, here, of a state showing its might at customs only to draw attention to its weakness; and of an author who, as well as that, is an ordinary citizen, whose forgone royalties are almost the least of the sacrifice, but are still a powerful emblem.This article was amended on 15 October 2026. An earlier version said that the Dunnes Stores strike of 1984 “cost [Mary Manning] £21 a week”. In fact, this was her weekly strike pay for the two years and nine months of industrial action.Explore more on these topicsSally RooneyProtestPalestine ActionActivismUK security and counter-terrorismPalestineMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Vermeer by Andrew Graham-Dixon audiobook review – a sharp and authoritative guide | Books | The Guardian
description: The author offers intriguing insights into the way this Dutch artist worked, including fresh perspectives on The Girl With the Pearl Earring
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The author offers intriguing insights into the way this Dutch artist worked, including fresh perspectives on The Girl With the Pearl Earring
Content: Vermeer's Girl With a Pearl Earring on display in Japan.Photograph: Jiji Press/EPAView image in fullscreenVermeer's Girl With a Pearl Earring on display in Japan.Photograph: Jiji Press/EPAAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewVermeer by Andrew Graham-Dixon audiobook review – a sharp and authoritative guideThe author offers intriguing insights into the way this Dutch artist worked, including fresh perspectives on The Girl With the Pearl EarringFiona SturgesThu 15 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the decades after the death of the Dutch artist Johannes Vermeer in 1675, few knew his name or work. He was so unknown that his paintings were sold with the forged signatures of more popular artists attached. All that changed in the mid-19th century, when his art was reassessed by French critics. Today Vermeer is one of the most admired painters in the world, although, says art historian Andrew Graham-Dixon, he has “proved stubbornly resistant to interpretation”.Vermeer: A Life Lost and Found, Graham-Dixon’s biography which was six years in the writing, endeavours to answer some unresolved questions, among them: what was Vermeer’s life like? Why did he paint the way he did? What was the intent behind his paintings, of which only 36 exist? Unlike the Dutch genre painters of his time, the Delft-born Vermeer painted solemn yet luminous works featuring women in domestic settings and engaged in activities such as reading, writing, playing music or pouring milk. His ability to render light, and its softening effect on rooms and people, was unparalleled.Graham-Dixon is the book’s narrator and his reading is sharp, authoritative and animated. As well as conjuring the world Vermeer inhabited and theorising about his relationship with his patrons, the author offers an intriguing new perspective – admittedly one that is impossible to prove – on the identity of the figure in The Girl With the Pearl Earring.Anyone doubting whether audio is the best medium to explore the life and work of a Dutch master will be pleased to find an attached file with the audiobook containing copious colour plates of Vermeer’s paintings.Available via Penguin, 15hr 1minFurther listeningKids, Wait Till You Hear This!Liza Minnelli, Hodder & Stoughton, 17hr 55minThe Cabaret star reads her uproarious and ferociously candid memoir, in which she reflects on her tumultuous love life, her relationship with her mother, Judy Garland, her struggles with alcohol and drug addiction and professional highs and lows.Good Good LovingYvvette Edwards,Little Brown, 7hr 47minSara Powell narrates this family saga about a British-Caribbean family spanning five decades. It opens with Ellen, the elderly matriarch, lying on a hospital bed waiting for the end while her family discuss her many shortcomings.Explore more on these topicsBooksAudiobook of the weekPaintingArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Floating World by Ben Eastham review – a compelling debut of art’s relation to money and power | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Following the death of his wife, a critic-teacher takes a job with an art-washing multinational, in a cinematic novel that is full of ideas
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Following the death of his wife, a critic-teacher takes a job with an art-washing multinational, in a cinematic novel that is full of ideas
Content: Slice of the art market … the National Museum of Qatar in Doha.Photograph: Patrick Baz/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSlice of the art market … the National Museum of Qatar in Doha.Photograph: Patrick Baz/AFP/Getty ImagesBook of the dayFictionReviewThe Floating World by Ben Eastham review – a compelling debut of art’s relation to money and powerFollowing the death of his wife, a critic-teacher takes a job with an art-washing multinational, in a cinematic novel that is full of ideasIan MaleneyThu 15 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 03.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the end of a night in a London pub, after last orders have been called, three friends are joking about what role they’d serve on a remote desert island, with no one but their fellow plane crash survivors for company. When one of them, an art critic turned reluctant schoolteacher, says that he would become an artist, he is, naturally, mocked. His friend Sybil, who actually is a painter, casts herself more sensibly as a demigod-queen of the island and employs her newly creative companion to “certify her glory”. “That’s what artists are for,” she says, “I pay you in fermented coconut water and you tell yourself you’re free and drink yourself to death.”This is about as clear a statement as one could wish for regarding the position of contemporary art as it relates to power: the boot of the latter is placed firmly on the former’s throat. This relationship is the central theme of The Floating World, Ben Eastham’s debut novel, which is narrated by the somewhat hapless and unnamed critic-teacher. And what has led to this existential pub conversation is an unexpected opportunity: following the death of the narrator’s wife in an unnamed war zone, he has been offered a job with the Morel Foundation, an art-washing spin-off of an arms-manufacturing multinational which extracts profit from all corners of a wartorn world while its cultural wing props up the ego of its eponymous overlord CEO.double quotation markIt's to its great credit that the novel's political awareness is more than stage‑dressing; it's the real heart of the bookThe narrator is unsure about taking up a position he knows to be morally indefensible, but which pays pretty well. Should he accept the nine-month contract – “helping with research, writing the press releases, editing the publications” – he would move from London to a tiny Greek island, where Morel is building “The Floating World”, a techno-utopian settlement inside a giant dome. A spectacular artistic event is planned to celebrate the official opening of what another of the narrator’s friends calls “literallya doomsday bunker for billionaires”. Is this really something he wants to be part of?Eastham knows this artistic milieu inside out. As a co-founder of the visual arts and literature magazine White Review and a busy and perceptive critic, Eastham has spent many years at the vanguard of contemporary art and literature. As a curator and writer, he has witnessed first-hand the tightening bonds between a globalised art market and international finance, from the widespread sponsorship of oil and opiate sellers to the geopolitical game-playing of projects like the Louvre Abu Dhabi, not to mention the use of artworks for money laundering, tax breaks and other kinds of financial engineering. Eastham threads examples of this interdependence throughout the book; sometimes as a nod to the knowing, but often more directly, as when a visit to a London museum is interrupted by a young woman throwing red paint at one of the paintings, screaming, “This is happening, open your eyes!”The narrator takes the job. He lands first in Athens, where he is welcomed by graffiti decrying the spread of short-term rentals for tourists, written deliberately in English – it is just about the only sign he can understand. Greece is the ideal setting for this book because there is arguably no place in Europe where it is easier to witness the contradictions of a world in which capital moves freely but people do not. In Athens, the most destitute struggle in statelessness and poverty, with the Acropolis as a backdrop. On the islands, victims of war, genocide, exploitation and climate catastrophe are airbrushed out of the escapist fantasies of the rich.It is to the novel’s immense credit that it manages to make this political awareness more than dutiful stage‑dressing; it is the real heart of the book. Eastham attempts an ambitious balancing act: on one side, the cynical gamesmanship of high-end contemporary art, and on the other, the emotional inner life of a man haunted by the memory of his deceased wife. The story becomes increasingly mysterious and action-packed, and it becomes inevitable that the two strands will be integrated through a conclusive narrative denouement. The form demands, and Eastham obliges with a blurry, dream-like conflagration of grief, panic and revenge. It’s all very cinematic, and neatly done – too neat, maybe, in the end. The Floating World is a book full of ideas and curiosity, but for all its well earned disillusion with the art world, it remains surprisingly sentimental.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Floating World by Ben Eastham is published by Fitzcarraldo (£14.99).
