title: Street Fighter review – nostalgia only goes so far in junky fighting game movie | Action and adventure films | The Guardian
description: There are brief, simple pleasures in the inevitable new big screen take on the classic game but like the recent Mortal Kombat movies, it’s a largely incoherent mess
Author: Radheyan Simonpillai
Headline: There are brief, simple pleasures in the inevitable new big screen take on the classic game but like the recent Mortal Kombat movies, it’s a largely incoherent mess
Content: Andrew Koji and Noah Centineo in Street Fighter.Photograph: Mark Rogers/Paramount Pictures, Capcom and LegendaryView image in fullscreenAndrew Koji and Noah Centineo in Street Fighter.Photograph: Mark Rogers/Paramount Pictures, Capcom and LegendaryAction and adventure filmsReviewStreet Fighter review – nostalgia only goes so far in junky fighting game movieThere are brief, simple pleasures in the inevitable new big screen take on the classic game but like the recent Mortal Kombat movies, it’s a largely incoherent messRadheyan SimonpillaiThu 15 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe just hadResident Evil, Zach Cregger’s giddy, nasty, devilishly fun spin on Capcom’s popular zombie franchise. It gave us renewed hope (after Sonic the Hedgehog, The Last of Us and Fallout) that video game adaptations could be good, actually.But now here comes Street Fighter, a garish and incoherent mess that amuses in fits and starts but barely improves on the Mortal Kombat movies before it, crushing those hopes in its atomic suplex.Whalefall review – slimy survival thriller traps us in a whale and struggles to make it digestibleRead moreFans certainly won’t mind. They’ve kept the box office’s life bar in the green for these one-on-one fighter adaptations going all the way back to the disastrous 1994 Street Fighter movie starring Jean-Claude Van Damme andhis $10,000-a-week coke problem. They’ll happily tolerate how the new Street Fighter, like those Mortal Kombat movies, can barely string together a cohesive plot, which has clearly been pencilled in as an afterthought between rounds of combat in yet another tournament-style narrative. None of that will matter because they’re just here for the dopamine hits by way of nostalgia.To that end, the movie exhaustively rolls out all the iconic characters and moves from the games – like Sumo warrior E Honda’s hundred-hand slap or military bro Guile’s flash kick – not to mention some at-times striking anime flashback sequences and a bevy of pop culture ephemera from its early-90s setting. Grainy, UHF quality MTV video segments show Ken (Noah Centineo) to be a self-destructive New Kids on the Block-era celebrity party boy with flashy blond curls, while the needle drops bring back bygone hits like MC Hammer’s 2 Legit 2 Quit and Montell Jordan’s This Is How We Do It.It’s all about keeping us pampered in those fond memories from our pubescent childhoods, including bits that bring back the way us preteen boys ogled the 16-bit version of hypersexualized Chun-Li. She’s played in the movie by the lively and commanding Callina Liang, who enters the frame thighs first and unfortunately plays the only character tasked with a gratuitous slow-motion shower scene.Liang doesn’t let that stuff drag down her performance, which is formidable, while her physicality during fight scenes is genuinely impressive. She’s one of the handful who bring some modest pleasures to the overcrowded mess. WWE wrestler Cody Rhodes, wearing a cartoonish trapezoid blond wig as Guile, is genuinely funny in the way he barks pleasantries and threats in equal measure. Indian movie star Vidyut Jammwal, who is trained in the ancient martial art Kalaripayattu, brings captivating authenticity and hypnotic movements to his all-too-brief scenes as yoga priest Dhalsim. Even controversial comic and manosphere podcaster Andrew Schulz gives a convincing performance worthy of an essay, playing Ken’s manager, who capitalizes on his bro’s brawn while coddling his wounded ego.But the likable performances get buried in a movie that often feels like it was made on a six-button control pad. Street Fighter is a barrage of character introductions and story arcs lifted from the games and animated spin-offs, colliding into one another in a way that makes a relatively linear plot (it’s a freakin’ fight tournament!) confusing. Did Vega edit this with his Wolverine-like claw hands?The movie’s most amusing fight arrives early, with Ken and Ryu (Andrew Koji) reunited in a hotel room after a years-long fallout, lured back together for a world championship tournament that the movie’s villain M Bison organized for nefarious purposes. Ken furiously takes wild swings at Ryu. Flying kicks miss the mark. Roundhouses hit nothing but air. Ryu quickly and calmly out-maneuvers, blocking with a pillow and then hilariously slipping the pillow below Ken’s head to catch his wipeout, or tiptoeing away from Ken while planted in a sofa seat. It’s a standout scene that really does feel like it belongs to another, smarter movie.Elsewhere, during a matchup between Ken and boxer Balrog (played by rapper 50 Cent), Sakurai learns the right lessons from Martin Scorsese’s Raging Bull, quick cutting between flashy hits and slow-motion impacts, the sloppy mix of blood and drool flying from Ken’s mouth hanging in the air long enough to appreciate its viscosity.And then there’s Liang’s Chun-Li, whose legwork delivers spectacular action, while her character tends to be the one dragging others down to earth with quick, frank, intermittently funny verbal jabs. She’s the grounded one, standing 10 toes down in purpose and principle. Whenever Ken or Ryu start emoting or waxing philosophical like Steven Seagal or Van Damme in those movies that inspire Street Fighter, Liang’s Chun-Li calls out in the most basic terms how stupid they sound.There’s several knowing winks at the fans like this, guarding against criticism by owning up to how silly this all is, which would land better if the movie ever rose above the stuff it’s making fun of. Instead, Street Fighter is satisfied punching down on itself, and everything that’s cringe about the 90s, while happily being stuck there, in the past, so it could pretend that this is as good as it gets for video game adaptations.We know better.Street Fighter is out in Australian cinemas now and in the UK and US on 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsAction and adventure filmsGamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘To succeed meant to leave’: inside the jolting film about Brummie estate kids knocked flying by demolition | Movies | The Guardian
description: The novel had no hero, no dialogue and little action. So how was I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning turned into such a funny, rousing and acclaimed film? Director Clio Barnard reveals all
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: The novel had no hero, no dialogue and little action. So how was I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning turned into such a funny, rousing and acclaimed film? Director Clio Barnard reveals all
Content: ‘You end up as ghosts’ … Anthony Boyle, Joe Cole, Daryl McCormack, Jay Lycurgo and Lola Petticrew in I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning.Photograph: Chris HarrisView image in fullscreen‘You end up as ghosts’ … Anthony Boyle, Joe Cole, Daryl McCormack, Jay Lycurgo and Lola Petticrew in I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning.Photograph: Chris HarrisMoviesInterview‘To succeed meant to leave’: inside the jolting film about Brummie estate kids knocked flying by demolitionXan BrooksThe novel had no hero, no dialogue and little action. So how was I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning turned into such a funny, rousing and acclaimed film? Director Clio Barnard reveals allThu 15 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a kid in 90sBirmingham, Keiran Goddard would gather with his friends to watch the tower blocks coming down. That’s what passed for entertainment back then. Controlled explosions, collapsing buildings. The demolition of the city’s postwar council estates marked the end of one story and the start of another. It was a dust-blown display of regeneration and progress. The housing that replaced it would be an improvement. The people of east Birmingham would move on to better lives.Goddard, specifically, moved on to study English at Oxford University. He now lives in London and writes books for a living. Physically, he has left his home town far behind. Emotionally and spiritually, not so much. “So I feel quite splintered,” he says. “I’m not sure anyone ever really leaves the world they grew up in.”double quotation mark‘Work hard, rise out of your class – that was the story’Goddard’sBirmingham-set second novelhas just been made into a film. Enda Walsh wrote the script; Clio Barnard called the shots. Set in and around an anonymous housing estate, I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning is a jolting, stirring ensemble drama in which a tower block’s demolition serves as a kind of societal big bang, spinning five childhood friends into a fraught adulthood.When writing the book, Goddard identified with the character of Patrick, the idealistic graduate turned zero hours delivery driver who argues that decent housing is a basic human right, not a capital asset. But he’s also like Rian, the group’s breakout star, who made a killing on the stock market and bought a sterile London flat. Rian is the chief investor behind a new apartment complex that is to be built on the bones of the old estate. The film shows it rising in time-lapse leaps and bounds, just as historic strains set to work on Rian’s close-knit gang of mates.View image in fullscreen‘Joy in itself can be its own positive protest’ … Clio Barnard.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/the ObserverThe story scaffold may be simple, yet the drama that follows is anything but. It’s nuanced, thorny and possibly irresolvable, with no easy answers or obvious hero to root for. Goddard wrote the book as a series of interior monologues then delivered it to his agent and editor in a spirit of wild optimism. “I said, ‘You know, I think it’s got some cinematic potential.’ And both of them replied, saying, ‘There’s no dialogue and not much happens. It’s got the least cinematic potential of anything that we’ve seen.’”I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning by Keiran Goddard review – growing up and apartRead moreThe film was a challenge, Barnard admits. It’s about the pull of the past and the sharp edge of the present, stitching an intimate human story against the broader social canvas. “It feels to me that there is an equality in this group of friends,” the director says. “And that the antagonist is the system, which is a hard thing to represent.” She was fired up, however, by its brand of political rage and its fine-grained depiction of an embattled working-class community. “Also, it made me laugh,” she adds. Shared jokes are the glue of all successful friendship groups. Rian’s mates mock his lifestyle – his posh girlfriend and big fridge – but they are ruefully, lovingly pleased for him, too.Barnard has always been drawn to the margins of the UK. She likes outsiders, pariahs, survivors and scamps. She made an eye-catching debut with 2010’sThe Arbor, a brilliant lip-synced documentary about the Bradford-born playwright Andrea Dunbar, who died of a brain haemorrhage at the age of 29.The Selfish Giantwas arguably harsher still: a devastating coming-of-age drama, foraging for scrap metal on the tatty fringes of town. One hesitates to say that she has since lightened up. All the same, 2021’sAli & Ava– an interracial love story, as tender as a bruise – and I See Buildings at least come with an air of hard-won optimism.“I think that’s been a conscious choice,” she says. “With Ali & Ava, I wanted the audience to leave with the feeling that they were able to act. And what I got from the group of people in this film was a massive amount of compassion and hope. I see a lot of Keiran in [the character of] Patrick. And Patrick’s a hopeful person. He believes that political change is still possible.”The world has now slipped seriously out of whack, she admits. “Just look at the protests in France at the moment. There’s an economic imbalance everywhere. It’s hard to find a regular income and a roof over your head, especially for young people. But hope in itself can be an active resistance. Joy in itself can be its own positive protest.”View image in fullscreenTender as a bruise … Adeel Akhtar and Claire Rushbrook in Ali & Ava.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyAs for the film industry, that’s arguably out of whack, too. I See Buildings lands in the UK fresh from a triumphant unveiling at the Cannes film festival. The international critics adored it. The Guardian’s ownPeter Bradshaw gave it a five-star review. But Barnard’s film might also prove to be among the last of a dying breed. It’s a blast of impassioned old-school social realism, folded in amid a glut of studio sequels and mythic heroes’ journeys, crying out to an audience that may no longer exist.I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning review – sweet, sad portrait of gen Z discontent and disillusionRead moreGoddard begs to differ. Like Patrick, he has hope; he puts his faith in the people. “We’ve seen it in publishing where the types of issues – the economic precarity – that traditionally affected only working-class communities are creeping more into middle-class society,” he says. “That means there’s a greater middle-class appetite for these kinds of stories. ‘Oh, you know that thing you’ve been moaning about for years? Well, it’s happening to me now as well.’” On the most basic level, he adds, the maths doesn’t add up. “The fact that the lives that are most frequently lived are the ones that are least frequently depicted. Economically, that’s stupid. You can’t simultaneously hold the view that people want to relate to stories and that the stories about the most common lives just aren’t viable. Those two things cannot be true. They can’t coexist.”Probably every human life is one of explosions and upheaval, and it can take a while for the dust to settle. Nowadays, Goddard has a clearer view of who he is and where he came from. He is a product, he says, of Blair-era social mobility: the beneficiary of a fleeting, fitful period of wealth redistribution. He was told that if he worked hard and behaved he might one day, God willing, rise out of his class. “That was always the story,” he says. “To succeed meant to leave.”In I See Buildings, Rian (played by Peaky Blinders star Joe Cole) winds up as a square peg in his fancy London apartment, pining for the streets, pubs and friends that he has left behind. Goddard can relate. “I’ve been very lucky. I’m not the victim here. As far as there is a right side of the equation to be on, I’m on it. The structures that enabled me to be here no longer exist. If you ran my life again now, it wouldn’t be the same. But yes, I think it does cause problems. You’re never truly accepted, and you can never properly go home. So you end up as a ghost, haunting the edges of two lives.”A film of his book could have been a disaster, he knows. “There are a number of different flavours of wrong,” he says. It might have wound up as poverty porn, or an earnest slab of liberal doggerel. It might have involved flat caps and misery, or poured out eight pints of mindless, bleary-eyed hedonism. Instead, he thinks that Walsh and Barnard have improved on his work. They’ve made the tale funnier, more rousing and hopeful.Best of all, Barnard filmed it on the streets of Birmingham. Goddard’s brother Tom helped integrate the crew with the community. The Crown social club served as the chief base of operations, where an open casting call drew as many as 800 local people. In a traditional story arc, the wayfaring hero eventually returns home. Odysseus arrives at Ithaca. Dorothy wakes up in her cosy Kansas farmhouse. The social mobility kids, Goddard feels, have been denied their third act. It’s the price they must pay for all the advances they’ve made. “But there was something very moving about going through this whole journey and literally returning to the estate I grew up on,” he says. “That was beyond special. That doesn’t normally happen. It’s as though, out of nowhere, I’ve been gifted the rare opportunity to close the circle and go home.”I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning is in cinemas on 4 DecemberThis article was amended on 15 October 2026. An earlier version said that Odysseus arrived at “Icarus”; that should have said Ithaca.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsFilm adaptationsPovertyClio BarnardBirminghamEnda WalshfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rebellion review – story of Bradford 12 revisits Britain’s ugly racist past | Movies | The Guardian
description: Ken Fero and Tariq Mehmood’s documentary recalls the fight against racism in 1980s Britain – even if its account of solidarity has a notable omission
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Ken Fero and Tariq Mehmood’s documentary recalls the fight against racism in 1980s Britain – even if its account of solidarity has a notable omission
Content: Shocking … some of the Bradford 12 in 1982.Photograph: Migrant Media/Ishaq KaziView image in fullscreenShocking … some of the Bradford 12 in 1982.Photograph: Migrant Media/Ishaq KaziMoviesReviewRebellion review – story of Bradford 12 revisits Britain’s ugly racist pastKen Fero and Tariq Mehmood’s documentary recalls the fight against racism in 1980s Britain – even if its account of solidarity has a notable omissionPeter BradshawThu 15 Oct 2026 06.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 06.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis fierce film from socialist film-makers Ken Fero and Tariq Mehmood gives us the story and the context of theBradford12. Twelve south Asian members of the United Black Youth League in 1981 were arrested on a charge of conspiracy to cause explosions for possessing dozens of molotov cocktails – milk bottles filled with petrol, with a rag through the lid – allegedly for throwing at the police. To the intense irritation of the British authorities, a mixed-race jury acquitted them, accepting their argument that it was in self-defence (and that the items themselves were closer to fireworks than bombs), because black and Asian communities were routinely and systematically attacked by skinheads and racists whose activities were shrugged at by the powers that be.It is a reminder of a particularly ugly, squalid, bigoted and mediocre era in British public life, when Margaret Thatcher, just before becoming prime minister, tried to siphon off some of the far-right National Front’s political energy by declaring that people felt “swamped” by immigrants, the most earsplittingly loud dog whistle in Tory history. It was also the era whenanti-racist protester Blair Peachwas killed by the Met’s yet-to-be-disbanded special patrol group, when thestill-unsolved New Cross firein London took the lives of 13 young black people, when thesouth Asian woman Anwar Dittawas subject to a spitefully obstructive move from the Home Office to prevent her bringing her children into the UK – supposedly because they weren’t really hers, though a DNA test finally proved her right. Perhaps most of all, it was an era when the witness-box testimony of uniformed police officers was increasingly seen as almost valueless in these cases; the film also reminds us how culpably lackadaisical and incompetent the Yorkshire police were in catching the serial killer Peter Sutcliffe.Rebellion is concerned with giving us a larger picture of liberationist politics, citing Frantz Fanon and bringing in Palestinian, South African, African American and Northern Irish voices. Here, however, I have one criticism: it is a shame, given the avowed importance of solidarity, that no interviewee can find it in their heart to say the word “antisemitism” – especially as the film uses a good deal of footage of the National Front, which had very open opinions about, and regularly attacked, Jews. It is clear that racism was something that was in the air then, along with casual misogyny and contempt for working people. Perhaps people conceal it better these days, but it’s still a shock to remember the sheer heavy weather of prejudice in those days, and to be reminded of those who stood up against it in court.Rebellion screened at theLondon film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsRaceLondon film festivalFestivalsFilm criticismPolicereviewsShareReuse this content

title: By Design review – Juliette Lewis turns into a chair in hypnotic Lynchian drama | Movies | The Guardian
description: A musician becomes obsessed with the haunted seat, but the potentially hilarious premise sleepwalks its way to an unsatisfying conclusion
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: A musician becomes obsessed with the haunted seat, but the potentially hilarious premise sleepwalks its way to an unsatisfying conclusion
Content: Glued to your seat … By Design.Photograph: Courtesy of Bulldog Film DistributionView image in fullscreenGlued to your seat … By Design.Photograph: Courtesy of Bulldog Film DistributionMoviesReviewBy Design review – Juliette Lewis turns into a chair in hypnotic Lynchian dramaA musician becomes obsessed with the haunted seat, but the potentially hilarious premise sleepwalks its way to an unsatisfying conclusionPeter BradshawThu 15 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe indie indulgences of US film-maker Amanda Kramer – which often contain big names making small appearances – are such a puzzle; sometimes they work, sometimes they don’t. I enjoyedher weird reverie about an imaginary 80s TV special, called Give Me Pity!, but not so muchthe 1950s-camp daydream Please Baby Please, with Andrea Riseborough. Now she gives us a film with a toweringly strange and potentially hilarious premise, on which the result does not in any way deliver. Yet there are moments of interest in the dreamy Lynchian drift that causes Kramer’s films to float away from the audience.By Design is an all but unbearable absurdist drama. The actors deliver halting dialogue as if in a hypnotic trance, paralysed by the film’s heavy conceit:Juliette Lewisplays a depressed single woman who turns into a chair. The scene seems set for some entertaining hijinks with visual effects, in which Lewis and the chair merge. But no – not really. What in fact happens is that Lewis’s own body is supposedly robbed of its animating identity or spirit, which migrates into the chair while she becomes catatonic, a body flopped down on the bed. The chair itself doesn’t look or behave in any way differently.Mamoudou Athie, doing his considerable best, plays a musician whose girlfriend buys him this haunted chair as a kind of guilt offering for walking out on him, and he becomes obsessed with it – although the comic or erotic potential of this transgressive idea is entirely neglected. The chair’s designer (a gamey cameo for thenow late Udo Kier) declares there is something strange about it but he can’t decide what it is. And so the film sleepwalks its way to a conclusion as unsatisfying as everything that has gone before. Someone somewhere should give Lewis a decent role.By Design is in UK cinemas from 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsJuliette LewisreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Faust review – FW Murnau’s silent masterpiece is a devilishly dazzling vision | Movies | The Guardian
description: The 1926 film of Goethe’s tragic tale of a man who sells his soul to the devil remains a spectacular feat of German expressionism
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The 1926 film of Goethe’s tragic tale of a man who sells his soul to the devil remains a spectacular feat of German expressionism
Content: World of knowledge … Gösta Ekman as Faust.Photograph: Courtesy of MubiView image in fullscreenWorld of knowledge … Gösta Ekman as Faust.Photograph: Courtesy of MubiMoviesReviewFaust review – FW Murnau’s silent masterpiece is a devilishly dazzling visionThe 1926 film of Goethe’s tragic tale of a man who sells his soul to the devil remains a spectacular feat of German expressionismPeter BradshawThu 15 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe centenary of FW Murnau’s silent fantasy-melodrama from 1926 is the occasion to ponder this mysterious film, taken from Goethe’s 19th-century depiction of the alchemist and natural philosopher who sells his soul to the devil but, in a very high-minded climax of German romanticism, is redeemed by love. (Not love of God precisely, but love of a good woman; the word “Liebe” finally appears at the centre of Murnau’s radiating vision of concentric circles conjured by the heavens, which annul his debt to the Evil One.) It is therefore very different from Christopher Marlowe’s scarier and more unforgiving account of Doctor Faustus.Murnau’s Faust is (obviously) concerned with and animated by evil, and there are echoes ofhis Nosferatu, made four years previously. In this film, Faust, having struck his bargain on a provisional 24-hour basis with Mephisto, finds that he is scared of a crucifix, like a vampire. It is also very much a film of Weimar Germany with its mad energy and streaks of garish satire and black comedy; the book-burning scene in which Faust immolates all his necromancy volumes, along with the Bible, is one which resonated with later events. (Perhaps it indirectly inspiredKlaus Mann’s novel Mephisto, later to be filmed by István Szabó.)Gösta Ekman plays Faust, ancient and grey-haired like an Old Testament prophet (or like God himself), and the veteran stager Emil Jannings (who, two years later, made Hollywood history by winning the first best actor Oscar) is the grinning, gurning Mephisto who makes a celestial wager that he can corrupt a decent man. This, of course, is Faust, who is wretched at the plague and devastation everywhere about and despairingly throws his learned books in the fire, but is then captivated by a charred page which tells of how to sell your soul at a distant crossroads. (Did this start the tradition carried on by bluesman Robert Johnson, who reputedly did something similar?)Mephisto offers him whatever he wants, including a “bacchanal” or orgy, and gives him an opportunity to dally with the Duchess of Parma, “the most beautiful woman in Italy”. But Faust ultimately wants to go back to his home village as the young man he once was, and there falls in love with comely innocent Gretchen (Camilla Horn), while Mephisto, that capering lord of misrule, has knockabout high-jinks with Gretchen’s blowsy Aunt Marthe (Yvette Guilbert). It is to lead to horror, with Gretchen sentenced to be burned at the stake for murdering the child she conceived with Faust, who is in turn wanted for killing Gretchen’s outraged brother Valentin (William Dieterle, himself to become an Oscar-winning Hollywood director) in a duel.The ambition, scale and drive of Faust are obvious: there is some wonderful model work for the landscape and cityscape that Faust and Mephisto look down on, flying above. And the still, painterly image of Mephisto as a vast evil angel, brooding over the city like a gigantic cloud, shrouding it in his black wings, is inspired.Faust is on Mubi from 14 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsFilm adaptationsJohann Wolfgang von GoetheFW MurnauGermanySilent filmreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Angèle: Instinct review – Belgium’s biggest star is determined to do pop differently | Music | The Guardian
description: Massive in her home nation but less so outside, Angèle is aided by Justice, Soulwax and Caroline Polachek in ​a bold bid for broader appeal – but her resultant album ​can be generic as well as daring
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Massive in her home nation but less so outside, Angèle is aided by Justice, Soulwax and Caroline Polachek in ​a bold bid for broader appeal – but her resultant album ​can be generic as well as daring
Content: Angèle.Photograph: Kenza Le BasView image in fullscreenAngèle.Photograph: Kenza Le BasAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewAngèle: Instinct review – Belgium’s biggest star is determined to do pop differently(RCA)Massive in her home nation but less so outside, Angèle is aided by Justice, Soulwax and Caroline Polachek in ​a bold bid for broader appeal – but her resultant album ​can be generic as well as daringAlexis PetridisThu 15 Oct 2026 07.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 09.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs has often been pointed out, we live in an era where the traditional Anglo-American stranglehold over pop has been broken. Partly because streaming has presented listeners with a far broader choice of music than would once have been imaginable, and partly as a result of social media accounts doing the promotional departments’ job for them, the charts are now as likely to include music made in Seoul or Lagos as London or LA. Spurs’ 62,000-capacity stadium has recently hosted not just Jay-Z, Gorillaz and System of a Down, but India’s Arijit Singh, South Korea’s BTS, BigBang and Stray Kids, and Puerto Rico’s Bad Bunny, who addressed the crowd almost exclusively in Spanish.View image in fullscreenCover art for Instinct.Photograph: Courtesy of Angéle and Grant James-ThomasClearly, British audiences’ disinclination to be welded to English-speaking artists is a cheering thing. Equally clearly, there seem to be limits: the same interest hasn’t been afforded Francophone pop. The biggest French-speaking stars in recent memory have either dealt in dance music or acquiesced to recording in English. Belgian rapper Stromae has attracted media interest and co-signs from Kanye West and Lorde without ever progressing beyond cult status in the UK.Likewise, Angèle Van Laeken, who kicked off her career in 2017, broke Stromae’s record for the most number of weeks at No 1 inBelgiumwith her 2018 single Tout Oublier – taken from a debut album that went seven times platinum in her homeland – and has been a household name to Francophone audiences ever since. The closest she has come to British success was her appearance on Dua Lipa’s 2020 single Fever, a minor hit.View image in fullscreenGlitterbeat stomp … Angèle.Photograph: Kenza Le BasYou could argue that some of her music is quite geographically specific. Her second album, Nonante-Cinq, opened with Bruxelles Je T’Aime, a song in praise of her her home town, terrible weather and all (one of its lyrics translates roughly, and rather splendidly, as: “Tonight the sky will certainly be covered by a storm / but after the storm people will party and get the beers in”). But it also fretted about the possibility that Belgium might end up divided between French and Flemish speakers, a topic that’s seldom hotly debated when the British get the beers in. Then again, Bad Bunny’s most recent album was at least partially consumed by the question of whether or not Hawaii was a suitable model for Puerto Rican statehood, and that didn’t stop it reaching the UK Top 10.You would struggle to call Angèle’s third album a concerted push for Anglo-American success, although there are more lyrics in English than on Nonante-Cinq and some of the names involved might cause ears to prick up. Justice collaborate on What You Want, a fruitful collision of maximalist rave synths and glitterbeat stomp. And Soulwax crop up on Trop, which is impressively noisy, with an edge to the electronics and its take on a house pulse; it’s driven by vocals that alternately lean towards rap and are scrambled into incomprehensibility. Love Triangle, meanwhile, involvesCaroline Polachekand French dance producer SebastiAn, a thrillingly discordant synthesiser arpeggio cutting through its killer chorus and sweaty-small-hours mood.Indeed, intermittently at least, Instinct makes a case that British audiences don’t know what they’re missing when it comes to Angèle, who has a penchant for suddenly grabbing the steering wheel and driving a song off road. On Verra starts out like a standard pop piano ballad – albeit with a hint of chanson about the melody – before it’s unexpectedly strafed with bursts of static and machine-gun-paced noise. You could initially imagine any number of pop stars essaying the sweet drift of Je Compte, but then it dramatically shifts gears, first into a four-to-the-floor rhythm topped with an assemblage of sampled gasps and warped vocals, then into a lo-fi piano ballad.This all carries the appealing sense of someone doing pop rather differently, although these moments are punctuated by more straightforward stuff. Some of it is great – the melody that floats above the chugging synths of Tout Décider is an unequivocal earworm – and some of it a little less so. The song F4ck 4ever is noticeably less diverting than its title; the cut-up samples and AutoTuned vocals that constitute Dis-le’s hook lie somewhere between unusual and tinnily annoying.Trash hits! Why a wave of hedonistic, feral female pop stars are rejecting respectabilityRead moreIt’s an album that is by turns really exciting and slightly frustrating, built for cherrypicking its highlights for a playlist rather than repeatedly listening to end-to-end. There’s enough here to grab the attention of anyone with an ear for left-field pop – one suspects any Caroline Polachek fans enticed by her appearance will be happy to stick around – but not quite enough to predict a broader shift in perceptions. One thing that unites all the disparate artists who have broken through pop’s language barrier is that they’re offering something that you really can’t get at home; so is Angèle, but only occasionally.This week Alexis listened toCameron Winter –$0 (Live at Carnegie Hall)A live version of the Heavy Metal highlight that alternately strips the song back – the string arrangement is gone – and somehow amplifies it: more simple, but more intense.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekPop and rockCaroline PolachekBelgiumJusticeDance musicalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Finding the groove: what’s the best genre of music to dance to? | Dance music | The Guardian
description: What is it about music that makes even non-professionals want to hit the dancefloor, and is it disco, funk or even classical that does it best? Four leading choreographers discuss their theories, with the science to back them up
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: What is it about music that makes even non-professionals want to hit the dancefloor, and is it disco, funk or even classical that does it best? Four leading choreographers discuss their theories, with the science to back them up
Content: ‘I get lost and distracted because the beat is so funky’ … The Brown Suite.Photograph: Deborah JaffeView image in fullscreen‘I get lost and distracted because the beat is so funky’ … The Brown Suite.Photograph: Deborah JaffeDance musicFinding the groove: what’s the best genre of music to dance to?What is it about music that makes even non-professionals want to hit the dancefloor, and is it disco, funk or even classical that does it best? Four leading choreographers discuss their theories, with the science to back them upLyndsey WinshipThu 15 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Idon’t know what it is about house music that makes me move, but I just can’t help it,” says Faye Stoeser. “And I don’t care what I look like. I just go for it.” “If a Missy [Elliott] track comes on, that’s me, I’m in the zone,” says Dannielle “Rhimes” Lecointe. “With hip-hop it’s something deep within the gut that makes you want to move. It has so many rhythms to it – a heartbeat, a pulse, a ricochet – that you feel in so many different places of your body.”What is the best music to dance to? Is it house music, it is hip-hop, is it disco or funk? Stoeser and Lecointe should have some insight since, as performers and choreographers, dancing is what they do for a living. When it comes to popular floorfillers, theDJ Intelligenceplatform found the most-requested track from UK DJs last year was Whitney Houston’s I Wanna Dance With Somebody (with Abba’s Dancing Queen second, and Mr Brightside by the Killers third). In the US,Billboard’s top wedding songis Uptown Funk by Mark Ronson featuring Bruno Mars. A 2013Mixmag pollnamed Daft Punk’s One More Time as the ultimate dance track, whereas Radio 2 listeners in 2008 voted forMichael Jackson’s Billie Jean.But what about those for whom dancing is more than recreation? When it comes to dance on stage, there is plenty that isn’t driven by music at all. Back in the 1940s, the US choreographer Merce Cunningham began to disconnect dance and music in his collaborations with the composer John Cage, rehearsing the dancers in silence. Some choreographers use music to create dance in the studio that is totally different from what they’ll perform to on stage.Dancethat’s focused on musical connection definitely went out of fashion for a while, but there are a bunch of shows coming up where music is the absolute driving force.View image in fullscreenEbony Scrooge with Danielle Lecointe … ‘I’m vibrating at different levels’Photograph: Rebecca Warrand/Johan Persson“We won’t choreograph until we have the music,” says Nahum McLean, of dance company BlacBrik, “which sometimes can be scary because it will be a week before the show, and we’re, like: ‘Still not found that music yet!’”McLean and his BlacBrik co-founder Darius Drooh had no trouble with the music for their current showThe Brown Suite, which is soundtracked by godfather of funk James Brown – a legendary dancer himself – along with songs by Etta James and Sam Cooke. “It’s so infectious,” says McLean of Brown’s music. “Sometimes I’ll have the music on in my headphones, and I’m trying to block [some choreography] mentally or write something down, and then I get lost and distracted because I’m like: This beat is so funky!”Drooh agrees: “Sometimes we’re just too busy dancing in the studio when we should be trying to choreograph.”double quotation markI can see people tapping their feet. It’s an involuntary reactionWhat is it about funk that makes it so irresistible? “There’s something about the bassline and the way they used it during that era, and you can’t help it, your body starts to have this natural response,” says McLean. “The way it’s layered with the percussion and the horns. In performances, I can see people tapping their feet. It’s an involuntary reaction.”There’s actual science that bears this out. Oxford professor Morten Kringelbach is one neuroscientist who set out to pin down what’s so funky about funk. Heplayed his test subjects funk drum breakswith different amounts of syncopation – meaning the beats that land between the regular pulse – and found an inverted-U shape; simply put, too little syncopation equals not funky enough, too much and your body can’t hook into the rhythm. James Brown hits the sweet spot. Plenty of others have also investigated “groove” – that’s the official scientific term for the quality in music that makes people want to dance.In a 2012study, cognitive neuroscientist Petr Janata used various measures, including tracking people’s spontaneous movements, to find the grooviest piece of music. The result: Stevie Wonder’s stone-cold classic Superstition (1972). Neuroscientist and musician Daniel Levitin has pointed to Wonder’s drumming and clavinet-playing on the track and how he varies the tones so that even though there’s a strong pulse, it never sounds uniform; “ear candy”, he’s called it.People have been put in brainscanners while listening to groovy musicand areas in their basal ganglia, which control motor activity and reward, lit up. Other elements that have a positive correlation with groove include: a prominent pulse or rhythm; a high number of different notes in each bar; short or accented beats; harmonic complexity – it should be low to medium; and the presence of low-frequency sounds, ie, heavy bass. Tempo matters, too. Superstition hovers around the 100bpm mark, slightly slower than the perceived optimum – 107-126bpm, according to one2018 analysis; other studies landed on 120bpm.View image in fullscreenEkleido … ‘When someone scores a goal in football and people lose their sense of self. We’re trying to bring that into the theatre.Photograph: Jack ThomsonHannah Ekholm, who along with Stoeser leads dance company Ekleido, would agree with that. “One hundred and twenty to 126bpm, that’s when it’s really groovy,” says Ekholm.“We make work to 130-135bpm,” adds Stoeser, “but I agree that between the 120-128bpm range it feels like it has that steady pulse but you still have that groove within it; the space to play.” Ekleido are specialists in “new way vogue”(a progression from the type of voguing Madonna sang about), which is danced to house music. On stage, their soundtrack isn’t just a steady four-to-the-floor – Ekholm’s partner Sam Shepherd, AKAFloating Points, writes music for them, including for their latest showFemina– but they do like a thumping beat.double quotation markThe orchestra is like an engine for me. Until I hear the music live I can’t really access my full capacityIt is also more than just the technical aspects of the music. “When you’re in a club space, you almost transcend together collectively,” says Stoeser. “I learned this term the other day: ‘collective effervescence’, the feeling when someone scores a goal in football and people lose their sense of self for a minute. We’re trying to bring a piece of that into the theatre.”I ask Lecointe,who’s about to take the lead role in her hip-hop dance showEbony Scrooge, where exactly she feels the music. “In the solar plexus,” she says. “Hip-hop sometimes feels to me a bit like a speaker. I’m vibrating at different levels: the bass, the snare, the hi-hat, can be the isolation in the feet, the hips, the chest.”Music doesn’t need to have a banging bassline to make you want to dance, though. When Anna Rose O’Sullivan, principal dancer with the Royal Ballet, says “the music almost makes me want to take off”, she’s not talking about techno but Tchaikovsky – specifically the Act II pas de deux she dances inThe Nutcracker. “It’s the emotion that it evokes, the melody, the swell. It’s something deeply romantic, but it has this soar,” she says. “Tchaikovsky wrote some bangers.” He certainly did, and some of the most danceable tunes in ballet have kept The Nutcracker in business Christmas after Christmas.It helps that when O’Sullivan performs at the Royal Opera House, the music is played live. “The orchestra is like an engine for me,” she says. “I could be doing something in the rehearsal studio for months, but until I hear it live I can’t really access my full capacity. It’s like if someone’s listening to a piece of music and their hairs stand up,” she adds, “but for us it’s not just hairs, it’s everything, every muscle feels alive.” That’s borne out by the science, too: tactile sensation makes you want to dance, whether that’s vibration from a subwoofer or the orchestra in the pit.There is definitely no single answer to the question of groove. James Brown may have taken over BlacBrik’s playlist, but McLean and Drooh insist there’s no music they couldn’t dance to. “My father is from west Africa and I have an African dance background. We will always hear the rhythm,” Drooh says. “We will always hear the bass in anything. You can put on Beethoven and we can find a boom-taka, boom-taka!”The Brown Suiteis touringnationwide to May.Ekleido: Feminais atGulbenkian Arts, Canterbury,29 to 30 October;and The Place, London,5 to 7 November;Ebony Scroogeis at Sadler’s Wells East, London,24 November to 3 January;The Nutcrackeris at Royal Opera House, London,3 December to 13 January.Explore more on these topicsDance musicDanceHip-hopBalletStevie WonderJames BrownEtta JamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mendelssohn: Songs Without Words review – Chamayou makes each piece feel somehow familiar yet fresh  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The pianist brings a singing quality and seeming effortlessness to the complete set of Songs Without Words
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: The pianist brings a singing quality and seeming effortlessness to the complete set of Songs Without Words
Content: Effortless playing … Bertrand Chamayou.Photograph: Le Philtre / Parlophone Records Ltd 2026View image in fullscreenEffortless playing … Bertrand Chamayou.Photograph: Le Philtre / Parlophone Records Ltd 2026Classical musicReviewMendelssohn: Songs Without Words review – Chamayou makes each piece feel somehow familiar yet freshBertrand Chamayou(Warner Classics)The pianist brings a singing quality and seeming effortlessness to the complete set of Songs Without WordsErica JealThu 15 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 10.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMendelssohn wrote 48 Songs Without Words for solo piano: eight sets of six, mostly under three minutes long, emerging over a 16-year period that spanned most of his short adult life. The handful that still regularly make their way on to recital programmes are only the tip of the iceberg; the complete set hasn’t been recorded as much as you might think, which makes this new release fromBertrand Chamayoustill more welcome.View image in fullscreenBertrand Chamayou: Mendelssohn Songs Without WordsThese pieces belong to the world of Schubert Lieder, and Chamayou brings a singing quality to them from the off. The Duetto that rounds off the Op 38 set is beautifully done, the melodic lines alternating like a female and male voice, each lingering just slightly as the other voice takes over. Compared to other interpreters, Chamayou is often softer-edged, his playing a little smoother and more flowing, although there are exceptions: Op 62 No 6 – known as Spring Song, but originally titled Camberwell Green after the then-elegant London suburb where it was written – is given a perky, almost frothy touch in the accompaniment: spring bubbling under like frogspawn in a pond.Chamayou doesn’t present these miniatures as if he thinks they are profound, yet thanks to his seeming effortlessness they come across that way. For him, going through these pieces has been like “opening a trunk of family photos faded by time”. It’s also a good analogy for listening to him play them: each new piece feels somehow familiar and yet demands your fresh attention.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com.
